── Where the writing about this page lives ───────────────────────────────
THE CONTRACT IS docs/APP.md for the app (routing, chrome, shared
gestures, boundaries) and docs/app-routes.csv for its views, one row each.
Those are the reader-facing account and the ones to update when
behaviour changes.

THE COMMENTS HERE explain the code they sit beside, and are addressed to
whoever edits it: why a control is where it is, what left and why, the
conventions a new view has to honour. Keep them beside their code.

A 5,962-word block used to sit at the end of this file doing both jobs at
once. Its contract half restated the doc and had fallen six views behind
it; its rationale half is now at the sites below. Retired 2026-08-10; the
measurement and the reasoning are in docs/text-content.md. Do not start a
second one: if a passage is not about the code it sits beside, it belongs
in the doc.

── GitHub jump-overs: the convention every view honours ──────────────────
GITHUB JUMP-OVERS: the app is a wrapper over GitHub, not a wall — every
view keeps a one-tap route to the GitHub presentation of what it is showing.
A jump-over for a FILE or a FOLDER is one link: the explorer's breadcrumb
links the current folder (ghFolderUrl), the viewer's actions link the open
file's blob, the sidebar's recent entries link theirs (fileGhUrl), each
staged item and finder row links its own repo@ref (stage.js itemGh), each
compare row links its blob at head, and every estate card and surface item
carries its github-logo link. A jump-over for a REPO or a BRANCH is a small
set, which is what earns a menu: the repo's is lib/kits/github-links.js, off
the sidebar row's github button and the Activity view's repo chip, and the
branch's is estate.js's branchMenuItems, off each Open row (tree, compare,
commits, the PR's files and checks, new PR). When adding a view, add its
jump-over, and prefer the shared list to a fresh one. ONE GLYPH, FOUR
MEANINGS, and the reader could not tell them apart. The github-logo marks a
repo MENU (a set of destinations), a repo or branch DESTINATION, the
MANIFEST behind a whole view, and an EXACT FILE. The ambiguity is not
theoretical: the Map's Transport (now Showing) header set a bare icon
immediately after the code span naming pages/toss-render.html while pointing
at docs/routes.json, so the icon read as belonging to the filename beside
it. Two rules separate them now. A manifest link is LABELLED — "Curate", as
the Tools view already did — and pushed to the header's far edge, away from
any filename; what the header names on the left carries its own jump. And an
exact-file link carries a SOURCE PEEK. THE PEEK (lib/kits/source-peek.js) is
a hover card showing the file: markdown rendered, JSON pretty-printed with
its top-level shape named, everything else as source, always the first 20
lines with a footer saying what was left behind. One attribute at the call
site (:data-peek="owner/repo[@ref]:path"), one delegated listener on
document, so a row Alpine renders later needs no wiring. gh-boot.js loads
it, alongside the FAB and for the same reason, so this page's boot block
does not: it belongs wherever a peek-bearing icon is rendered, and a page's
own boot list is the wrong owner of that. It first hung off the boot block
below and failed the one test that matters, since a page shell is served
from main even under ?use=, so a preview of the branch ran the new
components with no SourcePeek behind them and every :data-peek bound to
null. It is what makes the fourth meaning self-evident: an icon that can
show you the file is pointing at a file, and one that cannot is pointing at
something broader. So repo, branch and menu icons deliberately have none.
A project's folder icon peeks its README (2026-09-14): GitHub draws a
directory as its listing with the README beneath, so the card previews
where the tap goes. WHERE IT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT, beyond the broad
destinations: the viewer's GitHub action and the config view's, since both
sit above the file's full contents already on screen. A peek that repeats
what the page is showing is noise. POINTER AND KEYBOARD, NOT TOUCH: the card
opens on hover where the pointer can hover and on focus for a keyboard
reader; on a touch screen it never opens, and the icon keeps its single
meaning of a tap that jumps to GitHub. A press-and-hold would contradict the
finding recorded above about the repo menu, and an icon whose tap does one
clear thing needs no gesture.

The pre-build: one same-origin import carries the whole lib/ (the loader,
the gh-boot chain, every Alpine component, alpine-bundle) — no per-file
gh.load network for own code. The landing needs no token; the file browser
boots quietly and only prompts for auth on demand.

?use=<branch|tag|sha> re-pins the bundle to that ref for preview. It loads
by fetch + blob-import from raw.githubusercontent, NOT jsDelivr's /gh/ CDN
whose branch-tip listing lags a fresh push ~12h (a just-pushed branch used
to preview stale). raw serves public files anonymously with permissive
CORS, and a blob: URL imports despite raw's text/plain type because the
blob sets its own JS type; the bundle is one self-contained module (no
internal imports), so blob-import is clean. The fetch sets cache: 'no-store',
since a branch ref MOVES and the HTTP cache is keyed by URL alone: blob
import defeats the module cache and nothing was defeating the other one
(no SHA needed). The no-?use path stays the fastest same-origin import.

The bundle is the APP'S OWN since 2026-09-02 (dist/app.js, node/build/
build-app.mjs): the part of lib/ this page can reach, 22 components rather
than 32 registered at import, and the heavy on-demand kits (annotate, pdf,
dictate, xlsx) left to load on first use. dist/web-tools.js, the whole
library, stays for the pages that import it.

A branch NAME moves, which is why the fetch by name is no-store, and that
re-downloaded the whole bundle on every preview load. So a name is resolved
to its commit first (one small anonymous API call) and the bundle fetched
by SHA, an address that cannot move and that the HTTP cache may keep; a
SHA given directly skips the resolve, and a failed resolve falls back to
the uncached fetch by name.
The web-tools entry of the page's selection: `?use=`, or a `refs=` entry
naming this repository (docs/loader.md, "The selection"). A renderer
answers `use` for a framed app; gh-api.js inside the bundle installs the
rest of the selection once it runs.

daisyUI's :root:has() rules come out of the stylesheet above, which is
CORS-mode so it can be read: each one made every change in the page
restyle all of it. kits/root-has-prune.js has the measurement and what
the two families of rule did. A failure leaves the stylesheet as it was.

A 401 or 403 opens the This browser view rather than gh-auth's takeover,
registered here because this is the first moment ghAuth exists. Before the
shell has mounted there is no view to open, so the takeover still answers
(return false). Once it has, a failure during its boot route is parked for
the shell to pick up when the route settles (init), and one after that
routes at once.

gh-store rides in the pre-build cached but unexecuted; this load runs it
from the inlined cache (no network) so GH.prototype.save exists as before.

The `runs` ring every state/ cache carries: what a crawl cost, appended to
the commit the crawl was making anyway. Loaded before the three caches
because each writes one.

What the app's calls did that is worth reading, filed to
web-tools-private's logs/traffic/ (started in init).

What kind of browser this is, and the reader's name for it: the Here view,
the Traffic pane and the traffic log name a browser the same way.

The answer to the API's read-after-write lag: what this page last committed,
reconciled against what a read hands back. Loaded before the crawls because
each one folds a read into a write.
Config-aggregate builders for the private cache (state/configs.json).

The pure scan math + shared fetch orchestrators behind the branches view
and the activity crawl (window.BranchStatus).
Activity-aggregate builders for the private cache (state/activity.json).

The per-repo crawl that fills one of its entries (window.ActivityCrawl),
shared with node/activity-crawl.mjs so CI and this page crawl alike.
After branch-status and the builders, since it calls both.

The estate's file names (window.FileIndex), a leg of the same crawl: it
gates on the default-branch tips the activity pass has just read.

Every estate repo's Markdown with word counts (window.DocIndex), the same
crawl's other index; the Map's Docs tab reads it for repos past the hub.

What wrote a commit, read off the commit (window.WriteKinds). Beside the
activity cache because it classifies exactly what that cache stores.

Comma-separated parsing, shared. Loaded before the sessions cache, whose
title join reads the Dispatch export's CSV through it.
Sessions-aggregate builders for the private cache (state/sessions.json).

The marks for the parts of a call (background, proposal, commentary,
conclusion), which the Map's Icons tab lists as a drawn family.

The crawl that folds the records into it, shared with the headless runner
(node/sessions-crawl.mjs) the way kits/activity-crawl.js is.

The pure fold behind the Map view's Views tab: the app's own destinations
ranked by when the code behind each last moved (window.routeActivity), and
the fetching half that feeds it (window.RouteJoin), which the estate's
branch chips read too.

Errands: what a session needs this browser for, one record for reads of
your repos, code for you to run, and material only you have. The kit
performs the reads itself, when an errand's Run is tapped.
The write-side channel: proposed cross-repo edits, applied only on confirm.

What waits on the owner: user calls, and the Text collection's proposed
edits by file, behind the Waiting view and the Docs tab's markers.

Findings: the fold over the notes store that the Tending view lists and
the Activity panes show beside their subjects (window.Findings).
The owner/repo[@ref]:path grammar, and the inbox/outbox boxes built on it.
The allowlist that decides what a visit may store (window.VisitLog).
The PowerShell outpost's state derivation and its one write, behind its view.
The state icons the PowerShell outpost view shares with the shortcut views.
Which repository file a pasted piece of PowerShell belongs to (window.PowerShellMatch).

The estate's search calls (trees, file-name index, content index, session grep) with one
shared cache, behind the sidebar finder and the Search view.
Pure alignment assessment behind the Distribution/Repos view (window.PortableAlign).
Declared staleness checks, evaluated on sight from a repo's own config.

The GitHub destinations for one repo, shared by the sidebar's github menu
and the Activity view's repo chip (window.GithubLinks).

The line/word differ behind the stage's Diff lens, shared with
pages/diff-tool.html (window.textDiff).

The drag handle on the docked deck's edge. swipe-deck treats it as an
OPTIONAL dependency and mounts the seam only when `window.dockSplit` is
present, the same bargain session-render makes with session-export: the
host loads it, the kit notices. Nothing here loaded it, so this shell
installed both dock hooks, docked correctly, and never grew a seam, from
the day the splitter shipped until 2026-08-23. What hid it is that the
splitter's own test loads the kit itself before driving the app, which is
exactly the dependency the app was missing, so a passing check and a dead
feature were perfectly consistent. deck-dock-reflow.mjs now asserts the
seam is there on the app's OWN boot, which is the claim that was untested.

The one routing table (window.GuideRender): which address a repo file opens
at, and for a change set, whether a page is addressable on its own or is
framed by the app its repo declares. The branch rows in the Activity view
read it for their render chips, and a row is on the first screen, so this
is a boot load rather than a lazy one: a getter that loaded the kit on
first call would draw an empty strip and never redraw, since the component
has no reactive dependency on a global arriving later. pages/branch.html
loads the same kit for the same reason one step later.

A repo browser fronted by a per-repo landing page. The repo picker is up
front (header). The sidebar lists the repo's views — landing, atlas,
files, stage, branches — plus pinned and recent shortcuts; the actual folder/file
navigation lives in the main area (breadcrumb + listing, file content
beneath). The sidebar shows or hides at every width, out by default on a
wide screen and away on a phone; ?shell= sets how much of this frame a link
opens with. See the design notes at the end of this file.

App-wide drag cue. Purely visual (pointer-events-none), so the drop still
lands on the window handler wireAppDrop() registered. It stands down on the
Stage, where the bench draws its own cue over the thing being aimed at: two
overlays for one gesture is one too many, and the specific one is better.

z-[95], above the swipe deck's band: the overlay at 70, its seam and the
FAB drawer at 75, menus and the correspondence dialog at 80, source-peek at
85, the deck's sign tip at 90. At z-[60] until 2026-10-23, the row sat
under the deck, so a toast raised from inside an open deck (the
workbench's sheet count, a Copied) showed only the strip above the deck's
top edge. A toast is the newest thing on screen and short-lived, so it
covers rather than waits. pages/dictate.html's row uses the same level.

At most one action, and it takes the toast away with it. The Lists
view's undo is the only caller so far; see the toast store for why a
reversal lives here rather than on the row it undoes.

── Header: the app-level view nav (a closed set the app owns). That is all
it carries. The old repo-list dropdown and the desktop quick-links row went
first (repo selection happens on the Repos dashboard, which is nicer than a
dropdown); the auth shield followed, since everything it reached already had
an on-page home: the token control is the Repos dashboard's account row, a
repo's config is the sidebar's Config view, and "Refresh views" is the
State view's config row.

The BRAND went last, and for the same reason as the rest: it said nothing
the row beside it did not. Its tap was goDashboard(), which is Activity for
a signed-in viewer and Repos for a signed-out one, and both are the first
item of the nav it sat against, so the mark was a second route to a
destination already named a few pixels to its right. The mark still leads
the sidebar's crumb trail, where it is the route home from inside a repo and
is doing work; two copies of it on one screen were the redundancy, not the
mark itself. What the header buys is the width.

THE WHOLE HEADER IS CONDITIONAL under ?shell=none, which is what makes an
unframed link possible at all: every other view here is the shell's own,
with no standalone page behind it to link to the way an app view or a
custom landing has one. The way back is the FAB's Render tab, which
carries the mode as a bar. ───────────────────────────────────────────

z-[35], one past the Map's pinned tab strip (z-30 below lg), which would
otherwise paint over the find pill's bar hung from this header; still
under the sidebar's backdrop (z-40).

App-level views: Activity / Repos / Stage / Tools / Map, the
estate's own set, always labeled, inline on one row from the left
edge, at any phone width. Public browse left the
header (a signed-out affordance, still on the no-token banner and
every repo card); the nav scrolls rather than clipping on the
narrowest devices.

Then a hairline, then the REPO-SPONSORED views (appView:true): the
header now carries both classes of destination, the app's own and the
ones repos publish. Same set on every viewport, since the nav already
scrolls; the sidebar keeps its copy, which is what saves a phone from
scrolling the nav to reach them.

── What the header does NOT carry, and why each thing left ───────────────
The HEADER carries the view nav in TWO GROUPS, split by a hairline. First
estateNav, the app's own views — Activity (Open / To-do / Jots by pill),
Repos, Surfaces, Stage, Tools, Map — as labeled buttons, lit on the active
view, on every viewport. Then appNav, the REPO-SPONSORED views
(appView:true, e.g. News), each with the icon its repo declared, which is
what tells the two groups apart beyond the rule between them. The sponsored
group is the same on desktop and mobile; the sidebar keeps its own copy,
which is the phone's way to them without scrolling the nav. On a touch
device the FIRST group is also a SWIPE CAROUSEL: the active dashboard pane
follows the finger through a horizontal drag and slides out to commit one
step along estateNav (onSwipeStart/Move/End → _commit), an accelerator for
the tabs that stay the visible state. The estate sub-views share one
component, so the incoming content slides in on commit rather than
previewing live mid-drag; it rubber-bands at the ends, no-ops inside a repo,
and yields to any horizontally-scrollable region the gesture starts in.
Beside them the #repo component runs HEADLESS: it is the repo/auth
controller and hosts the shared dialog, but renders nothing (the old repo-
list dropdown and the auth shield are both gone). THE BRAND WENT TOO: its
tap was goDashboard (Activity if signed in, else Repos), and both of those
are the nav's own first item, so the mark was a second route to a
destination sitting a few pixels away. It still leads the sidebar crumb
trail, which is where a reader inside a repo goes home from, so the app
shows one copy of it rather than two, and the header keeps the width. The
sidebar toggle is its own hamburger, on every viewport since the sidebar
became closable on all of them, and it is the only button in the header
outside the nav and the rail. AUTH left the chrome entirely: the
token control is the account row on the Repos dashboard (estate.js
accountPanel → the dialog's estate scope), which is where an account-level
setting belongs, and every token-gated empty state points there. The
shield's other job, REFRESH VIEWS, was the Repos view's own Refresh button
when the shield went (both called refreshConfigs), so it needed no new home.
Both are now the State view's config row, which carries that crawl with its
age, its throttle, and what it costs. There is no repo-list dropdown and no
quick-links row: REPO SELECTION HAPPENS ON THE REPOS DASHBOARD (tap a card)
or from the sidebar Repos index. Repos reach the header through their
published VIEWS, not through a list of themselves.

data-slot names the unit slot an element fills (data/ui-units/
codebook.md, "Slots"): these view buttons are the shell's Tabs.

An entry's badge is a count waiting on the reader (Waiting's open
user calls, Proposals' pending edits); it carried a `badge` that
nothing drew until 2026-10-04.

The repo component runs headless here: the repo/auth controller plus
the token dialog it hosts, no visible readout of its own. The open
repo is shown at the top of the sidebar instead, so a header copy was
redundant, and the dialog is now opened from the page (the Repos
dashboard's account control, an estate card, the Map) rather than
from a header shield.

── The rail: the far end of the header ──────────────────────────
The `rail: true` items of the links board (loadRail), which are
destinations rather than views: they leave the app, or open a repo
in it. That is a different verb from switching a pane, so they sit
at the OPPOSITE END from the nav rather than as a third group in it.
Icon-only, because the set is small, recognizable, and daily; the
title and note ride the tooltip, and the Links view carries the full
board with every label spelled out.

Desktop only, and this is the one place the two viewports differ:
the nav already scrolls at phone widths, so a second header cluster
there would compete for the same overflow. Below lg the rail renders
in the sidebar instead (its own block under App views), which is
where a phone reaches it.

No rule on this side: the flexible gap after the nav is already the
separation, and a border with nothing after it reads as a stray line
against the window edge.

── The find pill: a view's filter, from the header ──────────────────
A view marked data-find-hoist hides its own filter box, and this
drives it instead, so a filter costs no view a row and opens from
one place on every view that has one. The same at every width: a
magnifier here, or the term as a chip once one is set, and tapped,
a bar that slides down from the header's edge over the top of the
view (#find-bar, teleported there because this row cannot hold
it), so opening it moves nothing. Below lg the view also scrolls
its list up under the bar, so the rows that narrow with each
keystroke sit above the keyboard rather than behind it. Ctrl or Cmd+F opens it
too (wireAppTypeahead). The input is laid out even while the bar is
shut, only at no height, because iOS raises the keyboard only for a
focus made inside the tap. No Done button: the keyboard's Search
key, the iOS bar's Done, Enter, and a tap elsewhere all close it;
Escape clears it as well.

Where else the word landed, when a view's one query runs
over several kinds of row (Activity's four panes): each a
count that opens its pane in a tap.

Recent terms, only while the bar is open and empty. The bar
lies over the view, so the row lengthens it without moving
anything, and it goes the moment a key lands.

── The ref switch: which ref THIS PAGE is running at ─────────────
Last in the row, past the rail, behind a hairline. The rail's items
are destinations you leave for; this one is a fact about the page you
are standing on, so it gets separated from them rather than added to
the set.

It is deliberately NOT the Files view's ref picker. That one chooses
which ref of the BROWSED repo you are reading; this one chooses which
ref of the app itself RUNS FROM, which is a different
question with the same vocabulary, so the panel spells out the repo
and path it acts on. The two are visually apart for the same reason:
the ref picker lives in the Files toolbar beside the tree it filters,
and this lives in the app chrome beside the shell it re-points.

The switch navigates to the toss renderer, since ?use= alone re-pins
only the lib a page loads and would leave this header, and every
other line of the shell, at the deployed version.

EVERY VIEWPORT, unlike the rail beside it. This shipped desktop-only
on the rail's reasoning (a second header cluster competing with a nav
that already scrolls), and that reasoning does not survive contact
with the header it describes: the nav scrolls, but the sidebar toggle
to the right of this is pinned and always visible, so the right end
of the header is already a place where fixed controls live and one
more costs the nav some of its scrolling window, nothing else. The
rail's exemption is not the same case and stands: it has a full
labeled copy in the sidebar, which is a phone's route to it, while
hiding this one left a phone with no route at all except the fab's
Render tab, several taps in. So the cost of hiding was an
inconsistency between viewports and no saving to show for it.

What it costs the nav is 2 rem, because below sm the control collapses
to a single branch glyph and moves its box, its newest jump and its
way home into the panel it opens (see ref-switch.js). A 10 rem box
was tried here first and was the wrong trade: it was the widest thing
in the header and the least likely to be used, since on a phone this
is picked from a list rather than typed into.

THE SIDEBAR TOGGLE, at every width. It was lg:hidden, on the premise
that a pinned desktop sidebar never needs summoning, which held right
up until the sidebar could be put away: the desktop then had a column
it could not collapse and a hamburger that would have collapsed it
sitting one media query out of reach. Now it toggles, it lights when
the sidebar is out, and the two viewports differ in one thing only,
which way the sidebar starts. Hidden on desktop where showSidebar
says there is nothing to show (a signed-out estate), since a control
that opens an empty panel is worse than no control; the phone keeps
it, where the sidebar is also the route back out of the view.

NO PASTE BUTTON HERE, and it is worth saying where one stood.
2026-08-19 the header carried one, for a real reason: iOS Safari
raises a paste event only when an editable is focused, so the window
listener wireAppPaste installs is the desktop's whole story and the
phone had no app-wide intake at all. A tap was the answer. It is
gone because the launcher's long-press menu now carries the same
call (the `menu` contract below), confirmed working on a device, and
the header is the scarcest row in the app: it holds identity, the
nav that already scrolls at phone widths, and the sidebar toggle. A
second permanent control for a verb reachable by a gesture is the
kind of thing that accretes until nothing on the row is findable.
pasteAnywhere() is untouched and still the one implementation.

The find pill's bar lands here: hung from the header's bottom edge and
lying over the view, so opening it moves nothing beneath.

── What the sidebar holds, and why the app views sit in two places ───────
The SIDEBAR holds only what is contextual: in a repo its views + pins +
recents; in the estate a compact Repos index (the estate members, grouped
like the grid; its header icon opens the full grid) and the same app views
the header's second group carries, both token-gated. The app views sit in
both places on purpose: the header is the one-tap route, the sidebar the one
that survives a header too narrow to show them. It hides on desktop when
the estate has neither (showSidebar), so a signed-out dashboard runs
full-width, and whenever the viewer has put it away. app.landingKind(repo)
is the one landing decision point within a repo.

TWO MECHANISMS, ONE STATE. Below lg the panel is a fixed overlay and
sidebarOpen slides it; at lg and up it is a static column, so closing it
has to REMOVE it (lg:hidden) rather than translate it off, or the main
area would keep the gap where it used to be. That is why the closed
desktop case reads as a hide and the closed phone case as a slide, and
why the class list no longer carries an unconditional lg:translate-x-0:
that one modifier was the whole reason the desktop sidebar could not be
put away.

Sidebar top bar: in a repo, a CRUMB TRAIL (crumbBar, sidebarCrumbs).
Two crumbs earn the bar back. The mark is the route to the dashboard,
and since the header dropped its own copy of it, the only one in the
chrome. The repo crumb drops the owner prefix
(always the same account), and that saved width is what pays for the
house; the full owner/name stays in its tooltip. Tapping the repo crumb
opens the repo menu, the same sheet a Repos row opens, so the trailing
icon cluster that used to live here has nothing left to carry. A third
crumb appears only when the ref is off the default, since browsing a
branch is state worth keeping in front of you.

One trail in both contexts. At the app level it is the mark alone,
which says the same thing the word "Views" did and says it in the
vocabulary the repo trail already established: the mark is where the
dashboard lives. In a repo the same mark leads the path.

── Why the crumb trail replaced the top bar label, in both contexts ──────
THE SIDEBAR CRUMB TRAIL (crumbBar, sidebarCrumbs) replaced the top bar's
dead label in BOTH contexts. At the app level it is the MARK ALONE, which
says what the word "Views" said and says it in the vocabulary the repo trail
already teaches; in a repo it is the mark, the repo, and the ref only when
off-default. The mark is the route to the dashboard, and since the header
dropped its own copy it is the only one in the chrome; it renders grayscale
at rest and in colour on hover, so it reads as a control rather than as
branding. Dropping the owner prefix (always this account) is what pays for
it, and the full owner/name stays in the tooltip. crumbHome is the one
navigation here that LEAVES THE DRAWER OPEN: the others swap the main area,
where the drawer is in the way, but this one swaps what the drawer itself
lists, so closing it would hide the change. THE DRAWER NO LONGER CLOSES ON
NAVIGATION AT ALL (see navActive); the scrim and the X are the only
dismissals, so crumbHome needs no special case. The repo crumb's menu is a
REPO SWITCHER (pickRepo) and nothing else: which repository is showing, with
the current one checked. A trail names where you are, so the only menu it
earns is the set of other places that slot could hold; acting on a repo
lives in the row menu above. The caret only appears when there is somewhere
to switch to.

Every width, now that every width can close it. It was lg:hidden
when only a phone could, and a panel that closes with no visible way
to close it is the defect that hid.

THE MARK'S MENU: the fixed destinations, then where you have been.
Anchored under the bar in the same panel idiom as the repo
switcher below (inset, top-full, rounded-box, shadow), because they
are two lists from one bar and a second geometry would read as a
second kind of thing.

HOME ON MAIN appears only off the default ref, and it is the row this
whole menu was built around: the mark used to run crumbHome(), which
swaps the view and stays on whatever ref the shell is running at, so
from a branch it reached the branch's dashboard and there was no
control anywhere that changed both at once.

THE VISITED LIST is coarser than browser Back on purpose: one row per
destination, deduped, most recent first. It also reaches what Back
cannot, since toss-render only ever calls replaceState.

A PAYLOAD ROW IS COUNTED AND NOT LINKED. Rendering a pasted document
records that it happened and its size, never its address, because the
address IS the document (kits/visit-log.js). It draws dimmed and
unclickable rather than being dropped: a gap in the list reads as a
bug, and a row that says what it will not hold is honest. The same
goes for an unrecognized address, which is the signal that a registry
has fallen behind the code.

THE REF IS SAID AS AN ADDRESS, not as the word "main" inside a
sentence. The repo already speaks one grammar for this
(kits/review-target.js states the family: `owner/repo` is the
repo, `owner/repo@branch` is it at a ref, and the ':' introduces
a path), so the row names where it goes in the vocabulary every
other address here uses, and the owner is dropped in mono the
way the crumb trail beside it already drops it.

One imprecision worth stating rather than hiding: this row goes
to the deployed APP at main, and `web-tools@main` names the repo
at main. They read the same to a reader switching off a branch
preview, since the app at a ref IS that ref's code, and the
alternative (`web-tools@main:app/index.html`) spends the row's
width restating the page you are already on.

Section header at the size the Recent block above uses, not a
smaller one: this sidebar carries hierarchy in opacity and weight
and keeps one size for everything a reader came to read.

ONE LINE: the thing, then the short context, then the revisit
count. The detail is short by construction rather than clipped
into shape, and it is a `span` on the row rather than a `title`,
since a fact parked in a title reaches no touch screen and no
screenshot (house style, rule 10).

The repo crumb opens a REPO SWITCHER: which repository is showing,
and nothing else. A breadcrumb names where you are, so the only menu
it earns is the set of other places that slot could hold. Acting ON a
repo (config, GitHub, its outbox) belongs to the Repos rows' menus,
not to the trail. Anchored under the bar in path-picker's panel idiom
(inset, top-full, rounded-box, shadow).

estateSwitcherRows: the members, plus the satellites of the
member in view, indented under its row by the sidebar's 1 px
rule (repoSatellites, beside repoProjects).

── The finder's query grammar, lane by lane ──────────────────────────────
Under the sidebar's crumb bar sits THE FINDER (quickFind,
lib/alpineComponents/quick-find.js): one always-ready input whose query
shape picks a lane — #123 opens an open PR's branch takeover estate-wide; @
is repo-then-file navigation (the mention picker's reading of the trigger:
pick a repo, walk or fuzzy-match its cached tree, open the file); a pasted
owner/repo[@ref]:path or repo@branch address resolves exactly with no
suggestions; +idea jots explicitly; plain text matches repos, the nav, file
names from cached trees (a tap-gated row extends the pass estate-wide, the
stage's loadAllTrees economy), and PR titles — with a token-gated "Jot this"
floor so an unmatched query lands in the pile instead of nowhere. Two deeper
passes sit behind their own tap gates: "Search file contents" routes to
the Search view, which searches the crawled Markdown index, and
"Search sessions" greps the captured records in web-tools-private client-
side, hits opening the Sessions pane's paged reader. Any bare printable
key reaches it, `/` included, through the shell's own router
(wireAppTypeahead) rather than a listener of the component's; a view
carrying its own search box (data-find-box) takes the keystroke first.
Branch and session hits travel the web-tools:open-branch-detail and
web-tools:open-session events, consumed in estate.js beside the &detail=
deep link they mirror.

── The finder: one input, always ready ─────────────────────────────
Directly under the crumb bar, above the scroll area so its results
panel takes the sidebar's height while it has rows, and the lists
below step aside until it closes. The query's shape picks the lane:
#123 finds an open PR estate-wide and opens the branch-detail
takeover; @ is
repo-then-file NAVIGATION (pick a repo, walk or fuzzy-match its
tree, open the file); a pasted owner/repo[@ref]:path or repo@branch
address resolves exactly, with no suggestions; +idea jots
explicitly; plain text matches repos, the nav, file names in every
estate repo (the registry's state/files.json), and PR titles, grouped
under a heading per kind, with tap-gated deeper passes: file
CONTENTS through the crawled Markdown index, and a client-side grep of the
captured session records. The last
row is always "Jot this", so a query that found
nothing is kept rather than lost. Sits in the SIDEBAR, not the
header: out and ready on a wide screen, one tap on a phone,
where the header's nav already scrolls and its right end is already
spoken for. Full lane doc in quick-find.js.

Steps aside while the finder's results show: they take this list's
height rather than floating over it (lib/alpineComponents/quick-find.js,
the `finder` store).

Estate-context sidebar. Two repo-sourced sections, both token-gated
(empty and hidden when unauthed): the Repos index on top, then the
app views. The app views also ride in the header now, behind the
hairline; the copy stays here because the header nav scrolls on a
narrow phone and this list does not.

Repos: a compact index of the estate members (repos declaring
estate:true in their OWN config), grouped and ordered like the Repos
grid. The header nav's Repos opens the full grid; this is the one-tap
jump list beside it, so the sidebar carries the repos even when no app
view does. The icon on the right opens that grid.

Three targets, all single-tap. The name opens the repo. The
two trailing buttons open the one anchored panel with two
different lists: the github-logo gives GITHUB LINKS for that
repo (repository, pull requests, issues, its task board,
branches, commits, actions) and the visibility marker gives
the REPO MENU (config, its outbox, copy link).

Splitting them is what let the GitHub side grow past the
single "Open on GitHub" row it used to be, which pointed at
the one destination a reader could have guessed. Two lists,
one panel: hovering from one button to the other swaps the
rows in place rather than closing a panel under the pointer.

On a pointer that can hover, either button opens on hover
after a short delay; a tap works everywhere and a second tap
on the same button puts it away. No gesture: a press-and-hold
was tried here and dropped, because a visible control that
answers a plain tap does the same job without having to be
discovered. The marker button is the old inert <span>
promoted to a real control, so the row still says
public/private with its glyph while carrying its menu.

PROJECTS, indented under their repo. A repo carrying several
workspaces declares them in its manifest's `projects` field
(the defining convention: a workspace running a tracker is a
project; the repo root's tracker marks the repo itself and
earns no row). The list rides the config cache the section
already read, so these rows cost no extra fetch. A tap on the
name opens the repo's Files view at the workspace folder, the
same route a folder pin takes.

NO LEADING GLYPH, AND A GUIDELINE INSTEAD OF AN INDENT.
Every row here took the same icon, since the field defaults
it, so a column of identical marks distinguished nothing
and read as a second list rather than as rows under their
repo. The indent then went through three positions before
landing here: pl-10 (past the repo label, on the reasoning
that a step says "inside"), flush at pl-2, and now a 1 px
rule down the block with the rows just clear of it.

The rule is the cheap version of what the indent was buying.
ml-4 puts it at 16 px, which is the CENTRE OF THE REPO
ICON above (pl-2 plus half of a 16 px glyph), so it reads
as hanging from the parent rather than as a stray margin,
and the -mt-1 above starts it inside the repo row's box
rather than below it. What it costs is 17 px of label
start, against the 32 an indent was spending, on a sidebar
where width is the scarce thing.

The rows are then the REPO SIDEBAR'S PROJECT ROWS, exactly:
same px-2 py-1.5, same text-base at /80, same gap-0.5, same
h-8 buttons. They were smaller and dimmer here for a while
(text-sm, min-h-7, /60), on the reasoning that a nested list
should read as subordinate, and the rule made that argument
unnecessary: once something says "these belong to that",
shrinking them says it a second time and costs legibility.
What still separates a project from a repo is the rule and
the project's own icon, drawn in its own colour at 14 px in
a 16 px slot where the repo rows draw a muted glyph, which
is enough. 14, because an SVG drawn edge to edge reads a
size larger than a Phosphor glyph in the same box, which
keeps a margin inside its own.

The two trailing buttons are the repo row's pattern at
project scale, and the pair is short because a workspace has
exactly two destinations worth naming from out here: its
FOLDER on GitHub, and its BOARD, opened here, which is the
thing that makes it a project at all. Both act directly
rather than opening a menu: the repo's buttons open panels
because a repo has seven GitHub destinations and a set of
actions to choose among, and a two-row menu would be a
gesture in front of a single answer.

GitHub FIRST, matching the repo row above it, so the
github-logo column runs straight down the sidebar and the
in-app action stays at the end of the row in both. It also
means a project that declares no board (`tracker: false`)
drops its last button rather than sliding the other one
into a different column.

NO NEGATIVE MARGIN ANY MORE, and the reason is worth
keeping because it is the same measurement twice. The gap
between a repo row and its first project was never a
declared margin: it was the repo row's own slack, since a
taller row centres its label with more air above and below
than a short one and half of that lands between the two. A
-mt-1 closed it while the rows were 36 px and 28 px. Now
both are 36 px, the slack is zero, and the same pull would
crowd the rows it used to align. The repo rows keep the
min-h-9 they came down to for that earlier arithmetic; at
equal heights it is simply the sidebar's row size.

The trailing buttons carry the REPO ROW'S OWN /30, and that
is now load-bearing rather than tidy. They were written at
/25, meaning to sit a shade below the repo's, and rendered
DARKER instead: this page's Tailwind browser build emits no
rule for text-base-content/20, so the glyphs fell through to
base-content at full strength while the repo's /30 above
them was honoured. Same family as the caret in
crumb-bar.js, where a utility that never appears in the
compiled sheet simply does not exist. So match a value the
page already uses rather than picking a fresh step, and if a
new one is wanted, check the computed colour rather than the
class list.

App views: pages a repo promotes to an estate-level entry (appView:true,
e.g. News), rendered live in the main area through toss-render. The
same set the header's second nav group shows (appNav reads this list),
so the two never disagree.

An entry that names a ref (an address like ?app=owner/repo@branch:path)
shows it, muted, after the label: the same promise the crumb trail
makes for a repo browsed off its default branch.

The rail again, spelled out. The header cluster is icon-only and
desktop-only; here each item gets its label and its doors, the way
the links board's own masthead band renders them, since a sidebar row
has the width for it. This is the phone's route to the rail, and on
desktop it is the labeled reading of the icons above.

Two icons, the same split the Repos section uses: one opens the
whole thing, one acts on it. The rail is a projection of a file, so
the question "how do I change what is up here" needs an answer in
the chrome that shows it, not only inside the board's own page. The
pencil opens the board's editor (?edit=1 through the toss address),
which is where the rail flags, order, labels, and doors live.

flex-wrap, not truncate: an item with several doors (GitHub's
notifications / PRs / agents) should spill onto a second line here
rather than losing them off the right edge. The sidebar is the wide
reading of the rail; that is the whole reason it renders twice.

Doors: further ways into the SAME destination, the board's own
idiom. They fit here and they do not fit in an icon cluster,
which is the other half of why the rail renders twice.

Per-repo views, hidden in the estate (global) context. The estate is
reached from the header nav and the sidebar trail's mark, not from
here, since it is a context above the repo, not a view of it.

WHAT A REPO VIEW IS FOR, after the 2026-08-14 pass: the things only
this repository can answer. Its README, its structure, its declared
pages, its manifest. Three rows left because the estate answers the
same question better for the whole constellation at once:

  files     the tree walk. Reading a file is central now, so this row
            hands the Files view this repo and leaves (the arrow says
            so). ?view=files is retired; ?file= and a pin open the
            central reader.
  branches  the per-repo branch review. Activity's Branches tab is
            the same rollup, same landed/stranded signal, across
            every repo, and opens the branch takeover. A per-repo
            copy of a cross-repo answer is a narrower view of a
            thing nobody wants narrowed.

Overview leads, and always: it is the README, for every repo.

A repo's own declared front page, when it names one. It renders
through the app view rather than a landing kind of its own, since
this shell already knows how to show a repo's page as an
addressable view.

The repo's own tree beside the file it opens. Until 2026-09-24
this row left the repo for the central Search view.

PROJECTS, inside a repo: the same list the estate sidebar indents
under this repo's row, at the level a repo view sits. One list, two
levels, one destination: a row there and a row here both open the
project view (openProject switches the repo first, goProject is
already in it), so a workspace reads the same however you reached it.
The rows are duplicated in markup rather than shared, the way the rail
is. They are also now sized ALIKE, which the duplication no longer
earns on its own: the two differ in exactly two ways, the estate's
extra repo argument and this one's active state. Keep them in step by
hand (a test checks the row class and the block class appear twice),
or fold them into a component the day a third difference appears.

The list is read from the OPEN repo's live manifest (repoProjects
prefers it over the estate cache), so it needs no token and follows
the browsed ref. The trailing buttons are the estate row's pair, and
the rows hang off the same 1 px rule at the same ml-4, which here
lands on the centre of the section head's own glyph rather than on a
repo row's. Three lists of projects, one treatment.

Satellites of the member in view (repoSatellites): in a member,
its own; in a satellite, the same list with itself marked, and the
head names the parent as a button.
Rows take the project rows' shape and rule, with GitHub's stored
size before the GitHub button.

The size gives way to the project hint, and both to the name
on a phone; the row's title-tip states both.

Needs attention: the repo's own declared checks (.web-tools.json
"checks"), evaluated on open. Only what is NOT passing renders, so a
current repo shows nothing here at all: badging green states would
make the block furniture, and furniture is what the eye stops
reading. Each row opens the file it is about.

Pinned: folders and files the repo designates in .web-tools.json. The
header carries a config gear, since the pins are a config field.
Recent: files touched by the newest commits on the current ref.

A recent entry opens the file in the app; the trailing icon is its
jump-over to the same file on GitHub, at the browsed ref. The row is
a button, so the anchor sits beside it rather than within.

── Main area: the selected view for the repo. On touch devices a
horizontal swipe here pages between the estate's dashboard views
(estateNav: Activity / Repos / Stage / Tools / Map; Activity's
Open / To-do / Jots sub-tabs switch by pill, not swipe; the header's
repo-sponsored group is out of the carousel, being iframes); see
swipeToView. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

@container so a view can size to THE PANE rather than the window. Under
the dock the two stop agreeing: the window is 1440 and the pane is 416,
and a grid keyed on `xl:` still reads three columns into a column that
fits one, which is how the first docked build produced a list of single
words. Viewport breakpoints were never really asking the right question
here (a 1280 window with the sidebar open leaves main 928px, and `xl:`
called that three columns too); the dock is just where being wrong got
loud. Adoption is per view, `lg:` to `@3xl:`, as each is touched.

Estate: the all-repo context, with two views of its own — the repo grid
(Repos) and the Stage (the cross-repo working set). One component
renders both and switches on the shell view, so both share this lazy
mount. Full width, so the repo grid runs three cards wide like the
pages index; the Stage constrains its own column.

w-full is load-bearing under listsFill and inert without it. An auto
inline margin on a flex ITEM sizes it to its content instead of
stretching it, so the moment listsFill turned the pane into a flex
column, mx-auto quietly capped this div at the width of its widest
row: the Lists pane came out 548px wide inside a 1280px window,
whatever !max-w-none said, and the Pin grid split that into two
266px columns and truncated a 26-character title for want of 5px.
In the ordinary block case width:100% is what the div already had.

App view: a page promoted to an estate-level entry (appView flag),
rendered live through toss-render's #gh= address mode, the same way a
custom landing embeds. Full-bleed, beside Repos / Stage.

Public browse: the no-token jsDelivr file browser (estate-level, beside
Repos / Stage). Lazy-mounted on first visit.

This browser: the token, the browser note, and what this origin keeps
in this browser. Where a 401 or 403 lands instead of the gh-auth
takeover (routeAuthFail). Estate-level, token-free, lazy-mounted. The
pane does not scroll: each tab scrolls inside itself, and Stored here
is two containers that split its height, as the Waiting view's are.

Pages: web-tools' own catalog, or any repo's `pages` entries, reached
at ?view=pages or via the repo sidebar/tabs.

data-pattern and data-part declare the div below a Card grid and
name its parts (data/ui-units/codebook.md, "Declaring a pattern
in markup"); nothing at runtime reads them. The folder chips,
the filter, the empty line and the catalog link are the
frame's, so the declaration holds the groups alone.

data-find-box: the Pages view's own filter, so a bare
keystroke narrows this list instead of opening the
sidebar finder (wireAppTypeahead).

Tinted, so the footer reads as the card's own rather
than as page under the shot.

Repo landing: the repo's front page, presented with the same structure
as the project view: the repo mark with the switcher menu, the name,
the App launcher when a companion app is declared, GitHub link,
and metadata badges. Below them, a tabstrip switches between Overview
(the README), App (live iframe), Board (root tracker), Pages (the repo's
catalog), Files (file browser), and Atlas.

A satellite usually has no manifest, so its page cannot say
whose it is; this badge does, and opens the parent.

Project: a workspace's front page, the repo overview one level down.
Same shape as that overview on purpose (name, a few facts, the front
door rendered), because a project is a repo-sized thing inside a repo
and a reader arriving at one wants what they want when arriving at a
repo. The header's three buttons are the routes out: the workspace as
files, its board, its folder on GitHub. Below them a segmented pill
(the shared internal-tab style) switches the body among Overview,
Board, Pages, and Docs; the header and pills stay put while the body
changes, so the reader never loses which workspace they are standing
in. A FILE board renders as the Board pill (navigable, links resolved
in-app) and drops the header button; a folder board keeps the button.

Overview is the repo's landing decision one level down: an entry
declaring a `landing` gets that page rendered live (toss-render #gh=,
same as a repo's custom landing), every other project gets its README.
Pages and Docs are DERIVED rather than declared: see projectPages and
loadProjectDocs below.

A project's masthead, on one line: the project mark, which is
the project's own icon (its manifest `icon`, an SVG in the repo,
drawn in its own colour on a neutral tile; the kanban glyph on
the primary tint where none is declared) and the switcher (the
repo's projects in the shared anchored menu, with the project's
folder on GitHub), then the name, the App button where the
workspace declares a landing (the App tab has no pill of its
own), and the repository, which opens the repo.

The tab row, full width under the masthead, every tab named.
Below sm a tab is its label alone, which is what lets five
fit a phone; the icons return from sm up. Outpost appears
where the workspace declares a PowerShell outpost and Board
where it has a file board. Pages is always offered, disabled
where the catalog claims nothing for the workspace, so the
place for pages is visible before there are any. Docs is a
mode of Files (the switch under this row), not a tab.
overflow-x-auto: a clipped tab is an unreachable one.

Files has two modes: the folder-at-a-time browser, and Docs,
the workspace's markdown as one tree (&tab=docs). The Map's
compact count chip, as the PowerShell outpost view's filters.

data-find-box: Docs' own filter, so a bare keystroke narrows
the tree instead of opening the sidebar finder.

App: the workspace's landing page itself, full-bleed under the
header, like a repo's custom landing, opened from the App
button beside the name, or at a route (a page query, stamped
as &item=) from a route card in Pages. The FAB carries the
bust-out to the full-viewport page.

Files: the project folder's tree beside the file it opens
(alpineComponents/file-browser.js), based at the project so the
crumbs never climb out of it. Remounted per project, repo and
ref.

THE OVERVIEW IS THE README, in every workspace, the promise a
repo's Overview makes one level up. A landing is the App (the
icon beside the name) and a PowerShell outpost its own tab;
until 2026-10-06 either one took this slot instead.

Board: the tracker board rendered in-pane, its relative
links resolved into the shell's viewer (onBoardClick), so a
row's task file is one tap without leaving the workspace.
The typed read, when board.csv exists on this ref.

data-pattern and data-part declare this a List and name its
parts (data/ui-units/codebook.md, "Declaring a pattern in
markup"); nothing at runtime reads them. The review line
rides inside the list element but is not an item.

The review line: what a grooming pass asks before it
reads any row. Each count states its own subject, so a
zero reads as an answer rather than a missing number.

A task an open user call decides links to it in
Waiting, where it is answered.

Last activity is the signal board.md cannot
carry, and the one that separates a live task
from one that has only been groomed.

The markdown fallback, for a ref whose generator predates
board.csv or that has not regenerated since.

Pages: the workspace's slice of the repo catalog. Lean cards
rather than the full gallery component (whose state lives in
a nested x-data the shell's selection cannot repaint): a lazy
live preview that is itself the link, the title, and the
GitHub source jump-over. The repo's own Pages view keeps the
shot/live/source toggles one level up.

A ROUTE card (an entry whose page is the project's landing,
with a query) is a door into the app rather than a page: its
face is the cached shot of that route, else the project's
icon, never a live frame, and it opens the App tab at the
route (openProjectApp) through a real link (projectAppHref),
so it still opens in a new tab. See projectPages for why.

data-pattern and data-part declare this a Card grid and name
its parts (data/ui-units/codebook.md, "Declaring a pattern
in markup"); nothing at runtime reads them.

Files › Docs: every markdown file in the workspace, from one
recursive tree read, as a folder tree with counts rolled up
(the Map's Docs rail, with the files nested). The first level
opens, deeper folders wait for a tap, a filter opens every
match, and READMEs lead their folder. A document reads beside
the tree, over it on a narrow pane, and rides as &item=; the
curated docs/README.md, where a workspace keeps one, is what
the reader shows before anything is picked. Source packages
are counted, not listed.

Outpost: the PowerShell outpost view, for a workspace that declares a
`powershellOutpost` manifest: its PowerShell material against
the work computer, which has no Git checkout
(lib/alpineComponents/powershell-outpost-view.js).
Mounted per project through a keyed one-row x-for, so switching
workspaces or leaving the tab remounts it with the right
manifest rather than repainting a component that read the
previous one at init.

Atlas: the treemap for the selected repo, embedded. Available for every
repo (the "ready mechanism"), even one with its own landing.

The Files tree walk and the per-repo Branches review stood here until
2026-08-14, and both were removed rather than moved: reading a file is
the estate's Files view, and the branch rollup is Activity's Branches
tab, which carries the same landed/stranded signal across every repo.
The ref compare went with the branch review, its only
caller anywhere; the component was deleted with nav-repo.html, its
last mount, a day later.

Config: the open repo's .web-tools.json as a full view (a Settings form
and a raw JSON tab), the roomy counterpart to the shared repo dialog's
config tabs. Per-repo, so it sits with the repo views (after Branches).
It is the only config surface for the OPEN repo now: the sidebar top
bar's gear was retired as a duplicate of this row.
Mounted lazily on first visit.

Wide, not 3xl: the form and the JSON pane sit side by side on
desktop, so a 3xl cap gave each about 360px and put the whole editor
in a narrow ribbon down the middle of a wide screen. The cap is high
enough that on a 1440 screen the pane's own width is what binds, and
a wider screen keeps using it.

No separate Stage pane: the Stage IS the estate pane's own view, in
lib/alpineComponents/estate.js.

The Map view: the coordination layer made inspectable — the portable
to-go bag (docs/portable.csv), and a per-repo card carrying the
repo-owned scope story plus a live adoption read. The operational face
of the constellation doctrine. Estate-level, its own component and lazy
mount.

The Proposals view: cross-repo edits an agent session proposed but
could not make, applied here on the user's confirm with the user's
token. Estate-level, token-gated, its own component and lazy mount;
the nav entry appears only while something is pending.

The Waiting view: what waits on the owner, the open user calls and the
Text collection's proposed edits by file (lib/alpineComponents/waiting.js,
lib/kits/user-calls.js). Lazy-mounted like Proposals. The pane does not
scroll: the view is two containers that split its height, a list over
a strip of detail cards, and each scrolls inside itself.

The Tending view: findings from tending passes, kept as notes in the
registry's notes store (lib/kits/findings.js), each linked to the
branches, pull requests, tasks, snags and sessions it concerns. Its own
component and lazy mount, like Tools and Proposals.

The Tools view: a curated gallery of the owner's utility pages (the
text-diff tool and the like), fed from the hub's docs/tools.csv.
Estate-level, public (no token), its own component and lazy mount.

The Search view: the central file surface (file names at any ref under
any folder, Markdown contents through the crawled word index, the captured session
records), over the same shared core the sidebar finder uses
(lib/kits/estate-search.js). The finder is for jumping; this is for
investigating, and it is where each mode's caveats are stated in
full. Estate-level, token-gated in effect, its own component and
lazy mount; the finder's "File contents" gate routes here with the
query carried over (goSearch → searchSeed).

It READS the file too, through the shared viewer embedded inside it,
so a results column and a file beside it want every pixel the window
has. It was capped at max-w-4xl, then at max-w-7xl, and both were the
same mistake one size apart: measured at a 1920 viewport on 2026-09-03,
the 7xl cap left 320px of dead margin down each side while the reader's
own column ran 455px. Uncapped now, like Tools and Map. A cap on this
pane is not a small size choice; it is the corridor.

The repo's Files view: alpineComponents/file-browser.js based at the
repo root, opening on filesPath with filesFile beside it.

The State view: the estate's derived state in one list, each piece with
when it was last built, when this browser last checked, what builds it,
and a Refresh where one is possible. It exists because "refresh" was one
icon over two unrelated verbs (a committed crawl that can be hours stale,
and a local recompute with no age at all), spread over six surfaces, with
the as-of reading that tells you whether to press hidden below `sm`.
Estate-level, token-gated, its own component and lazy mount.

── The repo menu: ONE panel, two lists (menuKind), opened by either of a
Repos row's trailing buttons and by the Activity view's repo chip. The
actions list is the marker button's; the github list is the github
button's.

Positioned FIXED from the trigger's rect rather than nested beside it,
because the rows live in an overflow-y-auto column that would clip an
absolutely-positioned panel at the list's edge; mounted out here, past
<aside>, for the same reason. z-[55] clears the drawer (z-50) that summons

── The shell mode: how much of the app is drawn around the view ──────────

A READING parameter, in the class ?use= and ?window= belong to:
it says how to PRESENT the screen, not which screen, so it gets no VIEWS
row and is stamped beside whatever the view table stamps. `full` is the
default and stays out of the URL, so every existing link is unchanged.

  nav   header, sidebar closed at every width (open it from the header)
  none  neither; the view alone, which is what an unframed link wants

THE DEFAULT IS PER VIEW, not one constant. An app view opens at `none`:
it is one page some repo promoted, framed whole, and a reader who
addressed it by name asked for that page rather than for the app around
it. A home-screen tile is the case that makes it obvious. Every other
route IS the app and keeps its header.

Derived per view rather than latched at boot, and that is the whole of why
this is a getter. A latched default would follow the reader out of the app
view and strand the estate dashboard with no nav, reachable only through
the FAB. Deriving it means the shell leaves when you enter an app view and
comes back when you leave, with nothing to remember or clear.

It also keeps the ADDRESS minimal in both directions, since the stamp
compares against this rather than against a constant: `?app=budget-drs`
carries no `shell` key and opens with nav chrome, and turning the header off there
stamps `shell=none`, which is the honest reading of a screen showing the
promoted page bare.

`none` is not a trap: the FAB's Render tab carries this as a bar (the
`modes` contract below), beside the ref and width bars, since which ref,
what width, and how much shell are three readings of one question. That is
the way back, and it is the same control that sets the mode in the first
place, so nothing needs a second escape hatch parked on the page.

Named `shell` because that is already this app's word for the header and
sidebar around a view (the ?shell= parameter in docs/APP.md, and window.__shell
is this object). `chrome` was the first name and was dropped: in a browser
the chrome is the BROWSER's, which is the one thing this cannot touch.
`frame` was dropped too, since the Render tab's width bar already means a
frame, and two meanings in one tab is how a bar gets misread.

The reader's explicit choice, '' for none made. Held apart from the mode
because the two answer different questions: what was asked for, and what
this screen opens as when nothing was.

Whether the sidebar is showing. One boolean at every width, which is the
whole of the mobile/desktop difference now: below lg it is an overlay with
a scrim, at lg and up a static column the main area sits beside, and the
only other difference is which way it starts (open on desktop, closed on a
phone). It used to be `drawer`, read below lg only, with an unconditional
lg:translate-x-0 pinning the column open on desktop with no way to collapse
it: the hamburger that would have done it was lg:hidden. So the desktop had
a sidebar it could not put away, and an unframed link had nothing to ask
for. The rename is the point, not tidiness: this is no longer a phone
affordance, it is the sidebar's state.

── The hide list ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Membership and every descriptive field are properties OF A REPO, written
in that repo's own config; this one is not. "I would rather not look at
this" is a statement about the VIEWER, not about the repo, and it has to
be reversible from here without a write to the repo it names, so it lives
beside the other viewer-owned estate content in the private registry: a
`hidden` array of owner/repo strings in the registry's own
.web-tools.json, read out of the config cache the sidebar already loads.
A hidden repo keeps `estate: true` and every field it declared, and comes
back unchanged when it is shown again. `conventions: 'optout'` remains the
repo-side answer to the neighbouring question (is this repo part of the
estate at all), and the two do not overlap: optout is a decision about the
repo, hiding is a decision about the dashboard.

── Live crawl progress, one channel for all three crawls ──────────────
A slot per cache key, null when that crawl is idle, and the shape is the
same in every slot: { verb, done, total, unit, active: [name, …] }. One
channel rather than three props because the readers are generic: the State
view draws a bar per row without knowing which crawl it is watching, and
the Activity pane draws the same bar for its own row.

THE CRAWL NAMES ITS OWN VERB AND UNIT. Only the crawl knows it is on the
scan pass rather than the quick one, or counting session records rather
than repos, so the words ride with the numbers instead of being inferred
by whoever draws them.

The unit is always the WHOLE thing the crawl was given to do (an account
repo, an estate repo, a session record), never the sub-work inside one.
Per-repo work ticks several times a second, reads as churn rather than
progress, and would suggest a precision the crawl does not have, since one
repo can cost an order of magnitude more than the next. `active` carries
every item in flight rather than the newest, because the pools run several
at once and naming one of them would describe the crawl wrongly. A crawl
that fans out all at once (configs) reports no `active` at all: "every
repo" is not a reading.

── The arrival crawls, while they are in flight ────────────────────────

Separate from the three `*Refreshing` flags beside them, and the split is
the whole point rather than a duplicate. Those flags belong to the Refresh
BUTTONS: they disable the control, spin its icon, and bracket a run whose
progress slot is opened and closed, and closing writes that run's call log,
which is a commit. An arrival crawl must not cost a commit per visit, so it
cannot borrow them.

What it can do is say it is running, which is the reading a row was missing
entirely: the number went from "1d ago" to "22m ago" with nothing in
between, so the one moment the view had something live to report was the
one moment it said nothing. No progress bar rides this, and the reason is
the same commit: `tickCrawl` no-ops without an open slot, and opening one
is what writes the log. A word is honest and free; a bar is not.

What each cache's last check left behind, in THIS tab: `at` is when the copy
on screen was last confirmed against its source (this browser's stamp, ms),
`tried` when a check last started, and `failed` the reason the last one
came back without confirming anything. The age pills read this and nothing
else; see "Freshness" for the rule that keeps `at` inside CHECK_MS.

A minute hand for the pills, so "checked 3m" advances between checks
rather than reading "now" until the next one starts.

Recently-committed files for the current repo@ref, shown in the sidebar.
Generated artifacts a build hook writes on every commit are noise here,
not real edits, so they're filtered out for web-tools specifically.

Read before anything paints, so the shell never flashes its full self on
the way to a ?shell=none load. Same read on popstate (restoreFromUrl).

Settled once the address has been routed, so a warm that keys on
`view` (the auth watcher's) waits for the view to be the linked one.

Changing the repo takes you to its overview. It used to bail out when a
file was open, because selecting one flipped the shell to the Files view

An open project is repo@ref-scoped like the rest: switching the ref
under it re-reads whatever its open tab renders from where you now are.

Estate membership needs a token to resolve, since it is read from the
cache in the private registry. Auth resolves after boot, so load then,
and reload when auth arrives. Editing any repo's config (config-saved)
can change membership, so that path rebuilds the cache and reloads.

Sessions rides beside activity here, and its absence was a real gap:
a load that lands straight on ?view=sessions routes before auth
resolves, so the pane's own arrival kick ran against no token and
declined, and nothing afterwards went back for it. Announced through
checkCache, so a commit reaches the pane.

ONE BOOT PATH. This watcher used to repeat the sidebar read, the
mailbox and the proposals count that init() had already fired, and
then ran the deep activity crawl and the sessions crawl whatever view
was open. Measured 2026-09-02 on a plain README landing: configs.json
read four to seven times, /user/repos five to seven, both crawls'
FRESH re-reads, and the estate pane reloading its 7 MB sessions file
a second time off the configs-refreshed that followed. The stored
token is all those reads need, so init() already made them when one
was there; what auth arriving adds is the case where it was NOT there
(a token pasted mid-session), and the crawl the open view reads.

Crawl, and RE-READ WHEN THE CRAWL MOVED SOMETHING. The sidebar is
built from the cache as it stood when the page opened, so a manifest
change merged since the last crawl is invisible to that read; the
crawl fixes the cache and the nav kept rendering what it read before
it, which is how two "Doc Growth" rows outlived the merge that
removed them (2026-08-28). refreshConfigCache reports whether it
committed, so the re-read costs one cache GET on the loads that
changed something and nothing on the rest.

Only what the pane on screen reads (ensureFresh), once the address
has been routed: a deep link to ?view=sessions lands before auth

Announced for views that mount before auth resolves and would otherwise
