── The per-repo manifest: .web-tools.json at the repo root ───────────────
The repo's web-tools config. A repo designates what this shell should
consider — a landing page, pinned folders/files, a staged-files list with
transfer targets — and its top-level fields are the repo's config for any
web-tools page, not just this shell. One GET per repo@ref; 404 means no
config. Parsed as data, never executed, so probing any repo is safe.
Consumers: the sidebar's Landing and Pages rows (landing, pages), its
Pinned block (pins), and the Stage view (stage).

── Declared staleness checks (lib/kits/repo-checks.js) ────────────────────────
Evaluated when a repo is opened and thrown away when you leave. No cache,
no crawl, no session hook: the answer is only wanted at the moment someone
is looking at the repo, so computing it then is both cheapest and most
current. A repo declaring no checks costs nothing (evaluate() short-circuits
before touching the reader).

The estate grid shows the same checks by a different route, and the split
is not duplication. Live evaluation is right for ONE repo you are looking
at; M checks across N repos on every load is the per-visit fanout the
activity cache exists to avoid, so the cards read facts the crawl already
probed (crawlRepoActivity) and judge them at render. Same declarations,
same module, one definition of each check.

The repo may have changed under a slow evaluation; same guard loadConfig
uses, or a stale panel lands on the wrong repo.

The batched reader a check set runs against: one tree read and one commit
read per distinct path, shared across every check in the batch. It moved to
lib/kits/activity-crawl.js with the crawl that is its other caller, and this
stays as the shell's name for it so the live config-view run and the crawl
cannot drift into two readers.

A check that could not run is its own finding (a rename usually), so it is
shown, distinctly from a plain failure rather than folded in with it.

A pin row carries its own icon. Config editing lives in the sidebar shield
dialog (repoModal, lib/alpineComponents/repo.js).

Build the estate-context sidebar from one read of the registry's config
cache (state/configs.json), the same source the quick-link row and the
estate grid use. Two lists come out of the one cache pass:
  estateRepos — every repo opting into the estate (estate:true), a compact
                 index beside the header nav's Repos grid, carrying each
                 repo's own icon/group/order so it groups like that grid.
  appViews     — a `pages` entry flagged appView:true in any repo, promoted
                 to an estate-level view (viewLabel/icon/order from the flag).
Token-gated: without a token there is no cache read, so both stay empty and
no private repo or page is named, matching the Stage and the private estate.

Every repo the crawl covers, config or not: the satellites rule
(satelliteClaims) reads names, and most satellites have no config.

The hide list rides in on the same read: it is a field of the
registry's OWN config, and the registry is one of the repos the
crawl already covers, so honouring it costs no second fetch.

Keep the raw config beside the derived lists: it is already read
and parsed, and menu-time questions (does this repo declare an
outbox?) should not cost a second fetch.

A hidden repo contributes NOTHING to the estate's lists: no
sidebar row, and none of its promoted pages as app views. Its
config stays in the map above, so the shell can still answer
questions about it (the menu's Show row is the first caller) and
opening it by address keeps working, which is what makes hiding a
display decision rather than a departure.

The rest of the mark (lib/kits/repo-mark.js): a drawn SVG, a
tone, a glyph weight. repoMarkHtml draws them; the session
brief reads them from this list rather than the manifest.

Filled by enrichSidebarPrivacy (the cache has no privacy); the
key is present so the later set is reactive. null === unknown.

A FULL APP brings its own shell (docs/APP.md, "Product
boundary"), so this app opens it at its own address rather than
framing it. The flag marks the page at that path, whichever of
its entries carries it, so route entries need not repeat it.

The render target may be a cross-repo page (owner/repo[@ref]:path):
home promotes the news view whose renderer lives in web-tools.

WHO PROMOTED IT, which is not where it lives. A cross-repo
promotion resolves `repo` to the page's home (home promotes
the hub's doc-growth page, so t.repo is the hub), and the
fact a reader needs is whose view this is. Only the
disambiguation below reads it; the address uses t.repo.

The short address, when the promoting repo declares one. It
is the page's name rather than its location, which is what
makes ?app=<slug> short: a path is most of an address and
none of the meaning. Optional, so a page that declares none
is reached by its address and nothing changes for it.

A page a repo promotes may need arguments to be the view that
repo means: home and web-tools promote the same doc-growth
page and differ only in which payload it reads. appViewUrl
already carries a query; without this it could only ever come
from the address bar, so a manifest could name the page but
not what it should show.

Query is part of the identity: two repos may promote the same
page and differ only in what they point it at, and a key that
ignored the query would make them one entry.

A ROW MUST NAME ITSELF. The sidebar and the header nav render an app
view as its icon and its label and nothing else, so two views sharing a
label are one view listed twice as far as any reader can tell. That is
not hypothetical: web-tools and home both promoted pages/doc-growth.html
as "Doc Growth", correctly (two payloads are two views), and the estate
nav said the same two words twice for two days.

The federated Growth view fixed that instance and manifest-registry's
slug gate stops one namespace collision, but neither reaches this:
viewLabel is free text, two repos may legitimately choose the same
words, and no gate should stop them. So the fix belongs where the
ambiguity appears. A repeated label takes the PROMOTING repo as a
suffix, which is the fact that actually differs: a cross-repo promotion
resolves to the page's own repo, so home's Doc Growth and the hub's
both address mehrlander/web-tools and suffixing by that names one repo
twice. `declaredBy` is whose manifest said so.

Only the repeats are suffixed: a unique label is already an answer, and
qualifying every row would spend the sidebar's width saying what the
Repos section says. `baseLabel` keeps the declared text for anything
that wants the name rather than the disambiguated display.

Two views from ONE repo cannot be told apart this way. The suffix
still points at the manifest to fix, which is the next question a
reader has.

independent; the list renders without it
likewise: one extra GET, off the render path

── The hide list: read, write, and who reads it ─────────────────────────
One resolver, so the sidebar and the Repos grid cannot disagree about who
is hidden. It takes the registry's own config and returns the effective
set, which is the stored list except while a toggle's override is still
waiting for the config crawl to catch up.

Flip one repo and write the registry back. The read is FRESH and its sha
rides into the save, so two hides in quick succession fold onto each
other rather than the loser overwriting the winner.

An empty list is dropped rather than written as []: the field means
"these are hidden", and a repo hiding nothing should read as a config
that never mentioned hiding.

The Repos grid reads the same cache on its own clock, so tell it the
list moved rather than waiting for the crawl that will confirm it.

The RAIL: the handful of destinations worth a tap from anywhere, read from
the same links board pages/links.html renders, so there is no second list.
A repo declares its board with `links` in its own .web-tools.json (a bare
path, or a qualified owner/repo[@ref]:path), the way `pages` declares a
catalog; the shell reads it and keeps the items flagged `rail: true`.

Why the shell reads the file rather than the page handing it up: promoted
as an app view, links.html renders in an iframe, and an iframe cannot paint
into its parent's chrome. That constraint is real but narrow, and it says
nothing about where the DATA comes from. The board is a file; the shell can
read a file. No cross-frame anything.

Independent of the sidebar render, like enrichSidebarPrivacy: a slow or
missing board must not hold up the Repos index. A 404 is not an error here,
just a repo that declares a board it has not written yet.

A board names its ref when it means one; otherwise the read follows
the page's selection for that repository, then main.

Same fallback links.html uses: an item's own icon wins, a plain
link borrows its area's glyph, so only the exceptions spend one.

A repo item is a destination in THIS shell, not an outbound
link, so it routes internally rather than reloading the page.

The config cache carries no visibility, so the sidebar Repos rows get their
public/private marker from the account repos list, one call matched by name.
Mutates priv on the existing objects (the key is present, so it is reactive);
an entry the list does not cover stays null (unknown) and shows no marker.
Sizes come in the same list, for the satellite rows (repoSizeLabel).

Manual config-cache rebuild for the estate refresh button. The app views,
Repos cards, and quick links all read a throttled (~6h) crawl of every
repo's .web-tools.json, so a just-merged config change (a repo newly
declaring an app view, say) can lag until the crawl next runs. This forces
the crawl now, then re-reads every consumer in order (the load path reads
before the async crawl commits, so a plain reload lags a step; awaiting the
crawl first is what makes the new entry appear immediately). The estate
component reloads its cards off the dispatched event.
Wait out a refresh ALREADY IN FLIGHT. refreshConfigs() returns immediately
when one is running, so awaiting it there would prove nothing and the
caller would retry against the same stale table it just missed on. Raced
against a timeout because the in-flight run can finish between the caller's
check and this listener, and a router that hangs is worse than one that
falls back.

── Config aggregate: crawl each participating repo's .web-tools.json and
fold it into a derived cache (state/configs.json) in the registry repo,
keeping a bounded on-change history per repo. Source of truth stays each
repo's own file; this is breadth + history a single read can't give. A
per-browser throttle (localStorage) keeps the crawl occasional, and a
material-change check keeps commits sparse, so nav triggers cost nothing.
── THE GATE IS MOTION, NOT THE CLOCK ──────────────────────────────────

Each of these three crawls used to be gated by an interval: six hours for
configs, thirty minutes for activity, fifteen for sessions. An interval is
not evidence about the source. It is a guess standing in for evidence, and
it is wrong in both directions at once: a repo pushed thirty seconds ago
waits out the clock while a quiet estate pays a full crawl for having
waited. The State view then printed the interval as "auto every 30m", which
read as a schedule and was not one, since nothing here ran on a timer then.
The crawls fired when a view that reads them was opened, so the interval
was only ever a floor with a promise written on it. There is a timer now
(see "Freshness"), and it is about the READING rather than the source: it
fires when what a pill shows turns five minutes old, and the gates below
still decide what that check costs.

The evidence was already in the building. Every one of these crawls can ask
its source what moved for about the price of one call: the account repo
listing carries `pushed_at` per repo, and the registry's own tree carries a
blob sha per session record. So the gate moves inside the crawl, per unit of
work, and the crawl simply runs: it looks, finds nothing, and costs a call.
A repo that moved is crawled the moment anyone looks, rather than at the
mercy of a stamp in one browser's localStorage.

What survives of the clock is this floor, and it is a debounce rather than a
policy: two views opened in the same breath must not fire the same crawl
twice. Nothing renders it, because a number that only prevents a double-tap
is not a reading anyone needs.

What each repo looked like the last time this crawl read its manifest.
Same store shape and same reasoning as the activity watermarks below.

READS MAIN, WHATEVER REF THE READER IS BROWSING: this crawl builds its own
GH clients pinned at main rather than borrowing the browser's, so a
session opened at ?repo=…&ref=<branch> cannot commit that branch's
manifest into the shared cache. node/test/shell-branch-addresses.test.mjs
holds it: every client the crawl constructs reads at main.
Returns {committed, changed} when it ran, {skipped:true} when it declined,
{error} when it failed. It reported NOTHING until 2026-08-25, which is why
the Repos pane could only be re-read by the manual Refresh: an announcement
needs a commit to announce, and there was no way to ask whether one had
happened. Every existing caller ignores the value.

Single-flight, the guard the other two crawls already had: the boot
path, an arrival kick and the Refresh button could run two of these at
once, each re-reading the account list and the cache FRESH, and the
loser saving a fold built on a pre-commit read. A call that finds a
crawl in flight joins it and gets that crawl's result.

Seed the crawl from the account's repos (the enumeration that discovers
estate members), so a repo opting in via its own config is picked up
without any registry list. If the enumeration fails, fall back to the
members already resolved from the cache: that re-crawls what is known
and cannot discover a new joiner, which is the honest degradation.
The floor is read BEFORE the enumeration, which is where the throttle
used to sit after it: a call this crawl is about to decline should not
cost a request to decline.

This listing is the enumeration that discovers estate members AND, from
the same response, the motion reading the gate below runs on. One call,
two jobs, which is what makes gating per repo affordable.
for the run record, appended below if this commits

A repo is QUIET when it has not been pushed since this crawl last read
it. Everything this crawl stores about a repo comes out of files in that
repo (its .web-tools.json, and the two files PortableAlign grades), and
no file changes without a push, so the reading is exact in the direction
that matters: a quiet repo cannot be hiding a manifest change.

It is NOT exact in the other direction, and does not need to be. A push
that never touched a manifest re-reads the repo for nothing, which costs
three calls and produces no commit. Gating tighter would mean reading the
files to find out whether the files changed.

The four ways to be wrong are the same four the activity gate closes
below, for the same reasons: a forced pass is never quiet, a repo with
nothing stored is never quiet, a repo with no recorded mark is never
quiet, and an unreadable pushed_at is never quiet. The fallback
enumeration above supplies no pushed_at at all, so a crawl that lost the
listing reads every repo rather than trusting a map it never filled.
Read up front, because a skip is only safe when there is a stored entry
to serve instead. The fold below re-reads this file after the fan-out,
for the same reason the activity crawl does: a crawl that runs for a
while must not fold onto the copy it read before it started.

One GH per repo (the shared store.gh is bound to the open repo). Read
the current manifest for each participant.
This fan-out is unpooled, so every repo is in flight from the first
moment: the count of finished repos is the only honest reading, and
`active` stays empty rather than listing the whole account back.

The gate, and it is the whole saving: a quiet repo makes no request
at all. Its stored entry rides forward through `carry` below, which
is the same path a repo the enumeration could not see already took.

The alignment grade rides this crawl. Two extra reads while already
standing in front of the repo, against three live reads per member on
every estate load, which is what putting the grade on the Repos cards
would otherwise have cost. The estate reads the cache it already
loads; nothing probes on render.

The repo's own committed skills ride the same free read. The
plugin's set is never here: a pulled skill lives in the plugin
cache, so a committed .claude/skills/ is by construction what
the hub did not ship this repo.

Stamped only for a repo this pass read, and only after it came back.
A repo whose pushed_at the listing did not carry records nothing, so
it stays un-gated rather than being marked with an empty string that
would match the next empty read.

Pruned to the current enumeration, so a repo that left the account
stops carrying a mark nothing will ask about again.

FRESH against the browser's 60-second cache, and reconciled against what
this page last wrote, against the API's own read-after-write lag. Both
failures look identical from here: a fold onto a base that is not
current. See readForFold above.

Every repo the cache already knew rides forward, whether or not this
crawl could see it. The enumeration above is this client's view of the
account, not the world's: a narrowly-scoped token, or an account past
the un-paginated 100 repos it asks for, produces a short list that is
not wrong so much as partial, and a partial list must not be written
over a shared file as if it were complete. See buildCache for how a
repo does leave.

Only commit when substance changed (buildCache always restamps
timestamps, so a deep-equal would never skip).

The run record rides the commit the crawl was making anyway; see
lib/kits/crawl-runs.js for why it cannot cause one. No `failed`: this
crawl swallows a per-repo read failure, so it has no count to give and
a zero would read as "none failed".
Optional by construction: the run record is an extra reading, and
nothing about it may stand between a crawl and the commit it exists
to make. A window without the kit simply carries the ring forward.

What the gate saved, recorded where the cost is. A run whose
`skipped` equals its `checked` made one request in total.

Force the activity crawl and tell the estate to re-read (the Activity view's
Refresh button and the estate refresh flow route here). Separate from the
config refresh because the activity crawl is much heavier (a capped branch
scan per repo), so it is not folded into every config refresh.

ONE PASS, and it shipped as two. The split ran the crawl quick-first
(commits, PRs, branch dates) so the list landed in seconds, then a scan
true-up behind it. What the call log showed (2026-08-17) is what that
actually cost: the deep pass repeats every cheap read the quick pass just
made, because `deep` gates the scan ALONE, so a two-pass refresh of 11
repos spent 66 calls, a fifth of the run, fetching the same commits and the
same two PR lists twice within a minute. The seconds it bought back were
real and the price was not worth them, and the reader watching the bar was
also being told a run had finished when it had not.

The quick pass keeps its caller: the State view's arrival kick warms this
cache for rows that need the repo list and the open PRs and no branch
verdicts at all, so `deep: false` stays a supported shape.

Announce a finished sessions crawl, handing the document along. The exact
sibling of announceActivity below, and it did not exist until 2026-08-27:
every caller dispatched the bare event by hand, so the Sessions pane went
back to the API for a file the crawl was holding, and its age pill reported
the last COMMIT rather than the last check. See the crawl's own note.
`sha` is main's blob sha for the copy handed over (the commit's, or the
base it matched), which is what a later freshness confirm compares.

Announce a finished activity crawl, handing the document along. A listener
that re-reads the cache on this event is re-fetching a file the crawl still
holds, so the detail carries it; a listener that gets no detail (the
throttled background path, or one that never looks) falls back to reading,
which is why this is an addition and not a change of contract.

The crawl's one moment of feedback, and the reason the toast belongs at the
end rather than during: the run takes tens of seconds (so a toast could not
outlive it) and commits only when something materially changed (so a
productive refresh and a no-op refresh used to end identically, with the
spinner stopping and nothing saying which happened). Per-repo failures are
surfaced here too; they were previously a console.warn and nothing else.
It took a `label` while the refresh ran in two passes, to tell their two
toasts apart; one pass reports once.

── Activity aggregate: crawl each ESTATE repo (estate:true, read from the
config cache) and fold a per-repo activity snapshot into a second derived
cache (state/activity.json) in the registry. This is the sibling of the
config crawl above, but heavier: besides cheap summary signals (pushed-at,
recent commits, open PRs, counts) it runs the capped landed/stranded branch
scan (lib/kits/branch-status.js) once and stores it, so the branches view and
the cross-repo Activity view render from the cache instead of a per-visit
fanout. The material-change gate keeps commits sparse; the watermark gate
below keeps the calls sparse.

30 MINUTES, down from 12 hours. The old number was set when every pass paid
for the whole estate whether or not anything had moved, and half a day was
the honest price of that. The watermark gate changed the thing the throttle
is rationing: a pass over a quiet estate is now about a dozen cheap reads
(one account listing, one PR watermark per repo) and no per-repo work at
all, so spacing it out by half a day buys nothing and costs a reader
looking at branch rows from this morning.

What a busy pass costs has NOT changed, and that is the number to watch: a
repo that moved still pays its summary, and one that was pushed still pays
its branch scan. The throttle is short because the FLOOR fell, not because
the ceiling did.
── The budget and the horizon, which used to be one number ──────────────

CAP is the BUDGET: how many older branches this pass may derive LIVE. That
is the request cost, and 30 is unchanged, so a crawl costs exactly what it
did before this split.

KEEP is the HORIZON: how many older branches keep a ROW. A carried row
costs storage and no request, so this buys coverage rather than calls.
Until 2026-09-09 the two were the same setting and the horizon was the
accident: web-tools stored 30 rows against 401 older branches and home 30
against 425, so the estate's stranded reading described its freshest fifth
while reading as though it described everything, and a branch that fell out
of the top 30 lost a verdict an earlier crawl had already paid for.

500 is the branch walk's own max, so this horizon is the whole list the
crawl can see. What it costs is the cache: state/activity.json was 508 KB
with 445 scan rows, and full coverage projects to about 1 MB, which every
app load fetches. Turn it down if that reads badly on a phone; the budget
above is what protects the API bill either way.
older branches SCANNED per repo per pass
older branches that KEEP a row
Errored scan rows retried per repo per crawl. A branch whose scan
failed usually fails again for the same reason (a rewritten history, a ref
the token cannot reach), so retrying every one on every crawl is how a
single repo came to spend 93 calls of a 183-call run with 56 of them
failing (2026-08-17, wa-bills). Three a run heals a transient failure
within a few crawls and caps what a permanent one can cost.

Newest commits fetched per repo per crawl, and STORED. Raised from 12 on
2026-08-19, when the behind arrow became a card: the crawl has always
fetched these for its own moved-or-not gate and read only [0].sha, so the
list was already paid for and already in the cache. 40 covers the estate's
usual spread (branches sit 20 to 40 behind) at one page of the same call
and about 5 KB per repo; past it the card says the count is right and the
list is not here, rather than showing a short list under a long number.

How deep the any-state PR read goes per repo (gh.branchPulls). 100 is the
API's page maximum, and it has to clear the branch scan's recent window
(BranchStatus.RECENT_DAYS, 14 days) or a fresh branch's merged PR would sit
past the reach and read as unknown. The busiest repo in the estate opens
roughly five PRs a day, so 100 covers about three weeks there and the whole
history everywhere else; anything past it is reported as unknown rather
than as "no PR", which is what `prReach` below is for.

repos crawled at once (each runs its own scan pool)
PR watermarks read at once (one cheap call each)

── The per-repo watermark store ───────────────────────────────────────
What each repo looked like the last time a crawl successfully read it:
its pushed_at, and its PR watermark (gh.prWatermark). The next crawl
compares against these to decide which repos it can skip entirely.

IN LOCALSTORAGE, NOT IN THE CACHE, and the reason is that the committed
file has no safe place to put them. Ride the material hash and a comment on
any pull request restamps and recommits a 700 KB cache for a field nothing
renders. Stay out of the hash and a crawl that learns a new watermark never
persists it, so the next pass sees the same movement, crawls again, and
never converges. Neither is a trade worth making for a number only this
browser's next crawl consults, and the throttle stamp beside it is already
per browser for exactly the same reason.

The cost of it being per browser is one full crawl on a new browser, which
is the correct behaviour anyway: a browser that has never looked has
nothing to carry forward.

One store shape, three crawls. Each keeps its own key; the reading and the
writing are the same two lines, so they are written once here.

Returns a summary of the run for the caller to report: {total, changed,
failed, committed}, or {skipped, reason} when there was nothing to do. The
background (unforced) caller ignores it; refreshActivity turns it into the
closing toast.
deep=false is the arrival path: current commits, PRs, branch dates and
sessions, no content scan. Complete for the recent window by
construction, since anything inside it is classified on date alone and
is never scanned even on a deep pass.

Single-flight: the tab-arrival kick and the Refresh button could run two
crawls at once, and the loser of that race saved a cache built on a
pre-commit read. A call that finds a crawl in flight joins it and gets
that crawl's result.

The floor, not a schedule: this crawl's real gate is the per-repo quiet
check inside it, which already reduces an unmoved estate to one listing
plus one watermark per repo. Holding it behind half an hour on top of
that only meant a repo pushed a minute ago waited out a clock that knew
nothing about it.

for the run record, appended below if this commits
Estate membership from the config cache (estate:true). The activity crawl
is estate-scoped, not account-wide: only repos on the dashboard need the
scan. No cache yet means nothing to crawl (the config crawl seeds it).

Hidden repos drop out here too, which is the point of the crawl being
estate-scoped: a repo nobody is looking at should not be paying for a
per-branch scan, and its rows would only render in views that already
exclude it.

Each member's own .web-tools.json rides along from the same read, so a
repo's declared checks cost the crawl nothing extra to discover.
One account-repos read for pushed-at / default-branch, matched by name.

The prior cache, read up front for the scan gate below, through the same
reconcile the fold uses: this crawl runs twice in a row (quick, then
scan), which is precisely the window in which a read can be answered
with the copy the pass before it replaced.

The scan gate: a repo not pushed since its last scan cannot have
changed any branch verdict (landed/stranded read git state alone, and a
branch delete counts as a push), so its stored rows carry forward
through mergeRepo and the tree reads go where something actually moved.
This is what makes the deep pass affordable enough to run routinely:
measured 2026-08-08, the estate held 167 scanned branches at two API
calls each, nearly all of them re-verifying repos that had not moved.
The margin absorbs clock skew between GitHub's pushed-at and the client
clock that stamped scannedAt; anything unmeasurable scans.
── The cheap half of the crawl, and now the first thing it does ─────
One PR watermark per repo, read before anything expensive. Together with
the pushed_at already in `metaByName` (one account listing, above) this
is the whole "did anything move" question, answered for the estate in
about a dozen calls against the 231 a full pass logged on 2026-08-21.

A read that fails records null rather than '', and null never gates: a
repo whose watermark could not be read is crawled, because skipping work
on a guess is worse than the calls it saves.

A repo is QUIET when nothing this cache stores can have moved: no push
since the last successful crawl, and no pull request touched since it
either. BOTH halves are required, and the second is the one that is easy
to leave out: openPRs, branchPRs and prReach all change with no push at
all, so a gate on pushed_at alone would freeze every branch row's PR
verdict until something happened to push. That is the bug this gate is
most likely to be reintroduced without.

Four ways to be wrong, each closed explicitly:
  * a FORCED pass is never quiet, because the Refresh button has to mean
    "go and look" or it means nothing
  * a repo with no stored entry is never quiet, whatever the marks say,
    since there is nothing to carry forward
  * a repo with no recorded watermark is never quiet (a new repo, a new
    browser, or a repo whose last crawl failed)
  * an unreadable watermark or a missing pushed_at is never quiet

The scan gate itself lives in the crawl kit (window.ActivityCrawl.needsScan),
so the headless runner gates on the same rule rather than on a copy of it.
This closure is the lookup: which entry, and which live pushed_at.

Bounded outer concurrency: each repo runs its own inner scan pool, so
a small repo pool keeps total in-flight GitHub calls reasonable. The
two progress ticks bracket exactly one repo's work, which is what makes
done/total a count of finished repos rather than an estimate.

Watermarks are recorded ONLY for a repo this pass actually read, and
only after it came back. Stamping one for a repo whose crawl threw
would make the failure permanent: the next pass would read the mark,
call the repo quiet, and carry forward the entry the failed pass never
refreshed. A skipped repo keeps the mark it already had, which is by
definition still current, since that is why it was skipped.

A deep pass that came back partial could not read the repo's
branches. It keeps what is stored (see the guard in
crawlRepoActivity) and says so, rather than reporting a clean run
over a repo it never saw.

Re-read the cache just before folding: the crawl can run for a while,
and folding over the copy read before it would silently revert whatever
another writer committed in between. Reconciled, so the one writer it
cannot be made to revert is this page itself.

`members` is the scope, so a repo whose crawl threw (it is in `failed`,
not in `fetched`) keeps its previous entry instead of being deleted by
a pass that never reached it.
`members` is the carry scope, so a repo this pass SKIPPED keeps its
stored entry untouched, with its own hash and its own crawl stamps.
That is the same path a failed repo takes, and it is why the skip is
safe: buildCache already had to answer "what about a repo I did not
fetch", and the answer was never "drop it".

Pruned to the current membership by construction: nextMarks is built
from `members` alone, so a repo that left the estate stops carrying a
mark nothing will ask about again.

was wrong on screen: a session ending is ONE event that moves both
readings, since its record lands in the registry and its commits land on a
branch, so wanting one without the other is the rare case rather than the

that reason; only the deliberate press merges.

guard inside each crawl already exists to avoid. Sessions first costs about

Each half keeps its own busy flag and its own progress slot, so both rows
still draw their own bar and their own wire line. What merges is the

One line for two crawls. The units genuinely differ and both are worth
saying (repos changed, records read), so the report names each half rather
than inventing a shared unit that would describe neither. A half that

is the one thing a merged report can get wrong that two reports could not.

A skip is not a no-op and must not be reported as one: "nothing changed"
over a crawl that never ran is the one reading this view exists to stop.

A pass that skipped every repo is not the same event as one that
crawled them all and found nothing, and reporting both as "checked"
hid the whole point of the gate: the first cost a dozen calls, the
second cost a couple of hundred. The word says which happened.

── The progress channel's two writers ─────────────────────────────────
openCrawl opens a slot (a Refresh button pressed), tickCrawl fills it.
Both reassign rather than mutate, so the whole shape lands on every reader
in one reactive step.

A tick into a CLOSED slot is a no-op, and that is the mechanism that keeps
the throttled background passes silent: they run the same crawl code and
hit the same ticks, but nobody opened a slot for them, so no bar appears
over a list the reader did not ask to have refreshed.
`calls0` and `t0` are the traffic ledger's call count and the clock at the
moment the RUN opened, so a reader can be told what this crawl has spent
rather than what the page has spent since it loaded, and so the call log
written at the end knows where the run began. The ledger (gh-boot's fetch
wrapper) counts every request the page makes, and the crawl is not the only
thing making them, so a bare total would answer a question nobody asked.

The activity refresh ran in two passes until 2026-08-17, so a slot carried
`pass`/`passes` and the bar spanned both rather than filling and starting
over. One pass now (the second was re-fetching the first's cheap reads), so
the slot is a plain run again: a bar that spans one pass IS the run.

Closing writes the run's call log, then clears the slot. Unawaited on
purpose: the log is a reading about a run that is already over, and nothing
the reader is waiting for may sit behind it.

── Folding onto the newest copy, not merely the fetched one ────────────
Every crawl here reads a registry file, folds into it, and writes it back.
GitHub's contents API is read-after-write eventual, so seconds after a
commit a read can still be answered with the version it replaced, sha and
all: the split refresh's scan pass hit exactly that and 409'd four times
(2026-08-16). `GH.FRESH` removed the browser's 60-second cache from the
picture; this removes the API's own lag, by preferring the copy this page
committed when the read comes back older than it. lib/kits/last-write.js
carries the argument.

Save a fold, then remember what was written. The sha rides in rather than
being re-read, which is the whole point: it is the one fact a lagging read
cannot supply.

── The call log: the last run of each crawl, as the calls it made ──────

The bar says how far along and the wire says what is in flight, and both
are gone the moment the run ends. This is the same traffic kept: every
GitHub call the run made, committed beside the caches, so the run can be
read after the fact by whoever opens the page and by anyone reading the
repo. It is the first thing here that makes the crawl's COST inspectable
rather than merely visible, which is what turns "it took 38 seconds" into
"167 of these 214 calls were one tree read per branch".

ONLY THE LAST RUN, per crawl, overwritten. A ring of runs would be hundreds
of rows times twenty, for a reading whose value is almost entirely in the
most recent one; the `runs` ring beside it already carries the shape of the
history (when, how long, how much changed) at four numbers a run.

THE PRICE, stated because it is real: this is a commit per run, including a
run that changed nothing, which is exactly what the caches' material-change
gate exists to avoid for THEM. It is a separate file for that reason: the
gate still holds where it matters, and a log whose whole subject is the run
has nothing to compare against. A run's rows are capped at what the ledger
holds (gh-boot trims at 400), and a run that outran it says so rather than
reporting a short list as complete.

The quota AT THIS CALL, kept only where it can explain something: a
failure. A run that comes back full of 404s reads as a broken crawl
until this says whether the answer was "gone" or "not allowed right
now" (2026-08-17, 86 of 183 calls 404 across every repo, with no way
to tell the two apart afterwards).

`calls` is the run's own count off the ledger's totals, which survive
trimming; `rows` is what could still be shown. They differ exactly when
the run outran the ledger, and saying both is what keeps a truncated
list from reading as a complete one.
Truncated means THIS RUN lost rows, which is `rows` short of `calls`.
It first read `trimmed > 0`, and that fired whenever the ledger dropped
anything since the run began, including the page's own boot traffic

first real run (2026-08-17, 373 of 373 rows, flagged).

The run's own header line for failures: how many, and the lowest quota

── Leaving a frame, which this app cannot do by writing window.top ───────

Inside a #gh= toss this app runs in an iframe whose sandbox grants
allow-scripts, allow-same-origin, allow-popups, allow-forms, allow-modals
and allow-downloads, and deliberately NOT allow-top-navigation. So
`window.top.location.href = url` is refused by the browser, and the
fallback beside it navigates THIS FRAME instead: the app reloads at main
inside the preview, the address bar never moves, and the reader is still
where they started. Reported from a phone as "it reloads but it doesn't
navigate", which is that failure exactly.

allow-same-origin is the way out. The subject may CALL into the shell, and
the shell is not sandboxed, so pages/toss-render.html exposes __tossLeave
and performs the navigation in its own document. window.top is still tried
after it, for a framer that is not our renderer and may permit the write.

Returns whether the trip was handed off, so the caller knows not to

was reported as one within a day.

This only fires from a framer that offers no __tossLeave and forbids the

frame. Navigating THIS frame stays out of the question, since that is the

new, since there is no hover to read and a tap already opens it. Guarded on

reports hover support (some hybrids) would otherwise open menus on a stray
finger. Memoized: the match cannot change mid-session in any way that
matters, and this is read from a getter on every menu measure.

long enough that crossing a row does not open it
long enough to cross the 2 px gap into the panel
The trigger's element is captured NOW, not read off the event later: by the
time the timer fires the event is spent and currentTarget is null.

The delay applies to a SWAP as well as to a first open, which is not an
aesthetic choice: the two triggers sit side by side and the panel opens
past both, so the pointer's route from one button to that panel crosses its
neighbour. Swapping on contact meant the github menu could not be reached
from the github button without the marker's menu replacing it on the way.
A crossing takes tens of milliseconds and a decision takes longer, so the
same ~140 ms that keeps a menu from opening as the pointer crosses a row
keeps it from swapping as the pointer crosses a button.

Leaving the trigger, or the panel, starts a short countdown rather than
closing: the pointer has to cross the gap between the two, and entering
either one cancels it.

Dispatch reads the ROW, not the key, since the combined list mixes three
kinds: a contributed row brings its own handler, a GitHub row carries a
url and leaves the app, and the rest fall through to the shell's own
navigation below.
What is left acts INSIDE a repo, so make it the open one first.

Any repo@ref on GitHub. The app is a wrapper over GitHub, not a wall, so
every view keeps a one-tap route to the GitHub presentation of what it is
showing; the sidebar's is the github button beside each Repos row, whose
first row this is. It takes a repo rather than reading the open one, since
the menu speaks for whichever repo summoned it, and the ref rides along
only for the OPEN repo (a ref is meaningless for one you are not browsing).

Pinned to the default branch, like the custom landing: the Files-view ref
picker does not re-point rendered surfaces.

── The view table ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

One statement of what a view is called in the URL, how a link opens it, and
what it stamps back. Read three ways: routeFromUrl() dispatches through it
at boot and again on popstate, and deepLinkParams() stamps through it.

It was three hand-copied else-if chains until 2026-08-11, and by then all
three ways of drifting had happened at once: ?view=pages stamped and
restorable but missing from the boot chain, ?view=proposals dispatched by
both chains and stamped by neither, ?view=estate stamped only beside a
repo/ref param on a premise that had expired. Each was a view the app could
reach and could not name. A row here cannot be half-addressable, which is
the promise three parallel chains could not make.

  key    the this.view value and the ?view= value
  open   what a link to it does. `u` is the parsed URL
  when   the address carries what open() needs; a miss falls through to the landing
  ready  the shell holds what stamp() needs; a miss stamps nothing
  stamp  the view's OWN keys. The caller has already set ?view=
  self   this view names itself another way, so the caller sets no ?view=.
         A function where the answer depends on WHICH spelling the view is
         about to stamp: `app` names itself only in its short form.

The landing names itself by naming its repo, not with a ?view=: a repo's
front page IS ?repo=owner/name, and stamping a view key beside it would
put a redundant param on the most-linked shape in the app. The one catch
is the DEFAULT repo, whose `repo` key is dropped above as redundant: that
left the hub's own landing with an empty query and no address at all, so
this row puts it back for this view only. Nothing else changes shape.

A project is repo-scoped, so its link carries the workspace beside the
?repo= already stamped; a non-default pill rides as &tab= so "open
budget-wa's docs" is one link.

The Stage's one tab value is not a tab: `&tab=errands` opens the errand
panel, which the courier navigates to from our own origin when it has
nothing to run on the page you are reading. Same key as Project and Map
use for a sub-address, so it parses, clears and restamps with them.

`next` is where This browser sends the reader back to, so a reload of
the view keeps its way out.

The open list rides as &tab=, To-do staying out of the URL as Map's
home tab does.

The branch open in the takeover, when one is. Being inside the swiper
is a state worth linking to and was the one state here without an
address: the list had ?view=branches, the branch had its standalone
page, and the reader in between could only be reached by tapping.

The window is a reading parameter, so it travels with the link:
without it a shared ?view=branches silently lands the reader on a
different slice than the one that was being discussed.

The session open in its swiper, the exact counterpart of `detail` on
the row above. Sessions were the one thing in the Activity group with
no address of their own: the branch rows beside them got a standalone
page and a copied link months ago, and tapping a session opened a
takeover that could not be pointed at. The id alone is enough,
because it is the record's filename stem and resolves against the
store by suffix.

The LIST, which is the pane's scope rather than one open record, so it
outlives the deck: closing a swiper drops `session=` and leaves the
reader on the list they arrived with, not on whatever the default
scope holds. estate.js's sessionListIds owns the grammar (short ids,
comma-separated, order kept).

The TOPIC, a filter on the follow-up's topics (estate.js,
sessionTopic), stamped for the reason the list is: a list narrowed to
one topic is the thing a link to it is for.

The default of each is silent, so the shortest address that means
"the Sessions pane as it opens" is still ?view=sessions alone.

Tending: the findings tending passes left, reached from the finding
lines in Activity rather than the header. `tab` is the list (Open is the
default and stays out of the URL) and `item` the finding a link was
minted for, the same two keys the project row uses for its own.

A restore onto Context re-reads its sub-address; onto any other tab
the held one stays, as the component's own state does.

Same `tab` key the project view stamps, and the same rule: the
default stays out of the URL so a plain ?view=map link keeps working.

A subview's keys ride with that subview alone: Context's four, Set's
one. Written straight onto the address by map.js and cleared by
nothing, Context's used to follow a picked question onto every later
tab and view.

The repo's Files view: its tree beside the file it opens
(alpineComponents/file-browser.js). It was folded into Search until
2026-09-24, when browsing and searching became separate surfaces again;
an old ?view=files&path=docs link lands here on that folder. An open
file rides as `file`, which routeFromUrl hands to openFile.

The Search view's address carries the ran search (sq + friends, stamped
from searchSeed, which the view updates on each run) AND the file open in
it (sfile, an owner/repo[@ref]:path address), so the screen can be shared
as what is on it rather than as the query behind it. A bare ?view=search
opens it empty. There is no `if (!sd.q) return` guard any more: since the
view browses on a repo or a folder alone, a screen with no query at all
is a screen worth addressing.

App views are estate-level, so the link stands alone (like the Stage):
the promoted page's repo and path ride it, independent of the open repo.
Three spellings, one destination. `?app=` is the short form and takes
either a slug a repo declared or the estate's `owner/repo[@ref]:path`
address; the five-key form is what this route was born with and still
resolves, so no minted link ever stops working.

A SLUG THE CACHE CANNOT ANSWER IS USUALLY A CACHE ONE MANIFEST BEHIND,
not a dead link. Slugs resolve out of the registry's config cache, so
the first load after a repo edits its .web-tools.json asks a cache
that predates the edit, misses, and lands on the estate. The refresh
that would have answered it commits moments later, too late for the
routing decision it just lost, and goDashboard's stamp has by then
rewritten `?app=<slug>` to `?view=estate`, so reloading retries the
wrong address and the reader cannot get back without the original
link. Hit three times between 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-08, twice on one
link, each time reported as "it didn't work".

So a missed slug buys one forced refresh and one retry. Bounded: the
guard fires at most once per load, and only a genuinely dead slug
pays for it.

Captured HERE, not read at render time, and the ordering is the whole
reason: goAppView stamps, the stamp deletes `on` (it is in VIEW_KEYS),
and a render-time read would then find the fallback already gone. So
the ?on= form worked in theory and delivered nothing, which a source
assertion could not have seen. Measured in a browser, 2026-08-25.

A slug naming nothing lands on the estate, the page's front door,
rather than on an app view with no page in it. Silent, because a
stale bookmark is not an error worth a dialog, and the estate shows
what the reader can reach instead.

Self-naming in the SHORT form only. `?app=<slug>` is a whole address,
since parseUrl reads the presence of `app` as view=app, so a `view=app`
beside it is a key that says nothing and the reader has to look past.
The five-key fallback writes no `app` at all, so there it is the only
thing naming the route and dropping it would make the address inert.
Hence a function: one row, two spellings, and only one of them answers
yes.

The short form is what gets WRITTEN, whenever the open view has a
slug to write. The alternative was to read it and stamp the long one
back, which turns every short link into a long one the moment the
reader touches anything, and an address nobody can keep is not worth
having minted. Precedented: ?view=branches rewrites to ?view=sessions.

The slug also makes appLabel/appIcon unnecessary. They exist so a
cold deep link is self-describing before the config cache resolves,
and a slug cannot resolve without that cache at all, so by the time
this view is on screen its label and icon are already known.

Carry the label/icon so a deep link is self-describing: the sidebar
entry reads "News" with its icon even before the config cache
(main-only discovery) has the entry.

Every key any row can stamp. Deleted unconditionally before a stamp, so the
result never depends on what the base happened to hold.
`file` and `path` are the retired Files view's keys, kept in the delete
list so a stale one is cleared rather than carried into a screen that does
not mean it; nothing stamps them now. `ref` is deleted here and re-stamped
above, being repo-scoped rather than any view's.
`on` is here to be DELETED and never written: it is the query fallback for
the subject's own params (appViewUrl), and the fragment is where they
belong, so an address arriving with ?on= leaves with '#'. That is the
self-heal, and it is why the key is in this list rather than a stamp.

THE SESSIONS ROW'S FOUR ARRIVED LATE AND WERE MISSING FOR A WEEK.
`session` and `list` (`set` until 2026-10-11) name the record and the scope; `lens` and `grain` are
how it is read. All four are stamped (PR #636 and #641, 2026-09-08 and
09-09) and none was listed here, so they were written and never cleared:
leaving Sessions with a record open put `&session=…&set=…&lens=…&grain=…`
on the Map, on the Atlas, and on every address copied afterwards. The
second harm is worse than the untidiness, because these four are seeded
from `location.search` at construction: a cold load of one of those
polluted addresses arms the Sessions pane with a record and a lens the
reader never asked for, which appears the next time they open it.

The rule this list states is not "list what looks stale". It is that a key
ANY row can stamp must be here, or the address carries it out of the only
screen that means it. node/test/app-routes.test.mjs now holds the two to
each other, so a stamp added without its key fails rather than drifts.

The one dispatch, shared by the boot and the popstate restore. Reports
whether the address named a view it could open, so each caller decides what
a miss means: at boot a #stage= fragment may still claim the screen, while
on a restore there is nothing left to try and the landing is the answer.

`app` joins the gate because it is a route key that names no repo and no
view: `?app=budget-drs` is a complete address and would otherwise parse
to null and land on the estate.

A row to land on in the file: ?col=<header>&row=<value>. Every
row stays; the table scrolls to the one whose cell matches.

`?app=` names its own route, so it implies view=app: the dispatch
in routeFromUrl keys on url.view, and a short address that named
no view would find no row to open and fall through to the estate.

The shell's state as URL parameters, built onto whatever base is handed in.
Split out of syncUrl() because two callers want the same answer for
different reasons: syncUrl merges it into the live address (so the base is
location.search, and foreign params like ?use= survive), while the header's
ref switch wants the app keys ALONE, to carry the current screen across a
ref change (there the base is empty, and ?use= must NOT survive, since the
switch is setting it). Every app key is set or deleted unconditionally, so
the result never depends on what the base happened to hold.

Set or deleted unconditionally, like `repo` and for the same reason, and
OUTSIDE the view table: the shell mode is a reading parameter, so it
survives a view change and travels with the address the header's ref
switch mints (which starts from an empty base, where ?use= must not
survive but this must, or a ref switch would silently reframe the page).

The browsed ref rides beside the repo, not on a view. It was the Files
view's key while the Files view was the only thing that read it; the
atlas, the config form, the gallery and mention all read it now, so it
is repo-scoped state and belongs where `repo` is.

One lookup where three parallel else-if chains used to be. A row that is
not `ready` stamps nothing rather than a half address naming a view the
shell cannot yet describe.

The estate's branch takeover reports what it has open, so the address can
follow a swipe. Empty when it closes, which is what makes Back leave the
takeover rather than the view.

SEEDED FROM THE URL, and that is load-bearing rather than tidy.
deepLinkParams rebuilds the query from a whitelist, so it deletes `detail`
and re-stamps it from this field. Left empty at boot, the first syncUrl
therefore erased an incoming `&detail=` before the estate ever read it, and
the link opened the plain Activity list with nothing to say why.

The same pair for the Sessions pane's own swiper. Two keys rather than one
shared one, because the two decks hold different objects and a link that
said `detail=` for either would have to be disambiguated by the ?view= it
rides with, which is a rule nobody reading the address could apply.
The Sessions pane's lens and, inside the table lens, its grain. Held here
for the reason mapTab is: the URL is the shell's to own, and a view whose
state it does not carry cannot be linked. That was not academic. The render
link handed over for this pane opened it on the List lens twice while the
thing under review was the table, so the reply had to end "now tap Table".

Defaults stay OUT of the address (see the stamp below), so a plain
?view=sessions link keeps meaning what it has always meant.

The session deck owns its history entry. Its active record and query
replace that entry, so Back leaves the reader in one step.

── The visit log ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Where the reader has been, as a short list the sidebar mark's menu reads.
Browser Back already walks the navigation, so this is not a second copy of
the history stack: it is coarser (one row per DESTINATION, deduped and
moved to the top on a revisit) and it reaches places Back cannot, since
pages/toss-render.html only ever calls replaceState and therefore leaves no
browser history at all.

WHAT IS STORED IS DECIDED BY kits/visit-log.js, NOT HERE, and that split is
the whole safety argument. An address in this estate is not always a
location: #gz= carries a document and a stage link folds local text in
beside its refs, so storing addresses verbatim would put pasted data in the
log and a workbench used on local material would leak it on the next
navigation. The kit matches against a closed allowlist and rebuilds the row
from the matched route's template, so nothing that arrived is written.
Read its head comment before changing anything below.

localStorage, capped, per browser. It has to be SYNCHRONOUS, because the
menu paints on the tap that opens it and a list that arrives a frame later
is worse than a short list that is right immediately. The full log, with
the tosses and the payload refusals kept for a Visited view, wants
IndexedDB through kits/persistence.js; that half is not built.

THE ALLOWLIST, held in code because the recorder runs on a navigation and
cannot wait on a fetch. Same trade the fab makes with _TOSS_MODES, and the
same guard: docs/routes-modes.csv and docs/routes-routes.csv own these
tables, node/test/visit-log-wiring.test.mjs fails if either drifts. App
routes need no list at all, since VIEWS IS the router and the kit takes the
keys straight off it, which is one fewer thing that can disagree.

Called from syncUrl's PUSH branch only, so the log inherits the browser's
own notion of a navigation rather than inventing a second one. A replace is
a no-op change or a popstate restore, and neither is a new destination.

A payload visit is COUNTED AND NOT LINKED. Dropping it would leave a gap
that reads as a bug; keeping the address would be the one thing this
whole design exists to prevent. The row carries its size and nothing else.

── What a row SAYS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

ONE LINE, like every other row in this sidebar and like the launcher menu,
which put the rule plainly when it dropped a two-line hint: a menu is read
in the moment before the finger lifts and has no room for a second line.
The first draft stacked a label over a muted detail at text-sm, which broke
that and rule 7 with it, demoting the half of the row that tells two
Sessions visits apart. Size carries nothing here; opacity does, the way
the Recent block above already works.

So the split is LABEL = the specific thing, DETAIL = the short context it
sits in, and the detail is short BY CONSTRUCTION rather than truncated into
shape. "CLAUDE.md · Files" reads; "Files · mehrlander/home:CLAUDE.md"
buries the filename behind a category and then clips it.

Route names join docs/app-routes.csv rather than being stored at write
time, since that registry owns them and a stored copy would be the
duplicate the registries rule warns about.

The PAGE leads here too, by the same rule: which page failed to match is
the specific thing, and "unrecognized" is the context. Labelling it the
other way round clipped a long word against a filename and told the
reader the one thing the dimming and the glyph already said.

The most specific thing the row names, falling back to the route itself
when the route IS the destination (Repos, Tools, the Map).

The right-hand half: short, muted, and never the address. It answers "which
one of these" rather than repeating what the label already said.
A payload row and an unrecognized row have nowhere to go, by construction.

The fragment is carried through untouched unless a caller has just asked
for a different one (goAppView, whose view owns its fragment). One shot:
cleared on read, so every other caller keeps the carry-through that has
always been the rule here.

Push a new history entry per distinct URL so the browser Back button walks
the navigation (repo, view, file, folder). A no-op change, or a change made
while restoring from a popstate, replaces in place instead, so Back never
needs a double press and popstate restoration doesn't re-push.

The tab names what the address names: the product, plus the open repo
exactly when deepLinkParams stamps `repo` (off the default only), owner
dropped the way the sidebar crumb drops it. Stamped here rather than in
a watcher so the title and the address cannot disagree.

AN APP VIEW NAMES ITSELF FIRST, which is the one place the order flips.
Everywhere else the product leads, because the repo is context on a Web
Tools screen. A promoted page is not a Web Tools screen: `?app=` is a
whole address and the three surfaces that read this title (the tab strip,
a bookmark, a home-screen tile) all truncate from the RIGHT, so leading
with the product spends the visible characters saying which shell rather
than which app. It takes the disambiguated `label` rather than
`baseLabel`, so two repos promoting one page are still told apart here.

Every route change passes through here, so this is the one place that
reliably sees an app view being LEFT. A watcher on `view` would miss the
boot case, where the shell arrives on a route without ever changing it.

PUSH, THEN RECORD ONLY IF THE PUSH TOOK, which is not defensive coding but
a measured fix. Inside a #gh= toss the renderer wraps pushState to swallow
a SecurityError (a relative push resolves against the stamped <base>, which
matches neither the frame's blob: document nor this origin), so the call is
a silent no-op. `cur` then never moves, `next !== cur` stays true forever,
and a recorder hanging off the branch alone logs a visit on EVERY syncUrl
of a previewed app. A blob inherits its creator's origin, so those rows land
in the same localStorage the real app reads: previewing the app on a branch
would quietly fill the reader's own log.

Measured, not reasoned about: a headless toss of app/index.html had two
visits recorded before anything was clicked. Reading the address back makes
the log depend on what actually happened rather than on which branch of an
if was taken, which is the same move recordVisit already makes by hanging
off syncUrl's own push/replace decision instead of inventing a second one.

Its own method because the mark arrives LATE, after the address is
already stamped, and re-running syncUrl for it would push a history entry
for a tab caption.

What an app view is called in a tab. THE DECLARED LABEL WINS wherever
there is one, because that is the name the sidebar and the header nav
render, and a tab disagreeing with them is worse than a plain tab.

The exception is the one case that has no declared label: a cold deep link
by address, before (or without) the crawl that carries the manifest, falls
back to the filename and reads `app.html`, which names nothing. The framed
page's own <title> answers exactly that case, and nothing else: it would
otherwise overrule a name its own repo chose for it.

Browser Back/Forward: re-derive the shell state from the URL through the
same routeFromUrl() the boot uses, so the two cannot disagree about what an
address means. `_restoring` makes syncUrl replace-in-place during the
restore, so the watchers this fires don't push new entries.

Back out of a mode change the way you back out of a view change: the
address is the whole state, so a restore re-reads this too.

A miss here is a real address the table cannot open, so land somewhere
honest rather than leaving the previous screen up under a new URL.

Point the file browser at a repo. web-tools boots identity-free via
pickByName; setup() fills the repo dropdown in the background (quiet: a
missing/expired token won't hijack the page).

Open a file of the OPEN repo, from wherever names one: a pin, a recent, a
?file= deep link, the repo menu. Every one of these used to drive the
explorer's own listing and viewer; they route to the central Files view
now, scoped to the file's folder so the walk around it is right there and
the file itself is the thing on screen.

The ref rides only when it is off the default, which is that view's rule
for '' and not a shortcut taken here.
A file or a folder opens in the repo's Files view, at the ref being
browsed: the tree opens on the folder and the file beside it. Search is
for finding; these callers already know where the thing is.

The Files view's state is its address: the folder the tree opens on and
the file beside it. filesKey remounts the component when either changes,
since the component does not follow a scope change on its own.
filesAt names the row of filesFile's table to land on, { col, row }; it
belongs to that one file, so any other open clears it.

The estate is a context above any repo, with views of its own: the repo
grid ('estate') and the Stage ('stage', the cross-repo working set,
belonging to no repo), mirroring how a repo has landing/atlas/files/…
isEstate gates the estate component (it renders the grid and the Stage,
switching on this.view, sharing the one lazy mount); estateCtx is the
wider context test the sidebar switches on.

The Lists view is the one estate pane that FILLS rather than flows: the
open list scrolls inside itself, so the page must not scroll and the chain
from the pane down to the component root has to carry a definite height.
Every other view keeps the ordinary overflow-y-auto column. Held here
rather than inside the component because the two ancestors that need the
classes are the shell's markup, not the component's.

App views are estate-level (peers of Repos/Stage), so they share
the estate sidebar context: the per-repo view list stays hidden and the
header reads "Repositories".

Whether the pinned desktop sidebar has anything to show: always in a repo
(its views / pins / recents), and in the estate whenever it has repo-sourced
content — the Repos index or the app views (News). Both are token-gated, so
a signed-out estate has neither and the dashboard takes the full width. It
is about CONTENT, not about the viewer's choice: sidebarOpen carries that,
and the aside is gone from a wide screen when either says so.

The sidebar Repos index, folded into its groups (core / data / tools …) in
the sorted order estateRepos already carries, so each group's rows stay
contiguous under one label, matching the Repos grid. Ungrouped repos ride an
empty-string group that renders without a label.

The dashboard front door: Open for a signed-in viewer (the richer
all-repo read), Repos for a signed-out one (Open is token-gated, so it
would land on an empty state). Brand tap and a bare open route here.
SESSIONS, not Branches, for a signed-in viewer. Both are Activity panes and
the group opened on Branches because Branches was the pane that existed
first. The front door should answer "what have I been doing", which is the
session's question; a branch is what a session left behind, and the Sessions
pane nests the branch row itself under the session that made it.

The header's app-level nav: the estate's own views, in
display order (Activity first). Repo-sourced app views ride behind it as a
second group (appNav below), separated by a hairline, so the header carries
both classes of destination while still showing which is which. It used to
carry only this set, on the reasoning that the header is fixed and repos do
not write it; what that bought was a header with unused room beside it and a
published view reachable only after opening a drawer. Each item maps to the
same go* method and `view` string the router already uses.

Activity is one nav stop over the estate's own motion, read several ways:
Sessions, the work; Branches (internal key 'branches'), the artifacts it
left; then Guides, State, Chats and Routes. The estate component's
segmented pill switches between them and the URL stamps the specific key,
so each deep-links on its own.

To-do and Jot used to be Activity's other two pills and are now their own
stop, Lists. They were never activity: a personal checklist and an idea
pile are not the estate moving, they sat there because the pill row
existed. Splitting them also gives each of the two remaining panes the
full column, which a cross-repo branch row and a session row both want.

`views` is the set that keeps this entry lit and `view` is only its
identity, so moving the door to Sessions is the `go` and the `view`;
?view=branches resolves to Branches, and the pill row leads with
Sessions, since a chip that moves is a target a reader has to
learn twice.

Waiting: the owner's queue, user calls and proposed edits. Standing
with a token, since proposed edits are rarely none and counting them
costs the Text collection; the badge is the open user calls.
One stop, named Stage, over the two things a surface is for, switched

Named for the thing, not the verb, so it sits with Repos and Stage
rather than beside them as an activity. It browses as much as it
searches now, and it is where every repo's files are read, so "Files"
is what a reader is looking for in this row. The ?view= key stays
`search`: an address is not a label, and every ?view=search link ever
shared still opens it.

State: what the estate keeps derived, and how old each piece is. A
standing entry rather than a conditional one (Proposals is the only
conditional): the answer to "is what I am looking at current" has to be
reachable before you know you need it, which is the failure the four
scattered Refresh buttons had.
Proposals is the one conditional entry: an empty channel should cost no
attention, so it appears only while something is pending (or while the
view is open, so the nav does not vanish under the user on the apply
that empties it).

The header's second nav group: the repo-sponsored views, the same list the
sidebar shows (sidebarAppViews, so a deep-linked view whose config has not
merged yet still appears, selected). They carry their icon where the app's
own entries are label-only: the hairline says a boundary, the icon says
which side of it a button sits on, and the icon is the repo's own choice.
One entry per view rather than a menu, since the set is small and the room
is there; a header this fills would be the signal to fold it into one.

The tooltip on an app-view entry, in the header and the sidebar alike. The
declaring repo, for the same reason the suffix uses it: a cross-repo
promotion's `repo` is the page's home, and "whose view is this" is what a
tooltip on a repeated label is being asked. The ref, when the entry names
one, because the label alone cannot tell a branch's copy of a page from
the declared one.

The board behind the rail, if some repo also promotes it as an app view:
the Links section's header icon then opens the full board, the way the
Repos section's icon opens the full grid. Matched on the page rather than
on a second declaration, since a repo that publishes both means one thing.

An app-view entry is active on its own key, not on the bare view string:
every sponsored view shares view==='app'.

NO go* METHOD CLOSES THE DRAWER. Navigating used to dismiss it, on the
reasoning that the drawer covers the main area on mobile. But the sidebar
is also the thing you navigate WITH: closing it after every tap means
reopening it for the next one, and it hides the fact that the list itself
just changed (a repo's views for the estate's, say). It now closes only
when you say so, by the scrim or the X. The pinned desktop sidebar never
closed, so the two behave alike now.
Repos consults the freshness rule on arrival, the way Branches and
Sessions do. It was once the one estate pane that did not, warmed only at

over to Repos an hour later read whatever the boot had left.

Lists: every list one at a time behind a row of tabs, at ?view=lists, the

keeps the open list, a route call's URL is authoritative. The key is not
checked against the lists here, since created lists are only known once

A tab tap from inside the estate, stamped so back and forward walk the

The Map view: the coordination layer made inspectable (the Distribution

The tab or subview is addressable (?view=map&tab=docs), on the same `tab` key the

falls back rather than leaving every section hidden.

A tab tap from inside map(): stamp the URL so back and forward walk the

Context and Set report their sub-addresses here and the map row stamps

The Tools view: the curated utility-page gallery (docs/tools.csv), public.

Open the Search view, optionally seeded ({ q, mode, repo, ref, path, file, kind }).
A seed reaches a mounted view by event (the component mounts once and

The gate is "any field arrived", not "a query arrived": the view browses on

The Proposals view: pending cross-repo edits awaiting the user's confirm.

With a call id, Waiting opens on that call: a mounted view hears the

A task held by an open user call says so in its awaiting line,
