State kicks ALL THREE, which is the reverse of what it used to do, and the
reverse is the point. It kicked nothing on the argument that a view whose
subject is age must not answer its own question before you read it. That
argument held while a crawl cost a full pass over the estate; it stopped
holding when the gate moved inside the crawls, since a look that finds
nothing now costs about one call per crawl.

And the old behaviour had a worse property than the one it avoided: this
is the view someone opens BECAUSE they suspect something is behind, and it
was the one view that would show them the lag and then decline to fix it.
Reporting a fault you are able to repair, to someone who came to you about
it, is not neutrality.

Un-awaited, so the rows render on the stored ages and re-read as each crawl
lands. Each one re-stamps `checked`, so the reading the view leads with is
about this visit rather than about whenever a pane was last opened.

EACH KICK ANNOUNCES ITSELF, and leaving this out made the whole change
invisible. The crawls ran correctly and stamped their `checked` keys; the
view had read those stamps once at mount and had no reason to read them
again, so a row sat there saying "checked 1d ago" over a crawl that had
finished seconds earlier. The three `*-refreshed` events the view already
listens for are dispatched by the manual Refresh wrappers alone, so an
arrival crawl landed in silence. Caught on a phone, 2026-08-22, by the
reading being obviously wrong.

Two passes, because they cost different amounts. Each kick fires the
cheap one as it lands: the `checked` stamps are localStorage and re-read
for nothing. When all three have settled, one more pass says so, and the
view re-reads everything once, since a crawl that committed also moved
the `written` date, which is a commit read per file.

checkCache marks `crawlChecking` for the row, announces whatever it
lands, records the outcome for the pills, and fires the cheap
cache-checked pass as each settles. The State view's arrival differs
from the freshness rule in one way only: it checks all three whatever
their age, since arriving here is asking.

Announced even when the view is already mounted: arriving from a second
age pill has to move the highlight, and re-setting `view` to the value it
already holds is not something Alpine reacts to.

Open is the estate's cross-repo live-branch view; the one estate component
renders it by reading the shell view (internal key 'activity'). A visit
consults the freshness rule (as Repos does), so the cache is warm and
self-healing.
days; the pane's question is "what am I working on", which is usually today (was 7 until 2026-08-08)

The window travels in the URL as whole days ('3') or hours ('1h'), so a
sub-day window never rides as a float. Bare numbers keep old links valid.

── Freshness: the rule behind every age pill ──────────────────────────

THE RULE. While a pill on screen reads a cache, its reading is at most
CHECK_MS old, or a check of that cache is running, or the last check failed
and the pill says so. "Old" is counted from when this tab last CONFIRMED the
copy it shows against the source, not from when the file was last written:
a check that finds nothing new commits nothing, so a write time keeps aging
over a store that was looked at a minute ago, and a pill reading it would
trip the rule forever.

WHY A RULE AND NOT A LIST OF EVENTS. Until 2026-10-05 the checks ran on
events: the boot, a navigation into a pane, a return after five minutes
hidden, a bfcache restore, and the pill itself. Each was added to close the
gap the one before had left, and the list still had one. A tab that stays
open and visible fires none of them, and on 2026-10-05 a Sessions pane sat
on "as of 23h" in front of its reader while session records landed all
night. The pill held the age and nothing consulted it. Now the age is the
trigger, and the events are only the moments it is consulted: load,
arrival, return, and a timer set for the moment the oldest reading on
screen turns CHECK_MS old.

A SKIPPED CRAWL STILL HAS TO ANSWER. The crawls keep their cost guards (the
one-minute floor, the per-unit motion gates), and those compare the store
with what THIS BROWSER last folded, a record every tab of it shares. A tab
whose sibling already folded the news is skipped, and used to keep showing
its own older copy. So a pass that hands back no document confirms
instead: one listing of state/ gives main's blob sha per file, and the
estate re-reads only a file whose sha is not the one it is showing.

The caches each view's pills read. Sessions draws a branch tile under every
row, so it keeps both current; State reads all three.

When a cache is next due: CHECK_MS after its last confirmation or its last
attempt, whichever is later. Counting the attempt is what stops a check
that keeps failing from being retried in a tight loop.

Consult the rule for the view on screen: check every cache it reads that
is due, then arm the timer for the next one. Safe to call on any event,
since a reading inside the window costs nothing. A hidden tab does no work
and arms nothing; its return is a visibilitychange, which calls this.

The settled pass makes the State view re-read its commit dates (a call
per file), and that view stays mounted once seen, so it is announced
only while State is the view on screen.

One check of one cache: the unforced crawl, then whatever puts the newest
copy on screen. A crawl that ran hands its document over; one that
declined (the floor, a motion gate) or that never hands one (configs)
confirms by sha. Every outcome is recorded, and `crawlChecking` is what the
pills and the State rows read while it runs. `deep` is the activity
crawl's content scan, which the State view's arrival leaves out.
A second call while one runs joins it, as the crawls themselves do, so the
State view's arrival waits on a check the timer had already started.

Work the page starts on its own, run as a job (gh-boot.js, the job ledger)
so the Traffic pane can name it. `cause` is why it ran: boot, arrival,
return, timer or tap. A page whose boot predates the ledger runs it bare.

Each check is a job (gh-boot.js, the job ledger), named for the row State
gives the cache and stamped with why it ran, so the Traffic pane can say
which calls a check made and what started it.

Record what a check came back with, manual or background. It counts as a
confirmation only when it ran without error AND this browser's stamp is
inside the window: a crawl that declined for want of input ("no estate
members in the config cache yet") looked at nothing, and the reason it gave
is what the pill reports. A failure keeps the last good `at`, so the pill
can say how old the copy it is still showing is.

Main's blob sha for one cache file, announced for the estate to compare
with the copy it shows. One FRESH listing of the directory: the contents
API's own lag can still answer with the sha before a write this page just
made, which is why the estate reconciles a re-read against LastWrite
rather than trusting the listing alone.

── Coming back to a page that never left ─────────────────────────────
On a phone there is no navigation to count as an arrival: Safari keeps the
page and restores it, so the boot ran once, whenever the tab was opened.
The return is therefore the arrival, and since the rule reads the age, a
tab flick costs nothing: a reading inside the window is left alone. A
bfcache restore (`pageshow` with `persisted`) brings the page back with no
boot at all, so it consults the rule as well.

Activity's other pill: the sessions that made the branches. TWO CACHES,
because this pane renders two: the session records are its rows and the
branch cache is its tiles, so arriving here on a stale branch cache would
draw current sessions over old branches. VIEW_CACHES carries the pair.

Chats warms nothing, and the absence is the design. The other three panes
read a crawl cache this shell keeps fresh; the archive's month shards are
immutable once committed, so there is no staleness for a crawl to chase.
What can be stale is the archive itself, which no crawl can fix: it
advances when an export lands in chat-histories. The pane states that
instead of offering a refresh that would do nothing.
Writes: the estate's commit stream read for who wrote it. No refresh
arm, unlike goActivity: the pane renders from the activity cache the
Branches pane already keeps, and its own deeper read is a control on
the pane rather than an arrival cost.

Traffic: the calls this page has made since it loaded and the work that
made them, from the job and traffic ledgers in memory. It warms nothing and reads no
cache, so arriving costs no call.

`repo` is a filter a Repos card or a branch row hands in, deliberately not
stamped: it narrows a reading, and a shared link should open the whole set.

The repo sidebar's Files row: hand the central surface this repo at the ref
being browsed, and go. The ref rides only when it is off the default, since
'' there means "the default branch" and is what the Files view holds.

The Stage's bench sub-view: the working surface. Every caller already
routed here (the explorer's "+", a #stage= link, a saved surface's Load),
and all of them mean "show me what is staged", which is this pill.

THE TAP-DRIVEN PASTE, which is the phone's whole intake: iOS Safari raises
no paste event without a focused editable, so the window listener above is
the desktop's story alone. Reached from the launcher's long-press menu (the
`menu` contract above) and nowhere else in the chrome. Same destination as
the listener: stage it, and if we are not already there, route to the Stage
and open the one thing that arrived. The read and the fold are
StageIntake.takeClipboard's, shared with the bench's own Paste button, so
there is one implementation behind two triggers.

pasteBusy survives the button it was written for: it guarded a :disabled
binding, and it still guards a second menu tap landing on a read in
flight, which would otherwise stage the clipboard twice.

Nothing is awaited before takeClipboard: see the preload in init() for why.

The PowerShell outpost view's selected file takes a page-wide paste or drop the way
an open Files result does: the view names the file, so a work copy
dropped anywhere on the page compares against it. That view is the
Outpost tab of a workspace declaring a PowerShell outpost manifest.

Capture at the gesture, before a clipboard/file read can change the view.
The workspace owns its live selection and pinned source; powershellOutpostItem
may still name a previous file while the Code explorer shows All files.

On the Outpost tab with no file open, pasted PowerShell goes to the
matcher, which finds the file it most resembles, rather than to the Stage.

The PowerShell outpost view compares a copy in memory and shows it in
its own Changes view; nothing is saved to the browser and the Stage
does not open. Every other surface keeps the stored check below.

A check landed in this browser: the PowerShell outpost view listens, since it
shows the checks beside the durable ledger and offers to promote one.

Only a code file is a work copy. A screenshot, a JSON file or any other
arrival is Stage intake, whether or not a file is selected.

Fold in whatever the fab parked on another page, and open the Stage on it.
Quiet when nothing is parked, which is every ordinary boot; a stale or
unreadable payload is dropped by the kit rather than reported, since the
paste it describes belongs to a session nobody is in any more.

The kit is loaded here rather than in the boot chain: nothing else on this
page reads it, and a boot that fetched it every time would be paying on
every load for the rare one that has something to collect.

Reported as information, not as an error: see the note on the bench's
pasteIn(), which this is the other trigger for. Tapping Paste with an
empty clipboard is the ordinary case, and the red alert it used to
raise read as a broken button.

LEAVING THE VIEW LEAVES THE TAKEOVER OVER IT. Newly reachable, and newly a
problem, because the deck stopped covering the chrome: the sidebar and the
header are live under an open takeover now, so a tap navigates while the
deck keeps painting the view you just left. Measured before fixing: opening
the workbench on the Stage and tapping Map left the workbench on screen with
the rail and the URL both saying Map.

It hangs off syncUrl rather than a $watch on `view`, and the reason is
ordering rather than taste. Every go* method routes through here
SYNCHRONOUSLY, so at the moment a paste calls goStage() no deck exists yet
and this is a no-op; a queued watcher could just as easily have fired after
the preview opened and closed the very thing the paste was routing to.

drop() rather than close(): close() walks history back, and the navigation
that got here is already the history event.

WHETHER A TAKEOVER IS INSET BY THE SIDEBAR, stamped on the root for the
--deck-left rules in <style> to key on. kits/swipe-deck.js frames itself
from that variable and defaults to the whole viewport, so a page with no
chrome beside its content needs none of this. See the CSS for why the
breakpoint alone will not do: the desktop sidebar is conditional, and a
deck inset by a column that is not there clips the view under it.
Docked is a reader's standing preference, not a per-deck choice: someone
who wants the list beside the file wants it on the next file too. Kept off
the address, since it describes THIS SCREEN rather than what is being
looked at, and a pane width in a shared link would arrive as a claim about
the reader's window that the sender could not have known.

THE SIDEBAR IS NOT THE DOCK'S DECISION. Showing or hiding it is already a
control the reader has, so docking only ever adds a column beside
whatever the sidebar is currently doing: --deck-side measures the aside,
and the dock offsets from there. Read as one chain rather than a nested
ternary, because the nesting was the part that made it look as though
docking and the sidebar were one decision.

The remembered seam, applied only while docked. Undocked it must go, or
the property sits on the root describing a split that is not on screen.

MEASURED, not stated. The header is h-14 plus a border, but it is also
conditional (shellMode) and a second copy of its height here would be a
number to keep in step with a class nobody would think to look at. A
hidden header measures 0, which is the right answer for free. This sets
--deck-head; the CSS maps it into --deck-top only at lg and up, so a
phone keeps the full-window takeover it already had.

MEASURED for the same reason the header is, and this one replaces a
literal that was already a second copy: the CSS used to restate the
aside's lg:w-80 / xl:w-[22rem] as 20rem / 22rem, so a change to the
sidebar's width would have moved the app and left the deck behind it
with nothing to report the gap. A sidebar that is closed or below lg
carries lg:hidden and measures 0, which is the right answer for free.

The deck's dock toggle calls this. It takes an INTENT ('dock' or 'pane'),
not a value of data-deck-pane: the kit knows it wants to sit beside the
list, and which attribute value expresses that here, with this sidebar, at
this width, is the shell's to decide. Installed on window rather than
passed to open() because the deck outlives no component and every surface
that opens one would otherwise wire the same argument.

`when` qualifies the claim the hook makes, and it closes a gap this shell
had: the CSS maps --deck-left in only at lg, so below it the shell CANNOT
dock, but the hook was installed unconditionally and the kit offered the
toggle anyway. Tapping it on a phone set data-deck-pane="dock", which
changed no layout (the rules are lg-gated) and did change one thing that
is not layout: the kit leaves page scroll UNLOCKED under 'dock', so the
background scrolled behind a full-window takeover. The same breakpoint the
CSS uses, stated once here, so the toggle appears exactly where docking
means something.

HOW WIDE, which is a separate claim from whether it can dock at all. The
kit asks for it as a percentage OF THE WINDOW given to the deck, because
that is the only quantity both sides can agree on: the shell's own
formula is sidebar-relative and the kit knows nothing about a sidebar.

Read by MEASURING the deck rather than by parsing the property, since the
property is a calc with a clamp in it and its computed value is a length
the shell would then have to turn back into a percentage. The overlay is
on screen and its left edge is the answer.

Stored per reader like the dock preference itself, and kept off the
address for the reason stated there: a pane width in a shared link is a
claim about the recipient's window that the sender could not have known.

── A DROP ANYWHERE STAGES ────────────────────────────────────────────────
The Stage's own view has always taken a drop, which meant the gesture
worked only once you had gone there: a file dragged onto Repos, a file, the
Map or the Activity list had nowhere to land, and nothing on screen said
so. The APP takes it now, from any view, and routes to the Stage with the
file already on the bench, opened in the preview when it is the only one.

The split is deliberate: what a dropped thing BECOMES is stage.js's
(window.StageIntake, one answer for the bench's drop-zone, a paste, and
this), and this owns the gesture and where it goes afterwards. The bench
mounts lazily, so there is nothing to call at drop time: the intake names
the staged item on the store and the stager opens it when it mounts.

Two drops it deliberately does not take. A drag over a form field keeps its
native drop, the way the paste path leaves a field's own paste alone, since
dropping a path into the destination box is a real thing to do. And a drop
the Stage view's own root already handled is left to it: that handler
preventDefaults on the way up, so `defaultPrevented` is the tell, and the
alternative is staging the same file twice.

Without a prevented dragover there is no drop event at all: this line is
what makes the window a drop target rather than the browser navigating
to the file. The note is refreshed only when it is missing, since
dragover fires continuously and re-deriving it on every frame would be
work nobody sees.

A null relatedTarget means the pointer left the WINDOW, not a child, and
the counter must clear rather than decrement: an enter/leave pair that
does not balance (dragging out over a scrollbar, say) otherwise leaves
the cue standing over an app nobody is dragging onto.

One file opens on itself, since seeing it is the reason to drop it. A
batch lands and stays listed: a modal over a set nobody has seen listed
is the wrong first look at it.

WHAT THE CUE CAN HONESTLY SAY MID-DRAG, which is less than it looks.
A drag in flight exposes `items` (a kind and a MIME type each) and nothing
else: `getAsFile()` returns null and `getData()` returns '' until the drop,
deliberately, so the browser does not leak a filename to a page you are
merely dragging over. "Drop release-notes.md to stage" is therefore not
writable from here at any effort. The count and the kind ARE answered
during the gesture, and so is what will happen to them, which is the part
worth saying: one file opens, several land.

── A PASTE ANYWHERE STAGES ───────────────────────────────────────────────
The same gesture as the drop above, over the same intake, and it had the
same defect for the same reason: the Stage has taken a paste since
2026-08-15, but through a window listener the STAGER registered and gated
on `view === 'stage'`, so the gesture was reachable only from the view it
was staging into, and only once the bench had mounted. A block of refs
copied while reading a repo's files, or a screenshot pasted on the Map,
had nowhere to land and nothing on screen said so.

Two things differ from the drop, both forced rather than chosen.

There is no `defaultPrevented` tell to lean on, because ordering runs the
other way. A drop on the Stage view hits that view's own ELEMENT handler
first and the window handler second, so the window can see it was taken.
Window listeners, by contrast, fire in registration order: init() runs at
boot and the stager mounts on the first visit to an estate view, so this
is always first and would read `defaultPrevented` as false every time. So
the stage's listener is gone rather than coordinated with, and this is the
only one. Being the only one is also what keeps the multi-flavor contract
whole: one reader of the clipboard, so nothing takes text/plain out from
under the bar that would have offered the HTML table beside it.

And the flavors a form field cannot hold are only worth reading when there
is somewhere to show them. On the Stage that is the offer bar, unchanged.
Anywhere else the bar is off screen, so a paste into a field is left
entirely alone: silently recording an offer nobody was told about is worse
than not reading the clipboard at all.

A FIELD KEEPS ITS PASTE. Nothing is preventDefault'ed on this path, so
the field pastes natively; what it cannot hold goes to the bar when
the bar is on screen to receive it.

AN ADDRESS IS A DESTINATION, NOT CONTENT. Tried before the intake, and
only ever declined into it: pasteRoute answers false for everything it
does not recognise, so the staging path below is unchanged for every
paste that is not one of the four shapes it names.

Reading text/plain here does not break the one-reader contract above.
That contract is about who TAKES the flavors and owns the offer bar;
getData on a DataTransfer consumes nothing, and this path ends in a
navigation with no bar to populate.

Off the Stage the paste is also a navigation, the way a drop is: it
went somewhere, and the somewhere is worth being shown. One item opens
on itself; a block of refs lands and stays listed.

── TYPING ANYWHERE FINDS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
The keyboard's version of the paste above, and it was missing for the same
reason: the app had one search box, in the sidebar, reachable by `/` and by
tapping it. On every view that carries no box of its own (Activity is the
one that showed it) a typed character went nowhere and nothing on screen
said where it should have gone.

ONE OWNER, like the paste. quick-find used to register its own `/` listener
and this rule is a superset of that one, so the component's listener is gone
rather than coordinated with; a page that mounts quickFind without this
shell wires its own. The box declares itself with an id the router names
(`quick-find-box`), and a VIEW's own box declares itself with
`data-find-box`.

THE VIEW'S BOX WINS WHERE IT IS ON SCREEN. Typing while looking at a list
and its filter means "narrow this", not "search the estate", so a visible
`data-find-box` takes the keystroke and the sidebar never opens. Visibility
is `getClientRects()`, not `offsetParent`, which is null for any fixed
element and so would have reported the phone's sidebar hidden while it was
out.

WHO CARRIES THE CHARACTER, which is the whole subtlety. Focusing an input
inside a keydown handler and NOT calling preventDefault leaves the browser
to run the default action against whatever is focused when it runs, which
is by then the box: the character lands, fast typing keeps landing, and
dead keys and IME composition are untouched. That only works on a box that
is already there. Where the sidebar has to be revealed first, Alpine's
class change lands a tick later and the default action has nowhere to go,
so that one path preventDefaults and seeds the character by hand, through
an `input` event so x-model writes it back to the component's own `q`.
── NO FOCUS ZOOM ON iOS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
iOS Safari zooms the page when a focused input's text is under 16px, and
leaves it zoomed. Sizing each box to 16px did not stop it for the
header's find pill opened through a toss (owner, 2026-10-21), and the
decisive control is the TOP document's viewport tag: maximum-scale=1
stops the focus zoom, while iOS has ignored it for pinch zoom since iOS
10 (kits/annotate.js guards its note box the same way, and restores the
tag as it found it, so the two agree). iOS only, since Android Chrome
does honor it for pinch; a cross-origin top is left alone.

CTRL OR CMD+F OPENS THE VIEW'S OWN FILTER, where the view has one:
its box if it shows one, else the header's find pill. The browser's
find reads the page as text, which on a list the view already knows
how to narrow is the weaker search. Pressed again with the filter
focused, it is left to the browser, so its find is one more press
away and never lost; on a view with no filter it is never taken.

A bare printable key, one character wide, so every named key (Tab,
Enter, Escape, the arrows, the function row) passes untouched. Space
goes with them: it scrolls, it activates a focused button, and no
query opens with one.

A deck or a modal is a screen of its own, and pulling focus to a box
behind it would type into something the reader cannot see. Those are
the app's two overlays that own the screen; the fab's drawer is
deliberately not one, since it passes pointer events through and
leaves the page beneath it live. A third that does own the screen owes
this router a tell of its own: a component whose panel sits in the DOM
at all times and slides cannot be found by its presence, so it has to
say `shown` in an attribute the way the deck says it in a stack.

WHICH BOX MAY WEAR data-find-box: a VIEW's own primary search, over the
content that view is showing. Only one view is on screen, so at most
one such box is ever visible and `first visible` is not a race. A box
inside something that OVERLAYS a view is disqualified for exactly that
reason: the fab drawer's debug console carries a filter, and marking it
would put two boxes on screen at once with DOM order deciding between
them. The membership is held by app-typeahead.test.mjs.

Below sm a hoisting pane hides its own box, and the header's find
pill stands in for it, so the key goes there rather than to the
sidebar finder.

showSidebar is about CONTENT, not about the viewer's choice: a
signed-out dashboard has no sidebar to open, so the finder is not
somewhere the key can be sent and the keystroke is left where a
reader's eye already is, which is nowhere. Measured 2026-09-04: without
this gate the seeded character landed in a box that stayed
display:none, and focus never moved.

Seed only once focus has actually landed. A reveal that did not take
would otherwise leave a character in a box nobody is looking at, and
the next keystroke would append to it.

── A PASTED ADDRESS OPENS WHAT IT NAMES ──────────────────────────────────

Until 2026-08-28 this app had exactly one paste behavior, unconditional:
everything went to the Stage as content, so an address pasted here became a
staged text file. toss-render has routed a paste by shape since it was
written (looksLikeAddress -> showAddress), and the estate, the one surface
that can actually OPEN what an address names, was the one that could not.

Three shapes route; everything else declines into the intake unchanged.
Two of them are RepoAddress.fromPaste's job (the bare grammar and a toss
link, whose subject is what pasting it means), and it is the whole of the
recognition so that the same answer is available to any other surface. The

── What the framed page is handed, and whose namespace is whose ──────────

THE SHELL OWNS THE QUERY. THE FRAGMENT IS THE SUBJECT'S.

That is the whole rule, and it needs no list of reserved names on either
side, which is the point: the shell's key set grows (VIEW_KEYS carries two
retired keys already) and a framed page's grows too, in another repo, with
nothing comparing them. Under a shared namespace the next addition on
either side is a silent collision that presents as "the deep link opened
the wrong screen". `?view=`, `?tab=` and `?q=` collide today.

It is also not a new rule. docs/routes.json states it for every parameter
in the estate ("read fragment first, query as fallback"), lib/kits/url-params.js
implements it, StageLink.read already applies it to stage/prompts/mode, and
this shell's own syncUrl has always rebuilt the query while carrying
location.hash through byte for byte. The fragment was a namespace the shell
preserved and did not use; this is the half that was missing.

Precedence, highest first:
  1. v.query      set programmatically. An action, not an address: the
                  Links pencil opens the board in edit mode this way.
  2. the fragment the reader's address carries, minus the three keys the
     shell claims there (stage, prompts, mode; see StageLink.read).
  3. ?on=<encoded>  the query fallback, for a context that eats the '#'
     (a link-preview crawler, a rewriter). Inbound only: `on` is in
     VIEW_KEYS, so the next stamp drops it and the address self-heals into
     the fragment form.

The delivery is a ?query on the addressed path, which the toss grammar
allows and the renderer's params shim answers inside the frame. So a framed
page reads its params exactly as it always has and needs no change to be
deep-linkable: budget-drs still reads ?view= and ?data= off its own search.

One honest limit: this is the address going IN. Navigating inside the frame
does not write back out, so the shell's fragment names where the reader
arrived rather than where they are now. The toss address has always had the
same property, so it is parity rather than a regression, and closing it
would need the framed page to postMessage its address to the shell.
The three keys the shell claims in the fragment, and the only exception to
"the fragment is the subject's". They are the stage link's, and they travel
as one unit; see StageLink.read.

Takes the PARSED url rather than reading `location`, and that is not a
style choice. parseUrl() snapshots the address at boot; by the time this
route opens, two unrelated syncUrl writes have already run (ensureBrowser
moves the browsed ref, and the ref watcher stamps), and each of them
deletes every VIEW_KEY it does not stamp, `on` included. So a live read
finds the fallback gone and the ?on= form delivers nothing, silently.
Measured in a browser on 2026-08-25, after the source assertions passed.
The fragment has no such problem, since syncUrl carries it through, so it
is still read live and only the fallback is threaded.

An app view's toss address, with whatever the subject's namespace holds
riding it as a ?query on the addressed path.

WHAT A VIEW INHERITS FROM THE APP, in appViewAddress below. Two
selections, each with the same order: the view's own, then an explicit one
of the app's, then the default the view derives for itself.

  Page ref. A view that names a ref (appRef) keeps it. Otherwise a
  web-tools view takes the app's own page ref when the app is tossed at a
  branch (window.__ref), since the app at a branch framing main's pages
  showed main inside branch chrome (docs/showing-consolidation.md, C5).
  A view of another repo has no app ref to take and opens at its default.

  Web Tools version. A `lib` in the view's own query wins, and the
  renderer reads it there. Otherwise an EXPLICIT selection of the app's
  rides as the renderer's ?lib=: window.__lib, which the renderer stamps
  only when a version was asked for, or on the deployed app its own
  ?use=, which is always an ask. It is forwarded even when it names main,
  because main is a selection like any other: an app tossed at a branch
  with ?lib=main, framing a web-tools view with no ref, addressed the view
  at the branch and dropped the main, so the view defaulted its library to
  the branch (reported against 70036ba). With no explicit selection
  nothing rides, and the view derives its own default (a web-tools view
  its own ref, any other main), the rule the renderer applies at every
  level.

A hub view with no ref of its own is DISPLAYED at the app's own version:
a view is a displayed file like the app, not one of its dependencies, so
a selection for the hub's dependencies (refs=, or ?lib=main) does not move
it; that selection rides along below and decides what the view loads.

Only a query that exists is parsed. Inside a toss the renderer's params
shim answers any EMPTY URLSearchParams with the app's own address,
because that is what new URLSearchParams(location.search) looks like in
a blob: frame; parsing an empty view query read the app's injected `lib`
as the view's own and dropped the forward (caught by the selection probe,
case X5d).

v.query only. A live subjectParams read here would hand the NEXT app view
the fragment belonging to the one before it.

THE SELECTION TRAVELS WHOLE (docs/loader.md, "The selection"): every
entry the link asked for, path entries included, rides to the view's
renderer as refs=. The web-tools repository entry rides as ?lib=, which
already yields to a view's own `lib`. What the app merely implies
(window.__refsImplied) never travels; the view implies its own.

An app view's toss address. Tossed (a renderer stamps __fabHosted; the
top-mode launcher stamps __tossTop), the app's explicit selection is
window.__lib; deployed, it is a real ?use=.

The page's selection as query parameters for a link to another page:
`refs=owner/repo@ref[:path]&…`, leaving out the repositories in `skip`.

── The app view's mark: what the tab, the bookmark and the tile carry ────

The shell ships one favicon for every route (lib/favicon.svg, the hex nut),
so budget-drs, News and the estate dashboard all read as the same thing in
a tab strip and in a bookmark list. An app view is a page some repo
PROMOTED, and its address names it; the mark should too.

THE MARK IS THE FRAMED PAGE'S OWN, not a reconstruction of it. toss-render

way than through the token, at the subject's ref) and announces the

a toss says it is a rendering and a promoted view does not. The two

from `.web-tools.json` shows a mark the page never chose, and parsing the

injects the default asynchronously).

Keyed on the app view it belongs to, so a mark can never outlive the view

apple-touch-icon's size; a tab renders it far smaller

the framed page's own <title>, when it announced one
the hex nut, captured before anything replaces it
the raster hex nut an iOS home-screen tile accepts

Replace rather than append. Two <link rel=icon> elements leave the choice
to the browser, which is not a thing to bet a mark on; toss-render's
setFavicon settled this the same way.
nothing of ours is on screen

One listener on THIS window, wired at init, because the announcement comes

The sidebar app-view list: the collected app views (from the config cache,

── The shell mode, and the sidebar it decides the opening state of ───────

returns null when the address names no repo, file, or view: a bare

Desktop opens with the sidebar out, a phone with it away, and only the
`full` mode takes that default: the other two are asking for the view.
Matched to the lg breakpoint the sidebar's own classes switch on, so the
default and the layout cannot disagree about what "desktop" means.

A CHOICE THAT AGREES WITH THE VIEW'S DEFAULT IS NOT A CHOICE, and
clearing it is what keeps a toggle local to the screen it was made on.
Turning the header off on an app view says "this page, bare", which is
already what that view does; latching it as a choice carried `shell=none`
out to the dashboard and left the estate with no nav and only the fab as
the way back. Measured in a browser: two taps on one app view and the
whole app had lost its chrome.

It also keeps the state and the address agreeing by construction, since

Which header-bearing mode to come back to. The drawer offers ONE control, a

someone who opened a ?shell=nav link, hid the header and brought it back

Deliberately NOT stamped into the URL. syncUrl pushes a history entry per
distinct address, so an addressable sidebar would put one on the stack
every time the drawer was tapped and make Back walk them; and the mode
already carries the part of this worth linking to, which is how the screen
OPENS. Toggling within a mode is reading, not navigation.

The FAB's opt-in contract for STATE, beside `actions` for verbs: each entry
is one on/off control the drawer's Render tab renders INLINE with the width
presets, since both answer how this view is being presented and a second
row for one question was the bigger half of the drawer's height. The shape
is { key, label, icon, on, title, set }; the FAB only reads and calls. The
row is one line and stays one line, so there is nowhere to explain a state
in prose: the tooltip carries the sentence, and the address carries the
fact, which is the point of putting the mode in the address.

ONE CONTROL, not three, and the sidebar is deliberately not among them.
The sidebar already has two owners a reader can reach: the header's
hamburger in the app, and ?shell=nav in the address. A third copy in the
drawer would be a control for the thing standing next to it. What is left
is the only part of the shell with no in-app control, since the header
cannot carry the button that hides the header.

The SAME switch, on the launcher's long-press menu, so a reader can easily
hide or show the header on any view. An app view defaults to 'nav' mode
(header visible, sidebar closed) for easy navigation, and this toggle offers
a fast 1-tap gesture to tuck the header away if they want the view bare.

fab.js's own description already claimed the app contributed this row,
and it did not: nothing declared `menu` anywhere, so readPageMenu found

── Swipe paging between dashboard views (touch only) ─────────────────────
The estateNav set (Activity / Repos / Stage / Tools / Map, plus
Proposals while it is showing) is a closed, ordered carousel. The header's
second group (the repo-sponsored views) stays out of it: each renders as an
iframe, which owns its own gesture surface, so a swipe could page IN and
never back out. Paging remains the app's own panes; the tabs reach
everything either way. Activity's three sub-views count as one stop
(navActive matches the alias list), switched by pill rather than swipe.

On a phone the active dashboard pane FOLLOWS THE FINGER through a
horizontal drag and slides out to commit, so paging reads as one continuous

one component (the estate pane re-renders its own content on a view
change), so a neighbour cannot be shown live mid-drag; instead the commit
slides the incoming content in from the dragged edge. It reuses the go*
methods a tab tap runs, so there is one navigation path and the lit header
tab stays the source of truth. Touch-only, so pointer users are never
affected; a drag outside the carousel (inside a repo) no-ops.

This is now the only hand-rolled swipe in the app. The estate's branch
takeover ran the same idiom against an embedded page until 2026-08-13, when

native snap track, and what it costs is that the panes must be real
siblings rather than one surface being translated.

The app sits beside pages/, not inside it, so pages.json's page-relative

through.

A page's live-render address in another repo: toss-render's #gh= mode at the

The gallery serves whichever repo is open, so reload its catalog when the
repo/ref changes (the component mounts once and persists behind x-show).

The watcher above settles once on every mount (config goes null then
set a tick later), and its comment called that redundant settle
harmless. It was not: on web-tools it re-fetched pages.json, 23 KB,
on every boot. Found by the fab's Traffic tab, which listed the file
twice. Keyed on what the catalog actually depends on, and set before
the await so a settle arriving mid-load is folded in too; cleared on
failure so a retry is still possible.
The key states what the catalog actually depends on, which is not the
same on both branches: web-tools reads one fixed pages.json and depends
on nothing else, so folding the ref into its key was what let the
duplicate through (init runs with the ref still empty, the watcher runs
with it settled to main, two different keys for one identical fetch).

Only repos with the gallery landing reach here (landingKind gates it):
web-tools, or a repo declaring a non-empty `pages` catalog. Bail
otherwise so a mid-switch to a non-gallery repo leaves the stale catalog
rather than clearing it.

web-tools: the generated page catalog. Live preview is the deployed
page at ?use=main; thumbnails are the committed shots. Flat since
2026-08-16, so the grouping the gallery renders is rebuilt here from
each row's own `top` and `group` rather than arriving as nesting.

Any other repo: one synthesized group from its declared `pages`. Each
tile gets its cached screenshot from the private thumb cache when one
exists (repo-pages-shots.mjs writes them there), defaulting to the shot
view so the card is a fast, clickable link to the page; a page with no
cached shot keeps the live toss-render (#gh=) default, lazily loaded as

(owner/repo[@ref]:path), so resolve the render target rather than
assuming the declaring repo.
`order` on a catalog entry, honored here the way it has always been
honored for app views (loadEstateSidebar): undeclared reads as 0, so
an entry with no opinion sorts ahead of one asking to be later.

The tiebreak is the entry's position in the catalog, NOT its label,
and that difference from the app-view sort is deliberate. App views
are collected across every repo, where array order means nothing and
a label sort is the only stable answer. A gallery is one repo's own
hand-written list, so its array order is already an editorial
statement; sorting undeclared entries alphabetically would scramble
every existing catalog to implement a field almost none of them set.

An entry's `query` rides into the page, so one page can be several
tiles. A tile whose page is a project's declared landing is a whole
app, so it never DEFAULTS to live: without a cached shot it opens on
the missing-shot face, and live stays one tap away on its toggle.
Project view's Pages, projectPages, says why at more length.

Fill in each tile's cached screenshot from the private thumb cache, keyed by the page's target repo, path and query (catalogThumbPath, in the registry repo, written by node/build/repo-pages-shots.mjs). Private-safe: read token-gated as a data URL, since a private repo's thumb has no plain URL and an cannot carry auth. A tile with a cached shot defaults to it (a fast, clickable link); one without keeps its default, live for a page and the missing-shot face for an app. No token, no cache read.
404: no cached shot, keep the live default

A catalog page carries its own target repo/path, so read it through
gh (token-authed, private-safe): reuse the open repo's gh when it is
the target, else a fresh instance for a cross-repo page. web-tools'
pages fetch by deployed URL.

The bridge: open a card's source in the file browser. Its repo path is the
github blob URL after /blob/<ref>/; that always names the real file, even
for the out-of-tree kit demos under lib/. Target the card's own repo, so a
catalog card opens its file in its repo rather than the default.

── Find pill: a view's filter box, hoisted into the header ─────────────────
The pill owns no query. It writes to the open view's own box (the
[data-find-box] input inside a view marked data-find-hoist, which that view
hides) and dispatches `input`, so each view's x-model, filtering and URL
stamp run exactly as if typed there. What it adds is placement: no row of
the view, one place for every view's filter, below lg a full-width 16px
field when tapped with the list lifted to just under the header so it
narrows above the keyboard, and the matches marked through the CSS Custom
Highlight API, which colors text ranges without touching any view's markup.
The list is the view's data-part="list" (the UI-units codebook's marker),
else whatever follows the box's row. Two boxes stay where they are: the
Search view's, which is that view's whole subject, and Config's key filter,
inside a reference panel that starts closed.

Elements stay out of Alpine's reactive state: a proxied node throws on
dispatchEvent.

The nearest ancestor that scrolls, which is the view itself for most and
an inner column for a project.

A view's box is hidden by its view's class, so whether its tab is the one
on screen is read off the row it sits in, whether it is shown there at
all off the label's own x-show (Docs' box is only on the Docs tab), and
whether it filters there off its search slot, which Activity drops on
State and Traffic.
A display:contents wrapper has no box of its own, so the row is the
first ancestor that does.
Retried because a view mounts its component lazily on first visit.

The placeholder is read even when the box is the same one: Activity's
four panes share a box whose placeholder follows the pane.

The lift is for a keyboard that covers half the screen; at lg and
up the field is in the header already and the list stays put.

Bring the list's top to just under the header, or under whatever stays
pinned over it: a sticky element whose parent spans the list (the
Map's tab strips below lg, the Sessions day lane), else the pane's
scroll-padding-top. A screen of padding below lets it stay there however
far the filter shrinks the list, where the browser would otherwise clamp
the scroll and drop it behind the keyboard. Scroll anchoring goes off
for the same reason: Chromium keeps a row on screen by subtracting the
rows filtered out above it, which walks the scroll back to the top.

Re-run after each render a keystroke causes (mark, below), since the
chips and notes above a list resize as it filters and would carry the
list off its line. Only then: a reader scrolling the results by hand
is not pulled back.

The bar lies over the top of the view, so the list lands below it
too: at its natural height, since it may still be sliding open.

Looked for inside the box's own section where it has one (a Map tab),
so a list belonging to another tab can never be picked.

The view can change its own query (a link, a reset); follow it
unless the reader is typing.

A count only where the view declares one on its box, with the
noun for its rows: rows read off the page's structure miscounted
wherever a list is grouped or holds its own empty line. A view whose
query reaches other kinds of row declares those too (find-also).

"1 session", "46 sessions"; a noun declared as "branch|branches" names
its own plural.

An Also entry names a method of the view's own component (the box's
scope) and its argument, so the view decides what opening its other
rows means: Activity widens the pane's scope to show every match.
The last few terms per view, offered while the field is open and empty.

── Overview: the default landing for a repo with no gallery — stats + README
+ a jump to the atlas. Reads the repo from the shared store; loads the README
through gh at the current ref. ─────────────────────────────────────────────

Every repo, the hub included. This used to skip the hub, because the hub
was the one repo whose landing was its page gallery rather than its
README, so fetching one would have been work nothing rendered. The
landing is the README everywhere now, and the gallery is its own view, so
the carve-out has nothing left to protect.

spec is one of two things, never a dialect: a bare color recolors mark's
layout-safe default (an outline), or a full CSS style string (any token
carrying a ':' passes through verbatim — your call, including its layout
cost). The rich prefix shorthand (bg-, p-, …) lives only in the console
formatter (f), for styling console *text*; mark deliberately does not
reuse it, so the two grammars can't drift into looking alike but differing.

help() with no argument opens the visual guide (tabbed reference + live
fixtures) in a popup; help(obj) still inspects an object via console.help.
The guide is the console-playground page — canonical hosted copy, so it
opens from any page the suite is pasted into.

console/mods/census.js — ping the page's shape: find and rank the
repeating structures, mark each in its own hue, and offer handles to grab
them. Orientation without reading any HTML. Requires console/base.js
(ea, glom, mark, unionArea).

  census()            top 10 groups (count ≥ 3), marked + console.table
  census(25, {min:2, mark:false})
  census.grab(i)      adopt group i as the glom working set
  census.clear()      remove census marks

Groups by unindexed tag path (html/body/table/tbody/tr). geoReg is
summary()'s kernel: union area over bounding box — near 1 means the group
tiles its region like a grid or list; near 0 means scattered or overlapped.

console/mods/columns.js — derive a table from a repeating working set:
pandas.read_html generalized to things that aren't <table>. Requires
console/base.js (glom).

  glom.columns()              one row object per member; console.table + return
  glom.columns({all: true})   keep constant (boilerplate) columns too
  packTable(glom.columns())   → columnar gzip+base64 on the clipboard

For each member, leaf texts are collected keyed by the member-relative
indexed tag path (td[2], div/span); links add an <path>@href column.
Columns whose value never varies across members are boilerplate and drop
(unless {all}); if nothing varies, everything is kept.

console/mods/core.js — shared kernels and the set event bus. Loads first;
every other glom mod requires base.js + this one (tap stays standalone).

  glom.core   { SCOPE, HUES, clean, own, upath, docOrder, upStep, overStep }
              the helpers the mods used to each carry a private copy of
  glom.onSet  subscriber list: every fn(els) runs after glom.set — and
              everything funnels through set (verbs, pick, grow, lasso,
              undo), so this is the suite's event bus. Subscribe instead
              of monkey-patching set; deck and recipe do.

Scroll-until-dry: run round() (which returns how many new items it saw),
then scroll + settle + round() until `dry` consecutive rounds surface
nothing or `max` rounds pass. harvest sweeps into memory, scan.sweep into
a store; both drive this one loop. Returns { total, rounds, hitMax }.

Debounced DOM-churn subscription: fire cb() `settle` ms after mutations
quiesce, and return a stop fn. The suite's SPA-fragility primitive —
watch heals the set on churn, scan captures on it.

A hued group layer for the rank-and-mark mods (census, templates): mark N
groups each in its own hue under data-<prefix>-<i>, grab group i into the
working set, and clear the marks. Owns the group list, so the two mods
stop each carrying their own verbatim grab/clear/mark copy.

console/mods/deck.js — a live side-window view of the working set: dense,
dark, monospace. Immediate visual validation without injecting any UI into
the host page: the deck is its own window (same-origin about:blank, driven
directly), so the page's CSS can't touch it and a rerender can't kill it.
Requires console/base.js (glom, sig, text).

  glom.deck()          open (or refresh) the deck; subscribes to glom.onSet
                       so verbs, pick, grow, lasso all show live
  glom.deck.close()    close and unsubscribe

console/mods/grow.js — by-example expansion of the working set.
Requires console/base.js (glom, ea).

  glom.grow()                expand current members to everything alike
  glom.grow({classes: false})  match on tag-path alone
  glom.grow({by: 'style'})   match on computed style (looks-alike; real
                             layout only — jsdom styles are uniform)
  glom.alike(el)             fresh set from one example element

Fingerprint: the unindexed tag path from the root (html/body/table/tbody/tr)
plus, when a path has two or more examples, the classes those examples
share. Two examples define what "alike" means far better than one (the
SelectorGadget insight): shared classes survive the intersection, hashy
per-instance classes (css-1a2b3c) wash out. A single example can't say
which of its classes matter, so it matches on structure alone.

Style fingerprint: "these LOOK like list items" — finds families in
class-less div soup where tag paths and classes both fail. Real layout
only (computed styles are uniform under jsdom).

console/mods/harvest.js — sweep a virtualized or lazy list. Virtualized
grids keep only the visible rows in the DOM, so any one-shot grab is
partial; harvest scrolls, waits, re-collects, and accumulates *records*
(text/html snapshots that survive element destruction) until the page runs
dry. Requires console/base.js (glom, ea).

  await glom.harvest()                      match via the set's tag-path fingerprint
  await glom.harvest({selector: '.row'})    explicit matcher (glom.infer() output fits)
  await glom.harvest({scroll, settle, dry}) custom scroller / wait ms / dry rounds

Returns [{key, text, html, el}] — el is the last-seen node and may be dead
by the time you look. Records dedupe by fingerprint + text, so identical
repeated rows collapse to one.

console/mods/infer.js — glom.infer(): synthesize a CSS selector that
matches the working set, and say honestly how well it does. Converts a
hand-danced set (picked, grown, lassoed, keep/dropped) into something
durable: replayable after a rerender, pasteable into Playwright or a
scraper. Requires console/base.js (glom).

  glom.infer()   → { selector, extra, missing }   (logs a verdict)

extra = elements the selector matches beyond the set; missing = members it
fails to match. (0, 0) is exact. Candidates: the members' shared atom
(tag + classes every member carries), then the same atom scoped under each
common ancestor with an id or classes. Mixed-tag sets infer per tag and
join with commas.

console/mods/join.js — relational joins over element sets: the spreadsheet
move that turns label/value scraping into one line. Requires base.js +
mods/core.js; composes with mods/sets.js (named sets via glom.peek).

  glom.join('labels', 'inputs', 'left-of')   each label paired with the
                                             input it sits left of
  glom.join(elsA, 'rows', 'inside')          arrays and names mix freely
  glom.join(a, b, (x, y) => …)               custom predicate

Relations (a REL b): inside, contains (structural); left-of, right-of,
above, below, same-row, same-col, near (geometric — real layout only,
jsdom boxes are all 0×0). When several b's qualify, the nearest by center
distance wins. Returns [{a, b, aText, bText}]; unmatched a's are dropped
and counted in the log.

console/mods/lasso.js — drag a rectangle, select what's inside. The
feature scraping libraries can't have: they don't have a screen. Requires
console/base.js (glom, ea).

  await glom.lasso()                  non-empty set → spatial refine (keep
                                      members inside); empty set → discover
  glom.lasso({mode: 'intersect'})     touching counts (default 'contain')

Esc cancels (set unchanged). Discovery keeps selection roots: contained
elements whose parent isn't contained, so a tight rectangle around a list
gets the items, not every span inside them. Zero-size boxes (hidden
elements, and everything under jsdom's inert layout) are skipped;
{zero: true} keeps them, which headless tests need.

console/mods/pick.js — click-to-collect mode for the glom working set.
Requires console/base.js (glom).

  glom.pick()        arm the page: hover shows a dashed outline, a tap or
                     click toggles membership (badges update live), Esc or
                     glom.pick.done() finishes and reports the set.

Picks are additive to the current working set; pick a member again to remove
it. Clicks are always swallowed (capture phase, stopImmediatePropagation) so
picking a link doesn't navigate.

TWO EVENTS, ONE SELECTION. A mouse sends pointerup and then click; iOS sends
pointerup and, for an element that is not itself clickable, NO CLICK AT ALL
to a document-level listener. kits/annotate.js carries the field report
(2026-08-14, "I tap and I don't get the outline") and moved its own picker
onto pointer events for it; this mod kept the click and would have failed the
same way on a phone, silently, since every mouse path works.

So both select, and a click arriving right after a pointerup this gesture
already handled is dropped rather than toggling the same element twice.

A pointerup that ENDED A SCROLL is not a tap, which a mouse never has to
distinguish. The browser says so itself by cancelling the pointer when it
claims the gesture; a distance check catches the slow drag it does not.

px of travel that still counts as a tap
ms a click may follow its own pointerup

console/mods/query.js — q(expr): a Playwright-flavored chain grammar,
implemented browser-native (Playwright itself is Node-side; its selector
grammar is just syntax). Requires console/base.js (ea, sig, mark, glom).

  q('#bills >> tbody tr >> has-text=hearing >> down=a >> nth=0-4')

Stages, separated by `>>`, each transforming the element set:
  <css>             querySelectorAll — document-wide as the first stage,
                    then within each member
  text=foo          own text contains "foo" (case-insensitive)
  text="Foo"        own text equals "Foo" (whitespace-cleaned)
  text=/re/i        own text matches the regex
  has-text=…        same three forms, against full textContent
  has=<css>         keep members containing a descendant match
  visible           keep visible members; visible=false for the inverse
  nth=2             pick by index (0-based; negatives count from the end)
  nth=1-4           inclusive range (ends may be negative: nth=1--1)
  up · up=2 · up=<css>   parent / nth ancestor / closest ancestor
  down=<css>        first descendant match per member
  down*=<css>       all descendant matches, unioned
  over=1 · over=-2  sibling hops

Returns a plain array decorated with .mark(spec), .glom() (adopt as the
working set), and .texts(). Results are deduped in document order.

Grammar notes: `>>` inside quotes or /regex/ literals is safe; a bare stage
named like an engine (e.g. an svg <text> selector) is read as the engine,
so write it as `svg text` or `*|text`.
Split on `>>` outside of "…", '…', and /…/ spans.

console/mods/recipe.js — the session journal: record every console-level
glom/q call and print the dance back as a replayable script. The export's
missing half: columns() gives the data, recipe() gives the provenance —
how the set was produced. Loads LAST in the suite so it can wrap the verbs
every other mod has installed. Requires base.js + mods/core.js.

  glom.recipe()         print (and return) the trail as one paste-able script
  glom.recipe.trail     the raw entries
  glom.recipe.clear()

Serialization is honest: strings/numbers/regexes/functions replay verbatim;
element arguments (from pick, lasso, census.grab…) can't travel through
text and appear as /* elements */ placeholders — replace them with a
selector (glom.infer()) when hardening a recipe.

Wrap the replayable ops in place: mods hold the same glom object, so a
wrapped method is seen everywhere; sub-properties (watch.stop, pick.done,
veins.grab…) ride along via Object.assign.

The glom(...) call itself: swap in a recording facade that shares every
property (same references) with the original.

console/mods/scan.js — durable capture over time. Every other mod takes one
snapshot of the DOM as it is now; scan adds the axis they lack, which is
time: define one or more streams (a selector + a format), then trigger a
pass on an interval, on DOM churn, or across a scroll, and each pass keeps
only the records whose key it hasn't seen (the fresh diff) and persists them
to IndexedDB. Poll-scroll capture is scan.sweep(): scroll to reveal what a
virtualizer hides, capture the fresh rows, repeat until the page runs dry.

The store is raw IndexedDB (no import, so the mod stays a single paste), and
because idb-nav / data-shelf read every database on the origin, whatever
scan writes is browsable there for free.

  glom('msg'); glom.grow(); glom.scan.define('rows')   seed a stream from the set
  glom.scan.define('rows', {selector, format})         or define it explicitly
  glom.scan.tick()                                 one capture pass now
  glom.scan.watch()                                capture on DOM churn
  await glom.scan.sweep()                          scroll-until-dry capture
  glom.scan.start(ms) / glom.scan.stop()           crude interval fallback
  glom.scan.grab('rows')                           adopt a stream back into the set
  glom.scan.data('rows')                           the in-memory records
  glom.scan.join('a', 'b')                         merge two streams
  glom.scan.highlight()                            outline captured elements
  await glom.scan.chat()                           preset: sidebar ↔ articles

This is a glom citizen, not a bystander parked in the namespace: a bare
define() reads the working set (infers the selector, snapshots each member),
and grab() writes captured elements back to it, so scan is the persistence
verb on the find → dance → grab loop. A stream's format(el) returns
{ key, ... }; key is what dedups a record across passes, so its stability (a
href, a content hash, an id, not a shifting ordinal) is where capture
quality lives. Requires base.js + core.js (mods/infer.js for set-seeding).

Default keyer/format when a stream is seeded from the working set instead
of a hand-written format: a stable key (id, own or descendant href, else a
text hash) plus a text/html snapshot. The same "prefer a durable handle
over an ordinal" rule the docs preach, applied automatically.
raw IndexedDB — one db, one keyPath:'key' store per stream.
gzip through base's single codec (pop.pack/unpack), not a private copy.
Ensure the db is open and holds `store`; adding a store means a version bump.
Pull a stream's persisted records into memory, decompressing as needed.
The fresh diff for one stream: live elements → formatted → minus what we hold.

Seed from the working set: glom/dance/grow to a set, and a bare
define() infers the selector (via mods/infer.js) and snapshots each
member, the same set-native shortcut watch and harvest take. Pass
{selector, format} to override either half.
One capture pass across every defined stream. Returns the fresh count.
Crude interval trigger — wasteful and it races scroll. Prefer watch/sweep.

Churn trigger: capture whenever the DOM mutates (debounced). The right
default for a live, streaming page — no idle polling, no missed rows.

Poll-scroll capture: scroll, settle, capture the fresh rows, repeat until
`dry` consecutive rounds surface nothing new. The harvest scroll engine
(core.sweep) with a durable sink. Returns total captured this sweep.

Adopt a stream's still-present elements as the working set, so a capture
flows back into the dance (census.grab / harvest, but keyed on record).

Left-join two streams into rows; unmatched members of b tail on. Default
relation: b's key contains a's key (the sidebar-link ↔ page pattern).
Outline the elements each stream has on record, one hue per stream.

Preset for chat UIs: a sidebar of conversation links (captions) joined to
the message bodies on the page (contents, content-hashed so distinct
messages persist rather than one blob per URL). A starting template —
retarget the selectors to the site in front of you.

console/mods/semantics.js — grab the structured data pages already carry:
JSON-LD blocks, microdata items, and og:/twitter: meta tags. Often the
whole scrape is sitting here, typed and labeled, before any DOM dancing.
Requires base.js + mods/core.js.

  glom.semantics()      → { jsonld: [...], microdata: [...], meta: {...} }

Microdata items come back as {type, props, el}: props read content/href/src
attributes before falling back to text, and nested itemscopes keep their
own props.

console/mods/sets.js — named working sets: park one dance, start another,
zip them later. Requires console/base.js (glom).

  glom.save('rows')     snapshot the current set under a name
  glom.use('rows')      restore it as the working set (badges return)
  glom.names()          {name: count}
  glom.forget('rows')   drop a name;  glom.forget()  drop all

Snapshots hold element references in memory: they survive the console
session, not a rerender (re-acquire via glom.infer()'s selector when the
page redraws).
read without switching the working set

console/mods/tap.js — capture fetch/XHR responses as they fly by. The DOM
is a lossy rendering of data that arrives as JSON; tap watches the wire
instead. Works when the API speaks JSON or text (nearly always); it sees
what's on the wire, so a payload the page decrypts client-side arrives
as-is. Standalone (no base.js dependency).

  tap()             arm, capture everything
  tap(/api/)        arm with a url filter (regex, or string includes)
  tap.hits          [{n, via, url, method, status, data}]  (data: parsed JSON or text)
  tap.last          most recent hit
  tap.find(v)       hits whose url matches v
  tap.clear()       drop hits;  tap.stop()  unwrap fetch/XHR, keep hits

  await tap.replay(0, {page: 7})               refetch hit 0 with mutated
                                               query params; returns parsed data
  await tap.walk(0, {param: 'page', to: 40})   walk a param across a range:
                                               paginate the API without
                                               scrolling; stops early when
                                               `until(data)` (default: empty
                                               array) says the well is dry

Each capture also dispatches window CustomEvent 'tap' ({detail: hit}) for
live consumers (e.g. the deck). Replays go through window.fetch, so an
armed tap records them as new hits.

Duck-typed regex check: instanceof fails cross-realm (console vs page
frame), and String.includes throws on a regex rather than coercing it.

A captured hit is a request template. GETs only — tap doesn't record
request bodies.

console/mods/veins.js — vein-to-skin matching: join captured API payloads
(the vein) to the rendered page (the skin). Flattens JSON to leaf fields,
matches leaf values against elements' own text, and reports which fields
actually feed the screen — so you learn "the column I'm scraping is
bills[].status" and can stop scraping the DOM for that site. Requires
console/base.js (glom, ea); pairs with mods/tap.js (uses tap.hits when no
data is passed).

  glom.veins()          join every tap.hits payload against the working set
                        (or the whole page if the set is empty)
  glom.veins(data)      join an explicit object/array instead
  glom.veins.grab(i)    adopt field i's matched elements as the working set

Fields rank by coverage (distinct values matched / distinct values seen):
a field whose every value lands somewhere on screen is a confirmed vein.
Matching is exact on whitespace-cleaned own text, with a containment
fallback for values of 4+ characters.

console/mods/verbs.js — set-wise navigation for the glom working set.
Requires console/base.js (glom). The set moves in lockstep: every member
takes the same step, members whose step lands nowhere drop out, and
glom.set dedupes and renumbers. The set stops being a bag and becomes a
cursor over N parallel subtrees.

  glom.up()            parent of each member
  glom.up(2)           grandparent
  glom.up('tr')        closest 'tr' ancestor (excludes self)
  glom.up(pred)        nearest ancestor passing pred
  glom.down('a')       first 'a' descendant per member (keeps cardinality)
  glom.downAll('a')    every 'a' descendant, unioned
  glom.over()          next element sibling
  glom.over(-2)        two siblings back

console/mods/watch.js — the self-healing working set. React-style pages
destroy data-glom attributes on every rerender, killing the selection
mid-dance; watch re-acquires it. Requires console/base.js (glom); uses
mods/infer.js for the automatic selector when no explicit one is given.

  glom.watch()                    infer a selector from the current set and
                                  re-apply it whenever the DOM churns
  glom.watch({selector: '.row'})  explicit selector (infer not needed)
  glom.watch.stop()               disarm

Mutations are debounced (`settle` ms, default 250) so a rerender storm
heals once, at the end. Healing logs only when membership actually changed.
