ONE FRESH READ OF THE CONFIG CACHE, SHARED. Four loaders read the
registry's state/configs.json (about 0.9 MB): work declarations, the data
census, estate columns and test execution. Each reads it FRESH, since a
loader caches its own result and a read it does make must see the file as
it is now, past GH's memo and the HTTP cache. Unjoined, those reads were
the Map's heaviest traffic: one load read the file seven times in four
minutes, and the traffic logs for 2026-10-16 to 30 came to 174 MB of it.
So a fresh read is shared: its in-flight promise, then its text, for
CONFIGS_SHARE_MS from when it started. A forced load (Refresh) always
starts a new read, which later loaders then share; a failed read is
dropped, so the next loader reads again; a different token or registry is
a miss; and dropConfigsShare(), called on a configs-refreshed or a
sign-in change, ends the share early. Each caller parses its own copy, so
no two loaders hold one object.
The cache is live registry state, written on main.

The Map view: the estate's coordination layer made inspectable. It is the
operational face of the constellation doctrine (home's
created/2026-06-27-constellation-architecture.md, kernel at the hub's
docs/CONSTELLATION.md), in top-level tabs, each a strip of
subviews; TABS and SUBVIEWS below are the list.
  Distribution the crosswalk from the hub's committed portable manifest
              (docs/portable.csv) into the inventories that own each
              artifact. It groups by HOW something travels, identifies
              WHAT it is, and points back to Skills, Docs, or Automation
              for the canonical description. Labelled "The set" until
              2026-08-07 and "Portable" until 2026-09-17; addressed as
              ?tab=set until 2026-10-11, when the address followed the
              label (the snag retired-address-kept-alive).
  Showing     how content moves, renders, and gets looked at, read from
              four hub files: the Showing table (which link
              reaches which kind of change), the shared
              owner/repo[@ref]:path address grammar, the delivery modes
              toss-render accepts (inline payload versus fetched
              reference, and the trust posture each one buys), and the
              toss routes mapping a content type to its renderer page.
              Named Transport until 2026-08-04; renamed because
              CONVERSATION.md already uses "transport" for the stage link,
              and the lead section here was titled Showing all along.
  Themes      prose two Markdown files repeat, read from docs/themes.csv,
              with similar wording from data/doc-overlap/ below it.
  Overview/Purpose the estate's mission, goals, and reading paths, beginning
              with the repo README, agent contract, and docs index. The
              `aims` URL key survives its move from the top strip.
  Docs/Growth a corpus as a moving picture: pages/doc-growth.html framed,
              every markdown file a bubble over the repo's history. Docs
              answers "is this document growing", one row at a time; this
              answers "what is the whole corpus doing". FEDERATED: the
              repo is a control, fed by each repo's own `growth` key, and
              the chart is one instrument pointed at whichever corpus is
              selected. It was two top-level app views until 2026-08-28,
              one per repo, which rendered as the word "Doc Growth" twice

              the Map's top strip into Docs on 2026-09-11.
  Docs/Inventory the documentation registry, read from the hub's
              docs/docs.csv: every doc's subject, status (living claims
              current truth, record preserves a moment, measured carries
              dated observations and is corrected by re-probing), reach,
              and maintenance. It also reads the doc-growth payload,
              turning its `words` snapshot into a trend, per row and
              per folder. Optional by construction, since that payload is
              refreshed on demand rather than by a hook; without it this
              reading renders exactly as it did before. Laid out as a
              folder rail beside the
              selected folder's files (2026-08-07); the flat
              directory-grid it replaced rendered docs/envelopes/schemas
              as a peer of docs and hid the hierarchy. A row's title
              opens the document in the house swipe deck, paging the
              selected folder's files, rather than navigating to the
              files view; its GitHub icon, inline with the badges,
              carries the source peek for the desktop glance, and the
              rendition helpers are SourcePeek's own exports so deck
              and peek cannot drift. A details toggle on the reach
              strip shows every row's maintenance at once. Reach is the one field here that is
              DERIVED rather than authored: node/build/docs-reach.mjs
              reads the skills and the app to see what names each doc,
              and docs-registry.test.mjs holds the registry's copy to it.
              It is the tab's headline because it is the number that
              moves when the estate improves, and it has already moved
              twice from being looked at: stripping comments from the app
              corpus (a mention is not a channel) and then adding the
              CLAUDE.md channel, which showed twelve docs the repo's own
              instructions name and the first cut had called orphans.
              Beside reach, each row carries its READERSHIP: the distinct
              sessions that opened the file, from the read counts the
              Growth chart draws (state/doc-reads.json on the private
              registry's background branch, python/doc-reads.py), else
              the sessions cache (docAttention) for a repo they do not
              hold, read here with the viewer's token, absent without one. Reach says who can
              get to a doc and this says who did, which is the pair worth
              reading together: an orphan nobody opens and an orphan
              opened in nine sessions are different problems. The column
              carries its caveats in the strip above it, because they are
              load-bearing rather than decorative: the two injected docs
              are the most-read files in the estate and are precisely the
              two no file tool can count. From 2026-08-27 the column

              context before the conversation began, from the record's
              startup_context) beside `docAttention` (what a file tool
              opened). The word "injected" survives only as the fallback
              for a cache older than that field, which is the whole
              difference: the exception used to be the mechanism. From
              2026-10-25 both numbers come from the read counts where
              they hold the repo: every session record and every
              Markdown path, where the cache keeps 400 sessions and
              docs/ paths, so this column and the Growth chart agree.

repo's card, which is what moved in August.

a helper the commit hook runs counts as running on an event, and a file
can count under more than one.

The events outside Claude Code, in the order each kind meets them, with
what each means. docs/harness.csv derives which file runs on which:
env:build, git:<hook>, and ci:<events> from a workflow's on: block.
How a check reaches its subject, which decides how much its pass proves.

The three closed vocabularies a row belongs to, each a separate question,
each filtering on its own axis and composing with the others. They are
labeled in the strip because they were not, and a reader had no way to
tell whether two pills competed or combined.

Only `kind` carries tone, and the asymmetry is deliberate rather than
left over: the kind badge repeats on every row, so a color lets a chip be
matched to the rows it selects. Method is the section heading and runner
is the row icon; coloring either would invent a mapping the rows do not
show.

What is NOT here is boot smoke. It was a chip until 2026-08-10 and did
not belong: a kind, a method, and a runner are each exactly one value per
file, while a boot check is a property of an individual assertion. The
chip had to pick a level to count and could not say which it picked, and
both readings happened to be 19. It is marked in the assertion list now,
on the one line it is true of.

Each dimension asks its question; each VALUE explains itself. The
per-value gloss is the one the reader wants (what is a `gate`?), and the
kind vocabulary's copy is the registry's own, read live rather than
restated here.

Tone in the strip is a small marker, kind only, and both halves of that
are deliberate. It was a tinted badge around the file count until
2026-08-10, which made one dimension's chips a different SHAPE from the
other two and read as arbitrary. A dot separates the colour from the
number: the colour keys the row badges below, the number is just a count.
And it stays kind-only because tinting method and runner was tried and is
worse: those colours decode to nothing, since no row anywhere wears them.

`dot` opts this dimension into the tone marker, and only this one can
have it: colour decodes to a kind because the per-row badge is tinted by
kind and nothing else. It stays a dimension-level opt-in rather than a
lookup per value, which is the shape that survives a domain gaining a
value another dimension already spends. The collision that forced it is
gone, since `kit` was a kind and a method at once until the kinds closed
on two, and a per-value KIND_TONE hit would have tinted the method chip
with a meaning it did not have.

Files and words are both shown because on this folder they disagree, and
the disagreement is the finding. Orphans are 40% of the files and 17% of
the words; one reachable document is 22% on its own. A strip carrying
only counts sends every reader to the tail.

── The doc deck's rendition ─────────────────────────────────────────
Full-length sibling of the peek's excerpt: same kind decision, same
frontmatter fencing, same JSON pretty-print, through SourcePeek's
exported pure helpers so the two can never disagree about what a file
looks like, with plain fallbacks for a page that never loaded the peek.
ref:path -> raw text
One recursive tree per repository/ref, shared by every slide. A rendered
document can then distinguish a repository file from code-shaped prose
without turning every backticked filename into a speculative link.
Escaping is window.esc from vanilla-bundle.js, first in the boot chain.

A user call's mark: the attention colour, on its row, its pill and its
edits' chips (paintCallChip).
Toned down from a solid orange (owner, 2026-10-20: "just a little bit too
intense"); still the one orange on the page.

WHAT EACH NOTE ON A CALL'S EDIT IS FOR (owner, 2026-10-20). `correct`
changes what the text claims, the test doc-audit's WRONG uses;
`clarify` keeps the claim and changes the wording, its WEAK. An edit
carries one note or several, every one shown, corrections first. A
`why` with no `notes` is one note of no kind.

One glyph per note, each its own tip; past four, three and a "+n" whose
tip holds the rest.

A list item's markdown without its own marker, dedented by the marker's
width, for a container drawn inside the item that already wears it.

The forms README's two tables, cell by cell as written and keyed by
their first column, and its paragraph on the forms that record no
answer. A table is the run of pipe rows under the header row whose first
cell is `first`; a cell holds no pipe, which the README's rows bear out.

kits/md-doc.js, lazily and once, beside marked: it is what puts a wide
table in its own scroller and a copy control on every heading, and a
deck that never opens a markdown file should not pay for it.

A registry as a markdown table. The estate's CSVs are one record per line
by construction (kits/csv.js says so, and every registry keeps its prose
single-line to hold that), which is what makes a line-oriented conversion
safe: no cell can carry the newline that would break a row in half.

A CELL IS DATA, so its markdown is escaped rather than run. The pipe has
to move because it is the table's own delimiter; the rest move because a
registry that describes markdown is full of markdown, and the first
rendering turned a registry's own `[caption](url)` into a link reading
"caption". A reader looking at the file has to be able to see the
brackets. Backslash escapes render as the bare character, so nothing is
added to what is on screen, and emoji are untouched.

Ragged rows are PADDED to the widest, never truncated to the header: a
row with an extra field is a file that has drifted from its header, and
dropping the field would hide exactly the thing worth seeing.

MOUNTED, not returned as a string. The section controls are listeners on
real nodes, and a string handed to innerHTML would drop them; the deck's
slide renderer therefore hands this the box to fill rather than asking it
for markup. The non-markdown branches still build a node, so the two
paths have one shape.

SOURCE MEANS THE FILE'S OWN BYTES-AS-TEXT. It must happen before CSV
conversion, Markdown frontmatter fencing, and JSON pretty-printing or
the switch would show a second presentation rather than the raw file.

A CSV IS A TABLE, and until 2026-09-04 every one of them arrived here as
wrapped raw text: SourcePeek.kindOf answers markdown / json / source,
which is the right set for a 28-line hover excerpt and the wrong one for
a full read. The Docs tab's deck pages docs/, which holds a dozen
registries, so the wall was the ordinary case rather than an edge.

Converted to a MARKDOWN table rather than built as one. Everything the
rendition needs already rides the markdown path: md-doc puts a wide
table in its own scroller, the house prose styling applies, and the
section controls work. A table built here would be a second table
treatment to keep in step with that one.

kindOf is left alone deliberately. Widening it would change the PEEK
too, and a hover card is a glance at the head of a file where the raw
line is what a reader recognizes. The extension test lives here because
the decision does.

Fenced FIRST, and the split runs on the fenced text, so the
sections the controls cut and the headings the reader sees come
from one parse. Fencing swaps `---` for ``` and keeps the block's
line count, so the line numbers in a copied reference still point
at the file the reader would open.
marked unavailable: fall through to source

Pill rows keep their labels intact and scroll within the available width.
`relative` makes the strip the containing block of what it scrolls, so a
pill's sr-only label is clipped with it rather than widening the pane.
`py-0.5` because a scroll box clips on every side: iOS Safari cut the
pills' bottom border where it met the box's edge (owner, 2026-10-21).

A list of questions, each answered by picking it. The Context tab's
questions and the Set tab's how-to questions are one form.

A chip is one pill in a row that narrows or regroups a list: the
repository row, Skills' source and subject rows, Agents' sets, Automation's triggers, the Gallery's Group by. One
shape for all of them, so a row of chips reads as narrowing rather than
as a third level of tabs; only
the two strips at the top are drawn as tabs. Toned chips, whose colour
keys the rows below (Docs' reach, Tests, Dimensions), keep their own.
Tighter on a phone, where three rows of chips cost a list its rows
(owner, 2026-10-24: "less pill padding, less space between rows").

A daisyUI join filled by x-for: the first button takes the group's
left corners (daisyUI's --radius-field, as the last one has), which
:first-child misses behind the <template>. The `!` is needed: daisyUI's
sheet is unlayered, so it beats any utility without one (snag
an-unlayered-rule-beats-every-layer).

The pinned stack below lg is navigation and the current group heading,
nothing more: the collection controls and filter rows scroll away with
the list, since a held chip row consumes a phone's viewport (html-style,
"Put filters in a header dropdown"). It held both until 2026-10-12, when
they took about 310 of the Map pane's 583 pixels at 320 by 640. Each held
layer carries data-map-sticky, which initMapSticky measures into the
offset the group heading reads.

Collection controls keep their own semantics and share this compact row.
`filters` is markup, or { html, show } when the filters row should hide
with what it holds (a repository row with no choice to offer).

A tab with nothing to put here (a diagram, a deck) draws no row: what
the tab is and reads lives in the app drawer's About tab, not here.

── Tallies: one form for every tab's count ────────────────────────────
A count was drawn five ways across the tabs (a sentence, a large number
over "of N", icon buttons on Tests, a right-aligned "N of M" on Policy,
or nothing), so each tab taught its own (owner, 2026-10-21: "use an icon
and try to make it consistent"). Now each is the icon of its kind of
row, the number, then the noun, which a phone drops for the icon alone,
as Tests already did. The icon is the one the tab listing those rows
wears, so a count and the tab it counts look alike.

A registry has a glyph of its own, since no stock icon says "a table
keyed one row per thing": a ruled table whose key column holds a mark
per row, drawn on Phosphor's 256 grid with its 16-unit stroke and painted
as a mask in the current text colour, so it sits in an <i> among the
font's glyphs at 1em.

`n` and `total` are Alpine expressions; "of N" shows only while a filter
leaves fewer than all.

── Repository choice: one row wherever a tab has one ──────────────────
It was a select on Data and Research, a tab strip on Docs and Growth,
and pills on Names. Now one row in the toolbar's filters slot: a
repository glyph, then pills in the Activity view's repo-chip form (mono
names and counts, rounded), which sets it apart from the tab strips
above so it does not read as a third level of tabs. It scrolls sideways
rather than wrapping, and shows only when it offers a choice. A tab
supplies `items`, an expression for [{ key, label, n, title }] (key ''
for All), the expression for the current key, and the statement that
picks `r.key`; it goes in mapToolbar's filters slot, which hides with it.

── Lens switch: the same rows shown another way ──────────────────────
A row that regroups what a tab lists rather than narrowing it (Peeves'
axes) is a segmented switch at the toolbar's right: "show these as", not
"go elsewhere", so it is drawn as neither a tab nor a chip. Every segment
keeps its name at every width; showing only the chosen one's below lg
read as an accordion. `items` is an expression for [{ k, n, i }]; `at`
names it for a look link. The x-for's <template> is the group's first
child, so daisyUI's :first-child rounding never reaches the first
button; mapJoin gives it the group's corners (owner, 2026-10-24).

Every declared column, rebuilt only when the registry pair or the
estate's column registries are read again, and every table, rebuilt
only when those or a census are: a getter rebuilding two thousand
columns would do it on every read in a render. Kept outside the
component so filling them is not a reactive write.

A column primitive's drawn mark (docs/favicons/primitives/), painted in
the primitive's colour. `p` is an Alpine expression; `size` a Tailwind
size class.

What opens the Data tab's panel-tip: hover or focus on a fine pointer,
a tap anywhere. `t` and `c` are expressions for a table and a column.

An event's row on the Events view, whatever its kind: the event and
what it means, then what runs on it, a matcher where Claude Code takes
one, the files the dispatcher runs, and the commit hook's steps, listed

strips do, so the board keeps its shape on a phone instead of wrapping.

A hook file's panel-tip, opened by a tap on its name in an event row,
as the Growth tab's file panel-tip is: its folder over its name, the
GitHub mark after the name (its peek reads the file in place) and the
file deck's icon at the top right; what the file does; and the chain of

outside and on Escape, and the name again closes it; it draws no ✕, as
the Growth tab's does not (owner, 2026-10-24). At z-82: over the FAB,
under the peek.

The deck icon floats, so only the line beside it gives
way and a long folder or name runs on under it.

The toolbar Automation's three addresses share: the file inventory
(?tab=harness), the events (?tab=events) and the schedule
(?tab=scheduled). Its filter row is what starts a thing running; the

Probes and Exploration share one control set; each section mounts it
in its own toolbar, so the toolbar stays that section's first child.

A source's panel-tip (kits/panel-tip.js owns the way out): hovering a
source opens it, a click pins it. It replaces an expander row, so the
table keeps its height and a reader can run down the sources one
hover at a time. The profile is the panel's body: every classified
property as its whole scale (CTX_SCALES), the same rows at the same

── Themes' card text ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
A file is read once per ref and path; its word positions once per read.
Both sit outside Alpine's reactivity, since nothing on screen watches
them and they can be whole documents. The swiper and its deck are kept
by their root element for the same reason.

Comments: every comment block and docstring in a repository's code,
written by python/comment-blocks.py. A repository offers its own by
naming a path under `comments` in its .web-tools.json.

A match at this cosine or above is the same text, which a run already
shows, so a card leaves it out (≥20 identical words always make runs).
The mark of a repeat to review first, on a row and on a run (themeReview).
A name that says nothing alone: a SKILL.md is its skill's folder.

Words as the scan counted them (python/duplicated-claims.py: [a-z0-9']+
over lowercased text), each with its place in the file.

Where a run sits in a file: its words in order, or, where the scan
dropped a table or a fence from inside it, its first and last eight.

A passage's runs in one file as excerpts, each run marked: runs closer
than a few hundred characters share an excerpt, so no context shows
twice, and an excerpt reaches out to its paragraph, at most 200
characters each side.

Markdown wraps a paragraph across lines; the card reads it as one, and
keeps the breaks before a list item, a heading or a table row.
Whether a span of a file overlaps a run placed in it (themeLayout).

── Themes' map ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Where a repeat sits in each of its files, in three views a card switches
between (themeView), every card at once. Ribbons and Bars give each file
a bar as long as the file against the longest, its runs in the accent
and its similar passages in grey; Ribbons join a repeat's place in one
file to its place in the next. Dot plot gives a pair of files that
share a repeat a square, one file across and the other down, so a repeat
that kept its place lies on the diagonal and one that moved lies off it.
A group draws a square for each file after the first, against the first
file it shares a repeat with, so five files make four squares, not ten.
A file is named by its number in the card's file list, so a long name
never shares a line with its bar.
The switch's segments, chosen and not, as lensSwitch draws them.

A span as drawn: never narrower than half a percent of the bar, so a
short run stays visible and its ribbon is as wide as its mark.

The tab strip. Who carries what is a property of each repo, so
that lives on the Repos cards, not here.

data-slot names the unit slot an element fills (data/ui-units/
codebook.md, "Slots"): this strip is the Tabs of every Map tab,
the sub-strip the Second-level switch of a tab that has one, and
the toolbar its controls and Sources action.

Both tab levels stay on one line at every width. Opening an
address reveals its selected tab within the scrolling strip.

A tab opens the route it names. Docs therefore lands on its
Inventory, the concrete index; Purpose and Growth remain
adjacent readings under the Docs subview strip.

The front door: every address the strip leads to, under its

where a reader arriving cold meets the sets before the rows. The

The family and the passage that discusses its icons,
as a peek; where each icon is declared is in its

Search, repository scope, count and Refresh sit in the shared

One table of workspaces: each repository first, as the workspace

Name: a repository in mono with its glyph; a project

Open tasks: one bar per board on the fullest board's

Parts: fixed slots, so a column reads as which

Markup, not x-for: a <template> inside <svg> is an SVG element,

The routes: one per use value, counted
The set: every repository a manifest read supplies

z-[60], under the swipe deck's z-[70]: a file opened from the

link at the panel's foot, never the default.

One header for every kind: what it is, then its ways out,
at the top beside the ✕ rather than in a footer.

A repository: the Repos card's grammar. Its one-line note,

A route: its files grouped by kind, each a count over

The declaration and the observation side by side, the

This is a delivery crosswalk, not a fourth inventory: the

Container widths, not viewport ones: this grid has to answer to

Declared a List with named parts (data/ui-units/codebook.md,

Inline with the badges, always visible, the way

One row per facet, each value always shown with its count

The list, one line a row, in a box of its own height.

One line: a path too long for it loses its start,

A file: its folder over its name, and its way out at the top

The deck icon floats, so only the line beside it gives

cache keeps its newest rows by last activity, so the weeks up to the
newest record it left out are partly covered; so is the week running.

A sequential scale on the one accent: the share of the week's
sessions that invoked the skill.

The tail on a skill row. Silent when the fold is absent, and explicit
when it is present and the skill is not in it: those are "not measured"
and "never fired", and a blank for both would collapse the one number
this tab exists to show. A skill nobody invokes is the finding.

The cache keys a file by repo-qualified path (`web-tools/docs/x.md`),
since a session spans repositories and `docs/README.md` alone would
collide across them. The registry rows are hub-relative, so qualify
before looking up rather than storing the same string twice.

A row's `formerly` names the paths the same document carried before a
rename (docs.json became docs.csv, and so on), so a read of an old path
is a read of this row, folded here.

What the italic tail says, and the honest empty. A never-opened doc
shows nothing rather than a dash, since an absence needs no ornament,
and the caveats the column used to state in a standing paragraph live
in the per-row title.

TWO FACTS, SIDE BY SIDE, NEVER ADDED. Presence in context and being
opened by a tool are different things, and a document present in forty
sessions and opened in three has not been read forty-three times.
Until 2026-08-27 this rendered that difference as the literal word
"injected" on the two rows tagged that way, because a count would have
ranked the estate's two most-read files last. The record now carries
startup context as data, so the word is the fallback for a cache older
than the field rather than the only answer available.

The "injected" label used to close with "not measurable here, and not
zero", which was two claims: the first true, the second an assumption
about a delivery path nothing was checking. It was wrong on 2026-08-26,
when the hook carrying both documents turned out to have been truncated
to a 2 KB preview since 2026-08-07. That is the strongest argument for
the receipts behind this column: a receipt states the BYTE COUNT the
hook actually supplied, so the same nineteen-day silence would now show
as a number that moved rather than as a label nobody could check.
The pre-receipt answer, kept for a cache older than the field.

Where the number came from is part of the number. A receipt is the
injecting hook naming what it supplied; a reconstruction is a
static walk standing in for a loader with no hook to observe it,
since Claude Code has no InstructionsLoaded event and its memory
loader logs a file count rather than the paths.

── The constellation's documents ─────────────────────────────────────
The hub's rows are its curated registry. Every other repo's are the
index the hourly crawl keeps in the private registry
(lib/kits/doc-index.js, state/docs.json): Markdown paths and word
counts, with no subject, status or reach, which only a repo's own
registry could state. The strip picks the repo; every getter below
reads docDocs, so the rail, rows, search, readership and deck serve
both.

A data repo's folder can hold 1,800 generated files; the list shows
the first DOC_ROWS and says how many more there are.

Search starts across the corpus and composes with reach. A folder
chosen during a search is an explicit scope; the folder that happened
to be open before the query is deliberately irrelevant.
One test for a row being in view, which the rail's counts share.

The rail: every directory in the registry plus its ancestors, in DFS
order (lexicographic gives it, since every path shares the docs/
root), rolled up so a folder's count and words include everything
below it. Structure comes from the full registry, so the tree never
changes shape under a reach filter; only the counts move, and a
folder filtered to nothing dims rather than vanishing.

Another repo's tree is not seven folders (home has 471), so there the
rail is the root, the open folder's ancestors and their siblings, and
the open folder's children; a search shows every folder it hits.

The selected folder's DIRECT files, filter applied; subfolder contents
stay behind their own rail rows.

Registry order is the default and stays the default: it is the order
the folder actually has, and a reader looking for a known file finds it
there. The sort is the other question, "what is nobody opening", which
registry order answers only by making someone read every row.

An injected doc sorts by its own channel, not by a zero. Nothing reads
it with a file tool by construction, so ranking it on reads would put
the estate's two most-delivered documents at the cold end, which is the
failure the readership column already refuses to make on a single row.

'' registry order, 'hot' most-opened first, 'cold' least. Cold is the
one worth having; hot is its inverse and costs one more state.

The folder's README subject doubles as the folder's description; a
folder without one shows nothing, which is itself information.

The counted half of swipeDeck.entry's title, spelled the way every
other template-driven door spells it (branch-brief owns the original).

Reading a doc: the house swipe deck, opened on the tapped row and
paging the selected folder's files as they are currently filtered.
Fetched full rather than excerpted (the peek is the glance, this is
the read), cached per ref:path so swiping back costs nothing. The
whole surface is imperative DOM: swipe-deck is framework-free, which
is also what keeps Alpine's moved-node hazards out of it.

docDeckRead, not docRead: the readership column's per-row accessor
(main's parallel work, merged 2026-08-07) already owns that name, and
a duplicate object key would shadow it silently.
A deck slide's path is a hub path, or owner/repo@ref:path for a file
in another repo (the Context tab's sources live in four). One parse,
so the fetch, the copied address and the link pass agree on which.

The address a copied SECTION carries, assembled here because this is
the only place that knows all four parts: which repo the deck reads,
which ref it is pinned at, which file the slide is, and the blob URL a
person rather than a tool would open. mdDoc adds the line span.

The registries are a useful immediate seed, but not the authority for
whether a repository path exists: a skill can cite an unregistered
sibling. The recursive tree fills that gap once per ref. Failure is
non-fatal; authored links keep their ordinary GitHub href and inline
code remains inert unless the paths already in hand prove the match.
a registry-seeded reader is still useful offline

A lazy rendered pass may finish after the reader has asked for raw.
Build off-DOM and commit only the newest request whose mode still
agrees with the file's state.

THE SLIDE IS THE DOCUMENT, and nothing above it. It used to lead with a
strip carrying the path, a GitHub mark and a "files view" button, which
named the file a THIRD time (the header's title and subtitle are the
other two, each elided a different way) and put two doors inside the
reading surface. kits/file-deck.js had already made this call for the
changeset deck and written down why; this half of the estate had not
followed. Both doors moved into the header, where the kit owns a `link`
slot and an actions row and the reader finds them in the same place on
every deck.
On the component only so the gate can reach it: the conversion is a
module-level pure function and renderDoc calls it directly, but a rule
about what a cell may not be reinterpreted as is worth holding, and
map-view.test.mjs mounts the component rather than the module.

IT RECORDS WHEN IT IS DONE, because a caller that wants to point INSIDE
a slide has to wait for three async steps it cannot see: the fetch,
marked, and md-doc. landDeckHash below is that caller, and without
this it would scroll an empty box. Keyed by path plus the deck generation
rather than by index, since the index is the deck's, the path is the
file's, and a reopened child must not inherit a detached prior box.

ONE DECK FOR BOTH LISTS, and that is the point of the shape rather
than a saving. The Docs tab read a row here; Distribution reached
its file by NAVIGATING to the Files view, which is a route change and
not an overlay, so the list the reader was working through was gone and
the way back was the browser's. Two tabs in one view answered the same
tap two different ways. The deck is the better answer, because it keeps
the set, the reader's place in it, and the return path.

A slide needs only `.path` (renderDoc decides the rendition by
extension and drops to a <pre> for source), so one renderer serves a
doc, a SKILL.md and a .py script alike. Kept as ONE function rather
than one per tab, since two would be two reading experiences a month
from now and nothing would report the drift.

`start` is clamped here rather than at each call site: a findIndex miss
returns -1, and a deck opened at -1 is a blank first slide with the
pager already wrong.

ONE LABELER, TWO READERS, which is what keeps the header and the
contents list from describing the same row two ways. `label(row)`
answers {title, subtitle, icon}; the HEADER takes the title and pairs
it with the locating half (the caller's context plus this file's
folder), and the CONTENTS list takes the title and the subtitle, which
is the gloss. The split is deliberate: a header answers "where am I"
and has one line to do it in, while a list is being scanned for "which
one did I want" and the subject is what answers that.
RE-AIM RATHER THAN STACK. Docked, the list stays on screen and stays
clickable, so a second tap is the ordinary case rather than the odd one,
and opening a second deck over the first would bury the reader one Back
press deeper for every row they looked at. Same list and a deck already
open: go to that slide. `key` is what "same list" means, since the two
tabs hand in different sets and the Docs tab a different one per folder.
A different key closes and reopens, which is the honest answer: the
pager, the title and the swipe range all belong to the old set.

Named rather than "Open": where a link goes is worth saying, which is
the same reason the kit lets a link carry its own mark.

Alpine proxies an assigned plain handle, so object identity is
not stable across `this._deck = handle`. A scalar generation is.

── The reference menu ────────────────────────────────────────────────

What the slide's old strip did, in the one place a phone has room for
it. Four of the five rows answer the same question the strip never
asked: how does a reader take this file WITH them. The estate has one
spelling for that, `owner/repo[@ref]:path`, which a toss, a stage and a
data view all read, so "copy address" hands over the qualified form
rather than a path that means nothing outside this repo. Copying the
contents costs no fetch: the slide already read the file into docCache,
keyed by the same ref this menu quotes.

The fifth row is the strip's "files view" door, and it keeps its words.
As a bare icon in the header it would promise a direction and name no
destination, which on a surface with no tooltips is a worse trade than
one extra row in a menu the reader opened on purpose.

The address as a HINT, which is a different job from the address. The
row still copies all forty characters of the SHA, the one place the
conventions call being approximately right being wrong; this line only
has to let a reader recognize what they are about to copy.

So it is budgeted from the RIGHT, which is the lesson kits/file-deck.js
learned about a deep path: CSS truncates from the right,
so the untouched address spent its whole width on `owner/repo@` plus
thirty-three characters of hex and dropped `:docs/APP.md`, the only
part that says WHICH FILE. Shortening the SHA was not enough on a
phone; the owner and repo had to go too, and they are the third a
reader of this menu already knows, since every row in the deck is this
hub's. The leading ellipsis says the copied value is longer.

IT HANGS OFF ITS OWN BUTTON. Pinned to the panel's right edge it
dropped from under the counter pill, two controls away from the thing
that opened it, which reads as a panel that arrived on its own. The
kit hands an action its button for exactly this. Falling back to the
header's measured height keeps it sane if a caller ever fires the
action from somewhere other than the header.

The elided hint in full, for a reader with a pointer. A phone gets
nothing from this and loses nothing by it.

Dismissal, and the Escape half is not decoration: the deck listens for
Escape on the window to close itself, so without a capture-phase
listener here the key would take the whole takeover down while a menu
was the only thing the reader meant to shut.
Next frame, so the click that opened this does not immediately close it.

A normal folder needs no extra context; a corpus-wide query does,
because its slides can come from several directories.

Reach: the derived channel by which a reader gets to a doc. The counts
are the tab's headline because they are the one number here that moves
when the estate improves: point a skill or a page at an orphan and it
leaves the orphan column. Tapping a count filters the registry to it, so
"which 18 are orphans" is one tap rather than a scan.

Mass, alongside the counts. A channel's file count says how many docs
sit there; its share says how much of the folder they are. The two
point in different directions here, which is the reason both render.

── Skills ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Two authored columns and nothing else, so the tab earns its place on
one affordance rather than on richness: the description IS the trigger
text a session matches against, so searching it answers "is there a
skill for this?", which 35 SKILL.md files and no index could not.

Name and description both, because a reader searching for a capability
has the words of the task, not the slug. Matching the description is
the whole point of holding it here.
── Outside skills ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Public, so it renders without a token. Matching runs on the id and the
rationale, the words a reader would search with.

A vendored or adapted copy ships in skills/, so it is one of Yours and
carries its origin there as a Source link; counting it here too would
be the double count the Yours set exists to end.

An upstream's address: a GitHub folder at its pinned commit, or the
page it was found on when it lives elsewhere.

The row a copied skill came from, joined on the registry's `ours`, so
the origin is stated once and a Plugin or Library row only points at it.

── The agent roster ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
Four sets on one tab row: the critics and the review panel's seats the
plugin ships, the readers hub skills spawn, and every other repo's own
agents from the crawl. A reader is grouped under the skill that spawns
it, since that skill's text is its prompt.

Icons arrive after the cards, the way the shell's project icons
do: a glyph stands in until each SVG is read, and a failed read
leaves the glyph rather than holding the roster back.

Token-gated and silent on failure, as the estate skills are: the
roster is public and renders without a token, minus this set.
the hub's own are the roster

moves a branch in an estate repository, with what starts it, the machine

The picked question rides in the address as ?setintent= while Set is
open (syncSetAddress), so a link or a reload opens on it.
The machine boxes, in order, with their labels, icons and glosses: docs/machines.csv.
A ref older than the machines registry still draws, one bare box per machine.
What each writer commits with, for its card; a ref older than the registry has none.
The intents are a lens on the diagram, so the diagram draws without them.

A machine's label and gloss are docs/machines.csv's. A page names no
machine: it runs in whatever browser opens it.

One box per machine in the registry's order, then one for the pages,
which run in whatever browser opens them.

An intent lights one path through the diagram, from what starts it to
where it lands, as a picked box lights what it touches; choosing either
clears the other. Off the path, boxes fade, so the path reads at a glance.

The shell owns the address (app/index.html, setMapCtx) and stamps
setintent only while Set is open.
The stacked box is the map pane's visible height under the pinned tabs.

On a phone a pick brings the box under the tabs and the diagram pane
to the path's first writer, so the lit path is in view.

Shown while the question is chosen, hover or not, so the boxes do not
move under the pointer.

Lit: the key itself, or anything one line away from what is hot. A
start lights its writers, a writer its starts, the writers it starts
and where it sets. Stacked there are no lines, so only the key itself is.
The card's rows, which say in words what the lines draw.

A program a person works through reads as authored by design; anything
else reading as authored is the residual, flagged.

The paths a writer sets on main directly, by docs/direct-to-main.csv's
`writer` column.

Lines between the boxes the grid placed, side by side only. A start
runs to its writer, a writer to each place it sets, and one writer to a
writer it starts by a loop out to the left of the column, so the loop
never crosses a box. A writer that finds its start by polling is dashed.
An intent lights the lines between consecutive steps of its path only.

── Relations: the joins between registries ─────────────────────────────
Each registry that holds another's keys, or is held, is a card; the
joins are docs/properties.csv's references column. A group is the
registries joined to one another, a registry's column is one past
every registry that references it, and a self-reference stays on its
card. relationsMeasure draws the lines once the grid has placed the
cards, as writersMeasure does for the Set tab.

── Watch: what to keep an eye on ───────────────────────────────────────
Triggers is one row per path by which something other than the owner
can make a machine run code, grouped by the machine it reaches. Public
is every file of the public repo with the marks the scan found in it;
Names is the email addresses in every checkout, grouped by domain. All
of it is read from the registry repo, at main unless ?regref= names
another ref.

What was decided about a path's worst case: kept on purpose, to narrow
to what the job needs, or narrowed. A row with none has no decision.

── Scheduled: the estate's scheduled tasks ─────────────────────────────
One row per task in the registry repo's data/design/scheduled-tasks.csv,
grouped by the machine that runs it. A task the registry schedules
itself carries its stages (scheduled-task-stages.csv) as a ladder,
cheapest first, each with the condition to go on and the outcome when
it stops: progressive action. Once the runner has written its state,
each stage shows how many targets reached it on the last run. Read
at main unless ?regref= names another ref, as the Context tab's
private half is.

A dispatched workflow's own file and newest run, read beside the
registry and non-fatally: the file says which events start it besides
the scheduled-tasks workflow, and whether it still carries a cron of its own (the one
thing the registry cannot see); the run is its last run of any kind,
the same reading the scheduled-tasks workflow makes to decide whether it is due.

The registry's `schedule` is cron in UTC (web-tools-private README,
"Scheduled tasks"). Parsed here as python/scheduled-tasks.py parses it, read into
words for the shapes the registry uses, and stepped forward for the
next firing, which is shown in the reader's own time.

The lines under the schedule: what else starts the task, what the
scheduled-tasks workflow passes it, and a workflow that still keeps a cron of its own.

── Changing a schedule ─────────────────────────────────────────────
The pickers speak local time and write UTC cron, which is what the
registry holds. A cron the pickers cannot express opens as Cron, so
nothing is rewritten by being opened. Save rewrites the one row's
`schedule` and `status` cells in the file as the tab read it, guarded
by the blob sha: a row or a file that moved since is refused, never
overwritten.
The cron the pickers name: a local hour on a local day, read back in UTC.

── The owner's pet peeves ────────────────────────────────────────────
Reviewed entries keep their source IDs for search, references and quotes.

The find lands the deck on the exchange, so it takes the opening
words only as far as they are plain: a curly quote or a dash in the
record would not match a straightened copy.

The library above is the hub's. This is every OTHER repo's committed

cards use, so the tab answers "is there a skill for this?" across the

Token-gated and silent on failure, like the Docs tab's readership: the

this section. A repo that declares nothing contributes no group, which
is the ordinary case rather than a gap.
the hub's own set IS the plugin

carries different fields: Yours as cards, the estate as name chips
under their repo, third parties as status cards. They now share one

Yours joins skills/manifest.csv (name, subject, trigger text) to
docs/portable.csv (the command a session types).
Until 2026-10-12 those were two sets, Your plugin and Your skills, of

The plugin's one-line role, or nothing. The trigger text is not a

A third party's SKILL.md: our held copy when we keep one, else the

Two small reads, each optional: a failed fetch leaves the Retired group
and the demo badges off rather than taking the tab down with it.

A retired skill has no subject and belongs to Yours, so a subject chip

An app view, the same door a kit demo opens through (kitDemoHref).

and the search box, so either strip says where the matches are before

Order is a reading order, not a count order: what the skill acts ON,

One line per set, carrying the rule rather than the history: what

The headline: what the search and both axes found, over what the

Sections by subject, in the reading order, then Unsorted; within one,
Yours first, then the estate, then third parties, each in source order.
docs/hook-legs.csv rows, read beside the harness registry

The dimensions the Gallery filters by, each a row of chips, and the

The Gallery section whose header is held at the top of the pane, and

The held header's height, where the current-card strip pins under it.
The unit the open deck shows, ringed among the Gallery's cards.

unit -> { desk, phone, store }
Which shot the cards show. Blank until the tab loads, then the one this

Any other dimension, split as frame is, so a dimension

test path -> [comparison rows]; null while absent or unread

Non-fatal on its own, the same posture as the growth payload on

rather than in the CSV itself, so the declaration and the rows say
the same thing. Then the drift: each row carries the blob hash of
its script as read, and one tree fetch says which scripts have
moved since. Both non-fatal; the rows render without them.

The join key is the `script` column and nothing else: a row's `where`
(function, section, line) is descriptive and never parsed. The first
cut joined on the text before the first space or punctuation mark in
one combined column, and a trailing comma was enough to make a row
count and not attach; the count said every row was attached because

Set of scripts whose blob hash moved; null while unknown
One tree fetch per repo, then a hash comparison per explained script.

an unstamped row makes no claim

carries both, split at the first comma.

What a repo's group shows, with the two absences told apart: a file

file whose reading says it stops nowhere is NOT A CHECK. Rows whose

Browser checks are counted as files and excluded from the assertion

The registry's test_count column counts test() declarations.

Mobile innerWidth can include offscreen shell content. The client

Focus once the panel stands where it will stay, so the ✕'s own

Invalidate a hover whose kit is still loading.

A qualification a row carries, filtered as a SECOND axis rather than
folded into the kind strip: a boot check and a browser check are not

These two used to be a sentence under the totals, which stated in prose

One labeled row per dimension, each row's chips carrying files and, where

One selection per dimension, so the three compose as an AND.

Which of a row's assertions are boot checks, as a Set for the list to

The suite as the strip has cut it, flattened out of its groups. The

A CHECK IS A DOCUMENT HERE, which is the whole reason the row moved off

`key` carries the filter, since two different cuts are two different
sets and a deck reopened on the same key would page the old one.

Non-fatal on its own, as the Docs tab's growth payload is: the
steps open one row, and a missing file costs that row its list.

The rail: every folder that holds a registry row, counts rolled up to
ancestors the same way the Docs rail rolls words, with the blank-role
count as the second figure. The invocation filter re-weights it.

A trigger folds its routes: the prefixed families (npm:showing,
git:pre-commit, ci:pull_request) match on the family, the bare routes
exactly.

path -> { events?, hand? }: each trigger a file reaches, valued '' for
its own route or the caller it reaches the trigger through. The suite
(node/test/) runs by npm test and in test.yml, so it carries both; a
document stands for a reader running the command it gives.

The caller a file reaches the picked trigger through, named for the
file list; blank when the file's own route is the trigger.
caller -> the files it runs, for the Events view.

A view trigger opens its address; a file trigger filters the inventory
(a second tap clears it) and moves the rail to the folder holding most
of its files when the open folder holds none.

The board: phases in the order the registry first names them, each
event with the registrations on it. A registration names the script
its command runs; the dispatcher's own row lists the session-*.sh
files it runs, which docs/harness.csv routes as session:SessionStart.

The release month, as Mar '26: the apostrophe keeps the year from
reading as a day. The registry keeps the whole date.

The kinds of event, in the order a change meets them. Claude Code's is
the board above; the others group docs/harness.csv's event-fired files
by the event their route names, in EVENT_WORDS's order.

A git hook's filename is its event, so a file under an env or git
event is named by its path rather than repeating the event.
What a file runs is listed under it, except the commit hook's, whose
steps already say it.

── A hook file's panel-tip ──────────────────────────────────────────
The Context tab's contract (showCtxTip): hover opens after 140 ms on a
fine pointer, a click or a tap pins, kits/panel-tip.js closes it. Keyed
by path; a registration whose command names no file is keyed by its
command and shows only where it runs.
The panel's content as a chain rather than as labelled rows: what
starts the file, the file, and what it starts, joined by arrows that
say "runs" so no label has to. A file a dispatcher runs takes its
place after the dispatcher.
A file's name: its panel-tip opens; the same name again closes it.

The Harness Automation subview's door, in the Docs Inventory shape: a
folder rail, a selected folder, and its direct files as filtered.

A part's value is a locator (owner/repo:path), a container path
(~/...), or words for an observation that arrives by hand. A folder
opens the tree; a file opens through the peek like every other tab.
The account's skills, needing attention first, each with its declared note.

The filter strip. The first two are facts a reader browses by; the
last three are the warning states, counted here so the figure the tab
exists to show is on the strip and not only in the row tone, and the
only pills that carry a tone.

The demo opens as an APP VIEW of this app rather than as a bare page:
the frame stack then reads app over renderer over page in the FAB's
layer strip, and every take the drawer offers aims at the demo. The
same door a promoted page gets; a kit demo is one this repo promotes.

An unchecked copy or paraphrase is the fact this tab exists to show,
so it renders in the warning tone; a pointer or live read needs no
check and stays neutral.

bare: drop the demo chrome (heading, helper, last-inserted panel) so the
picker embeds inside another component as a pure path designator.

roots: optional [{repo, ref?, label?}] (a bare "owner/repo" string is
accepted too). When present the picker opens one level up, at a choice
of repository: the chosen repo is the first path segment, so a single @
designates a fully-qualified path across repos. The mention-select
detail always carries repo/ref/path split apart, whatever the mode.
Absent: the picker follows the open repo through the shared browser
store, as before. Both are the same mechanism, one layer taller.

Repo-first: the root set is an explicit, mount-time argument, so the
picker does not follow the shared browser store.

Re-fetch the tree whenever the shared browser store points at a
different repo or ref, mirroring navigator/explorer/pages.

One recursive tree call per (repo, ref), the same primitive the Files
view uses, folded into the nested {name, children} shape the picker
walks.

Repo-first load: fetch each root repo's tree and present the set as the
top level, each repo a folder-shaped node ({kind:'repo', repo, ref})
whose children are that repo's own tree. Eager (one recursive tree call
per root) so typed and clicked navigation both resolve without a
mid-descent fetch; the root set is small (the open repo plus configured
targets). A root that fails to load still appears, empty.

Flat git-tree entries ({path, type:'blob'|'tree'}) → nested nodes.
Folders carry a children[]; files do not. Parent dirs are created on
demand so entry order does not matter.
Notify a host page that a reference was committed.

The chosen file as {repo, ref, path}. In repo-first mode the scope's
first node is the repo, so split it off: repo/ref come from that node
and path is the remainder. Otherwise the whole scope lives within the
open repo (the shared store's repo/ref).

A tap-through repo/path selector: a button-shaped trigger opens a navigable
tree panel right below (repos, then folders, then files), and selection is
taps all the way down — crumbs jump back up, "Here" commits a folder. Where
mention embeds a path inside prose (type @ mid-text), this component is for
the case where the path is the whole point. Anchored to the trigger rather
than a bottom sheet, so it stays inside the mobile viewport with visible
boundaries.

NO TEXT INPUT OF ITS OWN, which is not the same as no filtering. An input
here would invite the keyboard and iOS's focus zoom for what is mostly
navigation, and where a host already has a field (an address box the user is
typing in), a second one is worse than none. So the component owns `query`
and `active` but never renders a box: a host feeds keystrokes in through
setQuery/move/commitActive, and a host without a field just taps. The
scoring, the containers-first ordering, and the always-set active row are
mention's, deliberately, so the two pickers filter the same way.

Options:
  mode: 'file' (default) — choosing a file emits it and stays open for the
        next grab; 'dir' — the target is a folder: "Here" commits the
        current folder, and a file tap commits its containing folder.
  roots: [{repo, ref?, label?}], or a function returning them, or an async
        function, awaited lazily at first open (roots often resolve after
        mount: config, quick links, or a token-gated repo listing).
  placeholder, value: the trigger's idle label and initial committed label.
  trigger: false — render the PANEL ONLY and let the host own the opener.
        The built-in trigger is a btn-block, right where the path IS the
        control; a host whose chrome already names the path (the fab's render
        tab, where it sits in a compact row beside a menu) would otherwise
        have to show that path twice. The instance publishes itself on its
        root element as __pathPicker, so the host's own control calls
        toggle() on it.
  dense: true — tighter rows and smaller type, for a host with a narrow
        panel (the fab's drawer). Every row keeps a title with its full name,
        dense or not, since truncation is what a narrow panel buys.
  inline: true — the panel is part of the page rather than a dropdown: open
        from the start, no close button, filling its host's height. For a
        host whose job IS the tree (the project and repo Files views,
        alpineComponents/file-browser.js).
  base: {repo, ref?, dir?} — start inside that folder and never climb above
        it: the crumbs begin at the base, "Up" stops there, and `roots` is
        not consulted. The picker enters the repo and descends on first
        open, so a project's tree opens on the project.
  start: a folder under the base (a path from the repo root) to open on,
        with the floor still at the base: a repo's tree opening on the
        folder of a file it was asked to show, with the crumbs above it
        still walkable.
  gh: a GH instance, or a function returning one. The component's one hidden
        dependency used to be Alpine's `browser` store, which exists on
        the app and nowhere else; that quietly limited a general picker to
        one page. The store is still the default, so no existing caller
        changes.

A repo's tree loads when it is ENTERED, not at first open. It used to be the
other way round, on the reasoning that the root set was small and descent
should never pause. That reasoning inverted the moment a caller wanted to
offer every repo a token can see: one recursive tree call per root, up the
front, for the ninety-nine repos you were not going to open. Now the root
list costs nothing to show and one call to enter, so a roots list can be as
long as the caller likes.

Host-driven filtering (all no-ops for a host that does not use them):
  setQuery(text)   filter the current level; resets the active row to the top
  move(delta)      move the active row, wrapping
  commitActive()   choose the active row: descend a container, emit a file
  query, active    read them to render a hint or mirror state

Events (bubbling, from $root):
  path-pick — file mode: {repo, ref, path}; dir mode: {repo, ref, dir, spec}
  path-descend — after entering a container, so a host can clear its query

Registered at once when Alpine is already running (the fab's drawer, which
mounts this, is loaded after a page's own chain since 2026-09-02), and on
alpine:init otherwise.

A host that owns its own opener passes trigger:false; the panel then
anchors to whatever wrapper the host put this mount in.

Row density. The default is sized for touch in a full-width form, which
is where this picker started; dropped into a 22rem drawer those rows
eat the panel and truncate every name. `dense` is a host declaring it
has less width to give, not a preference: the tap target stays a row,
it just stops being 40 px tall.

with a base, the scope depth the reader cannot climb above
file mode: the last picked path, marked in the list
Always a real row, so Tab and Enter always have something to commit.

The trigger is a button, not an input: no keyboard, no iOS
focus zoom. It shows the last committed pick, else the idle
label.

A committed pick stacks: the repo on top, its @ref:dir under
it. One line could not hold all three on a phone, so the
branch and the folder were the parts that got truncated away,
which are exactly the parts a deposit is scoped by. A label
that is not a repo address (file mode, a bare path) has no
second part and renders as the single line it always was.

The FOLDER holds its ground and the branch truncates: a
branch name is long and recognizable from its front, while
the folder is short and is the half that answers "where
does this land". Truncating the whole line dropped the
folder first, which is backwards.

Two glyphs, not one rotated: a utility that only ever arrives by
toggling a class is never generated by Tailwind's browser build,
so this caret silently never turned.

Compact crumb row: a repo crumb shows its short name (full
name in the tooltip) so deep paths fit a phone width. Actions
bind to click, not pointerdown, so a touch that starts a
scroll never triggers them.

The count needs a loaded array; the caret only needs the
row to be enterable, which a repo is before it loads.

Shown only when a host is driving from a field: with taps alone
there are no keys to advertise.

Roots resolve lazily at first open, so sets that arrive after mount are
seen: config, quick links, or an awaited repo listing. A root node
starts with children === null, meaning "not loaded yet"; entering it
fills them in (see loadRepo).

Walk into the base: the repo, then each folder of `dir`. The floor is
where that walk ends, so the crumbs and "Up" treat it as the top. A
folder the tree does not have (renamed, or not on this ref) stops the
walk where it failed and says so, rather than showing the repo root as
though it were the folder.

A tree that could not be read already says so; the folder walk
would only replace that reason with a wrong one.

Then on to the start folder, when it lies under the base; a start
outside it is ignored rather than allowed to lift the floor.
A node's path inside its repo, for marking the picked file.

One repo's tree, on entry. Failure leaves an empty repo rather than a
broken picker: the row above it still reads, and the panel says Empty.
A root with no ref reads where the selection puts its repo.

The current level, filtered and ranked. Same scoring as mention:
exact, then prefix, then substring, containers before leaves, original
order breaking ties. An unranked substring match is what makes typing a
filename work without knowing where it sits in the list.

── host-driven filtering ───────────────────────────────────────────
The component keeps no input of its own; a host with a field pushes
keystrokes in here. Any query change puts the active row back at the
top, so the highlighted row is always the best current match.

The committed label, split for the two-line trigger: the repo, and
everything that scopes it. Regex rather than RepoAddress.parse because
this must also survive a label that is NOT an address (file mode
commits a bare path), which the parser rejects and the trigger still
has to render.
The current scope as a destination: null until a repo is entered.

An unentered repo loads here. Nothing is awaited for a node that is
already loaded, so descent stays synchronous in the common case.

A new level starts unfiltered, with the top row active. The event
lets a host reset its own field to match.
A file names its folder: the current scope is the destination.
File mode: emit the pick, stay open in place for the next grab.

Walking back up is a level change like descending, so the filter and the
active row reset with it. Otherwise a query typed three folders down
silently keeps filtering the level you just returned to.

One PowerShell or XAML file: the source in the editor, read-only until Edit,
with its browser draft, its Problems and its Outline beside it. The same
component serves two hosts, both in powershell-outpost-view.js:

  the file deck    one per slide (openFileDeck). The deck owns the header,

                   for the rest. Editing pauses the swipe, because a
                   horizontal drag in code selects text or scrolls a line.
  the view         one inline in the PowerShell outpost view, beside the
                   selected file's state (fileCtx). It draws the same
                   actions in its own bar after the view's Copy, puts Open
                   full screen in its menu, and keeps one
                   editor view across selections: show(item) swaps the
                   text in place.

Edits are browser drafts (PowerShellWorkspace.saveDraft). The PowerShell
outpost view lists them and publishes them together to a new branch;
nothing here writes to GitHub or records an observation.

The deck mounts it per slide by setAttribute('x-data', 'powershellFile()'),
the slide element carrying its context as `__psFile` ({ ctx, item, index }),
the back-pointer idiom docs/loader.md describes. The PowerShell outpost view
passes its context as the argument: x-data="powershellFile(fileCtx())".

With the host's tab row above (outerTabs), the bar is a header
row like the host's Changes strip: what the box holds, then
its actions.

Class bindings, not x-show: x-show defers a hide to the next
frame, so a quick flip between panes left the wrong one shown.

A host with its own tab row (ctx.outerTabs) shows these panes there,
so the component's tab list hides and the host reads `panes` and

The PowerShell outpost view's own hooks, so its tests and drop ring reach the parts
they name: the tab list, the editor box, its <pre>.

The deck steps slides on Left/Right and dismisses on Escape at the
window. Inside the editor those keys are the editor's.

Load a file into this instance. The deck calls it once per slide; the
PowerShell outpost view on every selection, so its one editor view is reused.
Back to the pinned GitHub source, not the draft's older base.
── Actions: the deck header when on screen, else this pane's own bar ─
Inline, Copy GitHub text is a button in the bar, so the menu leaves it out.

The PowerShell outpost view, shown in the Outpost tab of a project that
declares a PowerShell outpost manifest: one workspace's PowerShell material,
each file with where it is meant to go on the work computer and what has been
observed about the copy there. The work computer has no Git checkout, so
every fact about it arrives by hand:
a pasted or dropped work copy (the comparison flow, lib/kits/
file-correspondence.js, which stays browser-local), or a confirmed "I placed
this on the work computer", which lib/kits/powershell-outpost.js appends to the
workspace's observations.csv. The derivation is the kit's; this file is the
surface, and its one rule is that no gesture but the confirm writes.

npm test opens no browser, so a change to the file pane or the editor also
needs `npm run test:powershell-outpost-source` and `npm run test:powershell-file`.

Mounts by the crumb-bar idiom (template injected in init, then initTree),
reads the open project from the argument the pane passes, and reaches the
shell for the comparison hand-off.

One icon per file, in the list and the detail header, carrying the
state a reader acts on. "local state unknown" reads as Work set, a
dashed circle in no colour: the file as the repository holds it, taken
as what the work computer has. It names where the file came from and
claims no check, which a green "Assumed synced" did until 2026-10-13.
An observation confirmation is a filled check. The observations file and
the manifest are unchanged; this is how the list shows them. Titles stay
at two words, the repo's rule for an icon's label
(powershell-outpost-view.test.mjs).
The icons are the estate's shared tones (kits/sync-status.js), so a
shortcut behind GitHub and a file behind GitHub read the same.

The Office applications' marks, for the application pills. Phosphor has
no OneNote mark, so OneNote takes a notebook; an application outside
Office takes a plain window.

The adoption stages. Each state the kit derives belongs to one stage,
and the stage is what a row's icon, the State filters and a module's
count show: Work set, the repository's file taken as what the work
computer has; Shipped, a change on GitHub the work computer has not
adopted; Adopted, a recorded placement or a matching copy; Differs, a
recorded difference. The state's detail stays in the label, which the
status menu and the status line carry.

The status icon and its menu: tap or right-click. `side` anchors the
menu so it opens into the pane rather than off its edge. `part` is a
data-part for a list row's copy, which declares the menu its actions.

The whole-file line diff's rows, baseline against GitHub's text: the
Diff tab's body, and Changes' own for a file the parser cannot split.

One changed block, the card the Changes strip shows and the full-screen
deck renders in each slide (openChangeDeck, by addScopeToNode with `u`
and `deck`). The diff is always open: a change is what the card is for.
In the strip the card has a fixed height and its diff scrolls; in the
deck the slide scrolls.

A block's unchanged lines stay, for context; the strip opens the
card scrolled to its first changed line.

The source pane is the file component the deck uses
(alpineComponents/powershell-file.js), mounted inline once per detail

The Proposals view: pending cross-repo edits an agent session could not
make itself, waiting on the user's token and the user's say-so.

The channel is lib/kits/repo-proposals.js (proposals/pending -> applied in the
registry repo); this is only the review surface. Two rules shape it:

  Nothing applies without a confirm. The estate's other cached reads run
  on load because they read; this writes to a repo the session could not
  reach, so every apply is a two-tap gesture, the same one the stage's
  cross-repo copy uses.
  Show the bytes, not a description of them. Each row resolves against
  the target's current file and displays the exact content the write
  will send, so a reviewer confirms what happens rather than what was
  promised. For the JSON kinds that is a before/after on one key, which
  is the whole edit; for put-file it is a line diff via the shared
  text-diff kit (side-by-side panes when a diff cannot be computed). A
  removal reuses the JSON pane, with `(removed)` on the after side, since
  the edit it describes is the same shape.

Public browse: a no-token file browser for any PUBLIC GitHub repo. The
listing is one anonymous GitHub API call (GH.flatTree, git trees recursive)
and a file's bytes come from raw.githubusercontent (GH.rawUrl), which is not
rate-limited. This is the intentional non-auth capability of the app: the
GitHub API allows 60 anonymous requests an hour, and a browse spends one of
them rather than one per folder. It works signed in too, but earns its place
in the public case. Limits: public repos only, and a repo too large for one
tree response lists truncated. Registered as Alpine.data('publicBrowse').

alpineComponents/quick-find.js — the sidebar's always-ready finder.

One input at the top of the sidebar, sitting ready on desktop and one drawer
tap away on a phone. It is a DISPATCHER over what the app already holds, not
a search engine: every lane resolves from client-side state or a cached
read, and nothing is indexed or committed anywhere. The query's shape picks
the lane:

  #123 or 123     a PR in ANY state, estate-wide (the activity cache's
                  openPRs plus its any-state branchPRs index), the row
                  marked merged / closed / draft / ready; `#` alone lists
                  the OPEN ones, since that question is "what is in
                  flight". Opens the branch-detail takeover, the same
                  reader an Open row's name opens.
  @               repo-then-file NAVIGATION, the mention picker's reading
                  of the trigger: `@` lists the estate repos, picking one
                  completes to `@repo/` and lists that repo's root, folders
                  complete deeper, a file opens. Typing past the slash
                  filters the current folder AND fuzzy-matches the whole
                  tree, so `@web-tools/ghapi` lands on lib/gh-api.js
                  without walking. One recursive tree call per repo, cached
                  (the stage's Browse/Search share this economy).
  owner/repo[@ref]:path   a pasted address (RepoAddress, the estate's one
                  grammar) opens the file; the repo half accepts the short
                  name when exactly one estate repo matches. `repo@branch`
                  opens that branch's takeover. PASTE-ONLY lanes: they
                  resolve exactly and suggest nothing, because nobody types
                  a branch name from memory hoping for IntelliSense
                  (measured: the suggestion lists were noise).
  +idea           an explicit jot: the one row is "Jot this", Enter files it.
  anything else   substring match over estate repos, the app's nav
                  (estateNav + appNav), FILE NAMES in every estate repo, and
                  open PR titles. File names come from the registry's index
                  (state/files.json, lib/kits/file-index.js), read once on
                  first focus, so every repo answers on the first keystroke
                  with no tree read. A registry with no index yet falls back
                  to the trees already cached (the open repo's loads on first
                  use) behind a "File names, every repo" tap.
                  Two DEEPER passes ride a tap gate. "File
                  contents" ROUTES to the Search view (shell.goSearch) with
                  the query carried over: a content search wants parameters
                  and room for results, which a panel does not have, and
                  its caveats (Markdown only, default branches) live there.
                  "Sessions" greps the captured records in place
                  (EstateSearch.sessions: search.py's --grep in the
                  browser, hits opening the Sessions pane's reader via
                  web-tools:open-session). A ran search's rows replace the
                  lanes while the query stays put, under a clear row that
                  dismisses them; editing a character falls back. Every
                  fetch and cache is lib/kits/estate-search.js, shared with the
                  Search view, so neither surface pays twice.

RESULTS ARE GROUPED AND REPLACE THE SIDEBAR LIST. Each kind of answer sits
under its own heading with its count (Go to, Files, Pull requests, Search

takes the sidebar's height and the repo list under it hides (the `finder`
store), rather than a dropdown floating over it at 60% of the screen.

The registry's file index, once per page through the shared core

── Session search: the shared core's grep, kept in-panel ────────────
The corpus is small and the reader (the Sessions pane's paged

The index kit, loaded on the tap that asks for it. The lane reads

Every PR the cache knows of, in any state: the open rows above plus

per repo would crowd it with history. So the number lane reads this
and the text lane keeps to what is open.
The immediate children of `dir` in a flat path list: folders first.

which can exceed what it shows.

── The floor: nothing typed here is lost ─────────────────────────

A folder the index holds as a count: the Search view lists it, one
