alpineComponents/ref-picker.js — pick a ref OF A GIVEN REPO.

The estate already had three branch lists and none of them fit a fourth
caller, for one reason each:

  explorer.js's dropdown   bound to the browser store, so it can only ever
  repo.js's refDropdown    offer refs of the ONE repo the shell is browsing.
                           They are markup siblings of each other and say so.
  ref-switch.js            answers a different question entirely: which ref
                           the PAGE is running from. It navigates.

A view that scopes to any repo, the Search view being the first, needs the
list without either constraint: a repo handed in, and a picked ref handed
back, with no navigation and no store. That is the whole of this component.

PICKING IS THE VERB, typing is the fallback, which is the inverse of
ref-switch's arrangement and deliberate. There the box is the primary control
because the state it serves best is the default branch, where you know the
name of where you are going. Here you are reading files and choosing among
what exists, so the list leads and the box above it filters. A name that is
not in the list (a tag, a sha, a branch past the scan's reach) is still
reachable: the box offers to take it as typed, which is what keeps this a
picker with a paste in it rather than a picker instead of one.

Options (each may be a value or a function, read fresh on every open, since a
host's scope changes under a mounted picker):
  repo        'owner/name'. Empty disables the trigger: there is no branch
              list for "no repo", and offering one would be a lie.
  ref         the ref currently chosen; '' means the default branch, which
              is the honest empty (RepoAddress's rule: resolve late)
  defaultRef  the repo's default branch, when the host knows it
  onPick      (ref) => void. '' is handed back for the default branch, never
              the branch's name, so the host keeps the late-resolving form
  gh          a GH instance or a factory; defaults to the browser store's,
              re-pointed at `repo`

The scan runs ON DEMAND (hover, focus, or open) and once per repo: a view
nobody opens the control on pays nothing, and switching repos and back does
not re-fetch. branchesDated gives dates and the newest-first order that makes
the list worth reading; a tokenless or GraphQL-less caller degrades to the
REST list, undated and alphabetical, which is stated rather than hidden.

The instance publishes itself on its root element as __refPicker.
the repo the rows describe, so a repo switch re-scans
false once a scan has degraded to the REST list

The box FILTERS. It is not the way in, it is the way past a
list that is long or that does not hold what you want.

Offered only for something the list does not already hold, so
it never competes with a row one line below it.

The default branch, as itself. It is picked as '' rather than
by name, so a scope that means "whatever this repo calls its
default" keeps meaning that when the repo changes.

The trigger reads as the answer to "which ref", so an unset ref shows
what unset MEANS rather than showing nothing.

A typed value worth offering: only when the list has nothing to give
you. While anything still matches, the rows ARE the answer, and a "Use
newer" button one line above a `claude/newer` row is two ways to say
one thing where only the row is certainly a real ref. So the fallback
appears exactly where a picker runs out: a sha, a tag, a branch past
the scan's reach.

Two branches can share a tail, so the prefix stays, dimmed, rather than
being dropped: ref-switch's treatment, for the same reason.

A GraphQL failure is not a dead end here, only a poorer list, so
it degrades rather than reporting. What is NOT hidden is that it
degraded: the panel says so under the rows.

alpineComponents/ref-switch.js — the header control that says which ref this page is RUNNING AT, and switches it. The fab already answers this question, and answers it more fully: its launcher goes warning-tinted off the default branch, and its Render tab scans every branch carrying a different copy of the page. What the fab does not do is sit still. It is a floating disc that has to be opened before it says anything, and the ref a page is running at is the kind of fact that wants to be legible without a tap, in the chrome, beside everything else that says where you are. That is the whole of this component: the same fact and the same two verbs, promoted into a header. It is deliberately NOT a second scan. Three things only: 1. PASTE A REF. A text box, ALWAYS PRESENT, that takes a branch, tag or sha and goes on Enter. This is the primary verb, so it is not behind a tap: the state it serves best is the default branch, where there is nothing to report and everything to do, and a control that has to be opened first puts a door in front of the one thing it exists for. It is also the case the fab's scan list serves worst, since a branch you know the name of is quicker to paste than to find among three hundred rows. 2. RIDING. The same box is the readout: it holds the ref the page is running at as its VALUE, and goes warning-tinted off the default branch, with a house button beside it back to the live page. One slot answers "what am I running" and "take me somewhere else", rather than a chip and a field competing for the same corner. 3. NEWEST. One button that jumps to the most recently committed branch, the branch you are almost always looking for during a session. It hides itself once the scan says the newest branch IS the default one. The caret at the box's right opens the branch list, which is a convenience over the box rather than the way in. THE REF IT SWITCHES IS THE PAGE'S OWN, not the browsed repo's. On the app those are two different things and confusing them would be easy: the Files view's ref picker chooses which ref of mehrlander/home you are READING, while this chooses which ref of mehrlander/the app itself is RUNNING. So the panel names the repo and path it acts on, every time. HOW IT SWITCHES. Not with ?use= alone. ?use= re-pins the lib a page loads, which reaches dist/ and lib/ but never the page's own inline shell, so a branch that edits this header would preview as the old header. The toss is what swaps the shell: #gh=@:[?] The @ addresses the page AND pins its lib, since toss-render injects use= into a page of the hub. Until 2026-09-28 the switch also put ?use= on the renderer's own query, to pin the renderer's lib (its fab, its peek) to the same ref. That pin kills Safari's web process on an iPhone whenever the renderer hosts a frame (the snag shell-pin-kills-the-tab), and python/showing.py stopped minting it on 2026-09-08; this component kept minting it for twenty days. The cost of dropping it is that the drawer around a switched view is main's, which the fab's layer strip says. The page's current deep link rides along as the trailing ?query when the host supplies one, so switching refs lands you on the screen you were already looking at rather than at the page's front door. Usage:
repo the repo the PAGE lives in (not the one it is browsing) path the page's path within it defaultRef the guess until the scan lands; 'main' query function returning the page's current deep-link query string, carried into the switch. Omit and the switch lands at the page's default state renderer the toss renderer's URL; defaults to the deployed one The reads are the same two the fab makes (branchesForPath, degrading to branchesDated when there is no token), and they run ON DEMAND: hovering the opener starts the load, so by the time a pointer has traveled to the button the list is usually there, and a page nobody touches the control on pays nothing. The pure parts (URL construction, picking the newest) are on window.RefSwitch, where node/test/ref-switch.test.mjs reads them.

The one renderer. Hardcoded rather than derived because it is a property of
the estate, not of the page mounting this: a page in any repo tosses
through web-tools' deployed toss-render, the way fab.js does.

The switch address: the page addressed at the ref, and nothing on the
renderer's own query (see the note above).

The live page: the canonical github.io URL for a repo/path, which is what
"return to main" means for a Pages-served page. Empty for a repo that is
not Pages-served, and the caller falls back to dropping ?use= in place.

The most recently committed branch that is not the default one. The rows
arrive newest-first from branchesDated/branchesForPath, but sorting here
rather than trusting that keeps the pick honest against a caller that
filtered or re-ordered. Null when the default branch IS the newest, which
is what hides the button: "jump to the newest branch" is not an offer worth
making when the newest branch is the one you are already on.

An UNDATED row can never win, and that is the whole answer for the
token-free fallback: REST's branch list carries no commit date, so every
row ties, and a tie broken by array order would send "newest" to whichever
branch GitHub happened to list first. Undated rows are still perfectly
selectable by hand; they are just not evidence about which is newest.

Newest. Shown until the scan says otherwise, since before the
load there is no way to know whether the newest branch is the
default one, and an affordance that appears after a hover is
worse than one that quietly stops appearing.

── The phone trigger: one glyph, and the panel is the control ──
Below sm the three header slots collapse into this. A 10 rem
box was tried first and is the wrong trade: it is the widest
thing in the header and it is not what a thumb reaches for,
since pasting a branch name on a phone is rare and picking one
from a list is the whole interaction. So the box, the newest
jump and the way home all move into the panel, where there is
room to label them, and what stays pinned is 2 rem of glyph.

It still REPORTS without being opened, which is half of what
this component is for, and it now reports BOTH facts. The tint
answers "am I off the default branch"; the dot answers "and is
this the newest one". They are kept on separate channels on
purpose: they are independent questions, and folding the second
into the color would have amber mean two things at once and
imply one of them is better than the other, which being on the
newest branch is not. It is merely current.

The color is the whole tint signal; the glyph carried an
outline and a tinted background at first, which drew a box
around one glyph in a row of bare ones and said nothing the
color had not already said.

THE BOX ITSELF, not a button that reveals one. This is the
control: paste a branch, press Enter, go. It is present at the
default branch, where there is nothing to report but plenty to
do, which is the state a hidden input serves worst: the whole
point is jumping OFF main, and needing a tap to reach the box
puts a door in front of the one thing this exists for.

The box is also the readout, which is why it holds the current
ref as its VALUE rather than reporting it beside an empty
field. One slot answers "what am I running" and "take me
somewhere else", and off the default branch it goes
warning-tinted in place. Focus selects the whole value, so a
paste replaces it without clearing first.

The way out, one tap, without opening anything. Below sm the
panel's own "Back to main" row is the way out instead, which
has been there all along.

The panel hangs from the BOX's right edge, so what bounds its
width is the room to its left, and in a phone header that is
less than the panel wants: 24 rem hung off a box that ends
~40 px from the right edge of a 390 px viewport starts at
-26 px, off screen, with no scrollbar to reveal it. Clamped on
open by measuring, not by a media query, because a query cannot
know where this mount sits and the mount moves with whatever
else the header is carrying.

What this acts on, named every time. The control sits in a
shell that browses OTHER repos, so leaving it implied is how
it would be read as the browsed repo's ref picker.

── The newest slot, phone only: one corner, three states ──
This replaced a full-width row that spun and then, on the
branch you were most likely to be standing on, removed
itself. A row that sometimes vanishes is worse than a
smaller one that always answers, so the slot is always
here, at a reserved width, and says which of three things
is true:

  loading            a spinner
  there is a jump    a lightning button, tap to take it
  you are on it      nothing, because the GLYPH said so

The third state used to carry the word "newest" here, and
the word was the problem: a stray label in a corner, in a
panel that had just been stripped of everything else. It is
not dropped, it moved. The dot on the header glyph answers
it a few pixels away and without opening anything, which is
strictly better than answering it inside the thing you had
to open. Silence here is only correct BECAUSE the glyph
speaks; on its own it would be the vanishing row again.

A fourth case, no dated non-default branch at all, leaves
the slot empty too, since there is genuinely nothing to
report.

Desktop keeps its header bolt instead. It is one tap
without opening anything, which is the better deal where
there is width for it, and two lightnings on one panel
would be the duplication this whole pass has been removing.

Amber, not primary. Primary appears nowhere else in this
control at rest, only as a hover accent, while amber is
the switch's own colour: the ridden glyph, the box, the
way home, the current row. A blue bolt was the one
foreign note in the palette. It does mean amber now
carries a second sense here, "there is something newer",
alongside "you are off the default branch", and the two
never appear in the same place, so the reading stays
local: on the glyph it is where you are, in this corner
it is where you could go.

Reads showNewest rather than restating its rule, so this
and the desktop bolt cannot drift.

THE BOX, on a phone only. At sm and up it is in the header
where it needs no opening, and this is deliberately not a
second copy of it there: the two are display-exclusive, so
only ever one is interactive, and they share one typed value
so nothing can drift. No backticks in this comment, or any
other in here: the markup is a JS template literal and one
would end it mid-component.
Duplicated in markup rather than moved by
CSS because they sit in different parents, which is the same
reason the shell's rail renders twice.

── The list, and why a phone does without it ────────────────
Below sm the panel stops at the box, the newest jump and the
way home. The list is the one part of this control that is
genuinely duplicated elsewhere: the fab's Render tab scans
every branch carrying a different copy of the page, which is
the same question this list answers, down to the same signal.
Duplication is cheap in a desktop panel with room to spare
and expensive in a phone panel that then owns most of the
screen, so it is kept where it costs nothing and dropped
where it does. Typing still reaches any branch, and the fab
is the scan.

The hidden/sm:block pair sits under an x-show on purpose:
when x-show is true it removes its inline display style and
lets these classes govern, and when false its inline none
wins over them. Both halves land the right way round.

A branch carrying a different copy of THIS FILE. Not the
same question as "will the page look different", since
the lib the page loads is swapped too; it answers the
narrower one the scan can actually answer.

The row you are standing on is bold; it is warning-tinted
only when standing there means being off the default
branch, so the color keeps its one meaning. The name
carries its prefix dimmed rather than dropped: two
branches can share a tail, and a row has the width for
both when the emphasis says which half to read.

The box's value, seeded with the ref the page is running at (init) and
put back there by revert(). `dirty` is what separates "showing you
where you are" from "you are typing a destination": until the box is
edited its value is a readout, so it must not filter the list, and the
Go row must not offer to navigate to where you already are.

The ref the page is actually running at. One read covers both ways a
page gets here: a real ?use= in the address bar, and a toss, whose
params shim answers `use` with the addressed ref (see toss-render's
addressHtml). window.gh.ref is not used, because on a page whose boot
block ignores ?use= it would report the ref the LOADER settled on and
hide the fact that the address asked for another; the fab owns that
distinction and says so plainly, and a header chip is the wrong place
to relitigate it.
A deployed refs= entry, or a renderer's implied version, answers
when the address carries no ?use=.

A ref split at its last slash: `claude/thing-abc` -> 'claude/' + 'thing-abc'.
A ref with no slash is all tail, so both callers work unchanged.

Hidden once the scan says there is nowhere to jump: either the
newest branch IS the default, or it is the one already being ridden.
The second case used to leave the control up and do nothing legible
when tapped, because go() short-circuits on the ref you are already
at and revert() merely closes the panel. That reads as a dead button,
and it fires exactly when a session is riding its own newest branch,
which is most of the time this control is used at all.

The header glyph's dot: the branch being ridden is the newest one.
Only ever true while riding, since on the default branch there is no
branch for this to be a fact about. It is showNewest's complement
with a newest in hand, read through the same getter so the dot and
the corner bolt are guaranteed never to show at once.

The list, filtered by whatever has been TYPED. An untouched box holds
the current ref as a readout, and filtering on that would show one row
and hide the list you opened the panel to see. Substring rather than
prefix: branch names here are `claude/<slug>-<suffix>`, so the
memorable part is in the middle and a prefix match finds nothing you
remember.

How wide the panel may be, in px, measured at the moment it opens:
everything from the viewport's left gutter to this control's right
edge, which is the edge the panel hangs from. Empty until the first
open, so the CSS width stands on a desktop where nothing needs
clamping. The floor keeps a pathologically narrow mount from
producing a panel too thin to read; it would overflow left, which is
the lesser failure of the two.

One door for every way the panel opens (the caret, and typing into
the box), so the measurement cannot be attached to one of them and
forgotten on the other.

Escape puts the box back to the readout it started as. A half-typed
branch name left sitting in a header would otherwise misreport, for
the rest of the page's life, which ref the page is running at.

One load per page life. The rows are branch tips, which do move, but
a header control is not a monitor: reopening the panel in the same
session should not re-run three GraphQL pages, and a session that
pushes a branch reloads to ride it anyway.

The path-aware scan when it is available: same one call, and it
returns the repo's real default branch, which is what the chip's
"riding" test and the newest button both key on.

Last stop, and the only one a token-free viewer reaches: REST's
branch list, which is public for a public repo. It carries no
commit date, so the rows are unordered and the newest button
retires (see newestBranch) — the panel still takes a pasted ref
and still lists what there is to pick from, which is the point.

Navigation always leaves the TOP document. Inside a toss this
component runs in the renderer's frame, where assigning location
would nest a renderer inside a renderer rather than switch the ref.

Already there. Pressing Enter on an untouched box is the common way
to arrive here, and reloading the page for it would look like a
mystery navigation.

Load-then-go, so the button works on its first tap whether or not the
hover preload has landed. Two ways there is nowhere to jump, and both
say so rather than letting the button do nothing: the newest branch
is the default one, or it is the one already being ridden.

The second needs handling HERE and not only in showNewest, because of
the order: before the scan lands showNewest is true by design, so
the button is up and tappable, and the answer only arrives during
this await. Without the guard the tap fell through to go(), which
short-circuits on the ref it is already at and calls revert(), so the
panel shut and nothing else happened. Reported as the lightning not
working, and it was doing exactly what it was told.
Not Pages-served: drop the pin in place instead.

The dot exists to answer a question WITHOUT the panel being opened,
and it cannot answer anything before the scan lands. Desktop gets
that for free from the hover preload; a phone has no hover, so a dot
that waits for a tap would answer only after you opened the thing it
was meant to save you opening.

So the scan runs itself, once, and ONLY WHILE RIDING: on the
default branch no dot is possible, so a page nobody is previewing
still pays nothing, which was the whole point of loading on demand.
Riding is already a deliberate act, and this is the fact the control
exists to report, so one scan is proportionate. On idle rather
than immediately, because it is a garnish and the page's own
loading has the better claim on the network.

Dense on purpose: below the 44 px floor, which is for a COLD target in chrome, where these rows sit inside a panel the pointer has already aimed at and opened. The same reasoning lets path-picker run its option rows and crumbs below full size. .wt-menu-row (the app's

The estate (global) context, above the owner's repos. Only
on a host that has it (the app); guarded by hasEstate().

Fields a repo may self-declare, edited on the dialog (Settings form or raw

  Info      repo facts + token + a Public-browse shortcut

  Config    the same config as raw JSON (the whole shared file)

Settings and Config are two views of one object, synced on tab switch
(dlgTab). Fixed box size (w/h) with a scrolling body, so switching tabs

The token control is shared by both scopes, so it lives in one string and is

Inside the app only: the view that explains the token,
holds the browser note and lists what this origin stores.

Fixed box height in repo scope, so switching tabs never resizes
the dialog. The account panel has no tabs and one short control,
so it sizes to its content instead of standing mostly empty.

Header: target repo + tab switch (fixed). In estate scope the
title reads "Account" and the tabs are hidden, since the panel
is about the token, not a repo. In repo scope the repo name is
the one-tap GitHub link, since the dialog's old GitHub/CDN/
flat-tree link list was retired.

Body: a flex column filling the fixed box, so the box size is
constant across tabs. Info/Settings scroll their content; the
Config editor's textarea flexes to fill the height.

INFO tab (repo scope): the repo's facts and the token control.
The GitHub/CDN/flat-tree link list that used to live here is

ESTATE scope: the account panel, reached from the Repos
dashboard's account control. One job now, the GitHub token:
"Refresh views" left with the header shield, and the Repos

Shared editor header: the config's fully-qualified path and an

The rest of the mark (lib/kits/repo-mark.js), as on the

Headless in the app's header: the component is the repo/auth

A NOTE, since the icon alone is the fact: which of three auth
states this session is in. A daisyUI tooltip carried it to a

The dialog targets dlg.repo, which may differ from the open repo (opened

dlg.estate: the shield was opened at the all-repo estate level with no

The title-tip kit, for the auth glyph's legend. Delegated, so arriving

The estate context is either of its two views (repo grid or surfaces);

Account panel (the token) rather than a repo's config: asked for

Metadata: reuse the open repo's, else one direct read.

Only the raw-JSON (Config) tab can be malformed; the Settings form is

Pins as a newline list, so the form covers the common case; stage and any
other structured field are edited in JSON.
The Icon field's preview, as on the config view (config.js markPreview).
Drop empty/default keys so saved configs stay minimal (absent === off).
save() lives in gh-store.js, which not every host page loads.

The shell re-reads configs, refreshes the cache, and reloads the
estate / quick-link row on this event.

quiet: identity + repo-list failures stay non-fatal (no modal, no
gh-auth prompt takeover), for pages that already picked a repo
directly (pickByName) and only want the dropdown populated.
The "last accepted" the This browser view reports.

Signed out there is no account to list. The public fallback the
constructor's demo default reached (/users/anthropics/repos) answered
a question nobody here asked and spent the anonymous quota doing it.

Don't clobber a repo the page already picked (e.g. from URL state)
while this ran in the background.

Pick a repo by name without listing anyone's repos first: the
identity-free boot path. /repos/<name> works unauthenticated for

alpineComponents/search-view.js — the central file surface.

It began as a search results list and is now the place files are READ, which
is the same move made twice. The sidebar finder and this view split one job:
the finder is for JUMPING (few keystrokes, one destination, no controls),
this view is for INVESTIGATING (parameters, room for many results,
iteration). The finder's "File contents" gate routes here with the query
carried over; the header nav's Search entry opens it empty.

WHY THE FILE OPENS HERE. Every repo carried its own Files view (the
explorer's breadcrumb walk plus the shared viewer), so reading a file meant
first choosing a repository and then walking a tree, and a hit found here
bounced into that per-repo surface to be read. But a file is rarely wanted
as a position in a tree; it is wanted by name, by folder, or by what is
inside it, none of which a tree navigator answers and all three of which
this view already does. So the search IS the browse: a query, a repo, a ref,
and a folder scope are four filters over one list, and the list opens its
own file. `?view=files` stays exactly as it was for the tree walk that
wants it.

Three modes, each a mode pill, all served by lib/kits/estate-search.js (one
implementation, one cache, shared with the finder):

  Names        the repo trees, at any REF (which is what the trees API
               gives and the code index does not, so this is the lane that
               reaches branches) and under any folder. It is TWO READINGS
               of one corpus, and the query box is the switch between them:

                 a query   recursive and flat, every matching path
                 no query  ONE LEVEL, folders and files, walkable

               The second is the file browser. It has folders in it, which
               a recursive match structurally cannot, and it is why an
               empty query here is an answer rather than a miss.
  Contents     the estate's MARKDOWN, by word, from the content index the
               crawl writes (lib/kits/content-index.js), not GitHub's
               code-search API, which a page cannot read. Every word must
               be in the file, in any order; default branches, refreshed
               with the crawl. Each shown hit reads its file once for the
               line it quotes. A folder scope filters the hits, and the
               KIND pills facet them: what each file is by its path
               (DocGrowth.kind, the Map's Kind facet), one pill per kind the
               answer holds, with its count.
  Sessions     what was SAID, answered from the monthly search index rather
               than by opening every record, unioned with what each session
               row says about itself; hits share an inline and expanded
               reader with captured excerpts and a route into the source.
  Chats        the chat archive's catalog layers (what a chat was ABOUT, as
               a hand or machine summary describes it), across every month
               the frontier names; a hit opens the chat on its provider's
               own site. It is the sessions lane's opposite number and the
               pair is worth reading together: sessions quotes what was said
               and costs the whole record store, chats matches what a
               summary says and costs about 10 MB of shards. Neither reaches
               the chat snapshots' full text; that is CLI-only, in
               chat-histories tools/search_chats.py.

Every run re-executes the search; the caches underneath make re-matching
cheap, and "Refresh caches" (EstateSearch.reset) is the explicit way to
force fresh fetches, which is the view-level answer to "the results seem
cached". Deep-linkable: the shell stamps
?view=search&sq=&smode=&srepo=&sref=&spath=&sfile= through searchSeed, so a
search AND the file open in it are an address like any other view state.

Mounts by the crumb-bar idiom (template injected in init, then initTree);
lazy (template x-if="searchSeen" in the shell), like Map and Tools. The
reader is the shared viewer (viewer.js) embedded with bindStore:false, the
same way the stage previews a staged file: this view holds cross-repo hits,
so binding it to the browsed repo's activeFile would be the wrong subject.
The explorer's tab expansion, so a file reads the same here as there.

DOM handles stay outside Alpine's reactive proxy. The result list, inline
track and expanded reader share one selected id; records mount lazily.

A file's weight, from the tree read that already listed it, by the
estate's one rule for bytes (Traffic.fmtBytes).

A chip row led by its name: the Map's pattern (map.js, mapPillStrip and
mapChip), copied as the Activity view's pills are. One line that scrolls
sideways rather than wrapping, so the rows above the results keep their
height on a phone however many repos or kinds there are.

The name stays put while its chips scroll under it: sticky at the row's
left edge, on the page's own background so a chip passes behind it, and
a soft edge of that background so a half-hidden chip fades, not clips.

data-find-box: this view's own search, so the shell's
typeahead router sends a bare keystroke here rather than to
the sidebar finder. Typing while looking at Files means
"search here".

REPOS AS A RAIL, not a dropdown. The set is small, fixed, and the
thing you switch most, which is the case a select serves worst:
it hides every option behind a tap and reports the current one in
a slot that reads as a form field rather than as a place you are
standing. Single-select with "tap it again for all", drawn as
the Map's chip rows are: led by its name, one line, scrolling
sideways once the estate outgrows a phone's width.

The two scopes that are places rather than words, so both are
pickers rather than boxes: a ref is chosen from what the repo
has, a folder from what the tree holds. Each still takes a pasted
value, inside the panel, where it is the fallback rather than the
way in. The ref control needs a repo to list, so it stands down
under All, where each repo answers at its own default branch.

The ref is Names' alone: the content index reads default
branches only, so a branch picker there would scope nothing.

The x-ref sits on the WRAPPER, not on the picker's own element:
x-ref registers against the closest component root, so an
element carrying both would register the ref with itself and
this host would never find it. The fab's mount says the same.

The scope, as a walkable trail. A folder is reached by tapping one
on a result row as often as by the picker, so the way back out has
to be as cheap as either way in.
Only scope limits or a needed next action belong below the controls.

KINDS AS FACETS OF THE ANSWER, not a fixed filter: one chip per
kind the results hold, with its count, so no chip leads to an
empty list. The same row shape and the same "tap it again for
all" as the repo row above. Shown once an answer has more than
one kind, or while a kind is chosen, so it can be cleared.

Results and reader, side by side where there is room. Below lg
they are one column and the open file takes it, with a labelled
way back to the list: a phone showing a 40-row list above a file
is showing neither.

data-pattern and data-part declare a List and detail and name its
parts (data/ui-units/codebook.md, "Declaring a pattern in
markup"); nothing at runtime reads them. aria-current marks the
open hit in a standard attribute beside its class.

THE COUNT AND ITS TWO ACTIONS BELONG TO THE LIST, so they ride
the list's column rather than a band across the top of the
view. Above the grid they were the width of the whole surface
while describing one narrow column of it, which put the deck
button over the reader it has nothing to do with.

The row stays OUTSIDE the scroller and OUTSIDE the phone's
hide, which is what lets it move at all: below lg the list is
hidden while a file is open, and a deck button that went with
it would vanish exactly where swiping is worth most. So the
column hides its rows, not its header.

A folder listing is not a count of hits: nothing was searched
for, so nothing "hit". It says what is here, in the two kinds
it holds.

WHILE A MULTI-SHARD READ RUNS, what it has read. It sits
in the count's own slot and under the same column, so the
line the reader watches for the answer is the line that says
how far off the answer is. Only the chats lane fills it.

Read the results one at a time, opening where the reader is
standing (openIndex, else the top of the list), so the
reader's position counter and the deck are two speeds on
one position rather than two positions.

THE CLASSES AND THE WORDING ARE swipeDeck.entry()'s, and the
literal here is a COPY held to it by test
(node/test/deck-entry-parity.test.mjs) rather than a call:
the kit loads on demand, so it is not on the page when this
template first renders, and a host that waited for it would
show no button at all on the first paint. Unlike the other
two copies this one has no uncounted state, because it only
ever renders over a list already in hand.

The file's weight, off the same tree read that
listed it, so it costs no fetch. It is the one thing
the retired per-repo explorer showed that the cached
walk did not. Right-aligned and tabular so a column
of sizes reads as a column.

Scoping down is one tap from the row that revealed the
folder, which is where the reader is already looking. It
is shown at rest rather than on hover: a phone has no
hover, and this is an action, not a decoration. It
appears only where it would go somewhere, so a row sitting
directly in the current scope carries none.

The reader. The shared viewer carries the file's own chrome
(name, size, mode switch, GitHub / Raw / CDN / toss links), so
this bar holds only what the viewer cannot know: where in the
result set this file is, and the routes out.

The view is Files; these say by WHAT. "Names" and "Contents" are the
two halves of looking for a file and read as a pair; a mode pill
labelled Files under a heading labelled Files said the same word twice
and neither time said which half you were on.

The two lanes that search a CORPUS rather than the repos, so neither
takes a repo, a ref, or a folder: each one's subject is a single store
and picking web-tools out of it would mean nothing. Named once here
because three controls hide on it and a fourth mode would otherwise
have to be added to each of them by hand.

Which mode the reader opens a file in. Defined here until 2026-08-15,
when the stage's preview turned out to want the same policy; it now
lives on ViewRegistry, which owns it and carries the reasoning. This
stays as the name the template mounts with.

'' = every estate repo
names mode only; '' = default branch
folder scope; '' = the whole repo
how many hits the list holds; `more()` raises it
a search has executed (distinguishes "no hits" from "not run")

contents only: a DocGrowth kind key, '' = every kind
the last contents answer's kinds: [{ k, n, count }]

The file being read: { repo, ref, path } or null. Held apart from the
hit list because it outlives it: a re-run that drops the file from the
results should not yank it off the screen mid-read.

The deck over the hits: its handle, the list it was opened against, and
whether a tap is still resolving. The list is a SNAPSHOT rather than the
live getter, because a deck is a fixed set of slides and `fileHits`
moves under a re-run: a `count` taken at open and a `render` reading the
current results would disagree the moment either changed.

Whether every file in the deck sits in one place. The rule the hit rows
already follow one level up: a location repeated on every line says
nothing that tells the lines apart, and spends the width that the
filename wanted. So a deck of one folder's files lists bare filenames,
and a cross-repo answer keeps the location on every row.

Each mounted picker's config, built HERE and not in its own x-data, and
that placement is load-bearing rather than tidy.

Alpine evaluates an `x-data` expression with every registered component
NAME injected into the scope, so the estate's own component names are
live identifiers there. One of them is `repo` (alpineComponents/repo.js).
So the natural spelling, `refPicker({ repo: () => repo })` or a factory
method reading `this.repo`, resolves `repo` to that component's factory
function rather than to this view's scoped repository: the panel
rendered "[object Object]" where the repo goes and lost the default
branch, with nothing in either file looking wrong and both components
testing green in isolation. `defaultRef`, which is nobody's component,
came back undefined by the same route and looked like a separate bug.

init() runs in the ordinary component scope, where the injection is
gone, so `self` captured here is this view and the closures below can
read its fields by their real names. Any mount whose config closes over
host state belongs here for the same reason.

The seed: goSearch(opts) parked what the caller wanted (the finder's
gate, the explorer's hand-off, or a deep link's ?sq= family). Consume
once; run when there is something to run, since a seeded search is a
search someone already asked for. A seeded FILE opens after the run,
so a shared address lands on the file, not merely near it.

Back out of a source deck replays the Search address underneath
it. Keep the existing readers for that same result set; re-reading
it would dismiss the parent deck and lose its position.

NOTHING SEEDED IS STILL A REQUEST, and the request is "show me
files". A file surface whose front door is an empty box over an
empty list, with its own button greyed out, is a dead end that
reports nothing about why; the browsed repo is right there and is
what anyone opening this cold means. So a bare arrival scopes to it
and lists it, at the ref being browsed when that is off the default.
Only a bare arrival: a seed carrying a query meant that query, over
whatever scope it named, including every repo.

The component mounts once and persists behind x-show, so a LATER
routing (the finder's gate, with the view already open behind the
scenes) re-seeds through this event rather than through init.
Scroll only the list, so selecting a card never drags the whole page.

These readers belong to this result set. Invalidating it is a state
change already in progress, not another request to navigate Back.
Drop descendants first, including a source deck's own export view.

An Activity handoff often hits an already warm index, before this
first mount's queued initTree has registered the reader refs.

What the shell is browsing, in this view's own terms. The ref is
carried only when it is off the default, since '' here means "the
default branch" and is the honest thing to hold: the explorer's rule.

The select's options: the estate's repos, plus whatever is actually
scoped when that is not one of them. A repo can be browsed, handed over
by the explorer, or named in a ?srepo= link without being on the
estate, and a select holding a value it has no option for renders
blank, which reads as no scope at all while the list underneath is
scoped.

A run needs a query, EXCEPT in files mode, where a repo or a folder is
enough: that is the listing, and it is the browse half of this view.
Nothing narrows an all-repos listing of everything, so that one case
still asks for a query rather than reading every tree the token can see.

A corpus lane searches one store and takes no repo, ref or folder, so
the three controls that name those stand down together.

How far a multi-shard read has got, or null. Only the chats lane sets
it: forty shard reads is tens of seconds, and a spinner that cannot say
whether it is at month 2 or month 38 is the thing the estate's crawl
bars exist to avoid.

BROWSING vs SEARCHING, the one rule that decides what the list is.
A query is recursive and flat (which paths match); no query is one
level with its folders in it (what is in here). One repo, since a
level of "every repo at once" is not a place. The box is the switch,
which is why neither reading needs a control of its own.

Said as what typing DOES, since typing leaves the folder listing for
a recursive match and that is the surprise worth naming up front.

The folder scope, normalized once. The box is forgiving about slashes
because a pasted path routinely carries them; everything downstream
(the crumbs, the run, the address) reads this rather than the raw box.

Whether raising the cap can actually yield more. The names lane holds
the whole match set in memory, so it always can. Sessions returns
everything, so total never exceeds the list.

The line each Contents hit quotes, read from its file after the list
is drawn: the index holds words, not text. Four reads at a time, and
only for the rows on screen, so a broad query does not read the
estate; a row whose read fails simply quotes nothing.

Only file hits are readable here, so the position and the arrows count
those; a folder row and a sessions run leave the reader alone.

The bar over the reader names the file and where it came from. The
viewer's own header carries the full path, but it is the first thing to
lose its width on a phone, which is exactly where the list is hidden
and this bar is the only label left.

The row palette is the estate's, not this view's: `ph-folder
text-warning` and `ph-file text-info`, the pair the explorer, the
navigator, mention and path-picker all use. The rows here were built
generically and came out uniformly grey, which read as a results list
rather than as a file tree; the manila folder is what says at a glance
which rows you can walk into. The `..` row keeps the muted treatment on
purpose: it is a way out, not a folder in the listing.

One file hit's row, from either lane. Two things are dropped as
redundant, because a scoped listing otherwise repeats its own scope on
every line and truncates the only part that differs: the label is
RELATIVE to the folder scope, and the repo badge is dropped when a
single repo is the scope, since the control above already names it.
The full path stays on the hit for opening it and for the folder chip.
The placeholder names the corpus; only an otherwise invisible limit needs a note.

Contents carries no line: the placeholder says Markdown, and a repo
the index leaves out says so in the notice when it is chosen. A
standing line here cost a phone a row it could not read (owner,
2026-11-09).

── The scope controls ───────────────────────────────────────────────
Known only for the repo the shell scanned. Elsewhere '' is the honest
answer, and the picker renders it as "default branch" rather than
guessing a name.

A GH pointed at the SCOPED repo, for the folder picker's tree reads.
Without it the picker would walk the browsed repo while the list beside
it was scoped to another.

One root, the scoped repo at the scoped ref: the folder picker answers
"where in THIS repo", not "which repo", which the rail above owns.

The picker caches its roots at first open and would otherwise keep
showing the repo and ref you opened it on. Reset it whenever the scope
it was built for has moved, then open INSIDE the single root: a
one-row "pick a repo" level, in a control that exists to pick a folder
of the repo already named two controls to its left, is a tap that
asks a question with one answer.

Switching repos drops the ref and the folder with it: both name places
inside the repo you just left, and carrying them forward would scope a
listing to a branch and a folder the new repo very likely does not have.

A chosen chip scrolled out of its one-line row would hide which one
is on, so the row scrolls to it. Sideways only: scrollIntoView would
also move the page. The row is `relative`, so offsetLeft is measured
from it.

A kind is a facet of the answer already in hand, but the list, the
cap and the quoted lines all rebuild from a run, so a tap re-runs:
the shards are cached and the search itself is milliseconds.

A scope change is a new question, so the cap resets with it: carrying a
raised cap into a narrower scope would show a fuller list than the one
that was asked for and read as the scope not having taken.

Re-run only once something has been run: a control touched before the
first search is being set up, not re-asked.

ONE LEVEL, folders and all. An empty query is not a search with
nothing typed in it, it is the question "what is in here", and
that question has folders in its answer. Flattening a repo into
its blobs was a listing you could read and not one you could
walk, which is what a file browser is for; typing turns it back
into the recursive match below, so the box is the switch between
the two readings and needs no control of its own.

The way back out, at the top of the list where a file browser
has always put it. The crumb trail above says the same thing and
is the better target on a pointer; this is the one a thumb
reaches without leaving the list.

Every repo at its default branch is the question the registry's
file index (state/files.json) answers in one read; a repo, a ref
or a folder scope is a live tree read, as before. A registry with
no index yet falls through to the live reads too.

Both kits load on the first Contents run, as the sessions lane's
index kit does: a reader who never searches contents pays nothing.

What the index could not cover is said, not left for an empty
list to imply.

Every hit's kind, counted over the whole answer so the pills
say what a tap would show; the list then holds the chosen kind.
A plain Doc carries no tag: two thirds of the corpus would wear it.

The kit is loaded here rather than at boot, the way the chats
lane loads its own: this is the only consumer outside the

A registry whose crawl has not written a shard yet can only
answer on rows, which is a narrower search than the one that was
asked for. Saying so beats reporting it as a complete result.

Activity's order (including an explicitly curated set) travels
with its membership; opening the inspector must not reshuffle it.

The kit is loaded here rather than at boot: this is the only
consumer outside the Chats pane, and a reader who never opens

A month the frontier names with no shard in EITHER layer is a
hole in the archive, not a failed search, so it is reported
beside the hits rather than thrown over them.

Provider beside the date, because the archive is three corpora
and which one answered changes what the hit even is: a Gemini
row is a 30-minute-gap thread rather than a conversation, and
it has no address to open.

A routed query already owns its destination entry. Selecting its
first result completes that address; only a new submitted query
adds another entry for Back to walk.

The progress line is cleared HERE and not only on the happy path: a
read that throws at month 30 would otherwise leave "30 of 41" under
the error, reading as a partial answer rather than as no answer.

The address follows the search AND the open file, so this screen can be
shared as what is on it rather than as the query behind it.

A chat is READ where it lives. The archive holds a summary of it,
never the conversation in a form this app renders, so the honest
destination is the provider's own page. A Gemini row has no address
at all (Takeout keeps no per-conversation URL), so the row reports
that instead of opening a window on nothing.

Read a file in place. `ref` '' rides through to the repo's default
branch (RepoAddress's rule: parse honestly, resolve late), which is
what a name hit at the default branch carries. Every outcome shows something: a
failed fetch renders its reason where the file would be, so the
position counter never points at a blank pane.
A hit with no ref reads at the selection's ref; '' is the default branch.

── The deck ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The results, read one at a time. The pane beside the list is for
INVESTIGATING one hit (controls, a stepper, room to compare it against
the list); the deck is for GOING THROUGH them, which is what a fifty-row
answer to "where does this appear" is usually for and what a phone can
do at all. Same split the view's own header note draws between the
finder and this view, one level down.

THE DECK AND THE PANE ARE ONE POSITION, not two. It opens on the file
the pane has open, every slide change writes that file back to `open`,
and `open` is what the list highlights and what `stamp()` puts in the
URL. So dismissing the deck leaves the reader on the file they stopped
at, with the list scrolled to it, and a `?sfile=` link minted mid-deck
reopens on the same file. A deck holding a position of its own would
have made the stepper and the swipe disagree about "where am I".

Folders and session rows are not in it: `fileHits` is the readable
subset, which is also what the stepper counts, so a browse listing decks
its files and keeps its folders in the list where they are walked.

A deck already open becomes the parent, so this drills rather than
stacking: reached from a surface that is itself a deck, Back returns
there. Opened from the view there is none and it is the root.

The contents list, which this set needs more than most: fifty
hits is far past the footer's countable dots, and the rows are
the same two lines the header carries, so the reader recognizes
them from the list they tapped in from.

The slide is a file being read: the viewer owns the vertical axis
and a wide code view scrolls inside its own box rather than
widening the track.

A reading surface, so the chrome steps aside on the way down a
file and comes back on the way up or on the next file.

The starting slide fires no onSlide, so the pane is put on the same
file here rather than only from the second swipe onward.

The header for slide i: what the file is called, where it lives, and
the one door out. The filename is the title and the directory rides the
subtitle beside the repo, the split kits/file-deck.js settled: a header
truncated from the right otherwise spends its width on the path and
drops the one word the reader is looking for.

`HEAD` where the hit named no ref, as a default-branch name hit:
GitHub resolves it to the repo's default branch, which is exactly
what an unspecified ref means here (RepoAddress's rule: parse
honestly, resolve late). Guessing `main` would 404 on a repo that
calls it something else.

A slide is the shared viewer, driven the way showFile() drives the
pane's: one contents call, then show().

`identify: false` because THIS DECK'S HEADER IS THE FILE HEADER, set per
slide above; a viewer naming itself underneath would print the name
twice, elided two different ways, which is the call the stage reader and
kits/file-deck.js both made. What that drops with it is the viewer's own
control row: the mode switch and the Raw / CDN / toss links. Deliberate
and not carried up, because this is the READING pass and the pane is one
dismiss away holding all of it, on the same file the deck stopped at.

Every outcome shows something, the same promise the pane makes: a failed
fetch renders its reason where the file would be, so a swipe never lands
on a blank slide and the counter stays truthful.
A hit with no ref reads at the selection's ref; '' is the default branch.

The reader may be two slides past this one by now, and swipe-deck
empties what it has left; showing into a popped tree throws.

The one route back to the per-repo tree walk, for when the question is
where a file SITS rather than what it says.

alpineComponents/session-brief.js — one recorded session as a page.

The sibling of alpineComponents/branch-brief.js, and deliberately the same
shape, because the two answer the same kind of question about two different
objects: what is this thing, and what is inside it. A reader who has learned
where the deck button sits on a branch should find it in the same place on a
session.

This markup lived inside pages/session.html until 2026-08-27. Moving it here
changes nothing about that page and adds the host it could not have: the app's
Sessions pane mounts one per slide, directly, in the shell's own Alpine, so a
session can be swiped through the way a branch already is. That is the whole
reason for the lift; branch-brief.js took the same step on 2026-08-13 and its
header records why an iframe was the wrong way to do it.

A host passes:
  id        the record's short id: the eight hex characters that END its
            filename, not the whole stem, which carries the date as well
  day       the day it started, which with `id` derives the store path
  path      the store path outright, when the host already knows it
  branch    a branch name; opens that branch's latest session (resolveBranch)
  repo      the store, defaulting to the private one below
  record    a record already in hand; nothing is fetched
  framed    true to say the host supplies the identity chrome
  lent      false for a framed host that lends nothing (the standalone
            page's takeover), so the view reads its Now section, views and
            calls itself; defaults to `framed`
  compact   show the discussion search and its excerpts, without the overview
  fixedFind keep a compact reader tied to the host's submitted query
  matchNote plain text for a compact search with no matching captured prose
  pages     render chips for what this session's branches changed, lent by a
            host that can join a record to the crawl (see the Look row)
  facts     what the host already knows, so the head is right before the
            read lands (see `factsRecord`)
  warm      neighbours worth reading ahead: [{ id, day, path }]
  onMeta    called with what only a finished read knows
  pane      a tab of either region: 'overview' | 'turns' | 'outline' | 'log'
            | 'schema' above, 'calls' | 'views' | 'files' below ('raw' is
            taken as 'log')
  fileHref  (checkoutPath, record) => url, for the Files pane; see fileHref
  start     open the card deck on this card, once loaded
  find      find captured prose in this session after loading
  onFind    called with the submitted query, for an address-owning host
  onMatches called after a read or query change with exact local match counts
  onOpen    called with the full source deck, for a host that owns its lifetime

`facts` is the same contract branch-brief states and exists for the same
reason: the app's sessions cache holds every number on the strip, so a
slide can render its head immediately and only the outline waits on the JSON.
A cold pages/session.html has no such row and shows the strip when the record
arrives, which is the only thing it could do.

The store. Overridable per mount so this is not welded to one repo, which
is the same courtesy pages/session.html paid before the lift.

Records already read, keyed by store and path. Module scope, not component
state, because the deck reuses one mount per slide and a record is a
property of the session rather than of the visit: stepping back to a slide
must not refetch it.

A TTL at all, on a store whose records are written once and never revisited?
For exactly one record: the LIVE session's, which is rewritten and
republished on every Stop. Everything else is frozen and the expiry costs a
conditional request nobody notices. Same minute branch-brief uses.
[repo, path] -> { at, promise }

The store's own listing, for resolving a short id to a path. One recursive
tree read names every record, so a deck of twenty sessions addressed by id
pays for it once rather than twenty times. Keyed by repo, same expiry.
repo -> { at, promise }

Gemini's topics file for a record (sessions/topics/ in the store, on the
`background` branch the laptop daemon writes): the session's title,
summary and agenda, and a summary of every turn. Read here rather than
taken from the host, for two reasons. The host's copy is the rollup,
state/session-topics.json, which carries no turns. And a deep link into
the Sessions swiper opened it before the rollup was joined, so the slide
had no summary and the header named the session by its branch, "HEAD"
(reported 2026-10-22). Same memo, same expiry, as RECORDS.
[repo, path] -> { at, promise }
How long a slide's outline waits for that file before it is built without
it. Built once with the summaries, not once bare and again when they land:
a swiper builds three slides at a time, and on a phone the second build of
three large records was a spike of its own beside a page already near
Safari's memory ceiling (a crash on 2026-10-22 that did not recur). A file
slower than this still arrives, and the outline is rebuilt for it.

How far back a branch walk reads before giving up (see resolveBranch). A
ceiling on a loop that opens whole records, not a claim about the store: a
branch whose session is 25 records back is one nobody is holding on a phone
waiting to hear, and the error names the number it looked at.

WHAT A CLIPBOARD HOLDS, REDUCED TO A BRANCH NAME. The Claude app copies the
branch a session is on and nothing else about it, but what it copies has
varied: a bare name, a full ref, a GitHub tree or compare URL, a branch.html
address, or the name with a caption line under it. All of them reduce here,
so a shortcut passing a clipboard straight through does not have to know
which one it got.

The same reduction lives in lib/ops/session-menu.js as `branchOf`, and that
copy cannot import this one: an op is a single standalone function that a
phone evaluates with no page around it. Two copies on purpose; change one
and change the other.

ONE RULE IS DELIBERATELY NOT SHARED. The op also demands a `/` in the
result, because it is guessing whether a clipboard holds a branch at all
and needs a way to say no. Here the caller has already said it does, so a
slashless branch name is honoured rather than thrown away.

Every branch a record knows the session worked: each checkout's branch as of
the record's last write (`repos`), then every branch it pushed (`pushed`,
record schema 15). `repos` alone holds one branch per checkout, so a
session that worked several in one repo, or ended back on main, showed
fewer than it pushed: 15 of 54 records from 2026-09-29 to 2026-10-12.
The views strip's driver (swipeDeck.strip), outside Alpine's reactive state.

The branch to find a session FOR, resolved once at load. Not a filter:
the record it lands on is the whole subject of the mount.

Whether the host lends the session's work instead of this view reading
it, as the app's Sessions deck does (the crawl's `pages`, no Now section
or Views tab). Framed implies lent unless the host says `lent: false`,
which the standalone page's takeover does: it draws the identity and
lends nothing, so the view reads the work itself.

The shell's height when standalone: the viewport less whatever the
host draws above it (the page's address bar), measured at mount.

Gemini's topics file for this record, once read (see readTopics), and
how that read went: '' not tried, 'reading', 'found', 'none' (no file,
a 404) or 'unread' (anything else). The difference between the last
two is the difference between "not summarized" and "could not tell".

Each scope repository's mark, a RepoMark spec by short name (see
loadMarks): null while its manifest is out, '' where it declares none.
The facts panel-tip: the breakdown behind a strip glyph.

TWO REGIONS, EACH WITH ITS OWN TABS: the conversation above (overview,
turns, outline, log, schema) and what it produced below (calls, views,
files), the
shape the branch view has with its guide over its files. Each holds the tab the reader or the address asked
for, '' to let the region choose (topPane, bottomPane).

The record explorer's view, which the Log and Schema tabs share: the
Schema view's arrows open the tree or a table, and the tab follows.
The copy button's tick, for a moment after a copy lands.
The Now section's data: fetched by loadWork, standalone only.
The viewables strip's position, which swipeDeck.strip reports (viewDrive).

The action message (sessions/tools/now.py in the record store), read
from `nowRef`, main unless the address names another ref.
The component reads `now` off the address itself as well as taking it
from the host, because a `?use=` preview swaps this bundle and not the
host page: a host on main never learned to pass it along.

FULL WIDTH, NO CAP. This carried mx-auto and max-w-2xl, so a desktop
browser drew a phone's column down the middle of the screen with
the rest empty. The house style names that pattern outright (rule
3), and the estate's own branch list already made the same call
once nothing stood beside it to claim the space. A row here is a
wide thing for the same reason a branch row is: an ask, an answer,
a clock, a turn count and a tool tally all read across.

BOXED: the shell is the viewport's height and each region's pane
scrolls inside itself, as a framed slide's does, so the head stays
in view while the turns scroll. Standalone, the head scrolls
inside a cap of 45dvh where it runs taller, so a short screen
still leaves the regions a share. The document never scrolls, so
a phone's address bar stays expanded.

aria-busy while the record or Gemini's file is being read, which a
look link waits on (lib/kits/look.js) before it says its target is
not on the page. The data-at names below are its anchors.

The title, and the id beside it. Framed, the deck header already
carries both, so this line goes rather than being repeated at
half width in two places; the same rule branch-brief applies to
a branch name.

ONE LINE, AND THE ID KEPT OUT OF THE WRAP. sessionRender.describe
derives the title from the session's OPENING ASK, which the
outline then prints again as card 1's own row a couple of hundred
pixels below: at two lines that duplication cost 74px of a 932px
phone to say the same sentence twice. Truncated it still names
the session, which is all a heading over its own outline has to
do. A flex row with a shrink-0 id is what keeps the stem on the
line rather than wrapping alone under it, which is what a margin
on an inline span did once the title filled the row.

Inline (inside a toss) no header names the session, so this
line does, above the facts line and the tabs.

THE WAY OUT, to the app's Sessions view. Standalone only, since
a framed slide is already inside the app; target _top, so it
leaves a toss as well.

WHICH COPY OF THIS PAGE IS RUNNING. Everything else in this
head describes the SESSION; this describes the code doing the
describing, and without it a reader has no way to tell a branch
preview from the deployed page except through the FAB drawer,
which is one tap they may not have (branch.html grew the same
marker on 2026-09-04, after three rounds were lost to exactly
that). Framed it goes with the title, since a host that draws
the identity carries its own.

The facts line sits above the tabs, so it shows whichever tab is
up (owner, 2026-11-09); its panel-tip rides with it. One root for
the x-if.

The facts strip, drawn from whatever is known: the host's row
while the record is in flight, the record itself once it lands.
One implementation, two fidelities, so a slide never shows an
empty strip and then a full one.

GLYPHS WHERE THE SESSIONS ROW HAS THEM (2026-10-22). The Activity
view's Sessions row draws these counts as a wrench, a fan-out
tree and each repository's own mark, and each count is a button
that opens the breakdown behind it. This strip drew the same
facts as words, "72 tool calls · 0 failed · home, web-tools,
web-tools-private", which wrapped to three lines at 430px and
opened nothing. A date reads as a date and 1h 43m as a duration,
so those two stay text; a bare 72 does not read as calls, which
is what the glyph is for, and the panel under it names the unit
in words.

FAILURES FOLLOW THE ROW'S RULE: they ride the wrench, never a
fact of their own, as the Sessions row has since #710. The
wrench's panel states the count, a measured zero as "none
failed", and names each failing tool; the wrench's label carries
it for a screen reader.

EVERY TEXT FACT STILL CARRIES ITS DEFINITION through
kits/title-tip.js, for the reason it always did: a title reaches
no touch screen and no screenshot. A glyph fact carries its words
in its panel instead, since a hover opens the panel and a title-tip
on the same control would draw a second box over it.

ONE WRAPPING ROW, not a column of lines.

A counted fact is a CONTROL: tap pins its panel, a hover
opens it where the pointer is fine. Several facts open the
same panel (calls and agents are both the tool
list), as the Sessions row's agents count opens its tools
card.

THE SCOPE AS ONE PILL: each repository's own icon, declared
in its .web-tools.json (see loadMarks), which is how the
Sessions row and the branch chips below already draw it,
grouped so the set reads as one fact. A tap opens the
checkouts panel, which lists them with what the session
committed to each; it was a title-tip reading "Checked out:"
and the names for an hour, until the owner asked for the
structure the tools panel has (2026-10-22).

A microphone rode the end of this fact until the same day:
it opened pages/dictate.html with these repositories
chosen, to start a follow-up session. The owner had not
used it, and a note about what is on screen is the FAB's
Note tab, which every page has.

DECLARED MARKS, THEN A COUNT. A repository that declares no
icon drew the neutral bookmark, and bb88ffa7's nine
checkouts drew six of them in a row on a phone (owner,
2026-10-22); they are a number now, and the panel names
them.

A REAL SPACE between value and unit, not a margin, so a
screen reader, a copy and the tests read "40 calls"
rather than "40calls".

TRAILING, NEVER LEADING. Led, the dot rides the fact it
precedes, so a wrap took the separator down with it and
line 2 opened on a bullet. None between two glyph counts,
which the glyphs already separate, as on the Sessions row;
and none after the last fact.

The facts panel-tip: the breakdown behind a strip glyph, on the
branch panel-tip's machinery below (kits/panel-tip.js owns the
way out). Every number in it is already in the record or in
Gemini's file, so it is complete in its first frame.

The checkouts: a group each, the repository's mark and name,
then a line per branch with work on it (see scopeRows).

FILES CHANGED, not renderable views (owner,
2026-10-22): what a branch did, which the Views
tab already narrows to what renders. A tap opens
the branch deck on that branch's Files pane.
A PR pill already says the branch was pushed.

When it ran: the span and the turns in it, when it started and
last moved, and on how many days the owner spoke in it. The
turns ALONG the span are the outline's rail, which draws every
card on the same span; a rail here too drew it twice (owner,
2026-10-22).

The turns the rail below draws, counted where the span
is: how long, and how much happened in it.

── THE CONVERSATION: the top region ──────────────────────────
The overview, the outline and the raw record, under one tab row
with find, the card deck and the session link. It takes the
whole height when the bottom region has nothing to show, and two
fifths otherwise, so the views below get the larger share
(owner, 2026-11-09); the split holds whichever tab is up in
either (house style rule 15).

The switch and the exits: the cards button is the one coloured
control because it is what most readers came to do, and the
link that leaves sits ghost beside it, standalone only, since a
deck's header carries the session link.

The tab row and the search. (No backticks in this markup: it is
a JS template literal.)

WRAPS RATHER THAN SCROLLS. The buttons drop to a second line
when the tabs need the width, and the tablist keeps its own
scroll only for a screen too narrow for the tabs alone, since a
scrolling tablist hid every tab after the first. The buttons
take swipeDeck.entry's 'tight' size, 32px, as branch-brief's
header does. The tabs carry no counts (peeve P43); the Calls
tab in the bottom row keeps its count, tinted while one waits.

FIND, behind an icon: the field shows while it is open or holds
a search. The browser's own find cannot stand in, since the
outline draws each ask and reply cut short and this searches
every turn's full text.

COPY, ON THE LOG TAB: what the log shows, as JSON. The
explorer's own toolbar row is gone (owner, 2026-11-09), and
download with it.

THE CLASSES AND THE WORDING ARE swipeDeck.entry()'s, held to it
by node/test/deck-entry-parity.test.mjs rather than by a call:
the kit loads on demand and is not on the page when this
template first renders, so a host that waited for it would show
no button at all on the first paint. Same copy, same gate, as
branch-brief's file-deck button.

The estate's standard way to link a session: the logomark in
brand colour, no label, exactly as the Sessions rows and the
deck header draw it. Drawn from kits/claude-mark.js rather than
pasted, and called plainly rather than defensively: gh-boot
carries the kit as standing equipment, which is what
node/test/claude-mark.test.mjs asserts one test below the one
that runs every call site's arguments. A guard here would only
hide the case that test exists to catch.

── OVERVIEW: the session at a glance ─────────────────────────
The first tab, so the tabs sit right under the header and the
room a head above them took goes to the regions (owner,
2026-11-09). In reading order: where the work stands (the Now
section), the pages it changed when a host lends them, then
Gemini's topics and summary from the session's topics file
(web-tools-private sessions/topics/ on background, see
readTopics), or the host's row until it is read. The topic list
leads the summary, since each line opens the outline where that
topic starts. data-at-open names the tab a look link taps to
reach an anchor in here.

── NOW: where the session's work stands ─────────────────────
Not on a lent slide (the app's Sessions deck), which keeps the
lent Look row below.
What the session left for the owner: the action message where
the session wrote one, else its last closing state, and the open
asks from each branch's PR guide. The branches and what they
changed are read here too (one compare and PR list per branch),
and drawn elsewhere: the checkouts panel on the strip and the
Views tab. User calls are the Calls tab's alone; they were
listed here as well until the owner asked why (2026-10-22).

── THE ACTION MESSAGE ─────────────────────────────────────
What the owner should act on now, kept as a file beside the
session's record (web-tools-private sessions/tools/now.py) and
written only when that changes, so churn in the chat never
moves it. Collapsed it is the headline and each ask's question
with its options; a tap opens the reasons and the links, each
link one tap from the thing it names and a hover from a peek.
With no file, the chat's last closing line stands in.

AN ASK IS ANSWERED HERE. A tap on an option opens a confirm
with an optional note; Send appends the answer to the
message's answers file, and where the ask links a PR, also
comments it there, which wakes a session subscribed to it.

THE BRANCH ROWS ARE GONE (2026-10-22). A row per branch name,
a chip per repository coloured by its PR, each chip opening a
small branch panel: built on the premise that a session works
one branch name, which a long session breaks (bb88ffa7 drew
sixteen rows). The checkouts panel on the strip lists every
branch under its repository with its PR, and the owner judged
it the better presentation; a branch there opens the branch
deck that the rows' panel led to.

The peek: one viewable, beside the card that lists it. A page is its
live render scaled down; a document is its rendered Markdown.
Nothing in it takes the pointer except the way to open it.

── Look: what this session was building ─────────────────────
The pages this session's branches changed, each opening at the
BRANCH so it shows where the work got to rather than the commit
some crawl happened to see. branch-brief carries the same row for
one branch, in the same place and with the same chip; this is its
fold across the branches one session left behind.

GROUPED BY BRANCH, each group led by its repository's mark and the
branch's short name, so a chip says which branch it renders, as
each branch tile under a session card in the Activity view does.

LENT, NEVER COMPUTED: in the app the estate lends the crawl's
pages (estate.js sessionPages), and the app's slide has no Views
tab to hold them. A standalone pages/session.html is lent nothing
and draws no row, since its own branch reads fill the Views tab,
whose contents list groups the same pages by branch.

ONE LINE THAT SCROLLS, for the reason branch-brief's own Look row
gives: a wrap spends a whole band on the chip that did not fit,
and the partial chip at the edge is the affordance.

One line a topic, in the order the session reached it; a tap
opens the outline where it starts, under the same header the
outline draws there. The mark is how the topic's last stretch
ENDED (the closing state said inside it), so an unfinished one
reads as unfinished before anything is opened; a dot where it
ended on nothing. Minor asides are left to the outline's
headers. The provenance note rides a mark at the summary's
start, since title-tip underlines whatever carries it.

── TURNS: Gemini's summary of each turn ──────────────────────
One row per turn, numbered as the record numbers them, each its
headline: an index to scan, since the outline already prints
each turn's summary, and a tap opens the outline at that turn.
A turn that opens a stretch (the first, or one after a two-hour
break) carries the stretch's date and time above it; a mark sits
only on a turn Gemini did not summarize. The provenance lines
close the list.

── WHAT IT PRODUCED: the bottom region ───────────────────────
Calls, views and files under their own tab row, absent when the
session left none of the three; with one of them the row goes,
since a lone tab compares nothing and each pane names itself.
Calls lead, since what waits on the owner is the first thing to
see (owner, 2026-10-19), and their count is the one a tab keeps,
tinted while one waits.

FILES: what the session opened, which the strip counts and had no
route to. Alpine-rendered rather than imperative, unlike its two
neighbours: this is a list of plain rows with no state of its own,
so the reason those mount by hand (a kit that owns its selection)
does not apply.

Sorted by weight, not alphabetically: the question a reader brings
here is what the session WORKED ON, and an edit says more than a
read. The weighting is the sessions cache's own (fileWeight), so
this list and the row's hover card cannot order the same files two
ways.

── Addressing a session by the branch it worked on ───────────────────

The one address a phone can produce without knowing anything about this
store. The Claude app will copy the branch a session is on and copies
nothing else about it, so a branch name is the only handle that crosses
from there to here, and `Choose-Claude` in shortcut-tools hands it
straight to this page.

WHY THIS WALKS RATHER THAN READS AN INDEX. Nothing in the store joins a
branch to a record: the branch lives inside each record's `repos`, and
the one derived file that lifts it out, state/sessions.json, is 7 MB,
which is the wrong thing to hand a phone to answer one question. So the
tree listing (one call, cached, names every record and is already read
for #id=) orders the candidates and each is opened newest first. The
wanted session is the one being looked at while the branch was copied,
so it is the first or second read in the case this exists for.

The tie is the honest limit. A filename carries the day and the id, so
ordering is exact ACROSS days and arbitrary WITHIN one; `started` is
the real answer and only a fetched record has it. So the walk does not
stop on a match: it finishes that day and keeps the latest start, which
costs at most one day of reads and makes "the latest session on this
branch" true rather than nearly true.

Past the matching day, nothing left can be later. Also the only
exit that is not the cap, which is why the cap is generous.

Paths run newest day first, so the first hit fixes the day and only
a later `started` inside it can displace the record.

A record's serialized length, for one with no stored size (see rawSize).

── The two module-scope reads ────────────────────────────────────────────
Both are plain memos with the same expiry, kept out of the component for
the reason stated at the top: the deck reuses one mount per slide, and
what these answer is a property of the store rather than of the visit.

The PROMISE is memoized, not the settled record, and the difference shows
exactly where the deck lives: three slides mount at once and the reader's
two neighbours are warmed on top, so several callers ask for the same path
within a tick. Caching after the await lets every one of them miss and
fetch, which is the shape of bug that looks like nothing until the store is
private and every read is a rate-limited call.

The blob sha the record was read as, which is what Gemini's companion
names as its source (source_blob): the one exact answer to whether
the summaries were made from this version. Not enumerable, so Raw and
every export still show the record exactly as stored.

And its size in bytes, which is what the Raw tab prints: computing it
meant serializing the whole record again (see rawSize).
A failed read must not stand as the answer for a minute.
A failed read must not be cached as the answer for a minute.

Slotting without a custom element / shadow DOM. The host's children
are the slot content; Alpine has already queued their effects by the
time init() runs, so we must PRESERVE those nodes, not rebuild them
from a string — rebuilding orphans the queued effects and they throw
(e.g. "isDesktop is not defined") when they flush detached.

So: lift the existing children into a fresh body element (a move,
which keeps node identity + queued effects), assemble the chrome
around them synchronously, reattach, then initTree the new chrome.
initTree skips already-initialized nodes, so the slot isn't
double-bound. Net: the caller just drops bare markup inside — no
<template>, no wrapper — and it can read isDesktop / shown / close().
