in JavaScript, so a signed envelope can name its errand.
A pasted errand-result/1 envelope, or null for any other text.
An envelope's body as the one staged file the errand is graded against.
A glob of the only kind worth writing here: '*' is any run of characters.

The grade. For a read, `outcome` is the fulfill result; for any other
errand, it is { files: [{ name, text }] }, the text items staged for it.

The record that closes an errand, at its own name in the results folder.
A decline is served, not failed, and needs its reason: "nothing references
that, stop looking" is often worth more to the next session than the file.

Perform a read with an injected GH class and token. Returns an outcome and
never throws: errors land in it. Read-only, and called only from a tap.

  tree     recursive Git-trees listing of a repo (paths, types, sizes)
  branches branch names and tip shas
  fetch    contents of specific text files (paths)
main, not the selection: an errand is an operation, not a preview.

── Pinging Gemini ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A laptop-daemon `ping` errand filed by the app's Ping section, in the
shape web-tools-private sessions/tools/errand_runner.py files from a
session: daemon-<day>-ping-<base36 ms>. The Gemini home laptop daemon
forwards `prompt` to Gemini and writes the reply to
errands/results/<id>.json as data.reply.

A laptop-daemon `call-check` errand, filed from the Waiting view: one user
call's id, the evidence the browser gathered from GitHub, and the owner's
question when the Ask form carried one. The daemon asks Gemini whether the
call still holds, and the question first if there is one, and appends the
verdict to the notes store as Gemini's note about the call, voting up or
down on it. An empty question is left out, so the errand reads as the
plain check it was before questions existed.

The ping errands among a requests/ listing, newest day first. Pings filed
from a session's command line match too, so Ping shows every question.
Where one ping stands, from the claims/ and results/ listings.

A laptop-daemon `status` errand: the daemon closes it at once with its
host and tools version, so an answer means it is running.

Whether the Gemini home laptop daemon looks alive, from what it leaves on
BRANCH. It writes the topics rollup a minute or two after each session record
goes quiet, and it answers Pings and status checks. So:
  checking  a status check is out and unanswered
  behind    work has waited past the daemon's pace: a Ping unclaimed for
            5 minutes, a status check unanswered for 5, or a session record
            10 minutes old with no topics written since
  up        it did something in the last hour
  quiet     it did nothing for an hour, and nothing was waiting on it;
            silence cannot tell a running daemon from a stopped one
  unknown   nothing to read at all
Times are ISO strings; `at` is the moment the reading refers to.

The estate's search calls, in one place, with one cache.

Two consumers ask the same questions: the sidebar finder (a dispatcher whose
deeper lanes are tap-gated) and the Search view (the central file surface).
Each search existed first inside the finder component; extracting them here
is what lets the view exist without a second implementation, and what makes
the caches shared, so a tree the finder fetched is a tree the view never
re-fetches. Pure fetch-and-match: no Alpine, no DOM, no rendering opinions.
Consumers own reactivity by copying results into their own state.

The calls, and what each honestly covers:

  tree(repo, ref)    one recursive git/trees call per (repo, ref), cached
                     for the session (the stage's Browse/Search economy).
                     A FAILED fetch is not cached as an empty tree; it backs
                     off briefly and retries, so a blip does not kill the
                     file lanes until reload.
  names(...)         substring match over tree paths, any ref, any repos,
                     optionally scoped to a folder (`under`). Recursive and
                     flat: it answers "which paths match".
  level(...)         one level of one repo's tree, folders and files, off the
                     same cache. It answers "what is in here", which has
                     folders in it and is the question a recursive match
                     cannot fold back into.

Every file a caller gets back carries its SIZE IN BYTES, from the same
recursive read: the trees API reports a blob's size on the entry, so nothing
is fetched for it. This is the one thing the retired per-repo explorer had
that the cached walk did not, and it turned out to cost nothing to keep.
  contents(...)      the estate's MARKDOWN, by word, from the content index
                     the crawl writes into the registry
                     (kits/content-index.js: a manifest and each repo's
                     shards, default branches). Not GitHub's code-search
                     API, which a page cannot read: its answers carry no
                     CORS header (the kit's header has the measurement).
                     Shards are read once per registry and credential, like
                     the session shards. snippet(...) reads one hit's text
                     for the line a row quotes.
  sessions(...)      a client-side grep of the captured session records
                     (web-tools-private sessions/, via state/sessions.json):
                     what was SAID across every stored prompt and reply,
                     answered from kits/session-index.js rather than by
                     opening the records: 1.0 MB of monthly shards against
                     156 MB of store, 89 ms to load and 2 to 9 ms a query.
                     Unioned with what the ROW says (searchSegs: the two
                     names, the opening ask, attachments, repos, files),
                     because those are two halves of one question and the
                     rows are already in hand. A hit says which side
                     answered; the index holds terms rather than text, so a
                     match on the conversation has no fragment to quote.
  chats(...)         the chat archive's CHEAP PASS: the catalog month shards
                     in mehrlander/chat-histories (hand entries and machine
                     summaries merged), matched on title, tags and summary.
                     Read through kits/chat-archive.js, which owns the shard
                     memo, so this lane adds no cache of its own. It is the
                     sibling of sessions(...) and deliberately the opposite
                     trade: about 10 MB of model-written summaries across 41
                     months against 156 MB of verbatim records, so it finds a
                     chat you can DESCRIBE where the session lane finds words
                     that were SAID. Neither reaches the chat snapshots' full
                     text, which stays CLI-only (chat-histories
                     tools/search_chats.py, whose docstring names the split:
                     --catalog is the cheap semantic pass, full text the
                     exhaustive one).

Attaches to window.EstateSearch, loaded via gh.load('kits/estate-search.js').

a failed tree fetch may retry after this
"repo@ref" -> { paths, sizes, truncated }
"repo@ref" -> epoch ms of the last failure
"repo@ref" -> Promise
Each registry keeps only its current credential's cache. Requests retain
their cache object, so changing credentials or clearing caches detaches
unfinished old reads. Tokens never enter a cache key or statistics.

The registry's file-name index (state/files.json, lib/kits/file-index.js),
read once per page and kept: the crawl rewrites it at most once per push to
a default branch, so a second read in one visit would almost never differ.
`false` marks an index that could not be read, so a keystroke loop does not
re-request it; reset() clears either.

Months the chats lane has folded. The ROWS live in chat-archive's own memo
(immutable shards, never re-fetched once read), so this is a count for the
State view rather than a second copy of anything.

shard reads in flight at once
Successful session shards stay in the active cache. Failed months remain
retryable on the next query, and overlapping readers share their promises.

When this cache was last emptied, page load counting as the first empty.
It is the only age these caches have: nothing here is built, only fetched
and kept, so there is no build timestamp to report. The State view renders
it as "cleared 30m ago, 11 trees", which is the honest answer to the
question the Search view's own control kept being asked ("are these
results cached?").

~one line of context around the first case-insensitive hit.
`lead` is how much comes before the hit; a narrow row wants it short, or
the hit itself is what truncation cuts.

The blob paths of a repo at a ref ('' or 'HEAD' both mean the default
branch, resolved server-side), plus `sizes`, the same entries' byte counts
keyed by path. Throws on failure so a caller can say so; the failure is
remembered only long enough to stop a keystroke loop from hammering a dead
endpoint.

File-name search: substring over the trees of the given repos, each at its
own ref. Unreachable trees are reported, not thrown, so one bad ref does
not empty the whole answer.

`under` is a FOLDER SCOPE, applied before the substring match so the cap
counts scoped hits rather than spending itself outside the scope. It is
what makes an EMPTY query useful: with no q every path matches, so
`{ q: '', under: 'lib/kits' }` is a listing of that folder and the search
and the browse are one call. Leading and trailing slashes are forgiving.

ONE LEVEL of one repo's tree: the folders and files sitting directly under
`under`, rather than everything below it. Same cached tree as names(), so
browsing a folder costs no fetch after the first read of the repo, and
descending never costs another one.

This is the browse half, and it is a different question from names() rather
than a narrower one: names() answers "which paths match", which is
recursive and flat by nature, while this answers "what is in here", which
is one level and has folders in it. A consumer that folded folders out of a
recursive match would be answering neither.

A folder carries the count of blobs BELOW it, not in it, since that is what
the one recursive read knows and what says whether a folder is worth
opening. A file carries its own size, off the same entries.

WHAT A SESSION IS CALLED used to be folded in here, as `nameSegs`. It is
gone because RepoSessionsCache.searchSegs carries the same two names in
the same two spellings and eleven more fields besides, and one definition
of "what a row says" beats two that can drift. The argument it carried is
worth keeping: search.py holds --name apart from --grep because a name is
ASSIGNED and not said, so a hit on one must be distinguishable from a hit
on the other. The labelled segments do that here, and the sessions lane
below says which side answered on every hit.

Session search, over the index rather than the store.

IT USED TO OPEN EVERY RECORD. The registry holds 372 of them and 156 MB,
six at a time, and the first search of a session paid for all of it. What
that grep read was the prose, 22 MB of the 156, and kits/session-index.js
turns those into 1.0 MB of monthly shards over the wire. Measured: 89 ms
to load every shard and 2 to 9 ms a query, against tens of seconds and the
whole store.

TWO SOURCES, UNIONED, because they answer different halves and always did.
The INDEX answers what was SAID, across every prompt and reply. The ROW
answers what the session IS: its exported title, its derived name, its
opening ask, its attachments, the repos and files it worked
(RepoSessionsCache.searchSegs). Folding them keeps the old promise that
either spelling finds the session, and it costs nothing, since the rows
are already read for the shard months anyway.

WHAT A HIT CANNOT CARRY ANY MORE is a quoted fragment of the conversation.
The index holds terms, not text, so a match on what was said has nothing
to quote; the row's own ask stands in and the note line says which side
answered. Reading the sentence means opening the session, which fetches
that one record rather than all of them.
Pinned to main: the session store is live shared state written there.

Through the kit's constant, like every other read of this file. The
literal stays as the fallback for a boot where the kit has not loaded.

The months to read come from the rows, not from a tree call: every row
carries the day its session began, which is the folder its record sits
in and so the shard that holds it.
missing this time; a later query can retry

Activity can also match joined branch metadata that is absent from the
session row cache. Carry those known matches for this one query, so its
inspection list has the same membership after a cold link or refresh.

The quoted segment where the ROW answered, and a plain label where
only the conversation did, since there is nothing to quote.

`indexed` says whether the deep half ran at all. A registry whose crawl
has not written a shard yet answers on rows alone, and a consumer that
reported that as a complete result would be claiming a search it did not
perform.

Chat grep, over the archive's catalog layers. `repo` is the chat archive
(mehrlander/chat-histories); the shards load once per session through
chat-archive's memo and later queries match in memory.

WHOLE-ARCHIVE BY DEFAULT, which is what makes this a search rather than
the pane's filter. The Chats pane pages one month at a time on purpose and
its box narrows only what is loaded; this reads every month the frontier
names, about 10 MB across 41 shards, so it is a deliberate act and the
caller is expected to gate it. `months` caps the walk from the newest end
for a caller that wants a cheaper answer.

PROGRESS RATHER THAN A SPINNER. Forty shard reads is tens of seconds on a
cold pass, so `onProgress({ done, total })` fires per shard and the view
can say how far along it is. The crawl bars in the estate make the same
bargain for the same reason.

A MISSING SHARD IS NOT AN ERROR. Most months have exactly one of the two
layers, and chat-archive's loadMonth throws only when BOTH are absent,
which for a month the frontier named means the archive is inconsistent
rather than that the search failed. Those months are counted and reported
beside the hits, never thrown, so one bad month does not empty the answer.

Which field answered, for the note line. Same precedence the segments
are built in (title, summary, tags), so a hit whose title matched
says so rather than quoting a summary that happens to repeat it.

The shards are already newest-first inside a month and `take` is
newest-first across months, so this is only a tiebreak for rows whose
dates disagree with their shard.

One segment holding every term. The per-row test is chat-archive's
`matches`, which joins the segments; this narrower one exists only to pick
WHICH segment to quote, and a segment holding all the terms is the honest
one to show. Nothing is quoted when the terms are spread across fields.

What `clip` should centre on. It takes one needle, and a multi-term query
has no single one, so the first term stands in: it is the one the reader
typed first and the window is a courtesy rather than a claim.

Forget everything fetched, so the next search reads fresh. The Search
view's refresh control; a finder consumer clears its own copies too.
The index document, or null when the registry has none yet (a crawl has
not written it) or it cannot be read. Never throws: the callers fall back
to the live tree reads above, which is what they did before it existed.

A crawl that just wrote the index hands it here, so this page sees what it
committed without reading it back.

File-name search over the index: every indexed repo, default branches, in
one pass with no network after the first read. `repos` narrows it (the
estate's visible members, so a hidden repo stays hidden). Same row shape as
names(), plus `folders`, the capped folders whose path matched, and `at`,
the index's own age for the caller to show.

Contents, over the content index. Like sessions(), each registry keeps
only its current credential's reads, so a token change cannot reuse
another identity's shards.

`indexed` says whether a manifest exists at all, so a caller can tell
"nothing matched" from "nothing has been built yet".

One hit's quoted line: the file at its default branch, clipped around the
query's first term.

The chat shards are immutable once committed, so chat-archive keeps them
and only its failure backoff is worth clearing: a retry must not be told
to wait, and re-fetching a shard that read fine would be a reload of
everything already on screen for nothing. The count is this lane's own,
so it resets with the rest.

export.js — export a page to a portable, self-resolving copy: "download this
page plus the data it read()s" as one zip, optionally with its code inlined.

read() resolves a path local-first: a <script src=path> sitting beside the
page (page-relative) wins over the repo copy (root-relative). This kit emits
the page laid out so that wins with zero manual placement:

  <page-basename>.html      ← page source (baked, if offline), at the zip root
  <read-path>               ← each read() value, frozen to the local form

Because the HTML is at the zip root, page-relative and bundle-relative
coincide: a read path like 'data/sample.js' lands at 'data/sample.js' beside
the HTML, and read('data/sample.js') resolves it local on file://.

Which data? The data the page read()s. gh-boot.js wraps read() to record each
resolved read on window.__reads, so a page "declares" its data simply by
reading it. Callers can also pass reads explicitly (opts.reads) — handy when a
page already holds the value (the cross-repo-read demo does) or wants to export
data it hasn't read through read() itself.

Two zip modes, differing in exactly one thing: whether THIS REPO's code rides
along. Both freeze the read() data as sibling files beside the page.
  default          — code still loads from the CDN. Smaller.
  { offline:true } — also bakes the gh.load chain in (via build.js).
"offline" is the flag's name, not a promise: third-party libs (Tailwind,
daisyUI, Alpine, Phosphor) stay on their CDN tags in BOTH modes, so neither
zip renders on a machine with no network. What offline:true buys is
independence from *this repo*, which is what breaks on a private repo, an
unpushed branch, or a missing token. The FAB labels them "Zip" and
"Zip + code" for that reason.

renderCopy() is the third output and the odd one out: ONE HTML string, for
pasting into CodePen or any bare HTML preview. It is not an archive, so it has
nowhere to put sibling files: the code is inlined the way the offline zip does
it, and the read() data is inlined too (build.js `data`) rather than laid
down beside the page. Third-party CDN tags are deliberately left alone, because
the destination has a network and untouched tags are what make the paste small.
A page with no gh.load chain at all is already the finished artifact, and comes
back as its own source with nothing added.

Every entry point takes opts.gh / opts.scripts / opts.reads so a caller can aim
it at something other than the current window. The FAB does exactly that inside
a toss, where the page on screen is the subject in the frame and the globals
belong to the shell around it.

window.exporter:
  renderCopy(opts) -> { html, path, base, codeFiles, chainless, reads,
                        dropped, bytes, cdnRefs, relRefs }   (async)
  page({ offline?, path?, reads?, filename? })  build and download the zip
  build(opts) -> { path, base, filename, offline, codeFiles, reads, files }
                                                 same, minus the download
  localForm(path, value)  one read() value in its <script> deposit form
  cdnRefs(html)  count run-time references to our lib/ on GitHub Pages
  relRefs(html)  count page-relative script references (chainless pages)
The kits a demo injects into its proof frames ride along when code is
inlined: vanilla-demo.js lists them on window.__frameScripts, and
build.js collectCache gathers them with the loaded chain.

This is the "export" leg of the vocabulary: load → build → bake → export →
brief. The fifth leg (kits/brief.js) is this kit's reader-facing sibling: it
drops the boot chain the offline mode has to carry, because a review wants
the page's own code and nothing else.

Freeze a read() value into the local deposit form: the file read()'s local
probe injects as <script>, which sets document.currentScript.value.

The page's own repo path. The FAB stamps it on its host element
(data-path="pages/foo.html"); fall back to nothing so callers pass opts.path.

Bake the page's code into the HTML: collect the gh.load chain at runtime,
emit the build, and rewrite the entry.js import to carry it inline. The
result boots with no network (the data files below cover read() the same way).

Runtime references to this repo's own code by URL that survive baking.
Inlining covers the gh.load chain and the lib files a page reads to run in
a frame (vanilla-demo's injects, gathered by collectCache), so a page that
follows the loader leaves none. Anything else that reaches for lib/ on
GitHub Pages at run time breaks on a private repo or an unpushed branch,
so it is counted rather than silently left. data: URLs are stripped first,
or the inlined build would count itself.

Script references that resolve against the page's own location: a
relative <script src>, a relative import() or `from`. A chainless page
carrying one is not the finished artifact its shape suggests; it is a
page that renders only where it was served from. app/index.html is the
case: one import of ../dist/app.js and nothing for bake() to rewrite.

Assemble the file list without downloading — for previews/UI. With
opts.offline, the HTML is baked so the zip opens with no network at all
(code inlined + data local). Returns
{ path, base, filename, offline, codeFiles, reads:[paths], files:[{path,data}] }.
Default to the recorded reads; map to the {path,value} shape build needs.

Pristine repo copy at the booted ref — not document.documentElement
.outerHTML, which is the mutated post-Alpine DOM. On a ?use=<sha> page
gh.ref is that sha, so the export captures exactly the version running.

One HTML string that renders anywhere with a network: own code inlined,
read() data inlined, third-party CDN tags untouched. The output is for
pasting, so it is returned rather than downloaded; the caller decides
whether that means the clipboard, a file, or a fragment.

Returns { html, path, base, codeFiles, reads, dropped, bytes, chainless,
cdnRefs }. `chainless` is true when the page had no gh.load chain to
inline, which is not a degraded result: that page was already a standalone
artifact. `cdnRefs` counts what still reaches for our lib/ by URL at run time.

Only what survives a round trip through JSON can ride inside the file.
A value that does not (a live handle, a cyclic object) is dropped rather
than thrown over, and named in the result so the caller can say so.

Only meaningful on a chainless page: a baked one has had its import
rewritten to the carried build, which is a blob: URL and not counted.
Build and download. Same opts as build(); returns the manifest sans files.

Associate submitted text with one file at one repository revision. The
declaration names a PowerShell file; a selected XAML file supplies its own
address. Checks and unfinished submissions live in browser-local IndexedDB.

Recognize physical lines without changing the supplied source. A BOM
is already whitespace to this pattern. Repeated signatures may name
the same file; different identities must not silently choose the first.

Windows-1252 by table, not by TextDecoder: a Node built without full ICU
reads the label as ISO-8859-1, so 0x80 to 0x9F come back as C1 controls
where every browser gives punctuation (the snag
node-decodes-windows-1252-as-latin1). The five bytes the WHATWG table
leaves unassigned keep their own code point, as browsers do.

Every check under a folder, newest first: the PowerShell outpost view reads a
whole workspace's checks in one pass rather than one lookup per file.
The staged text and original pending record remain available.

kits/file-deck.js — a changeset's files, read one at a time.

The Files pane is a LIST, and a list is for scanning: thirty hairline rows,
each one a `fileReview` card that expands in place. Reading a diff through it
means expanding a row, scrolling past it, collapsing, expanding the next. That
is a good way to find a file and a poor way to read one.

This is the other half: the same cards, one per slide, in the house swipe deck
(kits/swipe-deck.js). It opens as a DRILL, one level below whatever deck or
takeover the reader was already in, so the header becomes the file's and
leaving it returns them to the branch. One deck visible, one meaning for the
swipe, and the nesting only in the return path. The reasoning for that shape
over a nested pager or a level picker is in swipe-deck's drilling note.

  fileDeck.open({ repo, ref, base, baseName, files, start, title, subtitle,
                  parent, onClose, actions, openOn }) -> the deck handle

  files      [{ path, previousPath, status, additions, deletions, patch }],
             the shape kits/branch-brief.js already assembles and the shape
             the compare API hands back. Pass the list the reader can SEE:
             a collapsed registry group is a group they chose not to open, so
             its files do not belong in the deck either. That makes the pane's
             group toggles the deck's filter, with no second control.
  start      index to open on, so "read from here" lands on the right file
  openOn     which PANE each card lands on ('mddiff' for the rendered
             comparison). Omitted, a card opens on the file itself, which is
             this surface's default and right for browsing.
  actions    extra header buttons, appended after the card's own controls.
             pages/approve.html puts its verdict button here, which is the
             only thing that makes an approval different from a read.
  parent     the deck handle to drill from, when there is one. drill() takes
             the crumb from its title and turns the dismiss button into a
             back chevron.
  The deck also LISTS itself, through swipe-deck's `index` labeler: the header
  mark opens every file in the changeset, current one marked. A changeset is
  exactly the case that wants it, since the footer draws dots only while they
  stay countable and a thirty-file branch is well past that. What a row says
  is the file and what happened to it, which is the pane's own reading of the
  compare rather than a second one.

  announce   default true: say what the reader is on through the subject
             channel the FAB listens to (see the note above open()). Pass
             false for a deck that should not retarget the sidebar.
  back       force the chevron without a parent DECK. The branch takeover is
             the case: it is chrome of its own rather than a swipe-deck, so
             there is no handle to drill from, but dismissing still returns
             the reader one level up and the glyph has to say so. An ✕ there
             would promise to close something it does not close.

Three slides mount at a time (swipe-deck renders the active one and its
neighbours), which is why every card here can start OPEN. The Files pane
cannot: it has to hedge with `open: files.length <= 12 && innerWidth >= 768`,
because twelve open cards is twelve fetches at once and most of a phone
screen. A deck is one file at a time by construction, so the hedge does not
apply and the reader gets the content without a tap.

Open on WHAT is the other half, and it is why the cards here are passed
`read` and `bare`. This is a reading surface, so a file opens as itself: a
doc rendered, an image shown, a `.gz` inflated, a source file diffed. And the
deck header already names the file, so the card drops its own collapsed row
rather than printing the path a second time, elided a second way.

Requires kits/swipe-deck.js, kits/subject-channel.js and the fileReview
Alpine component. All three ride in the pre-build, so a page that has the
bundle has them; a page on a gh.load chain names them itself.

The path, split the way the collapsed row splits it: the directory is
context and the filename is the answer. In the header the filename is the
title and the directory rides the subtitle, so a `claude/`-length path does
not truncate the one word the reader is looking for.

A directory, shortened from the MIDDLE so both ends survive.

The crumb is where the reader learns which branch and which corner of it
they are in, and a deep path defeated it: `sources/wayback/…` truncated at
the right by CSS, which keeps the segment nearest the repo root and throws
away the one nearest the file, exactly backwards. The two segments worth
keeping are the FIRST, which says which part of the tree, and the LAST,
which is the file's own folder. Everything between them is the part a
reader can infer, so it becomes one ellipsis.

  sources/wayback/url-corpora/corpora/drs.wa.gov/  ->  sources/…/drs.wa.gov
  lib/kits/                                        ->  lib/kits

The same trick on one string, and then on the whole crumb.

Eliding the directory was not enough on a phone: the crumb is
`<branch> · <dir>`, every branch here is a `claude/<slug>` whose slug runs
to twenty-five characters, and the header's own CSS truncation then cut
the RIGHT end, which is the dir. So the reader lost the specific half to
keep the general one, which is the wrong half to lose twice over.

Budget the crumb instead and spend it from the LEFT. The last part is the
file's own folder and survives whole; the branch gives way first, because
by then the reader has swiped into it and needs a reminder rather than a
full statement of it.

The budget is the VIEWPORT's, not a constant: 34 characters is what the
subtitle box holds at 390px beside the icon, the chevron and the counter
pill, so a wider phone gets a longer crumb and a narrower one a shorter.
Found by measuring in the browser, comparing the element's scrollWidth to
its clientWidth at 320, 390 and 430. Two things the divisor cannot fix and
does not pretend to: the chrome beside the crumb is a fixed width, so the
relationship is not really linear, and a floor of ten characters on the
branch means a very deep path can still exceed the budget. Below about
360px both bite and CSS truncation takes over, which is the same graceful
fallback as before rather than a regression.

What happened to a file, as a glyph and as words. `modified` gets no icon
of its own on purpose: it is the ordinary case and the majority of any
changeset, so marking it would spend the column on the rows that need it
least and leave the three that matter harder to pick out.

── Announcing the subject ──────────────────────────────────────────────

The FAB sidebar follows the reader from file to file, learning what is on
screen from the subject channel (kits/subject-channel.js): a repo, a ref
and a path, plus `route` for "a file an app is showing rather than the
renderer". That kit owns which windows are listening, saving and putting
back what it overwrites, and bridging the sidebar's answer back down into
a framed document. The deck's part is only to say which file, per slide.

`via` is left off deliberately: the fab already knows what page it is
mounted on (shellRepo/shellPath/shellRef, taken before any adoption) and
fills it in, so the deck never has to work out what app it is inside.

DECLARED HERE, ASSIGNED BELOW. render() hands this to every card as its
onChrome, and render runs while the deck is opening; the real one needs
the handle that open() returns. A const would be in its temporal dead
zone for exactly that window, so it starts as a no-op instead of as a
crash waiting on a race nobody would reproduce.

Same reason, one line up: render() runs while open() is still returning,
so anything it captures has to be declared before that call and assigned
after it.

The deck's cards read `__compareRef`, so it takes the bridge; the
navigate handle below is the deck's own and rides as a managed global.

One card per slide, mounted the way the Files pane mounts them, with one
difference that is not cosmetic: `open: true`. See the note above.

The options object is built HERE, in a closure, and not read off an
Alpine component. That is the same trap cardOpts documents in
alpineComponents/branch-brief.js: inside an x-data expression Alpine
injects every registered component name into scope, so `repo` resolves to
the repo DATA PROVIDER rather than to a string, and every content fetch
then addresses a stringified function. Here there is no x-data expression
to be caught by, because the mount is imperative and the options are
passed by reference through a global handoff.
Which global each built slide is holding, so `release` can let it go when
the deck evicts a slide the reader has left. Emptying the slide destroys
the card, but the options object carries the file's whole patch and would
sit on `window` for the life of the page.

The ref the slides are being read AT, which starts as the branch's and
moves when the sidebar's ref bar picks another (see navigate below).
Everything the compare told us is a fact about the branch, so the moment
it moves the patch, the status and the line counts stop being said.

Alpine evaluates x-data as an expression in the component's scope, so
the options travel through a keyed global rather than being serialized
into the attribute: a path with a quote in it would otherwise break the
expression, and a patch certainly would.

This is a READING surface, and the deck header already names the
file. So the card opens on the file's own presentation rather than
on a diff: a doc reads, an image shows, an archive shows what is
inside it. The diff is one tab away for anyone who wants it.

HOSTED, which since 2026-09-07 means the header carries the card's
controls too and not only its name. A slide was a row of chrome over
a document: the path (already in the header, truncated a second
way), three layout icons, a copy button and a github menu. Every one
of those is about the file the header is already naming, so they sit
beside the name and the slide is the document. What the card keeps
is the state behind them; see syncChrome.

WHICH READING TO LAND ON, when the caller has an opinion. A reading
surface opens on the file itself, which is right for a deck you are
browsing and wrong for one you opened to judge a change: there the
reader has to find what moved before they can weigh it, and the
rendered comparison is that same document with the change marked in
it. pages/approve.html is the caller that needs it. The card falls
back to the file where the pane it names does not exist, so passing
it costs nothing on a file that has no rendered comparison.

AND TELL THE HEADER A CARD EXISTS. onChrome covers every later change,
but not the first: the header is filled once at open, and a slide
built after that (the opening slide itself, since render runs while
open() is still returning) would leave it empty until the card
happened to move. A microtask, because `handle` is assigned by the
same synchronous block that called this.

The crumb's own context, minus whatever the parent already says. A host
that names the branch and drills from a deck TITLED the branch would
otherwise read "claude/some-branch · claude/some-branch · lib/kits/",
and asking every caller to know what its parent is called is a worse
rule than deduping here.

The breadcrumb: whatever the caller names as context, plus this file's
own directory. drill() prefixes the parent deck's title onto it.

The contents, which is the pane's list read back at deck scale. Off the
branch's own ref the status and the counts stop being true (see the
note by `moved`), so a row falls back to naming the folder, exactly as
the crumb does.

A slide is one file's dossier and can be long; let it scroll on its own
and keep the deck's own max-width, which the cards were designed for.

AND IT SETS ITS OWN EDGES. The deck's default padding is a reading
measure for a slide that is prose, and every slide here is a CARD,
which carries its own. Doubled up, a rendered comparison on a desktop
sat about 40px in from each side once the deck's `sm:px-8`, the
document's own inset and the reserved scrollbar gutter were added
together, and the changed blocks' tinted edges are meant to reach for
the sides. Reported 2026-09-18: "a lot less padding on the left and
right and top". Enough is left for the gutter to land on rather than
on the text.

`px-2` and not `px-1`: a changed block bleeds 8px past the text so its
ring is visible, and the document reserves 4 of that itself, so a slide
at 4 put the ring back on the viewport's edge. Measured at 390: `px-1`
gave 0, `px-2` gives 4. Above 640 the reserved scrollbar gutter adds 10
a side on top, which is the floor there and not something padding can
take back.

THE HEADER CARRIES THE FILE'S OWN CONTROLS, and nothing else. It held
a door to the sidebar until 2026-09-07, on the reading that a reader
would not otherwise know the drawer was aimed at this file. The reader
it was for asked for it back out: the deck still announces, so the
sidebar is still aimed here whenever it is opened, and the button was
a second thing to look at on a row that had none to spare. See
syncChrome, which fills this in per slide and REPLACES whatever is
here: the set is computed before a card exists to ask, so this is the
one frame before the first sync and not a second place controls live.

The crumb's head is normally the parent deck's title, which names the
branch. Once the reader has moved the deck off that branch the parent's
title is no longer what they are reading, so the ref they ARE reading
takes the slot: the crumb's whole job is to say where you are.

The caller's context gives way too where it was naming the ref, since
the crumb would otherwise carry both refs and say neither is the one.

The base rides along with the file. It is what makes the sidebar's
compare bar appear: the deck is not asking for a comparison, it is
saying that one is already in force and handing over the choice.

── Re-address, rather than be navigated away from ──────────────────────

The sidebar's ref bar renders a file at another ref by going TO the
renderer: outside a toss it navigates to toss-render, inside one it
re-addresses through `__tossNavigate`. Neither is right over a deck. The
reader is thirty files into a changeset, and answering "show me this at
main" by leaving for a single-file renderer throws away the list, the
position in it, and the way back.

A deck can do better because it already owns the slide: change the ref,
rebuild the two or three slides that are mounted, and the reader is
still exactly where they were. So the deck publishes a handle and the
fab tries it before it navigates, the same shape as `__tossNavigate` and
for the same reason. Borrowed and returned with the subject, since a
deck inside a toss must not leave the shell's own handle overwritten.

It answers false rather than swallowing what it cannot do: a file that
is not in this changeset, or another repo entirely, is a real navigation
and the fab should make it.

Every mounted slide is holding the old ref, and eviction is what
hands a card's own references back, so drop before building rather
than building over the top of a live tree.

── THE CARD'S CHROME, CARRIED BY THIS HEADER ───────────────────────

The slide is the document; everything about it is up here beside its
name. Same move stage.js's reader deck makes with its viewer, and for
the same reason: a control that acts on the file the header is naming
belongs next to the name, not in a second band under it.

Read off the card rather than rebuilt, so the layouts and the links
exist in one place (alpineComponents/file-review.js) and are only PLACED
in another. That is also why they arrive as buttons and a menu rather
than as the card's own markup: the card's is laid out for a row inside a
card, and the header is a different row with a different budget.

ONE ICON PER LAYOUT, not one menu holding three. They are a choice
between three readings of the same file, which is a thing to see at a
glance and tap once; behind a menu it becomes two taps and a memory
test. The github links go the other way for the same reason: four rows
of prose is a menu whatever it is anchored to.

A MENU IS THE EXCEPTION IN THIS ESTATE, and the rule it answers to is
how many places there are to go: 29 of the 31 github marks in lib/ are a
plain link, because a repo row, a pin, a peek's source each have exactly
one destination. The two that are menus are this file's set and the
branch page's, which offer this version, the base version, the last
commit and the raw bytes. Shape follows the destination count, not
taste, which is why these two do not read as inconsistent.

SMALLER WHERE THE ROW IS TIGHT. At 390px this header holds a dismiss,
the deck's mark, the file's name WITH its github mark inside it, the
pager, and these. Measured 2026-09-18: four of them at `btn-sm` left
the name 114px, of which the github mark takes about 30, so a
filename gets 84 and anything longer than `fund-600.md` elides. One
more control (pages/approve.html adds a verdict) took it to 48 and

syncChrome runs itself off the card's own onChrome, so this only has
to make the change; the header redraws when the card says it moved.

THE GITHUB MARK RIDES THE NAME, not the control cluster. It sat at the
cluster's end and then at its start, and both read as belonging to the
group of controls rather than to the file: which is what the estate's
own rule is against, since a github destination answers "which copy of
this file" and belongs with the identity. The card states the same rule
in flex order (alpineComponents/file-review.js: order-2 beside the name
on a reading surface, order-11 at the far end in a list); this header IS
the name, so the kit grew a slot inside its h1 rather than the mark
getting a better position among the controls.

THE CARET IS WHAT SAYS IT IS SAFE TO TAP. Without it the mark reads
as a link, so the reader expects to be taken somewhere and hesitates
over a control that only opens a list. Same glyph and size the card
and the branch page put on their own github menus.

The header follows the reader. This is the whole reason the deck knows
about files at all rather than being handed inert slides: the title has
to name the file you are looking at, not the one you opened on.

And once now, because drill() built the opening crumb by its own generic
rule (parent title, then whatever the child named) and that rule has no

is the one slide wearing the unfitted crumb.

The chrome too, and for a sharper reason than the crumb's: `actions` is
computed before the deck exists, so before any card has mounted, and a
reader who opens and never swipes would otherwise see a header with

kits/file-index.js — the estate's file names, kept in the private registry so
the sidebar finder can match a name in every repo on the first keystroke.

The finder used to read each repo's file list live: the open repo's on first
input, the other nine behind a "File names, every repo" tap. One recursive
trees call per repo per page visit, about 2.5 MB of JSON for the estate, and
a tap the reader had to know about. This file moves that read to the crawl,
which already knows when a repo's default branch moved, and stores the
answer as state/files.json beside the other caches.

WHAT AN ENTRY HOLDS. Per repo: the default-branch commit the list was read
at (`sha`), and its blob paths GROUPED BY FOLDER, `dirs: { "lib/kits":
["file-index.js", …] }`, which is about half the bytes of a flat path list
because a folder is spelled once. Measured 2026-10-01 over the ten estate
repos: 2.5 MB flat, 244 KB gzipped grouped.

THE FOLDER CAP. A folder holding more than FOLDER_CAP files DIRECTLY is
stored as its count, not its names: `dirs: { "bills/texts/2019-20/Htm/House":
2997 }`. One repo trips it today, wa-bills, whose 138,706 bill texts are
named by bill number and would otherwise be two thirds of the file. The
count stays, so the finder can say the folder exists and how much it holds,
and the cut is mechanical rather than a list of repos someone has to keep.

TRUNCATION. GitHub cuts a recursive trees response at 100,000 entries and
says so (`truncated`). readTree then walks: the root without recursion, and
each subtree recursively, descending again wherever a subtree is itself cut.
wa-bills costs about twenty calls this way, once per push to its default
branch. An entry whose walk still could not finish says `truncated: true`.

activity crawl already read; when it matches the stored entry's `sha`, the
entry carries and no call is made. A quiet estate costs this file nothing.

.gitattributes, resolved in the browser as git resolves it.

A page cannot run `git check-attr`, so this is git's own rule, from attr.c,
and node/test/git-attributes-kit.test.mjs holds it to git's answer for every
tracked file in this checkout. What git does, and so what this does:

  - Each line is a pattern and a list of attributes: `name` sets one,
    `-name` unsets it, `name=value` gives it a value, and `!name` returns it
    to unspecified. Blank lines and `#` lines are skipped.
  - A file takes, for each attribute, the first assignment met walking from
    the deepest .gitattributes to the root and from each file's last line
    up, so a later line wins and a folder's file beats its parent's. Within
    a line, a later attribute wins. `!name` counts as an assignment, which
    is how a later line clears an earlier one.
  - A pattern with no slash matches the file's name at any depth. Any other
    pattern matches the path relative to its own file's folder, with a
    leading slash dropped. `*` and `?` stop at a slash; `**` crosses folders
    only as `**/` at the start, `/**` at the end, or `/**/` between, and is
    `*` anywhere else.
  - A trailing slash matches a folder, never a file, and a negative pattern
    is ignored, so neither ever assigns anything here.
  - `[attr]name ...` in the root file defines a macro, and `binary` is
    built in as `-diff -merge -text`. A macro expands only when it is set.

Values are true (set), false (unset) or a string; `word()` spells one as
check-attr prints it. The input is the text of each .gitattributes by its
folder, '' for the root, so the caller chooses how to fetch them.

A bracket expression from `[` at i: [regex text, index of the closing `]`],
or null when it never closes, in which case `[` is literal.
A C-style quoted pattern, as git writes a path with spaces or controls.
One file's lines, as rules: { dir, line, pattern, match(path), attrs }.
The resolver for one tree: files is { '<folder>': text }.
Each specified attribute with the rule that assigned it.

The attributes git or GitHub act on by name, each with the section of the
document that defines it: the ones the estate sets, and the parts of the
binary macro above. Any other attribute means something only to the
repository's own tools, which define its values in docs/vocabularies.csv.

kits/git-change.js — pure browser-capable Git bundle & packfile unpacker,
delta patch resolver, and git-change/1 envelope validator.

Adheres to the repo's code layer rules (docs/code-layers.md):
  - Lives in lib/kits/
  - Registers window.GitChange
  - Uses dynamic lazy import for pako
  - Self-contained, pure, and testable in both browser and Node realms

Capabilities:
  - Verify git-change/1 envelopes (SHA-256 integrity, size bounds, schema)
  - Parse Git bundle v2/v3 headers (prerequisites and references)
  - Parse standard Git packfiles (PACK v2/v3, object streams)
  - Inflate object zlib streams and capture exact stream consumption boundaries
  - Apply Git copy/insert deltas (OBJ_OFS_DELTA and OBJ_REF_DELTA)
  - Fetch remote base blobs asynchronously when deltas reference base commits
  - Hash Git objects according to the Git object format (<type> <size>\0<data>)
  - Reconstruct head commits, trees, and changed files
gh-api.js's codec, kept under this kit's names for its callers.
The header is ASCII text ending with an empty line before the PACK signature

sha -> { type, data, sha }
packOffset -> { type, data, sha }
First pass: parse headers and inflate each object stream

A pack entry has one zlib stream. Pako 2 follows concatenated
wrapped streams, so locate the raw DEFLATE end first, then inflate
exactly that zlib member to validate its header and Adler-32 checksum.
Fetch missing base object asynchronously from GitHub
Guard against path traversal in tree entries
Recursively traverses tree objects present in the resolved objects map
Verify head tree SHA matches expected_tree
A top-level `root.<name> =` is the shelf's namespace shape (node/build/kits-index.mjs).

github-links.js — the GitHub destinations for one repo, as menu rows.

The app is a wrapper over GitHub, not a wall: every view keeps a one-tap
route to the GitHub presentation of what it is showing. For a REPO that route
used to be a single "Open on GitHub" row pointing at the repo root, which is
the one destination the reader could have guessed. The rest of a repo's
GitHub surface (its pull requests, its issues, its branch list, its Actions
runs) had no route at all, so this file names them once and both callers read
the same list: the sidebar Repos row's github button and the Activity view's
repo chip.

Pure: string building over owner/repo, no fetches, no Alpine. The URLs
themselves come from RepoAddress.github (lib/kits/repo-address.js), which
owns how a ref and a path are encoded; this file owns which destinations a
menu offers. window.GithubLinks, to match the other lib globals.

The row list is deliberately short and fixed. Insights, Settings, Wiki, and
Releases are all one more tap from the repo root and none of them is a place
this shell's reader goes daily; a menu that lists everything is a menu nobody
reads. `tracker` is the one repo-declared row (.web-tools.json), since where
a repo keeps its task board is a repo property, not a GitHub convention.
Read at call time: RepoAddress boots ahead of every kit.

The repo root, with a ref only when one is worth naming (browsing a
branch that is not the default). Same rule the old githubUrlFor used.

A path INSIDE the repo: a folder as a tree, a file as a blob (the last
segment carrying an extension is the test, the same one the sidebar uses
to decide whether a pin opens as a file). An empty ref means HEAD, which
is GitHub's own name for "the default branch, whatever it is called", and
saves the caller a lookup it may not have.

The REF here is a literal one to stamp, not a candidate: unlike `rows`,
this takes no defaultRef and makes no judgment about whether the ref is
worth naming. That decision belongs to the caller, which is the only side
that knows which ref a row stands for.

The sidebar's project rows are the reason this exists: they name a
workspace folder rather than a repo, and the task-board row below builds

One destination by key, for a caller that wants a link rather than a

kits/guide-render.js — a guide PR body, rendered as something you can walk.

A guide body is markdown written for GitHub: every file it names is a blob
link, which is the right answer for a reader standing on github.com and the
wrong one for a reader standing in the thing the guide describes. There the
link should reach the RENDERER that can show the file, not its source.

So this kit does two jobs over one parse:

  RE-AIM     every recognised blob link is pointed at the renderer for its
             kind (a page at the toss, a data-ish file at the data view) and
             stamped with its address, so a host can intercept the tap and
             render in place instead of navigating.
  COLLECT    the same links, deduped BY FILE, become a chip strip: the
             guide's file list as a menu rather than as prose to re-read.

Parsing the rendered HTML rather than string-replacing the markdown keeps one
definition of what a link is (the parser's), so a link written inline, as a
reference, or as an autolink all get the same treatment.

Extracted from alpineComponents/fab.js on 2026-08-06, where it had been the
drawer's alone. It moved because the FAB is not the only surface that shows a
guide: pages/branch.html renders the same body under the same rules, and the
estate's branch takeover renders that page full-viewport. One renderer, three
places it appears.

Pure but for `render`, which needs a DOM parser (the browser's, or jsdom's in
a test). No fetch, no Alpine, no `this`. Attaches to window.GuideRender.

THE TOSS'S MARK, and it is the chat convention's own glyph rather than a
second one. CONVERSATION.md writes a render link as 🥏 and has since the
primitive was named; the app drew ph-disc, so one mechanism had two marks
and a reader crossing from a reply to the row had to learn both. The
frisbee is the noun everything here already uses for the thing ("toss a
live view"), which a disc only resembles.

It rides on the TARGET rather than being typed into each template, for the
reason every other field here does: three strips render these chips and a
character repeated in three files is three places to disagree.

How a rendered body is styled: one injected stylesheet, not utility classes.

It was utility classes, in the arbitrary-variant form (`[&_a]:text-primary`,
`[&_ul]:list-disc`), and half of them silently produced nothing. daisyUI
ships its color utilities PREBUILT in its own stylesheet, so a bare
`text-primary` works while `[&_a]:text-primary` has to be generated by the
Tailwind browser build, which has no knowledge of daisyUI's theme tokens
and emits no rule at all. Core utilities in the same string (`underline`,
`list-disc`) generated fine, so a guide rendered with bullets and
underlines and never once with a blue link, in the FAB since PR #295 and
here since the day this kit was extracted, with nothing in any console.

Real CSS removes the whole class of failure: no generation step, no
dependency on when a class reaches the DOM relative to a scan, and the
daisyUI variables are read at paint time so a theme swap still follows.
The two sizes are one base class plus a modifier, since only the type scale
and the spacing differ between a full-width page and the FAB's drawer.

`drawer` is the FAB's right-side panel, `page` a full-width page. Injects on
first ask, so a host that never renders a guide pays nothing.

A blob URL's `<ref>/<path>` tail cannot be split by counting slashes,
because a ref may contain them and in this estate always does: every
session branch is `claude/<slug>`, so the naive first-segment split yields
ref `claude` and a path starting with the rest of the branch name. Both
halves are then wrong and the resulting address 404s.

The known refs are the disambiguator: match the LONGEST one that prefixes
the tail. Falls back to the first segment, which is right for a sha, a tag,
and any unslashed branch, and is the best available guess before a caller
has a branch list to offer.

Where a repo file opens. The one routing table, read by a guide's links and
by the FAB's path picker, differing only in `any`:

  .html            the toss, the renderer for a page
  data-ish files   the data view (markdown renders as preview there)
  anything else    null, unless `any` — a picker may be less careful than a
                   link, because a picker's user asked for that exact file

No ref is not a missing ref: the grammar reads a bare repo:path as the
repo's default branch, which is exactly what a cross-repo pick means.
Only the title has to say so, since "at " with nothing after it would
read as a bug.

`addr` rides alongside the url because an in-place re-address needs the
address, not the link: a renderer already open would otherwise reload its
shell to reach a state it can reach where it stands.

renderTarget answers for one file in isolation. This answers for a set of
changed paths, and it carries the one rule renderTarget cannot: in a repo
whose pages are framed by an app, a changed page is not addressable on its
own. The app is what mounts it, so a toss straight at the page renders a
document that boots into nothing, which docs/showing-mechanisms.csv records
as the route the session store got wrong most often.

`showing` is that repo's .web-tools.json `showing` block, the same three
fields python/showing.py reads, so the app and this estate's own script
pick the same mechanism from the same declaration rather than from two
codified opinions:

  app      the page that frames the others
  app_dir  the app's own folder; a changed page in it IS the app
  views    { <view key>: <path prefix it frames> }

Paths under one view collapse to ONE chip, because they are one thing to
open: the app on that view. A repo with no `showing` block, or a path
outside every declared prefix, falls through to renderTarget unchanged,
which is what makes this safe to call for every repo.

The LONGEST matching prefix wins, so a view nested inside another
one's folder resolves to itself rather than to its parent.

`short` is a SECOND label, not a replacement: a strip inside a list
row has about 220px and a mono filename runs 120 to 170 of it, so two
chips never share a line while a detail's full-width row fits four.
The extension is what goes, since the disc already says "a page" and
the title carries the path whole.

A file path in PROSE, styled as one. The caption convention writes
filenames plain ("Filenames stay plain and link words are tappable"), so
a rendered guide showed its most-scanned tokens in body type. This pass
wraps path-shaped tokens in <code class="guide-path"> after the parse:
renderer-side on purpose, so bodies stay plain markdown for GitHub and
every surface that renders through this kit (the FAB drawer, the branch
page, the takeover) styles them the same. The extension whitelist is what
keeps "e.g." and version numbers out; anchors, code, and pre are skipped,
a link's label being already styled by being a link.

Returns null for a link that should pass through untouched, so callers can
treat "no opinion" and "re-aim here" as the same branch.

markdown -> { html, targets, byAddr }.

`resolve(href)` decides where a link goes; the default reads blob URLs
against `knownRefs`. `preferRef` breaks a dedupe tie, which is not a detail:
a guide names each changed file three times by convention, [new] and [main]
and [diff], and the first two are the same file at two refs. Deduping on
the ADDRESS gave a strip listing index.html twice, which reads as a bug
and is useless as a menu. Keyed by kind and path, the ref the reader is
looking at wins. The PROSE keeps every link re-aimed individually, since
there both refs are meaningful: the sentence around them says which is
which.

Not something a host can render: a session link, a compare view, an
issue. Those still belong to GitHub and still open away.

A renderable link keeps its href so a long-press can still copy a
durable address; a host that wants in-place rendering intercepts the
ordinary tap on data-render-addr.

marked, lazily and once per page. Same URL and same shape source-peek.js
and chat-render.js use, so the three share one cached asset.

The `#gz=` payload, in one place: text gzipped, then base64url, so a page,
a document or a data envelope rides in a link with nothing hosted and no
token needed to open it.

The form is the estate's (docs/CONVERSATION.md, "Content in the link"). Until
2026-10-20 seventeen pages and components decoded it and nine encoded it,
each with a copy of its own. They agreed on the format and drifted at the
edges: six re-padded the base64 and the rest relied on atob forgiving its
absence, one page decoded through a second gzip library, and none but the
renderer tolerated whitespace a chat client wraps into a long link. This is
the one codec, and node/test/gz-payload.test.mjs fails on a new copy.

Encoding emits base64url ('-' and '_', no padding): a fragment value read
through URLSearchParams turns '+' into a space (kits/url-params.js).
Decoding accepts both alphabets, padded or not, and whitespace, as
pages/toss-render.html's decoder does, since links already handed over
carry every one of those. The renderer keeps that copy on purpose: its
critical render path loads no lib.

Attaches to window.GzPayload, loaded via gh.load('kits/gz-payload.js').

The base64 halves are gh-api.js's (GH.toBase64url, GH.decodeBytes), which
every page boots first: decodeBytes reads either alphabet, padded or not,
with any whitespace.

io.js — user data in and out of the page: file picker, file download, blob
preview, and the clipboard. JSZip loads lazily, only when saveZip is called.
Exposes window.io.

  await io.pick(accept)                 // file picker → ArrayBuffer
  await io.pickText(accept)             // file picker → string
  io.save(data, filename, type)         // download a Blob or typed array
  io.saveJson(data, filename, space)    // download as JSON
  await io.saveZip([{ path, data | url }], filename)
  io.show(data, type)                   // open a blob in a popup window
  await io.copy(text)                   // clipboard write → boolean
  await io.paste()                      // clipboard read → string
  await io.pasteItems()                 // every clipboard flavor → items[]

copy() and paste() try three branches in order. When the page lacks focus
they wait for the next click on the page and retry. Next is
navigator.clipboard in a secure context. Last is a hidden textarea with
execCommand. paste() throws 'Paste unavailable in this context' when all
three fail, as on Firefox desktop, where readText is gated and
execCommand('paste') is blocked. pick and pickText reject when the dialog
is cancelled.
Call paste() directly from the click handler: wrapping it in setTimeout may
break the user-gesture chain on iOS 16+.

The textarea write is vanilla-bundle.js's (window.copy.legacy), which
every page loads before this kit.

THE TEXTAREA PASTE, and the one rule it has to follow: READ THE VALUE, do
not ask execCommand whether it worked. On iOS `execCommand('paste')`
returns false and pastes anyway, because the actual read happens behind the
edit-menu pill the platform puts up; gating on the return value meant every
iOS paste resolved null and surfaced as "Paste unavailable in this
context", which is a sentence about the browser rather than about what
happened. The recipe is the ios-clipboard skill's, which was measured on a
device rather than reasoned about.

The attributes each earn their keep: the element must be focusable, so
display:none and visibility:hidden are out and offscreen-plus-transparent
is in; `inputmode="none"` keeps the soft keyboard down; and it must NOT be
readonly, which focuses fine and then pastes empty. The nested timeouts let
focus settle and the paste land before the read.

Empty resolves as null rather than '', so a caller can tell "nothing came
back" from "the clipboard holds an empty string" and fall through honestly.

Resolve the DEFERRED write's own answer, not `undefined`. Every
caller reads this as a boolean to decide whether to show a check or
a warning, so swallowing it made the one path that waits for a click
report failure on a copy that had just succeeded.

EVERY FLAVOR ON THE CLIPBOARD, the async sibling of paste(). paste()
resolves to a string because readText() does, so a caller reaching for
the clipboard through a button could never see that one copy out of a
spreadsheet carries the cells, an HTML table, and a picture of the range
at once. A paste EVENT has always carried all three; only this path was
narrow, which is why a keyboard paste and a button paste behaved
differently for the same clipboard.

Returns [{ kind: 'text'|'blob', type, text?, blob?, size }]. Falls back
to a single text/plain entry wherever read() is unavailable or refused,
so a caller never has to ask which path it got.

lib/kits/json-explorer.js — Native, framework-free JSON Explorer & Schema Profiler.

Four views of one JSON value, over one toolbar (views, filter, copy,
download) and a crumb trail once the tree is opened into a field:
  - Tree: a property sheet, key and value per row, collections closed until
          tapped, each with its item count and a size column; a filter that
          leaves out what does not match; an arrow into any collection.
  - Schema: the top-level fields with type, items and size, and the field
            types and fill rates of every array of records.
  - Table: the opened field as rows and columns, when it is an array of records.
  - JSON: the opened field, pretty-printed.

No external dependencies; copy delegates to kits/io.js when present.

Usage:
  window.JsonExplorer.mount(container, {
    data,        // JS object/array or raw JSON string
    name,        // optional file/subject name
    fill,        // boolean: true to fill container height and scroll internally
    mode,        // 'tree' | 'schema' | 'table' | 'raw' (default 'tree'); 'raw' is the JSON view
    chunk,       // initial path array to focus, e.g. ['repos']
    views,       // the views offered, a subset of the four keys (default all)
    tabs,        // false hides the view buttons, for a host that switches with setView
    filter,      // false hides the filter box
    toolbar,     // false drops the toolbar row: copy and download go (a host calls
                 //   copy()), and collapse and the record cards ride the crumb row
    onView,      // (view) => void, called on every change of view, the explorer's own
                 //   included (the Schema view's arrows open the tree and the table)
  }) -> { destroy, setView, focusChunk, updateSearch, copy, profile }

vanilla-bundle.js's window.esc, the one escape: it quotes as well, which
the textContent trick this replaced did not.
Infer table schema for record arrays

A PROPERTY SHEET, not a syntax-coloured dump. Reworked 2026-10-22 on the
owner's report from the session form's Raw tab: "it's all cluttered, and

items it has, and its size sits in a right-hand column the eye can run
down, which is the comparison a 5.7 MB record invites (where did the bytes

  - the chunk select, a second copy of the tree's own drill-in;
  - Collapse / Depth 1 / Expand: "Expand" laid every node of a 5.7 MB record
    into the page at once, and the other two were the default view and its
    collapse; one icon now returns to the top level, shown when there is

  - the per-row copy-path and copy-value buttons, revealed on hover, which a

  - the root row, which drew "nullnull" because Element.append writes a

Closed unless opened: the top level of whatever the tree is opened to
is always drawn, and everything below it waits for a tap.

How many children an open collection draws. A record's `calls` runs to
hundreds of entries and `attachments` to more, so a long one draws a
page at a time behind a "show more" row.

Profiled on first use: the Schema view is the only reader, and a walk
of a multi-megabyte record is not a cost to pay on opening the tree.
Bytes as UTF-8, of the compact serialisation, memoised per collection.

The views, as plain text buttons rather than a second boxed tab strip:

Its own row on a phone, inline from `sm` up: four views and four icons

After the input, or the input's own background paints over it.

Drawn only once the tree is opened into a field: at the top level the

A filter, not a highlighter: rows that neither match nor lead to a

A long string shows three lines and opens on a tap; the ellipsis the

What names a record in a list of them. A row of `calls` reading "11

The column to compare down, at the row's right edge. Below a kilobyte

The way into a collection, on every device: the hover-revealed

With no toolbar row, the two controls that depend on where the tree

The opened field as JSON, onto the clipboard: the toolbar's copy,

land.js — where the reader was just sent, and how they get told.

One question, asked after every address the estate resolves: DID THIS LAND
WHERE I MEANT. A surface that scrolls to a place and says nothing answers it
only by accident, since a mark that is simply present cannot be told from one
that was already there, and a reader who followed a link and saw no motion
cannot tell a hit from a miss.

LIFTED FROM A SECOND IMPLEMENTATION RATHER THAN INVENTED. mehrlander/home's
budget-drs submittal view has answered this for months, over two very
different subjects: a block of prose in an office document, and a rectangle
on a page of a PDF. Its `landOn`, `scrollerOf` and `.landed` lived inline in
projects/budget-drs/submittal/submittal.html until 2026-09-05, and the Map
view's Surfacing tab arrived at a near-identical scroller walk independently on 2026-09-04,
which is the second implementation that makes this a kit. The numbers below
are that page's, measured there; the smooth scroll and the reduced-motion
gate are new to this copy. home adopted the kit on 2026-09-05 and its inline
copy went, so the page that measured the numbers now calls this file for them.

  Land.mark(el, opts?)   scroll to `el`, tint it, fade the tint
  Land.clear(root)       drop every mark under `root`
  Land.scrollerOf(el)    the nearest ancestor that actually scrolls
  Land.route()           the address keys of the record last landed on, while
                         it is still displayed; null otherwise

NOT A HIGHLIGHTER, and the distinction decides the timing. A highlighter is
persistent and means "this matters"; a landing is transient and means "here",
which is a thing worth saying once. So it fades, and after that the reader is
looking at the document rather than at the app's answer about the document.

THE PDF CASE IS ALREADY BUILT, which the first draft of this file got wrong.
kits/pdf.js has carried a full find-and-land for months: `find(hits)` draws
a rectangle per hit off the text layer, `findGo(k)` moves between them, and
`repaint(i)` exists so a changed overlay reaches a page already on screen.
So the estate had EIGHT landings in seven files across two repos, disagreeing
about where a landing sits (centre, 0.28, a fixed 80px above a drawn region)
and what colour it is (warning at three strengths, an off-palette orange, and
primary). A first count said six and missed two, because both were reached by
grepping for the scroll and both do more than scroll. Three of pdf.js's
lessons are folded in below.

TWO OF THE EIGHT STAY WHERE THEY ARE, and saying which sharpens what this is:
  fab.js's `highlight` has no dwell and a "clear" button beside it. That is a
  HIGHLIGHTER, persistent and meaning "this matters", which the line above
  says this kit is not. Converting it would have taken the reader's control
  of it away.
  annotate.js lands on a foreign page the reader is annotating, and its 80px
  is a gap above a rectangle they drew rather than a fraction of a pane. A
  fraction is the wrong shape for a target with no container.
state-view.js's `aim` did convert, for the scroll only: its tint is Alpine's,
driven reactively off the selected item, and a kit adding a class beside that
would paint the sum of two owners.

Only the tints and LAND_AT are shared with it, and by COPY held to a gate
(node/test/land-parity.test.mjs) rather than by a call: pdf.js has no kit
dependencies, is loaded straight from jsDelivr on one path, and runs on
pages/pdf-inspect.html which loads nothing else. A copy that cannot be
eliminated is held two-way by test, which is the same bargain
deck-entry-parity makes for the deck door.

Attaches to window.Land. No CSS of its own: the tint and the fade are
Tailwind utilities, generated by the browser build the same way a class in a
component template is, so the page's theme owns the colour.

WHERE A LANDING SITS, and it is one number for every surface. Centred is
wrong twice, and both were measured in home rather than argued: for a SET,
the first of seven lit rows in the middle of the pane pushes its siblings
off the bottom; for a DOCUMENT, half a screen of the previous section sits
above the heading you asked for, which reads as having landed early.

A little over a quarter down leaves what was found near the top with its
context still visible, which is where a reader expects to have arrived.

Long enough to find with the eye after the scroll settles, short enough
that it is gone before it becomes furniture.

The tint, as utilities rather than a stylesheet. `bg-warning/30` compiles to
color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-warning) 30%, transparent), which is
character for character what home's `.landed` declares, so the two surfaces
are the same yellow by construction rather than by a matched hex.

TWO STRENGTHS, because a landing on a SET has a current member. That is
pdf.js's second lesson: its find draws the active hit strong with a ring
and the rest weak, so a reader stepping through seven hits can see both
where they are and how many there are. home's landOn lights every member
of a set identically and can only say "these seven", never "this one of
seven".

/10 rather than the /15 this was written with: Tailwind's opacity scale has
no 15 step, so the class compiled to nothing and the weaker mark would have
been invisible. node/test/dead-opacity.test.mjs is what said so, which is
the reason a tint in the FLOW is a class and a tint over a PAGE is a
color-mix string: the class is checkable and the string is free.

Left on the element after the tint comes off, because the removal is what
the transition is FOR: taking these off at the same time would cut the fade
and the mark would vanish rather than recede. A colour transition left on a
node costs nothing until something changes its colour again.

THE ROUTE THAT SENT THE READER, which outlives the tint. A route naming a
record stays in the address (web-tools house policy h:route), but a view
that lands on a record keeps nothing open: it scrolls, tints and forgets.
So the landing remembers the keys that sent it, and a page's address
writer asks Land.route() on each write. The answer holds while the landed
element is still displayed, which is the reader still being where the
route says: a tab change hides it, so the next write drops the keys, with
no bookkeeping in any view. Once seen hidden it is forgotten, so coming
back to the tab does not bring an old landing back into the address.
{ el, route }

jsdom has no checkVisibility and no layout; a hidden ancestor (x-show
writes display: none inline) is what a tab change leaves behind.

The nearest ancestor that actually scrolls vertically. Walked rather than
named because one landing serves panes the caller does not enumerate: a
list column, a document reader's own column, a deck slide. The `+ 4` is
slop against sub-pixel layout reporting a scrollable box that is not.

Every mark under `root`, off. The caller owns WHEN: a search that lights a
set clears before it searches, so a miss leaves nothing lit, while an
address naming one row by id has nothing to clear.

Land on `el`. Options:
  scroll    false to light it without moving, for every member of a set
            after the first: a count that lands on seven rows should move
            the reader once and light all seven, not walk down the list.
  ifNeeded  scroll only when `el` is not already fully in view, so a tap on
            something the reader can see does not jump under the finger.
  dwell     ms before the tint starts to go.
  smooth    false to jump; ignored (and forced off) under reduced motion.
  current   false for a member of a set that is not the one being read,
            drawn weaker so the set and the place inside it are two
            different things a reader can see at once.
  tint      false to move without marking, for the element the reader is
            ALREADY on: a list row whose detail just opened has to be kept
            in view when the layout reflows under it, and lighting it would
            answer a question nobody asked. The pair is one landing with
            two ends, and only the far end is news.
  settle    false to scroll exactly once. By default the scroll is
            re-asserted twice, on the next frame and again at 400ms, and
            only if the target has MOVED: see the note by `again`.
  route     the address keys that name `el`, as { piece: 'p-12' }: kept
            while `el` is displayed (Land.route), and announced with a
            `land:route` event on window so the page can write its
            address. Pass it on the landing a route caused, and for a
            set only on the current member.

ONLY THE SCROLLER MOVES. scrollIntoView walks every scrollable ancestor,
and a surface that keeps a list beside a document is a surface where that
is wrong: centring a paragraph in the reader scrolled the list it was
opened from off the screen. The fallback for an element in no scroller is
scrollIntoView, since there the page IS the scroller.

'instant', NOT 'auto', and the difference is the whole reduced-motion
gate. 'auto' does not mean "no animation": it means "use the element's
computed scroll-behavior", so on any scroller carrying Tailwind's
`scroll-smooth` this would animate the scroll of the reader who asked
that it not. kits/pdf.js states the same trap from the other end, which
is where this was found: it refuses `scroll-smooth` on its flow because
the CSS property reaches a plain `scrollTop =` too, and its opening seek
must land instantly.

Guarded rather than called, the rule branch-brief.js already settled:
jsdom implements no scrolling at all, and a landing is reached from
enough places that a throw inside one would break its caller's flow
rather than merely failing to scroll.

Where `el` sits in the scroller's CONTENT, which a scroll in flight
does not change: the rect moves and scrollTop moves by the same
amount. So two readings that differ mean the layout moved, never
that the scroll is still travelling.

SCROLLED AGAIN, and the second time is not belt and braces. A
scroll is taken against the scroller's size at that instant, and
the pane a landing runs in is often still settling: a docked pane
is laid out by its split, a deck slide sizes to a host that has
just been filled, a document column corrects its page heights in
a pass it does not await. Measured in mehrlander/home on
2026-08-29 from a search result on a phone: the element was found
and marked, and the pane still showed the document's first line,
because the scroller had grown under a scroll already taken.
Re-asserting once the layout has settled is cheaper than
detecting the settle, which has no event: nothing is recomputed
unless the target moved, so a pane that was stable costs two
comparisons and no motion, and a smooth scroll in flight is not
restarted toward the place it is already going.

Per element rather than one token for the surface, which is the same
guarantee home's dwell token buys and a narrower one: a second landing
elsewhere cannot clear this one's tint, and a second landing on THIS
element restarts its own dwell instead of racing an older timer.

── For a mark that is NOT a node in the flow ────────────────────────────

pdf.js's third lesson, and it is why a PDF mark cannot simply wear MARK: a
rectangle sized from the text layer sits OVER the glyphs it covers, so it
has to multiply against them rather than paint on top of them. That is the
"highlighter, not a selection" rule home states for its appendix mark,
implemented.
