And it needs a stronger percentage for the same reason. Multiplying against
a white page washes a tint out; the same number that reads clearly behind
DOM text on the app's own ground reads as nothing over print. Both pages
that draw one arrived at a higher number independently (home's appendix
mark at 42, pdf.js's find at 62), which is the substrate talking.

`tint(30)` and the utility `bg-warning/30` compute to the same value, not
merely a similar one: measured in the app on 2026-09-04, both resolve to
oklab(0.89172 0.0143011 0.0426671 / 0.3). So the flow mark and the overlay
mark are one colour function read two ways, and a theme change moves both.

behind live text
over a rendered page

── last-write: the copy this page just committed, for the next fold ───────

A crawl reads a committed JSON file, folds new facts into it, and writes it
back. That is safe exactly as long as the read answers with the current file.
It does not always: **GitHub's contents API is read-after-write eventual**, so
a read seconds after a commit can still be served the version that commit
replaced, blob sha and all. Measured 2026-08-16 in the estate's split activity
refresh, which commits twice in a row: the scan pass read the copy the quick
pass had just written over, and its PUT failed `409 does not match <sha>` four
times against a sha the API kept handing back. The browser's own 60-second
cache was ruled out first (`GH.FRESH` on every read that feeds a write); this
is the layer under that one, and no cache header reaches it.

The 409 is the guardrail, not the bug, and that is the whole reason this kit
is small: had the stale read carried a matching sha, the second pass would
have folded onto the first pass's base and silently reverted it. What is
needed is not a longer retry but a better answer to "what is the current
document", and this page already holds it: the bytes it just wrote, and the
sha the write returned.

So: note what you write, and reconcile what you read against it. Newest
stamp wins, and the stamp is the document's own (`generatedAt` by default),
never the clock, so two writers cannot disagree about whose copy is later
for any reason but the documents themselves.

WHAT THIS IS NOT. It is not a cache: nothing here is read to save a request,
and a reader that never writes never sees it. It is not a merge either. It
answers one question, for one file, from one page's own history: is the copy
I was just handed older than the one I put there?

After a successful save. `sha` is the blob sha the PUT returned, which is
the one fact a lagging read cannot supply and the next write needs.

What the caller should fold onto, given what the read returned.
`read` is `{ doc, sha }` or null for a 404. Returns the same shape plus
`ours: true` when this page's copy is the newer one, so a caller can say
so rather than silently substituting.

Strictly newer, not newer-or-equal: an equal stamp means the read caught
up, and preferring ours there would keep a superseded copy alive after
another writer legitimately replaced it with one stamped the same second.

A 404 after a write is the same lag wearing a different hat: the file
exists, the replica has not seen it. Ours is the honest answer there too.

Drop what is known about a path. For a caller that has learned its copy
is no longer relevant (a different branch, a signed-out client), since a
stale note would otherwise outlive its usefulness for the page's life.

linked-swiper.js — a list with a detail: the list beside, or over, a strip of
one card per row, the two moving together. html-style rule 11, held once.

Lifted from budget-drs's corpusSwiper (home, app/view/views/corpora.js), the
fullest version of the pattern in the estate, so every list-detail view can
share one implementation instead of copying the pick, the mark and the strip.

Framework-free, loaded via gh.load after kits/swipe-deck.js (the strip and the
door) and kits/dock-split.js (the seam), on a page whose chain has run
lib/vanilla-bundle.js (window.esc). Without swipe-deck the card is drawn
once and a pick redraws it; without dock-split there is no seam. Styling is
Tailwind and daisyUI classes, written out in full so a build that scans the
source finds every one.

  linkedSwiper.attach(o) -> { pick(id), show(id), mount(), paint(), step(d), destroy() }
    pick tells the host through onPick; show moves without telling it, for a
    host that keeps the selection itself; mount rebuilds after the rows change.
  linkedSwiper.head(name, i, n, noun, { deck, tight }) -> the head row's HTML
  linkedSwiper.mark(list, key, id) -> select a row and keep it in the list's view

attach() options:
  root        the element holding list and card; the kit sets its layout
  list        the list; the kit styles it and caps it when stacked
  card        the card; the kit fills it with a head row over a body
  key         the row attribute that holds an id: 'note' reads data-note.
              With it the kit picks on a row tap or key and marks the row
              (aria-selected); without it the host does both, using show().
              Up and Down in the list then step the selection the way a
              swipe steps the strip: the card follows, and focus moves with
              the row. Rows that carry a tabindex share one tab stop, on the
              selected row; where none does, the list itself takes focus.
              The head row, body and seam carry data-ls="head|body|seam".
  ids()       the ids in list order        sel()   the selected id
  body(id, el)   HTML for a card, or fill el and return nothing
  name(id)    { when, code, title } for the default head row
  head({ i, n, tight })   HTML for a head row of the host's own
  noun        one row, singular ('note'); names the arrows and the door
  empty       HTML for a card when no row is shown
  onPick(id, via)   the selection moved; via is list, swipe, step or api.
              The host records it here (its state, its address).
  deck()      opens the cards full screen; omit for a strip with no door
  drawn(el), release(i, el)   after a card is drawn, before one is emptied
  seam        a storage key: puts a dock-split seam between list and card and
              keeps the list's width under that key
  width()     the width the layout reads, default the root's own
  stackBelow  under this width the list stacks over the card (980)
  tightBelow  under this the arrows give way to the swipe (680)
  listMax     the stacked list's height cap, a literal class ('max-h-[38vh]')
  wide        the side-by-side columns without a seam, a literal class
              (default a 340px list: 'grid-cols-[minmax(0,340px)_minmax(0,1fr)]')
  innerClass, slidePad   passed to swipeDeck.core for each card

The estate's one escape helper, from lib/vanilla-bundle.js, which the boot
chain loads ahead of every kit.

The list's track is the seam's to set, and is held to leave the card 380px
so a width kept from a wider screen cannot squeeze the card on this one.

Inside the list, never the page: a swipe walks the selection down rows the
reader may have scrolled away from. The lead clears a sticky group label.

A focus ring drawn outside the row is cut off by the list's scroll
box, so it is drawn just inside. Inline, because the title-tip kit's
focus ring is unlayered and outranks a utility (snag
an-unlayered-rule-beats-every-layer).

Every move the strip did not make itself (the start, a pick in the list, a
track that changed width) means "be on this card", so it is instant.

A row's attribute is a string and a host's id may not be, so ids are
matched as strings and the host is handed its own value back.

A change reported while the strip is not the width it settled at is the
track re-snapping under a resize, not a swipe: back to the card it was on.

For a host that keeps the selection itself: be on this row, mark it, and
say nothing back.

Inline, because dock-split's stylesheet is unlayered and outranks the
`hidden` utility (snag an-unlayered-rule-beats-every-layer).

A host that answers a control inside a row claims the click first, in the
capture phase, with preventDefault, and the row is then not picked.

What was tapped takes focus (Safari does not give it to a tapped
button), so the arrow keys work after a tap as after a Tab.

The first mark runs before the icon font has set the rows' heights, and
the rows above a selection then grow under it, pushing a row a link
picked out of a capped list's view. Mark again once the fonts are in.

Lists: the registry's lists/ folder, read and written as one kind of file.

Every list is one JSON document in the registry's lists/ folder: an `items`
array beside whatever top-level keys describe the list. Four are built in
and carry behavior the Lists pane implements for them alone (To-do, Jot,
Pin and Snag, below). Any other file there whose top level has a `title` and an
`items` array is a list someone created in the pane, and it describes itself:

  { "title": "Aphorisms", "icon": "quotes", "capabilities": ["done"],
    "items": [ { "id": "l…", "text": "…", "note": "…", "created_at": "…" } ] }

`icon` is a Phosphor icon name without its `ph-` prefix. `note` is an item's
optional second line. A key nothing here reads survives every write, the
rule the built-in savers already followed for item fields.

A FILE WITH NO TITLE IS NOT A LIST. lists/autocorrect.json shares the folder
(the dictate page's find-and-replace table) and has `items` too, so the title
is the mark that a file was made to be read as a list.

CAPABILITIES ARE CLOSED; LISTS ARE OPEN. The rule the estate settled for a
jot's kind on 2026-08-26: a set is closed where code has to switch on its
values, and open where only a reader acts on it. Each capability below is
behavior the pane has to implement, so the vocabulary is declared here and
nowhere else; which lists exist is the folder's business. OPEN names the
capabilities a created list can turn on today. The rest are implemented for
the built-in list that has them, and join OPEN when a created list needs one.

EVERY WRITE IS A FRESH READ, THEN THE CHANGE, THEN THE SAVE, and only a
missing file (404) reads as empty. A writer that saved its own copy lost
whatever landed in between, and one that read every failure as "empty" (the
sidebar finder's jot until this kit) turned a dropped connection into a pile
holding only the newest jot.

ONE WRITE AT A TIME PER FILE, AND A LAGGING READ IS NOT BELIEVED. GitHub's
contents API is read-after-write eventual (kits/last-write.js has the
measurement), so two quick gestures on one list could each read before the
other's commit showed and the second save would drop the first. Writes from
this page to one file therefore queue behind each other, and the page keeps
the blob sha each write replaced beside the copy it wrote: a read that
answers with the replaced sha (or a 404 for a file this page just created)
is a replica that has not caught up, and the page's own copy stands in for
it. Any other sha is a newer write from elsewhere, and it is the one used.

Attaches window.Lists, loaded via gh.load('kits/lists.js').

The built-in lists, described in the shape a created list describes
itself. Their files carry no header: the pane's markup for them predates
this kit, and these records are what keeps the descriptions in one place.

Each file is named for its list, as a created list's file is.

Snag was a Markdown log, docs/SNAGS.md in web-tools, until 2026-10-20. Its
entries became items here, each naming the `repo` the trip belongs to, so
one list holds every repo's snags. An item's `id` is the slug the log's
heading carried, which is what citations elsewhere still name.

What the pane needs to draw a list's heading. A created list keeps only the
capabilities in OPEN, so a file naming one the pane cannot render for it
reads as a plain list rather than half of a feature.

The write in flight to each file, and what this page's last write to it
replaced and produced. Keyed by repo as well, since the pane can switch
registries without reloading.
`sha` is the file's blob sha, null when the file does not exist.

`was` is the blob sha the write replaces at `path`, null for a new file.
A save that reports no sha leaves nothing to compare a later read with.

`change(items, header)` returns the new items, or { items, header } when
the list's own description changes too.

The created lists, title order. A file that fails to read or parse is left
out rather than failing the folder: one hand-edited file with a stray comma
should not take every other list off the screen.
A list's file is named from its title, here and on every rename (move).

A rename to a title with a different slug moves the file, so its name keeps
matching its list. The new file is written before the old one is deleted:
a failure between the two leaves the list twice, which shows and costs one
delete, rather than not at all. A note about one of its items keeps the
old address, since notes are never edited.

Only an empty list, read fresh. Deleting a list's items is a gesture per
item, each with its undo, so the last step can never take content with it.

look.js — look markers: a link that lands on a place in a page, says why, and can ring the control to tap.

The address is the page's own fragment. Any page that boots the web-tools
loader answers it: lib/gh-boot.js loads land.js and this kit when a fragment
asks (LOOK_BOOT). Any other page loads both itself, Land first:

  #show=<anchor>[&say=<text>]   land on it, with a message when one is given
  #tap=<anchor>[&say=<text>]    land, then ring it and point at it until tapped
  #walkthrough=<name>                  a sequence the page declares, in
                                <script type="application/json" id="look-walkthroughs">
                                as { "<name>": [steps] }
  #steps=<base64url JSON>       a sequence carried in the link itself; a
                                value opening with '[' is read as plain JSON
  #intro=<text>                 a greeting: the first card's message when
                                that card points at something and says
                                nothing of its own, else a card of its own
                                ahead of the rest (or alone)

ONE MESSAGE PER CARD. A step is { at, say?, tap? }, or { say } alone: a
NOTE step, a message with nothing to point at, drawn as the dock on a page
left where it is. `tap` may be a string, the label by the hand ("Tap to
open"); without one the hand reads "Tap here" or "Click here", and a
control that opens another page says that Back returns here. A walkthrough whose
name or steps cannot be read still shows its intro, then the miss, so a
broken walkthrough costs the walkthrough and not the message.

A STOP'S ADDRESS MAY NAME ITS PAGE, the way a spreadsheet names a sheet and
then a cell: `pages/branch.html!files`, `app/?view=map&tab=showing!map-row`.
A stop on another page offers Go, a link carrying the walkthrough there, and a tap
step whose control is a link to the next stop's page carries the walkthrough itself.
The dock's number and its counter open every step as a list, and a row goes
to its step (stepList). Its speech bubble takes the reader's notes on a step,
kept as drafts in this browser and sent on Send to the estate's notes store,
where a session reads and answers them (composer, send; skills/notes).

A PAGE MAY DRIVE A WALKTHROUGH AS ITS OWN CHOOSER, as a lineup does, one
step per option: a step's `mark` (up to three characters) replaces its
number on the dock, the list and the target; `Look.start(steps, { folded:
true })` opens the dock folded to one row; `Look.go(j)` moves to step j; and
every step drawn dispatches `look:step` on window with `{ i, n }`, so the
page follows the reader's arrows and the reader's arrows follow the page.

A page the toss renderer runs top-level is named by the renderer's address,
`pages/toss-render.html?top&gh=owner/repo@ref:path`, so a walkthrough can cross
other repositories' pages; a framed toss has no address of its own, and its
walkthrough stays on the one page.
The walkthrough's position rides in the address as `stop=<n>`, so Back, a reload
or a copied link reopens at that stop; nothing is stored, so nothing expires.
The dock's braces show the walkthrough as JSON in a tooltip, in the shape a link
would carry.

A tap step is a DO step: its forward arrow is
locked until the reader taps the ringed control, the tap still reaches the
page, and the walkthrough stays on the step so the reader sees what the tap did.
Until then the dock offers a Skip past what the tap would make. Any other
step is a LOOK step and moves on with the dock's forward arrow. The arrow
keys do what the dock's arrows do. Other fragment keys are left
alone, so a page's own routing and a nonce ride beside these, and the five
keys plus `say` are reserved for this kit on any page that loads it.

AN ANCHOR IS A NAME THE PAGE DECLARES. `at` resolves, in order, to
  data-at="<at>"     the durable kind: a name the page gives an element
  id="<at>"          the same, for an element that already has one
  text:<words>       the smallest element whose whole text is those words
  css:<selector>     the first element the selector matches
The first two are checked against a page's source by python/look-link.py.
The last two exist for a page that declares nothing, which is what the toss
renderer injects this kit into, and they break when the wording or the
structure changes (docs/locators.md, the Quote and Selector rows).

A HIDDEN TARGET IS REVEALED BY ITS REGION. A hidden ancestor carrying
data-at-open="<anchor>" names the control that shows it, so a link into a
closed tab opens the tab first. Regions open outermost first, each opener
clicked once, since a second click on a toggle closes what the first opened.
A target that still resolves to nothing visible says so on screen: a miss
is an answer to "did this land", and silence is not.

EVERY SCROLLER MOVES, THE PAGE INCLUDED. A target in a pane that is itself
out of view has to be brought to the reader, not merely scrolled to inside a
pane nobody can see, so the scroll is the browser's own scrollIntoView,
centred, rather than land.js's climb to the nearest scroller, which rightly leaves
the page alone when a list beside a reader is the thing in view. Measured
2026-10-04 on the Land demo through a toss: Look ran before the page's
land.js arrived, scrolled only the window, and left the target clipped in
its pane with the tint drawn over whatever sat below it. The MARK is drawn
here, as an overlay, because it has to show on a page with no daisyUI theme
and no Tailwind build, where Land's class would compile to nothing; it is
clipped to every pane the target sits in, so a target scrolled out of its
pane takes its mark with it. It is Land's colour function with a fallback,
so on a themed page the two are one yellow.

The message arrives from a URL, so it is set as text and never as HTML.

  Look.start(steps, o?)  run a sequence now, replacing any running one;
                         o.wait caps how long an anchor may take to appear
  Look.stop()            take every marker down
  Look.fromHash(hash?)   the cleaned sequence a fragment asks for, or null
  Look.fromLocation()    start whatever location.hash asks for
  Look.find(at)          resolve one anchor, preferring a visible match
  Look.encode(steps)     base64url JSON, the value of #steps=

Starts itself: once the page has loaded, and again when the look keys in the
fragment change. A second copy of the kit on one page defers to the first.

Attaches to window.Look.

the label by the hand: a few words, not a message
how long an anchor may take to appear (a late render)
how long while the page says it is still reading (aria-busy)
how long a page that was busy must have been quiet before a miss
how long a page that has just started counts as busy (busy, below)
how long a revealed region may take to show
how long after a tap a change of address counts as the tap's
after a landing's scroll animation has had its time
how long a late layout may push the target away

the clearance a target keeps above the dock
A HIGHLIGHTER YELLOW, FIXED RATHER THAN THE THEME'S. The mark was
var(--color-warning), which daisyUI's light theme makes an amber; tinted to
30% over white that read as peach, which the owner took for a skin tone on
the app's Map view (2026-10-16). On a page with no theme it fell back to
this yellow, so the demo looked right and the app did not. The ring, the
step's number and the hand are yellow-400; the tint is yellow-300, which
stays yellow when thinned. Land still tints with the theme's warning
colour, so on a themed page a landing and a look mark now differ.
Land's FLOW strength, in the look mark's own yellow

The smallest: an element none of whose descendants also matches, so
`text:Export` lands on the button, not the toolbar around it.
Compared, not selected: an anchor needs no escaping to be a name.

A PAGE STILL READING ITS CONTENT says so with aria-busy="true" on any
element, and an anchor is looked for until that has been gone a moment, up
to BUSY_WAIT, rather than for `wait` from the load event: the session page
reads a record of several megabytes before its marks exist, which a phone
does not finish in 2.5 seconds. A page that never says so gets `wait`.
A page Alpine has not started yet says the same without trying: x-cloak
holds it hidden until the start lifts it, and the entities page took
longer than `wait` to start inside a toss (2026-11-09). Just after the
start the page is still drawing its first view, which may not yet say it
is busy: the app's Map drew the Icons tab, busy, a beat after the lift,
and inside a toss that beat outlasted QUIET_FOR. So a page counts as busy
for START_GRACE after its last x-cloak goes.

Found under x-cloak, the target is waiting for Alpine to start, not
hidden: wait for the start as for a busy page, then look again, since
the start may render the target anew.

FOUND BUT HIDDEN WHILE THE PAGE IS STILL READING. A tab that draws its
controls before its data keeps them hidden until the read lands, so the
anchor is there from the first frame and seek returns at once, leaving
only OPEN_WAIT for a read that can take seconds: the Map's Pages tab
answered "Hidden on this page" for its own axis buttons (2026-11-10).
A busy page gets the wait a missing anchor gets, on the same terms.

The steps as base64url JSON over UTF-8, through gh-api.js's codec where the
page has it. The toss renderer injects this kit into pages that boot
nothing, so gh-api.js is never there, and a walkthrough arriving at one read
as unreadable (2026-10-22); there the platform's codec reads and writes the
same encoding (node/test/base64-one-owner.test.mjs carries the exemption).

A link is untrusted input: keep the known fields, as strings and a flag.
`tap` may be a string, which is the label by the hand ("Tap to open").

Cleaned twice on the way in, so a page already lifted out of `at` is
kept from `page`.

Cleaned twice on the way in (fromHash, then start), so a label already
lifted out of `tap` is kept from `act`.

The authoring shape of a cleaned sequence, for the dock's JSON view: what
a link would carry to ask for exactly this walkthrough.
A step's badge: its mark, else its number.

A note step points at nothing; a miss step reports a link that could not
be read. Neither has an anchor to find.

AN ADDRESS NAMES A PAGE, THEN A PLACE ON IT, the way a spreadsheet names a
sheet and then a cell: `app/?view=map&tab=showing!text:Toss, data route`.
The first '!' splits them, and only when what comes before it reads as a
page (a path, a query or a .html name, and not a text: or css: anchor);
a '!' inside the page part is written %21. No page part means this page.
Checked across the three repos on 2026-10-17: no branch name, route table
or written page link held a '!', and one file did (a text file, not a page).

A page address is read from the site's root: /<repo>/ on a github.io
project site, / anywhere else (a local server). A document with no real
address of its own, such as a page framed by the toss renderer and served
from a blob: URL, cannot tell where it is, so there every page counts as
here and the walkthrough runs as it did before addresses.

Whether a URL is the page an address names: the same path, and every
query and fragment value the address names agrees. Keys it does not name,
such as a ?use= pin or the walkthrough's own, are the URL's business.
The query is read as text, not through URLSearchParams: in the toss
renderer's top mode a shim hides the renderer's own keys (`top`, `gh`,
`data`) from any URLSearchParams holding `top`, so two tossed pages read as
one and a stop on the other was walked on this page (2026-10-22).

A fragment's own text with the walkthrough's keys taken out and others given in,
edited as text rather than through URLSearchParams, which would re-encode
a page's own keys (gh=o/r becomes gh=o%2Fr) under it.

THE WALKTHROUGH TRAVELS IN THE ADDRESS, never in storage, so nothing is left
behind to expire. A link to stop i on another page is that page's address
with all of the walkthrough added to its fragment, so Back to an earlier stop
still works there, and `stop=` naming where to pick it up. The current
?use= pin rides along, so the next page runs the same code.

Where the reader is, less the walkthrough's own keys, so writing stop= is not
read as the reader going somewhere.

This page as an address a walkthrough can name: its path from the site's root,
its query less a ?use= pin, and its own fragment less the walkthrough's keys.

WHERE THE READER IS, kept in the address as `stop=<n>`, counted from 1, so
Back, a reload or a copied link opens at that stop, and the original link,
which has none, opens at the first. Written with replaceState, which fires
no hashchange, so a page routing on its own fragment is not re-routed. A
document with no real address of its own has nowhere to write it.
a history that refuses: the walkthrough still runs, it just will not reopen here

THIS DOCUMENT'S KEYS: the part of the fragment before a nested '#'. A toss
shell's fragment carries the framed page's address and, after a second
'#', the page's own fragment; URLSearchParams splits on '&' before it reads
a key, so a page fragment with two keys would surface as the shell's own
and run a second marker on the shell (lib/gh-boot.js says the same).

One message per card. The intro is the first card's message when that
card points at something and has none of its own, so the first card
shows a place and says one thing (the owner, 2026-10-16); otherwise it
is a card of its own, ahead of the rest.
The look keys alone, so a page rewriting its own keys is not a new ask.

The step's number, on the target and in the dock: dark on yellow in both
themes, since the yellow does not change with the theme. Shown with its
display named, since clearing an inline display drops this one with it.

ICONS ARE PHOSPHOR'S, as classes, like every page here. A page that does
not load Phosphor, which is what the toss renderer injects this kit into,
gets the two weights the marker uses from the CDN the pages use, since a
Phosphor class with no stylesheet behind it draws nothing at all. A page
that loads them already, by link or inlined, is left as it is.

THE HAND SAYS WHAT TO DO. A ringed control with a hand bobbing under it
was read as "tap this" and never said so (the owner, 2026-10-16), so the
hand carries a short label: the step's own (`"tap": "Tap to open"`), else
one chosen from the reader's pointer and from where the control leads.
Only the hand bobs; a label that moved would be harder to read.

Where a tap on a control takes the reader: '' for this page, 'tab' for a
new tab, 'page' for another document. Read from a link's href, so a
control that navigates by script is not caught, and a link that only
changes the query is taken to stay, since an app routes those in place.

A control that opens another page says how to come back in the label,
the one place the reader is already looking, unless the walkthrough goes along
with it (carry), when there is nothing to come back for.

THE TAP CARRIES THE WALKTHROUGH when the control is a link to another page and
the next stop belongs there: it names that page, or names none and so is
taken to be on the page the tap opens. The walkthrough's keys go onto the link
just before the browser follows it, so the next page opens at the next
stop with nothing stored (the owner, 2026-10-17: tap as directed and the
panel just updates). The stops up to the tap are stamped with this page,
so Back on the next page comes back here. A link to a page the next stop
does not name is left alone, and so is a control that navigates by
script, which the walkthrough cannot see in advance; Back still finds the stop,
since the address keeps it. carryTo answers whether a link would carry.

THE WORDS SIT IN A DOCK, the same place on every step: a card beside the
target had to find room near it on every step and every frame, covered
what sat there, and left the reader hunting for it after a scroll. The
dock is tied to its target by the step's number instead of by nearness,
and the page under it scrolls freely. A walkthrough gets a counter and arrows; a
lone landing gets its message and a close.
A LOOK STEP AND A DO STEP ARE DIFFERENT ASKS, and the dock says which. A
look step (here is the thing) tints its target and moves on with the
filled forward arrow. A do step (tap: true) rings its target and puts the
same yellow hand in the forward arrow's place until the reader's tap on
the page unlocks it: tapping the hand meanwhile says what to tap (tip()),
and the tap turns the hand into the arrow (complete()). A quiet Skip below
the message jumps to the first later step whose target exists now, past
whatever the skipped tap would have made, so leaving a do step undone
never lands on a step that cannot be shown; Back likewise passes over
steps whose targets are gone. Where those land is navOf()'s to say.

The counter opens the list as the number does, and goes on opening it
while the number is the way back to a target out of sight.

A SINGLE CARD ENDS ON DONE, in place of the corner ✕ (the owner,
2026-10-23): one way out, named as the end of something. The ✕ stays on
a walkthrough, which a reader may leave midway, on a Go card, whose stop
is elsewhere, and on a tap card not yet tapped, where Done would read as
finished.

THE FOOTER: the walkthrough's JSON behind braces and the note input on
the left; Send, once there are notes, and a do step's Skip on the right.
ONE MESSAGE PER CARD is the rule above it: a bold lead
over the message, and a line on how to come back from another page,
were each a second thing to read (the owner, 2026-10-16), so the intro
is a card's message or a card of its own, and the way back is the
hand's label.

ONE ROW OR THE WHOLE PANEL, the reader's choice, made in the number's list
and kept from step to step (the owner, 2026-10-23). Folded, the dock is the
number, the note field with the step's message as its placeholder, and
the check, so the page stays in view and a note is still one line away.
Typing opens it, since a note is written against the message, and it
folds again once the field is left empty. The dock is built whole and
folded by hiding, never redrawn, so the field being typed in keeps its
focus and a phone keeps its keyboard. A note step folds too, its message
in the field, which is what a lineup's options are: the page itself is
the content, and no mark is drawn on it. A step the reader must read
before anything else opens whatever the choice: a target not found, a
stop on another page, a step that needs an earlier one.
Folded again once the field is neither focused nor holding words.

THE ARROWS CROSS PAGES THE WAY THEY CROSS STOPS. Pressing Next or Back
toward a stop on another page goes there, carrying the walkthrough and the stop
in the address, so an arrow takes one tap wherever its stop is (the owner,
2026-10-17). Decided at the press, not when the dock is drawn: the dock
redraws the moment a tap lands, before an app has routed in place, and
an arrow fixed then as a link reloaded the app instead of moving on
(measured on the Map the same day). A Go card is left for a stop reached
any other way, such as a link that opens at a stop on another page.

BACK OVER A TAP THAT WENT SOMEWHERE GOES BACK THERE. When this stop was
reached by a tap that moved the page in place, Back to the tap's stop
undoes the move: the browser's own Back when the tap added an entry to
history, else the address the tap left from. The walkthrough follows the page
back (popstate, in start), so the reader lands on the tap's stop again.

Go: a real link, so it opens the way any link does (a long press offers a
new tab), carrying the walkthrough to the stop's page in its address.

THE WALKTHROUGH AS JSON, a tooltip over the dock rather than a section inside
it: an expanding card pushed the message around and was not liked
(2026-10-16). The braces toggle it; a new step closes it, since the dock
is redrawn. The steps are shown as the kit runs them, in the shape a link
would carry, with a copy control in its corner.

EVERY STEP, ONE TAP AWAY. The dock's number opens the walkthrough as a list,
the way the swipe deck's header mark opens its set, current step marked,
and a row goes to its step, on this page or another (the owner,
2026-10-22). While the target is out of sight the number is the way back
to it instead (paintMark), and says so with an arrow.

A NOTE ON ANY STEP, SENT WHEN THE READER SAYS. Each card takes notes, held
as drafts in this browser until Send appends them to the estate's notes
store (kits/notes.js; skills/notes reads and answers them), each about
the file its step shows, quoting the marked words when they are short
enough to quote, and naming the step it was written on (the owner,
2026-10-22). Drafts are the one thing this kit stores, since they are the
reader's own words and no address should carry them. They are kept per
walkthrough under a key read from its anchors and messages, which a page
stamped into a stop (carry) does not change, so they follow the
walkthrough from page to page on one site.

A note's subject: the file a page shows, read from the address that shows
it (the toss renderer's gh= or a route's key, a viewer's src=, in the query
or the fragment), else the page itself on its github.io site.

A step's drafted notes as text: on its card, each with a remove, and under
its row in the step list, where they are read rather than hovered (rule 10
of the house style, and a page the toss shows has no tip kit to lend).

THE NOTE IS ONE LINE, READY TO TYPE, beside the braces, with a green check
that adds it (the owner, 2026-10-22: a box that opened was more than the
job needed). Enter adds it too. The page under the dock may answer keys of
its own (Budget bills binds the arrows and letters), so a key typed here
stops here, and Escape leaves the field rather than the walkthrough.

GREEN ONLY WITH SOMETHING TO ADD (the owner, 2026-10-23): an empty field
leaves the check grey, so the colour says the press will act. Grey, not
disabled: a press on it finds nothing to add and puts the cursor in the
field (addDraft), and a value set without typing still adds.

Only words short enough to be the marked words: a container's whole
text (a footer of labels, 190 characters) quoted nothing.

SENDING TAKES THE ANNOTATION KIT'S PATH (kits/annotate.js, saveNotes): the
reader's token, the registry repository, kits/notes.js's compare-and-swap
append, one note per draft, all of them in one write, since each write
carries the whole store (seven sent one by one took seven, 2026-10-22). A
page the toss renderer showed boots none of that, so gh-api.js and the
kits are fetched from this site on the press. The drafts are let go only
once their notes are on main, so a failure keeps them for another Send.

The saved token has one reader, gh-auth.js (node/test/token-one-owner.test.mjs),
which a page that boots nothing has not loaded either.

The dock drawn again in place, for a change that is not a new step: a note
opened, added, removed or sent.

The dock's number turns into the way back when its target is out of
sight: an arrow toward it, or an eye when it is no longer shown at all, as
when the reader switched away from its tab.
Where Back, forward and a do step's Skip lead from step i, read now.

A missing target sends the reader back to the nearest tap NOT yet done.
It named the nearest tap of any kind, so a target missing for another
reason said "This step needs step 2 first" after step 2 was done
(2026-10-16, a Map row the screenshot's ref did not have).

DOING A DO STEP UNLOCKS IT; IT DOES NOT MOVE ON. The tap reaches the page
and the walkthrough stays put, so the reader sees what the tap did: the glow and
the hand stop, the step's number becomes a check, and the dock's hand
becomes the forward arrow. Moving on is the reader's next tap, as on any
other step. A bare tap link with no message has no dock to unlock, so it
simply ends.

A TAP THAT GOES SOMEWHERE MOVES THE WALKTHROUGH ON. An app routes in place a
moment after the tap reaches it, so the walkthrough watches for the address
to change (place(), each frame) and, if it does within ROUTE_WAIT, goes
to the next stop. A tap that changes nothing, such as a toggle, stays
on its step so the reader sees what it did. The address keeps this
stop, so the browser's Back returns to it.

A TRY TO MOVE ON IS ANSWERED IN TWO PLACES. Before the do step is done,
the dock's hand stands where the forward arrow will be, and a tap on it,
or the right arrow key, gets a short tip there and an answer on the page
(nudge()), where the action is. The tip says only what is wanted; the
ping from the ring says where. The kit draws the tip itself: a page the
toss renderer injects this kit into has no title-tip kit to lend one.

The target's answer: one sonar ping. A thin copy of the ring peels off
its edge and spreads about 18px outward as it fades, once per try; the
resting glow keeps breathing underneath. Picked on 2026-10-06 from six
options on a demo page (a flood of colour, a soft ripple, a colour
shift, a spotlight, a hop, and this), the last two proposed by an
independent agent. It is an outline, which paints outside the ring
without widening the page, and it is a single burst rather than the
endless one that read as stacked borders. A ping still running when the
reader tries again is left to finish rather than restarted.

Calls fn once el has stopped moving, so a ping goes off where the eye
lands rather than partway through a smooth scroll; a long one on a phone
outlasted the fixed delay this replaced, and iOS has no scrollend.
The JSON tooltip shares the spot above the dock, so it goes too.

`keep` is for a walkthrough being replaced rather than ended, so the step a
reader reached is forgotten only when the reader ends the walkthrough.

A miss from fromHash is shown as itself, after the intro it may follow;
anything else is cleaned here, since a page may hand over steps of its own.

One layer on the root, appended to <html> so a positioned <body> cannot
move its origin, and CLIPPING NOTHING. It used to clip sideways, with
overflow-x:clip on this zero-height box, so a ring at the right edge
could not widen the page; on an iPhone it drew nothing inside it at all,
the tint and the step's number gone while the fixed dock, which no
ancestor clips, stayed (2026-10-04, and Chromium draws exactly that with
the layer clipped both ways). The page keeps its width another way:
place() clamps every mark to it, and the pulse is a glow, a box-shadow,
which paints past its box without widening the page as a growing box
does.

ONE RING, AND A GLOW THAT BREATHES AROUND IT. The pulse was a second
line, an outline growing out from the ring and fading; filmed frame by
frame on 2026-10-05 it sat a pixel or two outside the ring for part of
every cycle, so the control wore two and three concentric borders at
once, which is what read as competing states on an iPhone. Now nothing
moves outward: the glow swells and fades in place, and only its opacity
animates, which a phone composites without repainting.

Fixed to the viewport, which the layer's sideways clip does not reach:
overflow clips only what the clipping box contains, and a fixed box is
contained by the viewport. Inset by the safe area, clear of a phone's
home bar, and at the bottom left, short of the bottom right corner where
the FAB's launcher sits: a 56px disc 24px in, measured 2026-10-04 over
this dock's close button through a toss. That launcher belongs to the
toss shell, outside this document, so the dock cannot move it and keeps
clear of it instead; on a wider screen the 28rem cap already does.
Above the hand and the step's number, which come after it in the layer,
so the JSON tooltip it carries is not drawn under the hand's label.

A walkthrough resumed after the reader left the page counts the taps before
the resumed step as done, since leaving was the tap.

Escape closes; the arrow keys do what the dock's arrows do, so the right
arrow does nothing on a do step, and neither key acts where the reader
is typing.
Brought back, it pings once it arrives, so the eye lands with it.

The page going back (the browser's Back, or the dock undoing a tap's
move) to where an earlier stop was shown takes the walkthrough back to it.

A folded dock opens when its field takes focus, and folds when the field
is left empty. A press inside the dock blurs the field before its click
lands, so folding waits for the press to finish: folding at the blur
would move the number out from under the reader's finger.
Any sign of the reader taking the page over ends the settling above.

Copy the walkthrough's JSON. Where the clipboard is refused, the text is
selected instead, so the reader's own Copy still works.

A STOP ON ANOTHER PAGE. Right after a tap, give the page a moment, since
the tap may have set an app routing there in place; still elsewhere, the
dock offers Go, a link carrying the walkthrough there. After a look step there
is nothing in motion to wait for.

A stop on another page is not written here, so browser Back returns to
the last stop the reader saw on this page.

A WALKTHROUGH IS ONE PAGE, but not one moment of it. A target an earlier tap
makes, such as a Save button that exists only while a row is being
edited, is missing once that tap is skipped, or undone by going on and
coming back, not because the page lacks it. Measured 2026-10-04 on an
iPhone: back from step 5 to the demo's step 4 said "Not on this page:
save-licenses" over the Summary tab. So Back and a do step's Skip pass
over steps whose targets do not exist now, read when the step is drawn,
and Next from a look step goes one on, since a target there may still be
rendering. Should that one turn out missing with a tap before it, the
dock names the nearest such step and offers to go there; missing with
none is a wrong name, and found but never shown is a third answer.

A control to tap is marked by its ring, not by a tint, which would
wash out a filled button's label.

The tap goes through to the page; the walkthrough follows it. Matched on the
anchor as well as the element, since a framework may re-render it.

A tint laid over the element, unblended. It was multiplied, meant to
leave text under it black, but the layer is a stacking context and so
an isolated group: the blend had no page beneath it, and Chromium drew
multiply and normal pixel for pixel alike (measured 2026-10-04). On an
iPhone the same step drew no tint while the rings drew, and only the
tint used the blend and color-mix; the blend was doing nothing here.
It stays while the dock is up, since the reader may scroll away and
back; a lone landing with nothing to say has no dock, so it fades and
goes, the way every other landing does. A brighter first moment
catches the eye where the scroll left it.

A LOOK LINK IS A POINTER, NOT A LANDING. Land's tint alone is right for
the app's own landings, which happen all day; a link someone sent is a
request to look here, and the tint alone was easy to miss beside a
dock the reader had not yet found (owner, 2026-10-16). So the target
also wears the ring a do step wears, and sends out one sonar ping once
the scroll has brought it in, the answer an early try already gets.

The browser's own scroll, since it moves every pane between the target and
the page. Centred, which keeps an ordinary target clear of a sticky header;
a target taller than most of the screen goes to the top instead, where a
sticky header can cover its first line. A step after the first moves only
when its target is out of view, under the dock included, so a tap does not
make the page jump under the finger.
Where the dock begins on the screen, or the screen's foot with no dock up.

ROOM BELOW THE DOCK. The dock covers the foot of the screen, and a target
near the end of its pane could not be scrolled clear of it, since the pane
was already at its end: the step opened with the target under the dock
and a down arrow for its number (the Map's Overview > Icons, its last
family, 2026-10-23). So before the scroll, the innermost pane the target
scrolls in, or the page where nothing inside it scrolls, gets padding at
its end, enough to centre the target, and only when the target could not
otherwise clear the dock. stop() takes the padding back.

A pane that clips without scrolling holds the target still; padding the
page around it would scroll the whole shell instead.

The panes that clip an element: every ancestor whose overflow is not
visible. Read once per step, since reading computed styles every frame is
what the per-frame placement cannot afford.

The part of an element the reader can actually see: its box cut by every
clipping pane and by the viewport, or null when nothing of it shows.

Every frame: the halo on the target, the pointer under it, the number at
its corner, and whether the dock's number should be the way back. In the
layer's own coordinates, so the page scrolling, an inner pane scrolling,
or the layout reflowing all come out right without a listener. The dock
is fixed and needs no placing.

A target scrolled out of its pane, or off the screen, takes its mark
with it; the dock stays, and offers the way back.

Clamped to the page's width, since nothing clips the layer: a mark
past the right edge would widen the page and scroll it sideways.

The hand points where it always did; its label sits to its right, or
to its left when the right edge would cut it off.
Under the dock counts as out of sight: the reader sees the dock there.

A done step's target may be gone, as a Save button is once tapped; that
is the step working, so its number stays rather than becoming a way back.

A PAGE STILL LOADING MOVES THE TARGET AFTER THE SCROLL. On the app's Map
the contents above the Showing entry arrived after the walkthrough had centred
it, and the first card opened with the target below the fold and a down
arrow for a number (2026-10-16). So for a few seconds after a step
lands, past the scroll's own animation, a target pushed out of view is
brought back, until the reader scrolls or touches anything.

A PAGE MAY REWRITE ITS FRAGMENT AS IT BOOTS, keeping only its own keys:
Budget bills writes tab, sec and bill with replaceState before the load
event, and a walkthrough arriving there lost steps= and stop= (2026-10-22).
The first start reads the fragment as it stood when this kit ran, when the
look keys have gone from it since.
`leave` is how the walkthrough goes to another page; a test replaces it.

kits/md-diff.js — a markdown change read as the DOCUMENT rather than as its
source.

The problem this answers. A diff is over source lines, and a rendered
document has thrown its lines away, so reviewing a documentation edit meant
reading `+` and `-` against markup: the reader judged the patch and then had
to imagine the page. That is the wrong way round for prose, where the
question is what the document now SAYS.

The assumption the whole shape follows from, and it is worth stating because
it is the one that can be wrong: a documentation edit is usually a change
here and a change there, not a rewrite. So the unit is a BLOCK, each changed
block gets a container of its own, and everything unchanged renders as
ordinary prose. A file rewritten end to end degrades into one container per
block, which is honest rather than broken, and the jump strip says so by its
count.

  mdDiff.blocks(md, { items })         -> [{ text, start, end }]
  mdDiff.align(old, new, { items })    -> [{ kind, old, new }]   full sequence
  mdDiff.restoreUnchanged(old, new, { items }) -> new, with the blocks align calls the same set back to old's exact text
  mdDiff.changes(old, new)             -> the changed entries only
  mdDiff.groups(old, new, { items })   -> align's sequence, each run of changes split
                                          into groups, an array per group
  mdDiff.revert(old, new, entry)       -> new, with that change (or an array of them) taken back
  mdDiff.runs(oldText, newText)        -> [{ type: 'equal'|'change', … }]
  mdDiff.mark(root, runs)              -> root, with <ins>/<del> laid over it
  mdDiff.render(host, old, new, opts)  -> { count, goto, next, prev }
  mdDiff.inline(old, new, { size })    -> one change's inline reading, an element
  mdDiff.one(old, new, { size })       -> one change's container, its three stops and
                                          swipe, with no listeners on the page; its
                                          handle (step, select) is el.__mdDiff
    opts.menu(entry, i) -> rowMenu items, opened from a change's index
    opts.note(entry, i) -> string | Element | null, said under the change
                           while its container is selected (or hovered)
    opts.actions(entry, i) -> [{ label, icon?, title?, run(entry, i, button) }], a
                           pill on the container's bottom edge, shown the same way;
                           with `icon` (a Phosphor class) the button is that icon
    opts.group      true draws each group as one container (see groups)
    opts.sign(entry, i) -> Element | null, a second pill at the bottom-right
                           corner, shown the same way; the actions then sit left

The host's half of the contract, all optional:

  opts.controls   an element to mount the controls in, for a host with a
                  header of its own. Without it the kit draws a sticky strip,
                  and `--md-diff-top` says how far down the host's top is.
  opts.layout     which layout the document opens on, 'swipe' or 'side'.
  opts.strip      false suppresses the kit's strip entirely.

The returned handle carries `controls` (the same element, to move later),
`setLayout`, and `next`/`prev`/`goto`, which is what a host wires its own
jump button to.

── Two layouts, and the document picks ─────────────────────────────────────

`swipe` reads, `side` compares, and which one you want is a property of the
document rather than of one change: nobody compares paragraph four in two
columns and paragraph nine by swiping. So one toggle in the strip moves every
change, and no block carries a control for it.

── Three readings on one axis, inside `swipe` ─────────────────────────────

Every version of old, new and combined is right for SOME change, which is why
picking one globally has never worked. The reader picks, by swiping:

  old      the block as it stood
  both     one column, the change marked in place   <- where a change opens
  new      the block as it now reads

One axis with three stops, so the swipe IS the interface and the line beneath
a change is a label that happens to be tappable. See the note above
`container` for what that replaced and why.

The track is a swipeDeck, so the gesture is the house one with the house snap
behaviour rather than a pointer threshold invented here.

── How the inline view is built, since this is the load-bearing part ───────

NOT by diffing markdown source and rendering the result: a word diff cuts
through `**` and `](` and the render collapses. Instead the NEW block is
rendered normally and the change is laid over the rendered text as standoff
marks, which is the move kits/annotate.js makes for a note. The diff runs
over the two blocks' PLAIN TEXT, so what is marked is what a reader sees, and
the markup underneath is never touched.

Deletions have no place in the new text, so each removed run is inserted as a
<del> at the boundary where it used to be. That is the one place this view
adds a node rather than marking one.

Two details keep that honest. Every offset is resolved against the text nodes
BEFORE anything is mutated, and the edits are applied back to front within
each node, so no operation invalidates the next one's coordinates. And a run
crossing an element boundary is wrapped once per text node rather than once
per run, so a change spanning `<strong>` stays inside the strong instead of
re-nesting the markup around it.

The coalescing rule is pages/shorter.html's, and it is a finding rather than
a nicety: a tiny equal run wedged between two changes is absorbed, so a
flipped word does not shatter a sentence into a dozen marks.

Marking runs before mdDoc.contain(), deliberately. contain() inserts a
language label above each fence, and that label is text the walker would
count, which would put every offset after the first fence off by its length.

And it is contained with `wrap`, so a fence's long line wraps rather than
scrolling sideways. A horizontal scroller inside a horizontal swipe is two
claims on one drag, and the swipe is what the container exists for; a line
running off the edge also defeats the point of showing two versions, which
is to see both of them.

Depends on window.Diff (jsdiff, as pages/shorter.html loads it),
window.GuideRender for the rendering, and kits/swipe-deck.js for the track.
All three are loaded on demand.
an equal run this short between two changes is noise

── Segmentation ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Top-level blocks, split on blank lines, with a fenced run kept whole: a
fence contains blank lines of its own, and splitting inside one produces
two halves that are each invalid markdown.
`items: true` also starts a block at each list item, so one bullet edited
is one block rather than its whole list (pages/dictate.html, 2026-10-01).
An item takes its continuation lines, indented or lazy, and a nested item
is a block of its own. A bullet or a "1." interrupts a paragraph, as in
CommonMark; any other number does so only after another item, since
"2. " opening a line mid-paragraph is text. A thematic break is no item.

Offsets index the caller's own string, so line endings are left as they
came. A Windows file's "\r" is whitespace to every rule below. Until
2026-10-01 this normalised "\r\n" to "\n" first, and every range then
ran one character short per line before it in the file the page edits.

A blank line outside a fence ends a block and belongs to no block,
which is two rules rather than one: an unterminated `if (buf.length)`
here pushes a run of leading blanks INTO the next block, and the
block's text then starts with whitespace that nothing downstream
strips.

── Alignment ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Blocks compare on their text with whitespace flattened, so a rewrap that
changes no words is not a change. What comes back is the NEW document's
sequence, each entry either an unchanged block or a change carrying both
sides.

Which old block became which new one, and what is left over.

The measure is shared words, as a Dice coefficient over the two token
lists: twice the overlap, over the two lengths together. It is deliberately
crude, and crude is enough, because what it has to get right is not which
rewording is closest but that prose never pairs with a table and a
paragraph never pairs with a code fence. Those score near zero whatever
the threshold.

Greedy, best score first. A stable-marriage pairing would be better in
principle and there is nothing here for it to fix: the runs are a handful
of blocks, and the case where greedy loses needs three blocks each of which
is the best match for the same partner.

Two rules cover what shared words cannot see, both reported from an edit
to a one-word heading ("Surfacing" to "Suacing"), which shares no word
with its old self and so came back as a removal and an addition. Blocks of
the same KIND (heading, list, quote, table, fence, paragraph) are also
scored on shared letter pairs, which a typo barely moves, at a higher
floor, since two unrelated paragraphs share plenty of letter pairs. And a
run of exactly one old block and one new block of the same kind is one
block edited, whatever the scores: nothing else is there for either to be.

below this the two are different blocks, not one edited
the same, measured on letter pairs, same kind only
A letter-pair match ranks below any word match: scaled under the floor.

Ordered by the NEW document, since that is the document being read. A
removed block has no place in it, so it is emitted just before whatever
now stands where it used to: the next old block that did survive.
`oi` and `ni` index the run's own olds and news, so align() can say where
in each text a change sits; `at` is the new block a removal stands before.

HOW A REMOVED RUN MEETS AN ADDED ONE, which is the whole of the alignment
and the thing worth getting right. diffArrays hands back a removed run and
an added run side by side; how those pair decides what each container
holds. Two wrong answers were tried first, and each was visible in the
demo page's own shot:

  fuse the whole run into one change   The reader loses the count, and the
    inline view's word diff then spans block boundaries, so a deletion
    belonging to a paragraph lands inside the code fence above it.
  pair by position when the counts match   A paragraph taken out shifts
    everything below it by one, so a paragraph pairs with a code fence and
    the container compares two unrelated things.

What is actually being asked is which old block BECAME which new one, and
position cannot answer it. So the blocks are paired on how much text they
share, best match first, and anything left over is an addition or a
removal in its own right. See `pairUp`.
Each entry also says WHERE it is, for a host that acts on one (a reject):
`oldRange` and `newRange` are { start, end, until } in each text, `until`
running to the next block so a block taken out takes its blank line with
it; a removal has no new range and carries `insertAt`, where its old text
would go back.
With `items`, a block can sit on the line after its neighbour with no
blank line between, and two ranges change to keep a revert exact. The
last item of a tight list reaches only to the end of its own line, so
taking it out leaves the blank line that parts the list from what
follows (taken with it, the next paragraph became the item before's
lazy continuation). And an item removed from the end of a tight list
goes back on the line after the block before it, not ahead of the
paragraph after the blank line.

A block's `end` is the start of the line after it, so the gap to the
next block is its blank lines, and a tight pair has none.

`from` only on the run's first block in each text, where the block
before is unchanged: after another block of the run, the gap is
that block's (see `swap`).

`b` with what align cannot see put back to `a`: every block it counts the
same is given a's exact text, and so is the gap after it when the next
block is the same too, or when it is the last, and the text before the
first block when that one is the same. Blocks compare with their
whitespace flattened, so a re-wrap, a doubled space or an extra blank
line between two unchanged paragraphs is no change and makes no card;
pages/dictate.html's Apply reverts the cards left unconfirmed, and
without this those edits went into the commit unconfirmed and unseen.
A gap beside a changed block is that change's, and is left alone.

And what comes before the first block, when that block is the same:
blank lines added at the top of the file belong to no change.

The new text with one change taken back, from an entry align() returned
for these same two texts: a changed block gets its old text again, an
added one goes with its blank line, and a removed one returns where it
stood. Positions are the entry's, so a caller re-aligns after each revert.

An array is one RUN, the entries align() returned between two unchanged
blocks, and it goes back as a span: the run is contiguous in both texts,
so its stretch of the new text is swapped for its stretch of the old.
Reverting its entries one by one would not do, since pairing is by shared
words and can cross ("Gone para." pairs with "Added para." below a block
that moved), which puts every block back but not in its old order.
AT THE END OF THE FILE a block's `until` is the end of the text, so its
span carries the file's last newline and not the blank line before it,
which belongs to the block above. Taking such a block out therefore takes
the blank line before it instead and keeps the file's ending, and putting
one back at the end brings the blank line that stood before it in the old
text. Measured by node/test/md-tracked-matrix.test.mjs: a paragraph
carried to the end of a file, or away from it, reverted one blank line
long or one short ("## Section\nDelta one." glued to a heading).

A block tight above a list item keeps a blank line above it and none
below, and when the item is taken out first (the cards reverted from the
last up) the item's blank line is left below it as well: a paragraph and
the item under it, carried down as one, came back one blank line long.
A cut with a blank line (or the file's start) above and a blank line
below takes the one below. Never so in the text align() measured, where
`until` reaches the next block's first line, or ends an item's own line
under the block tight above it.

A changed stretch put back, and the blank lines either side of it with it
when they differ. A gap belongs to no block, so a list item carried out
into a paragraph turned the tight gap above it into a blank line that no
card owned, and taking the card back left it there. Where both gaps are
as they were, this is the plain swap it always was.
The gap BEFORE is taken only when both sides carry `from`, which align()
gives only a run's first block: after another change the gap is that
change's, in its `until` or its `to`, and two cards taking one gap took
it twice when reverted from the last up (a paragraph added at the top of
a file and a split below it came back as "lpha" for "Alpha"). A range
without `to` (a hand-built entry) swaps as before.
`to` was measured before any later card was taken back. One that took out
the block after this one leaves that block's blank lines where this gap
was, so the gap runs on over them; otherwise the old gap came back on top
of them (a list item's last line cut to a stray "   *" came back with an
extra blank line).

The run's first block on each side gives the gap before it, its last
the gap after.

── Word runs ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Coarse runs first, then absorb the noise, as shorter.html does.

── Standoff marking ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
`coarse` is measured against the concatenated text of `root`, which is why
the caller must diff the text of the SAME tree it passes here.
Contrast, and the deletion is the one that needed it. It was a 20% wash
under `opacity-60` text, so the words a reader most needs to read were the
faintest thing on the page. The tint carries the signal now and the text
stays at full strength; the strike is currentColor, so it reads at the same
weight as the words it crosses.
The edge and marker of a wholly new block: the theme's success hue, which
is pale, deepened toward a saturated green so it reads at a glance.

`side` says which text `root` holds and therefore which coordinates the
runs are in, because a run list is measured against a PAIR and each half
indexes it differently:

  inline  the new text, additions wrapped and removals inserted (default)
  new     the new text, additions wrapped and removals left out
  old     the OLD text, removals wrapped, additions not present at all

The last two are the side-by-side halves. Marking each column rather than
rendering it plain is what makes the pair a comparison instead of two
paragraphs: the reader sees what left on the left and what arrived on the
right, in the same colours the inline reading uses.

The numeric filter and ownerDocument are kits/standoff.js's form, for the
same two reasons: NodeFilter is a bare global the suite's realm does not
have, and a tree built off-document belongs to its own document.

Absolute coordinates first, over the whole run list, before any edit.

A run that is only whitespace is passed over rather than marked. Marking
one adds a node that shows nothing, and the renderer's own newline
between two blocks is exactly that run, so the alternative is a stray
mark at the end of most changes.

An added run is also trimmed at both ends before it is marked. The
whitespace at the end of a run is the newline between two rendered
blocks, which belongs to neither, and a highlight over it wraps to the
next line as a coloured sliver under the paragraph. Visible on the demo
page's added block, where the whole paragraph is one run.

A wrap over [at, to), trimmed at both ends, in whichever tag the side
calls for.

The old column indexes the OLD text, so only `o` advances the cursor
and `n` is not in this document at all.
Then per node, since a run crossing an element boundary is two wraps.

A run over several blocks also covers the whitespace nodes between
them, and a wrap there is a sliver of colour between paragraphs.

Back to front within a node: splitText leaves the head intact, so every
offset still smaller than the one just used stays correct.

At the SAME offset the wrap goes first and the deletion second, which is
the opposite of how they read. A deletion is a zero-width point and its
split leaves the head node exactly that long, so running it first hands
the wrap an empty tail: the <ins> comes out containing nothing and the
added words are left unmarked. Running the wrap first puts the <del>
immediately before it, which is also where a reader expects the removed
words to sit.

`contain: false` is the inline view's, because the language label contain()
inserts would shift every offset after the first fence. The caller contains
it after marking instead.

`size` is the guide body's, set once by render() rather than threaded
through every call: a host in a drawer wants the small body for the whole
diff, never for one view of one change.

render()'s opts.menu, read by each container's index
render()'s opts.note, read by each container
render()'s opts.actions, read by each container
render()'s opts.sign, read by each container

bodyClass rather than the literal: it installs the stylesheet, and
`guide-body` styles nothing until it has.

A wholly new block is not marked: every word would be, and a paragraph
washed green is harder to read than the paragraph. Its container says it
is new instead (`NEW_EDGE`, below).
A change may carry its own `size` (one(), below): its slides render when
the deck reaches them, after the call that set bodySize has returned.
a shape the walker cannot mark still reads as the new text

The plain text a reader sees, for diffing the document rather than the
source. Rendered WITHOUT contain(), to match the tree inlineView marks.

A block that was taken out has no new text to lay marks over, so it is
shown as itself over a red wash. Strikethrough over a whole paragraph is
the obvious alternative and is much harder to read than the paragraph.

HOW FAST A READING SWAPS, and it is not one answer. A drag on a touch
screen is the reader's own motion, and animating the settle matches it. A
click or an arrow key is not a gesture, and Chrome scales a smooth
scroll's duration with the distance, so on a wide screen the same swap
takes proportionally longer: a reader on a desktop reported it as slow
while the same code felt right on a phone.

So the input decides, not the width. `prefers-reduced-motion` is folded in
here because it is the same question asked by someone with a stronger
claim on the answer.

WHAT A CHANGE LOOKS LIKE IN THE DOCUMENT, and the answer is: like the
document, with a little delineation. A bordered box per change turns a page
of prose into a stack of panels and the reader then reads the panels rather
than the text; a change with no edge at all is hard to aim at. So the block
keeps the left edge and the rhythm of the paragraphs around it, and carries
a faint tint that says where it begins and ends.

THREE READINGS ON ONE AXIS, which is what removed the controls. The first
version asked two questions (difference on or off, then which of that
pair), which needed two controls and a mode the reader had to hold. Old,
inline and new is one axis with three stops, so a swipe is the whole
interface and the stops are a label that happens to be tappable.
Two-column side by side went with it: at a phone's width it stacked into
old-above-new, which is what swiping to `old` and back already gives.

The reader lands on inline, the middle stop, so a swipe either way reaches
a whole version of the block.

The stops float at the top right rather than sitting under the block. Under
it they read as a caption belonging to the paragraph, which is the one
thing they are not, and they were easy to miss; over it they read as chrome
for the block they sit on. The backdrop is what keeps them legible where a
line of text runs under them.

SELECTION IS ONE IDEA WITH THREE WAYS IN. Tapping a stop, swiping, and
jumping from the strip all say the same thing: this block, this reading.
So the current block stays marked until another is chosen, rather than
flashing and going out, which left the strip's arrows saying nothing about
where they had put you.

A WHOLLY NEW BLOCK HAS ONE READING, as a wholly removed one does. It used
to offer `inline` and `new`, and with no old text those are the same
words twice: the marked reading is the paragraph washed green, the other
is the paragraph. A reader met three such blocks and asked what the
second stop was for, which is the question a control earns when it
changes nothing. So `added` collapses to the marked reading and says what
it is, the way `removed` already did.

THE BLOCK'S OUTLINE SAYS WHICH VERSION IS ON SCREEN. Without it, a block
sitting on `new` is prose with a faint wash, which is indistinguishable
from prose at a glance: the reader has scrolled past the marks and
nothing is left saying what they are looking at. Red for the old text,
green for the new, neutral for the marked reading, which needs no colour
of its own because the marks are the colour.

An outline rather than a fill, because a fill is a second background
behind text that already carries coloured marks, and the two washes
muddy each other; an outline is at the block's edge, where the prose is
not. It also leaves the background free to carry selection, which is the
one fact that has to be readable ON TOP of the version.
ONE HUE PER READING, and everything that says which reading is on screen
takes its colour from this table: the block's outline, the stop that is
lit, and the stops that are not. A reader should be able to learn the
vocabulary from the pill without tapping it, which is why an unlit `old`
is already faintly red and an unlit `new` faintly green.

The marked reading is neutral because its marks carry the colour, which
holds while a block has both kinds in it. A wholly new block has only
one, so the edge says green and matches what is inside it, the way a
wholly removed block says red.

The neutral reading is base-content, which at 80% would be nearly the
prose itself, so it alone is held down to an edge.

A WHOLLY NEW BLOCK says so with its edge and a New marker rather than
with marks (see inlineView). The theme's success hue is pale, so the
edge mixes in a deeper green to be seen at a glance, and on hover it
comes up to full strength over a faint wash of the same green.

`-mx-2 px-2` puts the tint's edge outside the text and leaves the text
itself on the document's own left edge, so the block is delineated
without being indented.

The index, top left, in the same pill the stops use. It is what joins a
block to the strip's `2 / 3`: without it the readout names a position
the document does not show anywhere. Tapping it claims the block, which
is a fourth way into the same selection and the one a thumb reaches for
when the stops are not what it wants.

It stays in both layouts, since it identifies the change rather than the
reading, and it FILLS when selected: with the background down at 4% the
badge is the strongest thing saying which block is claimed.

The index carries no version colour, since it names the change rather
than the reading. What it carries is weight: at 55% opacity it read as
an artefact of the layout rather than as a number worth reading, and it
is the one thing joining a block to the controls' `2 / 3`.
`md-diff-idx` is a hook, as `md-diff-note` is: a host that marks a change
its own way (the Map view's Docs tab, for a user call's edit) puts its
mark in this place.

The stops, floating. `-top-2` lifts the group into the gap above the
block so it clears the first line in the common case, and the backdrop
covers the case where a line runs under it.

NO HEIGHT TRANSITION, because there is no longer a height change to
ease. The box is sized once to the tallest reading and stays there; see
`swipe()` below for what that bought and what it cost. The transition
was written for a box that resized on every swap, and animating the
scroller's own box under a moving finger is what broke the gesture.

A NOTE AND ACTIONS, SHOWN WITH THE SELECTION. Dictate's change cards
(kits/md-surface.js) show their actions only on the card the reader has
selected, as a pill on its bottom edge, and keep the card's note one tap
away; a read-only container had neither, so a host could explain a change
only with a line that stood under every block at once. Both appear when
the container is selected, and on hover where there is a pointer, so a
document with twenty changes reads as twenty paragraphs until one is
picked. `group/chg` scopes the hover to this container.

The pill straddles the bottom edge: `!pb-4` keeps it off the note's
last line (the `!` outranks the `py-1` the layout sets), and `mb-4`
off the text of whatever follows the container.
Centred alone; beside a signature it sits left, so the two never
meet on a phone.

A SIGNATURE: who or what produced the change, in the same pill shape at
the right-hand corner. The host draws its content and owns its taps.

The reading on screen is FILLED, in its own hue, not merely less
transparent. A stop that differs from its neighbours only by opacity
reads as slightly clearer text rather than as a selection, and a stop
filled grey says which one is lit without saying what it is.

The pill's own edge follows the reading too, so the group reads as
belonging to a block showing `old` rather than as chrome parked on it.

Only a reader's move counts as choosing this block. The initial
`go(start)` scrolls the track, and the deck reports that as a slide
change like any other, so without a guard every container announces
itself on mount and the strip opens saying the reader is somewhere they
have not been.

The guard is the GESTURE, not a timer. A timer was tried first and is a
guess at how long a smooth scroll takes: 400ms held on the demo page and
not in the app, where a heavier layout stretched the same scroll past it
and the card opened on change 2 of 3. A pointer on the track cannot
arrive early.

AND IT OPENS WHAT A HOST OFFERS FOR THE CHANGE (`opts.menu`, a function of
the entry and its index returning rowMenu items), since the number is the
change's own handle: a reject belongs to the change, not to the document.

TAPPING THE BLOCK CLAIMS IT. Selection used to need a stop, the badge or
a swipe, so a reader who tapped the text of a change to look at it was
told, by the strip and by the badge, that they were somewhere else.
Reading a block is the plainest way of saying which one you are on.

SELECTION IS YELLOW, and the badge is where it is loud. A highlighter is
what a reader already reads as "this is the one I am on", and yellow is
the one hue the version vocabulary does not use, so it cannot be misread
as a reading. It is warning rather than a fixed yellow because every
other colour here follows the theme and this should too.

The badge carries it at nearly full strength while the block's own fill
stays at 4%. That division is the point: the fill would sit behind prose
that already carries coloured marks, and the badge sits on nothing.
An inline style rather than a class, because the pill already carries
`bg-base-100/90` and two background classes on one element are settled
by stylesheet order rather than by the order they are written in the
attribute. The first attempt added the fill as a class and it came out
pale, losing to the backdrop it was meant to cover.

slideScroll: false hands the vertical axis to the content, and takes
the slide's padding with it. Both matter here: the padding is what
would set a changed block in from the prose around it, and a scroller
inside the document is a second place to drag.

One stop per flick. Three readings on one axis puts the marked one
in the middle, which is where a reader is usually going, and
momentum carried straight past it to `new`. The property alone
never stopped that on iOS; the equal heights below are what did.
It stays because it costs nothing and it is correct where an
engine honours it.

ONE HEIGHT FOR ALL THREE READINGS, and it is the whole fix for the
gesture. The box used to follow the reading on screen: `fit(a)` from
inside the scroll handler, a fresh `scrollHeight` every animation
frame, and a 200ms height transition that therefore began at the
midpoint of every flick. On iOS that scroller then crossed the middle
stop and landed on the far side, or came to rest BETWEEN two stops,
which `scroll-snap-type: mandatory` is supposed to forbid.

pages/probe-snap.html measured it by hand on the device, five tracks
differing in one thing each. Deferring the write until the scroll went
quiet did not fix it. Writing it once before the drag did not fix it.
Removing swipe-deck's overshoot guard did not fix it. Giving every
slide the same height fixed it, and was the only lane that snapped.
So a scroller here is sized once and never resized, and the guard is
gone from the kit.

The cost is honest and small: a one-line `old` sits in a box built for
a three-line `inline`, so short readings carry whitespace below them.
That is the price of a gesture that lands where it is aimed, and the
readings of one paragraph are usually within a line or two of each
other anyway. `added` and `removed` have one reading, so they pay
nothing.

Every slide is built up front rather than lazily. Three is not a
number worth deferring, and a max across slides the deck has not built
yet is a max over nothing. `keep` is 2, so nothing is pruned back out.

The slide's own box is `h-full` under slideScroll:false, so measuring
it answers with the height already set. The content inside it is the
only box whose height is the content's.

Guarded, because the ResizeObserver below fires on every reflow and
an unchanged write is still a write on a box the engine is watching.

Highlighting and web fonts arrive after the first measurement, and a
