table that reflows changes it again, so the height follows the content
rather than being read once. This is the one write left after mount,
and it happens when content settles rather than when a finger moves.

── SIDE: both versions at once ───────────────────────────────────────
A reader who wants to compare rather than to read wants both halves in
view, and that is a property of the whole document rather than of one
block: nobody compares paragraph four side by side and paragraph nine by
swiping. So the layout is the document's and the stops stand down, which
is what keeps this from being a second control per change.

Each column carries the version tint the swipe layout puts on the block,
so red and green mean the same thing in both layouts.

TWO COLUMNS AT EVERY WIDTH. Stacking them on a phone made `side`
old-above-new, which is what swiping to `old` and back already gives,
so the layout stopped meaning anything at the width it is most often
read at. Narrow columns are the cost of comparing on a phone, and the
reader who does not want to pay it has `swipe`.

THE COLUMNS ARE THE CONTAINER. In `swipe` the block carries the
outline and the reading sits inside it; here the two columns carry
their own, and a third outline around them would be a box inside a box
spending width on nothing. So `build` strips the block's own edge and
padding for this layout and the columns take the full measure.

AND EACH COLUMN IS MARKED, which is the difference between a
comparison and two paragraphs side by side: what left is struck on the
left, what arrived is highlighted on the right, in the colours the
inline reading already uses.

Marked before contain(), for the reason the inline view is: the
language label contain() inserts is text the walker would count.

Right-aligned, because the index badge floats at the block's top
LEFT and a left-aligned label on the first column sits underneath it.

In `side` the columns are the container: the block gives up its own
edge and padding so the pair takes the full width, rather than sitting
in a box inside a box.

No initial build: render() calls setLayout once for the whole document,
which is the one place the layout is decided.

One stop along, for the arrow keys. Clamped rather than wrapped: a
reader holding a key down should stop at `new` rather than cycling
back to `old` and looking like it lost its place.

`group` draws each group (groups(), above) as one container rather than
each changed block: a new section is one change, not one per paragraph.

gap-2 is .5rem, which is exactly the margin guide-body puts between two
paragraphs. Each block renders as its own guide-body, and that rule zeroes
the first and last child's margins, so the gap here is the ONLY thing
setting the document's rhythm. Anything larger and the changes read as
cards with air around them rather than as paragraphs.
`md-diff-doc` is the one stable name on the rendered document, and it is
there so chrome OUTSIDE this kit can find the document it belongs to.
The handle's `next`/`prev` only reach a host holding the handle, and a
page that draws its jump button in a deck header two components away
does not: pages/approve.html renders the comparison inside a
file-review card inside a deck slide. A class plus an event is the
shortest path that does not thread a handle through both.
`px-1` IS THE ROOM THE CONTAINERS BLEED INTO. A changed block carries
`-mx-2 px-2`, which puts its tinted edge OUTSIDE the text so the block is
delineated without being indented. With a host at zero that edge lands
exactly on whatever bounds the document, so on a phone the coloured ring
ran off both sides of the screen and a reader could not see the box they
were swiping. Four pixels is the whole fix: the ring sits 4px inside the
host and the text is unmoved, since 4 of padding less 8 of bleed plus 8
of the block's own padding puts a changed line exactly where an
unchanged one already sits.

The kit reserves it rather than each consumer, because the bleed is the
kit's decision. pages/approve.html and kits/file-deck.js both mount this
and would otherwise each have to know the number.

── The controls, as ONE element the host may place ───────────────────

A position and a layout toggle, and nothing else. They used to sit in a
sticky strip of the kit's own with a pair of jump arrows beside them,
which put two jump mechanisms on a page whose header already had one,
and put the layout toggle somewhere that scrolled away. `next` and
`prev` stay on the returned handle, so a host that wants a jump button
wires its own.

Handing the host an element rather than drawing chrome it cannot move is
the same arrangement alpineComponents/file-review.js makes with its
`viewModes`: the controls exist in one place and are placed in another,
rather than being built twice and drifting.

The readout is what a host WITHOUT its own chrome needs, and a duplicate
for a host that draws the position itself. `readout: false` drops it and
`onMove` feeds whatever the host draws instead.
IT NEVER CHANGES WIDTH, because it sits in a floating pill and the pill
is anchored on its right edge: anything that resizes the readout slides
the whole control under the reader's thumb. Measured 2026-09-18 at 1200:
191px saying "10 changes", 162 at "1 / 10", 168 at "10 / 10", so it
shifted twice, once on the first tap and again crossing into two digits.

One shape for both states is what fixes the first shift: `– / 10` before
a change is claimed says the same thing "10 changes" said, in the form it
will take once the reader moves. `tabular-nums` and a `ch` floor fix the
second, since with equal-width digits the widest string this document can
show is exactly twice its digit count plus ' / '.

THE LAYOUT IS THE DOCUMENT'S, not each change's. Comparing and reading
are two ways of going through a document, and a reader doing one is
doing it to all of it: nobody compares paragraph four in two columns and
paragraph nine by swiping. One toggle, and every change follows it,
which is what keeps a second control off every block.

THE STEP BELONGS WITH THE COUNT. It sat in pages/approve.html's deck
header, which is where a reader looks for controls about the FILE: its
github links, which reading to show. Stepping change to change is about
the COMPARISON, which is what this strip is, and the readout beside it
already says which change of how many. Putting them together also gave
the header back its title, which at 390px had been squeezed to 38px by
ten buttons.

It wraps where a container's three stops clamp, since this is the walk
through the whole set and the tenth of ten should return to the first.

SHOW ME ALL OF THEM. The document reads as prose by design: an unchanged
paragraph is plain and a changed one carries a thin ring, which is right
for reading and wrong for the first ten seconds, when the question is
where the changes ARE. This lifts every block to the wash the claimed one
wears, so the shape of the change is visible at a glance, and drops it
again. A toggle rather than a mode: it is a way of looking, not a state
the document is in.

THE SAME WASH THE CLAIM WEARS, not a fainter one. Half strength was the
first try and it was barely there: the point is to answer "where are the
changes" across a screen, and a tint you have to look for does not. The
claim stays legible because the wash was never its loudest channel: the
numbered badge is nearly solid yellow while the wash sits at 8%, so with
every block lit the badge is still the only one of them that is.

Where the reader is, for a host drawing its own. Called on every change
of selection and once at mount, so a host has a value to render before
anything has been tapped.

Where they go. `opts.controls` is a host saying "I have a header, put
them in it"; without one the kit keeps its own sticky strip, which is
what a host with no chrome of its own (the review card) needs.

`--md-diff-top` is the strip's one host contract: how far down the
host's top is. A page with a sticky header would otherwise have the
strip slide underneath it and disappear.

IT FLOATS, rather than taking a row across the top. A full-width bar
was right when this kit drew the only chrome a card had; it is wrong
beside a deck header that already carries the file's controls, where
it reads as a second header and pushes the document down by its own
height. Reported 2026-09-18.

`sticky` and not `absolute`, because the reader wants the layout
toggle wherever they have scrolled to, and a `-mb-` equal to its own
height takes back the grid row it would otherwise occupy, so the
document begins where it would have begun with no strip at all. The
backdrop is what keeps the line behind it readable, since the prose
now runs underneath.

`--md-diff-top` is the strip's one host contract: how far down the
host's top is. A page with a sticky header would otherwise have the
strip slide underneath it and disappear.

`at` is -1 before the reader has claimed anything, which is a different
state from being on the first change and a host's badge should be able
to tell them apart.

ONE SELECTION, THREE WAYS IN. A container says `md-diff:here` when the
reader taps a stop or swipes it; the arrows set the same thing. So the
strip always names the block the reader is working in, whether they got
there by scrolling and swiping or by tapping an arrow.

Selection is the BACKGROUND, because the outline now carries the version.
The two facts need two channels: a reader working in a block still has
to be able to see which version that block is showing, so selection
cannot take the edge the version is using.

The same yellow as the badge, so selection is one colour rather than a
yellow badge on a blue block. A color-mix rather than `bg-warning/4`,
for two reasons: daisyUI ships its opacity ramp in tens, so 4 would be
composed by Tailwind and is dead on any page that has not registered
the theme names as colours (python/dead-opacity.py), and a kit has no
say in which pages load it. The arbitrary value resolves everywhere.

The same fact as an attribute, because the wash and the yellow badge
are the only OTHER places it is said and both are paint. A host
styling the current block, and a check asserting which one it is,
would otherwise be matching on a color-mix class string.

THE SAME JUMP, FOR CHROME THAT CANNOT HOLD THE HANDLE. `next` and `prev`
are for a host that called render() and kept what it returned. A page
whose jump button lives in a deck header, with a component boundary in
between, has the element and not the handle, so it dispatches here:

    doc.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('md-diff:jump', { detail: { d: 1 } }))

Wrapping rather than clamping, because this is the jump the reader uses
to walk the whole set and the tenth of ten should return to the first
rather than stop dead. That is the opposite of a container's stops,
which clamp; the two are different journeys.

CLICKING AWAY IS LETTING GO. Selection is a reader's claim on one block;
a claim nothing can release accumulates, and the strip keeps naming a
block the reader left some paragraphs ago. Listening on the document is
the only way to hear a tap that lands on nothing, and the listener
removes itself once the host is off the page, since a kit that renders
into a component has no teardown hook to hang it on.

INSIDE THE DOCUMENT, OUTSIDE A CHANGE. Scoping it to `host` is what
makes the rule safe to state: anything the host draws around the
document is its own business, including the jump button it wires to
`next`.

Clearing on any tap anywhere was the first version and it broke the
jump outright. The tap's pointerdown cleared the selection, and the
click that followed it computed `next` from nothing, so every press of
the arrow went to change 1 and the second press appeared to do
nothing at all.

It survived its own test because that test called `element.click()`,
which dispatches a click and no pointer events, so it never met the
listener it was meant to exercise. A probe driving this has to tap
the way a reader does (`page.click`), not the way a script finds
convenient.

THE ARROW KEYS, DELIBERATELY. They already appeared to work, and only by
accident: with focus inside a snap track, the browser's own horizontal
scroll nudges it and `snap-mandatory` settles on the next slide. That is
a whole reading changed by a side effect of where focus happens to be,
it moves by a scroll increment rather than by a stop, and it stops
working the moment focus leaves.

Keyed to the CLAIM instead, which is the thing the reader can see: the
yellow badge says which block the keys will move. Left and right walk
that block's stops.

ON SCREEN IS THE GATE FOR UP AND DOWN, not the claim. The claim was the
gate for both until 2026-09-18, and it meant a reader who had clicked the
document and pressed Down got a scroll: the keys only started working
once they had tapped a block, which is the move the keys were supposed to
save them. Down with nothing claimed now lands on the first change.

A deck mounts three of these at once, so "is this the one" has to be
answered by geometry rather than by the claim: every slide is in the tree
and laid out, and only the active one overlaps the viewport.

IN THE CAPTURE PHASE, and it stops what it handles. kits/swipe-deck.js
binds Left and Right on `window` to step the DECK, and both listeners
hear the same event: `preventDefault` does not stop a sibling listener,
and the deck's was registered first (it opened before this document
rendered), so it ran first and swiped the whole deck out from under a
reader who was walking one block's readings. Capture runs before any
bubble listener whatever the registration order, so this one decides.

Not while someone is typing, which includes a field a host put on the
page around this document.

UP AND DOWN WALK THE CHANGES, left and right walk one change's stops.
That is the same split the screen has: the readings of a block sit on
the horizontal axis and the blocks sit on the vertical one, so the keys
read as the directions they move in rather than as a mapping to learn.

From nothing, Down opens on the first change and Up on the last,
which is what each key means before there is a position to move from.

Left and right stay keyed to the claim, because with none there is no
block whose readings they would walk, and the deck's own use of them is
then the right one.

ONE CHANGE'S INLINE READING, on its own: the new text rendered, the words
that left struck in red and the words that arrived tinted green, as a
container's `both` stop draws them. For a host listing changes without a
document around them (the app's Waiting view), so a reader sees what each
one does before opening anything. Loads what render() loads.

ONE CHANGE AS ITS OWN CONTAINER, outside any document: the old, inline
and new stops and the swipe between them, with nothing installed on the
page. render() takes the arrow keys and the outside tap for a whole
document under review; a host that opens a single block in place of a
paragraph (kits/md-variants.js, a variant opened from its margin mark)
must leave the page's keys alone. The returned element is the
`.md-diff-change` section, built in the swipe layout, its index pill
hidden for the host to name it.

The container's handle rides on its element (`__mdDiff`), so a host
can step or settle the readings without reading the track itself.

needDiff is exported so a card counting changed lines loads jsdiff through
the one loader, and the counts come from the engine the rendered diff uses.
── Groups: which changed blocks read as one change ────────────────────

A split inside a link's text breaks the link, and the halves render its
markup: `[official` and `folder](https://…).` where the base reads
`official` and `folder.`. The second half shared no word with its old
paragraph, so it was a card of its own and the split showed no break.
Words are compared without that markup.

The texts' words laid end to end, each remembered as [block, word], and
which old word survived as which new one.

ONE CARD PER PARAGRAPH, UNLESS A JOIN, A SPLIT OR A STRETCH OF NEW TEXT
TIES SEVERAL TOGETHER (kits/md-surface.js's cards and render's `group`).
align pairs blocks one to one, so a join comes back as a changed
pair and a removal, and a split as a changed pair and an addition. What
ties them is shared words: an original paragraph whose words went into a
new one is linked to it, and a card is one set of linked paragraphs. A
link needs a fifth of the smaller paragraph's words, since a lone "the"
matches across two long paragraphs rewritten side by side.
A card must also be a contiguous stretch of both texts, which is what
reverting it swaps back, and cards must stand in the same order in both,
or each goes back in place and the pair stays swapped. So groups that
interleave or cross are merged.

A STRETCH OF NEW CONTENT IS ONE CARD. Paragraphs that are all added
share no words with anything old, so nothing above ties them, and a
new section came out as a card per paragraph. Neighbours that are both
additions, or both removals, are one stretch of one text and nothing of
the other, so taking them back together stays exact.

The sequence align() returns, each run of changes between two unchanged
blocks split into its groups: an unchanged entry, or an array of entries.

One entry standing for a group, for a container: its old and new text are
the group's blocks in order, and `entries` are the group's own, which
revert() takes as one run.

kits/md-doc.js — a markdown document rendered as something you can read and
take pieces OUT of.

Three jobs over one render, and the first two are the same job seen from
either end:

  CONTAIN    a wide table, code block or image scrolls or shrinks inside its
             own box rather than widening the column it sits in. Without this
             the widest thing in a doc sets the width of everything around it,
             and a reader dragging sideways to see column six drags the prose
             with it.
  CUT        every heading gets controls over THAT SECTION'S SOURCE: copy
             it with its address, edit it in place where the host says the
             render is the file as stored (`o.edit`, kits/md-edit.js), or
             open a note pinned to it. Wikipedia's [edit] link: the unit a
             reader wants to act on is the section, and what they want to
             act on it WITH is the markdown, not the HTML it was rendered
             into.
  DECLARE    the rendered box says which source and which address it is a
             rendering OF, so any node inside it can be answered for in the
             source's terms. That is what lets a note read
             `docs/APP.md § Mechanism (lines 16-28)` rather than
             `article > p:nth-of-type(3) [42-57]`.

The two arrived together because they are the same complaint from two sides.
A rendered document is a reading surface that has thrown away its source:
the table has lost the pipes that would have let it wrap, and the section has
lost the `##` that would have let it travel. Both are recoverable only by the
surface that still holds the source, which is this one.

WHY THE SOURCE AND NOT THE SELECTION. Copying a rendered section gives you
prose with the structure flattened out: a table becomes tab-separated runs, a
link becomes its label, a fenced block loses its fence. Handing that to a
model and asking for a revision gets you a revision of the flattening. The
source slice is the thing that can be revised and put back, which is the
whole point of cutting at a section rather than at a paragraph.

  mdDoc.split(src)                 -> [{ index, depth, title, slug, raw,
                                         start, end, startLine, endLine }]
  mdDoc.reference(sec, addr)       -> the provenance line(s), as an array
  mdDoc.payload(sec, addr)         -> reference + blank line + sec.raw
  mdDoc.html(src, o?)              -> a prose HTML STRING, tables contained
  mdDoc.render(host, src, o?)      -> mounts into host; returns { box, sections }
  mdDoc.enhance(box, src, o?)      -> the same over markup another renderer made;
                                      `src` must be the source that produced it
  mdDoc.contain(el, {wrap})        -> el, nothing left that can widen a column
                                      (`wrap` makes a fence wrap rather than
                                      scroll; see the note above contain)
  mdDoc.linkRepoFiles(el, o?)       -> make unambiguous repository file references navigable
  mdDoc.repoPath(file, href)        -> { path, hash } for a relative repository href
  mdDoc.locate(node)               -> { addr, sections, section } for any node in a render
  mdDoc.sourceRef(node)            -> "docs/APP.md § Mechanism (lines 16-28)"
  mdDoc.chain(sections, i)         -> section i and its ancestors by rank, innermost first
  mdDoc.children(sections, i)      -> the sections exactly one rank finer under i
  mdDoc.headOf(box, index)         -> the heading node for a section index
  mdDoc.stats(raw)                 -> { words, paragraphs, listItems, code, tables, ... }
                                      counted off the source, not the DOM
  mdDoc.KIND                       -> the frozen kind row every declaration carries
                                      (owned by docs/routes-kinds.csv)
  mdDoc.declare(box, state)        -> box, stamped with KIND through kits/src-doc.js
                                      (warns once and declares nothing without it)
  mdDoc.declaredIn(doc)            -> src-doc's declared render in doc, or null

`addr` is `{ repo, ref, path, url }`, all optional. It is what makes a copied
section worth pasting: a section with no address is a passage nobody can find
again, and the address is the half the reader cannot reconstruct.

THE VERBS ARE GLYPHS BY THE HEADING: copy always, edit where the host opted
in, note where the annotator is loaded. They were one ⋮ menu until
2026-10-25; "The section controls" below says why that changed.

SECTIONS NEST, the way Wikipedia's do: a section runs from its heading to the
next heading of EQUAL OR HIGHER rank, so copying a `##` section brings its
`###` subsections with it and each of those still has its own
control. A reader asking for "this section" nearly always means the part of
the document under that title, not the paragraphs before the next subheading.

Requires `window.marked` to be loaded already (the same lazy load every other
markdown surface here does), and reads `window.io.copy` when it is present
for the iOS clipboard path. No Alpine, no gh, no DOM opinions of its own: it
takes the host it is handed.

kits/chat-render.js carries its own copy of the table wrap, and keeps it: it
is a standalone script a page can drop in from jsDelivr with nothing else,
and node/test/chat-render-wide-table.test.mjs pins it there. The wrap is six
lines; the independence is worth more than the six.

── Contain ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Three elements can be wider than the column they are in, and each widens it
rather than being clipped by it. A TABLE's intrinsic min-content width (the
longest unbreakable run in each column) is a floor no ancestor can shrink
below. A PRE is `white-space: pre`, so a long command line does not wrap at
all. An IMG is its own pixel width. In a swipe-deck slide, the thing that
ends up scrolling is the SLIDE, which drags the headings and the prose
sideways along with whatever overflowed and reads as the document being
broken.

The table's wrapper does not force `max-content` on it. Typography's default
`width: 100%` still wraps cells, so a table that CAN fit still fits and only
one that genuinely cannot starts scrolling. Same call, and the same reasons,
as chat-render's.

INLINE STYLES, NOT UTILITY CLASSES, and that is the lesson kits/guide-render.js
paid for: a class that arrives in the DOM from a JS string depends on the
Tailwind browser build having generated a rule for it, and when it has not
there is no error anywhere, just a layout that quietly does not hold. The
`pre` case makes the point twice over, since the rule that normally saves it
belongs to the typography plugin: a page that renders prose without loading
that plugin has `overflow-x: visible` on every code block. Measured 2026-08-26
in the headless render, where the plugin ships no dist CSS and resolves to a
miss: a 922px command line inside a 398px column, slide scrollWidth 938
against a 430px track. The utility classes stay on the wrapper as the
readable statement of intent; the inline style is what makes it true.
── Fenced code: say what it is, and colour it ──────────────────────────

marked already emits `<pre><code class="language-x">`; nothing in this
estate's prose path ever read that class, so every fence rendered as an
unlabelled grey slab. A markdown file quoting markdown (a skill file
showing the marker shapes is the case) was the most confusing: a block of
plain text with no indication it was a sample rather than the document.

Two things, and the order matters. The LABEL is free and always right, so
it goes on whether or not the highlighter ever arrives. Prism is loaded
only when a labelled fence exists, and only its JS: its theme CSS paints a
light background and fixed token colours, which would fight the theme in
every dark render. The token colours live in guide-render's own CSS
instead, keyed to the daisyUI variables, so a highlighted block belongs to
the page it is on.

The same package the core came from, and a VERSIONED path. viewer.js
learned this the hard way: an unversioned components path 404s, so
every language the autoloader asked for failed and only Prism's four
bundled grammars highlighted. Pointing at npm/prismjs keeps the two
halves on one version.
no autoloader is still a working core

Positioned on the PRE rather than in a wrapper, so the block keeps its
own edges and the containment rule above still owns its scrolling.

`md-fence` is what reserves the strip it sits in. The label used to
share the first line of code: at .25rem down it ran from y4 to y14 and
the first line began at y11, so wherever that line reached the right
edge, which on a phone is most lines, the two sat on top of each other.
The class is on the pre rather than a `:has()` selector because
`data-md-fence` is also set for a fence with no language, which gets no
label and so needs no strip.

SPELLED OUT WHERE THE ABBREVIATION IS OPAQUE. A reader asked what `sh`
meant, which is a fair question about a two-letter label on a code
block. The map is deliberately short: only the cases where the token a
fence declares is not a word, since renaming anything else would
invent a language the document did not name.

A MARKED BLOCK KEEPS ITS MARKS AND GIVES UP ITS COLOURS, because the two
cannot share a block. Prism's highlightElement assigns innerHTML, so it
replaces everything inside the <code> with its own token spans, and any
<ins>/<del> that kits/md-diff.js laid over that fence is gone with it. A
documentation change inside a code block then rendered with no marking at
all: measured 2026-09-17 on the md-diff demo, three marks on the page and
zero inside the fence, in the one block whose edit was the point.

Marking wins rather than highlighting for two reasons. It is the reason
that surface exists, where syntax colour is decoration. And the two would
be arguing anyway: the token colours below are the theme's own primary,
success and accent, and red-on-removed over green-on-a-string is a worse
read than either alone.

TAKING THE CLASS OFF is what takes a block out of Prism's reach, and it
has to come off rather than be renamed. Prism's selector is four
alternatives, not one: `code[class*="language-"]` AND
`code[class*="lang-"]`, plus the same two through an ancestor. A first
attempt rewrote `language-sh` to `md-marked-lang-sh`, which still matched
the second alternative, so Prism claimed the block, found no grammar for
it, stamped `language-none` on it, and assigned innerHTML anyway: the
marks died exactly as before and the class said the fix had run. The
language moves to a data attribute, which no selector of Prism's reads.

The label above has already been read off the class by this point, and
`data-md-fence` on the pre is what stops a later pass relabelling, so
nothing downstream needs the class back. Token colours are keyed to
`.token.*` in guide-render's CSS rather than to the language, so they are
unaffected for every block that keeps its highlighting.
a grammar that will not load

`o.wrap` changes what a `pre` does with a line too long for its box: wrap
it rather than scroll it sideways.

WHY A CALLER WOULD ASK. A horizontal scroller inside a horizontal gesture
is two claims on one drag. kits/md-diff.js moves between a change's
readings by swiping, and a fence inside one took the drag for its own
scroll, so on a phone the reader could not reliably reach `old` from a
block whose content was code. The estate already met this with tables, in
a pane rather than a swipe (see the note by `.guide-body table` in
guide-render), and answered it by giving the table its own scroller; that
answer does not transfer, because the gesture the fence would be taking is
the one the whole container exists for.

It is a caller's choice rather than the default because the two readings
are both right somewhere. A guide body on a page is read down and a long
command scrolling in place keeps the prose measure honest; a fence inside a
comparison has to be legible at a glance, which means visible in full.
The containment choice a caller makes, pulled out so html(), render() and
enhance() forward it rather than each naming it again.

A pre scrolls as ITSELF: it is already a block with its own edges, so
there is nothing a wrapper would add.

`anywhere` rather than `break-word`: a shell command breaks at its
spaces, which is where a reader would break it, and the mid-token
break only happens for a single token wider than the box, which is
exactly when there is no other choice.

── Repository links ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Markdown already has a syntax for saying "this is a link". A repository
reader owes that authored intent one extra thing: `../markers/SKILL.md`
should open the repository file rather than resolve against app/index.html.
Inline code is different. Backticks say "code", not "link", so this kit
gives a WHOLE code span a door only when its text names exactly one known
file. Ambiguity stays visible and inert instead of choosing by accident.

The kit resolves and marks; the host navigates. That division keeps a
Markdown render reusable in a Files pane, a Swipe Deck, or a standalone
page without teaching this DOM-only kit what any of those surfaces are.
The child reader is a TEXT surface. Keep this list deliberately narrower
than "anything with a filename": handing an xlsx, image, PDF, or Word
document to the source renderer first decodes its bytes as text and then
presents the corruption as though it were the file. Authored binary links
still get their repository URL below; they simply keep the browser's
ordinary navigation instead of acquiring an in-deck click handler.

A fragment is still a repository-file reference: it names the current
file. Let the host land inside its existing reader so the browser does
not mint a history entry the Swipe Deck knows nothing about.

./ and ../ are authored resolution choices even inside code. A slash
without either prefix normally names a repository-root path. A bare
filename carries neither fact, so it links only when the entire tree has
one candidate: root README.md must not beat docs/README.md by accident.

The href remains a real GitHub address, so modified clicks keep the
browser's ordinary new-tab/new-window behavior. Only an unmodified
primary click belongs to the host's in-place reader.

With a known set, only re-aim a path the repository says exists.
Without one, leave resolution to the browser rather than manufacture
certainty this renderer does not have. Unsupported files still need
the repository URL: their authored relative href otherwise resolves
against app/index.html. They do not, however, become deck doors.

── Cut ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GitHub's own slug rule, near enough to link with: lowercased, punctuation
dropped, spaces hyphenated. Used for the blob URL's fragment, so a copied
reference opens on the section rather than at the top of a long file.

The headings, found in the SOURCE rather than in the rendered HTML, and
found through the parser rather than by a line regex. `# ` inside a fenced
block is not a heading and a regex cannot tell; the lexer already knows.

Only TOP-LEVEL heading tokens count. A heading inside a blockquote or a
list item is a nested token, and render() pairs this list against the box's
direct-child headings, so the two agree by construction: both take exactly
the headings that sit at the document's own level.

Offsets come from locating each token's `raw` forward from where the last
one ended, rather than from summing raw lengths. Summing drifts the moment
one token's raw is not byte-exact; searching forward re-anchors on every
token and cannot drift past the next match.

Line numbers, because the point of copying a section is usually to get a
revision back, and "lines 43-91 of this file" is what turns a revision into
an edit somebody can apply. One pass over the newlines, so a long document
costs one scan rather than one per section.

To the next heading of equal or higher rank: the section INCLUDES its
subsections. A `##` copied without its `###`s is a fragment of an
argument, and the reader who wanted the fragment has the subsection's
own control right there.

The address, in the estate's own `owner/repo[@ref]:path` grammar, because
that is the form every tool here can already resolve. The blob URL rides
beside it for the reader rather than for a tool, with the line anchor
GitHub understands.

The reference ALWAYS rides, and that is a decision rather than an
oversight. A section pasted into a chat without it is a passage the reader
then has to place by hand, which is the one part of the job they cannot do
from what is on their screen. A section pasted WITH it and not wanted costs
deleting two lines. The asymmetry decides it, the same way it decides the
annotator's preamble.

── Render ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
`proseClass: ''` means the caller's own container is already the prose box,
so what comes back is the BODY rather than a second wrapper. A stray div
between a `.prose` element and its children is not fatal (typography
matches descendants), but it takes over `> :first-child`, and a caller who
has said "I have a container" should get what goes in it.

YAML FRONTMATTER IS SHOWN AS WHAT IT IS, a code block of the YAML, since
marked has no notion of it: the opening `---` rendered as a rule and the
closing one turned the fields above it into a setext heading, so a skill
opened on a line and its name and description in large bold (reported
from the Dictate page, 2026-09-30). Only a leading `---` block whose first
line is a `key:` qualifies, so a document that opens with a real rule is
left alone. The YAML is carried verbatim, which keeps the rendered text a
subsequence of the source for any caller that maps one onto the other
(kits/md-surface.js). The block wears data-frontmatter for a caller to
style, and wraps: a skill's description is one long line, and a code
block's own scroll hid all but its first words.

THE CLIPBOARD WRITE IS kits/io.js's, and this two-line delegate is all any
kit keeps of it. Four of them carried the same textarea-fallback block,
pasted and lightly reworded, and the block is not boilerplate: it is the
iOS recipe io.js documents at length (focusable, not readonly, read the
value rather than trusting execCommand's return). Four copies of that is
four places for it to be subtly wrong, and three of them already differed
from each other in whether they returned anything.

It is FETCHED at load time rather than at click time. A clipboard write
has to run inside the user gesture that asked for it, and an await before
the write can spend the activation Safari is counting; loading the kit
when this one loads means it is simply there by the time a finger arrives.
The guard survives for the page that never gets it, and falls back to the
modern API alone, which is honest: no io.js, no legacy path.

kits/src-doc.js is self-loaded on the same principle: a page that loads this
kit has asked for a declared render, and the declaration is what that kit
holds. Every caller loads the pair explicitly too, since this arrives one
fetch late; this is the net under a caller that forgets, and declare()
below says so rather than silently doing nothing.

── Locate ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
THE DECLARATION, and it is what everything downstream of the render hangs
on. A rendered box says "I am a rendering of THIS markdown, at THIS
address", and any node inside it can then be answered for in the source's
own terms rather than the DOM's. kits/annotate.js is the first consumer:
its `Path:` line reads `docs/APP.md § Mechanism (lines 16-28)` instead of
`article > p:nth-of-type(3) [42-57]`, which is the difference between a
note a model can act on and a note it has to go looking for.

kits/src-doc.js OWNS THE DECLARATION: the attribute, the property and
the announcement for every kind that declares. This kit supplies the
markdown half: the sections, and the reference line that names one.

THE ROW THIS RENDER ANSWERS TO in docs/routes-kinds.csv, carried on the
declaration so a reader of the DOM gets the vocabulary without fetching a
registry. kits/annotate.js is that reader: its Section row is labelled from
`aimLabel` and `aimHint` rather than from strings of its own, so the aim
says what it is about instead of saying "Section" on a page that has four
other structures in it.

`aimIcon` IS PART OF THAT VOCABULARY, and it was not until 2026-09-06. The
label travelled and the glyph did not: both surfaces that draw this aim
hardcoded `ph-text-align-left`, so the next kind to declare would have
inherited markdown's icon along with its own name, and the row a reader saw
said "alignment" about a document. A kind that names its aim now names its
mark too.

ph-file-md, NOT ph-markdown-logo, and the difference is what the aim is
ABOUT. The logo is the format, and kits/annotate.js already spends it on
the serialization key that shows the set as markdown; two of them in one
card header, one lit and one not, would be the same glyph for two unrelated
questions. This aim points at a markdown DOCUMENT sitting on the page, so
it takes the document mark, which also pairs with the Page aim's ph-file
two buttons to its left: this page, or this markdown document.

The registry is the owner and node/test/routes-manifest.test.mjs holds the
two together, the same arrangement docs/routes-routes.csv has with
toss-render's inlined TOSS_ROUTES: the registry declares, the code inlines
so no render path takes a fetch, and adding to one alone fails.

Declaring is src-doc's, stamped with this kit's own row so a reader of
the DOM knows which kind it found.

Loud, once. A missing src-doc.js means nothing declares, which looks
exactly like a page with no markdown on it: the failure this kit's
consumers have already been bitten by twice.

`units` is what src-doc's aim test reads: this kind counts in
sections, and a heading-less file declares with none.

Kept as an alias so a markdown-specific caller reads as one; both
conditions (this kind declares an aim, and the render has sections in it)
are src-doc's now, since every kind needs the same pair.

Which section a node is in: walk up to the node's top-level ancestor inside
the box, then back through its previous siblings to the nearest heading
that render() stamped. That is the same rule the reader applies by eye,
which is what makes it the right one: a paragraph belongs to whatever
heading it is under.

The heading NODE rides along, not just the section data: a caller that
wants to outline the section (annotate's section pick) needs somewhere to
start walking, and re-finding the heading from a css path would be a
second answer to a question this call already answered.

The one line that says where a passage lives, in the source's terms. It is
deliberately not the machine address: `owner/repo@ref:path` is what the
payload's own header carries, and a note wants the part a person or a model
reads, which is the file, the section, and the lines.

── The section controls ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
ICONS BY THE HEADING, NOT A MENU. Until 2026-10-25 a ⋮ opened Copy section,
Copy for revision and Note this section, each with a line describing it, on
the argument that a heading has room for one mark. Read on a phone, the
mark was invisible at a quarter opacity, the menu was a block of chrome to
read through, and the verb a reader comes for (edit) was a row nobody found.
So the verbs are glyphs a reader can see: copy the section's source with its
address, and edit it in place. Copy for revision went with the menu, since
copying and pasting the answer into the editor is the same loop.

EDIT shows where the host has said the render IS the file as stored
(`o.edit.full`, the whole file it read) at an address that can take a
write, a branch rather than a commit. A diff, a variant reading or a paste
renders markdown that is not a file, and a pencil there would save
something nobody asked for. No token does NOT hide it: the editor asks for
one, which is the only way a reader without one learns that it exists.
NOTE shows only where the annotator is loaded, since a control that opens
nothing is worse than an absent one.
'branch' edits where it stands; 'pinned' is a commit on screen whose
branch is known (a `branch@commit` address), whose pencil shows disabled
(owner, 2026-11-02: "you would still see the edit button, but it would
show as disabled"; "Editing is available from live branch renders only").
A commit with no branch named keeps no pencil.
not a commit, full or short

The host's box drawn again from new source, for a host that did not take
the re-render itself (o.edit.onSaved). Sanitized the way the viewer does,
and not at all without the sanitizer: the box then keeps what it showed and
the next open reads the file.

THE KEYBOARD'S FOOTHOLD, as the FAB keeps one (alpineComponents/fab.js).
iOS raises the keyboard only for a focus made inside the tap, and the
editor's text box exists only after a preflight and a load. A field
focused here holds the keyboard up until the text box takes the focus,
and goes then; kits/md-edit.js removes it where no editor follows.
text-base, since iOS zooms the page to focus a field set under 16 px.

Deferred, because removing a focused field fires its blur in the middle
of the removal, and a second remove from inside it throws in Chromium
("no longer a child"), which took md-edit's open() down with it.
The editor loads on the tap, so a document nobody edits costs nothing.

Quiet but findable, and close together. At 60% in a 32 px box (40 px to a
finger) the pair read as louder than the heading beside them and set apart
from each other (owner's review, 2026-10-25), so they sit at 40% in a 28 px
box (32 px to a finger) and come up on hover or focus.

The controls live INSIDE the heading, appended after its text, rather than
in a row of their own. A row would push every heading down a line and give
the document a second rhythm; inside, they ride the heading's baseline.

`data-annotate-ui` is not decoration: kits/annotate.js walks the document's
text to anchor a quote and rejects any subtree carrying that attribute, so
stamping it here keeps the controls out of the text a note is taken on.
Without it a selection dragged across a heading would carry an invisible
glyph into the quote and the anchor would not re-find itself.
The pencil first, nearest the heading: it is the verb a reader comes for.

DISABLED MEANS DISABLED (owner, 2026-11-02: "let the disabled button be
disabled ... a simple tooltip is okay"): dimmed, aria-disabled rather
than `disabled` so the tip still shows on hover, and a click does nothing.

Turn it on first where it is off. noteSection returns false without
a mounted card, so the control would have flashed a warning and done
nothing; enable() is idempotent when the card is already up and aimed
at this document. The heading's OWN document, not window.document,
since a render inside a frame has to be annotated where it lives.

ENHANCE takes markup SOMEBODY ELSE produced and does the rest: contain it,
stamp its headings, declare its source. It exists because this kit is not
the only markdown renderer in the estate and should not have to be:
kits/guide-render.js renders a doc with the link re-aiming a guide body
needs, and the Files pane reads markdown through it. That reader wants the
containment and the section controls without giving up the re-aiming, and
a second renderer would be a second answer to what this estate's prose
looks like. So render() is enhance() with a parse in front of it, and a
host that already has a box calls the second half alone.

The `src` it is handed must be the SOURCE THAT PRODUCED THAT MARKUP.
Nothing can check that, and getting it wrong is the one way this misfires:
the headings would pair by order against a different document and every
section control would copy the wrong lines.

Pairing by ORDER, over the box's DIRECT children. Both lists are "the
headings at the document's own level", taken from the same parse, so
they line up one to one. A mismatched length means something rewrote
the HTML between the parse and here, and the honest answer is to attach
to as many as agree rather than to guess which side is right.

Declared even with no sections and even with the controls off: the
address is worth answering for on a document that happens to have no
headings, and a host that suppressed the controls has not said it wants
the source forgotten.

ATTACHED FIRST, then enhanced, and the order is load-bearing rather than
stylistic: enhance() ends by declaring, declaring announces, and a
listener's honest question is "does this document hold a render now".
Announcing about a box still detached answers no, so the Section chip
stayed hidden on a page that had just rendered a document. The other
caller of enhance() (the Files pane) was always in this order, which is
why only render() had the bug.

── The markdown hierarchy, which is not the DOM's ────────────────────────

A rendered document has two structures over it and they do not agree. The
DOM's is `article > div > ul > li`; markdown's is `## Scope` inside
`# Working conventions`, and the second is the one a reader of the prose
means. Nothing in a render carries it: sections nest by RANK, and `split`
already knows the ranks, so the chain is arithmetic over its output rather
than anything that has to be walked.

Ancestors of section i: the nearest preceding section of lower depth, then
ITS nearest preceding lower depth, up to the top. Innermost first, so it
reads like kits/peek.js's chainOf and the two can share a renderer.

The heading NODE for a section index, inside a declared render. `locate`
hands back the head for the node you asked about; this is how a caller
reaches the head of a DIFFERENT section, which is what walking the markdown
hierarchy needs. The attribute is this kit's, so the lookup is too.

The sections DIRECTLY under this one: the runs whose depth is exactly one
rank finer, before the next section of equal or higher rank closes it.

WHAT A SECTION IS MADE OF, counted in markdown's own units rather than the
DOM's. A reader asking about a passage wants to know it is four paragraphs
and a table, not that it is a div containing nine elements. Counted off the
source, so a fence's contents cannot be mistaken for the structures they
resemble: a ``` block full of hyphens is one code block, not a list.
its own heading is not a child

kits/md-edit-studio.js — the section editor as a studio: the source and a live
reading of the change on one full screen, with no mode to switch.

kits/md-edit.js owns everything around an editor (the save, the checks, the
drafts, the commit sheet) and mounts a variant through `api`. This is the
second of the two under comparison, ideas 2, 3 and 4 of
docs/prototypes/md-edit-ideas.json at once. Wikipedia's tabs
(kits/md-edit-tabs.js) make the writer choose between writing and seeing;
here the question "what does this do to the document" is answered while
typing, beside the cursor, rather than after a switch.

FULL SCREEN ON EVERY WIDTH. In place, the editor shares the width the
document gave the section, and a reading pane beside the source would get
half of a column. An overlay gives the two panes equal standing on a wide
screen, and on a phone it is the only way either gets room at all.

THE OVERLAY FOLLOWS THE VISUAL VIEWPORT, not `bottom: 0`. iOS does not
resize the layout viewport for the keyboard, so a fixed bottom edge sits
behind it. Sized to visualViewport, the overlay's last row sits directly
on top of the keyboard, and the same measurement says whether the keyboard
is up. With it up, the
reading pane folds to its bar, since half a phone is not enough for two
panes; the bar stays, so the reading is one tap away (a peek that ends when
the keyboard goes).

THE MARGIN IS MEASURED, because a textarea cannot mark its own lines and a
wrapped line has no fixed height. A hidden mirror with the textarea's font
and width measures each line of the source; a layer under the transparent
textarea paints the line numbers and the checks that point at a line
(idea 7). The numbers are FILE lines, so "Em dash on line 16" in a check is
line 16 in the margin.

THE READING RENDERS OFF TO THE SIDE and is swapped in, debounced, so a slow
tracked-changes pass never overwrites a newer one. Scrolling is kept
roughly level by proportion, driven by whichever pane the reader touched
last, so the two never fight.

NO FORMATTING BUTTONS: Markdown is typed, and a row of them cost a phone a
line of text above the keyboard (removed 2026-10-28). The shortcuts stay,
since they cost no room: ⌘B, ⌘I and ⌘K (Ctrl elsewhere).

ESCAPE NEVER DISCARDS A DRAFT ON ITS OWN: with nothing changed it closes,
otherwise it arms the discard button and puts focus on it. The network
checks (link targets, links to a renamed anchor) cost GitHub requests, so
they run only while the checks panel is open.

the reading follows the typing by this much
and the network checks by this much, panel open
px the visual viewport loses before it is a keyboard
Per viewer: which reading, and how much of a phone it takes.

── Header ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Not a btn-square, and named by its content rather than an aria-label:
confirmCancel writes "Discard changes" into it, and the name follows.
── Checks panel: a popover on a wide screen, a drawer on a phone ─────
── Layout: two columns, or stacked with a split ──────────────────────

The height a keyboard has not taken: the tallest seen at this width.
Read for the layout too, so a keyboard that shrinks the window (Android's
resizes-content) does not flip a tablet from two columns to stacked.
── The visual viewport: the overlay's size, and the keyboard ─────────
With the keyboard up the comparison switch gives its line to the text.

THE PAGE'S FAB floats over everything, in the bottom right corner, which
on a phone is where the folded bar's control and the checks drawer's rows
end. It is lifted over them through the property it reads for that
(kits/md-edit-tabs.js lifts it over its footer the same way), and given
back as it was found. With the keyboard up it stays behind the keyboard.

Changes and Clean share one typography because api.changes draws with
api.preview's renderer (lib/kits/md-edit.js, changesInto).

── Checks ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
What the network checks will look into, said while they run, in the
words the commit sheet uses for the same rows.

A row that points at lines steps through them on each tap; a row that
names link targets selects the first one where it is written.

The bar is the handle on a phone: drag it to set the split, tap it to
fold or open. Pointer capture throws on an id the browser no longer
holds, which is why it is guarded (kits/dock-split.js met it first).
Lock the page behind, and give back exactly what it had.

A class new to the page has no CSS until the current task ends, so the
margin is measured again once the browser build has compiled it.

kits/md-edit-tabs.js — Wikipedia's source editor for one markdown section:
Write, Preview and Changes over one text box, in place on a wide screen and
the whole screen on a phone.

kits/md-edit.js owns everything around the writing (the save, the checks,
the draft, the commit sheet, the receipt) and mounts an editor through `api`
(its "Variants" section). This is the `tabs` editor, the board's selection
(docs/prototypes/md-edit-ideas.json): idea 1, with the phone sheet (2), the
keyboard bar and margin checks (7), tracked changes (4) and the commit
sheet (6, the engine's) grafted on.

TABS RATHER THAN PANES, because a phone has room for one thing at a time and
Wikipedia's editors already know these three. They share one frame, so a
switch moves the body and nothing else, and the text box is the same element
throughout, hidden rather than rebuilt, so its undo history and selection
survive a look at the preview. A wide card keeps the box's height on the
other tabs for the same reason: the footer does not jump under the pointer.

ON A PHONE THE EDITOR TAKES THE SCREEN, because the keyboard takes half of it
and a card inside a scrolling document would leave the writer a strip. The
sheet follows window.visualViewport, not the layout viewport: iOS raises the
keyboard by shrinking and panning the VISUAL viewport and leaves `fixed`
elements where they were, so a bar pinned to the layout viewport's bottom
sits under the keyboard and the header can be panned off the top. Sized to
the visual viewport, the sheet keeps its header at the top and the text's
last row just above the keyboard. The document underneath is locked while
the sheet is open.

NO FORMATTING BUTTONS: Markdown is typed, and a row of them cost a phone a
line of text above the keyboard (removed 2026-10-28). The shortcuts stay,
since they cost no room: ⌘B, ⌘I and ⌘K (Ctrl elsewhere).

CHECKS IN THE MARGIN while typing, since an em dash is cheapest to fix on the
line where it was typed. The engine's rows name the lines they are about
(`at`); a text box cannot say where a line is drawn once it wraps, so a
hidden mirror carrying the box's computed font, padding and width lays the
same lines out to be measured. The mirror also sizes the box to its text,
which is what lets the gutter scroll with the lines rather than chase the
box's own scroll position.

THE CARD IS THE PANEL. The engine's panel is a padded card for its basic
floor; on a wide screen this editor is the card, so the padding comes off
while it is mounted and goes back on unmount, since a compare switch mounts
the other editor inside the same panel.

No loads of its own: preview, changes and formatting are the engine's, which
sanitize and load what they need.

⌘ on Apple keyboards, Ctrl elsewhere, and only that one: Ctrl+B on a Mac
is the caret's move back, which a bold shortcut must not take.
Everything that decides where a line wraps and how tall it is.

a wide card's box never opens shorter than this
margin checks settle this long after the last key
a check's text stays this long under its line

── The parts that persist across tabs and layouts ──────────────────────

The comparison switch would push the tab row past a phone's width, so
it gets a line of its own while the two editors are compared.

The root covers the layout viewport, keyboard area included, so a
keyboard sliding away never shows the page through the gap before the
sheet has grown back; the sheet inside it is what follows the keyboard.

iOS can scroll a locked page to bring a focused field above the
keyboard; the reader comes back to where they tapped the pencil.

A pinch zoom also shrinks the visual viewport; following it would
shrink the sheet with the zoom, so the sheet keeps the screen then.

Built once, and again only when the screen crosses the engine's narrow
line (a window resized, a tablet turned), with the same text box moved
across so nothing typed is lost.
── The box, its mirror, and the margin ──────────────────────────────────

Lay the text out in the mirror and size the box to it. Immediate on
every key: the box must never scroll inside itself, or the gutter would
drift from its lines.
A phone's box fills the sheet, so a tap anywhere below the text lands in it.
Select the line a check is about and say why under it.

The chip walks the warnings in turn; one about no line in particular
(the whole section removed) speaks from the top.

Bring [top, bottom] of the write pane into view: inside the sheet on a
phone, through the document's own scroller on a wide screen.

Where the caret is drawn, in the mirror: its line laid out again with a
probe at the caret's column.

The sheet scrolls rather than the box, so keeping the caret above the
keyboard is this editor's job, not the browser's.

"Draft restored" says where the text came from until the first key.
On a phone it stands under the title in place of the file's name,
since the tab row has no room to spare.

Tailwind's browser build styles a class new to the page after this task
ends, so the first measure can read unstyled geometry: measure again
once the classes have landed.

A phone opens with the caret after the heading, where an edit to the
title would start; a wide card opens at the top, as Wikipedia's does.

kits/md-edit.js — edit one section of a markdown file where it is rendered,
and save it back to the repository it came from.

kits/md-doc.js puts controls on every heading and already knows each
section's SOURCE: where it starts and ends in the file, and which file at
which address. This kit is the pencil among them, Wikipedia's [edit] link.
The pencil opens an editor over the section (a variant, see "Variants"), and
Publish opens a commit sheet with the checks, the message and where the
save lands.

  mdEdit.open({ sec, head, edit, rerender })
    sec       a section from mdDoc.split, of the body that was rendered
    head      its heading node inside a declared render (md-doc stamps it)
    edit      the host's opt-in: { full, onSaved? }. `full` is the whole file
              as read, frontmatter included, since the rendered body may be
              a suffix of it. `onSaved(text, info)` lets the host re-render
              from the saved text; return true when it did.
    rerender  md-doc's own re-render of the box, used when the host did not

THE SAVE NEVER WRITES OVER A NEWER VERSION, which the shared save would: on a
conflict gh-store refetches the sha and puts again. This reads the file fresh
first. If it is still what was rendered, the section is replaced where it
was. If it moved, the section's ORIGINAL text is looked for in the newer file
and replaced there when it occurs exactly once, which is how Wikipedia keeps
two edits to different sections from colliding. Anything else is a conflict:
the draft is kept and both are offered, and nothing is written. The PUT
itself goes out `strict`, so a race between the read and the write comes
back here to be rebased rather than being settled by overwriting.

WHAT RUNS AROUND THE SAVE. Before it: a generated file is refused (its
"do not edit" line, or a stage of the repo's commit hook in
docs/hook-legs.csv); the checks are the edit's own shape (heading kept,
level kept, a renamed anchor and who links to it, em dashes in added lines,
links that point nowhere). After it: the commit, its checks, and, where the
repo declares hook legs, which generated files the edit sets off and the
repair commit that refreshes them on the default branch.

Pure helpers ride on window.mdEdit for node/test/md-edit.test.mjs.
Literal paths, so the build walker sees each one (docs/loader.md).

A commit, full or abbreviated: links pin one as a short sha (showing.py
mints `@<12 hex>`), and a write cannot land on a commit. A branch named in
nothing but hex would read as one too, which costs it the pencil only.

github.com addresses have one owner (kits/repo-address.js), which boots on
every loader page.

Where the rendered body starts in the file. A host that strips frontmatter
before rendering (the viewer does) hands md-doc a SUFFIX of the file, and
every section offset is counted against that suffix. -1 when the body is
not the file's tail, which means this render cannot be written back.

Replace [a, b) with `next`. A section's raw ends at its last non-blank
character, so the blank lines that separate it from the next heading are
outside the range and survive; `next` is trimmed at the end to match. An
emptied section takes its trailing gap with it rather than leaving a hole.

The file moved since it was read: put the edit where the section's original
text now is, if that text is still there and nowhere else.
The first line as a heading: ATX (`## Title`) or setext (`Title` over ===).

Lines of `next` that are new, as indexes, with fenced code marked so a
check about prose can skip it. A multiset rather than a diff: a line that
moved is not new, and a check that fired on reordering would be noise.

The checks that need nothing but the two texts. `o.body` is the rendered
body after the edit, for same-document anchors; `o.line` is the file line
the section starts on, so a warning names a line the reader can find.
`at` holds the lines of `next` a row is about, 0-based, for an editor that
marks them in a margin.

Links that are new in `next`: their target as written, and whether it is
in this file (`#slug`) or another (`path[#slug]`). External addresses are
left out, since nothing here can say whether a website still answers.
── Pure: generated files and the hook legs ───────────────────────────────

The marker generated files carry near their top: "GENERATED from … do not
hand-edit", "_Generated from tasks/. Do not hand-edit._". One line, near the
top, so a document that merely discusses generated files does not trip it.
Letter boundaries rather than \b, since the board's line is italicized with
underscores and `_Generated` has no word boundary before the G.

A watch or a stage, against a path. `*.md` (no slash) is any file by that
name pattern anywhere; a glob with a slash is matched whole; anything else
is the file itself or a folder above it.

The legs an edit to `path` sets off: what they regenerate, and whether the
repair pass on the default branch runs them.
── Pure: what a reviewer gets, and what the checks say ───────────────────
Check runs on one commit, reduced to the one line a reader wants.

The section's rendered nodes: its heading and everything after it up to
the next heading of the same or higher rank, so a subsection travels with
its parent the way split() counts it.

A draft outlives a reload, keyed on the file and the section, and is only
restored onto the section text it was started from.
Per repo@ref: the repository's metadata and its hook legs, read once.

No header: the text box opens on the section's own heading line, which
says which section this is, and the sheet names where a save goes.

md-doc focuses a hidden field inside the pencil's tap so iOS raises the
keyboard for the editor that mounts a moment later. Where no editor
follows, the field goes, and the keyboard with it.

NO TOKEN ASKS FOR ONE rather than hiding the pencil, and carries on by
itself when gh-auth announces the token it saved.

── Variants ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
THE EDITOR IS A VARIANT; everything around it is this kit's. Two editors
are under comparison (docs/prototypes/md-edit-ideas.json): `tabs`,
Wikipedia's source editor (kits/md-edit-tabs.js), and `studio`, the source
and a live reading of the change side by side (kits/md-edit-studio.js).
Each mounts through `api` and hands back { text(), unmount() }. The save,
the checks, the drafts, the commit sheet and the receipt stay here, so the
two differ only in what writing is like. `basic`, a text box and two
buttons, is the floor when a variant fails to load.

Which one: `?editor=` on the page's address, else the last one switched to
(localStorage `mdEdit:editor`), else tabs. While `?editor=` is present the
variant carries a switch to the other, and the text goes across with it.
Literal paths, one per variant, so the build carries both.

Lines added and removed, as a multiset both ways: the count a status line
shows, which a moved line does not move and a blank line does not count in.

The section rendered as the document would render it, sanitized the way the
viewer is. Escaped text where the sanitizer is missing, never raw markup.

The change as tracked changes over the rendered prose: struck where words
left, tinted where they arrived. Drawn by preview() and marked with
kits/md-diff.js's word runs, rather than through md-diff's own renderer,
so Changes and Preview are one typography and switching between them does
not move the type (17 px against 14 px on a phone, found by the studio
variant). A mark over nothing but whitespace is the newline between two
blocks and draws as a sliver on a line of its own, so it goes.
no md-diff: the clean reading is the floor

Markdown formatting on a text box's selection. insertText keeps the
browser's own undo; setRangeText is the fallback where it is refused.
The switch between the two editors, shown only while comparing.
The floor: a text box, Cancel and Publish.

iOS ZOOMS THE PAGE INTO A FOCUSED FIELD set under 16 px, and leaves it
zoomed after the field lets go. Every field here is 16 px at the moment it
takes focus (measured headless), yet an iPhone still zoomed on a tap into
the text box (2026-10-28), so the size is not the whole of it. While an
editor is open, maximum-scale=1 on the viewport stops Safari's own zoom;
since iOS 10 Safari ignores it for a pinch, so the reader can still zoom
by hand. Only on iOS (the touch-callout test daisyUI uses for its own 16 px
fix), since Android honors maximum-scale for the pinch too. Counted, for
two editors open on one page; an editor dropped without its unmount leaves
the cap on, which costs nothing but that same automatic zoom. The double
tap's zoom is the other half, and touch-manipulation on each surface takes
it.

A phone, by its pointer or its width: where an editor should take the
whole screen and keep its controls above the keyboard.
The network checks, settled: resolves to the rows they end on.

Cancel, after a second tap when there is anything to lose. The draft
goes with a deliberate discard; it stays when the page simply closes.

── The commit sheet ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GitHub's commit dialog, since a save here is a commit: what changes, the
checks, the message and an optional description, and where it lands.

Checks that need the network: link targets, and who links to a renamed
anchor from elsewhere in the repository. Each job starts as a waiting row
and settles that same row, so a sheet can paint it as it lands.

The candidates come from the content index (kits/content-index.js):
Markdown files at the default branch holding both the file's name and
the slug. A page cannot read GitHub's code-search API, which this used
to ask. Each candidate is then read at this ref to confirm a link. A
repo the index leaves out, or has not built yet, cannot be searched.
Literal paths: the build reads gh.load calls to know what to bundle.

Read where the edit started, not on a branch made a moment ago: a new
branch is the same tree, and a read of it can be answered by a replica
that has not heard of it yet.

Refresh the browser's cached copy of this URL, so the next plain
read of the file (another view, a re-open) is not a minute stale.

Bottom LEFT on a wide screen and lifted on a phone, because the corner the
card would otherwise take is the FAB's.

The legs say what the repair MAY touch; the repair commit itself is
the record of what it did, so the row links it rather than repeating
the list as though it were a result.

A commit with no runs yet is usually a commit whose runs have not
started; "none" only after a minute of silence.

kits/md-history.js — a markdown document read WITH the history of its
passages: what each one used to say, the commit that changed it, and the
variants the Text collection holds of each earlier text.

Where the history comes from. Git, read through the page's GH client: the
commits that touched the file on its ref, newest first, and the file as it
stood at each one. Consecutive versions are aligned with md-diff's block
pairing, the same rule the Diff view uses, so a block's predecessor is the
old block that pairing matched it to one commit back. The walk reads one
version per commit and stops at the first of three ends: every block of the
open document has been traced to the commit that first wrote it, the file's
commit list runs out, or `limit` commits have been read (LIMIT, 20, by
default). At the third end the page says so and offers the next twenty.

Until 2026-09-22 this kit read a third collection file, revisions.jsonl:
eight rows from one bounded experiment, every field readable off git, and a
paragraph that became five recorded as five rows. Applied to those rows, the
pairing rule below reproduces the three one-to-one connections and matches
the split paragraph to one of its five successors, so the file was retired
and the walk replaced it. The pairing is an inference from shared words, not
a record: a block that became several is matched to the one sharing the most
words with it, and the rest appear as additions. A paragraph that moved
between files has no chain here, since git records that as a removal and an
addition.

The collection is consulted only once a chain exists, and quietly, so
History works on a public file for a reader with no token for home.

  mdHistory.gitSource(gh, repo)              -> { commits, read }, the two git reads
  mdHistory.walk(md, opts)                   -> { blocks, chains, commits, read, exhausted, truncated }
  mdHistory.plan(md, walked)                 -> { blocks, count }
  mdHistory.compose(md, plan)                -> the markdown with predecessors in place
  mdHistory.render(host, md, opts)           -> md-diff's handle, plus `plan` and `walked`
  mdHistory.index({ token })                 -> the collection, loaded

READ-ONLY, like every reader of the collection.
No ref: the collection is read where the page's selection puts home, else main.

── Git ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Two reads, both through GH.req with an absolute path so the client can
address any repository the page's token reaches, as the viewer's own byte
fetch does. A version is immutable, so the client's minute-long memo
serves a repeat read within a session for free.

── The walk ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
One chain per block of the open document, newest first: step 0 is the
block as it stands, and each later step carries the earlier text and the
commit that turned it into the step above. `origin` is the commit that
first wrote the oldest text, when the walk reached it.

Nothing older is listed. If the list is complete, this commit wrote
whatever is still untraced; if it was cut by the limit, that is not
known, and the chain stays open.

The collection's variants of each earlier text, by passage id. Step 0, the
text as it stands, carries its own marks in Preview and is left alone.
Which blocks have a predecessor, in document order, each with its chain.

The document with each planned block replaced by its predecessor: the
text one commit back. Offsets are md-diff's, measured on the
CRLF-normalised text, and the block's indentation and trailing newline
are kept, as md-variants does.

── The chain, under each container ───────────────────────────────────────
One line per step back: the commit that produced the step above it, then
the variants of that earlier text, each named by who and what.

The walk's own line under the document: how far back it read, and the
next twenty when the limit was what stopped it.

── Render ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
md-diff draws the document, old side being the predecessors; this attaches
a chain under each of its containers, matched by order, and the bound line
after the document. `opts.index` is the collection (or false to skip it);
absent, it is read quietly and its absence costs nothing but variants.

kits/md-surface.js — a markdown buffer shown RENDERED, and still aimed at by
character offset, so a text surface can edit its source while the reader looks
at the document.

Dictate.paint (kits/dictate.js) draws a plain-text buffer and answers the three
questions every gesture on pages/dictate.html asks: draw the buffer with its
caret and selection, turn a client point into an offset, and say whether a
point is over text at all. This answers the same three over RENDERED markdown,
so a surface that routes those three calls here keeps every gesture it has.

  MdSurface.paint(host, { text, interim, range, armed, handles, overlay, reach, caret })
                                   caret: the caret's color, red by default
                                   hideCaret: draw no caret, the range kept
                                   raw: draw each block as its source (below)
  MdSurface.offsetAt(host, x, y)   -> offset into text, or null off the text
  MdSurface.offsetOf(host, node, off, side) / domPoint(host, i, side)
                                   a Selection's end as an offset, and back
  MdSurface.rectAt(host, i)        -> the caret's client rect at offset i
  MdSurface.step(host, i, dir)     -> the offset one arrow key away, markup skipped
  MdSurface.hitsText(host, x, y)   -> is the point on rendered text
  MdSurface.tidy / backspace / enter  the rules for typing into the render
  MdSurface.changes(base, text)    what the marks draw: inserted runs, removals
  MdSurface.patch(path, base, text)  the edit as a unified diff git applies
  MdSurface.units(host) / unitsOf(base, text)
                                   every block on screen, unchanged or a card,
                                   with its span in the base and in the text

With `marks` and a `base`, paint also marks what changed since the base: a
green wash on inserted words, a red wedge where words were removed (it takes
taps, and carries data-md-del, the removal's index), and a bar in the margin
beside each changed block, green when the block is new and amber otherwise.

THE MAP IS Standoff.mapText (kits/standoff.js), which pages/audit-render.html
settled: rendered text is a subsequence of the source, so each text node is
found by a forward search and stamped with its offset. Markup is in no text
node, so no tap lands inside `**` or `](url)`. What cannot be found is left
unstamped and a tap there resolves to the nearest stamped text before it.

RAW draws every block as its markdown source rather than its render, in the
same blocks and the same cards. Since the drawn text then IS the source, the
map stamps every character, so the cards' readings, their marks, the notes'
blocks and every gesture carry over unchanged, and a reader sees the change
in the markdown itself (pages/dictate.html's Raw · Changes face). A blank
line after a block in the source is drawn as the gap a paragraph gets.

THE DOCUMENT IS RENDERED ONLY WHEN THE TEXT CHANGES. Everything that moves
with a tap or a scroll (the caret, the selection, the pins, the words being
spoken) is drawn in the overlay from client rects, so a scroll repaints a few
absolutely positioned boxes and parses nothing. The hypothesis is a chip at
the caret rather than words in the flow: splicing it into the rendered tree
would re-render on every partial result.

WHAT A CHANGE COSTS, measured 2026-09-24 in headless Chromium on a desktop
CPU: 12ms on docs/CONVERSATION.md (6k characters), about 80ms on docs/loader.md
(37k) and 210ms on docs/SNAGS.md (160k), mostly layout of the whole document.
A phone is slower by a factor not measured. The next step, if it is needed,
is re-rendering only the blocks that changed; content-visibility:auto was
tried and measured the caret a line off (see pages/dictate.html ensureMd).

Reads window.mdDoc (the render), window.Standoff (the map), window.Dictate
(the pins), window.marked and window.esc (raw blocks), all loaded by the caller.

A fence's language tag is text the source does not hold in that place.
Mapped, its search would run ahead to a later match and every node after
it would go unstamped, so it is set aside for the mapping and put back.

A LIST ITEM IS A BLOCK OF ITS OWN here (mdDiff.align with `items`), so
one bullet edited is one card and not its whole list. Rendered alone, an
item loses what its list gave it: a nested one indented four spaces reads
as a code block, and any nested one draws at the outer level. So an item
is drawn dedented, and indented by its depth, which is counted from the
items above it in the whole text. `whole` and `at` are that text and
where the item starts in it; without them it draws at the outer level.

And spaced as its list spaced it. Each item is its own <ul>, and the
house's list margin (.5rem, kits/guide-render.js) put 8px between two
bullets that sit 2px apart drawn whole. So the margin goes on the side
where the next or previous line is another item of the same list, and
the items' own 2px is the gap. `!` because guide-body's rules are not in
a layer and would win over a utility.

REFERENCE LINKS RESOLVE IN EVERY BLOCK. `[text][ref]` takes its URL from
a `[ref]: url` line elsewhere in the document, and a block drawn alone
never sees that line, so the link drew as literal brackets. Each block is
drawn with the document's definitions after it; marked draws a definition
as nothing, so the map, which stamps rendered text, is untouched. Held
for one text at a time, since every block of a paint shares it.

Set by paint for the length of one paint, so every block it draws is drawn
the same way. One host per page draws through here.

The Source face's type (pages/dictate.html), so Raw · changes and Raw ·
after differ only by the cards.

What a block reads as, for comparing old and new: its rendered words, or
under RAW the source itself.

── TRACKED: the edit as cards in the document ───────────────────────────
With a base, each paragraph that differs from it is drawn as a CARD in the
flow; unchanged blocks render as ordinary text. A card is one paragraph
unless a join or a split ties paragraphs together, and then it holds every
paragraph taking part: the original ones in `old`, the new ones in `inline`
and `new` (mdDiff's groupsOf). Two neighbouring paragraphs edited apart are two
cards; a stretch of paragraphs that are all new, or all removed, is one.

A card has up to three readings, named on its stops pill in order, and
every one but `old` takes the caret:

  old      the base's text for the whole run, read-only.
  inline   the default: the new text with the change laid over it, removed
           words struck in place (a <del>, never mapped, so the caret
           skips it), added words washed green, and a block taken out
           struck whole. Typing here is typing in the buffer.
  new      the new text, clean. Typing here is typing in the buffer too.

A run with both sides has all three; one that only removes has old and
