FIELD 3 IS THE claude.ai SESSION ID, and it is the field that lets the
back tap reach the conversation rather than a page about it. The whole
join already existed and stopped one hop short: the record carries
`agent_session`, the cache row carries it as `agent`, and session.html
renders an "Open this session in Claude Code" button from it, so the
menu was the only surface that had to spend a page load and two taps on
an address the index could have handed over. Measured 2026-09-19 on the
live store: 384 of 400 rows carry it, and all 13 menu branches missing it
are from 2026-08 and an older schema, so the op offers the row only where
the field is there rather than promising an address it may not have.

It costs about 34 bytes a branch, near 14 KB on a 57 KB payload. The bare
id is stored whole rather than with its constant `session_` prefix
stripped: three of those kilobytes are not worth a stored value that is
no longer the identifier it claims to be.

The branch moves to field 4 and only `recent` needs it: in `branches` the
key already is one. A row's label leads with the branch slug, which is
the ask already reduced to a topic and short enough to read on a phone,
so without that field the recent rows fall back to clipped prose.

A slash is what the op's branchOf requires before it will call a
string a branch, so a name without one could never be looked up here
and carrying it is dead weight. `branches` already excludes `main`.
Four fields here, five in `recent`: the key already names the branch,
so repeating it costs about a third of the file across 381 of them
for nothing a reader gains.

Same gate as the cache's, and for the same reason: the crawl stamps
`generatedAt` on every pass whether or not anything moved, so comparing
whole documents would commit on every crawl.

Only the records under YYYY/MM count. sample-record.json sits at the store
root precisely so it is not one, and tools/ holds the recorder.

lib/kits/report-layout.js: a report layout, meaning the declared shape of a
printed table, kept apart from the rows it prints.

The subject is a budget compare. One measure, a band of budget versions
across the top with a period inside each, a row hierarchy down the side, a
subtotal after each block, an opening line above them all, and a grand total
that is the opening plus the subtotals. That shape is the levels equation of
the budget-drs workspace (app/CARRY-FORWARD.md) widened from one budget to
several, which is why it is worth naming rather than drawing once.

WHY A SECOND OBJECT RATHER THAN A WIDER FLATTENER. The home estate's
app/report/rows.js already turns a {label, value, children} tree into
indented rows, and it refuses formatting on purpose: "a divisor and a
currency are the reader's business and a flattener has no opinion about
either." Everything this file adds is the opinion that flattener declines to
hold: which key bands the columns, where a subtotal sits, what a missing cell
looks like, which rows are emphasized. Folding those into the flattener would
put display back inside the data step. So a layout is declared beside the
rows, as JSON, and the pairing of the two is what a stored template is.

THE DISTINCTION THE FORMAT RESTS ON: a blank cell and a zero are different
claims. Blank means no row was filed. Zero means a row was filed at zero.
fold() therefore leaves a column absent rather than seeding it, and a
subtotal over a group with no rows in that column stays blank. In the source
table LEOFF Restatement is 0 in both chairs' 2026 and blank in the
Governor's, so collapsing the two would lose which budgets considered the
item at all.

THE ARITHMETIC IS BY CONSTRUCTION, so this file carries no check of its own.
Subtotals and the grand total are computed from the item rows, and asserting
that a computed sum equals itself proves nothing. What is worth holding is
the TRANSCRIPTION, and node/test/report-layout.test.mjs holds it: it builds
the model from the committed rows and asserts every subtotal and total
printed in the source table, typed in separately from the figures the rows
carry. A mistyped item is what that test catches.

A separator no label carries, so a composite key cannot be forged by two
labels that happen to abut.

Escaping is window.esc from vanilla-bundle.js, first in the boot chain,
so this file holds no second answer to the same question.

Declared order wins; otherwise first appearance, which keeps an authored
rows file in charge of its own reading order.

build(spec, rows) -> model
  columns: [{ key, band, within, gapBefore }]
  rows:    [{ kind, labels, values }]   kind: opening | item | subtotal | total
The model is plain data and is the stage the renderer draws from, so the
table can be checked, diffed or exported without going near markup.

One leaf per distinct level tuple, in first appearance order, then the
leaves gathered under the subtotal level in the order that level first
appeared. An authored rows file that lists an item's versions together
therefore prints in the order it was written.
Consecutive columns sharing a band, for the header's colspans.

The second way in: a PARTITION TREE rather than long rows.

transform-workbench.js's Pivot view already nests and accumulates, and its
pvDraw() says where the seam is: "this computes the partition, the host
decides whether to draw it as an indented table, a treemap or a till
receipt." A report is one more of those, so this adapts the tree it already
publishes instead of asking the workbench to re-fold its rows.

Two of that view's rules carry straight through and are the reason the fit
is close rather than merely possible. A node records only the column keys
it saw, so a missing cell is blank and never a zero, which is this format's
own distinction arrived at independently. And `res.partition` is true only
for sum and count: under avg, min or max a parent is NOT the sum of its
children, so subtotal rows are withheld rather than printed as numbers that
merely sit above other numbers.

ORDER IS THE READER'S, NOT THE TREE'S. pvTree sorts each node's children by
value descending, because reading by magnitude is what the Pivot view is
for. A printed report usually wants the other one: the order the analyst
wrote the rows in, where a residual block like "Other" sits last by
convention rather than wherever its size puts it. Neither reading is a
property of the partition, so the tree carries `seq`, each node's position
among its siblings before that sort, and `order: 'source'` reads it back.
The Pivot view is untouched by this: `seq` never reaches pvFlat, which
builds its row objects field by field.

With no column axis the tree carries no cells, so the node's own value is
the single column.

A node's children in the reading this report wants. 'source' needs seq,
so a tree built before pvTree carried it falls back to the tree's own
order rather than to an undefined sort.

One column axis means one header row. The band row is drawn only where a
band exists, so a pivot on a single column dimension does not get an
empty dark stripe over it.

Repeat suppression down the label columns, which is what makes the row
hierarchy read as a spreadsheet rather than as an indented tree.

The way back to a workbook. Raw numbers, not the formatted strings, so the
paste lands as numbers rather than as text Excel has to be argued with.

kits/review-target.js — parse and mint the address grammar for the review
page (pages/review.html). Pure string logic, no DOM, no fetch: the page (and
anything else that wants to speak the grammar) calls these; unit tests cover
them via node/test/bootstrap.mjs loadKit.

The grammar extends the family the repo already speaks — toss-render's
#gh=owner/repo[@ref]:path address and the app's #stage= refs — with a
comparison base:

  #gh=owner/repo                       whole repo, ref/base resolved later
  #gh=owner/repo@branch                changeset: base...branch
  #gh=owner/repo@branch:path/to/file   one file at branch, diffed vs base
  ...&base=main                        explicit base ref (else default branch)

The ':' before the path is unambiguous because git forbids ':' in ref
names. Pasted GitHub URLs are accepted too and normalize into the same
shape: /compare/a...b, /blob/<ref>/<path>, /tree/<ref>, /pull/<n> (returned
as kind:'pull' for the caller to resolve via the API), and a bare repo URL.
A blob URL with a slashed branch name is ambiguous (the URL does not mark
where the ref ends and the path begins); parse takes the first segment as
the ref, so prefer the #gh= form for slashed branches.

parse(input) -> null | { kind:'ref', repo, ref?, path?, base? }
             |        { kind:'pull', repo, number }
  input may be a location.hash ('#gh=...&base=...'), a bare fragment body,
  a 'gh=...' pair list, a github.com URL, or a bare 'owner/repo[@ref][:path]'.

mint({ repo, ref?, path?, base? }) -> 'gh=owner/repo[@ref][:path][&base=...]'
  (fragment body only; the caller prefixes '#' and the page URL). Path and
  refs are encoded per segment with '/' left readable, same policy as
  the app's #stage= links.

owner/repo[@ref][:path], read by lib/kits/repo-address.js, which owns the
grammar: a file address, or the same with no path.
Ambiguous when the branch name contains '/'; first segment wins.

Full URL: github.com normalizes into the grammar; a review-page URL
recurses on its own fragment/query.

Pair-list form: gh=<spec>&base=<ref>&... (order-independent). Split by
hand rather than URLSearchParams: that class would decode a second time
(parseSpec/dec already decode) and turns '+' into a space, corrupting
paths that contain either.

kits/root-has-prune.js — daisyUI's :root:has() rules, removed from the
loaded stylesheet so that a change anywhere in the page stops costing a
restyle of all of it.

MEASURED 2026-10-23, on the app with a nine-sheet workbook in the transform
workbench: one batch-chip click forced 15 to 17 style recalculations (the
grid measuring its height while it redraws), and they cost 264 to 349 ms
together. With daisyUI's stylesheet switched off the same click spent 40 to
60 ms recalculating; with only its :root:has() selectors taken out, about
96 ms. A selector anchored on :root that asks about the page's descendants
makes the browser re-check the root, and so restyle the whole tree, after
any change below it, which is every change. The page is large (8,500 nodes
with the reader open), so every recalculation is expensive.

WHAT THE RULES DO, and why losing them changes nothing here. daisyUI 5.7
carries 55 of them, in two families:
  - theme-controller: `:root:has(input.theme-controller[value=x]:checked)`
    beside `[data-theme=x]` on every theme, so a checked radio input can
    switch the theme. This estate sets `data-theme` and has no such input,
    and the `[data-theme=x]` half of each selector is kept.
  - page scroll lock: `:root:has(.drawer-toggle:checked)` and nested
    `:root:has(&)` under the modal and drawer states, which hold the page
    still behind an open modal. The app's views are fixed to the viewport
    and scroll inside their own panes, so there is no page scroll to lock.
A page that does use either would lose that behavior, which is why this
runs only on a stylesheet that opts in (below), never on every sheet.

HOW: a CSSOM edit of the stylesheet already loaded, not a second copy and
not a pinned fork. A selector list loses only its :root:has() alternatives
(`:root,:root:has(…),[data-theme=light]` keeps `:root,[data-theme=light]`),
and a rule left with none is deleted. Grouping rules (@layer, @media,
@supports) and nested rules are walked. Reading another origin's rules needs
the link to be CORS-mode, and jsDelivr answers `access-control-allow-origin:
*`, so the opt-in is two attributes on the link:

  <link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/…daisyui@5…" rel="stylesheet"
        crossorigin="anonymous" data-prune-root-has>

A sheet that cannot be read, or a rule the browser refuses to edit, is left
as it was: the cost of a miss is the old speed, never a broken page.

  RootHasPrune.run(doc?)        prune every opted-in link, now or on load;
                                resolves to { sheets, rewritten, removed }
  RootHasPrune.prune(sheet)     one stylesheet; { rewritten, removed }
  RootHasPrune.strip(selector)  the selector without its :root:has()
                                alternatives, or '' when none is left
  RootHasPrune.split(selector)  a selector list split at its top-level commas

Top-level commas only: a comma inside :is(), :has() or an attribute value
belongs to the alternative it sits in.

kits/route-activity.js — rank the app's own routes by when the code behind
each last moved, and join each to the work in flight against it.

The estate has three readings of its motion already (branches, sessions,
guides) and all three are keyed to GIT: a branch, the session that ran it,
the body that accounts for it. None of them says WHICH PART OF THE UI moved,
and the UI is what most of the work is. This is the fourth reading, keyed to
the ADDRESS: for each destination the app can be sent to, when did its code
last change, and is anything open against it now.

THE JOIN IS FILES, AND FILES ARE COARSER THAN ROUTES. This is the honest
limit and the pane states it rather than hiding it. Nine routes render out of
lib/alpineComponents/estate.js, so a commit there lights all nine; the shell
(app/index.html) holds the router and every pane's outer
markup, so a commit there lights everything and is therefore excluded from
attribution and reported on its own. What survives that is still a real
reading, and the exclusions are themselves the finding: a route with no file
of its own has no code of its own, which is a fact about the app the app
could not previously state.

Pure. No fetch, no DOM, no Alpine: the caller hands in the manifest, a
path -> last-commit map, and whatever branches it knows about, and gets rows
back. Same split as lib/kits/guide-index.js and lib/kits/repo-activity-cache.js
(pure fold here, crawl in the shell), which is what makes it testable.

  routeActivity.routesByFile(manifest)          -> Map path -> [route keys]
  routeActivity.rank(manifest, { touches, branches, now }) -> ranked rows
  routeActivity.shellRow(manifest, { touches })  -> the excluded shell's own row

Attaches to window.routeActivity, loaded via gh.load('kits/route-activity.js').

A file carrying more than this many routes says nothing about any one of
them when it changes. It is still listed on every row it belongs to, and
still dates the row when it is the only file there is; what it loses is
the right to be the row's REASON, so a row backed only by wide files reads
"shared" rather than claiming a date it did not earn.

The deployed app: the one page every route is an address INTO, so a route
link is this plus a query and never a path of its own.
The renderer a route link at a ref goes through (viewUrl below).

What the app loads at a branch. Named here because the staleness rule
below is about this file and not about lib/ in general.
the app's own pre-build since 2026-09-02; dist/web-tools.js serves the other pages

Which routes each declared file carries. Built from the manifest alone, so
"shared" is derived and never authored: a file becomes shared by being
named twice, which is the only way it could have become shared in fact.

Newest of a set of touches. A touch is whatever the caller read for a path
({ date, sha, subject, url, author }); only `date` is required, and a path
with no touch simply does not vote.

The row's date comes from its narrow files when it has any, and falls
back to its wide ones when it does not, flagged so the reading is never
silently borrowed from a file nine routes share.

The branch join takes the same rule as the date, and for the same reason.
A PR that edits estate.js touches nine routes' declared files, so a naive
join reports work open on all nine; the first render of this pane said
"11 with work open" off three PRs. A branch is OPEN ON a route when it
touches a narrow file, and merely NEAR it when its only hit is a file
several routes share. Both are shown; only the first is counted.

A route nothing is open against and nothing has touched still belongs
in the list: the inventory is the point, and an untouched route is the
one reading a recency list alone would never surface.

Three tiers, then date within each. The tiers are the whole point of the
ordering: a flat sort by date puts a route at the top because a file nine
routes share happened to move, which is the reading this pane exists to
avoid making. So a row dated by its OWN narrow file outranks every
borrowed one however fresh, a borrowed date outranks no date at all, and
an undated row falls to the bottom rather than to the top on an empty
string. Work open breaks a tie inside a tier, and manifest order breaks
what is left, so the order is total and stable.

The shell's own row: excluded from attribution above precisely because it
touches everything, and reported here so the exclusion is visible rather
than felt as a gap.

Every path the caller has to read a last-commit for, deduped, shell
included. The shell's own reading needs it and no route's does.

Fold ranked rows into their nav STOPS, which is the level the router lost.
Six sub-tabs are addressed as their own ?view= key because each used to be
a nav stop and kept its key when its pane moved under another; listing
those at the same rank as live destinations is what made a flat list read
oddly. `stop` puts the level back.

ORDER IS INHERITED, NOT RECOMPUTED. `rank` has already sorted by tier then
date, so grouping by first appearance gives exactly "stops by their
freshest member, rows by recency inside" with no second sort to disagree
with the first. An earlier draft grouped by a fixed manifest order and cost
the pane its headline, an hour-old route sitting below a six-day-old one;
taking the order from the ranking is what makes grouping safe here.

A stop owning ONE route is not a grouping and says so (`solo`), so the pane
can render it as a plain row rather than a section of one.

The stop's own reading is its freshest row's, which is its first: the
rows arrived in rank order and grouping preserved it.

The join run backwards: given a changed-file list, which routes does it
touch. `rank` answers "what is open against this route" for a pane that
starts from routes; this answers "what is this branch working on" for a
pane that starts from branches. Same rule in both directions, deliberately:
a hit on a narrow file is ON the route, a hit only on a file three or
more routes share is NEAR it, and the shell is never a hit at all. Two
panes disagreeing about the same pair of facts would be worse than either
pane not showing it.

WHICH SUB-TAB, when the caller says which files each of a route's tabs
reads (`tabFiles`: tab key -> exact paths). The app builds Map's from the
links in docs/map-tabs.csv (tabFilesFrom, below). The answer is the tab
most of the hits belong to, and only when one tab leads: a branch that adds
a CSV also restamps data/csv-census.csv, the Data tab's file, so "every hit
in one tab" would almost never answer. A tie, or no hit in any tab (the
component itself is every tab), names none, and the chip stays the route.
Carried from web-tools #850, where the same idea was five substring tests
hard-coded into this kit.

tabFiles from map-tabs.csv rows: each lede's `refs` (phrase=path pairs),
exact files only. A folder ref claims nothing, since `docs/` would put half
the repository on the Docs tab.

THE NEAR SET AS ONE SLOT, and the pixels are the argument. A file is wide
precisely by being declared many times, so a branch touching one brushes
every route that declares it: seven, for the app's own estate.js. Rendered
as a chip each, that is two lines of ghosted labels above the one line that
answers the question, on a phone, every time. The fact is worth keeping,
since it says the branch is not as narrow as the solid chips suggest, and
it is worth exactly one slot.

The note is here rather than in either view because both views draw it and
a second copy is a second thing to drift: branch-brief built this string
inline and the estate's rows rendered the near set as links instead, which
is the disagreement `routesTouched` exists to prevent. It is also the rule
against offering the link: every route in this set is one the rule says the
branch cannot be claimed to change, so a chip that opened one would hand a
reader the address the set exists to withhold.

── The manifest, and the address it yields ─────────────────────────────

Assembling the manifest was written out three times: in estate.js, in
branch-brief.js, and in the test that holds this file honest. Three copies
of a shape is three ways for a reader of one of them to be wrong about the
other two, and the shell row is exactly the part that reads as a sibling
key until you notice it is not. So the fold owns its own input shape.

Rows arrive PARSED, with `files` and `tabs` already split, because the two
callers reach for different CSV readers (window.Csv in the browser,
registries-load.mjs in the suite) and neither belongs in a pure fold. What
this owns is which row is the shell, which vocabulary rows are the groups,
and the fact that the shell is not a route.

`app` and `shell` are the same path under two names, and both are kept
because they answer different questions: the file to read, and the
path attribution has to exclude.

Whether a route can be OPENED from a row rather than merely named on one.
Only a bare `?view=<key>` qualifies: an address carrying a placeholder (a
repo, a file path, a promoted page) cannot be opened from a row that does
not know which one, and a link that lands nowhere is worse than no link.

The address that opens a route AT A REF, which is the whole point of the
reverse join being drawn at all. A chip that says "this branch is working
on Stage" and then opens Stage on main has dropped the branch at the one
moment it mattered.

At a ref it is a toss of the app: toss-render hands the framed app its
ref, so the app boots the branch's bundle. The toss supersedes `?use=` as
the preview link (docs/showing-consolidation.md); `?use=` links already
handed over keep working. The same address python/showing.py writes for
the lib-only case, deliberately, so the app and the script cannot hand a
reader two different links for one question.

The caveat that rides every link at a branch and is invisible without it.
Because the app loads the BUNDLE and not lib/, a branch that changed a
component without running `npm run build:lib` serves last week's code under
a link that resolves, renders, and looks right. The commit hook rebuilds,
so this fires on an unpushed rebuild or a --no-verify commit; either way the
reader wants to know before trusting what they see.

kits/route-join.js — the app-route join: the hub's own route manifest, and
for each open pull request against the hub, the files it touches.

TWO PANES READ THIS AND THEY ARE IN TWO COMPONENTS. Map's Views tab ranks
every destination the app can be sent to by when its code last moved; the
estate's Branches rows carry the reciprocal, a chip saying which destination
a branch is working on. Both need the same manifest, the same pull list and
the same file list per pull, so a copy in each would fetch all of it twice to
answer one question two ways.

It lived in lib/alpineComponents/estate.js until 2026-09-08, when the Views
pane left for the Map view and the two readings stopped sharing a component.
The obvious next home was the shell, which is where every other cross-pane
cache sits; that was wrong for a reason worth writing down. app/index.html is
a page, not a lib file, so node/test/bootstrap.mjs cannot load it: moving
this there would have traded fourteen assertions for one saved fetch, and the
suite said so on the first run.

FETCHES, unlike its sibling. lib/kits/route-activity.js is the pure fold over
what this returns and takes no client at all; the split is the same one
repo-activity-cache.js draws, and it is why the ranking is testable without a
network and the reading is testable without a browser. A kit that takes a
`gh` and calls it is ordinary here (branch-status, chat-archive, errands
all do); what a kit must not do is hold the state, which stays with whoever
asked.

  RouteJoin.manifest(gh)             -> the folded manifest (needs window.Csv)
  RouteJoin.branchFiles(gh, repo)    -> [{ repo, name, pr, title, ..., files }]
  RouteJoin.dates(gh, paths, ref)    -> { path: touch }
  RouteJoin.pool(items, worker[, n]) -> bounded-concurrency map

Attaches to window.RouteJoin, loaded via gh.load('kits/route-join.js').

Run `items` through a small pool. Bounded concurrency matters here for the
same reason it does in the branch scan: two dozen commit reads fired at
once spend the rate limit in one burst and gain nothing, since the wall
clock is set by the slowest, not the sum. A thrown worker yields null
rather than failing the batch, so one dead path costs its own row only.

Assembled from two CSVs since 2026-08-16. The shell is a row keyed `shell`
rather than a sibling key, and the group glosses live in the shared
value-gloss table, which is where every closed domain's do. Parsed here,
folded in route-activity: which row is the shell and which vocabulary rows
are the groups is the fold's own shape, and it was written out three times
before it was.

The failure names the address it could not read. A bare "404: Not Found"
sent the first diagnosis of this to auth, which the rate-limit figure in
the same message had already ruled out.

Every open pull request against the hub, with the files it touches. A
failed pull list is an empty join rather than a thrown one: the manifest is
the half that must be there, and a route with no branch against it is the
normal case anyway.

pulls() returns no html_url (it keeps the projection narrow), and the
address is fully determined by the repo and the number, so it is
built rather than fetched.

One last-commit read per path. `per_page=1` on the commits endpoint
filtered by path is the whole question: when did this file last move, and
in what commit. A path with no commits simply does not appear, which is
what leaves its route undated rather than dated wrong.

── row-menu: a tap on a row, and what you can do with it ───────────────────

  rowMenu.attach(table, opts)   -> detach()      Tabulator table + a gesture
  rowMenu.grid(el, config, opts) -> Tabulator    a new grid with a header menu
                                                 on every column and the row menu
  rowMenu.headerDefaults(opts)  -> columnDefaults  the header menu alone
  rowMenu.open({ x, y, items, square }) -> close()   the menu alone, for any host
  rowMenu.tsv(columns, rows)    -> string        the copy format, exported

THE GESTURE THE OTHER TWO KITS DECLINED TO IMPOSE. record-deck's header says
its way in "belongs to the host", and swipe-deck's `entry` says "a surface is
free to add a gesture of its own on top (a row tap)". Both left the row tap
to whoever owned the rows, and every host that wanted it wrote a button
instead, because a button is easy and a menu is not. So the row tap never
happened anywhere, and one host's button became the whole affordance.

WHAT IT COSTS, stated where a host will read it before adopting: swipe-deck's
same note warns that "a gesture nobody is told about is a feature only its
author can find". This IS that gesture. A host that drops its visible entry
for this alone is trading a discoverable affordance for a discovered one, and
should mean it. Two things make the trade defensible rather than merely
cheaper: tapping a row is what a reader already tries on a phone, and the
menu is not a deck opener wearing a disguise, since the copies are useful on
a table that has no deck at all.

WHY A MENU AND NOT A ROW ACTION. A row has more than one thing to say. "Read
from here" is the deck, "copy this row" is the row as data, and a host can
append its own. One tap that guesses between them is wrong half the time.

THE ROW MENU IS ABOUT THE ROW. It used to offer "Copy N rows" too, and
that item answered a question about the table from a menu opened on one
row (Marcus, 2026-10-24): the reader cannot tell from the row what a copy
of seven rows takes. Copying the table is the column menu's Table section
(copyTable below), where a host's own table menu can reach it too.

It follows the finger: the menu opens where the row was tapped rather than in
a corner, clamped into the viewport, because on a phone the distance between
what you touched and what answers is the whole of whether it feels connected.

NO TABULATOR IMPORT. `attach` assumes three calls of a table: `on`,
`getColumns` and `getRows`; `open` reads nothing and takes items, so a host
with a different grid can raise the same menu. `grid` and the header menu
are Tabulator's alone, and call the global the host already loaded.

io.js FETCHED AT LOAD TIME, never inside the click. A clipboard write has to
run in the user gesture that asked for it, and an await before the write
spends the activation Safari counts. Same idiom, and the same reason, as
md-doc.js and the other three delegates the clipboard gate names.

A CELL AS ONE FIELD OF ONE LINE. Tabs and newlines inside a value would
otherwise become column and row breaks in the paste, so a single cell
holding a paragraph turns into rows of garbage in the sheet it lands in.
Collapsed rather than quoted, because TSV has no quoting anyone agrees on.

TSV, HEADERS INCLUDED, for one row and for the whole list alike. It is the
one format that survives a paste into a spreadsheet, a chat and an editor
without a decision at either end. A single row keeps its header line for
the same reason: pasted alone, a row of bare values says nothing about
which column each one came from.

The visible, field-bearing columns, in the order the grid shows them. Same
filter record-deck's fromGrid applies, so the copy and the card agree about
what the row consists of.

── the menu ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

One at a time, held in a module-level handle rather than a stack: a second
menu opening while the first is up is a mis-tap, not a drill-down, and two
floating panels at once on a phone is the failure this is meant to avoid.

Placed after it is in the document, because its size is not known until it
has been laid out and the clamp needs the size. Hidden for that one frame
so the reader never sees it at the origin first.

items: [{ label, icon, run, keep } | { heading }]. `run` may return a string, which
replaces the label for a beat before the menu closes: that is how a copy
reports, since a clipboard write has no other visible effect and a toast
would be a second floating thing to dismiss. `keep` holds the menu open.
`square`: Excel's own look, for a host that is drawing a sheet (the
formula-bar copy menu): square corners, a hairline frame, tighter rows.
The phone hit target stays, since a mis-tap there costs an action.
`dense`: rows a third shorter, for a long list of short choices (a
filter's values); the phone target drops to 32px, about a fingertip.

A HEADING names the section that follows: the column a header menu was
opened on, then the whole table. A rule above every heading but the
first is what separates the two sections.

max-sm:min-h-11 is the phone hit target, the same 44px swipe-deck's
entry buys with max-sm:h-11: a menu is the one place a mis-tap costs
an action rather than nothing.

This menu's own close: one opened in the 700ms since, by a
second right-click, is not the one that reported.

Dismissal, four ways, all outside the menu: a tap elsewhere, Escape, any
scroll (the menu is fixed and the row under it is not, so a scrolled menu
is pointing at the wrong row), and a resize.

THE ROW IS TINTED while its menu is up, so the reader can see what
"this row" is. The cells carry the tint, not the row: Tabulator's
stylesheet paints the row outside Tailwind's layers, so a utility on
the row loses, while the cells are transparent (land.js's finding).

── attaching to a Tabulator table ────────────────────────────────────────

opts:
  deck      options handed to recordDeck.fromGrid ({ title, describe, … }),
            or false to leave the item out. The item is omitted anyway when
            record-deck is not loaded, so a host that never wants the deck
            can simply not load the kit.
  copy      false to leave both copy items out. Default on.
  items     [{ label, icon, run(ctx) }] appended, ctx = { row, data, table }
  skip      (event) => boolean, extra suppression on top of the link rule
  noun      what one row is, for the deck item's wording. Default 'record'.
  on        'tap' (the default) opens on a click or tap of the row;
            'context' opens on a right-click or a long press instead, for
            a grid where a tap already means something or nothing should
            interrupt it. Both answer with the same menu.

THE LINK RULE. A row whose cell holds a link, a button or a field is a row
where the tap already meant something, so the menu stays out of the way.
Checked on the tap's own target rather than declared per column, since the
host that renders a link into a cell is rarely the host wiring this up.

WHERE A MENU OPENS: at the pointer for a mouse, and below the element for
a long press. The finger is still down when a hold opens the menu, and a
menu drawn under it would take the release as a tap on its first item.
A touch is a TouchEvent, or a contextmenu that Android raised from one.

AND THE RELEASE IS SWALLOWED. Lifting the finger after a long press can
still send a click, which on a header would sort the column the menu was
opened on. One click, in the moment after the finger lifts, never more;
the outer timer only cleans up after a touch that never ended.

── the long press, owned here ────────────────────────────────────────────

NOT TABULATOR'S. Its rowTapHold and headerTapHold wait a fixed second, and
on an iPhone the press never got there (2026-10-24, Marcus's phone): by
about half a second Safari has begun selecting the cell's text, and the
gesture is Safari's. A Chromium touch emulation opened both menus, which
is why the browser this kit was checked in did not show it. So the hold
is timed here, shorter than Safari's, and the cells and header titles do
not select or call out on a touch screen. Header filter inputs keep both,
since an input that cannot select is an input that cannot be typed in.

A move past a few pixels is a scroll, not a hold, and cancels it.
A click that ends a drag across text is a selection, not a request.

On a touch screen the hold below is the context gesture; a contextmenu
Android raises from the same press is kept from opening a second menu
(and its own), not answered.

── a column header, and what you can do with it ──────────────────────────

Opened by a right-click on the header, or a long press on a phone, which
Tabulator routes to the same option (headerContextMenu). The function
opens this menu and returns no items, so Tabulator's own popup never draws
and the two menus a grid can raise look alike.

NO HEADER BUTTON. Tabulator's headerMenu draws a glyph in every column
header, and on a narrow grid that glyph is a share of every column's
width. The trade is discoverability: the menu is found the way a
spreadsheet's is, by right-clicking or holding the header.

TWO SECTIONS, under headings: what applies to the whole grid, then what
applies to the column the menu was opened on. The grid section repeats
on every column, which is the point: there is no other place in a grid's
chrome to put it without a toolbar, and the toolbar is what this replaced.

HEADER FILTERS ARE HIDDEN, NEVER REMOVED. Tabulator builds them with the
columns; hiding the row is a display change and a redraw, while removing
them would mean redefining every column. `filters` lets a host that keeps
the setting above one table (the workbench, across its grids) own it:
{ on: () => boolean, set: (on, table) => void }. Without it the setting
lives on the table.

COPY THE TABLE: what the filters show, in the columns shown plus any
grouped ones, as TSV.

THE COUNT IS THE LABEL, and it is the count of what is on screen. A
filtered grid copies what the filter left, so a label reading "Copy
table" over 74 of 322 rows would be describing the file rather than the
copy. Same promise swipe-deck's entry makes about its own count. Exported
as an item, so a host's own table menu (the explorer's Options) offers
the same copy under the same words.

session-export.js — a session as a list of exchanges, plus the pure function
that turns any part of one into markdown.

── The picker that was here, and the button that briefly replaced it ──────

Until 2026-09-06 this file ran a selection MODE over the list: a "Pick all /
Clear" bar pinned above the rows, a pick control on every row, and an export
bar carrying seven render toggles, an Options panel, a Preview panel, a size
readout, Download and Copy. It went through three designs in a week and the
reported objection never moved: it was hard to make sense of and it cost the
top of the screen for something nobody reached for.

It was replaced by one copy button per row, and that lasted a single commit.
The same objection arrived one size smaller: a control on every line of a
36-line list, offering an action whose payload is invisible until after the
tap, for a thing a reader would not do from a list they came to read. Both
removals are the same finding. The mode was too much machinery for the job;
the button was too much presence for the job.

So the list has no copy control at all. The two things a reader does from a
row are open its panel and enter the deck, and those are its two controls.

── What is left, and what has no caller ──────────────────────────────────

`markdown()` is the pure half and it survives both removals: give it a record
and a set of turn indices and it returns the excerpt, header block and all.
Nothing in the estate calls it. `index()` is the kit's only entry point that
anything reaches, from alpineComponents/session-brief.js.

That is stated rather than left to be discovered. Whether the estate should
be able to carry a session excerpt anywhere is a live question and a separate
one from whether this list is the place to offer it; the answer to the second
is no, and the first has not been asked. Deleting the pure half would also
make this file's NAME wrong, since what would remain is the outline.

Framework-free and DOM-rendering, loaded via gh.load after session-render.js
(which it reads) and swipe-deck.js (whose `h` and overlay idiom it borrows).

  sessionExport.model(record)               -> {cards, flat, cardOf, cardStart}
  sessionExport.markdown(record, sel, opts) -> string     pure; sel = Set|array|null

── What the output says about itself ─────────────────────────────────────

A record is a bounded capture, not a transcript: prompts are stored to 400
characters, prose to 8 KB a turn, result bodies to 1 or 2 KB, and receipts
and Reads are dropped by policy. An excerpt pasted into another session
carries none of that context, and a reader there has no way to tell a quiet
turn from an elided one. So the header block is not decoration: it names the
record, states the bound, and (with `caveats`, the default) carries the
record's own capture gaps. Turning it off is available and is a choice the
caller makes, not a default that quietly ships a partial record as a whole
one.

── Why detail is separate from selection ──────────────────────────────────

Which turns to take and how much of each are different questions, and the
second is where the size actually is: on the session that built this, tool
result bodies were 78% of the bytes. The first three flags say which roles a
caller wants and the rest govern how much of each renders, which is why
bodies default off and arguments default on: a Bash turn with no command in
it says nothing at all. The split is not cosmetic, and it is the caller's to
operate: emit() gives a tool turn a heading whatever the render flags say,
falling back to "(call only)", so a card holding 34 Bash calls cannot be
reduced to its ask by rendering alone. Something has to drop the turn, and
that something is the SELECTION the caller passes.

`asks`, `replies` and `args` decide WHICH turns of an open card are in;
`bodies`, `stamps`, `head` and `caveats` decide how much of them renders.
The split is not cosmetic: emit() gives a tool turn a heading whatever the
render flags say, falling back to "(call only)", so a card holding 34 Bash
calls cannot be reduced to its ask by rendering alone. Something has to
drop the turn, and that is what the first three do.

── The list ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Indices are positions in `flat`, which is the cards flattened. Deriving the
flat list FROM the cards rather than from turns() directly is what keeps a
turn index and a card index talking about the same sequence: groups() folds
a leading meta note into the first card, so the two orders are equal today
and there is no reason to depend on that.

A turn's own heading. The tool label already carries the tool name and its
failure mark, so it wins over the role word; nothing else has one.

The record's own capture gaps, as session-render states them. Read off the
rendered note rather than recomputed, so the exporter cannot drift into a
second, kinder account of what is missing.

The omission line is claimed only when something was actually omitted: an
excerpt of nothing but prose has no bodies to leave out, and saying so
would describe a decision that did not apply to it.

Pure: the whole point of the picker, minus the picker. `sel` of null means
every turn, so a caller wanting the plain "copy the session" has one call.

A rule marks a GAP, not a card boundary. The reader on the other end
needs to know where turns were dropped, so two consecutive turns run on
even across a card break, and a jump gets a rule even inside one card.
The earlier version ruled on every card change, which put a horizontal
line between every pair of turns in an asks-and-prose excerpt: each of
those turns starts its own card, so the mark that was supposed to mean
"something is missing here" appeared where nothing was.

── The overview ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
One row per card, titled by sessionRender.outline, and the same rows are
where an exchange is carried out. That is one surface doing two jobs on
purpose: both are "read the shape of this session as a list," and running
them apart meant the reader chose turns from a list of previews with no
titles while the titles lived nowhere at all.

Nothing is selected and nothing is copied, so there is no state to draw, no
bar to appear and nothing to clear. The list reads as an outline, which is
all it now is.

A title derived from tool calls rather than from prose is a weaker claim,
so it is styled as one. The reader can tell at a glance which rows the
session actually narrated and which are the renderer's best effort.

Role, said rather than colour-coded, and coloured only on the word itself.

Three treatments were tried. A blue dot against a purple dot asked the
reader to learn a legend printed nowhere. An accent border plus a tint on
the user rows made the asks scannable and read as a stray outline down the
left of the list, which is worse than the problem it solved: a border is
chrome, and chrome has to earn its weight against a row it is not part of.

What is left is the word, in Claude's own clay for Claude. That is the
same #d97757 as the estate's session logomark, so the colour already means
"Claude" everywhere else a reader has seen it and needs no key here. The
ask keeps the primary, and its title carries a little more weight, which
is enough to find the asks while scanning without drawing a single line.

── What the left edge marks, and what it stopped marking ────────────────

A guideline down each card keyed on `kind` until 2026-09-02: blue down the
asks, clay down the replies, nothing beside the work. Three things made
that wrong, and the row is two of them. Every row now shows a blue ask and
a clay reply, so the rule marked a SUBSET of them in the same two colours
for a different distinction; and the fact it encoded was `calls === 0`,
which the row prints in words as the tool tally. The third is that its blue
was a lie, since `ask` does not mean "you asked", it means the record kept
a prompt with no reply beside it, which is a capture gap.

Nothing runs down the edge now. The conventions' CLOSING STATE took its
place and then left it, since a state is the reply's claim and belongs on
the reply's line; it is a third row of the exchange, drawn in the card loop
below, and that block carries the argument and the two readings tried
before it.

The row's gutter glyph, and it is chat-render's ROLES table read down one
column: the same icon per role and the same two tints, primary for the ask
and clay for the reply. The other roles stay neutral, which that kit
measured rather than assumed: this theme's `warning` and `info` sit near
88% lightness, fine as a 2px rail and unreadable as an 11px glyph on white.

`mt` is optical, not structural: the glyph hangs beside a line of text and
has to sit on its baseline, and the ask runs a size larger than the reply.

── One line of markdown, reduced for a row and still emphasised ──────────

readAloud.speechText is the estate's one markdown-to-prose pass, and it
takes `**` off along with the fences, the link targets and the emoji. That
is right for a voice and wrong for a row: what an author set bold is the
half a reader scans for, and both of this row's reduced lines open on one
("Ready to continue.", "A term that names an intention instead of a
form."). Reported from the phone on 2026-09-02, on the state line.

So the runs are split on emphasis FIRST and reduced one at a time, which
keeps every bold span rather than only a leading one. speechText trims, so
the whitespace at each boundary is carried across by hand: without it
"Merged." and "It shipped." arrive as one word. A run that reduces to
nothing is dropped, so a line of pure emphasis cannot leave an empty span.

EITHER SIDE OF THE BOUNDARY, because emphasis puts the space on the
outside: `Yes. **A term…**` splits into a run ending in a space and a
bold run whose raw text is the inner slice and starts with a letter.
Testing only the incoming run gave "Yes.A term that names".

A role label. Clay is not a Tailwind token, so `assistant` takes it inline;
everything else rides a class.

*
The overview, as an element the caller mounts wherever it likes.
  opts.onOpen(i)   tapping a card's title or its deck glyph; omit and
                   neither is a link
  opts.agenda      the session's topic stretches, drawn as section headers
  opts.notes       Gemini's turn summaries, { [ask.at]: {summary, headline} },
                   drawn as one more line on each row they name; a list
                   where turns share an instant, taken in row order
  plus the DEFAULTS flags, which govern what a copied card renders
Returns { el }.

`opts.startCard` was here and is gone with the selection it opened: there
is nothing left for a card to be opened INTO. A host that wants to land a
reader on one card sends them to the deck, which is what `onOpen` is.

── Which stretch of the agenda each card belongs to ──────────────────────
The agenda is the follow-up's (web-tools-private sessions/topics/): the
session as stretches of user turns, each naming the topic it worked on,
joined onto the host's row by RepoSessionsCache.topicStretches. A card is
one exchange and opens on one user turn, so a card belongs to the last
stretch that began at or before its ask.

BY INSTANT FIRST, BY COUNT WHEN THERE IS NO INSTANT. A format 4 stretch
carries `at`, the time its first turn was sent, which is the same string
the record's prompt carries and so cannot drift from the card it names.
A format 3 stretch has only a turn index; it is looked up in the record's
prompts, and where even that is missing the card's own count of asks
stands in. A card with no ask (the closing summary) stays with the stretch
before it. Pure, and returns -1 for every card when there is no agenda.

── The peek panel, which replaced the expansion ──────────────────────

The row expanded in place until 2026-09-02, and the expansion rendered
every assistant turn whole. That is not what was asked for ("expand the
truncated part but not expand the whole thing") and the overshoot is what
the last two rounds were patching: a card opened to nine screens, so it
grew a height cap, and the cap needed a ring to say which card it was.

A panel under the line instead, and one per HALF: the ask has its own and
the reply has its own, because they are separate things to want and the
row now says so. Asked for as a tooltip; it cannot be one. kits/title-tip.js
draws its panel `pointer-events:none` on purpose and its own contract
draws the line here: the moment a tip's content needs a tap, which a
reply's links and code spans do, it is a panel-tip. So this is a panel, with
the reach a panel owes: focusable triggers, `aria-expanded`, Escape, and
a close button.

ONE PANEL, MOVED. It is appended into whichever card owns the open half,
which is what lets `offsetTop` position it: the box is the positioned
ancestor, so the panel hangs under the line that was tapped and scrolls
with the list rather than needing a scroll listener to chase it.

A MEASURE, not the card's width. It spanned the whole card, so at 1280
the panel ran 1,230px and its 13px prose crossed 150 characters a line,
which is not what a popover is. 34rem is about 68 characters at that
size. `left` and `right` are both still set, so a narrow screen keeps
the full span and the cap simply does not bite; with both set and no
auto margins the box is over-constrained and hugs the left, which is
the card's own edge.
26rem. It went to 14rem when the panel first held one comment instead of
an exchange, and came back the same day the chip became its trigger:
the reason to keep it short was that a panel could open on a hover
anywhere along a line, so its height was a cost paid on every pass of
the pointer. A chip is aimed at, so the height is only ever paid for
deliberately, and the panel's job is to hold the rest of the comment.

── Hover on a fine pointer, tap on a coarse one ──────────────────────
Asked for on 2026-09-02: a reader running a mouse down the list wants the
half under it, not a click per row. The timings and the shape are
kits/title-tip.js's, deliberately: a dwell before opening so a pointer
crossing the row does not flash a panel at it, and a grace after leaving
so a wobble does not.

THE GRACE IS ALSO WHAT LETS THE PANEL BE ENTERED, which is the one place
this parts from that kit. Its panel is `pointer-events:none`, so leaving
the trigger is the whole rule; this one scrolls and carries a close
button, so the rule is the full one from mechanics.md: close after
leaving BOTH. The panel clears the timer on the way in and re-arms it on
the way out, and the 220ms covers the gap between the two.

Gated on `(hover: hover)` rather than on the pointer type of the event,
because a touch screen synthesises a hover on tap: without the gate the
dwell and the tap would both fire and the panel would open and toggle
itself shut.

A second tap on the same half closes it, which is what makes the trigger
a toggle rather than a one-way door.
and it stays lit while open

── GATED ON A POINTER THAT CAN HOVER, like the trigger's pair below ─────
These two were not, and that is the whole of a reported defect: on a
touch screen, tapping INSIDE the panel closed it. Lifting a finger fires
pointerout with a null relatedTarget, `peek.contains(null)` is false, and
the leave timer ran, so the panel vanished 220ms after being touched.
Measured 2026-09-07 at 430x932 with hasTouch: open, still open at 50ms,
gone by 500.

The trigger's own hover handlers already carry this gate, for the
adjacent reason stated there: a touch screen synthesises a hover on tap,
so ungated they would open and toggle shut in one gesture. Same cause,
two symptoms, and this half was missed.

Dismissal on a coarse pointer is unaffected and is the whole set it ever
had: the close button, Escape, an outside pointerdown, or a second tap on
the row. None of those is a hover.

Dismissal, hung on the component root rather than on `document`: this
index is mounted per swiper slide, so a document listener would outlive
every copy of it. Capture phase, since a trigger stops propagation.

── AND IT MUST NOT REACH THE OPEN PANEL'S OWN TRIGGER ───────────────────
This ran BEFORE the click that toggles, so a second tap on the row that
opened the panel shut it here, cleared `peekAt`, and then `showPeek` saw
no open panel and opened it again. Shut and reopened inside one gesture
reads as nothing happening, which is not what the toggle above promises.
Measured 2026-09-07 with hasTouch: tapping row 7 correctly MOVED the
panel there, and tapping row 2 twice left it on row 2 both times.

It bites a mouse identically and is invisible there, because the hover
that opened the panel is still holding it open.

Excluding the owning trigger leaves every other route exactly as it was:
another row shuts this panel and opens its own, and anywhere else in the
list just shuts.

`role` and a tabindex rather than a real `button`. The reason was the
trigger being a CLAMPED LINE: Safari sizes a button from its unclipped
content, so the row stood at its full height with the text clipped inside
it, which this branch shipped once (snags:
safari-button-sizes-from-unclipped-content). The trigger is the chip now,
which is not clamped, so that hazard no longer reaches it. The mechanism
stayed because a chip wants exactly the same reach and a button buys
nothing more here.

NO OPEN-ON-FOCUS, which the title-tip kit does have. Focus lands before
click, so a mouse tap would open on focus and then toggle itself shut
on the click a moment later. Enter and Space above are what a keyboard
uses, and they run the same toggle a finger does.

chat-render's own chip, so the two surfaces cannot draw the same mark two
ways. Resolved per call rather than held, the same shape SR() takes: the
load order is the host's business, and a host that never loaded
chat-render gets a row with no chip rather than a thrown list.

Every clamped line, with the chip that reports what its clamp hid. Filled
as the rows are built and walked once by measureChips below.

── The chip, and what it reports ────────────────────────────────────
The row's two lines are clamped by CSS, not cut in the data, so unlike
the transcript card there is no dropped count to print: it is measured
off the rendered line (see measureChips below). The chip is chat-render's
own, exported for this, since a reader meets both marks within two taps.

INSIDE THE LINE, and the line is CUT to make room for it. The chip was
placed absolutely in a reserved padding-right, which made it a column at
the right margin and, worse, shortened EVERY line of a two-line ask to
hold room for a chip that belongs on the last one. Reported 2026-09-08:
"it should be in line. It shouldn't block and act like its own column."

So the text is truncated to what the clamp was going to show anyway, less
a little for the chip, and the chip follows it as ordinary inline
content. That also retires the circularity the gutter existed to break:
the count is no longer "what the clamp hides", which moves when the chip
takes space, but "what this line is not showing", which is exact by
construction whatever the digits are.

The original children are kept so a re-measure can put them back: a reply
line carries bold runs from richLine, so the cut has to preserve
structure rather than reset textContent.

The row elements, in order, which is what the rail below reads to say
which card the reader is standing on and what it scrolls to on a tap.

NO REPAINT PASS. There was one, an array of per-row closures run by
sync(), because "Pick all" changed twenty rows at once and a row could

gone every row owns everything it draws, and nothing on a row changes

── THE AGENDA AS SECTIONS, one per stretch, each under its own header ──
Asked for on 2026-10-02: "the topics are used to group the discussion
turns as they are displayed, a header where it changes", and the header
sticks while its stretch is on screen. Sticky inside a SECTION rather than
inside the list, so each header leaves with its own cards and the next
one takes its place instead of stacking under it.

It sticks under the rail. Framed, the rail sits outside the scroller and
the host publishes no chrome, so both numbers are 0 and the header holds

under the host's chrome, and --rail-h (set below, flow only) puts the

so you see a little bit more on the surface."

So the row carries the ask's own words at two lines closed and all of
them open, and the replies arrive under it. A card with no ask (the
capture note, the closing summary) keeps the titler's line, which is
the only text it has.

ONE TREATMENT FOR EVERY ASK, and it branches on whether the card HAS
one rather than on `kind`. It read `kind === 'work'` until

nothing to do with either of them. Reported from the phone as the ask
being bold "for some reason", which is exactly right: the reason was

It was the last mark of a distinction this file already retired
once. The guideline down the edge encoded the same fact and went for

and nobody looked at two rows side by side.

A card with NO ask keeps the heavier line, and that is not the same
rule wearing a disguise: the capture note and the closing summary

has no blue fill to mark it.
NO `block` HERE. It and `line-clamp-2` both set `display`, and `block`

The clamp utility supplies the display it needs.

Inline rather than a `bg-primary/*` class, so it tracks a theme change

── ONE COLOUR FOR THE ASK, AND IT IS BLUE ─────────────────────────
The row set it in `base-content/70`, a grey, while the panel showed

rather than a literal, so the text tracks a theme change the way its

AND DENSER WITH IT, 13px against the 14 it had. The ask was the
largest thing on the row while being its context, and the reply
preview under it runs 13; one size for both is what makes the pair

WHAT OPENS IS THE REST OF THE CONVERSATION, not the card. The ask is

THE OTHER HALF, ON THE SURFACE. Every closed row said "You" and showed

The LAST reply, not the first. A work exchange usually opens with the

Reduced through readAloud.speechText, which is this estate's one

So the box goes and the caret stays: a count and a state, set like the
clock beside it, with nothing left to read as tappable.
A COUNT, and nothing else now. It carried a caret while the row
expanded; with the expansion gone the caret pointed at nothing, and a
caret that opens nothing is the pill-that-looked-like-a-dropdown defect

AIR, BUT NO SECOND LINE. The mark was glued under the ask, which read as

a column of the same fact, and the clay glyph already says it in the
space the text was going to use. The deck's dense mode drops the word
for the same reason and this file follows it.

TWO CELLS, NOT A NESTED ROW. The mark rides the row's own gutter beside
the ask's, so both texts start on one edge; see the grid below.

SHOWN AND HIDDEN BY STYLE, not by `hidden`. That utility sets `display`
and so does `line-clamp-1`, which is the collision this file has now
shipped twice; an inline display beats both classes and restoring it to
'' hands the clamp back its own.

── Where the exchange arrived, on the reply's own side ───────────────
One line per closing state, under the reply it closes: the mark in the
row's gutter and the closing block's own words beside it, clamped to
one line like the reply above.

IT WAS A DOT BESIDE THE ASK until 2026-09-02, hung in the box's left
pad at the height of the first line, which put the ASSISTANT's claim
about where the work arrived on the row that carries what the READER
said. Reported the same day. Moving it under the reply also buys the
thing a bare mark could never carry: the 🟢 lead reads "Ready to
continue" on every row it appears, and the sentence after it names the
work that was on offer, which is the whole content of the state.

Deduped by key, last claim winning, and that is not the tidiness the
old dot's dedupe was. Two assistant turns in one exchange each closing
🟢 are two versions of one offer, and the later one is the live one; a
🆚 followed by a 🟢 is two different claims and keeps both lines, in
the order they were made.

A DISC, NOT THE EMOJI, in the same gutter the role glyphs use. The
marker drawn at 11px is a filled circle with the weight of an icon,
so it competed with the sparkle directly above it; at 6px it reads
as a mark on that line rather than a second role.

AND NO `data-title-tip`, which it carried while it was a bare dot beside
the ask. It is inside the row's button now, and the title-tip kit listens
on pointerdown in the capture phase without stopping propagation, so
one tap would open a panel AND expand the card: the two-doors defect
this file has already fixed twice. The gloss is not lost, because the
words are on the line beside it; the disc is the scan colour and
`aria-hidden` because the text says the same thing.

`mt-[10px]` is the third reading of this one pixel, and the two it
sits between are both defensible. At 6px the disc was 3.5px high and
simply wrong. At 9px it was centred on the LINE BOX to within half a
pixel and still read high, because the ink of a lowercase line sits
in the x-band, which for 13px system text runs from 6.8px above the
baseline and centres 1.6px lower than the box. At 11px it sat on that
band and read low, since the line opens on a capital and the disc
then hangs under it. So it splits them: 0.5px under the box centre,
0.6px over the band. Every number here was probed on the rendered
page with spans at `vertical-align: baseline` and `text-top`, not
taken from font tables.

INDENTED UNDER THE REPLY, not sitting beside it. It rode the row's
own gutter until 2026-09-02, which put it in the column the user and
sparkle glyphs occupy and made it read as a third turn. It is not
one: a closing state is a passage INSIDE the reply above it, and
drawing it as that reply's sibling says the exchange had three
speakers. Reported as exactly that, a peer where the content is
nested.

One step in, and the step is the row's own: a nested 11px track plus
the same gap makes 17px, which is chat-render's LEAD_INDENT and the
measure the open body already hangs on. So the state text starts
where a wrapped line of the reply would.
THE BOLD LEAD STAYS, and it is not decoration. Dropped, the line runs
"A alone, A plus the two proposed tasks, or hold everything", and the
only thing saying that was a decision put to the reader is a pink
dot; the row has to survive without its colour. It costs about a
third of the line for `ready`, which is the price of that.
And it is set bold, because it was bold where it was written; see
richLine, which the reply preview above goes through for the same
reason.

── What Gemini made of the exchange ──────────────────────────────────
The laptop daemon summarises every turn of a session (web-tools-private
sessions/topics/, `turns`), and the host hands those in as `notes`,
keyed by the instant the turn was sent, which is the ask's own `at`.
One more clamped line under the reply and its closing states, in the
row's own gutter and type, so the reader compares a summary with the
exchange it summarises without leaving the row (asked for 2026-10-22,
"get a sense of the summary as compared with the session detail").

GREY, AND GEMINI'S OWN MARK. Blue is what the owner said and clay is
Claude; a third speaker's colour would make the gutter a legend. The
mark's shape names the author and the grey says it is a reading of the
exchange rather than part of it.
Turns that share an instant arrive as a list, one per row in order.

── Where the context was compacted ───────────────────────────────────
One quiet line per compaction inside this exchange, set like the clock
and the tally rather than like prose, since what it names at rest is an
event and a size. Its panel carries the summary whole; the deck shows
the same summary as a fold among the turns. It sits above the reply
preview when it came before that reply (164 of the 166 in the store on
2026-10-30, and one more whose exchange has no reply), and under the
reply's closing lines otherwise, so the row keeps the exchange's order.

ONE CONTROL PER DESTINATION. Tapping the item opens it, which is the
cheap move and the common one; the glyph goes to the deck. It was the
other way round, with the title AND the glyph both entering the deck
and a pill doing the expanding, so the row offered two doors to one
place and hid the third behind a chip.

A GRID, BECAUSE THE ALIGNMENT IS THE POINT. The row was a numbered
gutter and one text column, with the reply's mark INSIDE that column:
so the ask started at the column edge and the answer started a glyph
and a gap further in, and the two halves of one exchange did not line
up. Asked for on 2026-09-01, against the Activity popover, which is
chatRender's dense mode: every glyph in one gutter, every text on one
edge. A fixed first track is what makes that exact rather than close,
and it is why this is a grid and not two nested flex rows.

AND THE NUMBER IS GONE, which the same ask proposed. It was a mono
column of digits the eye skipped to reach the sentence, and the gutter
it occupied is worth more as the role. The index survives where it was
doing work: `aria-label` here and the deck button's title, which is
what both name a card by.
NOT A BUTTON ANY MORE. It was one control for one destination while
the whole row expanded; the row now holds two triggers and a pick, and
a button cannot contain them. Its parts keep their own reach.

A stable hook, since the row stopped being the control that named
itself: `aria-label="Open card N"` went with the button.

11px + gap-x-1.5 is 17, which is chat-render's LEAD_INDENT exactly,
and not by coincidence: 11px is that kit's icon box, ink inside about
9 of it. Matching it is what lets the OPEN body line up under the
closed row, since those turns are rendered by that kit and hang on
that number. At 14px the two were 3px apart, which reads as a wobble
rather than as an indent.

Last of the chipped lines, so its chip is the last one pushed; the
ask's and the reply's are found by counting back from it below.

No "You" beside the clock any more. With both halves on the row the
ask is the lead and the clay mark names the answer, so a role word
labelled the obvious half and then sat between them. It survives
only where the card HAS no ask, a capture note or the closing
summary, which is the one case the lead does not name itself.

── NOTHING COPIES FROM THIS ROW ─────────────────────────────────────
A copy button sat in this rail for one commit, in the slot the pick
circle held, and it copied that one exchange as markdown. Removed on
the same day it landed, on the report that it read as a control per
item for something a reader would not do here: "I don't know what it
copies, and I don't think we would want to copy from this view."

That is the picker's own objection arriving one size smaller. The mode
was too much machinery for the job; one button per row was still a
control on every line of a 36-line list, offering an action whose
payload is invisible until after the tap. A list of exchanges is for
reading, and the two things a reader does from it are open the panel
and enter the deck.

No horizontal divider. The left rule already segments the conversation,
and an underline on every row drew a second grid that agreed with
nothing. `mb-1` is the gap between adjacent rules: without it a clay
row followed by a blue one draws a single unbroken line that changes
colour partway down, which reads as one rule rather than two.

NO BAND. What is in used to be a tint behind the head, and it went
through primary, then a neutral, and neither was right: at primary it
put a blue wash behind a blue ask, and at neutral it still washed one
(this theme's greys are cool, so ANY step off the page reads faintly
blue under the fill). Reported twice, 2026-09-01.

The band was answering a question the list stopped asking. Selection
used to be a checkbox and could differ from what was expanded; open IS
selected now, so the expansion is the mark, and an open row is already
taller with clay-marked replies under it. The band was a second copy of
that, and the copy is what collided with the accent.

What is left carries the state where the tint cannot: `aria-expanded`
for a screen reader, the caret's flip, and the count's own weight,
which is the one signal a card with NO replies has (it opens to
nothing, and that is the case the band was genuinely covering).

── The card as an ITEM ──────────────────────────────────────────────
The rows ran together, which is what "articulate each item" names: with
the guideline gone from the left edge there was nothing between one
exchange and the next but 2px of margin. A hairline under each is the
cheapest thing that reads as a list, and the objection this file used to
carry against one ("the left rule already segments the conversation")
went with the rule it named.

AND A SCOPE RULE, which does the job a band cannot. A tint behind the
head washes the blue ask sitting on it, since this theme's greys are
cool, and it was reported twice and removed for it. A 2px strip at the
card's own edge is outside every text, so it can light on hover and
stay lit while the panel is open without touching a colour.
The step is `/20` and not `/25` because 25 is not one Tailwind
generates: the class renders fully transparent and looks like a colour
that did not arrive. `dead-opacity` is the gate for exactly that, and it
named both the line and the nearest step that works.
3px at /40, up from 2px at /20 on 2026-09-08. It was drawn to be the
quiet answer to a fill and was quieter than that: at 2px and /20 it is
about a fifth of a hairline against a cool grey page, and a reader
asked for a hover effect on the row while this one was already there.
Still a strip at the card's own edge rather than a wash, which is the
part that must not change: a tint behind the head washes the blue ask
sitting on it, reported twice on 2026-09-01 and removed twice.

scroll-mt is what the rail's jump lands against: scrollIntoView puts
the box at the top of the scroller, and the top of the scroller is
under the rail and, in document flow, under the host's chrome too.
Without it a tapped card arrives hidden behind both.

── One panel per LINE, carrying that line whole ─────────────────────
The row is two clamped lines, an ask and the reply that answered it,
and the panel un-clamps the one under the pointer. It carried the whole
exchange until 2026-09-08 and was reported awkward on a desktop, which
it was for a reason the argument for it missed: hovering either line
opened a panel holding BOTH, so a reader who wanted the rest of a
sentence was handed a second copy of the line above it and a scroll.

What settles it is that the exchange has a better home. The deck reads
one card whole, with its tool calls, at reading size, and the glyph to
its right is one tap away on every row. So the panel does the small job
(this line, unclamped) and stops competing for the large one.

THE LINE IS THE TRIGGER and the CARD is still the scope: the rule at
the box's left edge lights on the row, and the panel hangs under the
line that opened it, since `box` is the positioned ancestor and
showPeek reads offsetTop against it.

THE ASK IS RESTYLED AFTER IT IS DRAWN, and both halves of that are
reported defects rather than taste. chat-render renders a prompt
through `rawPre`, verbatim in a `<pre>`, because a prompt is typed text
and not markdown; in DENSE mode it then drops it to 11px sans, so the
ask reads under the reply it is context for. Here they are in one panel
and the reply is 13px prose, so the shrink puts the ask two sizes down
from what the row shows. And the verbatim whitespace shows every double
space after a sentence, which the row directly above collapses: the
same words, twice, differently.

So: the reading size, and a squeeze of runs of spaces that do not START
a line. Line-leading whitespace survives, which is the indentation of
anything pasted, and so does every newline. The deck stays verbatim.

Awaited, because `card` resolves chat-render's ready() first: without
it the restyle runs against an empty node and finds no `<pre>`.

── THE CHIP IS THE TRIGGER, and the line is not ─────────────────────
The line was, from 2026-09-08 morning, and a whole line is a large
target for a panel: on a desktop the pointer crosses one on its way to
anywhere, so the panel opened on the way past. Reported the same day.
A chip is aimed at, so the panel only ever opens on purpose, and
hovering the prose is left to say the two quiet things it should: which
tick this row is, and that the row is under the pointer.

It also gates itself on there being anything to show. A chip exists
only where the clamp actually hid something, so a line that fits has no
trigger at all, which is the honest shape: a panel repeating a line the
reader can already see whole is the copy this row does not need.

The TURN'S own clock labels it, not the card's, which is the card's
first turn and so is wrong on the reply by however long the work took.

The compaction's line is its own trigger, since it is short and set at
its own width: a pointer aims at it rather than crossing it.

The panel carries the summary whole, under the headline Gemini gave
the same turn, which is the one thing the row does not show.

── NO PICKED STATE TO DRAW ──────────────────────────────────────────
A repaint closure sat here and marked the picked row: the turn count in
a heavier grey, the circle filled, and an INSET ring on the box, which
was itself the third answer to that question. A tint behind the head
came before it, through primary and then a neutral, and both washed the
blue ask sitting on them, since this theme's greys are cool and any
step off the page reads faintly blue under that fill. Reported twice on
2026-09-01 and replaced by the ring; the ring is inset rather than a
border so it takes no layout and cannot move the grid the row's
alignment depends on.

All three answered "which rows are in the excerpt", and nothing asks
now. Kept in the record because the FILL is the part that must not come
back: any future row state here is an edge, never a wash behind an ask.

Under a sticky header, a card the rail scrolls to must land below it.
Two lines of header is the most it draws, so that is the margin.

CONTAINED, for a page opened in a phone's sheet: a pull past the top of
the turns otherwise chains to the host and dismisses the sheet
(docs/ios-sheet-drags.md, path 2).

── THE SESSION'S OWN TIMELINE ────────────────────────────────────────
One tick a card, placed by WHEN it happened across the session's span
rather than evenly, so the rail draws the shape of the conversation: a
burst reads as a cluster, an hour away as a gap, and a session that ran
overnight reads as one. The vocabulary is the transcript card's, in the
estate (estate.js, "THE SESSION'S OWN TIMELINE"), which is the surface
this was asked to match; both descend from the State view's pulse rail.

IT LIVES HERE, NOT IN THE HOST, because it needs two things the host does
not have: the card boxes, to say which one the reader is standing on, and
the lead instants that place the ticks. A host that mounted its own would
be reading into this kit's DOM.

AND IT IS A CONTROL. Tapping or dragging scrolls to the nearest card,
which is the one gesture that crosses forty of them; that is why the
whole strip carries the pointer and the height, rather than each 1px
tick.
One element per card, kept so a row can light its own; see lightTick.

Full strength, wider and taller than a tick, so a cluster still says
which card the rail is naming.

touch-none, or the drag belongs to the scroller behind it and the rail
gets one frame before the page takes over. h-4 rather than the rail's
own 12px, so the strip a finger has to find is the row and not the
hairline.

STICKY, and the offset is the host's to declare. Framed, this sits
above a scroller as a plain flex item and never moves, so top-0 is
inert; in document flow the whole pane scrolls and the rail has to
clear the host's own sticky chrome, whose height sessionBrief publishes
as --chrome-h. One class covers both, and a host that publishes nothing
gets 0, which is the correct answer for a host with no chrome.

── Placing the ticks ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
The span is the RECORD'S, start to end, not the first card to the last:
the last card's lead is said before the session's final write, and a rail
that ended there would draw the tail as if nothing happened in it.

PLACEMENT IS PER TICK, AND THE MIXED CASE IS THE NORM. A card with no
instant falls back to its index, spaced evenly, while its dated
neighbours are placed by time. That reads as a rare schema-3 path and is
not one: every record in the store ends with the renderer's own summary
card ("What this session touched"), which carries a sort sentinel rather
than a time, so the fallback fires on all 345 of them (measured
2026-09-08 over web-tools-private sessions/).

It is correct because that card is LAST, where the fallback puts it at
100%, which is the right end for a summary of the whole. session-render's
turns() appends it positionally, and groups() folds a leading meta note
into the first card rather than leaving it a card of its own, so an
undated card in the MIDDLE is the shape that does not occur. It is also
the shape this would get wrong: placed by index among neighbours placed
by time, it would land wherever the count fell rather than where it
happened. Held by node/test/session-export-open.test.mjs.

Where NOTHING is dated the whole rail spaces evenly and drops its clock
labels: even spacing claims nothing about time, which is honest, where a
label over it would not be.

The rail's ends: clock times for a session that kept to one day, and
dates for one that did not. Clock times alone read "4:55 PM ... 1:28 AM"
over a nine-day session (bb88ffa7), which hides the nine days.

Where the topic changes, the full height of the strip: the agenda's
shape drawn on the session's own clock, so a session that jumped about
reads as one before a header is read.

── Where the reader is standing ──────────────────────────────────────
The rail's own bottom edge is the reference line, and it is the right one
in BOTH layouts without either being detected: framed it is the top of
the scroller, and in flow the rail is stuck under the chrome, so it is the
top of what can be seen. Measured in viewport coordinates for the same
reason: `scrollTop` would need to know which box is doing the scrolling.

The card the line falls INSIDE, not the last one that started above it.
Those differ exactly at a boundary, which is where a list scrolled to its
end sits.

One read a frame. A scroll fires far faster than the layout it is asking
about can change, and every read here is a forced reflow.

CAPTURE ON THE WINDOW, which is the only listener that catches both
layouts: a scroll event does not bubble, so a listener on `el` sees the
inner scroller and never the page. It outlives this element, which is
exactly the leak the panel handlers above are hung on `el` to avoid, so
this one is handed back for the host to release.

Tap the rail, land on that card. The one control here that can move a
reader a long way in one gesture. Held down it scrubs, and a tap is the
