── traffic-log: the app writes down what its calls did worth reading ──────

The Traffic pane shows one open page's calls, and only to the person looking
at it, and only until a reload. The question it was built for (is the app
making calls it does not need, or pulling data nobody reads) needs the record
where a session can read it, across tabs and devices and days. So the app
files it: a JSON file per finding window in web-tools-private's logs/traffic/,
committed through the viewer's own token, the channel kits/page-report.js
already uses for logs/page/.

IT WRITES WHAT IS OF INTEREST, NOT A SCHEDULE. Every five minutes, and when
the tab is hidden, it reads the calls the window held and asks
Traffic.trafficFindings for what stands out: a call repeated, calls made while
the tab was hidden, a failure, a large download, a heavy window, or the
token's calls falling fast. A window with none of those writes nothing. A
finding filed within the hour on this device is left out, so a steady poll
is filed once an hour with its rate rather than every five minutes.

WHAT IT NEVER WRITES: the token or any header. URLs name private repos and
paths, which is why the log lives in the private repo.

Its own writes are calls too. They run as the job "Traffic log", so the
Traffic pane lists them, and a window leaves them out of its findings.

Off for good with TrafficLog.disable(), or for one load with ?report=off, the
switch page reports honor.

IT ALSO KEEPS THE LAST MONTH, in this browser only. Every minute, and when
the tab is hidden or closed, each app tab adds its own calls since it last
did to two stores in localStorage (Traffic.addBins), which outlive a reload
and add up every app tab in the browser: quarter hours for the pane's 24
hours, and hours for its 7 and 30 days. Each keeps only as far back as the
longest range it serves (Traffic.RANGES), so the options the pane offers are
the record's extent. The stores are local and write nothing to a repo, so
the off switch above leaves them running.

Started by the app (app/index.html); loading this file starts nothing.
Attaches window.TrafficLog.
The signatures filed lately on this device, with when.

Where the last window ended: the ledger's running call number, the clock,
and the token's remaining calls with the hour they count against.

As page reports ask it: gh-auth fills the instance's token only when a
request is about to be made, so the saved token is the answer before that.

The last month, as above: this tab's calls since it last added them, into
each of the browser's stores. Returns the stores by name, as RANGES
name them.

The memory the page holds as it writes: the JS heap (Chrome alone
reports it) and the elements on the page.

The browser that filed it: its kind ("iPhone Safari") and the
reader's own name for it from the Here view, if they gave one.

Remembered before the write, as page reports learned to: two triggers
racing would otherwise both pass the quiet check and file twice.

A tab going to the background is the moment its record is most
likely to matter and least likely to be looked at; a minute's floor
keeps flipping between tabs from checking on every flip. Its calls go
to the stores then too, and as the tab closes.
For a reader who wants the next occurrence of everything filed.

traffic.js: the pure read of what a page has pulled over the network, and the
vocabulary the FAB's Traffic tab renders. Collection lives in gh-boot.js,
which wraps window.fetch and GH.prototype.get to fill window.__traffic and
window.__ghFiles. Everything here is a pure function over that ledger plus the
browser's Resource Timing entries, so it unit-tests against plain objects and
costs nothing until the tab is opened.

Three questions get called "size" here, and they do not share a unit:

  BOOT      what one page load cost. Fixed, cacheable, measured by Resource
            Timing. Answers "why is this slow on a phone".
  API       what browsing has spent since. Grows as you go, measured by the
            fetch wrapper reading content-length. Answers "what is this
            pulling", and it is the one a rate limit bounds.
  RESIDENT  what the app is holding locally. Not traffic, same question.

The honesty rules are most of why this file exists rather than a few inline
sums in the component:

  - transferSize 0 against a NONZERO body size means served from cache. It is
    not a free resource, it is a resource you already paid for.
  - all three sizes 0 on a cross-origin row means the origin sent no
    Timing-Allow-Origin header, so the size is UNDISCLOSED, not zero. jsDelivr
    sends it (verified 2026-08-05), api.github.com does not. An undisclosed
    row must never be summed into a figure that reads as complete, which is
    why every total here carries its own undisclosed count.
  - transferSize counts response headers along with the body, so a boot total
    runs a few hundred bytes per row above the payload it describes.
  - content-length on an API response is the COMPRESSED body as sent, which is
    the wire figure we want. It is absent on chunked responses; absent is
    recorded as null and reported as unknown, never as zero.

── Formatting ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
THE ONE RULE FOR A BYTE COUNT, for every view, not only this kit's: binary
units, one decimal while it still buys something, so 9.5 KB, 408 KB, 1.4 MB,
2.1 GB, with the unit chosen by the figure as rounded, so a count just under
a boundary reads 10 KB or 1.0 MB rather than 10.0 KB or 1024 KB.
bytes-one-owner.test.mjs fails on a second copy. `missing` is what a count that is not a number
reads as: this kit's tables say '?', because an absent figure is unknown,
not zero, while a view that would rather show nothing passes ''.

── Classification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Grouping by endpoint SHAPE, and it is worth being exact about what that
does and does not tell you, because the obvious reading is wrong.

What it gives: a mechanical, unfalsifiable statement of WHAT KIND of call
was made. A URL cannot lie about which endpoint it hit.

What it does NOT give: who made it. The endpoints are shared, heavily.
`contents/` is hit by gh.get (so every load() and read()), gh-fetch,
gh-store's WRITES, gh-transfer, and the config crawl. `commits` is hit by
branch-status's crawl, recentFiles, gh-fetch's history reads, and
the app's per-file sidebar lookup. So "forty calls to commits" does not
identify the crawl, and an earlier version of this comment claimed it did.

Caller attribution needs the callers to tag themselves, and since
2026-10-15 the work a page starts on its own does: it runs inside
window.__job (gh-boot.js), and a row that job made carries its id (jobRows
below). What is still NOT possible is inferring a caller from nothing: the
scripts registry refused stack sniffing because gh-api.js runs loaded files
as anonymous Function bodies, where a stack names nobody, and a row no job
claims is reported by the view it went out under, not by a guessed owner.

The method column is the axis that does separate something real, and it
separates the thing that matters most: a write from a read.

{ host, group, label } for one URL. `group` is the roll-up key, `label` its
human name. Anything unrecognized groups under its own hostname rather than
a catch-all, so a page pulling from somewhere unexpected says where.
The repo a call was aimed at, pulled straight out of the URL. Free, and it
is the axis that separates a crawl from browsing: an estate crawl touches
many repos, browsing touches one. Null where the URL carries no repo, which
is honest rather than awkward: a GraphQL POST names its repo in the body,
and the ledger does not read bodies.

A call carrying `via` was the loader fetching own code or data through
gh.load()/read(). It hits the same contents/ endpoint as everything else,
so nothing in the URL could tell you, and the difference is the one a
reader actually wants: the library pulling itself in, versus the page
reading something.

A readable name for a URL row. jsDelivr's /combine/ URLs carry every
package in the path and are the widest rows on the boot table, so they
collapse to "first +N" rather than wrapping over four lines.

A generic filename names nothing on its own, and a list of eight rows
all reading "style.css" is worse than no list: borrow the folder. Seen
for real on the first render of the Boot band, where daisyUI's
per-component stylesheets collapsed into one repeated word.

── Boot: the Resource Timing read ────────────────────────────────────────
One row per resource the browser fetched declaratively or otherwise, with
its state resolved to one of three words. `state` is the whole point: a
number without it is a claim the data does not support.

  network      real bytes crossed the wire
  cached       served locally; the body size is known, the transfer was 0
  undisclosed  cross-origin with no Timing-Allow-Origin; size unknowable

Boot rows group by ROLE, not by host, because the question the band answers
is "what did this page spend its weight on": the app's own code, the
third-party CSS and JS it stands on, the fonts, the document itself.

The whole boot read: rows heaviest first, plus the totals and the two
counts that qualify them. `ms` is the wall clock to the last resource's
end, not the sum of durations, since the loads overlap.
Roll boot rows up by group for the summary line above the table.

── API: the ledger read ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
Entries are what gh-boot's fetch wrapper recorded: { url, t, ms, status,
wire, error }. `wire` is null when the response carried no content-length,
and that stays null all the way to the display rather than becoming a zero
that quietly deflates a total.
A call that changes something on the other end, which is a different kind
of event from a read and has to be countable as one. Anything that is not
plainly GET or HEAD counts, including an absent method: the ledger records
what it saw, and "unknown" is nearer to a write than to a read for the
purpose of deciding whether to look.

The same ledger cut the other way. Endpoint shape says WHAT was called;
this says WHERE it landed, and the two answer different halves of "what is
this pulling". Rows with no repo in the URL are collected under one bucket
rather than dropped, so the counts still add up to the total.

Named repos first, heaviest first; the unattributable bucket last, since
it is a caveat rather than a finding.

── The header readout ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
One line, three facts, in the order they go wrong: what the load cost, what
browsing has added, and how much quota is left. The rate figure is omitted
rather than guessed when no response has carried the header.

A load whose every row withheld its size has no weight to report. Saying
"0 B" there would be the strip's most confident wrong number, so it says
nothing and leaves the explanation to the band.

── Resident: what is held locally ────────────────────────────────────────
Not traffic. Included because it is the same question ("how big is this
thing") and has no other home. Web Storage counts UTF-16 code units, so the
byte cost is twice the character count; keys count too.

── Jobs: why the calls went out ──────────────────────────────────────────
gh-boot's job ledger (window.__jobs) names the work a page started on its
own and stamps every ledger row it can attribute with that job's id. These
read the two together, for the app's Traffic pane.

How a job ended, in a few words, from the primitives the collector kept.
The crawls' own conventions: { error } is a failure they reported rather
than threw, { skipped } a decline, { committed } a write or its absence.

The page's own files: the document and what its tags and styles pulled
(scripts, stylesheets, fonts, images), whenever they arrived. A call made
with fetch or XMLHttpRequest is left out, since the traffic ledger counts
it, and counting it here as well would weigh it twice.

The pane's two lists. `jobs` is every job in the ledger, newest first, its
counts taken from the job itself, which outlive the traffic ledger's cap.
`free` is the calls no job claimed, one row per view that was on screen
when they went out, so the two lists together account for every row the
ledger still holds. Free counts come from those rows and shrink with them,
which is why the pane reports the trimmed count beside them.

The page's own load, as one row beside the jobs: the files it loaded
(pageFiles) and the calls it made before the app had a view on screen
(`where` empty), so what opening the page cost compares on the same bars
with everything the page did after. `fileCalls` turns the files into rows
the calls table can take: a file's time is the page's
start plus its own offset, a cached file transferred nothing, and a file
whose server disclosed no size has none, never zero.

The browser's calls over time, in bins. The traffic log
(lib/kits/traffic-log.js) adds each tab's own calls to stores in
localStorage, so the record outlives a reload and adds up every app tab
in this browser. A store holds bins of one size, `step` minutes, keyed by
the bin's start on the reader's clock ('YYYY-MM-DDTHH' for an hour,
'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM' for less; `offset` is minutes behind UTC, as
getTimezoneOffset gives it). A bin counts calls, those made while the tab
was hidden, the bytes known, the failures, and the calls by owner
(`o.owner(e)`: a job's name, or the view on screen).

RANGES are the Traffic pane's options, and the stores keep exactly what
they draw: `n` bars of `span` minutes each, read from the store whose
bins are `step` minutes. So the options state how far back the browser's
record goes, and the record goes no further.
How long a store keeps its bins: the longest range it serves, and a bar.
A key back to the time its bin starts.

A range's bars, oldest first, the current one last: each with its start
and end and the sum of the store's bins inside it, empty where nothing
was counted.
When the store's record begins: its oldest bin's start, or null.
A round top for a lane's scale: 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten.

Where a range's axis is marked, as bar indexes: `line` on a boundary the
reader keeps time by (midnight, or a Monday for a month), `label` where
the axis is named. A day is named every `every` hours; a week names each
day at its midnight; a month names each Monday.

What the traffic log files (lib/kits/traffic-log.js): out of the calls one
window of a page's life held, only the patterns worth a reader's time. A
finding carries `sig`, its identity across windows, so the log can leave
out one it filed within the hour. The kinds:
  repeat  one method and URL called `repeat` times or more
  hidden  calls made while the tab was hidden, by owner
  failed  calls that failed (isFailed), by method and URL
  large   one response of `large` bytes or more
  heavy   the window's bytes reaching `heavy`
  burn    the token's remaining calls falling by `burn` or more; the token
          is shared by every tab and device on it, so `mine` says how many
          of those calls this page made
`o.owner(e)` names who made a call, `o.rate` is { from, to } remaining.

A GraphQL call's key carries its operation (gh-boot.js's `op`), since
every query shares the one URL and would otherwise read as one repeat.
The ledger rows behind one of jobRows' rows, newest first.

The header's figures for the whole tab: every call since the page loaded,
how many of them went out while it was hidden, and how many a job claimed.
Calls and bytes come from the running totals; the hidden and claimed
shares can only be read off rows still in the ledger, so they say so.
`errors` (the running total) splits, over the rows held, into `notFound`,
a 404, which is usually the app checking for a file a repo does not keep,
and `failed`, everything else: another status of 400 or more, or no answer.

The live read, for a browser: this page's Resource Timing entries and its
navigation entry, folded by `fold` (boot or pageFiles). Kept apart from the
pure functions above so the analysis tests without a performance object.

treemap.js — pure logic for mapping a file tree as a treemap.
Extracted from pages/repo-atlas.html so the kernels are testable (npm test)
and reusable by other visualizers (IDB stores, zip contents, …).
No DOM, no colors — rendering choices stay with the page.

window.treemap exposes:
  CATS                         category key → label (seven keys)
  categorize(name)             file name → category key
  buildTree(entries, rootName) git-trees entries → node tree with rollups
  catTotals(node)              { cat: { bytes, files } } under a node
  squarify(items, x, y, w, h)  weighted items → rects (squarified layout)
  fmtBytes(n)                  byte count → '6.4 MB'

── Category taxonomy ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Seven keys: six identity families + 'other'. Colors are the caller's
concern (repo-atlas assigns the dataviz palette's dark categorical slots).

── Tree build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
entries: git-trees-API shape — [{ path, type: 'blob'|'tree'|…, size }].
Returns the root of a node tree: dirs { name, path, isDir:true, size,
children, fileCount, dirCount, parent }, files { name, path, isDir:false,
size, cat, parent }. Children sorted by size desc; sizes rolled up.
Aggregate bytes/files per category under a node.

── Squarified treemap (Bruls, Huizing & van Wijk 2000) ────────────────────
items: [{ weight }] sorted desc. Returns rects [{x,y,w,h}] aligned to
items, tiling (x,y,w,h) exactly; each row is laid along the shorter side,
rows accept items while the worst aspect ratio improves.

guard: the 0.0001 area floor (and float drift) can exhaust the region
before the items run out — emit zero rects rather than negative ones
region taller than wide → row spans the width

The row's worst aspect ratio is max(thick²/minArea, maxArea/thick²),
so a min/max/sum triple scores each candidate in O(1) — no row copy,
no rescan (matters in files mode, where flat dirs make √n-long rows).

── Formatting ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Kept on the surface for repo-atlas, which reads it from here; the rule is
the estate's one (Traffic.fmtBytes).

Reading a page's own input params, fragment first, query as fallback.

Every page in this repo that takes input by URL wants the same precedence,
for two reasons that pull in opposite directions:

  The fragment is the DEFAULT and the private form. It never reaches a
  server, so it carries unbounded payloads (GitHub Pages' edge 414s a URL
  past roughly 8KB, which is what drove the payload to '#' in PR #165) and
  leaks nothing to logs on the way.

  The query is the FALLBACK, for contexts that eat the '#': a toss-render
  frame (whose params shim answers ?query lookups, which is how a routed
  toss delivers ?src= to the page it mounts), an email or chat client that
  strips the fragment, a deep link pasted through a rewriter.

So: put payloads in the fragment, put short addresses wherever is
convenient, and read both here rather than picking one per page. This is
the general form of the rule StageLink.read already applies to stage links
and toss-render applies to its own params (toss-render keeps a private
two-line copy on purpose: its critical render path loads no lib).

Values come back URLSearchParams-decoded, so a base64 payload must use the
URL-safe alphabet ('-' and '_'); a literal '+' would decode to a space.
Every encoder in this repo emits base64url, and the decoders normalize it
back, so this is a constraint on new callers rather than a live bug.

withKey() is the write half, for a page that addresses its own view back
into the fragment. It is the same contract read backwards, which is why it
lives here rather than beside its one caller.

subject() is the same precedence applied to a whole half of an address rather
than one key: which params belong to a page being FRAMED, when the framer
owns the query and the subject owns the fragment. See its own comment.

Pure: no DOM beyond the location it is handed, no network. Attaches to
window.UrlParams.

The location to read when a caller passes nothing. Guarded so the module
loads in a non-browser realm (the tests import it against a stub).

One key, fragment first. Absent and empty are both misses, so a stray
'?src=' in a URL cannot mask a real '#src='.

The first key that has a value, as [key, value]. Lets a page declare its
input modes in precedence order (payload before address, say) and take
whichever arrived, in one read.

Which half holds the value get() would take: 'hash', 'search', or null,
under the same rule (fragment first, absent and empty both misses). For a
caller whose several keys must ride together from one source, or whose
fragment payload must be parsed raw rather than URLSearchParams-decoded
(the stage spec encodes '&' inside paths, which get() would decode into a
live delimiter): pick the source here, read it with your own parser.

Set one key in a param string, leaving every other segment byte for byte.
The write half of get(): a page that addresses its own view in the
fragment (data-view's `#item=`) has to edit one key of a string it does
not own the rest of.

Deliberately string surgery on the '&' segments rather than a
URLSearchParams round-trip. A fragment here routinely carries a '#gz='
payload beside the view key, and re-serializing re-encodes the payload:
correct in principle, a rewrite of tens of kilobytes in practice, and
wrong outright for a segment that is not 'k=v' shaped.

A null, undefined, or empty value removes the key. A leading '#' or '?'
is preserved when the input has one, and dropped when the result is
empty, so an assignment never leaves a bare marker behind. Pass '#' for
an empty fragment to get one back on the result.

── The whole of the other side's params, not one key ────────────────────

For a page that FRAMES another page and has to decide which half of its own
address belongs to the thing inside it. The rule the shell settled on, and
the reason it is stated here rather than there:

  The framer owns the query. The fragment is the subject's.

A shared namespace needs a reserved list on both sides, and the two sides
live in different repos with nothing comparing them, so the next key either
one adds is a silent collision that presents as "the deep link opened the
wrong screen". Split the namespaces and there is no list to keep.

`reserved` is the small, closed set the FRAMER still claims in the fragment
(the app claims stage/prompts/mode there, for stage links). Everything
else in the fragment is handed on untouched, including keys nobody has
thought of yet, which is the property the split is for.

Returns a param string ('a=1&b=2'), not a URLSearchParams, because the
caller's next move is to concatenate it onto an address: re-serializing
would re-encode a payload segment that was never 'k=v' shaped, the same
reason withKey() above does string surgery.

Fragment first, query second, under the file's own rule: `?on=` is the
fallback for a context that eats the '#', and it arrives percent-encoded as
one value, so it is decoded before the same filter runs over it.

kits/user-calls.js — what waits on the owner (window.UserCalls).

Two queues, read together because the owner meets them together:

  USER CALLS: one decision a session needs from the owner, one file each in
  web-tools-private user-calls/ (user-call/1, written by user-call.py). A
  call is open while its status is open and no answer line has come back in
  its <id>.answers.jsonl. Calls are filed straight to main
  (docs/direct-to-main.csv), so main is the ref read.

  PROPOSED EDITS: the Text collection's proposals in mehrlander/home
  (projects/text/proposals.jsonl), each a passage pair put forward for one
  file. The collection keeps a proposal after it is applied ("the file
  either carries the new text or it does not"), so what counts is what
  Dictate's &proposed would stage on the file as it stands: its own matcher,
  mdVariants.plan, run over each named file at main, counting the blocks
  whose picked variant is proposed for that file. Raw rows overcount badly
  (582 rows, 2026-10-04), and so does any looser match: a passage spanning
  two blocks, or one found only inside a longer block, is never staged, so a
  marker promising it would open on nothing. Those are kept apart, each with
  the reason Dictate cannot stage it, so a view can say they exist rather
  than leave a file silently short. The plan needs the collection's
  passages (4.5MB), so this is read when a view asks, never at boot.

  UserCalls.list({ token, fresh })          -> every user call, newest first,
                                               each with `answers` and `open`
  UserCalls.pendingEdits({ token, fresh })  -> Map 'owner/repo:path' ->
                                               { file, calls, staged, items, bases, unstaged, moot }
                                               items: [{ from, to, author, purpose, kind, basis, gloss,
                                                         fromId, toId, notes }]
                                               gloss: the purpose's definition in purposes.csv
                                               fromId, toId: the passage ids a review row names
                                               notes: the comments reviews.jsonl holds on the pair
                                               A proposal a reader voted down is not pending:
                                               rejecting is what that vote records.
                                               kind: mdVariants.kind(purpose), 'edit' | 'tighten'
                                               unstaged: the file's other open proposals, which
                                               Dictate cannot stage (mdVariants.unstaged) and a
                                               person still could by hand: the items' fields,
                                               less the ids and notes, plus `reason`
                                               moot: the same for those whose text or file is
                                               gone (reason 'gone' or 'file'), which no one
                                               can act on; an applied one is left out
  UserCalls.where(call)                     -> owner/repo[@ref]:path of a call
  UserCalls.href(call)                      -> where a call is answered
  UserCalls.sessionHref(call)               -> the session page that filed it
  UserCalls.dictateHref({ file, call, proposed })
                                            -> Dictate on a file, the call's
                                               edits or its proposals staged;
                                               `proposed` true stages all of
                                               them, 'edit' or 'tighten' one kind

Links are built at the version of web-tools the page runs at (the
selection, GH.refFor), so a view opened from a branch hands the reader the
branch's Dictate rather than main's. Both reads are cached for the page;
`fresh` reads again.

'owner/repo@ref:path' and 'owner/repo:path' name the same document here:
a proposal names no ref, and a call's ref only says where to read it.
The reasons no one can act on: the text a proposal changes, or its file, is gone.
one unreadable call is not the list failing

A file main no longer holds is a reason, not a failure; any other
failed read is said nothing about, since it may be this reader's.

A rejection is a down vote in reviews.jsonl (Text Lab's and the
Docs reader's), and it sticks: a proposal some reader voted down and
none voted up is no longer waiting on anyone.

Each staged block as the detail draws it: the file's block as it
stands, the proposed text, and who proposed it on what basis.

What Dictate cannot stage, so a file is never silently short: an
applied pair and a rejected one have been answered, and are left out.
One whose text or file is gone is moot, apart from the rest.

A hub page at the version this page runs at: main's own address, or the
toss renderer at the selected ref, which carries the query and fragment
through to the page.

A pick call is answered on its image board; every other kind, a
documentation call included, on its call page.

vanilla-demo.js — the living-documentation demo format, distilled from
pages/drop/live-docs-concept.html. A page hands it a `sections` config; it
renders the whole literate document: numbered sections, each holding compact
examples that pair prose with an editable snippet and a live proof (rendered
markup, markup in a host context, JS drawing into a frame, or console output).

Sibling to vanilla-bundle.js: a framework-free, DOM-rendering module loaded
via gh.load. Not a logic kit (it renders), not an Alpine component (no
framework). Depends on kits/cm6.js for the editor and kits/proof.js for
the sandboxed proof documents (load both before this file), and on
Tailwind + daisyUI + Phosphor being present on the host page for styling.
The proof iframes are isolated (sandbox allow-scripts, opaque origin) and
bring their own minimal CSS — plus Tailwind (`tw:true`), the full daisyUI
stack (`daisy:true`), and any `inject` scripts a block opts into. The
`parent` kind is the deliberate exception: it runs in the host page,
unsandboxed.

  demo.mount({ sections, sectionsEl, displayEl?, legendEl? })

  A repo-relative `inject` path ('kits/x.js') is read through the page's
  loader (gh.get, at the page's ?use=<ref>) before the blocks build, and
  rides into each frame inline. Absolute http(s) entries load as <script src>.

Config shape:
  sections: [{ title, intro?, examples: [example] }]
  example:  { title, prose?, lang: 'html'|'js', code,
              kind: 'render'|'context'|'jsrender'|'console'|'parent'|'stage',
              tw?: bool,        // inject Tailwind into the proof frame
              daisy?: bool,     // inject Tailwind + daisyUI + Phosphor (implies tw)
              inject?: string[],// <script src> loaded into the frame head, in order
              context?: string  // host template with a {{slot}} marker (kind:'context')
            }

The six kinds:
  render    — the snippet is body markup; the proof is what it renders.
  context   — the snippet is injected at {{slot}} inside a host template.
  jsrender  — the snippet is JS that builds nodes into the frame body.
  console   — the snippet is JS run in a sandboxed frame; the proof is
               captured console output (Run / Mod-Enter). Wrapped in an async
               IIFE, so it can `await` and use any injected globals.
  parent    — the snippet is JS run in the HOST page (not isolated), for code
               that needs real storage, downloads, the clipboard, or the
               page's already-loaded kits. Runs only on Run / Mod-Enter,
               never on edit, so file dialogs don't fire while you type.
  stage     — `parent` with somewhere to draw: the snippet is handed a
               `stage` element in the proof area, cleared before each run,
               and its console is captured under it. For demonstrating what
               a reader USES rather than what a call returned: a drop
               target, a paste surface, a mounted Alpine component.

THE CLIPBOARD WRITE IS kits/io.js's, and this two-line delegate is all any
kit keeps of it. Four of them carried the same textarea-fallback block,
pasted and lightly reworded, and the block is not boilerplate: it is the
iOS recipe io.js documents at length (focusable, not readonly, read the
value rather than trusting execCommand's return). Four copies of that is
four places for it to be subtly wrong, and three of them already differed
from each other in whether they returned anything.

It is FETCHED at load time rather than at click time. A clipboard write
has to run inside the user gesture that asked for it, and an await before
the write can spend the activation Safari is counting; loading the kit
when this one loads means it is simply there by the time a finger arrives.
The guard survives for the page that never gets it, and falls back to the
modern API alone, which is honest: no io.js, no legacy path.
── shared editor settings, applied across every block via the Display control ──

inline block hosts, checked once by the load fail-safe
per-host loading spinners, live-updated from cm6.loadStatus()

── isolated proof documents — built by kits/proof.js ──
Repo-relative inject paths, read once by mount() through the page's
loader and handed to proof.doc as inline code. Inline because the frame is
sandboxed (opaque origin, no token) and no host that tracks a ref serves a
script as a script; the loader already reads every other file this way.
── Display control: a small popover that drives every editor at once ──
── host-template dialog (kind:'context') — read-only CM6 view of the harness ──

WHO OWNS THE CONSOLE. A host snippet's output is captured by patching
console for the duration of its run, which is right for `parent` and wrong
for `stage`: a stage snippet's job is usually to WIRE something, and the
handler it wires runs long after run() returned, with the patch already
lifted. The first thing built on the stage kind logged from inside a drop
handler; the line went to the browser's console and the box under the stage
stayed empty (measured headlessly, 2026-09-13).

So the patch is installed once and never lifted, and what moves is the
SINK. `parent` claims it for its run and drops it after; `stage` keeps it
until another host snippet runs. Every level still forwards to the real
console, so nothing is swallowed either way.

── the live demo block: editor + proof. Returns the card synchronously;
the CM6 editor mounts async and wires the proof once ready. ──

`stage` is `parent` plus somewhere to draw. Both run in the host page on
a real Run click and capture its console; the difference is that a stage
snippet is handed an element, so a demo can show a thing you USE (a drop
target, a paste surface, a mounted component) and not only what it
logged. A sandboxed frame cannot stand in: the whole point of these two
kinds is the host page's own capabilities.
console-style output area + line painter, shared by `console` and `parent`.

Runs in the host page — no iframe, full page capabilities. Never fires
on edit; only Run / Mod-Enter execute it, so a real user gesture backs
file dialogs, downloads, and clipboard calls. console is patched for
the duration of the run and restored after.

The stage sits ABOVE the console box: what the snippet drew is the
proof, and the log is the running commentary beside it.

Cleared per run, so a second Run is a second demonstration rather
than a second copy stacked under the first.

`stage` is a declared parameter only for the stage kind: naming it
for every host snippet would shadow whatever a `parent` snippet
happens to call its own variable.

A stage keeps the console until another host snippet takes it, so
whatever it wired still reports.

TWO TRACKS ON A WIDE SCREEN, stacked on a narrow one. The commentary
takes a rail and the editor with its proof takes the rest, so the prose
gets its measure from a grid TRACK rather than from a cap on the text
element, which is what house style rule 3 asks for: the page's own
layout sets the width. The caps this replaces (max-w-[66ch] here and
max-w-[64ch] on a section intro) were Tailwind's 65ch reading column in
a third disguise, invisible to the scanner that refuses the named sizes.

`min-w-0` on the right track is load-bearing: a grid column's default
`auto` floor is its content, so one long line in an editor or a proof
widens the track and pushes the page into a horizontal scroll.

── editor load fail-safe ──────────────────────────────────────────────
Every block's editor awaits one shared module load (cm6's modsPromise,
surfaced as cm6.preload()). cm6 retries transient import failures itself;
this is the backstop for when retries are exhausted or the load hangs. We

kits/visit-log.js — turn an address into a storable visit, by allowlist.

A visit log stores where a reader went. The hazard is that in this estate an
address is not always a location: #gz= and #html= carry a whole document in
the fragment, and a stage link folds local text in beside its refs
(alpineComponents/stage.js: "Refs are pointers, so their content stays behind
the token; everything else is authored or carried, so it rides the link
itself"). A log that stored addresses verbatim would therefore store pasted
documents, and a workbench you used on local data would leak it into the
record the moment you navigated away.

THE DEFENCE IS NOT A FILTER. A filter is a list of the payload forms someone
thought of, so the next form nobody thought of rides straight through. This
module never carries its input forward at all: it matches the address against
a closed list of recognized routes, pulls out the fields that route declares,
checks each against a narrow grammar, and REBUILDS the stored row from the
route's own template. Nothing that arrived is written. A payload has nowhere
to ride, even when the match is wrong, because a matched template has no slot
shaped like a payload.

The three outcomes, and only one of them is a defect:

  matched        rebuilt from the template. Safe by construction.
  unrecognized   nothing stored but the PATHNAME and a count. Costs a gap in
                 the log, and is the signal that the registry has fallen
                 behind the code. The pathname is safe because every payload
                 form in this system rides in the fragment or the query and
                 never in the path.
  misrecognized  a row labelled as route X that was really route Y. Costs a
                 wrong label and a link that opens the wrong screen. Still
                 cannot leak, since X's template decided every field written.

A live case where a filter and an allowlist disagree, from this repo rather
than from a thought experiment: pages/toss-render.html reads
`param('url') || param('u')`, and until 2026-09-17 docs/routes-modes.csv had
no row for `u`. A filter stripping known payload keys would not have known
`u` and would have stored the payload. This module never matched it, so it
recorded an unrecognized visit and nothing else. `u` has a row now, which is
the misalignment the unrecognized outcome exists to surface.

THE ALLOWLIST IS DATA, AND NOT THIS FILE'S. Delivery modes come from
docs/routes-modes.csv, whose `carries` column is already `inline` against
`reference`; typed toss keys from docs/routes-routes.csv; app routes from
docs/app-routes.csv. All three are governed
registries (docs/registries.csv), so this module joins rather than
classifying, and a new mode is described once rather than twice. The caller
hands the tables in.

Pure: no DOM, no network, no clock, no storage. The caller supplies the
address, the tables and the timestamp. Storage is the shell's, the way
route-activity.js folds and the shell crawls.

  VisitLog.classify(href, { modes, routes, tossRoutes, now }) -> row | null
  VisitLog.key(row)                               -> the dedupe key

Attaches to window.VisitLog, loaded via gh.load('kits/visit-log.js').

── The grammars ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Narrow on purpose, and narrower than the parsers that READ these forms.
repo-address.js accepts `(.+)` for a path because it has to parse whatever
git allows; this module is deciding what to WRITE, so it accepts only what
it is willing to store. A path carrying '?' or '#' is refused rather than
trimmed: trimming is the sanitizing move this file exists to avoid, and a
refusal lands in `unrecognized` where it is visible.

LENGTH IS THE CONTROL THAT ACTUALLY STOPS BULK, and saying so is the point
of this note. A character class does not separate a path from a payload:
base64url is [A-Za-z0-9_-], which `[\w.\-\/]+` accepts happily, so an
unbounded PATH stored a 226-character gzip blob arriving as
`?view=project&project=<blob>`. The corpus test caught it; the fix is a
bound sized to what each field legitimately holds, plus the row-size cap
below as the backstop no single grammar has to carry.

The honest residue: a SHORT string that is not a path can still be stored
as one. That is the misrecognized outcome, and it is acceptable by design,
because a wrong label costs a wrong link while bulk costs the document.

A view key, a tab, a lens: the short vocabulary words the app's own query
uses. Never a free string.

A record id: a session stem, a branch spec, a commit-ish. Bounded, because
an unbounded "id" is a place for anything to hide.

Why an address was not stored. A CLOSED VOCABULARY: the value written is
looked up here by a key this file controls, so no rejection reason can be
assembled out of the address it is rejecting.

── The route templates ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

One row per storable shape. `fields` names what may be written and the
grammar each must satisfy; nothing outside it is ever read off the address.
`kind` is what the row IS, which is what a reader groups by.
A toss of a repo file, the estate's one durable render address.
A typed toss: the key names a renderer, the value addresses the content.

The app's own routes. `view` is the route key; the rest is whatever that
route's row in docs/app-routes.csv is entitled to carry.

A stage link's REFS only. The `gz` segment beside them is local content
and is never a field here, so it cannot be written even by a caller
asking for this template by name.

Which delivery modes may be stored at all, read off the table's own
`carries` column rather than named here. An unknown value is treated as
inline, so a typo in the registry fails closed.

Every mode the table describes, storable or not. A mode that is described
and inline is REFUSED by name; a mode that is not described at all falls
through to unrecognized. Both end with nothing stored, and the difference
is only what the log can tell you afterwards.

The TYPED TOSS keys, from docs/routes-routes.csv. routes-modes.csv carries
a single `<route>` row standing for all of them, which is right for a table
describing delivery modes and useless as an allowlist: a key has to be
matchable by name. So the third registry is read here rather than inferred.
The app's route keys, from docs/app-routes.csv.

Re-mint: take a template and a bag of candidate values, and emit ONLY the
fields the template declares, only where the grammar accepts them. This is
the whole safety property, in six lines.

Split `owner/repo[@ref]:path` with repo-address.js, which owns the
grammar, without inheriting its permissive path: mint() holds each part to
the narrower grammars above, so a trailing ?query or #frag makes the whole
thing refuse rather than get trimmed. See the note on the grammars.

The fragment, as key/value segments. Read by slice rather than
URLSearchParams, matching toss-render's own readFragment: a payload
segment is not 'k=v' shaped and must not be re-encoded on the way past.

── classify ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Returns a row, or null when the address is not a visit at all (an empty
string, a parse failure). An unrecognized address is a ROW, not a null:
the count is the point, and a silent drop would hide the drift this whole
design is built to surface.
THE BACKSTOP. Every grammar above is a judgement about one field; this is a
fact about the whole row. A visit row is a handful of short identifiers, so
anything past this is carrying something, whatever it claimed to be, and is
refused as unrecognized rather than stored. It exists so that no future
field, and no combination of fields each individually plausible, can smuggle
bulk past a per-field check.

The pathname is always safe to carry, so every row gets it and an
unrecognized row gets nothing else.

`why` IS A CODE FROM A CLOSED SET, never a sentence built from the
address. It read `'view=' + view + ' is in no route registry'` for an
hour and that was a leak: a payload arriving as ?view=<blob> reached the
row inside its own rejection reason. The corpus test at the foot of
node/test/visit-log.test.mjs caught it, which is the whole argument for
testing the property rather than the cases. Interpolating input into a
diagnostic is the same mistake as storing it, and a refusal path is the
easiest place in a design like this to make it.

1. THE FRAGMENT FIRST, because a delivery mode outranks whatever query
the page also carries: a #gz= toss of a page whose own ?view= rides
along is a payload visit, not an app route.

A described mode that carries content: refuse it BY NAME, so the log
can say a local document was rendered without holding a byte of it.

REFS ONLY. The spec half is stored; every other segment of a stage
link (gz, prompts, cmp, view, dest) is left behind, and `gz` is
content by the grammar above rather than by this exclusion.
A typed toss: the key is a registered renderer, the value an address.

A fragment that carried something this module does not recognize is
unrecognized, never "probably fine". Anchors are the one exception, since
a bare '#heading' is a scroll target rather than an address.

2. THE QUERY, for the app's own routes. `?on=` is the fragment's query
fallback and may carry a subject's whole param string, so it is a
payload here exactly as a fragment mode would be.

── key ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

What makes two visits the same destination. The READING PARAMETERS are
deliberately out of it (lens, grain, window, smode, set): revisiting a
screen at a different lens moves the one row rather than splitting it, so
the list stays a list of places. `tab` IS in the key, because Map's twelve
tabs are twelve panes rather than twelve readings of one.

Every unrecognized visit to one pathname collapses to one key, which is
what turns a leak-proof refusal into a countable signal.

wring.js — single-document template induction: give it one document with
repeated structure (a log, an HTML page) and it returns the recurring
templates (fixed boilerplate with variable slots) plus the values filling
each slot. Lossless: templates + slot values reconstruct the original
exactly.

Load via gh.load('kits/wring.js'); exposes window.wring.
  const run  = wring.induce(logText, { group: 'align' });   // text → templates
  const sigs = wring.extractSignaturesFromNodes(document);  // DOM → signatures
  const res  = wring.groupByTemplate(sigs);                 //   → templates

  run.result     // { groups: [{ template, members, score }], ungrouped }
                 //   template uses ${N} slot markers; each member is
                 //   { original, slots }
  run.fidelity   // { pass, total }: members that reconstruct exactly

The stages individually:
  wring.tokenize(text, mode)             // 1: 'punct'|'word'|'char'|'line'
  wring.induceGrammar(tokens)            // 2: Re-Pair grammar of repeats
  wring.groupByTemplate(strings, opts)   // 3-4: Bookend Merge + MDL
  wring.groupByAlignment(records, opts)  // 3: positional alignment
  wring.selectTemplates(input)           // 4: full MDL selection
  wring.reconstruct(template, slots, delimiter = '.')
                                         // 5: rebuild a Bookend Merge member
  wring.reconstructAlign(template, slots)  // 5: rebuild an aligned record

The pipeline runs Stage 1 (segment) → Stage 2 (grammar) → Stages 3-4 (group
and select) → Stage 5 (reconstruct); the stage sections below are in that
order. Edit this file directly: it is the live copy. It began as a
concatenation of the modules in mehrlander/wring (archived read-only;
reference snapshot under archive/wring/, design notes in
archive/wring/ARCHITECTURE.md), and stopped being generated on 2026-09-06.

Two choices differ from ARCHITECTURE.md. Stage 2 is Re-Pair (Larsson &
Moffat, 2000) where that document names Sequitur: both build a hierarchical
grammar of exact repeats, Re-Pair is offline and greedily replaces the most
frequent digram, and the { start, rules, ruleUses } interface takes either.
Stage 3 has two groupers because Bookend Merge groups on the longest shared
literal, which on a log line is an incidental field: records sharing a
client IP group together while the real template fractures.
groupByAlignment groups on positional agreement instead (the Drain and
LogMine idea), and induce(text, { group: 'align' }) selects it.

kits/write-kinds.js — what wrote a commit, read off the commit itself.

Five writers share one GitHub identity in this estate: the Web Tools app,
the phone (through Log-Repo in mehrlander/shortcut-tools), the workflows that
write with the owner's token (the hourly cache pass, the scheduled-tasks
workflow), the Gemini daemon on the home laptop, and a pull-request merge all
commit as the account owner. Only a Claude session stands apart,
authored as `Claude`. So `%an` answers almost nothing and the subject line is
the signal, which is why the app's own messages are a contract rather than a
courtesy. Every new write a person makes by tapping in the app ends
` via Web Tools` (TAP below), and a change to any subject's shape changes this
file in the same commit.

The split that matters is not who typed but WHAT KIND OF RECORD a commit is:

  development history  a session, a merge, a person's own commit, CI
  application state    the app's crawl, a tap in the app, the phone's log,
                       a workflow run

Both are real commits on a real branch. Nothing but this reading separates
them, and the second kind is the one that surprises a reader of `git log`,
because nobody deliberately made most of it: the crawl refreshes its caches
on a tab-arrival kick, not only on the Refresh button.

Every kind carries `sure`. Seven read a signal the writer emits deliberately
(an author name the platform sets, a subject this repo writes on purpose).
`device` alone is a heuristic over an OBSERVED vocabulary, so it is marked
unsure and a consumer may say so. A guess that cannot be told from a fact is
the failure this field exists to prevent.

Attaches window.WriteKinds. Pure: no network, no DOM, no clock.

The app's five cache refreshes. These are exact: this repo writes them, in
app/index.html, and each names the derived file it rewrites. The phone's
session-menu copy joined on 2026-09-08, in a merge, which is the reason this
list is a regex here rather than a rule someone remembers: a new crawl write
lands in `authored` until it is added, which is the honest failure direction.
The traffic log (kits/traffic-log.js) joined on 2026-10-16: not a cache, but
the same kind of record, written by the app on its own clock.

A write a GITHUB ACTIONS RUN made with the owner's token, so neither the
author nor, for a cache refresh, the subject told it from the app's own
crawl: until 2026-10-09 the hourly pass's writes read as the browser's.
The runners append the trailer on purpose (node/activity-crawl.mjs,
node/sessions-crawl.mjs, python/scheduled-tasks.py), and it is tested
before the crawl, whose subjects it extends. Older run writes stay crawl.

A write the GEMINI DAEMON made on the home laptop (web-tools-private
sessions/tools/poll_followup.py, errand_runner.py and schedule_runner.py
append the trailer).
Its sessions-cache refresh carries the app's own crawl subject, so it too is
tested before the crawl. Older daemon writes stay authored, or crawl.

A write a PERSON made by tapping in the app. `the app` is the same
trailer under the app's old internal name and stays readable, since 608
commits already carry it and history keeps the name it was written with.
Both merge shapes GitHub produces: the merge commit and the squash.

OBSERVED on 2026-09-08, not a contract: the subjects Log-Repo has actually
produced in the registry repo. A new op lands in `authored` until it is
added here, which is the honest failure direction.

Order is the classifier. The run and daemon trailers go first, then the two
exact app signals, because a trailer, a crawl subject or a tap trailer
settles the question outright; author tests follow; the residual is
`authored`, which claims nothing.

commit: { msg, author } — the shape lib/kits/repo-activity-cache.js stores
in recentCommits. Anything else returns `authored`, since a classifier that
throws on a short row would take a whole pane down with it.

Counts in KINDS order, so a caller renders a stable row rather than one
that reshuffles as the data changes. Zero-count kinds are kept: an absent
category and a category with nothing in it read differently.

How much of a set is application state rather than development. The one
number this kit exists to make available, and the reason the pane's accent
marks that split and nothing else.
