What the legend lists: the categories when colour varies by point, the
series otherwise, each with the mark its chart draws.

Where the legend sits and the margin it takes from each side of the frame.
Excel writes r, l, t, b or tr; tr and anything unrecognised read as r, the
schema default. Excel has placed new legends at the bottom since 2013, so
the row form is the common one rather than the exception.
A row legend wraps into as many lines as the frame's width needs.
Zero is always inside the value range, as Excel's automatic axis keeps it.

lib/kits/xlsx-extract.js — PICK PART OF A WORKBOOK AND CARRY THE ANSWER
AWAY. kits/xlsx.js already reads every part of an .xlsx and returns plain
objects; what was missing was a way to ask for SOME of that reading and hand
the result to something else. This kit is that selection, and nothing more:
it writes no file back, reconstructs no workbook, and renders nothing.

SHEETS FIRST. The current picker selects kinds independently within each
sheet, then selects modeled objects individually. A related pivot or cache
is never included merely because its associated sheet is selected. The
original two-axis cross-product remains as extract() for v1 callers.

THE ANSWER IS A data-view ENVELOPE, with provenance. Every kind here
serialises to a table of rows or to a block of source text, which is exactly
what a data-view item carries, so an extract renders in pages/data-view.html
today with no new page and no new viewer. The one thing that envelope has no
slot for is where the extract CAME FROM: which workbook, at which ref, what
was picked, and what was left behind. v1 and v2 are both data-view profiles,
and the reasoning for making it a profile over data-view rather than a
sibling of it is in docs/envelopes/workbook-extract.md.

EVERY CUT IS REPORTED, never silently applied. The habit is pivotRecords':
each item carries the rows it returned against the total it could have, so a
reader can see the edge rather than discover it. The same fact is written
into the item's `note`, where today's data-view reader shows it without
knowing this format exists.

Pure: no DOM, no network, no zip. Takes an already-analysed result (what
xlsxKit.readZip or .analyze returns) and returns a plain object. Attaches to
window.XlsxExtract. Contract and worked examples:
docs/envelopes/workbook-extract.md.

  catalog(result)                 survey() plus objects: pivots, cached
                                  records, connections and queries
  extractSelected(result, pick, opts) -> v2 envelope (SELECTED_KIND);
                                  pick: { sheets: [{ name, kinds }], objects }
  survey(result)                  every sheet by every sheet kind, with counts;
                                  a zero is reported, not omitted
  extract(result, pick, opts)     v1 envelope (KIND); pick: { sheets, kinds,
                                  headerRow }, opts: { source, maxRows, title,
                                  note, now }. No sheets takes every sheet;
                                  no kinds takes nothing
  profileRows(sheet, xl, headerRow)  profileColumns as table rows
  sheetTables(result)             every sheet as typed rows keyed by column
                                  letter: [{ name, hidden, visibility, rows }]
  receptions(cat, declared)       match .web-tools.json receptions to a catalog:
                                  [{ reception, pick, omitted, never, cap }]
  receptionTarget(r, source, now, sheet) -> { dest, file }, with {date},
                                  {time}, {stem}, {slug} and {sheet} filled
  KINDS                           the readings on offer, with scope and view

Read at call time rather than at load: this kit is registered before a
page's gh.load chain finishes, so binding the namespace here would capture
an undefined. The throw names the missing load, since the alternative is a
TypeError three frames down that reads as a bug in this file.
A1 address from a zero-based column index and a 1-based row.

A sheet's rows keyed by the column letter, which is what sheetRows returns
and what every tabular kind below either is or joins to.

---- the kinds ----------------------------------------------------------

One entry per kind. `count` is the cheap answer for a picker's matrix and
`parts` is the expensive one that actually builds rows; the two MUST agree,
since a matrix cell showing 400 beside an item holding 12 is a lie about
the file rather than about the cut. Where a cheap count could not be made
exact the kind counts the same way it produces (`columns` scans the row
keys, which is the set profileColumns itself enumerates).

`parts` returns a LIST, because three kinds legitimately produce more than
one item: a workbook has one records table per pivot cache and one M
section per query part, and folding those together would lose which cache
or which section a row came from.

One sheet in the serialized-workbook shape:
  { SheetName, Dimension, MergedCells: ['A1:B1', …],
    Cells: [{ Address, Formula, Value }, …] }
Formula is '' for an entered cell, '=<text>' where the file stored text,
and '=[fill N] <master text>' for a shared-formula follower, whose own
text the file never stored. Value is the cached value as a string, which
is how the PowerShell exporter writes it too.

A number a cell holds, for the formula table's Value column: the raw value
as stored, since a formula's result under a date format is a different
question from the formula itself.

A dxf index turned into the few words a reader needs: what the rule paints.
The full record is available through xlsxKit.dxfStyle; a table cell wants a
label, and an empty one is honest where the rule names no format at all.

A rule that names a dxf the file does not carry, and a rule whose dxf
sets nothing a renderer can draw, are different facts and read
differently: the index alone says "there is a format here that this
reading could not turn into anything".

Only the rows that travel are read through their formats, which is
the expensive part: on a 100,000-row sheet under the 2,000-row cap,
formatting every row and keeping 2,000 was most of a tick.

THE SAME ROWS AS DATA. Values reads each cell through its number
format, as the sheet draws it ("32,570.17", "3%"), which is what a
person reading the extract wants and what a reader computing on it
has to parse back. Here a number is a number, a date an ISO date and
a tick a boolean, from the rows sheetTables gives the workbench.
Added 2026-10-23, for an extract handed to a model.

The rows typedRows keeps (any cell with a value), counted without
building them: a survey counts every reading of every sheet, and
building 100,000 typed rows to count them was most of its time.

As with Values, only the rows that travel are typed. A sheet already
typed in full (the workbench door reads it so) is sliced instead.

The first maxRows rows that hold a value, as the full read would
keep them: an empty row in the file is not one of them.

THE SERIALIZED-WORKBOOK SHAPE, one object per sheet: every cell as
its address, its formula and its cached value, plus the sheet's
declared range and merges. It is the shape home's PowerShell
exporter (Get-WsDetail) writes and the fund view's reader consumes,
so an extract taken here lands where that export already lands. Raw
values on purpose: a number formatted "33,912,780" is a string the
reader cannot parse, and the cached value is what the file holds.
Never cut, since a partial sheet in this shape reads as a whole one.

A SHARED formula's followers store no text of their own. The
kit reports those as `true` rather than as an empty string, so
the distinction survives to here: an empty Formula cell means
the file did not store one, and the note says how many.

A border is four edges and a table cell is one string: the
sides that are drawn, named. The full record is one
xlsxKit.cellStyle call away for anything that needs it.

The options as the file lists them, joined: a choice list is the
fact, and the reader wants to read it rather than expand a nested
array in a tree.

WHAT THIS KIND IS NOT. These are the rules as the file states them.
Which cells Excel would actually paint is a second question, and the
kit answers it only for the rule types decidable from a cell alone
(xlsxKit.cfApplies); an expression rule needs a formula engine.

A cache has no name of its own, so it is named by the range it was
built from. The part filename says nothing a reader knows.

What the part held against what the definition claims. The two
disagreeing is a fact about the file, not one to reconcile away.

The caches that actually carry rows. A workbook saved to refresh on open
has a definition and nothing behind it, which is a different answer from
"the pivot has no rows", so those are not offered rather than offered empty.

ONE RENDERING OF profileColumns, here rather than in the tab that draws it.
The Structure mode's Columns tab reads this too: two spellings of the same
table is how a column reads `Role` in one place and `role` in the other.

---- every sheet as rows, for a tool that computes over them ------------

The transform workbench's way into a workbook. `values` above reads a
sheet as Excel draws it, which is right for a reader and wrong for a
pivot: a number formatted `33,912,780` arrives as a string, and a sum over
strings is nothing. So each cell here keeps the type the file gave it.
Text stays text (a zero-padded code stays `01234`), a number is a number,
a boolean is a boolean, an error is its own text, and a date is ISO,
since a five-digit serial is the one raw value nobody can read.

KEYED BY COLUMN LETTER, with `Row` beside them, and no header guessed.
A form's row 1 is a title band, so promoting it would name one column and
blank the rest; letters and row numbers are also what the Sheet view
draws, so a row here can be found there. Promoting a header row is a
`rows => rows` step the workbench exists to run.

RECTANGULAR: every row carries every column the sheet uses, a blank as
'', in column order. A table tool reads its columns off the FIRST row
(the workbench's grid does), and a form's first row is often a lone
title in A, which showed one column of a sheet that used three.

Every sheet in workbook order, hidden ones included and flagged: this is
an inspection, and a hidden sheet is the one most worth seeing. A row
the file stores with no value in it (formatting only) is dropped, and a
sheet left with no rows is reported with an empty list, not omitted.
One sheet's rows as typed data, keyed by column letter plus `Row`, every
row carrying every used column. Shared by sheetTables and the `raw`
reading, so the workbench and an extract read a sheet the same way.
Kept per sheet object, since a survey counts it and a pick builds it.

---- the survey: what is on offer, and how much of it --------------------

The picker's whole input. Every sheet against every sheet-scoped kind,
plus the four workbook-scoped kinds once. A zero is REPORTED rather than
omitted, for the reason the Structure mode keeps an empty tab in its strip:
a cell that disappears when empty cannot say "this workbook has no pivots",
it just looks like a workbook with fewer kinds.

A filename stem from a sheet name. A sheet may be called "Q1 / Q2" or
"2024 Budget", and both have to survive into a name a link can address.

Names are the envelope's addresses (#item=), so a collision is a link that
opens the wrong item. Deduped by suffix rather than by throwing: two sheets
may legitimately reduce to one stem.

The one sentence an item's note carries, derived from the item's own
record rather than written beside it: the cut first, because it is the
thing a reader must not discover later, then whatever the kind had to say.

A label may already carry the extension (`Section1.m` is the part's
own filename), and appending it again minted `workbook.Section1.m.m`.

An empty kind produces NO ITEM rather than an empty one. The survey
already said the cell was zero, and a file of `[]` in the envelope
reads as a finding rather than as an absence.

WHAT WAS PICKED AND WHAT WAS LEFT, both stated. The second is the half
an envelope normally cannot express, and it is the difference between
"this is the workbook" and "this is four kinds out of fourteen".

A sheet-centered catalogue. A pivot table belongs to the sheet where it
is placed; a cache belongs beside its source sheet when that source is in
this workbook. Neither relationship implies that checking a sheet checks
the object. Cache rows can disclose data from another sheet, so objects
always require their own explicit selection.

v2 keeps the data-view item shape but records independent per-sheet kinds
and individual workbook objects. The v1 cross-product API above remains
available to existing callers; the Structure picker uses this contract.

---- receptions: a receiving repo's standing pick -----------------------

A repo's .web-tools.json may declare `receptions`: for a workbook whose
sheets match, which sheets to take, which to leave, which readings, and
where the extract lands. The receiver declares it and the picker runs it,
so nothing about any one workbook has to live in this kit or the page.

  { id, label, match: { sheets: [name…] }, omit: [name… | 'hidden'],
    never: [name…], readings: [kind…], cap, dest, file }

A reception with no `match.sheets` applies to every workbook; one that
names sheets applies only where all of them are present, by sheet set
rather than by file name because a workbook is renamed more often than
its tabs are. Declarations are tried in order, so a specific one listed
before a general one wins. Every sheet not omitted is taken, with the
readings it has any of. `omit` takes names and the token `hidden`, which
leaves behind every sheet the workbook hides: a gesture already made in
Excel, and one a rename does not undo. `cap` defaults to null (no row
cut), since a landed extract is a file rather than a link. `dest` and
`file` may carry `{date}`, `{stem}` and `{slug}`.

`never` NAMES SHEETS THAT MUST NOT LAND, and it is returned rather than
applied. Omitting them here would be the quiet fix: the reader would see a
clean pick and learn nothing, and the case this exists for is precisely
the one where the usual signal lapsed (a private sheet unhidden to work on
it, then forgotten). So a named sheet that is selected BLOCKS the handover
and says which, leaving the reader to re-hide it or untick it. `omit`
decides what is taken; `never` decides what may not be.

The declared names, not the ones currently in breach: a pick changes
with every tick, so the caller tests against this as it repaints and
there is one statement of the rule rather than two.

Where a reception's extract lands: `{date}` is the day (UTC) and `{time}`
the hour and minute (HHMM), both from `now`, which a caller passes as the
extract's own `taken` stamp so files sort in the order the sheets were
read; `{stem}` the workbook's name without its extension reduced to
filename characters, `{slug}` that stem lowercased, for a folder
convention that wants it, and `{sheet}` the one picked sheet's name
slugged, or `workbook` when the extract holds several.

kits/xlsx-map.js — HOW A WORKBOOK'S PARTS CONNECT, and what each sheet holds,
read from what kits/xlsx.js already parsed. Nothing here opens a file.

kits/xlsx.js joins each part to its neighbours (a pivot to the sheet it sits
on and the cache it reads, a table to its sheet, a chart to its drawing) and
stops there. The questions a reader brings to a workbook they did not build
are one step further: which sheets feed which, where a pivot's rows come
from, what a query loads and from where, which sheet is a table and which is
a form. Those are answered here, as rows a view can draw and a test can hold.

  XlsxMap.links(result)        every link, [{ kind, from, to, count, cells, via, detail }]
  XlsxMap.gist(result)         per sheet, in workbook order: size, shape, header, facts
  XlsxMap.queries(result)      each Power Query by name, [{ name, section, m }]
  XlsxMap.refs(text, ctx)      the sheets, tables and names one formula reaches
  XlsxMap.words(link)          a link as { from, verb, to }, for a table's columns
  XlsxMap.phrase(link)         the same as one line a reader can check

A link's `from` and `to` are nodes, { type, name, sheet }: `type` is one of
sheet, external, table, pivot, query, connection, chart. `sheet` is the
sheet a non-sheet node sits on, where it sits on one. Direction is the
direction data moves: Ledger -> Summary means Summary reads Ledger.

WHAT IS NOT READ. Formula references are found by pattern in the stored
text, after string literals are removed; INDIRECT, OFFSET over a computed
address and VBA can reach any sheet and are invisible to this. A shared
formula's followers are counted against their master's text, which names the
same sheets. Attaches to window.XlsxMap; loaded via gh.load('kits/xlsx-map.js').

kits/xlsx.js's own rule for a relationship target, repeated rather than
exported: a target is relative to the folder of the part that owns it.
---- the context a formula is read against -------------------------------

Sheet, table and defined names, each to the sheet it lives on, plus the
external workbooks in the order a formula's [n] counts them. The order
comes from workbook.xml's <externalReferences>, which kits/xlsx.js records
as an attribute set in document order; the filename's number is a
convention and is not used.
The sheets a reference text names, quoted or bare, by their real names.

`'Q1 / Q2'!A1`, `Ledger!A1`, `[1]Rates!B2`, `'[2]Year 2024'!C3` and the
two ends of a 3D `Jan:Mar!B4`. Bare names start with a letter or an
underscore, which is when Excel leaves a name unquoted.

ONE FORMULA'S REACH: the sheets it names, the tables its structured
references name, and the defined names it uses, each resolved to a sheet.
`self` is the sheet holding the formula, so a reference to its own sheet
is dropped rather than drawn as a loop.

EACH QUERY BY NAME. kits/xlsx.js returns the mashup's M files, and one
file (`Formulas/Section1.m`, usually the only one) holds every query as a
`shared Name = …;` member. The member is what Excel's Queries pane lists,
so it is the unit here. A member is found at the start of a line, so the
word inside a string or a comment does not open one.
Formulas: every computed cell, its own text or its master's.

One count per cell per source, however often the text names it;
every route it took (a table, a defined name) is kept.
A dropdown whose list lives on another sheet.
Charts: each series' ranges, to the chart on the sheet that draws it.

Pivots: the cache's source, to the table drawn from it. A source named
rather than addressed (a table or a defined name) is followed to its sheet.
Queries and connections: what each loads, and what each reads.

Which query a connection runs. Excel names it in the connection string
(`Location=AFRS`) and usually in the command; older files say it only in
the connection's name or description.

A query's connection that loads no table here (to the data model, or
only as a connection) is still the query's way out of the workbook.
A connection that is not a query reads from outside the workbook.
A query's own sources, by the M functions that name them.

Another query named in this one's text, unless the name is one of
this query's own steps (`Source` is a step in nearly every query and
occasionally also a query's name) or appears only inside a string
literal, comment, or bracketed field/record selector (`[Base]`).
Strings and comments go in one left-to-right pass, so the `//` of a
URL inside a string is not read as a comment opening.

A link as words: the subject, what it does, the object. The names are
the file's own; the verb is the only thing this decides.
A stored number arrives as its <v> text, so a string of digits is a number.

WHICH ROW NAMES THE COLUMNS, guessed once so a reader is shown headings
rather than a title band. The first of the top rows that is mostly text,
fills at least half the used width, and has rows under it.

HEADINGS OVER ROWS, and enough of either to be a list. Three headings
over two rows is a table; two are a form's label and value ("Prepared
by | Budget office") unless ten or more rows sit under them.

What a visible sheet keeps out of sight, which Values still
carries: hidden rows by number, hidden columns by letter, the
columns only within the used width (a <col> range may run to XFD).

lib/kits/xlsx-people.js — WHERE A WORKBOOK NAMES PEOPLE, and whose names
they are, found before any of it is shared. The question it answers is the
one asked before an extract leaves the device: does what I picked carry
anyone's name, and whose?

A NAME IS A FIRST NAME BESIDE A SURNAME, read off three public lists rather
than guessed from the shape of the text:

  first     about 8,800 English first names (@stdlib's two datasets, Apache-2.0)
  surnames  88,799 US Census surnames, most common first (@zxcvbn-ts/language-en, MIT)
  words     about 39,000 common English words, with no proper nouns (SCOWL
            sizes 10 to 35, US and shared spellings, via wordlist-english, MIT)

Two words in a row (`First Last`, `First M. Last`, `Last, First`), both
capitalized or both in capitals, are a name when the second is a Census
surname and either
  - the first is a listed first name, unless both are ordinary English words
    and the surname is outside the 1,000 most common ("Job Class", "Fair
    Start" are out; "Mark Smith", "Grace Young" are in), or
  - the first is neither a listed name nor an English word, and the surname
    is not an English word or is among the 1,000 most common ("Mateo
    Garcia", "Jayceon Smith").
A name is found anywhere in a cell, so "Prepared by Dana Whitfield" and
"Contact: Rachel Kim (360) 555-0100" each give one. An email address is a
name of its own.

MEASURED, 2026-10-30, on the 87 DRS and OFM workbooks in mehrlander/home
(209,845 text cells) and on 1,800 planted names. The rule this replaced,
any two capitalized words beside a heading or label that read like a person
field, flagged 722 distinct texts there, nearly all org units and fee
titles ("IS Administration" beside "Central Reception Unit Contact Team").
This rule flags 23, finds 88% of the planted names, whose first names were
drawn evenly from the 2,000 most common US baby names of the 2020s, and every
pairing of a common adult first name with one of the 120 most common
surnames. compromise's people() found 71% of the planted names and flagged
182 texts. A tagger is the wrong tool in any case: pages/entities.html ran
spaCy's small English model over this estate's prose and 7 to 9 percent of
its PERSON tags were people, and a cell gives a model less to go on than a
sentence.

A MISS IS POSSIBLE AND SAID SO by the page that shows this: a surname
outside the Census list, a first name that is an English word and not on
the first-name list ("Promise Dugger", "Meadow Buck"), a lone surname or
first name, and a nickname. A place, a product or a title can still read as
a person ("Walla Walla", "Rock Pointe", "Bail Bond").

OUTSIDE THE CELLS is where a name travels unnoticed, so those are read too:
the file's creator and last-modified-by, its Manager property, the people
behind threaded comments, and every comment author. The properties never
travel in an extract; they travel only if the file itself is sent.

Pure apart from loadLists(): takes an analysed result (xlsxKit.readZip or
.analyze) and returns plain objects. Attaches to window.XlsxPeople.

  loadLists()               Promise of the lists, fetched once per page
  makeLists(first, surnames, words)
                            the lists from plain arrays, surnames most
                            common first: what loadLists() resolves to
  scan(result, { lists })
      -> { findings, lists, sheets }; a finding is
         { id, kind, sheet, object, col, cell, header, label, evidence,
           count, filled, names }, kind one of column | cell | author |
         property; `lists` is false when the scan ran without them, which
         leaves addresses, comment authors and the file's properties
  namesIn(text, lists)      the names and addresses a text holds
  carried(found, picked)    the findings an extract pick carries; picked is
                            the Overview's { sheets: Map(name -> Set of
                            kinds), objects: Set of ids }
  rows(found)               findings as rows for a table
Read at call time: this kit can load before the workbook kit does.
A failed fetch is not cached, so the next scan tries again.
Capitalized (with Mc/Mac, O', hyphens) or all capitals.

Words never part of a name here, though a list holds them: the nouns a
budget workbook puts beside a word that is also a name, months and days,
and the parts of an address or an institution's name.
A place in a Washington workbook long before it is anyone's first name.

The surnames common enough to be names even beside a first name that is
also a word: Mark Smith, Grace Young, Will Hall.

The text cut into words, keeping a comma and an initial's period; any
other mark breaks the run, and so does a word cut short by a period,
which is an abbreviation ("Res. Grad", "Auth Del:").
A double surname is two surnames: Perez-Carrillo, not African-American.

A COLUMN IS SAMPLED BEFORE IT IS READ IN FULL. Every distinct text is
read once per scan, which covers the usual workbook, whose cells repeat a
few thousand texts. A column of distinct texts past SAMPLE values is read
cell by cell only when its sample holds a name, half from the top and
half spread evenly down, so a 100,000-row column of codes costs a sample.
What that can miss is a long column whose few names all fall between the
sampled rows.

A column with at least GROUP cells naming someone is reported once, as
the column; fewer are reported cell by cell, where they sit.
The distinct names a finding keeps, for the roster and the table.

A sheet's columns, each as its values below its heading. The heading is
the column's first filled cell when that cell is text and names no one,
which finds a table's header wherever the table starts.

The el map (every element path in every part, with its distinct text and
attribute values) is where the file's own properties are, so they are
read from there rather than taught to the workbook kit as fields.
Cached pivot rows, which can hold data from a sheet that is not picked.
Comment authors, per sheet where the workbook kit placed the comment.

Authors in a comments part the kit did not attach to a sheet, and the
people behind threaded comments: in the file, in no extract.

The readings that carry a sheet's cell text into an extract. `styles`,
`conditional` and `validations` describe cells without their values.
Where, in a reader's words: a sheet column, a sheet cell, a cached field.

lib/kits/xlsx-write.js — build a new workbook holding a chosen subset of
another workbook's sheets. The companion to kits/xlsx.js, which reads a
package and never writes one.

REPRODUCTION, NOT SUBTRACTION. The other way to do this is to edit the
package in place: delete the parts a dropped sheet owns, then patch
workbook.xml, [Content_Types].xml and the rels around the hole. That is
more faithful, because everything not touched survives byte-intact. It was
deliberately not chosen. This kit loads the source into a writer library,
drops the sheets, and lets the writer re-emit every part, so what survives
is what the writer models. Loss is expected; the manifest is where it is
declared rather than discovered.

WHY ExcelJS AND NOT SheetJS, measured 2026-09-14 rather than assumed.
Round-tripping three of the OFM budget forms (a macro workbook with 2,795
formulas, a 218-merge form with an image, and the TECM pivot template)
through each library and re-reading the output with kits/xlsx.js:

  cells kept      ExcelJS 17144/17148, 1640/1642, 458/502
                  SheetJS 13872/17148,  327/1642,   52/502
  cellXfs kept    ExcelJS 49/56, 287/305, 29/34
                  SheetJS  3/56,   7/305,  1/34
  conditional formats, data validations
                  ExcelJS all
                  SheetJS none

SheetJS's community build does not write cell styles, and it drops the
empty-but-formatted cells a blank form is largely made of. On the TECM
template that is 90% of the cells. The size argument that favoured it does
not survive contact either: its output was 2.0 MB from a 56 KB source,
because it emits 32,768 column definitions. ExcelJS is ~938 KB over
jsDelivr against SheetJS's 882 KB, which is the wrong 56 KB to save.

SheetJS still earns a place, as the INDEPENDENT READER in the check suite
(node/test/xlsx-write.test.mjs): a defect both the producer and
kits/xlsx.js share is invisible to a check that only uses those two.

THE GRAFT is what makes the sheet picker's checkbox list real. A writer
models no VBA, no pivot cache, no customXml and no workbook connections, so
offering them as options with only a writer behind them would be offering
inert checkboxes. After the writer emits the base package, the source's own
bytes for those parts are copied in with JSZip, along with the source's own
content-type and relationship ENTRIES, copied verbatim rather than
reconstructed from a hardcoded table of type URIs. A graft that does not
take is reported and skipped; the workbook still opens.

window.xlsxWriteKit:
  rebuild(bytes, keep, { grafts? }) -> { bytes, manifest, suffix, mime }
      (async) `keep` is a list of sheet display names; kits/xlsx.js must be
      loaded first, since it reads both the source and the output.
  plan(read, partNames, keep)  what keeping `keep` implies; no writing
  manifestText(manifest)       the manifest as markdown, to travel with the file
  verify(bytes) -> { ok, problems, parts, sheets }   package consistency (async)
  FEATURES, GRAFTS, resolveTarget, relsPathFor, closure, ownership

WHAT THE REBUILD DOES NOT CARRY, each named in FEATURES and the manifest:
the calc chain (dropped on purpose; the output sets fullCalcOnLoad), printer
settings (nothing models or grafts them), a sheet-local defined name's scope
(the writer emits every name workbook-global), two hyperlinks on one cell
(they collapse to one) and a link with only an in-workbook location, and
empty cells whose style is the default in every field.

Both loaders copy kits/xlsx.js's spelling exactly, and the spelling is
load-bearing rather than stylistic: node/test/bootstrap.mjs rewrites
`import('<url>')` to pull the vendored copy, but it first MASKS the
sequence `await(await import(` so that kits/compression.js's user-facing
template literal survives byte-intact. A kit written that way is never
rewritten and every test of it reaches the live CDN, which Node refuses.

ExcelJS ships one browser bundle in two wrappers and the loader has to
accept both. jsDelivr's `/+esm` is that bundle rolled into a module, whose
namespace carries the constructor; a plain UMD copy (a page that loaded it
through a <script>, or a harness that serves dist/exceljs.min.js for the
same URL) exports nothing and assigns `window.ExcelJS` as a side effect.
So the resolution is by CAPABILITY rather than by shape: take whichever of
the global, the namespace's default, or the namespace itself actually has
a Workbook.

Worth recording what this replaced. The first browser run failed with
`process is not defined`, and the obvious reading was that the CDN bundle
needs a process shim; a shim was written and it moved the error rather
than removing it. Neither bundle contains a single unguarded `process`
reference. What served the page was exceljs's NODE entry, because
node/render/cdn.mjs resolved a /+esm request through package.json main
and exceljs declares no module field. The fix belonged there, and the shim
would have shipped a fake `process` global to every page that opened a
workbook, in order to satisfy a library that never asked for one.

OPC part paths are package-absolute with no leading slash. A relationship
target is relative to the FOLDER of the part that declares it, which is
why '../comments1.xml' out of xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml is xl/comments1.xml
and not xl/worksheets/comments1.xml. External targets (http:, mailto:,
file:) resolve to null and are not package parts.

Every part reachable from `part` by following relationships, transitively.
This is the map the task hangs on: a sheet's drawing, its VML comment
boxes, its printer settings and its pivot table are reachable from that
sheet's rels and from nothing else, so the closure says exactly what
travels with it. kits/xlsx.js's `conns` view is coarser and calls
drawing1.xml workbook-wide.

Which sheets own which parts, and which parts no single sheet owns.
A part reachable from two kept sheets belongs to both; a part reachable
from a dropped sheet AND a kept one is not a dropped part.

Workbook scope: reachable from the package root without going through
any worksheet part.

What keeping `keep` implies, entirely from what kits/xlsx.js read plus the
zip's own part list (binary parts like vbaProject.bin are not XML, so the
reader never sees them and they arrive here as names).

`keep` is a list of sheet DISPLAY names, because that is what the reader
ticks. Workbook order, not part-file order, decides the output order:
xl.sheets[k].index is the workbook position.
Parts no kept sheet reaches and the workbook scope does not hold.

THE PIVOT TRAP. A pivot's cache is built from a range on some sheet,
and that sheet need not be the one the pivot sits on: in the TECM
template the pivot is on HeadCountCheck and its cache reads
HeadCounts&CostPerCredit. Keeping the pivot's own sheet is therefore not
enough to keep the pivot meaningful.

Defined names whose reference names a dropped sheet. ExcelJS writes
every name workbook-global and drops the localSheetId, so the
zero-based-index trap cannot fire here; a name pointing at a sheet that
is gone is a #REF! either way, so it is reported and left to the writer.

Each graft names the parts it carries and how the package should point at
them. `parts` are copied byte-for-byte; `linkFrom` is the part whose rels
gain an entry; `bodyPatch` is the one case (a pivot cache) where a
relationship alone is not the link.

TABLES, AND THE REASON THIS GRAFT EXISTS AT ALL. The writer re-emits a
table, so on paper it needs no graft. What it re-emits is not a table
Excel will open: on the OFM central-service form it wrote
`headerRowCount="0"` onto a table that still carries an
`<autoFilter ref="C3:E863">`, which is self-contradictory, because an
autofilter's dropdowns live in the header row. It also dropped
`tableType="queryTable"` and both `xl/queryTables/` parts, so a table
built from a database connection came back as a plain range still
claiming the connection's name.

Excel refused that file and offered to repair it, reported 2026-09-14
from the gold set. The mechanical check passed it and both readers
parsed it, which is the whole argument for the third check existing.

Matching is by displayName rather than by part filename: the writer
numbers table parts in its own order, so table1.xml on one side is not
reliably table1.xml on the other. Here they happened to line up.
Which sheet owns each table, from that sheet's own rels.

Splice a child element in before a container's closing tag. Crude on
purpose: [Content_Types].xml and every .rels file are machine-written with
a fixed shape, and a DOM round trip through XMLSerializer is where
namespace prefixes get rewritten. If the closing tag is missing the splice
REFUSES rather than appending to a malformed file, which is what turns a
failed graft into a skipped one.

CALC CHAIN, the free win. calcChain.xml is only a recalculation order
cache, and every index in it is a sheet index that moves when a sheet
goes. The writer emits no calcChain at all, so instead of repairing the
indices we tell Excel to recompute on open, which is what a workbook
with no calcChain does anyway and what makes the omission correct rather
than merely tolerated.

ACTIVE TAB, which is the index trap that does not fix itself. The writer
carries workbookView.activeTab through untouched, so a workbook whose
third sheet was selected when it was saved comes back pointing at index
2 with two sheets left, and Excel opens on a tab that is not there.

Worth saying how this was nearly missed: on all thirteen OFM budget
forms the rebuild's activeTab was absent, which reads as the writer
dropping it and the trap being free. It is not. Those workbooks were all
saved on their first tab, so activeTab was 0 and therefore omitted. The
fixture in node/test/xlsx-write.test.mjs sets it to the last sheet on
purpose, and that is what caught this.

Map each source sheet to the part path the WRITER gave it. ExcelJS names
a worksheet part after its own internal id, not its position, so
sheet1.xml in the source can be sheet4.xml in the output. Anything
grafted onto a sheet has to be aimed by this map rather than by the
source path.

Content-type entries are copied from the SOURCE package, never built
from a table of type URIs here. A Default for an extension is added only
when the output has none.

The source's own Relationship element, re-Id'd so it cannot collide with
one the writer emitted, and re-targeted relative to the output part that
declares it.

TABLES are aimed by displayName, not by part path. The writer
renumbers table parts in its own order, and its sheet rels already
point at whatever it named them, so the graft overwrites the part
the writer produced rather than adding one. Nothing needs a new
relationship for the table itself; what does need adding is the
table's OWN rels and the queryTable parts behind them, which the
writer models not at all.

The pivot graft is the one that needs a body edit, and its link runs
through two parts rather than one.

The worksheet reaches its pivot table through a relationship
only, so aim that one at the writer's part path.

The cache is the exception the comment above promised: workbook.xml
names it in its BODY, so the relationship alone is not the link.

Link only the parts the source itself links from this part. An
itemProps or a signature is reached from its own item's rels, which
was copied above, so it needs no entry here.

A workbook holding vbaProject.bin must declare the macro-enabled main
type, or Excel rejects the package rather than merely losing the macros.

ONE FIXED TIMESTAMP ON EVERY ENTRY, so two rebuilds of one workbook are
byte-identical. JSZip stamps `new Date()` on each entry it is handed, and
the writer's own output arrives already stamped, so without this the
output changes on every run: measured on the OFM forms, two runs a second
apart differed in 31 of 34 entries with the CONTENT of all 34 identical.

That is not cosmetic. A derived artifact is only safe to regenerate
rather than store when its builder is deterministic, so an output that
drifts for no semantic reason forces the file itself into a repository,
which is the thing the estate's size discipline exists to avoid. It also
makes two rebuilds impossible to compare. 1980-01-01 is the zip epoch's
own floor and what reproducible-build tooling uses; nothing in OOXML
reads an entry date, and the workbook's real dates live in
docProps/core.xml, which is copied through untouched.

THE HONESTY MECHANISM. Every row is derived from what kits/xlsx.js read,
on both sides: `found` from the source and `out` from the OUTPUT, re-read
by the same reader. Re-reading is the point. A manifest built from what
the writer was asked to do records intent; re-reading records result, so a
feature the writer silently dropped shows up as a gap rather than as a
claim that held.

AND A THIRD COLUMN, because the second one on its own accuses the tool of
doing its job. Dropping a sheet is supposed to take that sheet's cells,
comments and merges with it, so `out` below `found` is the normal case and
flagging it makes every manifest look like a failure. `expect` is the
source count restricted to the KEPT sheets, which is what a lossless
rebuild would produce, so the only gap worth a warning is out < expect.

A workbook-scoped row has no honest restriction to compute: the style
tables, the defined names and the connections belong to the package rather
than to any sheet, and a font that only the dropped sheet used is pruned
legitimately. Those rows declare scope 'workbook', show no expectation and
are never flagged. That is a real limit of this manifest and not a
rounding of one: genuine style loss hides in exactly those rows, and what
finds it is re-reading the output, which is the next check rather than
this one.

The raw count, and the one that reads as alarming for a reason that is
not loss. A blank form is full of `<c r="A8" s="15"/>`: an empty cell
whose style record is the default in every field, which the writer
drops because it is indistinguishable from no cell. classifyCellLoss()
below separates those from cells that carried something, so this row
is flagged on the second kind only.

Not loss when it falls. A run is a width applied to a column range, and
the writer merges adjacent runs of equal width: 2-10, 11-11 and
12-16384 all at 9.14 come back as one run 2-16384. Same widths, fewer
records, so the row is reported and never flagged.

Parts the reader never sees, counted off the zip's own listing. A binary
part has no model to restrict, so every row here is workbook-scoped except
the two that are named per sheet.

WHY THE CELL COUNT NEEDS A CLASSIFIER RATHER THAN A CAVEAT. Rebuilding all
thirteen OFM budget forms and diffing each kept sheet cell by cell, the
writer lost 292 cells in total and every one of them was an empty cell
whose style record is the package default in every field. Not one cell
carrying a value, a formula, or a style that renders differently from no
style was lost. A note saying "some of this is probably harmless" would
have been true and useless; separating the two kinds is a check, so the
manifest flags the count only when something other than a stub goes.

The limit worth stating: "renders like no style" is judged from the xf
record's own fields, so a style that is default in all of them and still
means something to Excel would be miscounted as a stub. Nothing in the
corpus is such a style, which is evidence and not a proof.

A cell inside a merged range that is NOT its top-left. Excel renders a
merge from the top-left cell alone, so text sitting in a slave is in the
file and not on the screen. Calling its loss harmless would overstate the
case, since a formula can still address the cell; calling it plain data
loss would overstate it the other way. It gets its own count.
kits/xlsx.js hands a merge back with a ONE-based row and a ZERO-based
column, which is worth stating rather than inferring: reading r1 as
zero-based makes every lookup miss by a row and the classifier then reports
ordinary loss where there is a merge.

Two ways to lose a cell: the writer omits it, or it survives with
its value emptied. The second is what a merge slave does.
The classifier, not the count, decides whether the cell row is short.

The value row answers to the same classifier, so a merge slave's text
does not read as a lost value.

A per-sheet binary part's expectation is the count of matching parts the
KEPT sheets reach, which the ownership closure already answered.

A reader's version of the same manifest. Markdown, because it is meant to
travel next to the file it describes.

CHECK 1 OF 3, the mechanical one. It proves the package is internally
consistent. It cannot prove Excel likes it, which is what the gold set is
for, and it cannot prove the content is right, which is what re-reading
with an independent parser is for.

Every part has a content type. The honest limit: an OPC package
normally declares `<Default Extension="xml" ContentType="application/xml"/>`,
so every .xml part passes this rule whether or not it carries the
Override its role requires. The rule catches an untyped binary (a
grafted vbaProject.bin whose Default went missing) and does not catch a
styles part that lost its Override. The one XML Override Excel refuses
the file over is checked separately below.

The workbook's own part must be typed as a spreadsheet main part, and as
the MACRO-ENABLED one whenever a VBA project is in the package. Excel
rejects the file outright on either, rather than opening it and losing
the macros, which is what makes this worth a rule of its own.
every rels target exists; every r:id in a body resolves

A calcChain cell's `i` is the sheet's sheetId (ECMA-376, CT_CalcCell),
not its position: a workbook whose sheets were added and removed has ids
past its sheet count, and Excel's own files read fine with them.

A PART THAT CONTRADICTS ITSELF. Everything above checks the wiring
BETWEEN parts: does this id resolve, does this target exist, is this
index in range. None of it looks inside a part, and that is the gap the
gold set found on 2026-09-14. The writer emitted a table carrying
`headerRowCount="0"` and an `<autoFilter>` over its whole range, which
cannot both be true, because an autofilter's dropdowns live in the header
row it says it does not have. Every check here passed, both readers
parsed it, and Excel refused the file and offered to repair it.

One rule, not a schema validator. A validator is the right answer and a
large one; this is the specific contradiction that cost a round trip,
added so it cannot cost a second.

AND IT MAY BE NARROWER THAN THE FAULT. A bisect in Excel showed
headerRowCount="0" is the operative attribute: setting it back to "1" on
both tables made the file open. It did not isolate whether the autoFilter
is required for Excel to object. The pairing is kept because a headerless
table is otherwise legal OOXML and flagging every one of them would be
wrong, but if a case turns up that this misses, widen it on that
evidence rather than on this comment.
orphan parts: reachable from the package root, or nothing points at them

lib/kits/xlsx.js — OOXML (.xlsx) structural inspector: unzip, walk every
XML/rels part, and surface the internal cross-references (shared strings,
styles, sheet rels, comments, calc chain, defined names) plus reconstructed
sheet data. Pulled from three dropped prototypes (home repo's chron/dump/,
"Excel drop dive" being the most complete of the three) into one pure kit:
no DOM rendering, no jQuery/Tabulator. analyze() takes already-extracted
XML strings and is synchronous and part-order-independent — cross-file
resolution (shared-string values, "which sheets does this file touch")
happens in a finalize pass after every part is walked, which also fixes a
real bug in the source prototypes: they resolved shared-string cell values
inline during a concurrent, unordered zip read, so a sheet processed before
sharedStrings.xml got empty string values. readZip() is the thin
JSZip-backed convenience wrapper a page actually calls.

2026-08-15: the prototypes' own lineage was recovered from the chat archive
(mehrlander/chat-histories, excel.md), and they turned out to be the weaker
of two contemporaneous browser builds. A separate 2025-11-17 viewer resolved
sheet names through workbook.xml plus its rels and handled inline strings;
neither reached the three that were dropped here, so this kit shipped
without both. Both are now in, along with the index confusion the first of
them was hiding: see the finalize() join and connectionsView.

  readZip(fileOrArrayBuffer) -> result (async; JSZip loads lazily)
      result: { el, connectedPaths, conns, xl: { sheets, strings, styles,
      fonts, fills, borders, xfs, comments, definedNames, calcChain, ... } }
  analyze(parts)             the synchronous core readZip wraps
  views.{paths, connections, unconnected, files, sources, pivots}(result)
  summary(result)            { total, connected, unconnected, connectedPct }
  sheetRows(sheet, xl?)      [{ Row, A, B, ... }], values formatted when xl given

                             sizes, styles, images, cf, notes, links; stops
                             at opts.maxRows (2000) / maxCells (30000) and
                             says so in `truncated`
  formulaText(sheet, row, col)  a cell's stored formula as '=<text>', the
                             master's text under '=[fill N] ' for a
                             shared-formula follower, '' for an entered cell
  formulaFor(sheet, row, col)  a cell's own formula, a shared follower's

  shiftRefs(text, dr, dc)    relative A1 references moved, as a fill does

THREE BOUNDARIES, each a place the kit declines rather than guesses. An
`expression` conditional rule is a formula, so it is skipped and counted in
sheetLayout's `cfSkipped`. Pictures are read from DrawingML anchors, not
from legacy VML, so a comment's text is read but not the box Excel draws it
in. A list validation resolves an inline list or a cell range; a defined
name returns null and the cell carries only its prompt.
'AA5' -> 26 (zero-based column index); ignores the row digits. -1 if unparsable.
'B7' -> 7. The row half of an A1 reference.

'A1:C3' -> { r1, c1, r2, c2 }, rows 1-based and columns 0-based to match
colIndexFromRef. Normalised, since a range may be written either way round.

'FF4472C4' or '4472C4' -> '#4472c4'. An ARGB alpha byte is dropped rather
than honoured: Excel writes FF for everything a cell fill or font uses.

A node's tag without its namespace prefix. Every part of a workbook except
the theme is written unprefixed, so directChild's nodeName comparison works
there; theme1.xml writes `a:clrScheme`, and matching it by the tag as
written silently returned nothing. That failure is invisible rather than
loud: the theme resolves to an empty palette, every theme-coloured fill
becomes null, and a form's gray areas disappear while the text on them
still draws. Cost me one round of screenshots to find.

'A1' or 'A1:C3', space-separated, which is how every range list in the
format is written: a conditional format's `sqref`, a validation's, a merge.

Excel escapes a character it cannot write literally as `_xHHHH_`, and a
validation prompt written on several lines arrives as `_x000a_`. Left as
written it reads as a typo in the middle of OFM's own field instructions.

English Metric Units, the measure every drawing offset is written in.
914400 to the inch, so 9525 to a CSS pixel at 96dpi.

A colour as written, resolved in finalize(). `theme` needs the palette and
`indexed` needs the legacy table; `rgb` is already an answer but is kept in
the same shape so one resolver serves all three.

Text of an <is> (inline string) or an <si> (shared string). A plain one is
a single <t>; a rich one splits into <r> runs each carrying its own <t>,
and the value is the runs concatenated. Every <t> descendant, in document
order, covers both without a special case.

Except <rPh>, which is a phonetic hint (furigana over a Japanese reading)
and carries its own <t>. It is not part of the value, and concatenating it
would interleave a pronunciation guide into the cell.

── READING XML AS TEXT, for the two parts that are large and regular ───

A worksheet's <sheetData> and sharedStrings.xml grow with the data, and
every other part grows with the workbook's design. MEASURED 2026-10-24 on
a 100,000-row, 12-column sheet: readZip took 41 s, about a third of it in
DOMParser building some 2.5 million nodes and most of the rest walking
them, each node through every branch below. Those two parts are read by
position instead (analyze's scanSheetData and scanSharedStrings), into
the same structures; every irregular part, and everything in a worksheet
outside <sheetData>, still goes through the DOM.
The `>` that closes a start tag, skipping any inside a quoted value.

Whether `<name` at `at` opens that element and not a longer one (`<c`
against `<col`): the next character ends the name.
richText's rule as text: every <t> joined, except a phonetic run's.

The inventory keeps every path's count and attribute names, and at most
this many distinct values of each, which is what the File parts and
Unmapped tables show. Without a cap a sheet's cell references alone were
1.3 million strings held for those two tables.
OpenXML Chart parser (<c:chartSpace> -> structured chart model).

A DrawingML colour as written under a fill: an explicit rgb, a theme slot,
or a system colour's last value, with the modifiers Excel applies to it.
Resolved by paintChart, since a theme slot needs theme1.xml.
DrawingML names a theme slot; xl.theme holds them in SpreadsheetML order.

Shade mixes toward black and tint toward white; lumMod and lumOff scale and
shift HSL luminance, which is how Excel writes "Accent 1, Lighter 40%".
Applied in that fixed order rather than document order, an approximation
that only matters when one colour carries both kinds.

Series colours against the workbook's theme, which a chart part cannot see
on its own. A line takes its stroke. A bar or slice takes its FILL and never
its outline, which Excel often writes white or as noFill.
The point index is a position, not a sorting hint. Absent points stay null.

Absent, varyColors is on for a pie and off otherwise; present without a
val, the schema's boolean default makes it on.
A point's own fill (c:dPt) overrides the series', keyed by point index.

Resolve direct worksheet references only after sheets and shared strings
are complete. A chart cache can store zero for a genuinely blank cell.
Formula cells use their saved value; this reader does not recalculate Excel.

---- style records, read the same way from <cellXfs>'s tables and from a
conditional rule's <dxf> ------------------------------------------------

A dxf writes `<i val="0"/>` to turn italic OFF, so the presence of the
element is not the answer; its val is, wherever it has one.

A fill is a pattern, and only `solid` is a flat colour a renderer can
reproduce honestly. Excel's default fills are `none` and `gray125`, and
both mean "nothing to draw"; the second is the diagonal hatch Excel
reserves as fill index 1 and it is never what an author chose. For a solid
fill the colour is fgColor, which reads backwards; bgColor on a solid
pattern is almost always the meaningless `indexed="64"` sentinel. A
DIFFERENTIAL fill, the kind a conditional rule carries, inverts that and
takes bgColor: reading fgColor there returns nothing, and the rule then
paints no colour while still looking implemented.

A CACHE VALUE, in the six shapes OOXML writes it. The same element names
serve a cacheField's <sharedItems> and a record's cells, so one reader does
both. `x` is the seventh and appears only in a record: an index into its
field's shared items, resolved in finalize because the records part may be
walked before the definition that explains it.

A boolean is kept as a boolean and a missing cell as null rather than as
the empty string, since "" is a value a text field can hold and a blank is
not the same fact.

A pivot cache can hold every row of its source, so the records are capped
and the cap is REPORTED rather than silently applied: a reader comparing a
record count against what is on screen has to be able to see the cut.

<connection type="N">. The code, not the provider: a reader wants to know
a query is a web query without the kit claiming to understand the URL.

parts: [[path, xmlString], ...] or {path: xmlString}. Walk order doesn't
matter for correctness — see the module comment above.
`opts.dom` reads every part through the DOM, the scanners off: the
reference the two text readers are tested against, and a way back if one
ever misreads a file.

THE READ IN SLICES, for a page that must keep painting. analyze() is the
same read run to the end in one go; here it stops every `sliceMs` (40 by
default), lets the browser paint and take input, tells `onProgress` the
fraction read, and goes on. On a 100,000-row sheet the read is about
three seconds of work either way; sliced, the page holds still for none
of it, and the reader can be told how far it has got.

The read itself, yielding the fraction of the parts' text read so far:
between parts, every 2,048 rows of a sheet, every 16,384 strings, and
every 4,096 rows as they are frozen at the end.
sheetN -> { usedStrings:Set, usedStyles:Set, cellCount, formulas, mergedCells, dimension, sharedFormulas, cols, merges, freeze, rawRows:Map<row,{cols,ht,hidden}> }

workbook order: [{ name, sheetId, rid }]
custom format id -> format code
cellXfs index -> numFmtId (a cell's `s`)
the workbook's epoch; see serialToDate

---- APPEARANCE, which is everything below and is the half this kit
ignored until 2026-09-04. A cell's `s` indexes cellXfs; that entry
names a font, a fill, a border and an alignment as well as the number
format the kit already read. Without the other four a form drawn by
OFM (a title band, a gray input area, a ruled box) reaches a reader as
a bare grid of strings, which is what it did.

Colours are stored as SPECS here and resolved in finalize(), because a
theme colour is defined in theme1.xml and analyze() is deliberately
part-order-independent: styles.xml may be walked first. This is the
same reason shared-string values resolve there.
theme colour index -> '#rrggbb'
fontId -> { bold, italic, underline, strike, size, color, name }
fillId -> '#rrggbb' | null (null is "no fill", not white)
borderId -> { top, right, bottom, left } of { style, color }
cellXfs index -> { numFmtId, fontId, fillId, borderId, align… }
dxfId -> the differential format a conditional rule applies
drawing part -> [{ from, to, ext, embed, name }]
chart part -> parsed chart model
'xl/media/image1.png' -> data: URI, attached by readZip
comments part -> [author name], authorId is the index
comments part -> [{ ref, authorId, text }]
The inventory record at a path, as the DOM walk keeps it.

The DOM walk's inventory over a fragment of text: every tag under
`prefix` by its path, its attributes, and a childless element's text.
For the few cells and strings that are not plain, so the inventory
matches the DOM's without a DOM.

A worksheet cut at its <sheetData>: the cells' text, and the part with
an empty element in their place. Null where there is nothing to cut:
no cells, or a main namespace written with a prefix (`<x:sheetData>`),
which the DOM path reads as it always has.

THE ROWS, as the DOM branch for <row> and <c> builds them: the same
rawRows entries, counters and shared-formula masters, and inventory
records at the same paths. The inventory stops at the cell's own
children; the runs inside an inline string are counted as its <t>.
<v>, <f> and <is>, each at most once, found by position.

`<is><t>text</t></is>`, which is how most writers other than
Excel store every string, is a plain cell too.
The counters the DOM branch for <c> keeps.

THE STRING TABLE, by position: one entry per <si>, empty or rich alike,
since the index is the position and a skipped entry shifts every
string after it. False when the part does not look like one, so the
DOM path reads it instead.

A plain entry, one <t> with no attributes, by hand; a rich one
or one carrying xml:space through the fragment walk.

A worksheet's cells are read as text and the rest of it through the
DOM with an empty <sheetData/> standing in, so every branch below
still sees the part's merges, rules, validations, links and panes.

The used range as the file declares it (`<dimension ref>`), and
the text of each shared-formula master by its `si` index.
Geometry, which is what makes a sheet a page rather than a list.

Three kinds of content the sheet carries beside its cells, each
invisible in a value grid: the rules that repaint a cell, the
field-level instructions and choice lists OFM attaches to its
form inputs, and the drawings anchored over the grid.
The links the sheet carries, resolved in finalize().

A value can sit in three places, not one. t="s" indexes sharedStrings and is
resolved in finalize(); t="inlineStr" puts the text in <is> and
has NO <v> at all, so reading <v> alone silently produced an
empty cell (fixed 2026-08-15); everything else is <v>, whether
that is a number, a date serial, a boolean, or a formula result.

THE FORMULA, as the file writes it: no leading '=', since that
is Excel's UI rather than the stored text. `true` where the cell
is computed and the text is not there to have, which is what a
SHARED formula's followers look like: the master carries the
text and every cell after it carries `<f t="shared" si="0"/>`
and nothing else. Recovering those means rewriting relative
references per cell, which is a formula engine, so the honest
answer is "computed, text not stored here".

Truthy either way, which is the contract profileColumns already
reads (a computed cell counted apart from an entered one). It
was `true` for every computed cell until 2026-09-14; nothing
read the value, so widening it costs no caller.

THE SHARED-FORMULA INDEX rides beside the text, or beside the
absence of it: the master carries `si` and the text, a follower
carries `si` alone. Kept per cell, and the master's text kept
per sheet under that index, so a serializer can write a
follower as `=[fill N] <master text>`, which is the form the
PowerShell exporter (Get-WsDetail) already emits and the fund
view's reader already resolves. Still not a formula engine:
nothing here shifts a reference.

`ht` is the row's own height in points and only counts when the
author set one; a row with customHeight off follows the sheet
default and must not be pinned to whatever Excel last measured.

A <col> covers a RANGE of columns (min..max, both 1-based), so widths
are stored as the ranges the file wrote rather than expanded: a sheet
may declare one width for columns 5 through 16384 and expanding that
is 16k entries for one fact.

A RULE THAT REPAINTS A CELL. The ranges live on the parent element
and the rule on the child, so both are read here rather than in two
passes. `priority` is ascending: 1 outranks 2.

WHAT A FORM SAYS ABOUT ITS OWN INPUTS, and there are two kinds. A
`list` names the choices a cell accepts; a validation with no type
at all carries only Excel's input message, the note that appears when
you select the cell. OFM's fee form has thirteen of the second kind
and every one is a field instruction the reader could not otherwise
see ("Enter the four digit fee code from the 2008 Fee Inventory").

Which drawing part holds this sheet's pictures. Resolved through the
sheet's own rels in finalize(), for the same reason the workbook's
sheet list is: the rels part may not have been walked yet.

A sheet points at its comments through <legacyDrawing>, which names
the VML shape that draws the little red corner, NOT the comments part
itself. The comments part is a plain relationship of the sheet with
no element referring to it, so it is found by TYPE in finalize rather
than by an r:id anything here carries.

A LINK ON A CELL. Excel writes one element per link with the cells it
covers and one of two destinations: `r:id`, a relationship of the
sheet whose target is the URL (resolved in finalize, since the rels
part may not have been walked yet), or `location`, a place in this
workbook written as 'Sheet'!A1. A HYPERLINK() formula is neither and
is not read here.

Frozen panes. `state` distinguishes a frozen split from a dragged
one, and only the frozen kind is a fact about the document rather
than about where somebody left their scrollbar.

WHERE the merge is, not only how many there are. The count answers a
structural question ("does this sheet merge at all"); a renderer
needs the range, and the DP Addendum's 218 of them are most of what
makes it read as a form.

sheets resolved in finalize(), once every sheet is known
THE INDEX IS THE POSITION, so every <si> pushes exactly once even
when it has no text. Two kinds used to be dropped instead, and a
dropped entry does not blank one cell: it shifts every string after
it by one, so the sheet fills with real text belonging to other
cells and nothing looks broken.

A RICH <si> is the common one. It holds <r> runs rather than a bare
<t>, so the old directChild(node,'t') found nothing. The OFM decision
package addendum has 6 rich entries among 163, and read through this
kit its form drew "Total Square Feet" where the workbook says
"Section One: Current Facility Information and Utilization". Found
2026-09-04 by rendering the sheet and comparing it to Excel, which is
the first thing in this estate that could have caught it: a grid of
plausible strings in plausible places reads as correct.

A cell's `s` attribute indexes cellXfs, and that entry's numFmtId names
a format code: either a custom one declared in <numFmts> or a built-in
id with no code written anywhere in the file. Without this join every
date is a bare serial and every currency a bare float, which is the one
gap in this kit with consequences a reader can see.
Document order IS the index, so these are pushed as walked.

`applyFill`/`applyBorder`/`applyFont` are Excel's own switches for
"use the named record or inherit". Absent means apply, which is
why the test is against an explicit '0' rather than for a '1'.

A DIFFERENTIAL format: the font, fill and border a conditional rule
applies ON TOP of whatever the cell already has, so every part is
optional and an absent one means "leave it alone". Its fill reads
the OTHER way round from a normal one, bgColor rather than fgColor,
which is the trap: reading fgColor here returns nothing and the rule
paints no colour at all while still looking implemented.

A PICTURE ANCHORED OVER THE GRID. A twoCellAnchor pins both corners to
cells and resizes with them; a oneCellAnchor pins the top-left and
carries its own extent. Both are read; absoluteAnchor is not, since it
positions against the sheet rather than against any cell and there is
nothing to attach it to in a table.

THE DUPLICATION TRAP: Excel wraps an anchor in <mc:AlternateContent>
with the same picture in <mc:Choice> and again in <mc:Fallback>, so a
walker that takes every anchor draws the OFM addendum's logo twice,
slightly offset. Only the Choice is read.

The blip's r:embed or chart's r:id points at the media or chart part through
the DRAWING's own rels, not the sheet's.

The palette a `theme="N"` colour indexes, in <clrScheme> order, with
one correction: the scheme writes dk1, lt1, dk2, lt2 and Excel's
indices are lt1, dk1, lt2, dk2, so the first two pairs swap. Getting
that backwards turns a white title on a dark band into black on
white, which reads as plausible and is wrong.

A COMMENT IS A NOTE SOMEBODY LEFT ON A CELL, and in these workbooks it
is where OFM's own staff wrote the hint that does not fit on the form.
The kit counted them and read no text until 2026-09-04.

Two things make the part hard to place. Its number is its own, not the
sheet's: comments1.xml can belong to sheet5. And the text is a run
sequence, whose first run is conventionally the author's name with a
colon, which Excel adds and a reader does not want repeated beside the
author field. The join is done in finalize; here the parts are read.
`comments?`: Excel names the part comments1.xml, and openpyxl writes
xl/comments/comment1.xml, which the plural alone missed, so every
comment in such a workbook read as absent.

EVERY EXTERNAL SOURCE THE WORKBOOK DECLARES, in one part. `type` is a
numeric code and CONNECTION_KIND names it; the kit classifies the code
rather than interpreting the provider string, the same line cellFormat
draws around a number format. The detail is whichever child element the
kind puts it in, which is why one field cannot be read off `connection`
alone.

A Power Query connection is an OLE DB connection whose provider
is Microsoft's Mashup engine, so the M it runs is NOT here: it is
in the DataMashup blob readMashup() opens. Flagged so a reader
following a query lands there instead of on this string.

A PIVOT CACHE IS THE DATA; A PIVOT TABLE IS ONE VIEW OF IT. They live in
separate parts and several tables may share one cache, so the two are
collected apart and joined in finalize through the workbook's own
cacheId map rather than by part number, which nothing guarantees.

The range the cache was built from, named by DISPLAY sheet name
(the one thing in an .xlsx that addresses a sheet the way a reader
does) or, for a cache over a table, by that table's name.

Parallel to `fields` by index, the shape the row record already
uses for styles and types. A field with no <sharedItems> keeps an
empty list, which is what a records part's <x> would then index
into and miss, honestly.

EXACTLY the shared-items path. A cacheField may also carry a
<fieldGroup><groupItems> of the same element names, and folding those
in would shift every <x> index in the records by however many groups
the author made.

THE ROWS BEHIND A PIVOT. Stored as read and resolved in finalize: an
<x> cell is an index into the cache definition's shared items and the
definition may not have been walked yet, which is the same reason
shared strings resolve there.
narrowed to its own sheet in finalize
The measures, which are the only fields with a name a reader wrote.

The workbook's cacheId -> relationship map, the only statement of which
cache part a pivot table's `cacheId` means.

The <sheets> element is the ONLY place a sheet's display name and its
workbook order live. Everything else in an .xlsx addresses a sheet by
part file (sheetN.xml) or by workbook index, and the two are unrelated
once a workbook has been reordered or a sheet deleted. Collected here
and joined to the part files in finalize(), once the rels are known.
The 1904 epoch is a workbook-wide switch, off by default, and getting it
wrong shifts every date by four years and a day rather than failing.

r:id is namespaced; getAttribute wants the qualified name as
written, and DOMParser keeps the prefix on a non-namespace-aware
read. Fall back to the local name for a document that omits it.

Omitted means visible. `veryHidden` is kept distinct from `hidden`
rather than folded in: only the second can be unhidden from
Excel's own menu, so a reader auditing a workbook wants the two
apart.

`id` rides along because the workbook's <sheet r:id> points at a
part through this map and nothing else resolves it.
---- finalize: cross-file info that needs every part already walked ----

Give every sheet its display name and its workbook position, which is
the join no other part of the file makes. Until 2026-08-15 the kit knew
a sheet only as `sheetN` from its part filename and treated N as the
workbook index, which is wrong the moment a workbook is reordered or a
sheet deleted, and wrong for `localSheetId` and calcChain's `i` always,
since both are ZERO-based. Anything the workbook does not claim keeps a
null name rather than a guessed one.
The rels target is relative to xl/, and may be written absolute.

A workbook with no <sheets> at all (a fragment, a hand-built fixture)
falls back to part order, matching what the browser prototypes did.

Resolve shared-string cell values now that xl.strings is complete, and
freeze each sheet's rows in row order.

Parallel to `cells` rather than folded into it, so the existing
shape is untouched and a consumer that does not care about formats
pays nothing. Only cells carrying an `s` appear.

Likewise for the `t` attribute, which is what separates a number
from a string of digits and therefore decides how a cell aligns.

The formula text where the file stored one, `true` where the cell
is computed and it did not. Only computed cells appear.

The shared-formula index of each cell that has one, master and
follower alike; the master's text is sheet.sharedFormulas[si].

Colours last, because a theme colour needs theme1.xml and analyze() does
not promise it was walked first. Every spec collected during the walk
resolves here, once, against the finished palette.

Each sheet's pictures and charts, joined through the sheet's own rels to the drawing
part and through THAT part's rels to the media or chart. Two hops, and the second
is the one worth naming: a blip's r:embed or chart's r:id is scoped to the drawing, so
resolving it against the sheet's rels finds the wrong part or none.

A sheet's comments, found BY TYPE among its relationships. Nothing in the
sheet XML names the comments part: <legacyDrawing> points at the VML that
draws the red corner, and the comments themselves ride a relationship
with no referring element. Matching on the part name rather than on the
relationship type, which arrives with a full schema URL, keeps this from
depending on how the writer spelled it.

Excel writes the author's name as the first run followed by a colon
and a newline. It is the same string the author field already
carries, so a reader shown both sees it twice; dropped here rather
than at the render, since every consumer would otherwise repeat it.

A sheet's own visibility, which lives only in workbook.xml. A sheet the
workbook never claims keeps `null` rather than a guessed 'visible', the
same rule the name and index join follows.

Each pivot table to the sheet it is drawn on and to the cache it reads.
The sheet comes from the sheet's own rels, the cache from the workbook's
cacheId map; a table whose cache the file does not declare keeps a null
part rather than the nearest-numbered one.

Each cache definition to the records part it declares, through its OWN
rels. Not by matching the number in the filename: the pairing is
conventional rather than guaranteed, and the rels state it.

An <x> cell is an index into its OWN field's shared items, so the
column position is what picks the list. A record longer than the field
list, or an index the list does not reach, resolves to null rather than
to a neighbouring field's value.

The sheet each pivot part actually belongs to, now that it is known: a
pivot table touched every sheet while it was only reachable as ALL_SHEETS.

A link's URL lives in the sheet's rels, keyed by the r:id the element
carries; a `location` link needs no join.

The author's name, off the front of a comment's own text. Excel writes
"Name:\n" as the first run; a comment somebody typed without that prefix is
left exactly as written, which is why this matches rather than slices.

A rels target is relative to its owner's directory and may be written with
a leading slash or with `../` hops, neither of which a zip entry name has.

Excel's legacy indexed palette. Only the first 24 entries and the two
sentinels matter in practice: 64 is "automatic" (the window's own text or
background colour, so no answer of ours) and 65 is the window background.

A tint lightens (positive) or darkens (negative) a theme colour. Excel
applies it in HSL luminance; the linear approximation below is within a
couple of levels for the shades a workbook actually uses, which are the
-0.15 and -0.35 grays every OFM form is banded with.

A colour spec to '#rrggbb', or null where the file declines to say. Null is
not white: a cell with no fill shows whatever is behind it, and painting
that white would erase a banded row underneath a merge.

---- number formats ----------------------------------------------------

Excel writes no format code for its built-in ids, so a reader has to carry
them. Only the ids that change how a value READS are listed: the rest are
decimal-place and thousands-separator variants that leave a number a
number, and guessing at their exact codes would add nothing.
Every built-in id now, not only the ones that change a value's KIND. The
list grew on 2026-09-04 with formatValue: a code like `#,##0` used to be
classified `number` and printed raw, so the id behind it was not worth
carrying. Now that the code is applied, `1234.5` under id 3 is `1,235` and
the code has to be there to say so. Ids 5 to 8 and 41 to 44 are the
currency and accounting pairs, written out because their negative and
zero sections are what make an accounting column line up.

The built-in currency and accounting ids, which carry a symbol we do not
reproduce; naming them as currency is the useful part.

What a format code MEANS, which is all a reader needs to decide how to
print a value. Literal text in quotes and the bracketed sections (colours,
conditions, [h] elapsed hours) are skipped first, since a code like
`"day "0` would otherwise read as a date on its `d`.

An elapsed-time code is a duration, not a clock reading, and printing it
as a time of day would be wrong rather than merely ugly.

`m` is month or minute depending on neighbours, so it is never the sole
evidence for a date; `s` and `h` are unambiguous.

The format a cell's `s` resolves to. Returns null for a cell with no style,
which is the common case and is not the same as a General style.

An Excel serial to a Date, in UTC.

25569 is the serial for 1970-01-01, so the subtraction lands on the JS
epoch directly. The correction below it is the famous one: Excel counts a
1900-02-29 that never existed, deliberately, to stay compatible with Lotus
1-2-3. Serials at or below 59 sit before that phantom day and are one short
of the linear count; from 61 the two agree again. Serial 60 IS the phantom
day and has no correct answer, so it lands on 1900-02-28.

A private-use sentinel standing in for literal text while the numeric part
of a code is substituted. It has to be a character no format code and no
value can contain, which rules out the obvious ASCII choices.

WHICH SECTION OF A CODE APPLIES. A format is up to four sections separated
by semicolons: positive, negative, zero, text. Two sections mean the second
is for negatives; one means it covers everything. A negative under a code
with its own negative section is printed WITHOUT a minus sign, because the
section supplies the notation, which is how `(1,234)` accounting columns
work and why prefixing a minus there would print `-(1,234)`.

One section applied to one number. The grammar handled: `0` and `#` digit
places, `.` decimals, `,` grouping, `%` (which scales by 100), `"…"` and
`\x` literals, `[…]` conditions and colours (skipped), `_x` width padding
(dropped, since a browser has no fixed-width space to pad with) and `*x`
repeat-fill (dropped for the same reason). Scientific and fraction codes
are NOT interpreted; they fall through to the plain number, which is
honest rather than wrong.
Each trailing comma before the decimal point scales down by a thousand.

`#` before the point means "no digit here if there is nothing to show",
which is what makes `#.##` print `.5` rather than `0.5`.

One section applied to one date. Tokenised first and substituted second,
so a replacement's own letters cannot be re-read: replacing `mmm` with
`September` and then scanning for `d` would find the `e`, and then the `p`.

`m` IS THE ONLY REAL AMBIGUITY IN THE GRAMMAR: month, or minute. Excel
reads it as minutes when it sits next to an hour or a seconds token, and
as a month otherwise. The neighbour that decides it is the previous or
next DATE-LETTER token, not the previous character. Reading the character
instead is a bug that hides well: in `m/d/yy h:mm` the token before the
final `mm` is a colon, so the rule missed the `h` behind it and printed
the month, which under a March date drew 12:03 for noon exactly.

A cell's value printed the way its format says to read it.

Until 2026-09-04 this decided the KIND of a value and printed that plainly,
on the argument that reproducing Excel's glyphs meant implementing the
whole format grammar. The consequence was that every number and every
currency fell through to `String(raw)`: an accounting cell read `1234.5`
where the workbook showed `$1,234.50`, which is the single loudest way a
rendered sheet says "this is not your spreadsheet". The subset above is
the answer, and it is a subset on purpose. What it does not interpret
(scientific notation, fractions, conditional sections) falls through to a
plain number rather than to an approximation.

A ROUNDED VALUE IS WHAT EXCEL DRAWS AND IS NOT THE WHOLE TRUTH. `0%` on
