dim the label at once. There the first tap shows the tip and the next
tap on the same chip, which closes it, dims. A pointer that hovers gets
the tip on hover, so every click dims. In Review a chip carries no tip,
and a tap picks the category the list holds.

── REVIEW: one category's units as a list over a strip of the document ──
The list holds the category the chips pick: Notes (every unit with a
note, the default where any unit has one) or a label. Below it a strip,
one slide per unit: the whole document painted as in Doc, that unit
current and its note set under it, scrolled into view. A swipe moves
the list's selection and a pick in the list moves the strip (html-style
rule 11). Stacked at every width, since the page sits in a deck, whose
frame is vertical.

What the list holds, said on the page: a tap on a chip picks the
category, so a chip cannot also open a tip that explains it.

The unit a view treats as current: the selection in Doc, the list's row
in Review, and while a slide is painted, that slide's own unit.
The strip, built again whenever its rows change: a category, an edit.

ONE SLIDE: the whole document with this unit current, its note set under
the block that holds it, and the slide scrolled so the unit sits a third
of the way down.

Move to row i, the strip following: instantly for a jump, smoothly for
a step to a neighbour.

A row under the pointer tints its unit in the document, with an outline
in the text colour so a pale label still shows; leaving puts the unit's
own shade back.
A tap on a unit in the document picks it, where the list holds it.
The current row kept in view inside the list, never by scrolling the page.

A unit as one line of plain text: list markers, emphasis and link
targets taken out.

WHERE IN THE DOCUMENT, and only that. This opened with the target's path,
which is the same for every unit on the page and is already in the
header, so the first 21 characters of the panel's TALLEST line never
varied. num() makes exactly this argument about the uid's shared prefix;
the location line had not been given the same reading.

ONE RENDER, THEN PAINT OVER IT. This used to render each unit on its own,
`markdown(text.slice(u.start, u.end))` sixty-odd times, concatenated. Every
trouble the boundary editing had came from that: a slice can open a `**` it
never closes, so there was a balance check and a red outline; a slice can
carry a `##` its neighbour lost, so half a heading rendered as a heading and
half as prose; a slice can be a list item's later sentence with no marker,
so there was a rule handing it back its indent. Each was a patch over the
same decision.

The document is rendered ONCE and keeps its own element tree. Units are
painted as tinted ranges over the text nodes, so a unit no longer produces
an element and therefore cannot cut one. A boundary inside a heading now
leaves the heading whole and gives it two tints, which is what it should
always have done. What fragments is the DOM at paint time, never the
annotation: the standoff stays a flat partition of character offsets, which
is the whole point of standoff.
`range` renders one section rather than the document, for the deck. A
section starts at a heading, so its edges are block edges and slicing
there cuts nothing: the reason per-unit slicing was wrong does not apply.

The type classes go on an inner element, never on the host: paint() does
not own its container's layout, and assigning className to the host wiped
the padding the page and the deck slide had each given it.

Source shows the bytes, Read shows the document. Both are ONE node tree
over the whole text, so the painting below is the same operation on each
and Source no longer has to reassemble the document from slices.

Every text node, its offset into the source. What it cannot find it
leaves unwrapped, and an unwrapped run carries no offset, so it is
simply not painted rather than painted in the wrong place.

MATERIALIZED IN PLACE, AND ONLY IN PLACE. An insertion holds text the
document does not contain, so drawing it here is the whole of what the
page can honestly do with one: the reader sees how the document would
read, and nothing is written. It carries no uid and takes no tint from
either axis, because it has neither a label nor a verdict to paint, and
it is added AFTER the map runs, so no boundary can land inside text that
has no offsets. Its own boundary is what it answers to, so a tap selects
the unit that anchors it and arms that edge.

Placed between BLOCKS, since that is where a boundary between blocks is.
Dropping it beside the piece would put a block element inside whatever
paragraph or heading that piece belongs to.

A section deck paints one range, so an insertion anchored outside it
has nothing to sit after and is simply not drawn here.

ONE PIECE OF ONE UNIT, inside whatever element the document put it in. A
unit is several of these when it crosses a block or an inline construct,
and they answer together: every treatment keys on data-uid rather than on
one element, so hover and selection reach the whole unit.

`first` and `last` say whether this piece carries the unit's own edge. The
tick marks are the boundary the reader is being shown, so they belong on
the outer edges of the unit and not on every internal seam the document's
markup happened to create.

A PIECE IS ALSO A MAPPED RUN. mapText wraps each text node and the
pieces are cut out of it, so the piece is what actually holds text now
and the whole pin stack (nodeAt, offsetAt, rectAt) reads data-src. Both
carry it: an outer span whose text no unit claimed keeps its own, and
one that was cut has element children, which nodeAt skips. `atomic` is
inherited so a boundary still cannot land inside a link or a bold span.

Hover tints the unit in whichever painted host it sits in, Doc's or
Review's.

TEXT DECORATION IS THE FREE CHANNEL, which is why the remove marker can
ride beside the label rather than displacing it: the tint, the ticks and
the opacity are all spent on the label, and this is not.

One property, one colour. Red wins where both apply: the selection is
where you already are, the verdict is the finding. Review's current
unit takes the primary colour, whatever its label's tint.

── EDGES ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A BOUNDARY IS THE OBJECT, not an edge: the end of one unit is the start of
the next, so there is one draggable thing per junction and the partition
survives by construction. Overlap is therefore not a mode this offers, and
since 2026-08-30 it is also a complaint the checker makes.

TAP TO ARM, NOT DRAG TO EXTEND, which is lib/kits/annotate.js's measured
answer for the same problem on the same phone: dragging a handle puts the
finger over the words being aimed at, which is what every platform then
patches with a floating magnifier. Two taps also survive a scroll, a
mis-hit and a change of mind, and a drag survives none of them.

EDGES ARE A READ-VIEW AFFORDANCE. Source shows the bytes, markup and all,
and a boundary placed inside `**` or `](url)` leaves one side holding an
unclosed delimiter; the rendered view cannot offer one, since markup is
in no text node and an inline construct is atomic. Two views that
disagreed about what is legal would be worse than one that edits.
EVERY UNIT HAS TWO BOUNDARIES, one before it and one after. The first
unit's "before" is the head of the document and the last unit's "after"
is its tail, and those two follow or precede no unit: `shift` refuses
them because it needs a unit on each side, `insert` takes them because it
needs one. That asymmetry is the whole of `shiftable`. This list used to
omit both, which was right while shift was the only boundary op and left
a document unable to gain a lead or a closing sentence once insert
arrived.
The insertion standing at a boundary, if any. `after: null` is the head.

THE SHAPE IN FORCE at the armed boundary, or null where the question does
not arise: no insertion stands there, or it is the head, where a run has
nothing to run into and the check refuses it. `document` is an answer and
not the absence of one, which is why the button group reads it from here
rather than from `as` directly.

A getter because x-for renders inside x-show whether or not the group is
displayed, so an expression reaching through a null armedEdge throws on
every repaint with nothing on screen to show for it.

The shape, restated as a whole insert. The op is keyed by its anchor and
REPLACES what stands there, so setting the shape is the same operation as
setting the text and needs no op of its own. `document` writes no field
at all, which is why it cannot be a third value of one.

A tap in the text is two different requests, and which one is a state the
reader set by tapping a pinhead. Armed: put this boundary here. Otherwise:
make that unit the active one.
A CLICK IS NOT ALWAYS A TAP, and on a touch screen the difference is what
broke this. Measured 2026-09-07 with a real finger: tapping a pin puts

  click(touch), pointerdown(touch), touchstart, pointerup, touchend, click

on the document. The FIRST click arrives before any pointerdown, because
a tap on the pin synthesizes a click into the document underneath it, and
hit() runs on click while lastTapOffset is recorded on pointerdown. So
that phantom ran with no offset of its own: it consumed the arming and,
where an earlier tap had left an offset standing, placed the boundary at
a point the reader had tapped for some other reason entirely. A mouse
orders pointerdown before click always, so none of it is visible there.

The offset is therefore CONSUMED, once, by the click that follows its own
pointerdown. A click carrying none is a phantom: it does nothing at all
and leaves the pin armed, rather than spending the arming on a placement
nobody asked for.

A tap relocates a boundary that HAS two sides. The head and the tail
have one, so there is nothing to relocate them between: the tap falls
through and selects, which is what it would have done unarmed, rather
than pushing a shift both implementations would refuse.

A boundary lands between words, never inside one. caretRangeFromPoint
answers in characters, which is finer than any judgement being made here:
a unit divides a sentence at a word, and a pin parked mid-word reads as a
slip every time. Snapping to the nearer end of the word under the pointer
keeps the drag continuous and the result legible. All three placers go
through here (drag, tap, pad), so they agree.

The client rect of the collapsed range at a document offset, which is
what the pin painter measures from.

A BOUNDARY IS SHARED: it ends one unit and starts the next, and
Standoff.nodeAt answers with the FIRST span containing the offset,
which is the earlier one. Its rendered run is followed by the
separator text node and both units' padding, so the mark landed 8 to
9px short of the text it opens, measured at 390 and 1280 alike. The
later span's offset 0 is the same boundary at the place a reader sees
it, so prefer it and keep nodeAt for the end of a paragraph, where
there is no later span to ask.
MARKUP HAS NO CHARACTER TO PIN, and until now that meant no pin at all.
Every list item opens with its marker, so every list item lost its
START handle and its opening boundary could not be moved from the page
at all. The honest place for a boundary that falls in markup is the
unit's nearest RENDERED character on the correct side: before its first
for a start, after its last for an end. That is a position, not a
claim about which character the offset is, and the drag reads its
offsets from the pointer rather than from where the pin was drawn.
Scoped to the selected unit, or a missing start would borrow a rect
from the next unit and mark a boundary somewhere else entirely. An
ATOMIC run counts here, unlike everywhere else: a boundary may not go
INSIDE a link or a bold span, but the unit's own first and last
characters are outside every construct it contains, and a unit that is
bold end to end has no other run to offer. Dragging such a pin inward
is refused by offsetAt, which is the correct answer; dragging it
outward, to swallow the sentence before it, is the move it exists for.

Whitespace-only runs are excluded, and that is not tidiness: see the
wrapped-space case at the bottom of this method.

A COLLAPSED RANGE AT THE END OF A RUN MEASURES ZERO, which is not the
same as having no position: the boundary at the end of a paragraph is
exactly where the last character stops. Measure that character and take
its trailing edge, which is the same point by another route.

Landing at the END of a run means the boundary is a junction. Which
side of it the mark belongs on depends on which edge is being drawn:
a START edge OPENS the selected unit, so it belongs at that unit's
first character, while an END edge CLOSES it and belongs at its last.
nodeAt always answers with the earlier run, which is right for an end
and 8 to 9px short for a start. An exact data-src match cannot find
the later run either: mapText trims the slice's leading whitespace, so
its data-src sits past the boundary by whatever white space separated
them. Step to the next run instead.

AND A SPACE THAT WRAPPED MEASURES NOTHING AT ALL, which is the case the
two measurements above both miss. A split hands the separator to one
side (ops.py's halves meet, and openSplit's regex takes the whitespace
with the first half), so a unit can end on a space; when the line breaks
exactly there the browser gives that space a zero-width box and a Range
over it no box, so the edge reported itself unpinnable while the reader
could plainly see where the unit ended. Measured at 390 on
conven-063a, which pins at 900 and did not at 390.

The unit's own last non-blank character is that place. Same fallback as
the markup case above, for the same reason: a position, not a claim
about which character the offset is.

THE PINS ARE THE DICTATION PAGE'S PINS, painted by Dictate.pins: a ball
on a stem that covers the line, above on the left and below on the right,
red with a light centre when armed. It was settled there against a thumb
and it is one implementation, so this page hands over two rects and gets
the same marker rather than an approximation of it.

`reach: 0`, the same as pages/dictate.html, and for its reason: the
clearance comes from the drag's vertical deadband, so the reader takes
exactly as much as they need and the pin stays where it is pointing.
`arrows: false`, since this page has a pad.
An edge with no rect gets NO PIN. Two ways that happens and both are
honest: the unit is the document's first or last, so the edge is not a
boundary at all; or the boundary sits in markup, where the render has no
position for it. The second is a legacy condition rather than a gap in
the map: the segmenter cuts at block starts, and a block starts at `## `
or `- **`, which the placement rule now forbids. Drawing a pin at zero
for either puts a marker in the corner pointing at nothing, which is what
the painter does when handed a null rect.

The panel opens down and right of the POINTER, the way a context menu
does, rather than aligned to the unit. Aligning it to the span put it in
a fixed place no matter where the tap landed, which for a unit spanning
three lines is nowhere near the words that were actually touched.

Flips back over the pointer on whichever axis would overflow, so a tap
in the bottom-right corner opens up and left instead of being shoved
sideways. Falls back to the unit's own rect when the selection did not
come from a pointer at all (the standoff table's rows, a re-place after
an edit), which is the only case with no point to work from.

THE VISUAL VIEWPORT, NOT THE LAYOUT ONE, and this is the whole of the
mobile fix. A fixed element is positioned against the LAYOUT viewport,
and every CSS measure available to the panel describes that one too:
`100vw` does not shrink under pinch-zoom, and inside the toss iframe it
is the frame's width rather than the phone's. So a panel sized in CSS
can be wider than what is actually on screen, and a clamp computed from
the same measure agrees with it and still puts the panel off the right
edge. Sizing and placing from `visualViewport` makes both answers come
from the region the reader can see.

Only the viewport half is replaced. The design cap (20rem, 70%) stays
where it is written, and the class on the element keeps it as the
before-JS floor; what changes is that the second term now measures the
region the reader can see instead of the one the document was laid out
in. Inline wins over the class, so this tightens and never widens.
The 7rem gutter is not slack. Tapping outside is how the panel closes,
so a popover filling the width is a sheet with no way out; the floor
keeps that true on a viewport too narrow for the subtraction. Narrow
and tall also beats wide and short here, since the content is short
lines and a label the eye has to find, not a paragraph.

A PANEL ALPINE HAS NOT YET UN-HIDDEN MEASURES 0 BY 0, and a clamp
against a zero width is not a clamp: it leaves left at x + GAP, and the
panel then paints its real width off the right edge. Placement has to
wait for a box, and one frame is usually it. Bounded, so a panel that
never gets one stops asking instead of looping every frame.

THE PINS ARE OBSTACLES, NOT DECORATION. Each is 32px of tap target on
the selected unit's own boundary, which is exactly where a panel
anchored to the tap wants to sit, and a panel over a pin does not look
broken: the pin is drawn, it is simply unreachable, so arming reads as
a dead control. Found by asking elementFromPoint what is under the
pinhead rather than by looking, since both cases are the same picture.

Down-right first, the direction asked for, then the three flips. Those
four are not enough on a phone and the geometry says why: the panel is
most of the width, so any vertical band it occupies that a pin's band
touches collides no matter where it sits horizontally. The freedom is
vertical, so the last two candidates clear the pins OUTRIGHT, below
them or above them, which is the only move a narrow screen leaves.

The pin drag, from pages/dictate.html: the aim point is the BAR's centre
carried by the finger's delta, one to one, so what moves under the ball is
what the ball was already marking. `lead` is the ball's own offset from
its stem, measured at the grab, which is what makes the two pins hold back
by different amounts and arrive at the same thumb-below-the-aim distance.

WHICH PIN THE FINGER MEANT, which is not always the one the browser
hands over. A pin's touch target is a 32px box padded above and below
the line it marks, so two pins on adjacent lines overlap wherever their
x values are close, and elementFromPoint then answers with whichever was
appended last, which is always `end`. Grabbing the start pin and
watching the end boundary move is what that looks like from the outside,
and it is what this page did until 2026-09-07: measured at 430px on the
stored CONVENTIONS.md run, the start box sat at (132,301,32x53) and the
end box at (117,328,32x53), so the start pin's own centre was inside the
end pin's box.

Resolved by distance to the BAR, which is the thing a pin actually
marks, rather than by stacking order. Only boxes containing the point
are considered and the gate above is unchanged, so a point inside one
box alone still answers with that box.

MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING IS REPAINTED. The bar is the pin's first child
and it IS the text line; the painter restyles in place but a repaint
still moves it, so both rects are read now.

Armed on the way DOWN, so the ring is under the finger before it moves
and a drag never has to be told apart from a tap to paint it.

ARMING IS NOT DRAGGING, and at the head and the tail only the first is
available: a boundary with a unit on one side holds text and cannot be
relocated, since there is nothing to relocate it between. Returning
here leaves it armed, which is what the insert field in the panel
reads, and never starts a drag that ops.shift would refuse mid-gesture.

Moved live and recorded once: one drag is one judgment, so the patch
gets a single shift when the finger lifts.

A TAP IS A DRAG THAT WENT NOWHERE, and it toggles: tap to arm, tap
again to put down.

Where the last tap landed, recorded on the way down so `hit()` can use it
on the way up. One delegated listener, bound once: paint() rebuilds every
span, so a per-span listener would be re-bound on every repaint.

One source of position beats two that must agree, so the pins are
re-measured rather than offset. Cheap: at most two of them.

The deck is a CONTAINER, not a viewer: one section per slide, same units,
same paint(). Nothing about the audit changes to ride it.
THE VIEWER. The page opens in the house swipe deck, the frame other
files open in: one slide holding the whole document as one vertical
scroll, the view controls in the deck's header and the legend in its
subheader row. The Stage's transform tool mounts the same way. Closing
the deck puts each piece back where it came from, so the plain page
underneath is whole again rather than empty.

The elements themselves, held here: $refs is resolved against the DOM,
so a ref detached by the deck (the legend in Spans) stops resolving.

The legend row is the document's; in Spans the deck carries no
subheader at all, rather than an empty bordered strip.

Each label's share of the section's words, drawn as the legend's
strip draws the document's, in place of a line of totals. The
section's own heading opens the card below it.

Busy until the payload has loaded, so a look link waits for the header and
legend it renders (lib/kits/look.js, seek).

Tenant chrome: this page is routinely tossed inside an iframe, so it
sticks rather than taking the viewport, and it does not narrow itself
to a reading column. No line of totals: each legend chip counts its
units and its note gives its share of words, the strip under the
legend draws those shares, and Review counts what has been removed.

Reporting is the normal state, so this is a fact about the page
rather than a warning, and there is nothing on it to act on. It
stays visible because a page that files reports must be answerable
to whoever is holding it; the address carries ?report=off for one
load, and the kit's disable() for good.

Two different objects: the document, tinted by its annotation, or
the annotation itself as data. How the document is shown (rendered
or raw markdown) is a display choice, so it sits on the legend row
with the other two.
The view controls. In the deck viewer they ride in its header.

Rendered, on or off, for whichever object is on screen: the
formatted document or the spans table when on, the markdown or
standoff.json when off.

On a phone the pair shrinks to undo and the count, so the deck's
header keeps its title: redo stays in the unit panel and on the
keyboard.

The legend is the explanation. Each chip carries the treatment it
names, so a label chip is tinted as its units are. Hovering one
lights its units. Tapping one dims its units in place rather than
hiding them, which keeps the document readable while one category is
set aside. In Review the chips are the category the list holds, one
at a time, with Notes, every unit with a note, first.

One line at any width. The chips take whatever the controls leave and
scroll sideways when a vocabulary has more labels than fit.
How the document's units are drawn.

How a unit is drawn, Doc only: its label's tint over the whole
span, or an underline. Icon toggles carry their state in the
icon's colour alone: no outline, no fill.

Each label's share of the document's words, in its chip's hue and
in the chips' order: the part-to-whole the chips' notes give one
label at a time, drawn whole, so its figures stay in those notes.
A chip set aside dims its segment.

Everything below the header. In the deck viewer this is the one slide,
and it scrolls inside itself: the whole document, top to bottom.

The pin layer. It overlays the doc box exactly, takes no taps of its
own, and hands each pin back its own: the painter writes the box's
whole style attribute, so the exception is a rule here rather than
an inline property there. While a pin is being dragged the pins stop
hit-testing, so the aim point reads the text and not the pin on it.

REVIEW: the chips' category as a list over a strip of the document.
A caption says what the category is; the list under it is one line
per unit and as tall as its rows, up to a third of the height; the bar
under it steps through the list and edits the current unit; the strip
below holds one slide per unit, the whole document with that unit
current and its note under it. Stacked at every width, and it fills
the viewport under the header as Spans does.

A row under the pointer tints its unit in the document. The current
row carries the primary bar, the colour of the document's underline.
A row names its label only under Notes, the one category that mixes
labels.

The label as a pill over the platform's own select, and the
verdict as Keep or Drop, both as in the unit panel.

rBuild() mounts the strip here. data-no-swipe: a sideways drag here
is the strip's, never the deck's.

The annotation as the thing it is: rows over spans, and the committed
bytes underneath. The page never re-derives this; the builder copies
standoff.json in verbatim, so what is on screen is what is in the file.

Fills the viewport under the header, and the table or the JSON scrolls
inside it, so the column headings stay in view. The height is bound
as an object, here and in Review: a string :style rewrites the whole
style attribute whenever inDeck or hdrH changes, which drops x-show's
display:none and left this table under every other view.

Above the shared FAB (z-80), which is fixed to this same corner and was
covering the split candidates. dictate.html's sheet takes the corner the
same way: while a page's own bottom UI is up, it owns the bottom.

A PILL IS SIZED BY ITS TEXT, AND A SELECT IS NOT. A native select
takes the width of its WIDEST option plus a chevron, so `KEEP` was
carrying `REWRITE`'s width and `NAV` was carrying `PROV`'s, which is
the padding that read as awkward. The span sizes the pill to the
value actually shown; the select lies over it at zero opacity and
takes the tap, so this is still the platform's own dropdown rather
than a menu reimplemented.

Whether the unit stays: Keep, or Drop from the document. The one
edit the tools carry out; anything else, a rewording included, goes
in the note below. Both values are named, so the control reads as
a decision about this unit rather than as a delete.

GROUPED BY THE QUESTION EACH LINE ANSWERS, which nothing said before:
the block above is what this unit IS and what was decided about it,
this one is where it sits and how big, the next is how it came to
have these boundaries. The no-drag notice moved up here because it is
a fact about this unit's edges, and it used to sit below the note
with the two position lines separated by everything between.

Wrapping rather than truncating is what lets the panel be narrow:
this line was the widest thing in it, and a truncated one still
claims the width it was cut to.

THE ARMED BOUNDARY IS THE INSERTION'S ANCHOR, so the row that already
belongs to a boundary takes the second boundary operation rather than
a control of its own. Drag is offered only where the boundary has a
unit on each side: the head and the tail have one, which is enough to
hold text and not enough to relocate.

HOW THE TEXT MEETS WHAT IS AROUND IT. Three choices, not two,
because `document` is a distinct state and not a synonym for one of
the others: it leaves the field unset and hands the answer to the
boundary, which is the honest default at every boundary but the
tail, where a document's final newline is a terminator rather than
a paragraph break. Absent at the head, where a run has nothing to
run into and the check refuses it.

Undo BESIDE the operations, not only in the header. A drag ends
with the finger on the panel and the header a screen away, so the
one control a reader wants immediately after an edit was the one
furthest from it. The header pair stays: it is the only undo
reachable with nothing selected.

The patch is the artifact of an editing session: what you decided,
reviewable as a list of judgments rather than as a JSON diff.

Two ways out, and the page says which one is open. Saving writes
the edited standoff to the ref being read; where that ref is main
there is nothing to write to, and the command below is the route.

bench.html — a page a shortcut calls into, rather than a page a shortcut opens.

EVERY OTHER PAGE IN THIS ESTATE IS A DESTINATION. Show-Html navigates Safari
to a data: URL, Show-WebView raises a sheet, show.py gzips a page into a link.
In all three the shortcut's flow ENDS when the page appears, which is why the
return channel has been such a preoccupation and why Log-Repo exists at all.

Run JavaScript on Web Page is the other direction and it was already on the
device. It runs inside a shortcut and hands its value back through
completion(), so a page becomes callable. Three facts settle the model, all
read out of the corpus rather than guessed (shortcut-tools
docs/shortcuts-format-notes.md, "The browser is a coprocessor"):

  1. completion() returns structured values, not only text. Get-Nice ends a
     card with completion(window.siriData), an array of objects.
  2. The page is a HEAP BETWEEN CALLS. One Get-Nice card writes
     window.siriData, a later separate card reads it back. Same run, same page.
  3. WFJavaScript may be a token string, and in AI Run JavaScript On Page it is
     ENTIRELY one variable. So the sent script can be built at run time.

EACH DEPENDENCY NAMES ITS UMD DIST FILE, and that is not tidiness. A jsDelivr
combine of bare package names takes each package's DEFAULT entry, and js-yaml's
and papaparse's are CommonJS: the first unguarded `exports` throws, and because
combine concatenates into one script, the throw takes out every package after it
in the bundle. The symptom is that marked works and Papa is not defined, which
reads as a CDN outage rather than as the bundle being one file. Caught by
node/test/bench-page.mjs on 2026-08-29.

WHAT THAT BUYS, AND WHY THIS PAGE EXISTS. The documented performance cliff on
that action scales with SOURCE LENGTH (JavaScriptCore, no JIT), not with work
done. So the discipline is not "avoid JavaScript in Shortcuts", it is "put the
heavy code somewhere that already parsed it and send one line". A page that has
already pulled marked, js-yaml, papaparse and turndown off the CDN is exactly
that somewhere. The shortcut then sends:

    completion(bench.call("md", "<base64>"))

which is short enough that the cliff never applies.

INPUT ARRIVES BASE64, DELIBERATELY. It is interpolated into the script by
Shortcuts, so raw text would end the string literal on the first quote,
backtick or newline it contained. Base64 with WFBase64LineBreakMode "None" has
none of those characters, and the estate already base64s on this boundary
(Log-Repo does). bench.call decodes as UTF-8 on the way in.

OPS ARE SYNCHRONOUS ON PURPOSE. completion(bench.call(...)) has to receive a
value, not a promise. An async op is still reachable, it just has to be written
by the caller as bench.call("x", b).then(completion).

THE CALL LOG IS THE POINT OF THE UI. Leave this open in a tab, drive it from a
shortcut, and watch each call land with its op, its input size and its result.
That is the diagnostic the estate never had for this boundary: everywhere else
a failed call is a shortcut that stops with no explanation. The try-it box
below exercises the same bench.call the shortcut uses, so the page is testable
in a desktop browser with no device in the loop.

Built as nodes rather than interpolated markup. A call's output is arbitrary
text, and `md` returns HTML by definition, so this is the one place on the
page holding a value that must not be parsed. textContent settles it without
a local escape helper, which the estate keeps to exactly one (window.esc,
lib/vanilla-bundle.js) and this page does not boot the chain to reach.

Three layers, and the split is the point:

  DERIVED   read from the API on every load: state, ahead/behind, lifespan,
            authoring sessions, the PRs, commits, the changed files. Because

            needs no sync step. A link to it is current whenever it is opened,

            is where the judgment has always been written, so this page reads

            FAB drawer uses, which re-aims each file link at what can show the
            file and lifts them into a chip strip. Arrows step through every
            PR the branch has had, since a merge ends a PR but not a branch.

            branch with no PR to carry it: intent, what is open, what was left

            family is (docs/envelopes/):

              ?src=<owner/repo[@ref]:path>   fetched through the contents API
              #gz=<base64url>                gzipped into the fragment

            than by asking, mirroring lib/kits/data-payload.js. A `branch-review/1`

The ready gate, and why it is a plain script ABOVE the module.

Importing the pre-build boots Alpine as part of the import: alpine-bundle.js
is the last entry in its auto-boot chain. So by the time the module below
resumes to run its own gh.load calls, Alpine has already started, walked the
DOM, and run this page's `init()`. Any kit the page loads for itself is
therefore undefined at component-init time, and which one you notice depends
only on how far init gets before it touches one: `reviewTarget.parse` in
resolve(), or `BranchBrief.fetchBrief` one await later. Both were live, and
the second was reported from a real browser on 2026-08-07.

The build already solved this once, for itself: url-params.js and
repo-address.js are forced into the auto-boot chain precisely because "a
page's own gh.load chain runs AFTER this import" (node/build/build-lib.mjs).
That fix does not extend to a kit only one page wants, so the page has to
state its own readiness.

So this draws the ROUTES. One origin at the top, three paths down through

TWO MECHANICS THIS PAGE IS BUILT AROUND.
1. An x-for inside <svg> draws nothing: Alpine clones a <template> into the
   HTML namespace and <rect> parses as an unknown element. So the diagram is
   built in JS instead, as real nodes through createElementNS, driven by
   x-effect. Nodes carry data-node for a delegated listener rather than
   Alpine bindings. Building nodes rather than interpolating a markup string
   also settles escaping at the root: attributes go through setAttribute and
   labels through textContent, neither of which parses markup, so the page
   needs no local escape helper (the estate keeps exactly one, window.esc in
   lib/vanilla-bundle.js, and this page does not boot the chain to reach it).
2. No modal, and no daisyUI tooltip. Every node explains itself in place, on
   hover where the pointer is fine and on tap everywhere, per the house
   style's compliant-tooltip rules.

dictate.html — the blank page you talk at.

Every other caller of kits/dictate.js attaches the voice buffer to something:
the annotator pins a note to a passage, the stage makes a file out of it, the
FAB's menu stages a note about the page you are reading. All three are right
and none of them answers "I want to say a thing." That address did not exist,
which is why the dictation stack could be complete and still not be reached
for. This page is the missing address and nothing else: a full viewport of
text, a pad under your thumb, and somewhere for the words to go.

IT IS A PHONE PAGE FIRST. Not responsive-so-it-also-works: the shell is the
viewport (h-dvh, no document scroll, so no pull-to-refresh and no rubber
band), the controls sit at the bottom where a thumb already is, the type runs
large enough to read at arm's length while speaking, and the bottom row
clears the home indicator. A desktop gets the same thing centred, which costs
nothing and is the honest way round: the hard constraints are the phone's.

THE GESTURE LAYER IS THE NOTES COMPOSER'S (kits/annotate.js), not the
stage's. The first cut of this page took the stage's dictation card, which
is a version behind: it keeps the painter's arrow cluster because it has no
cursor pad, and it still carries a pencil into the keyboard. What came
across on 2026-08-23 is the composer's answer to both. The PAD is held and
dragged, the caret moves and the button does not, so placing one no longer
means putting a thumb over the two words either side of it; `arrows: false`
follows, since an armed pin is dragged the same way. A DOUBLE TAP opens the
keyboard where it landed, and the pencil is gone. What did NOT come across
is the composer's vertical mark column, for a reason measured rather than
preferred: see "The text" below.

WHAT IT ADDS TO THE KIT, since the kit is where the composition rules live:

  THE ENGINE IS KEPT ALIVE. Not here, in the kit, but this page is why it
  was fixed. `continuous` is a request WebKit does not honor past its own
  silence timeout, so the microphone switched itself off at every thinking
  pause. Survivable for a one-sentence note; fatal for the thing this page
  is for. See "Keeping the engine alive" in kits/dictate.js.

  THE DRAFT SURVIVES THE PAGE. Every change writes the buffer to
  localStorage, and it is restored on the next load. A phone call, a swipe
  to another app that comes back cold, a stray reload: none of them should
  cost ten minutes of talking. The draft is cleared when the words reach
  somewhere durable, so a session that ENDED properly opens blank and only
  an INTERRUPTED one comes back.

  THE SCREEN IS HELD AWAKE while listening, because a phone that dims and
  locks takes the microphone with it, and nothing about that failure tells
  the reader what happened.

  TWO MODIFIER TAPS, for the desk rather than the phone, where the hands are
  free and idle. Both say something only the reader can know, because it is
  about words not yet spoken: CONTROL un-ends the sentence the pause just
  closed, so the words still coming belong to it; SHIFT capitalizes the next
  word, or recases the selected one. Tapped alone, acted on release, so a
  chord is not mistaken for one. See "The two modifier taps" below.

  IT COMES BACK FROM THE BACKGROUND. Switching apps kills the recognition
  outright, past anything a relaunch timer can see, so returning to a
  visible page restarts it if the reader never asked to stop.

  THE WORDS GO SOMEWHERE. This is the half that makes it a tool rather than
  a textarea. Copy and Share read the buffer; Jot files it in the estate's
  pile (the registry's lists/jot.json, which the app already renders at
  ?view=lists) and Drop writes a dated markdown file into home's chron/dump/,
  the tray /drain reads. The two that file it durably clear the buffer; the
  two that only read it leave it alone.

  AND SEND, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT DOES NOT FILE THE WORDS AT ALL. It reads
  them as an INSTRUCTION and hands them somewhere that can act on it: the
  system share sheet, a new Claude Code session with repositories
  preselected, or a chat. It stands where Share stood, because Share is one
  of those rows rather than a peer of them.

  THAT ALSO FIXES WHAT SHARE COULD NOT SAY. The button carried
  `x-show="canShare"`, so on a browser without navigator.share, which is
  most desktops, it was simply absent: no reason given, and no pointer at
  Copy. The button is unconditional now and the share ROW carries the
  absence, greyed with its reason, exactly as an unreachable link target
  does.

  IT IS ALSO WHY THIS PAGE IS THE ONE THAT CAN DO IT. The composer on a page
  (kits/annotate.js) has room for the words and nowhere to put the aiming;
  the estate's session rows have the repositories and nowhere to write. Here
  both fit, which is the whole reason the annotator's expand button points at
  this page rather than growing a target picker of its own.

  NOTHING IS SENT BY SENDING. The link prefills a composer at the far end and
  the reader still presses the button there, which is the documented
  behaviour for Claude Code and the reason a one-tap control is safe. The one
  target that does submit on arrival is named as such in the sheet, on the row
  itself, because a reader cannot be expected to know which is which.

  AUTOCORRECT, and the plain word is the right one: it is find and replace
  over a list, whole words, longest first, applied to each segment as it
  lands (kits/dictate.js `opts.fix`). It earns its place only because iOS
  Text Replacement reaches the keyboard and not a page's speech results,
  and because the Web Speech API's own SpeechGrammarList does nothing in
  WebKit. The list lives in the registry and the menu row adds to it from
  whatever is selected, so it gets better the more it is wrong. What it
  cannot do is context: homophones are out of its reach entirely, and only
  a model reading the sentence around a word would go further.

WHERE THE CONTROLS SIT. The HEADER is a three-column grid: the session on
the left (record, and how long it has run), the TARGET on the centre line,
and the history plus the menu on the right (undo, redo, the keyboard). The
BOTTOM is two rows, and they are split by what a tap DOES rather than by
how it looks: the KEYS that compose (the marks, the shift, backspace) and
the DESTINATIONS that end it (Copy, Share, Jot, Drop). Record doubles as
the state readout, since red and pulsing answers "is it hearing me" from
across the room and the page then needs no word for it.

BACKSPACE IS A KEY, and its two earlier homes were both reasoned from
something other than how often it is tapped. In the header it sat beside
undo and redo, on the reading that the three all take something back: true,
and beside the point, since undo is reached for a handful of times in a
session and backspace is reached for mid-sentence, over and over. Moved
down on 2026-08-25 it landed in the row that ends the note, which was the
only room there was, so the key that removes a word sat against the button
that filed it. It is the fifth key now, at the right end, where every
keyboard the reader has ever used puts it. Five across a phone is 73px
each, still half again the composer's column key.

THE DESTINATIONS ARE FOUR BUTTONS, not a Save that opens four. The sheet
they were in was a CHOOSER and never a confirmation: tapping Jot in it
filed the note there and then, so the extra tap bought no safety, only
distance. Flattened 2026-08-27.

AND THE FOURTH OF THEM IS A CHOOSER AGAIN, which is not a reversal. Send
took Share's slot on 2026-09-06 and Share became one row inside it, beside
the two that start a session somewhere. The rule above forbids a sheet
wrapping choices already MADE; which destination, and for a session which
repositories, are choices nobody has made yet. Share was always a chooser
with a single option, opened by the operating system rather than here. What the sheet carried and the row cannot
is a line of description under each name; those are titles now, and the one
that says something a reader cannot infer, where Drop writes, is also in
the toast that lands after it writes.

THE TARGET IS TWO GESTURES ON ONE BUTTON, because they are one job: this is
the control that aims. DRAG it and the caret moves (the pad, below). TAP it
and the caret becomes one end of a selection whose other end is your next
tap in the text. Two taps for an arbitrary range, where the long press gives
only a word and the pins give one edge at a time.

AND THE TARGET IS RED WHENEVER A PIN IS. There is one armed state, not two:
arming a pinhead lights the target, tapping the target puts any pin down,
and the second tap of the two-tap selection disarms rather than leaving one
lit. So the red target means one thing, "the next tap in the text moves
something", and the reader gets a full-size button for the exit that the
12px pinhead was: a near miss there used to clear the selection outright.

AND NO HAPTIC ON THE LONG PRESS, though the platform's own long-press
selection answers with one. Measured on the device rather than assumed:
docs/ios-haptics.md. The reachable buzz belongs to a real user activation of
a native control, a scripted one earns nothing, and navigator.vibrate has
never existed in WebKit. There is no way for this page to fire one at the
moment its own gesture does.

FILE MODE opens an existing file instead of a blank page, so the same pad,
voice and keyboard revise a document rather than start a note. Added
2026-09-24, because nothing in the estate opened an arbitrary markdown file,
took edits, and committed it back. Five things change and nothing else does:

  THE BOTTOM ROW IS COPY AND SEND. Jot and Drop file a note somewhere new,
  which is the wrong act for words that already have a home. Send opens the
  same sheet as ever with two things added: WHAT GOES (the record of changes
  and notes, the edit as a patch, or the whole file) above the rows, and
  SAVE TO GITHUB as the first row, so committing is one destination among
  the places the edit can go rather than a button of its own.

  SAVE WRITES WITH THE SHA IT LOADED, AND NOTHING ELSE. It does not go
  through GH.prototype.save, whose recovery answers a 409 by fetching the
  current sha and writing again: right for the estate's own JSON, and a
  silent overwrite of somebody else's edit here. A conflict is reported, the
  buffer stays, and Reload is the way back to what GitHub holds.

  THE DRAFT IS KEYED TO THE FILE and carries the sha it was begun from, so an
  interrupted edit reopens in the file it belongs to, and a save of it still
  conflicts if the file moved in the meantime.

  NOTHING STARTS LISTENING ON ARRIVAL. The remembered grant opens a blank
  page into the microphone, which is what a blank page is for; a document is
  opened to be read first, and words landing at its end unasked are damage.

  THE TYPE IS SMALLER, 17px against 21, since a document is read at reading
  distance and a note is spoken at arm's length.

  AND IT HAS TWO FACES, on a toggle in the header. SOURCE is the buffer as
  this page has always drawn it. RENDERED is the document as it reads, and
  it is not a preview: kits/md-surface.js answers the same three questions
  Dictate.paint does (draw, point to offset, on the words or not) over the
  rendered markdown, so every gesture here works on it and every edit is still
  an edit to the markdown string. A markdown file opens Rendered. A third,
  read-only CHANGES face (kits/md-diff.js) was retired on 2026-09-29: with
  the change cards below it showed the same edit a second time, and what it
  alone had, a count and next and previous, moved onto the Rendered face.

  TYPING WORKS IN THE RENDERED FACE TOO, through an invisible textarea that
  holds the caret's line of source (see startTyping). A wrapper such as
  `**…**` stays while one character of it remains and goes with the last;
  backspace at the start of a heading or item drops its marker; Enter makes a
  paragraph, or the next list item.

  AND IT TRACKS CHANGES IN PLACE, the way a word processor does. Each run
  of blocks that differs from GitHub's copy is drawn as one CARD in the flow,
  open to typing: removed words struck, added words green, both where they
  stand, and a block taken out struck whole. Deleting an original word strikes it; typing shows green; deleting
  your own green text simply removes it, since the changes are the difference
  between the buffer and the base rather than a log. Struck words are drawn
  and never mapped, so the caret cannot land in them; tapping one offers it
  back. A card's stops pill reads original, marked and new: original is
  GitHub's text, read-only; new is the text clean, still open to typing. A
  tap on a stop or a sideways swipe picks one, a tap on the original returns
  to marked, and an edit forgets every original; its number wears an × that
  discards the change. A pill in the pane's corner counts the cards and
  steps between them. The faces pill's Rendered · after shows the text without them. kits/md-surface.js (tracked) draws them.

  AND THE SAME CARDS OVER THE MARKDOWN, as Raw · changes on the faces pill,
  whose six faces are a grid: Rendered and Raw, each Before, Changes and
  After (owner, 2026-10-04). md-surface's `raw` draws each block as its
  source, so the cards, their readings, the notes and the gestures are the
  same ones, and a change to markup (a bold added, a link moved) is read
  where it is. Typing there takes keys as their own characters: Enter is a
  newline, and backspace at a line's start takes the newline before it.

  PARAGRAPHS ARE JOINED, SPLIT AND CARRIED BY HAND. Backspace at a
  paragraph's start joins it to the one above; a long press on the space
  between two sentences offers Split; a long press inside a selection (a
  drag, under a mouse) carries it, to between two words or onto a gap as a
  paragraph of its own. Each is one undo step, in kits/dictate.js (join,
  split, move); the methods beside paintExtras below say how they are drawn.
  In a change card, a gray bar in the text marks where a paragraph break was
  closed, or in the original, where one will be opened.

  THE PLATFORM SELECTS, by default since 2026-10-01 (an option from 09-27):
  selecting in the Rendered face is its long press, handles and callout on
  a phone, and its drag, double click and shift-click on a desk. The
  buffer's range follows the platform's selection, a tap or a click still
  places the caret, and a Move pill under a selection carries it to the
  next place tapped. Split then comes from the shifted ¶ at a caret. On a
  desk a click no longer opens typing; the first key does. The page's own
  painted selection with its pins is Native selection unchecked in the
  menu, or ?sel=painted. See nativeSync.

  A CHANGE IS DISCARDED FROM ITS OWN CARD, the × on its number, which puts
  that block back as GitHub has it (mdDiff.revert). The whole edit leaves by
  Send: a Claude Code session gets the patch with a line saying
  where it belongs, Share and Copy in the sheet's foot get the bare patch
  (`git apply` takes it). Copy in the bottom row copies the whole buffer.

  AND IT REVIEWS THE PROPOSAL QUEUE, with `&proposed`. A proposal is a
  request in the Text collection (mehrlander/home, projects/text/
  proposals.jsonl, filed by tools/propose.py there) to replace one passage
  of a named file. With `&proposed` the buffer starts as GitHub's copy with
  every proposal queued for this file put in (stageProposals), so each is a
  change card like any edit: confirm and Apply commits it, the × discards
  it. A held draft still wins, being the reader's own progress through the
  queue, and Clear all edits stages the queue again. Two limits. A block
  with several proposals stages the first and hides the rest. And a discard
  here lives only in this browser's draft, so once the draft ends it is
  staged again; a rejection in the Docs reader is a down vote in
  reviews.jsonl, and a rejected proposal is not staged.

  AND IT ANSWERS A DOCUMENTATION CALL, with `&user-call=`. A user call
  (web-tools-private user-calls/user-call.py, kind documentation) is one
  action item: a question, a brief, a recommendation, the session and PR
  it came from, and its edits written into it. The page draws that head
  under the header and stages the edits it can find in GitHub's copy
  (stageEdits), so each is a card like any other. Answer, on the head or the
  Apply pill, opens one sheet: each edit's decision, read off the page rather
  than logged (callDecisions), and four ways out. Record the answer beside
  the call with the confirmed edits as a patch, for a session to apply where
  the repo's commit hook runs (the default, see answerCall); commit them to
  the file's branch, or to a new branch cut from it, and record; or copy the
  answer as JSON, patch and all, and record nothing. A discard is a decision
  here, so the "no" the
  proposal queue cannot record is in the answer. So are the reader's notes:
  one on an edit's card goes with that edit's decision, and any other goes
  by the words it is on.

  A NOTE IS ON A BLOCK, CHANGED OR NOT, and is not part of any commit.
  The block the caret is in (on a desk, the one under the mouse) wears a
  dashed outline at the extent the card would take, and a badge in the
  margin opens its note, one per block; a card's note is written in its
  Info, which holds the note and nothing else, hung from the card's number
  as a dropdown: under a documentation call the note starts as the call's
  why for that change, and the reader edits it as their own. Notes are
  records anchored to GitHub's copy (kits/dictate-record.js), so they keep
  their paragraph through edits, through Apply and Save, and through Clear
  all edits; they are kept with no edit at all; and they leave in the
  RECORD, `dictate/1` (kits/dictate-record.js), which Send hands over as
  markdown or JSON beside the patch and the whole file, with a preview of
  exactly what goes. Until 2026-10-01 a note was a string per card that went
  into the commit message, and could not be written on an unchanged block.

THE ONE TAP ON ARRIVAL is not a design choice. WebKit needs a user gesture
before it will raise the microphone prompt, so a page cannot start listening
on its own the first time. Once the reader has allowed it, the grant is
remembered here and the next arrival starts listening with no tap at all;
a refusal or a throw falls back to the tap target rather than asking again.

NO FOCUS ZOOM. Safari zooms the page when the keyboard opens on a field it
judges too small, and reported 2026-09-24 on file mode's 17px textarea
inside a toss. The cause at that size is not established; the remedy is
the one kits/annotate.js settled on for the same report at 16px:
maximum-scale=1 on the TOP document's viewport meta, which stops the focus
zoom and leaves pinch zoom alone (iOS ignores it for gestures since iOS 10).
This page's own meta carries it statically; a same-origin shell around it
(the toss) gets it here. A cross-origin top is left alone.

THE PAGE ADOPTS ITS OWN PRE-BUILD (dist/dictate.js), and the reason is
arrival time on a phone rather than bytes. The gh.load chain below is a
WATERFALL: each await is a round trip that cannot start until the one
before it ends, and gh-boot's own eight sit inside the first of them.
Measured 2026-09-08 on this page: 25 requests, fourteen of them serial
contents-API calls to api.github.com, which is uncached and rate-limited.
On a phone that is seconds of pure serialization, and it is exactly what
"slow the first time, fast on the second" describes: nothing was wrong but
the cache was cold.

The build is the same loader with GH.prototype.get served from an inlined
cache, so every gh.load below still runs and simply costs no network. One
same-origin request of 189k (64k over the wire) replaces the fourteen.

It is walked from THIS page's reach (node/build/build.mjs), not the whole
library: dist/web-tools.js would be 1.4 MB gzipped for a page that touches
a tenth of it. Tracked, refreshed by the commit hook, and held to its
sources by node/test/derived-artifacts.test.mjs.

?use=<ref> keeps working the way the app's does: the build is fetched from
raw.githubusercontent at that ref and blob-imported, since jsDelivr's /gh/
cache holds a branch name for hours and a preview has to be the tip.

happen and commits nothing; the second one does it. A repair that
rewrites a sentence somewhere off screen is the one edit on this page

rather than a highlight over it, so the look is worth the tap.

THE PAD, ported from the notes composer (kits/annotate.js) rather than
from the stage's card, which is where this page's first cut came from
and which is a version behind. Three keys and a shift, four faces:

  PRIMARY   . , ?          the marks ordinary prose runs on
  SHIFTED   ; ! ¶          reached for deliberately, worth a second tap

The page's own six-across row is retired with the arrow cluster: it was

THE STITCH IS NO LONGER ONE OF THESE FACES. It used to replace the full
stop whenever a caret sat in a sentence gap, on the reasoning that a
full stop cannot be wanted where one already sits. That reasoning held
for a caret and broke the moment the key learned to reach back on its
own (kits/dictate.js): a buffer with any invented break in it can now
be repaired, which is nearly always, and a key that swallowed the full
stop nearly always would leave no way to type one. So it has a slot of
its own in the row below, always there, and this face is a full stop
again.

FILE MODE TRADES TWO MARKS FOR FORMATTING. A document is headed,
listed, bolded and coded far more than it is exclaimed at: measured
across this repo's markdown, inline code is 69% of inline marks and
bold 22%, and headings and list items with paragraphs are 91% of
blocks. Heading and list act on the caret's line, so they need no
selection and take the shifted face; bold and code wrap a selection,
so they take the selection face, and casing moves behind its shift.

THE PLATFORM'S OWN DRAG, under native selection: a phone lifts held
selected words and a desktop drags them. The Rendered face is not a
text field, so nothing would take the drop, and it is taken here:
the dragover says where the words would land (the carry's marker),
the drop moves them through the kit, one undo step.

WHILE WORDS ARE HELD FOR A MOVE, NOTHING ELSE MAY TAKE A DRAG, and
above all not the sheet an iPhone presents this page in, which
closes on a downward drag (docs/ios-sheet-drags.md). Holding is a
deliberate opening act, the one thing that note says a scrolling
pane needs before it can hold a drag at all, so here the whole page
takes variant D: a cancelled touchstart, so no scroll begins, and a
cancelled touchmove on the node the touch started on, since a
listener on an ancestor goes quiet if that node is rebuilt. A
control keeps its touchstart, or its tap would be lost with it, and
loses only its touchmove, which a tap does not need.

WORDS landing end the armed state: the seam they were aimed at may
not be the newest any more, and a marker that survived the change
would point at a break the reader has stopped thinking about.

A CHANGE IN THE TEXT, not any call. The kit reports through onText
after a caret move too, and the step-back key IS a caret move: a
blanket disarm here would put the marker out on the very tap meant
to re-aim it. Moving the caret re-derives the marker instead, which
is why nothing here has to special-case the jump.
Words held for Move name offsets, and an edit moves them.

A CARRY IS OVER WHEN THE TEXT MOVES UNDER IT: its range names
the words it picked up, and a final result from the microphone
replaces exactly those. The drop's own edit arrives after the
carry has ended, so it never cancels itself.
Only a change that reaches the carried words ends it: words
appended further on leave the range naming what it named.

A refusal invalidates the remembered grant, so the next arrival
asks with a tap rather than starting into a denied microphone.

An interrupted session comes back. A finished one does not: `save`
is cleared wherever the words reach somewhere durable, so a blank
page here means the last note was filed, not that one was lost.
A HANDOFF REPLACES A STORED DRAFT, and does not join it. Both are
"words that were here before", but one was sent HERE, deliberately,
seconds ago, and the other is whatever this page was last left
holding.

IT USED TO JOIN THEM, on the reasoning that nothing should be lost
and the reader could cut what they did not want. What that missed is
that this page SAVES what it is shown: an arrival was joined, saved
over the draft key, and then joined again by the next arrival, so
expanding a second note opened on the first one stacked above it and
a third opened on both. The pile grows by one note per expand, which
is what "it is showing content it held from storage" describes.

NOTHING IS SILENTLY DISCARDED EITHER. The draft that was here is set
aside under its own key and offered back in the band above the words,
one tap, above whatever is there by then. That is the same join, made
when the reader asks for it rather than guessed on their behalf.
File mode takes neither: the buffer is the file, and a handoff left
untaken stays in its slot for the next blank page.

The newest set-aside wins: an older one the reader has walked past

The remembered grant. WebKit will not raise the microphone prompt

── The two modifier taps ─────────────────────────────────────────
A desk is not this page's home, but it is where a long note actually
gets dictated, and there the two hands are free and idle. Both keys
say the same kind of thing, which is why they are a pair: the engine
is about to guess a sentence boundary wrong, and only the reader knows
it, because only the reader knows what they are about to say.

  CONTROL   this is not a new sentence. The pause wrote a full stop
            and the words still to come belong to what came before.
  SHIFT     the next word is a capital: a name, a product, an
            initialism the recognizer has no way to hear as one.

A TAP, NOT A CHORD, and that is the whole difficulty. The reader's
hands are not on the keys and there is no second key to press, so the
gesture is press-and-release with nothing in between. `keydown` alone
cannot serve: it fires as the first half of Ctrl+C, it repeats while
held, and Shift is held through every capital typed in the edit half.
So the press only ARMS, anything else that happens cancels it, and the
release is what acts. That is the standard read of a bare modifier and
it is the reason this is fifteen lines rather than two.

Control acts at once and shows its work: the full stop disappears.
Shift cannot, since the word it capitalizes has not been said, so it
arms the kit and the header wears the indicator until a word spends it.

The key that went down alone, or null. Any second key, any pointer,
and any focus leaving the page clears it: all three mean the press
was part of something else.

Escape puts away the undo pill, before anything else. Info's
Escape is kits/panel-tip.js's; this only keeps it from also
reaching a card held for the keys.

UNDER THE NATIVE SELECTION A DESK IS NOT TYPING UNTIL IT TYPES (a
click no longer opens it), so the keys the sink would handle, the
travel keys and undo, redo and select-all, are handed to it from
here, and the editing keys open typing the way a character does.

A character typed at the Rendered face with no keyboard open opens
it, and focus moving inside keydown carries the character with it.
a held key is not a tap

A chord that ends with the modifier released last (Ctrl+C held
through the C's own keyup) already cleared `tap` on the C's
keydown, so nothing reaches here.

Inert where there is nothing to take back, which is the point of it
being its own act rather than the backspace: a mistaken press on a
buffer ending in a word must not eat the word.

With a word selected the reader is pointing at a capital that already
exists and can simply be changed, so the same key means recase. With
nothing selected there is no word yet, so it arms.

WORDS ARRIVING is the proof, and the only one available. Starting an
engine is not: r.start() succeeds whether or not the microphone is
allowed, and the refusal comes back asynchronously, so a flag written
at start time would remember a permission that was never granted.

GATED ON THE ENGINE. onText fires for every write to the buffer, a
restored draft and a typed edit included, and treating those as
speech wrote a microphone grant nobody had given and cleared the
banner announcing the restore in the same breath.

A phone that dims and locks takes the microphone with it, and the
reader is given no reason. Absent in a browser without the API,
which loses nothing that was working before.
Before the file has loaded, the buffer is not an edit of anything.

The confirmations ride with the edit they belong to, and the notes
with it or on their own: a note on an unchanged file is kept too.
`base` is the blob the notes are anchored in, so a later load can
tell whether GitHub's copy moved under them. The text is kept only
when it is an edit, or a notes-only draft would restore GitHub's

── The painted surface and its gestures ──────────────────────────
The notes composer's set, which is a version on from the stage's and
differs in what the reader is given to aim WITH:

  long press ON the words   take the word under the finger
  ...and keep dragging      extend from that word, arming as it goes
  long press OFF them       open the keyboard, caret where it was
  double tap                open the keyboard, caret where it landed
  single tap                place the caret, or move an armed edge
  tap a pinhead             arm that edge, or put it down
  drag a pinhead            move that edge, one to one
  drag a finger anywhere    scroll, and only scroll
  mouse drag                select, for a pointer that has no problem

THE LAST TWO ARE ONE DECISION. A finger has exactly one way to scroll
this pane, so a finger drag cannot also mean select; a cursor has a
wheel, so a cursor drag can. The page spent two days trying to split
the difference by direction, sideways selecting and vertical
scrolling, and the rule worked without ever being legible: nothing on
screen could teach it, and the reader who dragged the wrong way found
a surface that looked broken. On touch the long press is the way in,
which is what the phone already means by it on a page you are reading.

No triple, and no arrow cluster. The triple's select-all cannot
survive the double opening a keyboard: the second tap swaps the read
surface for a textarea and the third lands somewhere this listener
cannot hear. The arrows are retired by the pad below, which drags an
armed pin with the same gesture it drags the caret.
A CLIENT POINT AS AN OFFSET INTO THE BUFFER, which is the one question
every gesture here asks. Three of them used to carry their own copy of
this, differing only in which local named the host.

── THE VERTICAL AIM OF A THUMB'S DRAG ────────────────────────────
Horizontal is always the finger, one to one. Vertical is HELD BACK
until the thumb has cleared the words, then resumes, quantized to
lines and measured from where the hold ended rather than from the
grab. So placing an edge a line down costs about two lines of thumb,
and the first is spent getting the hand off the text.

`lead` is how far the grip sits from the line it marks: a pin's ball,
signed, positive below and negative above. ZERO when the finger is on
the text itself, which is the long-press extend. A grip already below
the line spends the base hold; one above spends that plus twice its
own offset, which is exactly the travel that carries it down across
the line to where the other one started.

Upward is immediate in every case. That direction is clearance for
none of them, and a hold there only makes the drag feel stuck.

ONE RULE FOR THE TWO DRAGS A THUMB DRIVES, the long-press extend and
the pin, because they are one question: where is the reader aiming,
given that their thumb is in the way of the answer. It was three until
the plain drag became the mouse's alone; a cursor occludes nothing, so
it aims with the raw pointer and this is not in its path. The extend
went without it at first, on the reading that a finger on the text IS
the aim point and holding back would read as lag. It reads as the
thumb covering the boundary instead.
On the words, in whichever face is showing.

── Holding a drag against an iOS sheet ───────────────────────────
`touch-action: none` IS NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT, which is the one
thing to remember here. A page opened from an app on a phone is
presented in a sheet the reader dismisses by dragging down, and the
host decides that from the web view's SCROLL rather than from touches,
so a handle carrying only touch-action still lets the sheet go. This
is variant D of five measured on device (docs/ios-sheet-drags.md):
touch-action, plus a cancelled touchstart and touchmove.

`{ passive: false }` is not optional, since a passive listener cannot
cancel anything and browsers default both events to passive. Nothing
is lost: preventDefault on a TOUCH event suppresses the compatibility
MOUSE events, not the pointer ones, so every drag below runs as before.
It does suppress the compatibility CLICK, which costs nothing here
because the pad and the pins are driven from pointerdown.

The word a long press took, kept for as long as the finger stays
down. Its presence is what turns the rest of the gesture into an
extension rather than a fresh selection. See the move handler.

Native selection: when the press began, and whether it began on the
end of a live selection, where the platform's handle is.

── Holding the iOS sheet for the length of a long-press drag ─────
The pad and the pins can carry `touch-action: none` because neither
scrolls. THE TEXT PANE MUST SCROLL, so it cannot, and the sheet has
to be held by the only lever left: cancelling `touchmove`, which is
variant E in docs/ios-sheet-drags.md and measured to hold. Gated on
`word`, so an ordinary swipe scrolls and only an extension is held.

Cancelling touchSTART is not available here for the same reason it
was right on the pad: it would kill the scroll outright, and at
touchstart nothing yet knows this touch will become a long press.

THE LISTENER GOES ON THE NODE THE TOUCH STARTED ON, captured at
pointerdown. paint() clears the host and rebuilds every span on
every frame of the extension, and a touch keeps its original target
after that target leaves the document, so a listener on the pane or
on the document would never see the events: a detached target has no
path to an ancestor. Same trap as the pins, one layer deeper, and
here there is no repaint hook to re-attach from.

It also keeps the gesture alive at all. A browser that decides a
touch is a scroll fires pointercancel and stops sending pointermove,
so without this the extension does not merely fight the sheet, it
ends.

IT USED TO CANCEL PRE-EMPTIVELY TOO, on the first touch that had
opened far enough sideways to be a selection rather than a scroll,
because the browser rules on a gesture before the move handler does
and a claimed pan fires pointercancel. That test went with the plain
touch drag it protected: nothing now becomes a selection without a
long press first, and by the time a press has taken its word there
is a `word` to gate on.
A mouse press inside the selection: a drag from here carries it.
A card's number and label are controls, not text: no caret, no long press.

ANY TOUCH ON THE WORDS ENDS A PENDING STITCH. It was reported as
the missing exit: the marker went up and tapping the canvas left
it there, because the only disarm was a change in the text and a
tap changes none. Whatever this gesture turns out to be, a caret,
a word, the keyboard, it is the reader looking somewhere else.

A mouse or a keyboard means the pins can go: drag and shift-click
do the extending, so the handles are furniture for a job the
platform already does. The selection stays painted.

A MOUSE PRESS ENDS TYPING UNDER THE NATIVE SELECTION, so the
platform can select: while typing the sink holds the focus, and a
selection drawn in the words needs it back in the document. The
next key typed starts typing again (bindKeys), over whatever the
mouse selected. Without this a desk kept the native selection only
until its first click, which opened typing for good.

THE PLATFORM SELECTS, under the native option: no long press
here, no mouse drag, no carry by holding. Only the tap is ours.
AND WHILE WORDS ARE HELD FOR A MOVE, a finger anywhere on the text
is the target's pad: the caret moves in parallel with it, off to
the side of the thumb rather than under it. A press that goes
nowhere is still a tap, and the tap drops the words where it
lands (pointerup, below).

PRESSED INSIDE THE SELECTION, a mouse is picking it up rather than
starting a new one: the drag below carries it if the press moves.

OFF the words a held finger is not an aim that missed, it is a
request for the keyboard. Nothing is collapsed on the way in.

HELD INSIDE THE SELECTION, a finger picks it up, the way the
platform does: the words follow the finger until it lifts.

REMEMBER THE WORD, because the finger has not lifted and what it
does next decides whether this gesture is over.

── A LONG PRESS THAT KEEPS GOING IS ONE GESTURE ────────────────
The press takes the word; carrying on past it extends from the
word's OUTER EDGE, so a range is one press-and-drag rather than a
press, a lift, and a second gesture to widen what it found. This
is the platform's own reading, and it was half here already: the
ordinary drag below would fire and select from the raw character
under the press, which threw the word away and lit no pin, so the
gesture appeared to work and quietly did something else.

The edge under the finger arms as it goes, so the moving end is
visible while it moves. The release puts it down again, like every
other drag here.

Back inside the word is not a shrink. The word is the floor of
this gesture, the same as on the platform, and treating a wobble
as a request to cut into it would make the press feel unstable.

Pins off for the duration, or caret-from-point answers with the
pin this drag just lit rather than with the word under it.

── A PLAIN DRAG IS THE MOUSE'S ─────────────────────────────────
Press the button, drag across the words, and the selection follows
from where it went down to where it is. On a desktop that is what
every text surface does and there is nothing to weigh it against:
a mouse does not scroll by dragging, so the gesture is free.

ON A FINGER IT IS NOT FREE, and that is why this branch is gated
rather than shared. The pane has to scroll, and a drag is the only
way to scroll it, so a drag that also selects has to be told apart
from one that scrolls. The page tried the one discriminator there
is, direction: sideways selected, vertical scrolled. It worked and
it was still wrong. Nothing on screen can teach a rule like that,
a refused vertical drag fell through to the tap path and moved the
caret to wherever the finger lifted, and the reader who tried the
obvious thing found a surface that looked broken.

So on touch the long press is the way in, which is the convention
the phone already uses for a page you are reading rather than
typing into. What that costs is one thing and it is worth naming:
a press floors the anchor at a word, so a selection can no longer
BEGIN mid-word on a finger. Everything after stays character-level,
the far end as it extends and either edge afterwards by pin drag,
and the target's two taps place both edges to the character. The
precise route survives; it stopped being a drag. Decided
2026-08-25, retiring the touch half added two days earlier.

Under the slop, a click that wobbled. Turning that into a
one-character selection is how a text box comes to feel twitchy.

NO VERTICAL HOLD-BACK HERE, unlike the two drags below. `dragY`
exists to get a thumb off the words before the aim starts moving,
and a cursor covers nothing: quantizing it to lines and charging
it a line and a half of travel would only make it feel broken.

And it arms the edge it is moving, the same as every other way of
extending here, so the pad or that pinhead continues on release.

WHILE TYPING, A TAP MOVES THE CARET AND KEEPS THE KEYBOARD. The
compatibility mousedown would move focus off the sink, so it is
cancelled, and the release puts focus back in case the platform took
it anyway.

A CARRY ENDS WHERE IT IS DROPPED, and claims the release: nothing
below may read it as a tap.

A drag claims its own release: the tap logic below would read it as
a click and drop a caret where the selection just finished.

AND EVERY DRAG ENDS WITH THE PIN DOWN. The edge arms as the drag
runs, which is what says which end is moving while it moves, and
letting go is the end of that: the selection stands and the pin
goes back to blue. One rule for all three drags, the pin's own
included, so a lifted finger never leaves a mode behind.

`pinDrag` is cleared HERE and not above, which is not tidiness. A
pin's own drag has no `dragging` and is caught by the guard below,
so clearing the flag before that guard reads it lets the release
fall through and drop a caret over the selection just made.

A RELEASE FAR FROM ITS PRESS IS NOT A TAP. On touch every drag is
now a scroll, and a scroll that lifts should leave the caret where
it was. Usually the browser claims the gesture and fires
pointercancel before this runs, but a drag under its own scroll
threshold reaches here, and without this the caret jumped to
wherever the finger came up. That was the quiet half of the old
sideways rule: a refused vertical drag did not do nothing, it
moved the caret to the far end of the gesture. Same 10px slop the
move handler uses, and the count resets so a scroll cannot become
the first half of a double.

A sideways swipe on a card is the card's own scroll (md-surface,
the snap track), settled into a reading by md-card-reading. It
arrives here, if at all, as a release far from its press.

Under the native option a long press was the platform selecting,
and a press on a selection's end was its handle: neither is a tap,
and reading one as a tap would drop a caret over what it made.
With words picked up by Move, the tap aims them; Move here lands them.

A mouse has no long press and no handles: its click is a click,
however long it was held and wherever it landed.

A mouse beside a card's words takes the card for the keys, on any
reading, before the original's tap below would turn it back.

The original takes no caret, so a tap on it returns the card to the
marked text, where the next tap, or a double, lands as usual.

A MARKED WORD, TAPPED, OFFERS ITS UNDO, struck or added alike: one
pill, one word, so "no thanks" never needs the keyboard. A struck
word is the base's, not the buffer's, so the tap stops there; an
added word is the buffer's, so the tap also places the caret.

An underlined change is the buffer's words too: the same pop, and
the caret lands as usual.

ARMING ENDS A RUN. pointerdown already armed the pin, and counting
the tap too made "tap a pin, then tap the text" a double and opened
the keyboard on the gesture meant to move the edge.

A MOUSE IN THE RENDERED FACE GETS A DESKTOP EDITOR'S CLICKS, not the
phone's: see mouseClick.

The double opens the keyboard from the canvas too: tapping the
empty space under the words is the most obvious way of saying
"let me type here", and it used to be the one place that did
nothing, because the canvas won before the count.

The armed anchor takes the tap first, canvas included: a tap past
the last word means the end of the buffer there as everywhere.

AND THE PLACEMENT SPENDS THE ARMING. An armed pin takes this tap,
moves its edge to it, and goes back to blue: the arming asked
"where should this edge go", the tap answered, and there is
nothing left for it to be live for. Wanting to move it again is
one tap on the pinhead, which is the same cost as leaving it lit
and cheaper than the alternative, since a pin left live turns the
NEXT tap anywhere in the text into a move nobody asked for.

Completes the one rule the rest of the page already follows: every
drag ends put down, the two-tap maneuver ends put down, and now so
does this. An arming is spent by the action it enables.

── A pinhead is tapped OR dragged ────────────────────────────────
Tapping arms the edge so the pad can walk it, which is the gesture
this surface was built around: a finger dragging a selection edge
covers the words it is aiming at. But the BALL sits off the line, one
diameter above it or below it, so a finger on the ball is not over the
