text either. The objection never applied to the handle itself, and
dragging one is what every reader already expects a handle to do. So
both, and neither costs the other anything.

The aim point is the BAR's centre carried by the finger's delta, not
the finger. One to one, so what moves under the ball is what the ball
was already marking, and the offset between thumb and line is whatever
the reader chose by where they grabbed it.

THE WAY OUT OF THE ARMED STATE, and it is the thing you are looking
at. A confirm step with no cancel is a trap, and this one had none:
the stitch key commits on its second tap, so it cannot also be the
escape. Tapping the badge dismisses it and changes nothing.

MEASURED BEFORE ANYTHING IS PAINTED. The bar is the pin's first
child and it IS the text line, its last is the ball, and paint()
replaces the whole element, so reading either afterwards reads a
detached node, whose getBoundingClientRect is all zeroes and reports
no failure.

Where the GRIP sits relative to the line it marks: positive below,
negative above. This is the whole difference between the two pins.

Armed on the way DOWN, so the ring is under the finger before it
moves, and a drag never has to be told apart from a tap to paint it.

The vertical aim is `dragY`, shared with the other two drags. What
this one supplies is `lead`, the ball's own offset from its stem,
which is why the two pins hold back by different amounts: the end's
ball hangs below the line so its thumb starts clear, the start's
hangs above so its buffer must carry the thumb down across the line
first. Measured at the grab rather than set as a constant, so both
arrive at the same thumb-below-the-aim distance.

It also fixes the commoner accident, which is not aiming at the
wrong line but drifting onto one. A thumb sliding along a line to
place an edge does not travel straight, and without the hold a few
pixels of wander step the edge into the line above.

Fixed at the grab, not read per frame. Which pin you hold can change
mid-drag when the edges cross, and where your thumb physically is
cannot, so recomputing would jump the aim at the crossing.

Held against an edge, scroll, the same as the pad: an edge dragged
to the bottom of a buffer longer than the screen would otherwise
stop at whatever happens to be visible.

LANDING EXACTLY ON THE OTHER EDGE IS SKIPPED, not clamped. A
zero-width range takes both pins off the screen mid-drag, and a
clamp one character short means the edges can never cross at all.
Skipping the frame keeps a live selection and lets the next move
land past it.

AND A CROSSING RENAMES THE PIN UNDER THE FINGER. setRange sorts,
so dragging start past end makes the dragged edge the end; follow
it, or the label the rest of the page is holding quietly lies.

CLEARED ON THE NEXT TICK, not here. These listeners are on the
document in the CAPTURE phase, so they run before the same
pointerup reaches the text box's own handler, and the pin is
destroyed and rebuilt on every paint, so that handler hit-tests
fresh and sees the WORDS rather than the pin it started on. The
pad has no such trouble: its button survives the drag and holds
pointer capture, so the release never reaches the text at all.

A TAP IS A DRAG THAT WENT NOWHERE, and it toggles, which is the
behaviour the pinheads have always had: tap to arm, tap again to
put down.

A DRAG PUTS IT DOWN, and so does every other drag on this page
(see the text box's own release). The arming is what says which
end is moving WHILE it moves; letting go ends that, leaving the
selection and a blue pin. Same shape as the two-tap maneuver,
which also sets rather than staying live.

── The cursor pad ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Press it and drag: the button does not move, the CARET does. On a
phone the only way to place a caret was to touch the text at the place
you were aiming at, which puts a thumb over the two words either side
of it, and a second tap there takes the word instead of moving
anything. So the one gesture for "put it between these two" hid its
own target and had a homonym. Here the finger is somewhere else and
the eye stays on the text.

Ported from kits/annotate.js, constants and all, because the feel IS
the three numbers: crawl and the caret creeps at well under 1:1, flick
and it runs ahead of the thumb, so a short button reaches a long
buffer and the overshoot is walked back without lifting.

A fine pointer from the start, so a desktop never sees the pins it would
only lose at the first click; any mouse press sets it too.

A DESK: a mouse that hovers, read once at load. Unlike `precise`,
which a single mouse press turns on, this does not change under the
reader, so the on-screen keys do not vanish mid-session on a phone.
A desk has a keyboard, which types every key of the upper row, so
that row is not drawn and the formats move to shortcuts (shortcut).

── One armed state, three ways in ────────────────────────────────
`armed` is the whole aiming state and it has four values: null, the
two pin names, and 'anchor'. That is a merge, not a widening. The
page used to carry a separate `anchoring` flag beside it, and the two
said the same thing in different words: SOMETHING IS LIVE AND POINTED
AT THE TEXT, so the next tap in the buffer moves it rather than
placing a caret. Two flags for one fact meant the target could be red
while a pin was red, or neither, and the reader had to learn which
red meant what.

So: the target is red exactly when `armed` is set, whichever way it
got set, and tapping it walks the state rather than reaching into the
text. That gives the tiny pinhead a large, safe control, which is the
thing that was missing: a miss near a pinhead used to clear the
selection outright, and no tap on the target ever can.

  tap a pinhead                arms that edge
  tap the target, selected     end → start → null → end (toggleAnchor)
  tap the target, not          null → 'anchor' → null

ARMING IS ALWAYS MOMENTARY. Whatever lit it, the thing it enables puts
it out again: a drag ends put down, the two-tap maneuver ends put
down, and a tap that places an armed edge ends put down. Nothing here
leaves a mode behind for the next tap to fall into.

'anchor' is the special case with no pin to show, since there is no
range yet. It needs none: the target itself is the affordance, and
painting a lone red pin at the caret would be a fourth thing to read.
The caret, with a selection counting as its far end. Extending from
the far end is what shift-click does everywhere, which makes the one
rule cover the collapsed case, the selected case and the empty case
without a branch for any of them.

TAPPING THE HEADER'S OWN BACKGROUND PUTS ANY PIN DOWN. The target
cycles and the pinheads toggle, so both are ways of CHANGING which
edge is live; this is the way of simply ending it, and the header is
the largest piece of nothing on the screen that is not the text. A tap
in the text would move something, which is exactly what a reader who
is done does not want.

Buttons are excluded rather than stopped from propagating, since the
header's controls each own their own tap and this must not eat any.

The target's tap half, and it reads the buffer rather than being one
switch. WITH A SELECTION it cycles the two pins and off, since that is
the only question left to ask: which edge am I about to move. WITHOUT
one there are no pins to cycle, so it arms an anchor at the caret and
the next tap in the text is the other end.

  selected      null → end → start → null
  not selected  null → anchor → null

END FIRST, because the far end of a selection is the active one
everywhere else here: `caretOffset` returns it, and the anchor extends
from it. One rule, not a second convention for this control.

The anchor is not lost by this. Arming a pin and tapping the text does
exactly what the anchor did, extending from the other edge to where
you tapped, so with a selection the cycle is the same tool with the
edge named rather than guessed.

The completing tap. Returns whether it consumed the tap, so the
gesture handler can fall through to its ordinary reading when the
anchor was never armed.

The anchor is read HERE rather than at the tap that armed it, so the
pad can be dragged to the exact start and only then tapped shut. An
arm-time capture made that flow silently wrong, selecting from
wherever the caret had been before the drag.

AND IT DISARMS. The maneuver is finished when the selection exists,
so leaving a pin lit would mean a third tap to close it, on a target
12px across, with the selection lost if that tap missed. Refining an
edge afterwards is still one tap on its pinhead.

What the pad is aiming, in client coordinates: the armed pin if one is
armed, the caret otherwise. One gesture, two subjects, and which is a
state the reader set by tapping a pinhead. That is what let the arrows
go: an armed edge is dragged exactly the way the caret is. 'anchor' is
not a pin, so it aims the caret like the unarmed case.

The virtual point ACCUMULATES, one move at a time, each step scaled
by how fast that move was. An absolute mapping cannot accelerate:
the gain would be a property of the whole drag rather than of the
moment, and "flick then creep" is two moments.

Clamped as it accumulates, not only where it is read: an unclamped
accumulator drifts outside the box on a flick, and the drag back
spends its first inch returning from somewhere invisible.

Vertical lands on LINES rather than between them, so a slow drag
steps one line at a time and a flick crosses several.

Held against an edge, SCROLL rather than stop: the buffer runs
longer than the screen, and a pad that could only reach what
happens to be visible would be worst on exactly the long notes.

Aiming held words: the pad's caret replaces a tapped aim. No loupe:
the pad moves the caret off to the side of the finger, so nothing
is under it to magnify, and a lens would cover the view being aimed.

A TAP IS A DRAG THAT WENT NOWHERE, and it means the other half of
this button. Measured against the raw thumb travel rather than the
accumulated virtual point, since the gain would call a 6px twitch
a 14px move at a flick.

`el` is what took the press and `onTap` what a press that went
nowhere means: the target's own tap for the button, nothing for the
text (whose own tap handler has the release). See padFrom.
the keyboard brings its own caret

The flag the text box reads to stand down. It has to: a capture can
be lost mid-gesture (a browser deciding the touch was a scroll) and
the box would then read the tail of a drag as a tap.

And the document holds still. A pad drag is not a scroll, but the
page under it will happily take one, and a page that scrolls at its
top edge inside a sheet-presented in-app browser is the gesture
that dismisses the sheet.

Listeners on the DOCUMENT rather than the button: pointer capture
is best-effort and a lost one must not strand the drag.

`retry` is not a caller's parameter: it is how this defers itself once.
EVERY POSITION HERE IS MEASURED, off `getClientRects` on the painted
spans, and a hidden element measures zero, so a paint that runs while
the read pane is `display:none` puts both pins at the layer's origin
and leaves them there. Nothing about that looks like a measurement
failure on screen: it looks like two pins stuck in the corner.

`editClose` is how it happened. It sets the flag and paints in the
same breath, and Alpine does not clear `display:none` until the
reactive flush, so the paint measured the pane one tick before it came
back. Measured 2026-08-25: pins at 34,88 and 82,88 before a trip
through the keyboard and both at -16,71 after it, with the pane
computing `none` at the paint and `block` at `$nextTick`.

Guarded HERE rather than at that one call site, because the trap
belongs to painting and not to the keyboard: any caller that repaints
across a visibility change has it. The deferral is a FRAME, not a
tick, and up to three of them: once the FAB mounted on this page (its
selection listener hears the textarea let go) Alpine's flush could
outlast one $nextTick, and a trip through the keyboard came back with
no pins about half the time. Bounded, so a host that is hidden for
good costs three frames rather than a loop.

Block by block even with nothing changed, so the block under the
caret can be marked and noted (markBlock).

Under the native option the platform draws the selection, unless
Move has picked it up, when the page holds it until the drop.
Red is the phone's precision caret; a mouse gets the text's own color.

Wider than the kit's 2px on a phone: at 2px, fading on the pulse,
the caret was hard to find in running text.
A card taken for the keys shows no caret; the range waits for Enter.

Read fresh rather than stored: the caret may have moved under the
armed state (the step-back key), and the marker has to follow.

NO ARROW CLUSTER. The pad drags an armed pin the same way it drags
the caret, so a pair of arrows chasing the pin around is furniture
for a job already done. This page carried them because its first
cut came from the stage's card, which keeps them for the good
reason that it has no pad.

And no pins once a mouse or a keyboard is in play: drag and
shift-click do the extending. The selection stays painted; only
the thing you would have tapped goes.

NOR WHILE THE TEXTAREA IS UP, which is not the same reason. The
read pane is hidden then but the pin layer is not: it sits outside
the scroll box on purpose, so a pin can hang above the first line
rather than being cut in half, and that also puts it outside the
`x-show` that hides the words. It never showed while the only way
in was a double tap, which lands on a point and collapses the
selection to a caret. The keyboard button carries a selection
across intact, so two pins were suddenly drawn on top of the
textarea's own native one, marking the same words twice.

NO STALK. The armed pin was pushed out on one, first 36px and then
18, to keep the thumb off the words it was aiming at. THE DRAG'S
VERTICAL DEADBAND does that instead, and does it better: the
clearance comes from the gesture, so the reader takes exactly as
much as they need and the pin stays where it is pointing. A stalk
on top of that was a second answer to a solved problem, and it
moved the one thing on the screen whose job is to not move.

The painter keeps the option, tested and off. It is a number away
if the pin ever needs to say "grabbable" louder than the red ring
already does.

Only once there is something to be at the end OF. On an empty
buffer the end caret is a red bar alone in the corner, behind the
start prompt, and it reads as a rendering fault.

THE PINS ARE REPLACED EVERY PAINT, so the touch hold is re-attached
every paint. It cannot live on the layer instead: a touch keeps the
element it STARTED on as its target even after that element is
removed from the document, and a detached target has no path to an
ancestor's listener, so the hold would go quiet on the first repaint
of a drag, which is the one moment it is for.

ARMING WITH NO CARET PLACED WALKS ONE BACK, rather than only
lighting the marker where the reader is. Two things follow from
it, and neither needs a second notion of "where".

The step-back key keeps working while armed. It moves the caret
to the seam BEFORE the caret's, so with the caret still resting at
the end it would have landed on the very seam the marker was
already showing: a tap that looked broken because it changed
nothing. Measured in the browser before this line was written.

And the caret it places is BORROWED (kits/dictate.js jumpBack), so
committing hands it back to the end and dictation carries on where
the reader is speaking. A caret they placed themselves is theirs,
so the 'caret' aim arms in place and keeps the old behaviour of
staying on the join.

The marker is derived from the caret, so stepping back while armed
re-aims it rather than disarming.

A shifted mark drops the shift, the way a phone keyboard does: the
sticky case is the one asked for by tapping again.

── Typing into the Rendered face ─────────────────────────────────
A phone raises its keyboard only for a focused field, so an invisible
textarea (the SINK) takes focus and every keystroke goes through it.
It holds the caret's line of source, caret placed to match, so the
platform's autocorrect and capitalization see real context; each input
is read as a difference against what the sink held and applied to the
buffer at the same place, through the kit's type() and erase(), whose
undo coalesces a run of typing into one step. The document re-renders
around it. The rules for Enter, a line-start backspace, and a wrapper
losing its last character are kits/md-surface.js's.
── The Rendered face under a mouse ───────────────────────────────
The red caret, the pins, the long press and the double tap that opens
the keyboard are all answers to a phone: to iOS raising its own
selection, callout and loupe over a surface it does not own. A mouse
has none of those problems, and on a desktop the phone's gestures
only got in the way: a double click opened the keyboard instead of
taking the word, and typing did nothing until it had. So under a
mouse the face behaves like any text editor. A click places the caret
and types there, shift-click extends, a double click takes the word,
a triple click the line, and a drag selects (the move handler). Keys
are sinkKey's. The model underneath is the same range the phone
drives, so dictation, the pad and the format keys see no difference.

The block, not the source line: a hard-wrapped paragraph is one
paragraph on screen, and that is what a triple click means.

Under the native selection a click places the caret and no more:
typing starts on the first key, so the mouse stays the platform's.

A CARD FOR THE KEYS, on a desk. A click in a change card's blank space,
beside its words rather than on them, takes the card without a caret,
so the arrows turn it rather than walk the text: left and right step
through its readings, up and down go to the card before or after,
Enter puts the caret back to edit, and Escape lets it go. A click on
the words is an editor's click, as ever.

Set, not scrolled to: a key has no slide to show, and a scroll
left for the snap to settle was re-snapped back to the reading it
left when the card's layers changed under it (measured headless).
Typing while a card is held does nothing: Enter is the way in.
A collapsed range moves; with shift, the end away from the anchor does.

Typing follows the click, except while the microphone is live: starting
to type stops dictation, and a click to move where the words land must
not. A key pressed then starts typing on its own (bindKeys).

The keys a textarea would handle itself, if it held the document. The
sink holds only the caret's line, so travel is computed here against the
render: left and right by MdSurface.step (markup skipped), up and down
by the caret's screen position, keeping the column it started from.
THE SHORTCUTS, for any keyboard, a desk's or one paired to a phone.
The formats are file mode's shifted keys under the chords Google Docs
and Notion use for them, and Send is the chord chat apps send with.
  ⌘/Ctrl B       bold            ⌘/Ctrl E        inline code
  ⌘/Ctrl ⌥ 1-6   heading level   ⌘/Ctrl ⌥ 0      plain paragraph
  ⌘/Ctrl ⇧ 8     list item       ⌘/Ctrl Enter    Send
Digits are read off e.code, since ⌥ and ⇧ change e.key.
A chord as this platform names it: the Mac's symbols, or Ctrl+ Alt+
Shift+ elsewhere.
off the pane: scroll it, then look

A point in the gap between blocks resolves to the nearest text,
often a line's end; asking again at that line's middle puts the
caret back under the column it came from.
The caret's line kept on screen after a key moved it.

In Raw · changes the markdown is on screen, so a key means its own
character: Enter is one newline, and backspace at a line's start
takes the newline before it. The markdown rules below are for the
render, where the markers cannot be seen.

The sink holds one line, so a forward delete at its end has nothing
to take there; the next character of the document is taken here.

The wrapper rule, after a deletion: markers whose last character just
went go with it.

── The edit as a patch ───────────────────────────────────────────
Discarding one change lives on its card (rejectCard); these are the
whole edit, as a unified diff to copy or to hand to a Claude Code
session.

Only while the menu is open: Alpine evaluates the menu's bindings even
hidden, and a whole-file diff per keystroke is not free.

What rides to Claude Code: where the edit belongs, what it was made
against, and the patch. Addresses plus the change, which is what a
session with the repository cloned needs; it reads the rest itself.

── Paragraphs: the seam between two, and carrying words across ──
The Rendered view draws a document block by block, so the gap between
two paragraphs was nowhere a finger could aim. It is a drop target now.
Joining needs no target: backspace at a paragraph's start joins it to
the one above with a space (kits/dictate.js join). A Join pill on a
tapped gap was tried and dropped as a second route to the same edit.
The shifted ¶ splits at the caret.

HOLD A SELECTION AND DRAG IT to move the words (kits/dictate.js
move). A touch picks the selection up with the same long press that
otherwise takes a word, pressed INSIDE what is already selected; a
mouse picks it up by dragging it. The drop marker says where it will
land: a bar between two words, or a line across the gap between two
paragraphs, which lands the words as a paragraph of their own. So a
sentence carried out to the gap below is a split, and a paragraph
carried onto the end of the one above is a join. A touch aims a
little above the finger, where the carried words are drawn, so the
finger does not cover the place it is pointing at.
A LONG PRESS ON THE SPACE BETWEEN TWO WORDS places a caret, as it
always has; where a paragraph could be cut there, a Split pill rides
under it. Spent by the next touch. There is no Join pill: ⌫ at the
start of a paragraph joins it to the one above, with a space.

Drawn into the pin layer, after every paint, since both follow the
layout: a scroll, a re-render or a keyboard all move them.
NATIVE: words held for a move stay washed while the caret aims.

Where words dragged by the platform would land, and the loupe that
shows it above the thumb covering it (drawLens).
Held words aimed by a tap on a gap show the same drop line.

The carried words, drawn where they are aimed and KEPT INSIDE THE
PANE: a label hanging past the edge widens the page, and a phone
answers that by zooming the whole view out mid-drag (measured
headless: the viewport grew from 844 to 896 and everything fixed to
it jumped).

WHERE HELD WORDS WILL LAND, pointed at from both sides: yellow
wedges above and below the caret (or the middle of a gap's drop
line), and on whichever side has room, a small Move here tag that
lands them. The tag is the confirm, at the place it confirms.

And the caret holds still: its pulse fades it to a fifth, which is
the moment it is hardest to find.
Below unless that would run under the bottom of the pane.

THE LOUPE. A drop point is under the finger that is dragging to it,
so a lens above the thumb shows it: the rendered text around the drop
point, enlarged, with the pulsing caret (or, over a gap, a line) at
its centre. The text is a
copy of the Rendered face made once per drag, with the card readings
not on screen left out, so each dragover only moves it.

Shaped like the platform's own: a capsule, a hairline edge, a soft
drop shadow, and a sheen across the top half, as glass has.

WHERE THE DROP POINT IS IN THE COPY, measured rather than assumed.
The copy does not lay out exactly as the page: card readings not on
screen are left out of it, which shortens a card, and a first
margin that collapses through the page's host does not collapse
out of an absolutely placed box. Assumed, the lens sat half a line
off on the phone. So the copy is laid out scaled at the origin, the
drop offset is found in it by its data-src runs, and the copy is
then moved so that point sits at the lens centre. Its position and
transform origin are inline, not classes: a class new to the page
exists only once Tailwind's browser build has written it, a frame
later, and the origin moving after the measurement slid the text out
of the lens. The focus is
taken relative to that offset's own caret on the page, which is
what carries a gap's midpoint across too.

The caret rect at a source offset inside the loupe's copy: the run
stamped with the offset (data-src, copied from the page), or the end
of the last run before it where the offset sits on markup.
The drop marker: a line across a gap, or a bar between two words.

INSIDE CODE A SPACE IS NOT A SENTENCE GAP: a split there cuts an inline
code span or a fenced block in two, so Split is not offered. Read off
the source: an odd count of backticks before the offset on its line,
or an odd count of fence lines before it in the file.
Every move lands through here, and none lands in code: words dropped
into a fence, an indented block or inline code cut it in two, or
became code (refused from 2026-10-01; Split already was).

An indented code block: a run of lines indented four spaces or a
tab, opened by a blank line, and not under a list item, where the
same indent is a continuation paragraph.
Inside a fence: an opening ``` or ~~~ is closed only by its own kind.

A PILL MUST NOT TAKE FOCUS. While the keyboard is up, the press on it
would blur the typing sink; the blur ends typing and repaints, which
rebuilds the pill before the tap lands, so the tap did nothing and the
keyboard closed. The press is refused focus; the click still fires.
How far above a finger the carried words are drawn and aimed.

A mouse carry starts only once the pointer has left the slop, so it
is already moving; a touch carry starts at the press and is not.

Repainted once so the pins come off: the words are lifted, and a
handle left on them would read as a second thing to drag.

NOTHING IS AIMED UNTIL THE FINGER MOVES. A touch aims above the
finger, so a target taken at the press would sit on the line above
the words, and a long press let go where it began would drop them
there. Inside the same slop the tap uses, the words are only lifted.

WHERE A DROP AT A POINT LANDS: a paragraph break (the gap between two
blocks, above the first, below the last, or a blank line in the
source), else the nearer edge of the word under it. Null when it
would land inside the words being carried.

The aim stays inside the pane: above the finger near the top is
over the file bar, and a gap scrolled out of sight is no place to
drop words the reader cannot see land.

A word target out of sight (the nearest text to a point in the gap
at the top is the end of the paragraph scrolled away) steps inward
until it lands on text the reader can see.

Held near the top or bottom of the pane, the pane scrolls, so a drop
can reach a paragraph off screen. THE SPEED RAMPS WITH THE SQUARE OF
THE DEPTH into the edge band: a linear ramp ran at 200px a second a
few pixels in, which is where a reader aiming at the last visible
line already is, and carried a headless drop to the end of the file.

── Native selection ──────────────────────────────────────────────
THE OPTION HANDS SELECTING TO THE PLATFORM. The words are made
selectable (the stylesheet's data-native-sel rule), the page stops
painting a selection and its pins, and the platform's long press and
handles make one. The buffer follows it: every selectionchange inside
the Rendered face is read back through the map (MdSurface.offsetOf)
into d.range, so dictation, the keys and backspace act on it as on a
painted one. The other way round, a range the page sets (undo, a
drop) is written into the platform's selection (nativeReflect).

WHAT IT GIVES UP. The page's long press did three jobs and the
platform's does one. Taking a word is the platform's now. Split on a
held space goes: a tap and the shifted ¶ split at the caret. Carrying
by holding goes too, since a held selection opens the callout, so a
Move pill rides under the selection: tap it, then tap where the words
go, between two words or in the gap between paragraphs.

`_lastNative` is the platform's selection as last read or written
here, as "a:b" or '' for none. A selectionchange that reads the same
is this page's own write coming back, and is not adopted: adopting it
is how a range set on markup drifted a character wider each round.

THE PLATFORM LET GO without a tap (a press it kept, a handle
nudged off): the range is still live, so it is written back rather
than left unhighlighted for the next words to overwrite unseen. A
real tap places the caret, and that paint takes the selection away.
A new selection made while words are held for Move replaces them.

The platform moved first and its selectionchange is still queued
(a handle drag, with a repaint from the microphone in between):
the platform is right, and writing the old range back would pull
the handle out from under the finger.
Near either end of the platform's selection, where its handles are.

The start's knob sits above its line and the end's below, so each
zone reaches past its own line on that side only, not into the
line beside it where a tap is a tap.

THE TARGET'S TAP. Under native selection, with words selected, it
holds them for a move and puts the caret at their end for the pad to
aim; held, it drops them at the caret. Otherwise the anchor, as ever.

A tap on the text while words are held AIMS: the caret goes where
they would land, and a gap is kept as a gap (moveAim, drawn as the
drop line) so Move here makes them a paragraph of their own there.
Inside a word, the nearer of its edges, as a dropped carry does.

── The change cards ──────────────────────────────────────────────
Each run of blocks that differs from GitHub's copy is one card in the
Rendered face (kits/md-surface.js, tracked), shown with its change
marked and open to typing. Its stops pill reads original, marked and
new; a sideways swipe moves the card's text with the finger and
settles on one (md-card-reading), a tap on a stop scrolls there, a
tap on the original returns to marked, and a tap on its number
selects it. THE SELECTED CARD SHOWS ITS PILL (markCardBar): the card the
caret is in, or the one picked by its number, or on a desk the one
under the mouse. Only one at a time, so the document still reads as
one.

A LINK IN THE DOCUMENT IS TEXT HERE, not a way out: this face is an
editor. A click on one followed its href, which is written relative
to the file on GitHub and resolved against this page, so it left the
editor for an address that does not exist (measured 2026-10-01 with
either selection). The click still places the caret, as on any word.

INFO LIVES ON THE CARD'S NUMBER (owner's call, 2026-10-01; it was a
word in the pill). A click PINS it: a hover-opened one stays; a pinned
one closes; any other opens pinned, which is every tap on a phone.

The same three ways for a block's badge, which opens the same panel
with no change to show: the block's notes, or a field for one.

A mouse resting on a card's number opens its Info unpinned, after the
house 140ms; moving off before then opens nothing.
A block's badge does the same once it holds a note; an empty one
opens on a click, since an empty field is nothing to read.

A resting mouse on an underline opens its pop, as on info; off the
words and off the pop, a hover-opened one goes after the grace.

THE CARD PILL: the selected card's actions, as the words "confirm" and
"remove" in a small pill (Info is the card's number) centred on its bottom edge. kits/md-surface.js
draws one in every card, hidden, from `cardActions`; this shows the
selected card's and hides the rest. Being in the card, it scrolls with
the text rather than being moved on each scroll. Centred because a
neighbouring card keeps its number at its left and its stops at its
right. The shape is the convention and the words are the page's: a
page reviewing someone else's text would put its votes and comments
in the same pill, the destructive one last.

It grows in when the selection reaches a new card, and a repaint
(which rebuilds every card, so every bar is born hidden) shows the
same card's at once rather than replaying that on each keystroke.

The card's own border turns amber, nothing drawn outside it: a
second ring made the card read as a text field, which it is not.
Important, since the kit sets the border's colour per card.
A bar just built has no style to transition from until it is laid out.

── The block under the caret, the one under the mouse, and the notes
AN UNCHANGED BLOCK IS A UNIT TOO, and two of them can be marked at
once, each its own way, so neither takes the other's mark:

  THE CARET'S BLOCK  a light dashed outline at the extent the card
                     would take: the scope an edit there would have.
  THE MOUSE'S BLOCK  a light wash, on a desk only, and kept while its
                     panel is open.

They were one mark until 2026-10-01, the mouse's block taking it while
the mouse was over one and the caret's taking it back when the mouse
left, so the outline jumped between two paragraphs as the pointer
moved (owner's report). Neither takes room: the outline is an
`outline` and the wash is a background spread by a box-shadow, so
marking moves no text. Blocks are drawn one by one even with nothing
changed (MdSurface.paint `blocks`), so there is always one to mark.

EACH MARKED BLOCK WEARS A BADGE AT ITS TOP LEFT, where a card keeps
its number, and it opens the block's note: "+ note", or "note" once
there is one. A block holding a note keeps its badge
unmarked, so a note is found without visiting every paragraph; a card
holding one shows it beside its number. An unchanged block has only
the 8px between paragraphs where a card has padding, so the marks sit
4px out and the badge is a compact 18px pill centred on that line,
which clears the line above's descenders and this line's capitals.

One note, so one mark: the call's while the note is its why, the
reader's once they have written over it.
The blocks: a badge on each marked block and on each holding a note.

The card's number pill, compact: 18px, its centre on the marks' line
4px above the text. AMBER, AND IT SAYS WHAT IT DOES, since a bare
pencil in grey went unnoticed (owner, 2026-10-01): amber is the
card's action pill's colour, the one pill that acts. Words and no
icon, "+ note" or "note" once there is one, the owner's pick of four
shot side by side (an icon with "Add note", this, a solid fill, and
bare text on the outline). The ::before widens what a thumb can hit,
sideways and upward only: reaching 8px down it covered the first
line's opening words, so a click meant for the caret there opened the
note instead (measured 2026-10-01 on a desk).

The title-tip only where a pointer hovers. On a phone the tap that
opened the note panel below also opened the tip above, over the
previous line, saying what the panel already showed (owner's
screenshot, 2026-10-02). The aria-label carries it for a reader.

── Confirm, then Apply ───────────────────────────────────────────
A CARD IS CONFIRMED FOR APPLY, and Apply commits the confirmed cards
together, one commit, to the branch the file was opened from. The
two steps are the confirmation: confirming is local and taken back by
the same word, and nothing reaches GitHub until Apply. Owner's design,
2026-09-29: reject is per change (the word pop's Undo), commit is per
card, never part of one.

A card is known by a key that survives edits to it and elsewhere:
where its GitHub text starts ('o' + offset), or for a card that only
adds, the line just above it ('a@'). That card's own text was its key
until 2026-10-01, so an edit to it orphaned its note. A confirmation
holds the card's text as confirmed, and lapses when that text
changes, so what is applied is what was seen.

── Notes ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A NOTE IS ON A BLOCK, changed or not: written from a card's Info, or
from the badge an unchanged block wears under the caret or the mouse
(markBlock). Each is a record anchored to GitHub's copy
(kits/dictate-record.js), so it stays on its paragraph through any
edit, through the edit being taken back, and through Apply.

The units are md-surface's: every block on screen, unchanged or a
card, with its span in GitHub's copy. The painted ones when they are
current, otherwise worked out from the two texts.

A card's confirmation key from its unit, the same key cardId reads
off the painted card, so the record can say which changes are
accepted from any face.

The notes as they should be stored or sent: a note on added text
quotes that text as it reads now.

The notes a unit holds, by its span in GitHub's copy, which no edit
moves, so an Info opened on a block keeps finding its notes while the
reader types elsewhere.

ONE NOTE PER SECTION (owner, 2026-10-04). The field is the unit's
note: typing makes it, emptying it deletes it, and it stays the same
element throughout, so the keyboard stays up while it is written.
Two noted paragraphs joined into one card still hold two records;
the field shows them as one text (noteText), and the first edit folds
them into the first record, so a section never shows a list.
UNDER A CALL THE NOTE STARTS AS THE CALL'S WHY (owner, 2026-10-04):
the why is the section's note until the reader writes one, and it is
the field's text, so the field never offers "Add a note" over a note
already there. An edit makes it the reader's, a record like any note;
written back to the why's words, or emptied, it is the call's again.

READ, THEN EDIT (owner, 2026-10-04: "it should let you change the
note"). A note opens as text, with a pencil; the pencil, or a tap on
the text, turns it into the field, and Done turns it back. A section
with no note opens on the field, since a note is what the badge was
tapped for. The field is shown and focused inside the tap, for the
reason openBlockInfo gives: iOS raises the keyboard for no later focus.
Leaving the field does not end the editing, since on a phone the tap
on Done arrives after the blur, and a button swapped out under it
would hand the tap to whatever took its place.

THE TRASH ON A NOTE'S ROW removes the note and closes the panel, so
the badge going back to "+ note" is the confirmation. Emptying the
field still removes it too, but nothing said so, and on a phone it
took a select-all first (owner, 2026-10-02). The page's Undo walks the
text and not the notes, so the way back is the toast's, which puts the
same record back, id and anchor and all.
The section's note, every record of it, so the trash empties the
section whether or not a join left two.
Under a call the same button reverts rather than deletes, since what
is left is the call's why; it keeps the panel open on it, as proof.

A draft from before notes were records (2026-10-01) kept them by card
key; once the cards are drawn each is put on the card it named.

Each paint: confirmations whose card changed or went lapse, and the
confirmed cards wear it, a green number and "confirmed" in the pill.

A title-tip, not a `title`: this is what the word does, and a
phone would never have shown it.

WHAT A COMMIT WOULD SEND: GitHub's copy with the confirmed cards'
changes in it, which is the text now with every OTHER card taken back
(mdDiff.revert, the same take-back as remove), from the last card up
so each revert's positions still hold.

And what no card shows (a re-wrap, spacing, a blank line between
unchanged paragraphs) goes back to GitHub's, so the commit holds the
confirmed cards and nothing else.

APPLY: one commit of confirmedText. To the file's own branch, it then
is the base, so the applied cards go and the rest stay as edits,
keeping their notes. To a NEW branch (a call's answer can ask for
one), the file's branch has not moved, so the page keeps everything as
it was and the commit is reported by its link. Returns the commit as
{ target, url }, or null when nothing landed.

What changed, by each change's opening words, and nothing else:
notes are not commit text. They stay on the page and leave in the
record (see `record`). A call's commit names the call it answers.

Every note moves through the commit: one on an applied change
lands on its text, now GitHub's; one on a change still pending
stays on it; one whose text went out is kept unplaced.

WHAT THE CHANGE WAS, line by line in the markdown source, since a
change the rendered marks cannot show (bold added, an indent, a
doubled space) left the card looking unchanged and the two copies side
by side left the reader to find it. Each changed line is numbered as
the file numbers it, the characters that changed are lit within it,
with spaces and tabs made visible there, and unchanged lines beyond
one either side fold. The header counts the lines and says when the
change is only whitespace, or only formatting.

IT IS A PANEL-TIP, by the house rule (daisy-alpine mechanics.md,
"Title-tips and panel-tips"): it scrolls, so it takes the pointer.
kits/panel-tip.js owns the ways out and this owns the opening: hover
opens it unpinned where there is hover, and it closes when the
pointer is demonstrably elsewhere; a click pins it, and pinned it
closes on Escape, a press outside, or a scroll.

NO ✕, BY THE OWNER'S CHOICE (2026-09-29), and a deliberate departure
from the rule, which draws the kit's ghost ✕ when pinned and on every
screen with no hover. The rule's reason stands and is accepted here:
a press outside lets the tap through to what was under it, so on a
phone closing Info means finding somewhere safe to press. The page
around a card is text more than controls, which is why the owner
judged the trade worth it; revisit if that stops being true.

The kit's pointer guard would close a pinned panel the moment the
mouse left it, so a pinned one is wired without it.

Hover-opened, the card itself counts as near, since reaching the
panel from the number means crossing the card; pinned, a press on
the card is outside like any other.

A card's source, both sides: { s, a, line } for GitHub's copy (O) and
the text now (N), each the span from its first entry to its last.

CHANGES THE WORDS CANNOT SHOW, underlined where they are. The marks
come from a word diff, so bold added, italics taken off, or a doubled
space changed the file and marked nothing: the card read as unchanged.
Here each card on its marked reading has its source compared by
character, and what changed only in markers or spacing gets a dotted
amber underline, on the overlay, so the rendered text is untouched.
  paired markers (** __ * _ ` ~~) added or removed: the words between
  spacing added or removed: the word after it
Info names it exactly. A card whose character diff is a rewrite (many
pieces) is left alone, since its words are already marked and a
marker found in a rewrite is noise. Memoized by the two sources.

Each find: u, the words underlined; s, the span of the text now
that an undo replaces; old, GitHub's text for that span; what, a
word for the change. Offsets are relative to the card's source.
Markers pair in order, like with like: the first opens, the next closes.

WHERE THE WORDS ARE ONE ELEMENT (the bold, italic or code the
markers made), the underline is that element's own decoration,
so it moves with the text. An overlay measured at paint stayed
where the words had been when the text shifted afterwards, a
late style reflowing it: reported on a desk, the underline ran
on past "demonstrated" into the next word.

The rest are drawn, so they are drawn again once late styles
have landed, the same two frames and a beat the kit waits.

The underlined change under a point, or null: its words' own boxes,
not the nearest offset, so a tap beside the words is not a hit.

AN UNDERLINE OPENS THE SAME POP AS A MARK, with the raw change above
its Undo: GitHub's source and the source now, the markers lit, since
the rendered words are the one place the change cannot be seen. A tap
opens it anywhere; a resting mouse opens it where there is hover, and
it goes again once the mouse has left both the words and the pop.
Above the words when below would run into the key rows.

THE INFO IS THE NOTE (owner, 2026-10-04): no diff, and since the same
day no header either. The change is read in the card, and as markdown
on Raw · changes; what the panel carries is what the card cannot, the
section's one note, which under a call starts as the call's why.

The field takes focus inside the tap, as a block's does (openBlockInfo),
unless the call has something to be read first.

A DROPDOWN FROM THE BADGE (owner, 2026-10-04), as a panel-tip hangs
from its trigger: under the number, its left edge on the number's, or
over it when the text pane has no room below. Until then it stood
clear of the whole section, which put a short note a long way from
the badge that opened it; covering a few words is what a dropdown does.

AN UNCHANGED BLOCK'S PANEL is a card's Info with no change in it: its
note, and a field for one when it has none, focused, since a note is
what the badge was tapped for.

THE FIELD TAKES FOCUS INSIDE THE TAP. iOS raises the keyboard only
for a focus made while the tap is still being handled, and $nextTick
is far too late: Alpine holds it until the panel's fade has run, a
frame and 90ms on, so the field was focused with no keyboard and
wanted a second tap (owner's question, 2026-10-02). A microtask
queued here runs after Alpine's own render of the field and still
inside the tap. The fade would show the panel a frame later, so it
is shown here, still clear, and fades in from there.

CLEAR ALL EDITS: the file as GitHub holds it, the local edit gone and
the notes kept (loadFile). One undo still reaches the edit. Offered
from the unsaved mark itself and from the menu.

The next card below the top of the pane, or the previous one above it,
wrapping; brought to just under the top.

THE UNDO OF ONE MARK. Every undo is one replacement, [a, b) of the
buffer by `text`: a struck word goes back in at the caret its tap
would have placed (just before it), an added word comes out, and a
struck word right against an added one is a REPLACEMENT, which undoes
as a pair from either side, since keeping half of it is a third text
nobody wrote.

THE PILL GOES UNDER THE FINGER: at the tap's x, below the line the tap
was on. A mark that wraps has one box per line, and its bounding box
is their union, whose centre can be a line away from anything tapped.

THE CHANGE IN THE RAW MARKDOWN, which is what is being edited: one
line of source around [a, b), GitHub's text struck in red and the
text now in green, the context plain and dimmed. The same for every
pop, a struck or added word or an underline, so a red beside a green
shows which the undo is about, and bold added shows as the ** it is.
Spaces are dotted only where they are the change itself.
ONE DIFF FOR EVERY VIEW OF A CHANGE (owner, 2026-10-01). The card
marks words with mdDiff.runs: a word diff whose short unchanged gaps
between two changes fold into them. Info and the pops used a character
diff where two lines were mostly alike, and a rewrite came out as
letters ("kind" against "knowing") beside a card marking whole words.
Here is runs again, as jsdiff-shaped parts, for both. The exception
is a change only in markers or spacing, which the card shows as
markFormat's dotted underline, found by character: that comparison
is the card's mechanism there, and a word diff would light all of
"**para**." for two pairs of asterisks.

A long change is shown by its ends: the pop is a glance at the
edit, and a sentence-long insertion printed whole filled a phone
screen. Changed text keeps 40 characters of its start and 20 of its
end, unchanged text between changes 12 either side.

Kept on screen once drawn: the pop is centred on the words and as
wide as its line of source, so near an edge it slides inward.

Taking a word out leaves its space: of two spaces, or a space before
punctuation, one goes with it.
An underline's undo is exact: its span is GitHub's own, spaces included.

── The faces ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Six, as a grid: Rendered and Raw, each before, with changes, and
after. Changes and Rendered-after are the Rendered view with the change
cards on and off; Raw-changes is the same cards with each block drawn
as its markdown source; Raw-after is Source. A before face hides the text
now behind GitHub's copy and draws nothing else, and the text changing
under it (a phrase dictated, an undo) brings the text back: paint()
drops the before face first, so nothing lands unseen.
A removal's wedge was tapped: the same undo pill as a struck word.

── Formatting, file mode ─────────────────────────────────────────
Each is ONE write to the buffer, so one undo takes it back, and each
leaves the words it acted on selected, so a second tap undoes it or the
next key stacks on it.
The lines the caret or the selection touches.

'H' cycles as the key does; 'H0'..'H6' (the shortcuts) set a
level, and asking for the level a line already has clears it.

── The keyboard half ─────────────────────────────────────────────
THE PENCIL IS RETIRED, as it is in the composer: a double tap is the
only way in, and it is both shorter and better aimed than a button,
since the reader has already pointed at the place they mean. Opening
with the caret at the end would make them point again through a
textarea their thumb is now half covering.

The way out is the keyboard's own: blur, or Escape. There is no
control of its own to find.
`at` is an offset the reader POINTED AT, which only the double tap
has; the button has none and takes the selection instead. Both end at
the same call, so the textarea is always opened somewhere deliberate.

In the Rendered face the keyboard types where the caret is, into the
document as it reads, rather than swapping in the source.
the phrase on screen is part of what is being edited

READ THE RANGE AFTER THE FLUSH, not before. A flush with a selection
live is a REPLACEMENT: the running hypothesis lands over the
selected words and the kit leaves the range over what replaced them.
Read first and the offsets describe a buffer that has since moved.
after the flag, so the pins come off with it

SYNCHRONOUS, INSIDE THE TAP, and that is the whole of why the
textarea is never `display:none` (see its markup). This used to run
in `$nextTick`, which focused the field correctly and left the
keyboard down on a phone: WebKit gives a programmatic focus the
keyboard only from the call stack of the gesture, and a microtask is
past it. Nothing on a desktop can show the difference, since a
desktop has no keyboard to raise.

The VALUE has to be written by hand for the same reason. `x-model`
assigns on the reactive flush, so at this instant the element still
holds the previous text and `setSelectionRange` would be measured
against it. Alpine writes the same string a moment later.

A SELECTION CROSSES INTACT, which is the whole point of the button:
the first thing typed replaces the words that were picked out, which
is the one repair a keyboard does better than a voice. A caret is
the same call with the two offsets equal, and nothing selected opens
at the end, where dictation would have carried on.

Read the caret BEFORE the assignment, because setting the buffer
drops the range by design, and restore it after. That is the whole
of "the red caret is where you left the keyboard": without it,
leaving sent the caret to the end and the next spoken words landed
there rather than where the reader had been working.

── Corrections ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
Read once at boot, held as one alternation so a segment costs one
pass rather than one per entry. Longest first, so "web tools app"
cannot be eaten by "web tools" before it is reached.

Case is carried across: a correction fired at the head of a sentence
keeps its capital, since the recognizer's own capitalization is the
only signal available about where a sentence started.

Add and remove share one read-modify-write, since they differ only in
what they do to the list in between. A list you can only add to makes
a mistyped entry permanent from the page's side, which is the state
the reader is most likely to want out of.

The buffer is corrected too, since the reader is looking at the word
that was wrong and a list that only helps NEXT time reads as a
control that did nothing.

The sheet STAYS OPEN. The list under the fields is the confirmation,
and closing on save would hide the one thing that says it worked.

── Where the words go ────────────────────────────────────────────
Committing the hypothesis first, always: the reader has READ the grey
text and tapped save, so accepting it is what they asked for.
A METHOD, not a getter: it commits the running hypothesis, and a
getter with a side effect is a trap set for the first template that
reads it. Committing is right whichever way the words go out, since
the reader has READ the grey text and then tapped save.

?to= names the destination a link already has in mind, and the row
paints that one primary rather than acting on it: choosing is still
the reader's, and a URL that could file a note on arrival would be a
different and much less safe thing. It is the only difference between
the four buttons, so it is a class rather than a branch.

Copy and Share only READ the buffer, so they leave it standing and
leave the draft in place: nothing durable has happened yet and a
clipboard is not a place words live.

Rather than a silent no-op: a clipboard write can be refused, and
a reader who thinks they have the words and does not is worse off
than one who is told to use Share.

Jot and Drop file it, so both clear: the note has a home now and the
page goes back to being blank, which is the state it is for.

── Send: the fifth destination ────────────────────────────────────
It reads the buffer and leaves it standing, like Copy and Share and
unlike Jot and Drop: nothing durable has happened here either. The
words are still on this page when you come back, which matters more
for this one than for the other two, since the far end may refuse
them (over the cap) or the reader may change their mind about where.

FILE MODE SENDS A FILE, not a note: the edit or the whole of it, and
one of the places it can go is back to GitHub. With changes, the
sheet opens on the edit and on Save; without, on the file and on a
session, since there is nothing to save.

The account's repositories, most recently updated first. Fetched once,
on the first open, because a page that is usually only dictated into
should not spend a call on a sheet nobody opens.

CAPPED, and the cap is a phone rather than an API limit: a bottom
sheet holding a scrolling list of a hundred repositories is a worse
control than one holding the dozen you have touched this month.
Anything preselected by ?repo= is pinned above the cap, so a link can
always name a repository this list would not have reached.

Named rather than swallowed: with no list and no message the sheet
reads as "you have no repositories", which is a different and
wrong claim.

Preselected first and in the order given, then the rest of the
account's. A link's repositories are the ones its author meant.

SHARE IS NOT A ROW, IT IS THE OTHER BUTTON. It was a row for one
commit, which made reaching the system sheet two taps: pick the row,
then confirm. That is a confirm step over a choice already made, and
the sheet it opens is itself a chooser, so the second tap bought
nothing at all.

It belongs at the foot beside the primary because that is what it is:
a second way to finish, not a third destination. The rows above are
the ones that need a repository or a warning read first; Share needs
neither and should cost what Copy costs.

What rides. A session or a chat gets the patch WITH a line saying where
it belongs; Share and Copy get the bare patch, which is what git and a
paste want. The whole file is the buffer either way.

THE RECORD: this file, the version its line numbers count in, then the
changes and the notes, either of which may be empty (`dictate/1`,
kits/dictate-record.js). Only while the sheet is open, as the patch
is, since it aligns the whole file.

The link, and what it could not carry. Recomputed on every change
rather than stored, so the sheet's own summary line cannot drift from
the button beside it.

Over the cap is a REFUSAL, not a truncation: a prompt cut at a
character boundary reads as a complete instruction and gets acted on.
The sheet says the number so the reader can cut it themselves, which is
the only edit that knows which sentence matters.
The cap belongs to the query string. Share hands the buffer over as
text with no address to fit it into, so it is never over.

A new tab, never this one. The words are still here and the draft is
still in storage, so navigating away would be recoverable, but a page
you are dictating into should not vanish because you aimed it.

BRING BACK WHAT THE ARRIVAL DISPLACED, above whatever is here now.
It is the join the arrival used to make by itself, and the difference
is the whole point: asked for rather than guessed. Spent on use, so
the band stops offering something that is already in the buffer.

Back to blank, and still listening if it was. The buffer goes through
the kit's setter, so undo can bring it back for one step, which is
the whole safety net a clear needs here.

Starting fresh means the set-aside too: a reader clearing the page
is not asking to be offered an older draft on the next line.

── The status bar ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
Three facts and a menu, because a capture surface has to answer "is it
hearing me" without being asked, and answer it from across the room.

── The header ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A THREE-COLUMN GRID, so the target lands on the viewport's centre line
rather than on the midpoint of whatever space the two side groups leave
over. In file mode the target is in the bottom row instead, between
Copy and Send, and the centre column stands empty.

Left is the session (record, and how long it has run). Centre is the one
control that AIMS. Right is the history and the menu. Backspace joins
undo and redo rather than staying in the bottom row: it undoes a word
the way undo undoes an act, and the three read as one group.

IN FILE MODE THE FILE LINE LIVES HERE TOO, rather than in a second band
under the header. The empty centre column takes the file's name and
whether it is unsaved, and the two faces join the right group. On a
phone the name is the file's own (SKILL.md), with the repository and
its folders on a small second line, and unsaved is a dot; from
the sm breakpoint up, the whole repo@ref:path and the badge. The clock
and word count give way on a phone, and the count moves to the menu.

RECORD, and the state readout as well as the switch: red and pulsing
while live, so the one question a capture surface has to answer
without being asked is answered by the control that changes it.

The armed capital has nothing on screen to show yet: the word it
applies to has not been said. So it wears the ring red the pins and
the target wear, which is this page's one word for "live".

The target in the header, for a note; in file mode it is in the
bottom row. See the one there for what it does.

Which file, and whether the buffer differs from it. The name links to
GitHub, the only place a reader can check what Save would overwrite.

Cut from the LEFT when it does not fit, so the folder nearest the
file is the part that shows: right-to-left for the ellipsis,
the path itself isolated left-to-right so its order holds.

THE KEYBOARD, on a button rather than only on a double tap. The
double tap stays and is still the better aim, since it says WHERE
as well as that you want to type. What it cannot do is carry a
selection: it lands on a point, and a point collapses one. This
does the other thing, and it is the reason it exists rather than
being a second route to the same place: whatever is selected comes
across selected, so the first thing typed replaces it.

The menu is a DROPDOWN, not a band. As a band it inserted itself
between the header and the text and pushed the words down the screen
to show controls that are not about the words at all.

File mode's New: back to what GitHub holds, the local edit discarded.
One step of undo still reaches the edit, as it does for New.

Notes whose text left GitHub's copy, kept in the record until
the reader lets them go; only here when there are some.

On a desk the upper keys are not drawn, so their shortcuts are
listed where the rest of the page's options are.

TWO ARRIVALS, ONE BAND, and they are told apart because they mean
different things. A restored draft is this page's own history; words
handed over by a composer on another page are somebody's sentence from
somewhere else, and a buffer that gained those without saying so is a
buffer the reader cannot trust. Same band, same Start fresh, different
first clause.
"Bring back" appears only on the second, and only where the arrival
displaced something: it is the way back to the draft this page was
holding, which an arrival replaces rather than joins (see init).

NOT IN FILE MODE: there the unsaved mark in the header already says the
words on screen are an edit, and tapping it clears them.

THE CALL'S HEAD, under the header: what is being asked, why, and where
it came from, so the edits below arrive as one action item rather than
as unexplained changes. A band, which the menu's comment above warns
against, and earned here: it is the subject of the page while a call is
open. Two lines until tapped; the rest (the recommendation, the edits'
standing in the file, the session, the PR, the call itself) one tap
down. Answer is the same sheet the Apply pill opens.

── The text ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The whole width and the whole remaining height. THE COMPOSER'S MARK
COLUMN DID NOT COME ACROSS, and it is the one piece of that card's
shape that could not: a column beside the text holds 56px of the width
for the full height in order to carry four keys at the bottom of it,
which on a 390px phone is 14% of the measure spent on whitespace. The
composer can afford it because its text box is capped at 172px, so the
column is the height of the keys; here the box is the height of a
phone. Shot both ways before deciding.

What DID come across is everything that is behavior rather than
geometry: the key set and its four faces, the cursor pad, the retired
arrows, the retired pencil, and the bottom row.

The LAYER is the handles' home: outside the scroll box and unclipped,
so a pin may hang above the first line rather than being cut in half.

ALWAYS RENDERED, hidden by opacity rather than by `x-show`, and the
reason is the phone's and not a style preference. WebKit raises the
keyboard for a programmatic `focus()` only from inside the call
stack of a user gesture, so the focus has to happen in the tap
itself. `x-show` writes `display:none`, a `display:none` element
cannot take focus, and Alpine does not clear it until the reactive
flush, which is after the handler has returned. The field therefore
has to exist and be focusable at the moment the button is pressed,
which is what this costs and what it buys. Measured 2026-08-25:
display was `none` synchronously after setting the flag and `block`
by `$nextTick`, and focus landed there, which is why the button
opened the textarea and left the keyboard down.

It sits UNDER the read pane, and by DOM ORDER rather than by a
z-index: it is written first, so the pane paints over it, and the
pin layer above them both keeps painting over the pane. A `z-10` on
the pane did the same job for the pane and hid the pins behind it,
since they are the layer's own children with no z-index of their
own. Order costs nothing and disturbs nothing.

It takes no taps while it is invisible, and `tabindex` goes to -1 so
a keyboard user does not land in a field they cannot see; -1 still
permits the programmatic focus this is all for.
The before faces: GitHub's copy, drawn and never edited.

File mode's Rendered face. Its classes are set once from
GuideRender.bodyClass() when the renderer loads, so the document
reads in the house markdown type.

Nothing said yet. The whole empty surface IS the start button,
which is the one tap WebKit's gesture requirement makes
unavoidable and the largest target a page can offer for it.

THE SINK: the Rendered face's keyboard input. Invisible, 16px so a
phone does not zoom to it, and holding the caret's line of source so
autocorrect has context (see startTyping).

A REMOVAL, SHOWN AGAIN. The marks can only point at where words went,
since the buffer no longer holds them; this is where they are read.

A card's Info, as the house panel-tip (see openCardInfo): the note
and nothing else. Why a call proposed the change, when one did, and
the reader's own note. The change itself is read in the card, and as
markdown on Raw · changes; until 2026-10-04 the lines were drawn
here, under a line saying where they were. No ✕: it closes on a
press outside, Escape or a scroll (see openCardInfo). It arrives as
every house tip does, the title-tip's 90ms fade and nothing more
(kits/title-tip.js); the word pop below does the same.

THE NOTE ON THE SECTION, a card or an unchanged block, one per
section: a record kept with the draft and handed over in the record
Send carries, never in a commit. Under a documentation call it
starts as the call's why for the change (see infoWhy), and is the
reader's once edited. Read, it is text with its controls on its
first line, their right edge on the panel's: a pencil, and for a
note of the reader's a trash, or under a call the arrow back to
the call's note. Written, the row is the field: tinted, its margin
and padding together the read row's padding, so the words do not
move when it opens, and Done where the pencil was, inside the tint
as an input's trailing button is. Done holds its place while the
field is empty, so the first letter typed reflows nothing (see
editNote), and each control is 15px wide whatever its icon font
has done, since the bold check can load after the pencil and the
field would move under it. The field stays the same element while the note is
made, and its text is not reset under the caret.

A CHANGE'S POP, for a struck or added word or an underline: the
change in the raw markdown (rawSegs), one line of source with
GitHub's text struck red and the text now green, and under it the
Undo, an action, so in the Split pill's blue. Under the tapped line,
or above when below is out of room. The tap that opened it is
ignored by the outside-click, which otherwise arrives as the same
gesture.
w-max, AND IT MATTERS: a fixed box placed by its left edge and then
pulled back by half its width is laid out in the room to the right
of that edge, so near the middle of a phone it was squeezed to a
column a word wide. max-content, capped by the screen, lets the
line of source take the width it needs.

THE FACES, ONE PILL (owner, 2026-10-01). Top right under the
header, it names the face on screen and opens six as a grid: rows
Rendered and Raw, columns Before (GitHub's copy, read-only), Changes
(the text now with each change a card) and After (the text now).
Rendered · changes is the main one, named Changes on the pill. Raw ·
changes is the same cards over the markdown source (owner,
2026-10-04), which is where the raw change is read now that a
card's Info holds only notes. It replaced the header's eye button, which flipped
only between Rendered and Source, and the menu's Track changes,
which was the Changes and Rendered-after pair under another name.
Green while the text differs from GitHub's, the flat badge with a
border the owner picked on 2026-09-30, on a solid ground because it
floats over the document; plain when the two agree. A file that is
not markdown has no rendered faces, and shows the pill only while
there is a before to differ from.

THE CHANGES, COUNTED: how many cards the edit makes, and a step to
the next or the previous one, wrapping at the ends. It is what the
retired Changes face had that the cards did not. Bottom left, since
the launcher holds the bottom right.

Apply, the second step: shown once a card is confirmed, naming
how many and the branch they will be committed to. Under a call it
opens the answer sheet instead, where the branch is chosen and the
answer is recorded with the commit.

The keyboard half, and it has no controls of its own: blur or
Escape is the way out, which is the keyboard's own gesture and the
one a reader already reaches for.

ITS TYPE CLASSES MATCH THE READ PANE'S EXACTLY, and the list has to
be read as one thing rather than tidied per side: the same size,
the same leading, the same tracking, the same wrap rule, the same
padding, over the same 358px content box. A word wrapping one
character earlier here than there is the whole paragraph reflowing
under the reader at the moment they switch, and it reads as the
text having moved rather than as a font detail.

Measured 2026-08-25, when it did not match: the read pane carried
`tracking-[-0.01em]` and this did not, so 21px type ran 0.21px wider
per character, 16.8px over a 79-character line. Everything else was
already identical, which is what made it hard to see and easy to
fix. `break-words` went the other way, onto the read pane, so a URL
too long for the measure breaks in both rather than scrolling in
one.

── The keys ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TWO GROUPS PAST A HAIRLINE. On the left the composer's three marks and
its shift, laid across instead of down: the keys that WRITE. On the
right the three that take something back: step to a break, close it,
delete a word. The rule between them is what a thumb reaching without
looking reads first, and it is why the backspace no longer has to be
found by counting cells from the end.

Seven keys measure 50px each at 390 and 48 at 375, and every one holds a
single glyph, so what each needs is a touch target rather than a label.
At 320 they are 40px wide, under the platform's 44, and that is accepted
rather than fixed: the row is 56px tall, so the target is 40 by 56 and
generous in the axis a thumb actually misses in. Tapped over and over
inside one note, so they are the tall row, and being the tall row is
what qualifies a control to be here.

Sticky in fact, momentary in feel: a shifted mark drops the shift the
way a phone keyboard does. It used to become a ✕ that dropped the
selection, on the composer's reasoning that the pad and the selection
are one state and a mode needs an exit. The exit was already there,
since a tap anywhere outside the selection collapses it to a caret,
so the key does one thing.

── THE REPAIRS, past a rule ───────────────────────────────────────
Four keys write and three take back, and until this rule they sat in
one undifferentiated run where a thumb had to count cells to find the
backspace. The line says which half of the row it is in before the
glyph says what the key does, which is what a thumb reaching without
looking actually reads.

It is a hairline WITH room either side rather than one or the other. A
gap alone at this size reads as a layout accident; a line alone was
drawn in base-300 between two base-200 keys and disappeared into
them, which a shot showed before this comment was written. Inset from
top and bottom too, so it separates the keys without drawing a box
around either group.

STEP BACK, the key that changes nothing. It walks the caret to the
previous sentence break so the reader can SEE which one they are about
to close, and tapping again walks past it to the one before.

IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE STITCH CANNOT GUESS. For a few hours on
2026-09-06 the stitch reached backwards by itself, and no ordering of
its targets was right: during dictation the buffer almost always ends
in the full stop the pause just wrote, so "the most recent break" is
that one. Taking it back is exactly right when the sentence should
keep running and exactly wrong when the reader meant to keep it and
repair an earlier break, and nothing in the buffer tells the two
apart, since the difference is in what they are about to say.

BACKWARDS ONLY. Forwards is a tap on the text, which every reader of
this surface already knows and which lands anywhere rather than on a
break, so a key for it would spend a cell duplicating a gesture.
Getting back is the hard direction and the one worth a key.

The caret it places is a LOAN: the stitch hands it back to the end, so
the next thing said still lands where the reader is speaking. See
`jumpBack` in kits/dictate.js.

THE STITCH, IN TWO TAPS. The first shows where it would happen and
changes nothing; the second does it. This is the one edit on the page
that rewrites a sentence somewhere other than where the reader is
looking, so it is the one worth a glance before it lands, and the
marker is a badge hovering over the spot with a stem down to the line,
drawn in the overlay and changing nothing in the text: a first cut
previewed the edit in place, which read well and reflowed the whole
paragraph, since a capital and its lower-case twin are different
widths.

Step back between the two taps and the marker re-aims, since it is
derived from the caret rather than stored. Tap the badge, or anywhere
in the words, to back out.

IT LOOKS LIKE THE OTHER KEYS UNTIL IT IS ARMED. It wore a warning tint
whenever it was live, which at 20% over a ghost button read as a
disabled control rather than an available one, and it was reported as
a glitch. There is nothing to distinguish anyway now that it is out in
the open with a cell of its own; the tint is worth something only for
the armed state, where it means "this tap commits".

DIMMED RATHER THAN GONE where there is no break to close. A key that
came and went in the middle of a row would move the ones beside it
under a thumb that had already learned where they are.

BACKSPACE, at the right end, where every keyboard the reader has ever
used puts it. It is red because it is
the one key here that takes a WORD away, and the tint is the aim: the
marks are reached for by position and this one has to be found in a
hurry, mid-sentence, without reading. The stitch beside it takes
something away too and wears the warning tint rather than this one,
which is the same distinction the pad's shift already draws: amber is
a state or a repair, red is a deletion. It needs no
`:disabled` for the keyboard half, since the row it is in is hidden
there and the software keyboard has its own.

── The destinations ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Four buttons, one tap each, in the row that used to hold one button
that opened a sheet holding these four. The row is the same rhythm as
the keys above it and half a step shorter, which is the whole visual
statement that it is a different kind of control: keys compose, these
end it. Copy and Share leave the words standing, Jot and Drop file
them and clear the page, and the pair that needs a token is the pair
that writes to a repository.

A phone at 390px gives each of four 92px, so the name fits beside the
icon and neither has to go. The row lays out `grow basis-0`, so
Share dropping out on a browser with no `navigator.share` widens the
other three rather than leaving a hole.

NO TOKEN DOES NOT DISABLE Jot and Drop, which is the one place this row
departs from the sheet it replaces. The sheet could afford to grey them
out because it had a paragraph underneath saying why; a row has nowhere
to put that sentence except a permanent line between these buttons and
the keys, costing 34px on every screen to explain a state most readers
are never in. So the tap is left live and `commit()` answers it with the
toast it already carried and the sheet made unreachable: no token here,
use Copy or Share. The explanation arrives when it is asked for.

THE TARGET, IN FILE MODE, small and on the centre line between Copy
and Send, where a thumb rests. A note's row has four destinations and
no room for a fifth, so there it stays in the header. Two gestures on one button, because they are one job:
drag it and the caret moves, tap it and the caret becomes one end of
a selection whose other end is your next tap. Armed it wears the ring
an armed pin wears, which is this page's one word for "live and
pointed at the text". touch-action:none inline is what makes the drag
work rather than scrolling the page under it.

UNDER NATIVE SELECTION it is also the Move, in two steps that say
what they are. With words selected it lights, and a tap holds them:
the held words stay washed, a cancel appears beside the target, and
yellow wedges above and below the caret point at where the words
would go, with a small Move here tag (markAim). Then aim: drag the
target, or drag or tap anywhere on the text, and the caret and its
markers follow. Nothing lands until Move here is tapped, on the tag
or on the target. Tapped without aiming, the words stay where they
were.

Two buttons side by side, not a daisyUI join: a join squares its
members' inner corners by DOM position, and with the cancel hidden
the target was still its second member, square on one side.
NOT ON A DESK: a mouse points at the text itself, drags a selection
to move it, and has the arrow keys, so the pad has nothing to add.

inside this one, beside the two that start a session somewhere. That
is what it always was: a chooser with a single option, opened by the
operating system instead of by this page.

button simply was not there on a browser without navigator.share,
which is most desktops, with nothing on screen to say why or what the

── Answer a call ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
One sheet for the three ways a call's answer can leave: committed to
the file's own branch, committed to a new branch cut from it, or copied
out as JSON with nothing committed. The first two also append the answer
beside the call (and comment it on the call's PR when ticked, which
wakes a subscribed session). With nothing confirmed there is no commit
to make, and the primary button records the answer alone.
Each edit is a row with its decision, read off the page when the sheet
opens (callDecisions); a row is a way back to that edit's card.
