diff-tool.html — compare two texts, full window.

A window-filling app shell rather than a centered document: the app bar and
the control bar are fixed, and only the diff body scrolls. That holds from
390px to a wide desktop, which is the point of the layout. At no width does
the tool sit in a narrow column with dead margins.

Four tabs, left to right in the order you use them:

  Sources   two slots, A and B. Each holds editable text and can be filled
            from a URL, a GitHub address (owner/repo[@ref]:path, read through
            the stored token so private repos and un-pushed branches work),
            a local file, or the clipboard. Contents persist in localStorage
            under 512 KB a side, so the tool still holds your text tomorrow.
  Diff      split or unified, word-level highlighting inside changed lines,
            unchanged stretches folded behind expand bars, prev/next change
            navigation. Defaults to unified below 768px, where two columns of
            code do not fit.
  Patch     a unified diff with a context selector, copyable as text, as a
            fenced markdown block, or downloadable as .patch.
  Apply     apply a unified patch to a source text and load the result into B.

NORMALIZATION is the stage between the sources and the diff, and it is what
makes comparing two documents (rather than two source files) readable. It
descends from pages/drop/diff-tool.html, the legislative version-comparison
tool this page absorbs: strip HTML to text, then an ordered list of regex
rules. The `Prose` preset breaks on sentence ends so two drafts diff sentence
by sentence instead of showing one enormous changed paragraph. When either
side looks like HTML the tags found in it appear as chips, and clicking one
adds a rule that strips it.

THE ENGINE is kits/text-diff.js, patience diff over lines, shared with the
stage's Diff lens rather than inlined here. It replaced an O(n*m) DP table
that allocated n*m int32s and could not survive two long documents. The why,
the trade, and the caps are documented in the kit.

Built to skills/html-style. The three rules that shaped it, since a first
draft broke all three:

  No stat cards, and no line of totals standing in for them. Each count sits
  on what it counts: the selected repo's button carries its DENOMINATOR (files
  scanned against files present), because the scope of the scan is the fact
  about this page most likely to be misread; the list's name and mention

  explained in a paragraph, and an unjudged label reads "not judged" in the

guides/code-layers.html — the decision document behind the lib/ reorganisation.
Written because the migration task had a file list and a recommendation but no
statement of what the categories ARE, and the one rule that had been written
down was refuted by measurement a day later.

FOUR TABS, one question each: what the tree looks like now, what could be done
about it, what is proposed, and what the move costs. The tabs are the structure
rather than a convenience: the four are read at different moments and by
different people, and stacking them into one scroll was what made the first
version open on a wall of prose instead of on the measurement.

Table columns are held to four and every cell wraps, because a horizontal
scrollbar hides the column that decides each row. vanilla-bundle.js alone
registers sixteen globals, so the attaches cell summarises past the first two
rather than setting the table's width from its worst row.

DATA IS BAKED IN, on purpose. Every number comes from
scripts/code-shape.py (npm run code-shape), run at the date in the
header, inlined rather than fetched so the page renders identically through a
#gh= toss, a #gz= toss, or a local file open. A guide resting on measurement
describes a specific state of the tree; a live re-read would silently restate
the argument against a tree that had already moved.

Icons drop below sm so five tabs fit one row on a phone. The label
is the thing being read; the icon was what pushed Migration onto a
second line.

The record, in the register of a court's statement of facts: third person,
past tense, no advocacy. It never argues, and the closing paragraph declines
to decide, which is what lets the rest read as fact rather than as a brief.
The recommendation lives in Options, where a reader can weigh it as one.

Numerals describing the CURRENT tree are bound to the data, so re-running the
scan cannot leave the prose asserting a count the table contradicts.
Numerals describing the RECORD are hardcoded on purpose: "seven of twenty-one"
is a fact about what the 2026-08-06 retraction found, not about the tree, and
binding it to live data would silently rewrite history to match the present.

No heading. The tab already says Facts, and the opening sentence names
the subject, so a "Statement of facts" banner said the same thing a
third time before the reader reached a single fact.
the finding, as two claims side by side
the table: four columns, every cell wraps, no horizontal scroll

Precompute the two derived display fields once, rather than in the
x-for. attachShort is the reason the table needs no horizontal scroll:
vanilla-bundle.js registers sixteen globals, and letting one row set
the column width costs every other row its legibility.

Blob links point at the SHA the scan was RUN against, not at main. The
page reports a specific state of the tree, so a link that followed main
would eventually open a file that no longer matches the row describing it,
and it would do so silently. Pinning costs nothing and cannot drift.

The scan script is not a subject of the measurement, it is the
instrument, and it does not exist at the measured SHA because this branch
introduces it. Pinning it there gives a 404, which a link check caught and
an eye would not have. It rides the branch until this merges; repoint it
at main then, or drop the helper and use blob() once the two agree.

Spelled out, because the statement of facts is prose and "31 files" reads
as a table cell dropped into a sentence. Falls back to the digits above
the range it knows, which is the honest failure: a wrong word would be
worse than a bare numeral.
Bound to the data: these describe the tree as measured.

inquiry.html — renders an `inquiry/1` surface: a SELF-ADDRESSED envelope.

Every other envelope in this repo carries content outward and stops there. A
stage's `&prompts=` asks are one-click-copied INTO another chat; nothing comes
back. This one carries the address its answers return to, so the person who
taps through it never has to describe what they were answering.

Three layers, and keeping them separate is the point:
  the OBJECT     an inquiry/1 surface, self-addressed via context.reply_to
  the RENDERING  this page, a dynamic form drawn from the items
  the CONSTRAINT the profile schema, which names the boxes and requires them

reply_to is NOT stage/1's `destination`. That field is defined as "a claim
about the set" (where these files are proposed to go). Answers are a different
subject and do not exist when the envelope is authored, and an inquiry can
legitimately carry both, which is the test that made it its own field.

Addressing, the same grammar the other envelopes use:
  #src=owner/repo[@ref]:path     fetch the envelope through the stored token
  #gz=<base64url gzip>           carry it inline, for a token-less reader
Both also read from ?query, for contexts that strip fragments.

The return leg is gh-store's save(), the same read-modify-write the annotator
uses for a jot. Answers append to one file per submission rather than mutating
a shared one: a run is a record, and two runs of the same inquiry are two
facts, not a correction.

A framed inquiry is a broken inquiry, and silently so. toss-render mounts
its subject with `allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-popups allow-forms
allow-modals allow-downloads` and NOT allow-top-navigation, so a custom
scheme in an ACTION link cannot navigate anything: the tap does nothing and
reports nothing. This page exists to launch such links, so the toss is not
a delivery route for it and the page has to say that itself.
One card per step. The form is drawn from the items, never hand-built.

autolink one and neither will a bare string here.

  dossier   an area's own markdown, opened full width below the columns,

pdf-inspect.html — the visual half of kits/pdf.js.

The kit's numbers are checked by three headless suites, but a table extractor
is a geometry tool and geometry is judged by looking. This page draws every
layer the kit produces on top of the page it was read from: text containers,
per-character boxes, the vector rules with their detected roles, both column
detectors, and the lattice grid with its cell indices.

Everything visual here goes through pdf.view(), the kit's projection, and
nothing on this page converts a coordinate by hand. That is deliberate: if the
overlay lines up, the projection is right, and if it drifts, the projection is
wrong. The page is the assertion.

The sample PDF is built in the browser with pdf-lib (already loaded by the
kit), so no binary is committed and the fixture is visible as code. It is the
same geometry as node/test/pdf-kit-browser.mjs, including the white rule that
a naive extractor turns into a phantom column.

Affordances worth knowing, since none of them announce themselves:
  - drop a PDF anywhere on the stage
  - hover or tap a text box to read its own numbers, font, and cell
  - drag a rectangle to select, which re-runs the column detector on it
  - keys: arrows page, p/s mode, c controls, +/- zoom, 0 reset, 1-6 layers

Headless: npm run shot -- pages/pdf-inspect.html [--width 390] [--script ...]

Toolbar: one row at every width, and it never scrolls. What cannot fit on
a phone moves into the panel rather than wrapping into the layer list.

Where an addressed document came from, linked to the file on GitHub.
Absent for the sample and for a drop, which have no address to state.

Drop anywhere on the stage. The file input stays for the phone, where
there is nothing to drop from.
controls: a static column from lg up, an off-canvas drawer below it

What the pointer is over. An inspector should answer "what is this box"
without a console, and this is the only place the item's own numbers,
font, and decoration are visible at all.

One axis at a time, one big slider, and a nudge at each end. Three
thin sliders stacked was a desktop answer: on a phone the target is a
few millimetres tall and the value you want is usually one of them.

Saved views. The presets are the four that ship; anything beyond them
is a place you found by hand, and losing it on the next drag is the
whole reason this exists.
The four hues carry meaning and nothing on the canvas says so.

The canonical boot (README.md). entry.js boots window.gh and chains
gh-boot.js, which auto-loads gh-auth.js, gh-fetch.js, kits/console.js, and
vanilla-bundle.js, and mounts the FAB.
?use=<branch|tag|sha> pins everything entry.js loads to a ref; defaults to main.

The colours are the page's only opinion about the kit's output. One hue per
layer, and the same hue in the legend, so a stray box is traceable to the
function that produced it without reading any code.

pdf.js objects use private class fields, and Alpine deep-proxies every
property of a component's state, which detaches them from their own class.
So the live objects live here, outside reactivity, and only plain data
(counts, strings, the matrix) crosses into the component.

What each hue means in the stack. The canvas cannot label itself without
becoming unreadable, so the key lives in the panel beside it.
The four that ship. A preset is a whole view, not just an orientation, so
recalling one restores the spread too; a stack read at 8pt spacing and one
read at 60 are different pictures and the name should mean both.

The address this document came from, when it came from one. Null for the
sample and for anything dropped, which is what keeps the header honest:
a local file has no address and must not be shown wearing one.

Keyboard, for the desktop half of the audience. Nothing here is the only
way to reach a function; every one of these has a control too.

An address in the hash wins over the sample: someone who linked a
document meant that document. hashchange keeps the page addressable
after boot, which is what lets the drawer re-aim it in place rather
than reloading, and what makes a second link land where it says.

--- addressed documents -------------------------------------------------

`#gh=owner/repo[@ref]:path`, the estate's one address grammar, so a PDF
anywhere in any repo is a link rather than a download-and-drag. Until
2026-08-15 this page had no entrance but the file picker and the drop
zone, which made it the one tool in the estate that could not be pointed
at the estate's own files: the DRS budget submittals it was built to read
sit in a repo it had no way to name.

Token-gated like every #gh= address, and honest when the token is missing:
a 404 here usually means "not signed in", not "no such file".
The addressed file on GitHub. Blob rather than raw, since the point of the
header link is to reach the file where it lives, with its history beside it.

TWO SPELLINGS, because two callers write them and neither is wrong.
`#gh=` is the estate's address form, what a person links and what the
drawer re-aims. `?src=` is what toss-render hands a registered renderer
(docs/routes.json), so `#pdf=owner/repo:file.pdf` lands here without the
router learning anything about this page. The hash wins when both are
present: it is the one a reader can see and edit.

WHICH PAGE the address asks for, in the same two spellings as the address
itself. This page's main mode is page-scoped, so a link into it from a
reader that has a position ought to carry it: the viewer's pdf mode hands
over the page under the reader's thumb, and without this the workbench
opened on page 1 and the position was thrown away at the door. Silent
loss, since a link cannot report what it dropped.

Clamped after the document is parsed, not here: `numPages` is unknown
until then, and a page past the end should land on the last page rather
than fail the load.

A fresh GH rather than the page's own: this address names another repo.
gh-auth patches the prototype's headers getter, so the stored token
reaches every instance and a private repo resolves without passing it.
An address with no ref follows the link's selection for that repo.

After `parse`, which sets pageNum to 1 unconditionally, and only when
the document actually loaded: a failed fetch leaves numPages at 0 and
there is no page to go to.

The value of whichever axis the picker has selected. A getter rather than a
template expression: `this` inside an Alpine expression is not the
component, so `this[axis]` there is undefined and the readout reads NaN.

Whether the current orientation IS this view, within a degree. Cheaper and
more honest than tracking a selected name: a slider nudge silently leaves
the preset, and a flag would keep claiming otherwise.

--- saved views ---------------------------------------------------------

Through the persistence kit rather than localStorage, because that is the
repo's answer for this and its store is already namespaced per page.
Failures here are never fatal: the page works without saved views, so a
blocked IndexedDB degrades to an in-memory list for the session.
A name that says where you are, so an unnamed save is still findable.
Steps through the same ladder the select offers, from wherever `fit` landed.

Built here rather than committed, so the fixture is readable as code and
the page has something to show on first load with no file and no network.

The white rule: a reader never sees it, a naive extractor rules the
header into two columns because of it.
A dotted leader, drawn the way a budget report draws one.

An unruled block below, so the stream detectors have something the
lattice cannot see.

Eleven more pages, so the stack has something to be about: the same
running head and a changing folio on every one (the furniture the
detector should find), over body text that moves.

A dropped file replaces whatever the hash named, so the address goes
with it. Leaving it set would caption local bytes with a repo path.

One entry point for every source, so the busy state, the error surface, and
the reset of per-document state cannot drift apart between them.

pdf.js refuses a second render() on a canvas whose first is still in
flight, and a fast toggle or page step gets there easily.

'fit' is the default because the first thing a phone showed was a page
squeezed into a sliver beside a panel that could not be closed.

Every coordinate below comes from the kit's projection. Nothing here
multiplies by scale or subtracts from height.
Painted back to front, so the fine detail is never buried.

Stagger the labels down a short ladder: adjacent columns are routinely
a few points apart (a 60pt body margin beside a 66pt cell inset), and
at that spacing the captions overprint into an unreadable smear.

Dashed where the kit inferred an edge no rule draws: an open perimeter
or a header split. Solid means every side traces to ink.

Three states, three treatments, because "what was extracted" and "what
the lattice walks" are different sets and the gap between them is the
whole white-rule story. Solid: a rule that survives geom.usable and
will be walked. Dashed and faint: extracted but discarded, because it
is the page colour or too short. Rose: a rule the kit resolved as
decoration, which is how underline detection becomes visible instead of
staying a boolean in a console dump.

--- the stack -----------------------------------------------------------

Pages laid out along a third axis, so what repeats becomes a column through
the stack and what is unique to one page stands alone. The projection is a
plain axonometric: two rotations, no perspective and no camera, because the
question this view answers is "does this element recur at this position",
and perspective would make two elements at the same (x, y) on different
pages land at different screen points, which is precisely the comparison
being made. Foreshortening would look better and read worse.

Drawn to one canvas rather than as DOM planes: a hundred pages of item
boxes is tens of thousands of elements, and the browser has no reason to
lay any of them out.
Model space to a flat plane, with no scale and no offset applied. Keeping
those out means the caller can project the volume's corners first, measure
the result, and derive a scale that fits: the view then never clips, at any
orientation, which the first version did the moment it was rotated.

Depth is centred on the middle page, not on page one. Rotating about the
front sheet swings the whole stack sideways out of frame, which reads as
the wrong pivot because it is.

Fit the volume, whatever the orientation. Project the eight corners,
measure the extent, and pick the scale and offset from that.

Two kinds of recurrence, and the distinction is the finding. In a tabular
document the body rows recur positionally too, so "appears at the same
place on most pages" is not by itself a footer detector. What separates
them is whether the text repeats: a running head says the same thing every
page, a folio and a data row do not.
Back to front, so nearer pages occlude further ones.

Barely-there sheets. The first attempt filled each at 0.72 alpha and
twelve stacked into an opaque slab: the near page was legible and the
eleven behind it were gone, which is the one thing this view exists to
show. A stack has to be seen through.

Depth cue by opacity rather than by size, since the projection is
deliberately parallel: far pages fade, near pages read.

The cut planes, drawn through the whole stack so a bound is visible as a
surface rather than as a number that changed somewhere.

Any change to the view raises the readout and schedules its retirement.
Called from the orbit, the sliders, and the presets alike, so the feedback
does not depend on which control you reached for.

Turn the detector's output into a proposed cut, which is the point of
having a detector: the sliders start somewhere defensible rather than at
the page edges.

Orbit. The pointer handlers on the stack canvas are separate from the
page-mode drag, because one selects and the other rotates.

Claim the gesture. Without this an enclosing sheet (the Claude app's
in-app browser, a mobile drawer) can read a horizontal drag as a swipe to
dismiss and take the pointer away mid-orbit. Capture plus preventDefault
keeps it here; the View sliders exist for where that is not enough.

Normalized per axis, so a drag across the canvas turns the same amount on
a phone as on a desktop. The rates are deliberately unequal: a full-width
horizontal drag is 120 degrees of yaw, a full-height vertical one is 90 of
pitch, and a shared rate made the vertical axis feel twice as fast because
the canvas is taller than it is wide on a phone.

The comparison the kit exists to make, and it is only meaningful over the
same region: run stream across a whole page and it reads the title, the
leader row, and the unruled block too, so it "differs" from any lattice
table by construction and says nothing. Scoped to the ruled area, the two
readings are actually answerable against each other.

An edge placed from text is the evidence stream reads, so agreement over
it is weaker than agreement over drawn rules; say which edges those are.

Drag selection. Screen coordinates go straight to the kit; the only thing
this page computes is the rectangle the pointer described.

The reading under the pointer, whether or not a drag is in progress. Uses
the kit's own hit test against the projected boxes, so what the panel
reports is the same box the overlay drew.

Which lattice cell, if any, claims it. Answering "where did this land"
is most of the reason to hover something in the first place.

peek.html — kits/peek.js, armed, over a page built to make the walk matter.

Arm it, then tap anything below. Tap the same spot again to walk up the
ancestor chain. The structures here are chosen to make the walk matter: each
one buries the thing you would actually want several levels under whatever
your finger lands on.

?use=<branch|tag|sha> pins the lib chain to a ref for previewing edits.
A table: a tap lands on a link, the row is three levels up.
A card grid: the card is what you mean, the tap lands on a word.
Deep nesting with no useful classes: the case where the tag path is the
only thing that tells you where you are.
Prose: a tap lands mid-sentence, the section is the unit.

pip-steps.html — a walkthrough that stays on screen while you work somewhere else.

THE PROBLEM IT SOLVES. Handing over "do these nine taps in Settings" fails in
a way a link cannot fix: the reader leaves the message to do the taps, and the
instructions leave with it. They come back, re-find their place, and go again.
iOS has exactly one mechanism that survives the app switch, and it is
Picture-in-Picture, which floats video and nothing else. So the steps are
shipped as frames of text: python/pip-steps.py renders one still card per
step and encodes them at a fixed seconds-per-step, which turns the player's
own scrubber into a step navigator.

This page is the launcher, and it exists to remove the taps a bare video URL
cannot. `autopictureinpicture` floats the window on its own when the app is
backgrounded, so the reader opens the link, switches to the app they are
actually working in, and the steps follow them: no PiP button to find. The
Float button stays for the explicit route, and asks inside the click handler
because iOS grants PiP only on a live user gesture, preferring
webkitSetPresentationMode as the iOS spelling.

Media Session gives the PiP transport real card boundaries, so a tap lands on
the start of a card instead of wherever a fixed skip interval falls. The card
duration is set to the skip interval anyway, which makes the bare video behave
too, but only the page can be exact.

Where no PiP API exists the same steps render as a list, from the same JSON the
video was built from, so the page is never a dead end.

IT MUST BE OPENED IN A BROWSER, not in a web view. Whether a Shortcuts or
in-app web view permits PiP is unmeasured; Safari is the known-good venue, so
a shortcut reaches this through Open-URL rather than showing it inline.

A CARD HOLDS WHAT THE READER CAN ACT ON WITHOUT LOOKING BACK, so grouping two
or three shortens the loop. That is the cost this format has to keep down: a
reader who misses their card waits for the whole cycle to come round.

ADDRESS. ?v= the MP4, ?steps= the cards JSON behind it; both default to the
probe-automation pair. The JSON's title names the walkthrough.
Feature-detect on the element, since iOS ships the webkit spelling only.

The property, not just the attribute: Safari reads the IDL attribute, and
this is what floats the window on its own when the app is backgrounded.

Card boundaries are exact, so the transport buttons land on a card start
rather than wherever a fixed skip interval happens to fall.

Both calls stay synchronous inside the click: iOS drops the PiP request
once the gesture that authorised it has been awaited away.

An idea board for the pivot builder: five ways to say which fields are
rows, which run across, which is the value and which filter, each live on
the shared engine (lib/kits/table-stats.js, TableStats.pivot) over the same
sample, and one result view whose layout is chosen separately, so a
builder and a result shape can be compared in any pairing. The filters
sit in their own strip over the table in every builder. Menus are the
estate's own (lib/kits/row-menu.js). A pill drags as soon as it moves,
by mouse or finger; a tap picks it up, lights every place it can go,
and a tap on one of those puts it there.
The filters, over the table they narrow, whichever builder is up.
The pill under a finger or a mouse while it is dragged.
Where the dragged pill will land.
A field's card, from the caret on its pill.

── the sample ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A state budget's shape: agency › program, fund, object of expenditure,
fiscal year, dollars, and FTEs only on salary lines (blank elsewhere, so a
pivot of FTEs shows the skipped-row count doing its job).

field -> Set of values left out
grid outline: paths folded shut
tap and drop: { field, from } picked up
number filter: field -> { lo, hi }
what a list joins its values with

The value's functions as its pill shows them: three letters or fewer, so
the pill keeps one width. A tap steps through the ones that fit the field.

A field holds one of rows, across and value at a time; a filter rides
beside any of them. Placing a value that is not a number counts its rows.

A text filter leaves out the values unticked; a number filter keeps the
rows between its bounds, either bound open.

A list's cell is text, truncated to a column's width; the card and the
Cards view show it whole.
Ten steps of the accent, the only opacities a daisyUI colour takes.

── pills ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
data-pill marks a draggable field; data-from names where it sits. A pill's
role shows in its icon, so a pill means the same thing in every concept.
A PILL IS A CAPSULE, not a daisyUI button: 28px tall, a 1px border, the
name truncating before the pill outgrows its line. Its colour says what
the field holds (numbers in the secondary hue, text in the page's own);
placed pills are tinted, tray pills plain, the picked-up pill ringed. Its
segments, each a tap of its own: the name (pick up, or drag), the value's
summary when it is the value, and a caret for the field's card. Only the
Tap builder, which has no shelves to say a pill's role, shows a role icon.

THE VALUE'S FUNCTION, a small pill inside its pill: sum, avg, min, max,
each three letters, so the pill keeps one width whichever is in use. A
tap steps to the next; count, which no longer summarizes the numbers but
the rows, is on the field's card. A text value can only count, and its
inner pill does not step.

The three roles as labelled groups on one wrapping line: as many rows
as the pills need, rather than one per role.
Every field on one wrapping line; a tap moves it to the next role.
An addition is a small worded chip, so it says what it adds.

No builder of its own: the tray, and the result's header as the drop
targets (see grid()).

── the result ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GRID: one label column, the row fields nested in it as an outline rather
than a column each, which is what keeps a phone's width for the numbers.
A group row carries its subtotal and folds. The header and the label
column stay put while the body scrolls both ways.

CARDS: one card per top group, no sideways scroll at all. The across
values become label-value pairs, and a deeper level becomes lines.

── the field's card ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
What TableStats.profile reads in the column, the same figures the
explorer's Columns view and the workbench's Profile show. No buttons of
its own: a field becomes a filter the way it takes any role, by drag or by
tap and drop onto the strip.

The header says it all in one line: the name, what it holds, how many
distinct values (the figure that decides whether a field can group),
and its role. Fill and blank counts were a row of tiles nobody read.

A PILL'S FACTS are the house title-tip (kits/title-tip.js). Not its name,
which the pill already shows, nor its role, which its place shows: the
lead is its type as an icon pill, then what it holds as a row of pills,
its distinct count and a number's range or a text field's commonest
value. A mouse gets it on hover; a tap opens it, and since the same tap

A SIDE TEST FOR ONE FAILURE, not a demo of the deck.

md-diff's change container is a three-stop swipeDeck.core. On iOS a flick
crosses the middle stop and lands on the far side, and it can also come to
rest BETWEEN two stops, which `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` is supposed to
forbid. Neither reproduces headless: Playwright's touch emulation has no
momentum phase, so the only instrument is a thumb.

Four tracks, identical content, differing in exactly one thing each, so a
swipe on each says which mechanism is responsible rather than that something
is wrong.

  A  as shipped: snapStop (the property AND the kit's overshoot guard), and
     the height written from inside the scroll handler on every frame, which
     is what the container does.
  B  the property only, guard removed. Isolates the guard: if A sticks and B
     does not, the guard's corrective `go()` is fighting the engine's snap.
  C  the guard kept, the height written only once the scroll has gone quiet.
     Isolates the write: `scrollHeight` is a layout-flushing read, and the
     value changes at the midpoint of every flick, so the scroller's own box
     animates under a finger that is still moving.
  D  neither, and all three stops the same height, so nothing about the
     scroller changes during a gesture. The floor: if D sticks too, both
     hypotheses are wrong and the cause is in the engine or the page around
     it.
  E  the candidate fix, if C or D clears it: the box opens to the tallest
     stop on touchdown, before momentum exists, and eases to the exact
     height once the scroll is quiet. Unequal heights are kept, since they
     are what the readings actually are.

Each track reports where it came to REST, in slide widths. A whole number is
a snap point honoured; 0.70 is the failure in the screenshot. It also reports
how many stops the last gesture crossed, which is the other half of the same
complaint.

THE ANSWER, measured by thumb on an iPhone 2026-09-18: D, and only D. Not B,
so the guard was not the cause. Not C, so deferring the write until the
scroll went quiet was not enough. Not E, so one write before the drag was not
enough either. Every lane that resized the scroller at any point failed, and
the lane that never resized it worked.

What shipped from that: md-diff's change container is sized once to its
tallest reading and never resized, its height transition is gone, and
swipe-deck's overshoot guard is gone with it. The invariant is held by
node/render/scenarios/md-diff-one-height.mjs. This page stays as the
instrument, not as an open question.

Plain DOM, no Alpine. The code under test is framework-free (lib/kits) and a
probe that wraps it in a component is measuring the wrapper too.

Three stops of deliberately unequal height, because that difference is
what turns the container's per-frame write into a real layout change.

Every lane reports the same two numbers, read when the scroll goes quiet.
`scrollend` where it exists, a 160ms lull where it does not, so the lane
says the same thing on every engine.

`snapStop` is the kit option that turns on BOTH the property and the
overshoot guard. A lane that wants the property without the guard asks
for neither and sets the property itself, so the kit stays untouched.

Lane D gives every stop the same text, so without a number a reader
cannot tell a landing from an overshoot. Every lane carries it, so the
lanes stay comparable.

The candidate shape rather than a bare deferral: the box opens to the
tallest stop BEFORE the drag, so nothing clips while the reader moves,
and eases to the exact height once the scroll is quiet. One write, and
it lands before momentum exists rather than in the middle of it.

  ...&base=main                        explicit base (else default branch)

Pasted GitHub URLs normalize into the same shape: /compare/a...b, /blob/,
/tree/, /pull/N (resolved via the API: branch names while the PR is open,

apply: at most 300 files listed, per-file patch text absent for large or
binary files; the contents API caps a fetched side at ~1 MB (the card then
falls back to its links).

CAN A WEB PAGE MAKE AN iPHONE TAP BACK?

One cell per technique, in the shape docs/ios-sheet-drags.md prescribes,
because this cannot be answered anywhere but on the device: no emulator
reproduces a Taptic Engine, and every claim about it found in writing is a
claim about some particular iOS version.

  A  navigator.vibrate()   the standard. WebKit has never shipped it, and
                           the estate calls it in three places anyway.
  B  a `switch` checkbox toggled BY SCRIPT. THE QUESTION: Safari 17.4 gave
     the switch control real haptics, and a page can only use them if a
     synthetic toggle earns them too.
  C  the same switch toggled BY HAND. The control.
  D  a label wrapping a switch, tapped. A real tap, not on the input.

ANSWERED, 2026-08-25: C and D buzz, A and B do not. So the haptic belongs
to a real user activation of a switch, the activation may arrive through a
label rather than the input, and a page still cannot fire one on demand.
The reasoning and what it costs the long press: docs/ios-haptics.md.

Kept, not deleted, because WebKit can move and no emulator can tell us.

RUN 1 (same day) ANSWERED C AND NOTHING ELSE.
C buzzed, so the device is willing. A, B and D reported nothing because the
page was broken in a way it could not tell anyone about: Alpine and Tailwind
rode one combined jsDelivr URL, that request did not land, and the result
was a page that looked nearly right, had dead buttons, and printed empty
values where its own feature detection should have been. It reproduced
perfectly in headless, which is exactly the trap.

So this version DEPENDS ON NO EXTERNAL JAVASCRIPT. Plain listeners, plain
textContent, one inline script. The CSS may still fail to arrive and the
page will be ugly and completely usable. And the first line it prints is
whether its own script ran, because a probe that cannot report its own
failure will report someone else's instead.

The one this page exists for. A scripted click is what a long press would
do, and a control that answers only a real finger is no use to one.

B drives C's own input, so C's change handler fires too and its counter
would climb for a toggle no finger touched. C is the CONTROL: it has to
count human taps and nothing else, or the two readings blur exactly where
the answer lives.

(the snag shell-pin-kills-the-tab). That matrix ran on 2026-09-08,
when the unpinned shell imported its modules from jsDelivr. Since 2026-09-26
both routes read everything after gh-api.js through the contents API, so the
delivery difference left is narrower: HOW gh-api.js arrives (native import
from Pages, or blob import of raw's copy) and WHICH ref the shell's gh names.

level, and a probe must not change the production shell's boot. The replica
is only trustworthy if its positive control (cell D, the recorded crash
shape) dies on the device. If D survives, the replica is not reproducing the
failure and no other cell here means anything; cell G, the real toss-render
pinned with ?use=, was there to say which. Since PR #825 the renderer ignores
?use=, so cell G no longer tests the pin.

toss-top-probe.html — top mode: the renderer replaces itself with the
selected page, so the page runs as the top-level document.
Experiments E6 and E10 of docs/showing-consolidation.md.

THE QUESTION. A toss frames its page, so the tab's title and icon, the
address bar and history, the viewport a phone gives a page, and the FAB all
belong to the renderer, whose code is main's. `?use=` on a deployed page has
all of those, at the ref, and nothing else a toss has. Can the renderer
instead fetch the page at its ref, prepend the same prelude a toss stamps,
and document.open / write / close itself into that page?

THE ADDRESS, and the one change from the first prototype. The address rides
the query as ONE key, `gh`, beside the page's own real parameters:

  toss-top-probe.html?gh=owner/repo@ref:path[&lib=<ref>][&<page params>][#<page frag>]

so the page's query and fragment are its own, as on the deployed page. The
first prototype carried the page query INSIDE the gh value, and the app, which
writes its whole query back on every view change, copied the address into
itself until it nested (measured 2026-09-28). Now the prelude hides the `gh`
entry from the page's reads of its address, and folds it back into every
history write, so a page that rewrites its query keeps the address without
knowing it exists. The old form (page query inside the gh value) is still
read, for the device cells minted before this change.

THE VERSIONS, by the renderer's rule (docs/loader.md, "Under the toss"): the
page at the address's ref; Web Tools at `lib` if the link names it, else the
page's own ref for a web-tools page, else main. A real `lib` in the query
stays visible to the page, since it IS the version the page should load.

NOT THE PROPOSAL'S RENDERER: no inliner, no fetch shim, no payload mode, no
forced width. It exists to measure what top-level execution buys and costs,
headlessly and on a phone, and it is small enough to be the one file merged
to main that lets a branch's page, or a branch's renderer, run top-level on a
device before its own merge.

THE SELF-DRIVING CHECK (?probe=<errand id>&steps=…), the `device-link`
errand method in docs/run-methods.csv. A person opens one link on the device
and does nothing else: this runs in the page it launched, walks the steps,
shows where it is in a banner, and closes the errand by writing
errands/results/<id>.json on the registry's `background` branch, where
errands live (kits/errands.js BRANCH), with the device's stored token. Steps:
  fab       open the FAB drawer as a tap does and wait; armed first, so a
            tab that dies here is recorded as `died` when Safari reloads it
  write     the page writes ?view=tools without the selection
  reload    reload the tab (the run resumes from sessionStorage)
  back      history Back
  go:<q>    replace the page's query with <q> and reload
Every step records whether the URL and window.__refs still carry the whole
selection the link named. Serialized into the page, so it is self-contained.
A `go` that opens a view mounts its frame after boot; give it time.

The address: `gh` read by slice up to the next '&' for the current form,
or to the end for the old form whose page query rode inside the value.

The page's own parameters: every real key but `gh`, plus, in the old
form, the query that rode inside the gh value.

Appended, not set: a key the page repeats keeps every value (set kept the

THE SELECTION, in the renderer's grammar (docs/loader.md, "The
selection"): repeatable refs=owner/repo@ref[:path], lib= as the web-tools
entry. The target is read at its address @ref, else where the selection
puts it; the rest of its repository follows the selection first.
Raw media type, or the JSON envelope from a server that ignores it.

Only the parameters the page's own query does not carry are injected:
the old form's page query, and `use`/`lib` when they are defaults.

`use` carries the effective ref; `lib` is never invented (the renderer's
rule), so a page reading `lib` or __lib sees only a real selection.

The link's selection, restored into every URL the page writes, or a
page that writes ?view=x would drop it and a reload would lose it
(measured 2026-09-29: this history shim kept only gh). What the
page's URL carries is read before anything is restored: `lib` comes

__ref is the displayed file's version, stamped only when known, as
the renderer stamps it (a default-branch read leaves it unset).

The address stays out of the page's sight: every read of a params
object that holds gh=<this address> skips that entry, and `use` and

History: whatever the page writes, the path stays this file's and

with the link's selection restored (keepSource, below). Relative
URLs resolve against the <base>, which is the deployed page's
directory, so the target's own path is ignored.

session.html — one recorded session as a readable conversation.

The sibling of branch.html, and the same argument: every session surface was
a LIST (the app's Sessions pane, search.py's rows), and each ended in a
summary because there was nowhere of ours to go. 🌿 is where you read a
branch; this is where you read the session that made it.

Address grammar, fragment preferred and query accepted:

  #gh=owner/repo[@ref]:sessions/2026/08/2026-08-07-abc12345.json
  #id=abc12345                     the short id, resolved against the store
  #branch=claude/some-branch-ab12  that branch's LATEST session
  #gz=<base64url>                  a gzipped record, for a reader with no token

Any of the four takes `pane=outline|files|raw|calls` and `card=<n>`, which say where
in the session to land: `card` opens the deck on one exchange, the session's
answer to branch.html's `file=`.

`#branch=` is the address a phone can produce. The Claude app copies the branch
a Claude Code session is on and nothing else about it, so this page takes that
string and finds the session behind it; shortcut-tools' `Choose-Claude` is the
caller, off the double back tap. The walk it costs, and the tie it settles, are
in alpineComponents/session-brief.js at resolveBranch.

The record is web-tools-private/sessions/**.json (its README is the schema).
The store is private, so #gh= and #id= read through the viewer's stored token
and a tokenless browser gets nothing; #gz= is the fallback that needs none.

What the page is NOT: a transcript. A record is a bounded capture, and the
bounds are real (prompts at 400 characters, prose at 8 KB a turn, result
bodies at 1 to 2 KB, receipts and Reads dropped by policy). session-render.js
states each gap in the deck's first card rather than letting an absence read
as a quiet session. Nothing here reconstructs what was never captured.

?use=<branch|tag|sha> pins this page's own lib chain to a ref, fetched from
raw.githubusercontent with `cache: 'no-store'`. Both halves are needed: the
blob import defeats the MODULE cache, and no-store defeats the HTTP one. A
branch ref MOVES, so a plain fetch happily served a bundle from an earlier
push and the preview showed old code with no way to tell (2026-08-07).

Full account in pages/branch.html, where the failure was first measured.

shortcut-edit.html — a proposed hand edit to a shortcut, shown where it goes.

A shortcut whose only copy is the device cannot be replaced by paste without
losing its file settings (share sheet, input types, icon), so a change to one
is a hand edit: cards pasted at one place in the editor. The editor has no
line numbers and no search, so the place has to be recognisable by what
surrounds it. This page is that reference, open in Safari beside the editor.

THE LINK CARRIES EVERYTHING. shortcut-tools' tools/edit.py applies the cards
to the newest exported copy of the shortcut, sketches it before and after,
and gzips {name, before, after, cards} into #gz=. No token and no fetch, so
the page opens anywhere and cannot disagree with what was proposed.

WHAT IS SHOWN. The after listing, in the Workflows view's form (index gutter,
nesting kept as indent, verb in bold), with added lines marked and removed
lines struck through where they stood. Lines are matched on their text
without the index, since an insertion renumbers everything below it.
Unchanged runs far from a change collapse to a count. Each change names its
place as the blocks that enclose it and the lines either side, which is what
a reader scrolling the editor can actually match.
The list: every open proposal, with where it stands.

shortcuts.html — home base for the shortcut estate.

WHAT WAS MISSING. Three surfaces existed and none of them was an entry point.
shortcut-log.html answers "what ran"; library.html in web-tools-private answers
"what is on the phone", all 606 of them; workflows/README.md answers "what have
we built", in 12,500 words ordered by the date each thing was discovered. The
question a reader actually opens with, "what do we maintain and is the phone
carrying the current copy", had no surface at all, and could not have one while
the answer lived in 75 separate workflow files.

So shortcut-tools publishes catalog.json, one row per workflow, and this page is
its reader. The two are the same split every other page here runs: the
structured stage is committed and checked in the repo that owns the data, and
the render holds no judgment of its own.

THE JOIN IS THIS PAGE'S JOB, AND ONLY THIS PAGE'S. catalog.json carries what
the workflow files state and nothing about any device, deliberately, so it stays
deterministic and its --check can be exact. Whether a shortcut is installed, which
build ran, and when, are facts about a phone. They live in web-tools-private,
they need a token, and they are layered on here.

WHICH MEANS THE PAGE HAS TO WORK WITHOUT THEM. catalog.json is public, so the
table renders with no token at all and the Device column stays empty. That is
the repo's standing rule about unknown answers: "current" and "not looked up"
must never render the same, so an unread device is blank rather than green.

THREE SOURCES SAY "ON DEVICE" AND ALL THREE ARE PARTIAL. library.json is a
snapshot of the last dump, so anything installed since is missing from it. The
newest manifest is the device's own list and is newer, but still a moment in
time. The log holds installs and runs and only for shortcuts that report. Reading
all three together is what run.py's own audit does, and it is the reason a name
installed yesterday does not read as absent.

THE INSTALL LINK PICKS ITS RECEIVER FROM THAT READ, which is the one thing
this page can do that tools/plist.py cannot. Library-Import and
Library-Replace take an identical two-line payload and differ only in whether
they delete the old copy by name first. Importing over a name the library
already holds leaves both copies and the OLDER one keeps the index, so every
link and every runworkflow card naming it still resolves to the copy that was
supposed to be replaced. This page knows which names the device holds, so it
emits Replace for those and Import for the rest; the CLI has no device read
and correctly defaults to Import. One rule, two owners, split on what each can
actually see. While the signing worker both receivers depend on is down
(SIGNER_DOWN below), every install goes through Library-Paste instead.

AND A NAME OFF THE CATALOG GETS AN ANSWER. 77 workflows here against 606
shortcuts surveyed on the device means most names a link can carry have no
workflow here, and the page used to answer all of them alike whether the name was
a device shortcut, newer than the dump, or genuinely nothing. It now says
which, and offers Open rather than Install, because a device shortcut has no
plist here to install.

NO STAT CARDS, AND NO LINE OF TOTALS. Each filter is a pill carrying the count
it would show under whatever the search box holds, so "how many need
installing" is read off the control that lists them (html-style rule 1).

ONE PAGE, TWO VIEWS. ?name=<Name> opens that workflow on its own: its sentence,
every action in order, what it calls, what calls it, and the same install and
run links its row carries. A view rather than a second page, because the two
halves share a boot, one catalog fetch and one read of the device, and because
a listing's `run X` line is then a link to X's own page. Unnamed workflows are
reachable the same way as ?file=<file>, since half the catalog is probes and
demos and a row that cannot be opened is a dead row.

WHY IT EXISTS AT ALL. A handover in chat carries the listing in its own table,
and used to carry a path into GitHub beside it. The path answered "where does
this come from" and nothing else. This view answers the question that follows
it: what the shortcut calls, what would break if it changed, and whether the phone
is holding this build.

Shorter: a proposal-adjudication tool.

You bring two things: your original text, and a shorter version of it
(pasted from any model, or drafted here by the local model). The page
word-diffs them and lays the shorter version out as a stream of discrete
edits, each one defaulting to ACCEPTED. The work is then subtraction:
skim, reject the cuts that went too far, regenerate any span you don't
like, and copy the assembled result. Getting a shortening is cheap; this
page is the part that was expensive: going through it piece by piece.

The local model (Llama-3.2-1B via web-llm, WebGPU) is OPTIONAL and lazy.
Nothing is fetched from huggingface.co until you press a ✨ Shorten
action, so the review flow works with zero model, and a network that
can't reach the weights (cert/proxy) no longer breaks page load. web-llm
still needs a real https origin (github.io) and a WebGPU browser; when a
✨ action can't get there, the failure is reported inline, on the span.

text-lab.html — the front page of home's Text project (projects/text), the
estate's text analysis as one reading surface. Five panes over one subject: what we tried, the variants we
retained, what we read with, what we read against, and what came out.

Named Text LAB, not Text Instruments. That name collided twice: with Texas
Instruments on sight, which no amount of context undoes, and with this page's
own `instruments` tab, so the whole and one of its five parts wore one word.
`-lab` is the suffix the tools themselves already use (termlab, registerlab,
entitylab, concept-lab), so it names the whole without renaming a part.

  probes       projects/text/probes/probes.csv, the registry docs/probes.md
               specifies. One row per bounded question, with a recorded
               standing and four badges (asks, grain, method, checked), each
               a value from projects/text/vocabulary.csv. The pane groups by
               date or by any badge, and a tap on a badge filters by it.
               Failures are recorded at the same weight as successes, so the
               standing counts lead the header.
  variants     The shared Text collection, read from its committed files
               in home (passages.jsonl, variants.jsonl, proposals.jsonl):
               every variant, as passage, alternative wording, author, and
               purpose, with a chip naming each file a variant has been
               proposed for, linked to the proposal's basis.
               Searchable, filterable by author and purpose, addressable by
               variant id. A variant does not claim to apply to the
               document a reader has open, and nothing here applies one.
  instruments  projects/text/INSTRUMENTS.md, rendered. Organised by
               unit of analysis (word, term of art, named entity, speaker,
               sentence, document), because that is the question a session
               actually arrives with: I have text at this grain.
  resources    projects/text/resources.csv, the word lists and norms
               tables, grouped by whether the estate holds one, fetches it at
               run time, or does not have it. A coverage grid leads the pane:
               property by state, so the empty cells read as loudly as the
               full ones.
  runs         projects/text/runs/runs.csv, one row per dated run of
               work, with its kind, method, thread and what it left behind.
               A row is one link: to the run's page when it has one, to its
               README when not, opened in this view so Back returns. A run
               that declares its documents in a files.jsonl also opens as a
               deck of them, and a run that settled probes names how many.

Reviewing. Under every pair, in the list and in both decks, one line carries
the variant's facts and a reader's three acts: vote it up, vote it down, and
comment. Each act is one line appended to home's projects/text/reviews.jsonl
through the viewer's token, written straight to the ref being read, the way
approve.html writes a verdict. The details that used to sit behind a row's
expander are a panel-tip (kits/panel-tip.js), opened from the same line.

Reading one at a time. The variants list is the index, and a deck is how it
is read: the house swipe-deck, with the same door (the cards glyph) every
other list here uses. Two decks. The filtered variants, one pair per slide in
md-diff's old/both/new swipe, so a variant reads exactly as it does in the
file viewer. And a text run's documents, one file per slide in md-variants'
full-document reading (kits/md-variants.js), so a pass is seen where
it lands rather than as loose pairs.

Data contract. Everything is read live from mehrlander/home through the
viewer's token (gh-api + gh-auth). This page holds no copy of the probe
records or the register, so it cannot drift from them; the cost is that home
is private, so a tokenless reader meets the auth prompt, exactly as
links.html does over the same repo.

Standing is derived here from the first sentence of the verdict, by the same
rule probes/build-index.py uses to derive it for the generated README. Two
readings of one field, so the page and the README cannot disagree.

Colour appears on one thing: a probe's standing. Nothing else takes an
accent, so any colour on this page is a verdict and nothing else. The four
values are a scale, not four decorations.

  ?use=<ref>   pins this page's own lib chain to a ref.
  ?data=<ref>  pins which ref of home is read (defaults to main).
  ?pane=<name> opens one pane.
  ?q=<text>    searches the variants.

toss-render.html — full-viewport render of HTML that GitHub Pages isn't
serving. Formerly embed.html. Three ways in: a URL param, a paste, or the
on-page GitHub-file field. Two trust levels, opposite handling:

Payload modes (the 🥏 toss — content rides in on the URL, UNTRUSTED):
  #gz=<base64url of gzipped HTML>   inline HTML, gzip-compressed
  #html=<base64 of HTML>            inline HTML, plain
  #url=<base64 of absolute URL>     iframe src points at the URL
Anyone can craft a toss link, so payloads render in a sandbox WITHOUT
allow-same-origin: scripts run, but under an opaque origin that cannot read
this origin's localStorage (which can hold a gh token). Pasted HTML and
pasted URLs are payloads too, on the same terms. Caveat for #url=: a site
sending X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors refuses to load at all.

Address mode (fetched by reference, TRUSTED via allowlist):
  #gh=<owner>/<repo>[@<ref>]:<path>[?<query>][#<frag>]
  e.g. #gh=mehrlander/web-tools@some-branch:pages/index.html
Fetched through the GitHub API with the stored token, so private repos and
un-deployed branches work, and rendered SAME-ORIGIN. Same-origin means the
rendered page could read that token, which is why this mode accepts only
repos owned by the OWNERS allowlist below; a crafted link to anyone else's
repo is refused outright, so the token can neither fetch it nor be exposed
to it. Read the other way, that is what makes address mode the preview route
for a page that NEEDS the token: an un-deployed branch copy reaches the same
localStorage the deployed page will, which a #gz= payload cannot. The ':'
before <path> is unambiguous because git forbids ':' in ref names, and no
@ref means the repo's default branch (and no ?use shim). A pinned address,
@<branch>@<commit> with the commit 7 to 40 hex characters, reads the commit
and carries the branch as a label (splitPin). Neither the ?query
nor the #frag reaches the API: both are handed to the PAGE, by the shims
addressHtml assembles.

Host query (how to show, never what):
  ?w=<px>      lay the subject out at that width (the forced-width section)
  ?lib=<ref>   the Web Tools code the framed page boots, and a routed toss's
               viewer page, apart from the page's own ref (libRef, and the
               channels addressHtml stamps)
  ?top         run a trusted address as this tab's own document instead of a
               frame: the page's title, icon, history, viewport and FAB, with
               the same prelude, inlining and fetch shim a frame gets. The
               address then rides the query as ?gh= beside the page's own
               parameters. Not with ?w=, and never for a payload.
  ?refs=owner/repo@<ref>[:path]
               repeatable: the ref to read a repository, one file, or a
               folder (`:dir/`) at, for whatever the displayed file's code
               reads. ?lib= is the mehrlander/web-tools entry spelled short.
               Stamped into the page as window.__refs and forwarded by the
               apps to the views they frame; never applied to this renderer's
               own code. docs/loader.md "The selection" has the rules.

The on-page field and a pasted github.com/.../blob/<ref>/<path> URL both
route here.

Toss routes (typed content tosses, built on address mode):
  #<route>=<owner>/<repo>[@<ref>]:<path>
  e.g. #data=mehrlander/home@main:projects/budget-drs/data/rows.csv
The key names a registered renderer page and the value is a content
envelope's address, so a caller addresses the CONTENT, not the renderer, and
this file stays schema-blind: it never parses the envelope. See showRoute
and TOSS_ROUTES, whose owner is docs/routes.json.

Empty state (the page's second job, and the reason it is listed as a tool):
with no input, the panel is a look at whatever is on the clipboard, whether
or not you know what that is. What arrives is routed by shape rather than

Params are read from the fragment (#) first, then the query string (?).
Payloads MUST use the fragment: a query string travels in the HTTP request
and GitHub Pages' edge rejects URLs past ~8KB with a 414. Addresses are
short, so either form works. All base64 params accept the standard or the
URL-safe alphabet, with or without padding. One key per fragment, read by
slice rather than URLSearchParams, which is what lets a page query keep its
bare '&'s: readFragment.

Everything else is stated beside the code it governs. Page actions live in
the FAB (alpineComponents/fab.js), which the tossRender x-data component
feeds; the shell owns the one fab per viewport and the subject stamping
(guardHtml, setSubject, addressHtml); the frame is mounted on a blob: URL
rather than srcdoc, and the microphone granted in address mode only
(mountFrame); a private or un-deployed page's own relative deps are inlined
ahead of render (inlineRelativeDeps) and its runtime fetches rerouted
(fetchShim); the tab shows the subject's own favicon, dimmed (the favicon
section); and `?w=` lays the subject out at another device's width (the
forced-width section).

The 🥏 bookmarklet feeding the gz mode lives at bookmarklets/toss-render.js,
which is the canonical copy: edit it there.

THE FRISBEE, not ph-disc, and it is the chat convention's own mark:
CONVERSATION.md writes a render link as 🥏, so the page a reader lands on
from one now opens with the same glyph rather than with a disc that only
resembles it. No opacity: a Phosphor glyph mutes by losing contrast and
an emoji mutes by looking faded, so the size carries it here.

The one page action, "Link", is surfaced through the FAB's take grid via
the x-data `actions` contract, not a floating pill.
Toolbox: page actions, zip/offline export, component/script/console tabs.
Repos whose HTML may render same-origin (with token access) via #gh=.

Fragment first (never sent to the server, so no edge URL-length cap),
query string as fallback.

The fragment is read by SLICE, not URLSearchParams. A toss fragment carries
exactly one key, and that key's value routinely contains a page query of
its own (#gh=…:app/index.html?view=app&appRepo=X&appPath=Y).
URLSearchParams splits the whole fragment on '&' before it looks at any
key, so everything past the first '&' is torn off the address and becomes
sibling fragment params nothing here reads: the page gets ?view=app and its
other two params arrive null, silently. Reading the one key by slice keeps
a bare '&' inside the value. Percent-escapes are still decoded, so links
minted with the old %26 workaround keep working, and a value that is not
valid escaping is used verbatim rather than throwing. The '+' is left alone
here; the params shim re-parses the page query with URLSearchParams, which
decodes '+' there, where it means something.

The query string keeps URLSearchParams: there a '&' really does delimit, so
a page query with more than one param has to ride the fragment (or encode
its '&' as %26) to survive the trip.

THE SELECTION (docs/loader.md, "The selection"). A link can name, for any
repository the rendered file's code reads, the ref to read it at:
repeatable refs=owner/repo@ref, or @ref:path for one file, or @ref:dir/
for a folder. `lib=` is the web-tools entry spelled short. An outer
document's selection (the top-mode launcher running this renderer) is
inherited, and this query wins over it. SELECTED holds only what a link
asked for; it is stamped into the page as window.__refs and is what a
page forwards to the views it opens.

The selection is for the PAGE, never for this renderer's own code (its FAB
and drawer). A renderer running Web Tools at a chosen ref while it hosts a
frame is the shape recorded as killing Safari's tab (the snag
shell-pin-kills-the-tab), so this document's own globals are emptied here,
before its FAB boots, and the boot below imports entry.js at main.

TOP MODE (?top): the page becomes this tab's document instead of a frame
inside it, so its own title, icon, history, viewport and FAB are the
tab's. The address rides the query as `gh`, beside the page's own real
parameters, and the same prelude a frame gets (the <base>, the fetch shim,
the inliner's output, the selection) is written in with the page. Set here,
before anything awaits, because the FAB boot below is a separate module
that must not start in a document about to be replaced.
A forced width (?w=) needs the frame it lays the page out in, so it keeps
one; so does a payload (#gz=, #html=), which must stay opaque-origin and
never reaches showAddress.

The resolver, one function for this renderer and for the page it mounts,
whose prelude receives its source (refForSource). Path entries first,
longest match wins, then the repository's entry, then what the page
implies. gh-api.js and the launcher carry the same function;

Again once the document is in, since swapping src or srcdoc lands focus

── THE FRAME IS THE CONTENT, so give it the keyboard ─────────────────────

A FRESH IFRAME NEVER RECEIVES A KEYSTROKE. Focus stays on the top document
until something is clicked, so a rendered page's own shortcuts do nothing
here until the reader clicks into the frame first: `document.hasFocus()`
inside it reads false and no keydown arrives at all. One focus() on the
frame ELEMENT takes it, with no user activation, and does not scroll the
frame into view.

THE COST, named because it is real: the shell's paste-anywhere below then
reaches the framed page instead of re-rendering here. That window was
already only open until the reader's first click, so this closes it rather
than removing something dependable; and the empty panel, where paste is
the primary action and carries its own button, is untouched.

Never taken from a field that SURVIVES the render, which is the only kind
this can protect: a re-render from the drawer must not pull the caret out
of the address input the reader is typing in. The empty panel's own field
is a different case and needs no guard, since the reveal hides the panel
and the browser blurs it a moment before this runs.

── Forced frame width: seeing a page at a shape the device is not ────────

A FRAME IS A VIEWPORT, which is the whole mechanism. Give the subject a
frame W CSS px wide and every width question agrees: media queries, a
boot-time innerWidth read, a container measure. Nothing is faked, so
nothing has to be kept consistent; the page really is laid out at W.

Both directions come off this one lever, which is why the shell owns it
and the drawer only calls it. A phone at 1280 gets a frame wider than the
screen, scaled down to fit, without touching this document's own viewport
meta. A desktop at 390 gets a narrow frame at scale 1, centered, with an
edge so it reads as a shape rather than as a page that failed to fill the
window.

The transform is presentation only and does not shrink the layout box, so
a frame wider than the screen still pushes out a horizontal scrollbar.
Hence overflow:hidden on the body for as long as a width is forced, and
the height divided back out by the scale so the frame still fills.

What no width can fake, and the drawer says so rather than implying
otherwise: `pointer` and `hover`. A phone rendering at 1280 still answers

interaction model.

Read from `?w=` on the renderer's own query, never from inside the address:
the address is what to show, the width is how to show it, and keeping them
apart is what lets a width ride any of the render modes unchanged.

Only while a frame is actually under it: a width asked for on the URL is
applied at boot, before anything has rendered, and the input panel that
may be all the viewer ever sees has to keep its own scrolling.

0 (or anything falsy) is "actual". A real width is floored at 240, since
below that there is no page left to look at, only a column of wrapped
words, and a typo should not render something unreadable in silence.

Keep the address honest, so the width survives a reload and travels when
the address bar is copied. replaceState fires no hashchange, so the
reload listener above stays quiet.
Rotating the device, or resizing the window, changes what "fit" means.

Mount HTML in the frame at a real URL, so a trailing #frag reaches the
page as its own location.hash.

Why not srcdoc: an about:srcdoc document's location.hash is always "" and
the property is non-configurable ([LegacyUnforgeable] on Location), so no
prelude can shim it the way the params shim covers ?query by patching
URLSearchParams.prototype. A blob: URL carries a fragment for real, and
sandbox flags (not the URL scheme) still decide the origin, so the two
trust levels are unchanged: address mode keeps allow-same-origin, payload
mode stays opaque and unable to read this origin's localStorage. The one
observable difference for a rendered page is document.URL, about:srcdoc
before and blob:<origin>/… now.

What the switch does NOT buy: the history shim in addressHtml still earns
its place. A relative history.replaceState('#x') resolves against the
stamped <base> (github.io), which never matches the blob: document URL, so
it throws exactly as it did under srcdoc. Only the initial hash is new.

THE MICROPHONE, granted in ADDRESS MODE and withheld in payload mode.
For pages/dictate.html, which is a page whose whole job is hearing you
and which is handed over for review as a toss.

This is an EXPLICIT grant standing in for an implicit one, not a fix.
Permissions Policy defaults `microphone` to `self`, and an address-mode
frame is same-origin (allow-same-origin, over a blob: URL that inherits
this origin), so Chromium already answers allowsFeature('microphone')
with true without this line: node/test/toss-microphone.mjs. Safari is
not measured, and WebKit has been the stricter of the two about capture
inside a frame for as long as it has had one. The line is worth keeping
because the implicit grant is load-bearing on a sandbox flag several
hundred lines away: drop allow-same-origin from address mode and the
frame goes opaque and the microphone goes with it, silently.

Payload frames are opaque-origin, so withholding is also the only honest
option: a delegation to an opaque origin grants nothing either way.

charset=utf-8 is load-bearing, not decoration. A blob: document takes its
encoding from the Blob's type, and with none declared the browser sniffs,
finds no <meta charset> in a page that never had one, and falls back to
the locale default (windows-1252). The Blob is built from a JS string, so
its bytes are always UTF-8, and every non-ASCII character then renders as
its mojibake: 🎉 as ðŸŽ‰. Held by node/test/toss-charset.mjs.

Revoke the previous render's URL only after the new one is committed, so
a rapid re-toss can't pull the document out from under a pending load.
--- base64 helpers (standard or URL-safe, padded or not) ---

Standard alphabet, padded: what a data: URI needs. The URL-safe form below
is the same bytes with the two substitutions and the padding stripped.

Singleton guard for the sandboxed modes: stamp __fabHosted so a fab in
the tossed HTML declines to mount (the shell's fab owns the viewport).
Render-time only — tossLinkFn keeps encoding the original text.
`<head(\s...)?>` rather than `<head[^>]*>`, which also matches a <header>
and so put the stamp inside the header of a page with no <head> of its own.

── The subject's favicon, dimmed ────────────────────────────────────────

A toss is a rendering OF a page, so the tab says which page: the subject's
own icon, dimmed so the tab never impersonates the deployed page. The
frisbee is the fallback, and means no addressable subject behind this
render.

Read the <link rel=icon> href ATTRIBUTE, not the property: the property is
already resolved against the <base> addressHtml stamps, and a private
repo's icon file is not fetchable from that URL without the token. Read it
live off the same-origin frame rather than reconstructing it from the
fetched source or from .web-tools.json, so gh-boot's runtime injection and
any page that sets its icon late both come through.

Rasterize through a canvas to a PNG data URI rather than wrapping the icon
in an SVG <image>: SVG favicons render under a restricted mode whose
handling of nested images is not worth betting the feature on, and a PNG
data URI also sidesteps escaping a data URI inside XML.

Dimming rather than a badge, because a favicon is 16 CSS px in the tab
strip where a corner badge is five pixels of mush; desaturating and fading
keeps the silhouette, which is the channel that survives. Most of the
signal is cheaper to buy in saturation than in alpha, hence the split
between the two constants below. Picked against real icons on BOTH a light
and a dark tab strip: fading harder (alpha ~0.55) reads well on light and
goes muddy on dark, and full grayscale (saturate 0) is unmistakable but
throws away the colour that makes an icon recognizable at a glance.

On caching: Chrome keys the favicon cache by ICON url, and a data URI is
its own content, so every subject gets its own entry and none can go
stale. History and bookmarks key on the PAGE url instead, which is
identical for every toss (the address rides in the fragment), so those
surfaces keep whichever icon was recorded last. Not fixable from here.
0 = grayscale, 1 = untouched

covers the 16 and 32 px tab renditions
how long to keep watching for a late icon

The frisbee, captured before anything replaces it: the mark for a render
with no subject behind it.

Build and verify a GitHub contents-API URL for a file inside owner/name.
Rejects empty, dot, backslash, or pre-encoded segments and confirms the
URL parser's normalized href stays under /repos/<owner>/<name>/contents/,
so a crafted name or path cannot climb out of the repo the OWNERS check

TOP MODE'S TWO SHIMS, where a frame's differ. The page's address is this
tab's real query, and this renderer owns some of its keys: `top`, the
address (`gh`, or a route key such as `data`), and the selection (`refs`,
`lib`) and width (`w`). History: whatever the page writes, the path stays
this renderer's, `top` and the address lead the query, and the selection
is kept when the page's own write leaves it out, so a view switch, Back and
a reload all keep the page and its versions. Relative URLs resolve against
the <base>, the deployed page's directory, so the target's own path is not
this document's. Params: a URLSearchParams holding `top` is the page's
address, and its reads skip `top` and the address key and answer the
defaults (`use`, a routed page's `src`) a frame's shim answers.

Interpret a contents-API response fetched with the raw media type. The
Content-Type label alone cannot be trusted to say which body arrived: a
raw success may be echoed as text/plain OR as the raw media type itself
(whose name contains "+json"), and caches/proxies can mislabel either way
(Safari surfaces the mismatch as "The string did not match the expected
pattern"). So classify structurally: parse as JSON only when the label
suggests it, and accept the parse only if the result actually is
contents-API metadata (content + encoding fields); anything else is the
file itself. Directory listings throw; >1 MB metadata (content "") falls
back to the git blobs API by sha (served up to 100 MB).

Distinguish the four reasons an address fetch fails instead of guessing
"not found, or the stored token lacks access" on every 404:
  1. No token is saved in localStorage.ghToken.
  2. A token is saved, and GitHub rejects it (401 on the read or on /user).
  3. A classic token is saved and accepted by /user, but x-oauth-scopes
     lacks `repo`, so GitHub hides private repositories as 404.
  4. The saved token has `repo` scope and /user accepts it, which means a
     404 is a missing repository, ref, or file path rather than a token
     problem (so the token link stays hidden).

Word Select: a touch-first, word-level selection engine. The unit of selection is the word. There is no character-level selection and no native selection at all: `user-select: none` is set everywhere, so iOS never raises its magnifier or callout bar, and every highlight on screen is ours. What the page draws instead is a run of word spans and the gap spans between them, so a contiguous selection paints as one unbroken band with no structural artifact between words. DOM shape, per paragraph: word A gap span holds one real space, so it is a genuine wrap opportunity and the text flows exactly as unmarked prose would. A gap paints only when the words on both sides belong to the *same* range, which is what keeps two adjacent but distinct selections visibly isolated. The one thing a painted gap could have cost is a stub of highlight hanging past the end of a wrapped line; measured, it does not: a gap at a line break collapses to exactly zero width at the last word's right edge, because collapsible white space at a soft wrap opportunity is not measured, so there is no box left to fill. Model: `ranges` is a sorted list of disjoint, non-adjacent {a,b} inclusive word-index pairs. `drag` is the single in-flight range, painted tentative. Committing merges the drag range into `ranges` (touching ranges coalesce). Gestures (pointer events, one pointer at a time, extra fingers ignored): tap on an unselected word -> new one-word range, pins appear tap on a selected word/pin -> context menu, bounds untouched hold 350ms then drag -> new range, snapping word by word drag a pin -> that range detaches and re-forms live mouse press then move -> drag immediately, no hold required Viewport lock: the body is a fixed app shell (no document scroll, so no pull-to-refresh and no rubber-band), the reading pane scrolls internally with `overscroll-behavior: contain` and `touch-action: pan-y`, and while a drag is live a non-passive touchmove listener calls preventDefault(), which is the one thing that reliably stops a scroll mid-gesture in both Blink and WebKit. A hold cannot have scrolled yet, so the cancel window never opens. No dependencies, no CDN, no lib chain. The page is self-contained on purpose: it has to survive being opened from a file, a data URL, or a 🥏 #gz= toss on a phone, and its whole job is precise control of inline text flow, which is not something a utility framework helps with.

Annotations that point into a document, checked against the document now.

Two kinds are stored, each pointing its own way (docs/locators.md, "Kinds"):

  a note's anchor  in the notes store (the checkout whose .web-tools.json
                   declares "notes"): a note whose `about` is a file,
                   owner/repo[@ref]:path, quoting its passage as a W3C text
                   quote selector (`exact`, `prefix`, `suffix`). Found again by
                   its words, so it survives edits anywhere but the passage.
  a standoff       a JSON file of `"kind": "standoff/1"` in any checkout:
                   character spans into its target, valid while the target's
                   bytes still hash to `target.sha256` (lib/kits/standoff.js).

Each gets one of docs/locators.md's verdicts:

  ok            the quote is found once, or several times with its context
                picking one; the standoff's hash matches
  changed       the quoted words were edited and a close match remains
                (reanchor.py's FUZZY tier); the standoff's target changed
  broken        the quoted words are gone, or the file is
  unverifiable  the repo is not checked out beside this one, the note pins a
                ref that is not here, or the standoff pins no hash

    anchors.py              every stored annotation, against each working tree
    anchors.py --staged     only those pointing into files this commit changes,
                            against the staged text, printing only what is not
                            ok (the pre-commit hook's warning). A standoff whose
                            target was unchanged at HEAD is re-anchored from
                            HEAD to the staged text and its lost units counted.
    anchors.py --json       one JSON object per annotation
    anchors.py --strict     exit 1 when anything is changed or broken

The quote matching is reanchor.py's: exact, exact with context, then a fuzzy
match against the document's segments. Checkouts are found beside this one (the
estate's sibling layout); a repo not there reads as unverifiable, never broken.
Everything is read locally: the notes store at its origin/main as last fetched.
